posts.author: outapips
posts.text:
Hi Whiteout, IF,

I've read thru the compression book and the video several times and I'm still not grasping the difference between compression and a flag.

In the video the definition of compression is taking out the last decision point and its orders. That I understand and can follow on the chart taking out each supply/demand area and seeing what has been consumed and what hasn't.

Where I'm stuck is between a flag and compression as a flag to me indicates price may continue to the price projection from the flag.

Maybe I'm harping on this needlessly but to me until I can understand it fully I'm always going to be unsure and have doubts about what I'm seeing.

If I spot a bull flag (and by that I mean a defined rectangle but skewed on an angle) then I do the measuring thing with the pole and extend it out from the break to get an idea of how far price will move. If this occurs just before a supply area and indicates that price may move deep or thru the supply then I am very wary about going short.

If I see price narrowing into a wedge/funnel type shape then I figure that is compression and I am happy to trade from the appropriate level.

When I watch LF's video to me I'm seeing a flag (rectangle skewed on an angle) where he is saying its compression into the start of the supply zone. To me I would be hesitant to go short even tho price is moving into daily supply as by the flag price projection it could almost all the way into the zone.

When watching the video fast forward to 6 min 30 sec and watch from there and the area I have as a flag is referred to as compression.

I have also attached a chart showing the H4 chart with what I see as compression and what I see as a flag pattern.

I feel a bit silly for not being able to understand the difference and appreciate your patience while I grasp the concept.

I hope I have explainded things clearly enough.

ttfreitas wrote: Thanks, Mel! With respect to the comment that you made about price compressing to the upside before reaching Demand: why does that indicate that price will brake through demand?

TT,

Here, price did bounce from the demand level, but in wich fashion? It bounced up in a compressed way. Since we also had a previous demand level that got broken (see chart), you know that you have a decison that have been made there.

In other words, we have a demand level but also a previous decision point that had been made right above it. Since price traded up to the decision point in a compressed way, we can expect that it will bounce back down from this decision point. If it bounce back down like it did, you also have to take into consideration the fact that the demand (that I pointed out) isn't fresh anymore... We can not know 100% that there are no buy orders left there anymore, untill this demand breaks to the downside.

Now, fresh demand and supply zones is another topic,I believe it's up to each trader to decide for him/herself wether he/she wants to trade every possible unfresh zones or not.

Does that makes sence to you?

Hi Lockhart

CPLQ is where price compressed towards S or D then in one point we have a liquidity imbalance toward the S or D. It is a place where decision is made among buyers and sellers. You can also explain it as a place where no supply or demand left and price can freely go its way.

I marked in your chart, you see price compresses, consuming Demand down to where no Demand orders left

Hi Nasgato,

Nice that you opened a "homework thread". I took a look at your charts and notticed a few things that I would like to point out to you. I have marked a few things on your charts.

An important point for you would be to not forget about the supply and demand zone first. A broken supply or demand level is also a zone (very important) so before searching for any compression on a chart, maybe it would be beter to look for the the supply and demand zones that are above and bellow current price, then look to see if ther are "fresh" or not and only after finding your s/d zones you can look for compression in order to make a decision. If a supply or demand zone has been tested several times, you know that the zone weakens by every revisits, so looking at how price behaves around the zones is smethig very important too.

Hope that makes sence, Best, Mel

Hi Mel, Thank you for your time.

In my words CP is price moving up with no pending buy limit order left below. Or price moving down with no pending sell limit order left above. Basically, it cleared the way for a possible quick moving back.

I have a few thought about CP, correct me if not right. 1. A bull flag on an up trend (in HTF) is a valid CP (in LTF). 2. A mild trend with a few deep enough pull backs is also a valid CP (in HTF). 3. CP doesn't tell which direction price will likely to go, it only tells if price moving back, it could be a quick big move.

Thanks in advance

UC

posts.author: @mel
posts.text:
Nice explaination Ucego!

Cp is all about price taking the pockets of Supply (while going down)and the pockets of Demand (while going up) in order to clear the orders.

1)About your first point. I would say if you see compression on a higher TF, then you have CP on this timeframe. You can have cp on a higher TF and clean s/d levels on a small TF...

2) Yes, if you see that there was pockets of supply or demand where price pulled back.

3) You always have to look at the bigger picture that has been paint. I wouldn't look for cp just in the middle of a chart. If you see a clean fresh demand level and there is cp wile price goes down to this demand then this would be a very good sign of a potential reversal Up at the demand level.

However, if you see an unfresh demand level, that has been tested several times and you see cp while price goes down, you will still have to look at your chart to see if price will like to break the demand or just bounce back up.

But Cp is Cp... Price thinks ahead of time. If price cleared the pockets of supply while going down and price broke the demand than the cp that was made there will still be valid, only not for the imediate term but probably for later...

Best, Mel

posts.author: naughtypip
posts.text:
Hi Oedipus, I think you are on the right track.

Compression is basically accumulation of orders or distribution of orders, depending which way the market is going. So if we are heading to a supply area and the big guys want to have a bulk of orders to sell with ready for when the supply zone is hit, they will keep knocking price back down whilst it is climbing, creating dips, so that the small guys buy the dips, and this allows the big guys to filter their sell orders into the market as there is now someone on the other side to buy them. If they didn't create this price dynamic then they would get awful fills and lose money.

Having all of these sell orders already in the market for when they reach the supply zone means that the one last order that shoots price down probably gets quite a bad fill, but it doesn't matter because they already have lots of other sell orders sat in the market which will be gathering a nice profit.

This is just my understanding of it, I might be wrong - I'd get some clarification from more senior members before you take this as how it really works.

posts.text:
Just to check I understand it:

I'm reading the Red explanationof what compression is, and its difference from a flag. This is what I understand, on a bull trend:

1.- Compression is price rising to supply, but spiking south to fill small pockets of demand orders. Why? because: 1.1.- This small pockets of demand helps price to reach supply 1.2.- The way down is cleared of demand orders allowing price to make a fast big drop when it reaches supply. This clearing of orders is what we call consumption. 1.3.- Big money starts to sell slowly to this demand orders. So through compression big money finds also liquidity to fill their big orders. (?) 2.- Compression is a reversal signal, because is showing that price is clearing the way for this reversal ("PRICES THINK AHEAD OF TIME").

3.- Flag is price going down, stopping momentum on a bull trend, but spiking north for: 3.1.- Clean the supply orders so price could continue its way up. Consumption again. 3.2.- Take the price to a better demand level to have cheaper price before continue the move up. (?) 4.- Flag is a continuation pattern, as it tell us with their cleaning of supply, that wants to continue on its way up.

So the essence of both, compression and flag, is the consumption of orders. It seems that this concept is very important. Why price needs to consume the orders? 1.- Because there is the need to consume the orders for find a counterpart, so to reach liquidity, other fundamental concept. 2.- And because to price move further and faster, there is the need to have no orders stopping the movement.

Are you agree with this definitions of CP, flag and consumption, or I'm wrong or forgetting something?

Thanks

Compression, in and of itself is neither a continuation nor a reversal pattern. It's (in the above example) simply consumption of novices buy orders. The wicks on the bottom of the candles are longer because the big money is stretching price to find the buy orders then snapping back filling it's short position. If it's useful for you, I tried to put what I understand CP is on here: www.acegazette.com/en/community/ace-foru...n.html?start=25#6391

On a word, CP when price is going up is price spiking down to consumed the demand orders. So when price reaches supply, there aren't demand orders that stop the price in its way down.

This is, I think, a good example of CP: www.acegazette.com/media/kunena/attachments/208/nu_cp3.png Price goes up from demand to supply, spiking south on the way, so consuming all the small demand orders. When price reaches supply it drop fast because the way is clean.

Other good example: www.acegazette.com/media/kunena/attachments/208/nu_cp5.png Keep an eye on how price goes up and down, filling every new demand zone, so consuming all the orders there are. When arrives to supply, it drops.

And other example: www.acegazette.com/media/kunena/attachments/208/nu_cp.png from demand to supply, consuming small demand orders, and when it reach supply, big fast drop

After looking this examples, could you locate more areas of compression on your last chart?

Hope this helps

posts.author: benhur

Adam.

For better understanding of compression, you should ask yourself: why should I care for compression. So it is better to begin with a clear definition: A Compression is when price move away from a level (Supply or Demand) while clearing the orders flows on its way.

Exp. if price move away from demand, a compression price action would be clearing more demand on it way up to supply.

Why should you care about it? Because when price is back to the compressed area you can assume there are less order flows against the move. so back to the example, now when price hit supply and turn back toward last demand, you can assume it will show less buying power against this move.

So now you know why you need it, find PA that clears orders in a way that when price is back - it be more likely to go through fairly easy.

Here is how I would mark CP areas on your chart.

posts.author: madwt
posts.text:
This is my first post on this forum.

I like to digest an idea, mull it over for a while and then express the idea verbally to see if it makes sense. This is what I am doing here. Once I am comfortable I have digested the idea, the practice may begin. In this post, I am going to verbalise my understanding of compression, but more importantly, how it is of benefit to a trader.

Trading charts is similar to playing sport. In sport, we need to use different tactics at different places on the field. Have you watched Australia Ruby League (Australia football)? If so, what do you find in the middle of the field? You will find mud, blood, injuries and so on. It is not where you look to execute your key plays.

Rather, you want to execute your key plays where they count. This is near the try (score/goal/touch down) line. You do not use your key plays anywhere on the field. You wait until your team is in position, a place where you have an opportunity to score. Then, when the conditions are right, you execute your key plays. In trading, your key plays are your entry techniques and where you use them matters.

As a trader, we need to identify areas of opportunity, a place on the chart where the odds are significantly in our favour. Strong supply and demand levels provide this opportunity. These are places on a chart where a move may start from. This is where we can bring out our key plays out and score a touch-down.

At a strong supply level, we expect there to be an overwhelming volume of sell orders and price to fall. At a strong demand level, we expect there to be an overwhelming volume of buy orders and price to rise. However, like in our sports analogy, the team may be at the right place on the field, but your key players may not yet be positioned for the best possible opportunity. However, once everyone is in place, it’s time to go for the touch-down.

Once we are in the right position on a chart, how can we tell if the odds are significantly in our favour? That is the important question. In other words, if we are at a significant demand level and ready to short, what conditions would prevent price falling rapidly?

The only thing which will stop price falling (sessions times, news, etc. aside) are buy orders waiting to be consumed, pushing price back up, or stalling the fall. However, if there were no buy orders waiting to be consumed below the current price level, the selling pressure at a supply level would cause the price to fall rapidly. Price is free to drop until it once again reaches a demand level where new buyers are waiting.

This can be summarised as follows:

- We want to short at a strong supply level if we believe the buy orders lurking below the current price were consumed in the up move.

- We want to buy at a strong demand level if we believe thee sell orders lurking above the current price were consumed in the down move.

We know when we are at a supply or demand level. We can see this on the chart. The problem is, we cannot see how many buy orders are sitting below us, nor can we see how many sell orders are sitting above us. However, we can make an educated guess about what orders may be lurking by visually recognising what the consumption of previous orders looks like on a chart.

The visual recognition of the consumption of orders on a chart is called compression.

If price is moving up and compressing, the buy orders are being consumed. If the buy orders have been consumed, they are not lurking below the current price. As such, when price hits a strong supply level and selling pressure kicks in, price has a clear path to drop straight back through the area of compression. Price is free to drop as there are no pockets of buy orders waiting to be consumed. Price will drop until it reaches a demand level where new buyers are waiting.

Likewise, if price is moving down and compressing, the sell orders are being

consumed. If the sell orders have been consumed, they are not lurking above the current price. As such, when price hits a strong demand level and buying pressure kicks in, price has a clear path to climb straight up through the area of compression. Price climbs as there are no longer pockets of sell orders waiting to be consumed. Price is free to climb until it reaches a supply level where new sellers are waiting.

For this reason:

- An ideal reversal point for a short position is at a strong supply level where price compressed into the supply.

- An ideal reversal point for a long position is at a strong demand level where price compressed into the demand.

By knowing this, the demand and supply zones can define where you want to bring out your key plays, and the compression tells you it’s an ideal time to place your chips on the table. This is why recognising and understanding compression is important to price action trading.

In my next post, I will describe what compression looks like on a chart and what is happening inside the compression. I hope other people find this post useful.

posts.author: madwt
posts.text:
In my last post, I described what compression is and why it is important. However, I did not describe what compression looks like on screen. In this post, I will describe what compression looks like on screen so that compression may be more easily recognised.

Price will rise when there are more buy orders than sell orders. We can see this visually. Price is rising and making higher highs and higher lows. Therefore we know that the buyers are in charge and driving price higher. In the same way, price will fall when there are more sell orders than buy orders. We can see this visually. Price is falling and making lower lows and lower highs. Therefore, we know the sellers are in charge pushing price lower.

If prices are rising and the buyers are in charge that is good. We need the buyers to push prices up to a major supply level where we are patiently waiting to sell. However, when we are ready to sell, we want the buyers which have moved price up to our major supply level to be exhausted. We do not want to get into a fight with the buyers. If they are exhausted, the will put up a small fight, and then crumble under the selling pressure. In order words, we want their buys orders to have been all consumed. We do not want buyers to still be vigorously chasing price up.

What is important is the way price is moving on screen, not just the fact price is moving up or moving down. If price is moving up, buyers will be keen to join the up-trend, or add new longs to their existing bullish position. However, buyers will generally prefer to buy at a price which they perceive to be good value. In order to buy at a price of good value, buyers wait for a pull-back to get in at a better price. However, they dare not wait for too much of a pull-back or they may miss the boat. Buy orders will usually be placed and sit eagerly awaiting price to come back to the most recent minor demand level. This is the last place from which price moved up or the most recent minor swing low.

If this is the case, price dips into the most recent minor demand and the buy orders are consumed. The consumption of these orders shoots the price back up. How this looks on screen depends on the time frame, though will often appear as candles with long lower wicks. How far price moves up depends on the how many excited buyers there are. If there are a significant number of buyers, price will zoom! However, this is not the price action that forms compression. In compression, there will be enough buyers to push prices up, possibly creating long lower wicks, but once the buy orders at perceived good value are consumed, price will move up steadily again.

As the trend continues, the process repeats over. Price dips, buyers step in at the most recent minor demand and price makes a new higher low.

- When price is rising, but with dips which spike down, you are seeing compression in the up move. When you see this, you know that the buys orders are being consumed on the pull-backs in the up move.

- When price is falling but with spikes up, you are seeing compression in the down move. When you see this, you know that the sell orders are being consumed on the rallies in the down move.

An example of compression is shown below. In my next post, I will show some ways compression can appear on screen. I hope other people find this post useful.

I am looking at the break down of price on the Euro as per the chart below. I was expecting the break down for other reasons, but from a price action perspective, the question to ask is why did price choose that level from which to break down? Why not 20 pips below that level or 20 pips above that level? Is there a reason for that exact level?

It's all about decisions on price. The question the market is asking is this. Is price too cheap or is too expensive?

Decisions are made all the time. However, important decisions are remembered. If the market decided that $1 is way too cheap, there is a mad rush to buy driving price up. That is strong demand. When price comes back to $1 the market remembers this and it is time to buy again, assuming market conditions have not changed.

I refer to the market, but what is that? Most people consider the market as the collective of traders. I would challenge that thought as the collective of traders is the crowd. When the market makes an important decision, it is not the crowd that decides. The crowd would most likely get it wrong. Let’s assume the market is getting it right. As such, important decisions on price, the decisions that count, are not made by the crowd. These decisions are made by the smart money and their decisions determine where price goes at important price levels.

The collective of smart money are still people and it pays to understand how people make decisions. It is often said that successful people make firm decisions. That is, important decisions once made are carried out with enthusiasm and energy. The question is, can we see this decision making process play out visually on our charts?

When decisions are made, especially if there is significant money on the line, people will pause and consider their options. Traders will look at lines, levels and indicators. They may check the fundamentals. They may check for signs of confirmation in many ways. They pause and ponder if the decision they are about to make is the right one. We see this when price stalls.

Goods examples are the rally-base-rally, drop-base-drop, rally-base-drop and drop-base-rally price patterns. In these examples, the decision is happening in the base. Is price now too expensive or is it still too cheap? If it is an important decision, once it is decided, the orders pile on. We see the result of that decision when we observe a pole.

The market is going up and down all the time. So in effect, decisions are being made all the time, tick by tick, candle by candle. What we are concerned with is recognising when a significantly important decision has been made and what that decision looks like on screen. If the market decides that $1 is way too cheap, then it pays to listen to that decision. If Warren Buffett whispered in my ear that company X shares were cheap at $1, it would pay to listen to that. When price pulled back to $1 dollar, it would be time to buy, and buy aggressively.

Let’s assume for the moment that the exact price from where the Euro collapsed was at a prior decision on price. It was not at some random price point. That is, it was decided earlier that the Euro at price was too expensive and that was an important decision. When price comes back to that price, this is something we would want to know about it. Before the Euro collapsed, we had a rally and then a base. When the price stalled, the market had to make a decision. Is price still too expensive?

The market decided that the Euro was still too expensive and price collapsed. In my next post, I will go back and see what that prior decision looks like.

I am looking at the price where Euro collapsed and asking myself why the market decided that price was too expensive. More importantly, I am interested in observing what that decision looks like on screen. I can see that the Euro fell from there, but the market does not pay for noticing things in hindsight. The market pays when we correctly anticipate what may happen in the future and we are rewarded for our ability to act on that in a well risk defined manner. However, in order to do this, we need to know at what places we should to be paying attention, perched ready to pounce.

Prior to the collapse there was a rally and a base (see post #8 above). In the base the market was making a decision. The market was deciding if price was too cheap or too expensive. If the market decides price is too cheap, we will see a rally-base-rally develop. If the market decides price is too expensive, we will see rally-base-drop. It turns out we had a rally-base-drop, but that was only seen after that fact.

The weekly chart shows important decisions were made around this price level in the past.

The daily chart is more insightful, showing with more clarity the decisions being made around this price.

The 4hr chart shows the level being crossed up and down numerous times.

The 1hr chart shows some historical significance at this price level. The last time was around the 10th of October. I will take a closer look and see what happened at this time.

The 5min chart shows the market making decisions. The market decides price was too cheap on the 11th of October. The challenge I have is that I can see these decisions playing out at all different price levels on the chart. As mentioned, this is all in hindsight and I cannot trade in hindsight.

To me, the most useful piece of information on the chart, and what I would most likely be looking at in real time is the most recent demand marked in the green box. I say this as it just sticks out so clearly. When price reached this level, the market considered the Euro as cheap and there was strong demand for the Euro at this price. On the last test of the level, the demand was very strong and price zoomed away. The demand created a traditional support level.

What catches my eye was is fact that price moved away abruptly on testing the level. That is, the market did not wallow around at this price making a decision on the value of the Euro. The smart money had decided well before the Euro reached this price that it was cheap and the buy orders were eagerly waiting price to reach that level.

The question is, when prices comes back to that level again, what will happen? Will there still be demand at that price. If so, how much? If there is demand, the price will move up once again. However, there is only a finite amount of demand for a commodity at certain price. Once all the buyers have made their purchase, the demand disappears. The market is big, but it is still finite. Once the buyers have had their fill, the demand will have been all consumed.

When the Euro comes back to the level, price bases. That is, it forms a drop-base structure. Price did not zoom away. It’s during that base the a decision is being made. Is price still cheap? Or, is it now too expensive? It's time to decide? This is what the decision making process looks like zoomed out.

And this is what it looks like zoomed in.

The market decides price is too expensive. All the demand is consumed. Price falls away, leaving fresh supply. In the decision making process, what I see on screen is a S/R flip.

When price comes back to a S/R flip zone, a place where market changed its mind on the value of the Euro, that is the price at which the Euro collapsed. It's somewhere I should be looking at. In this case, it was a place where there was prior demand. But once that demand was consumed, what was left was fresh supply.

posts.author: Ifmyante
posts.text:
Yes, there's a very good reason for that PA

Firstly, there were a mass of buy orders remaining at the bottom of your yellow box -supply breaking like that will nearly always leave unfilled buys These needed to be consumed before price could drop

Then we come to the break above the spike high. If you want to sell lots and lots of something, you need lots and lots of buyers So what do you do to get lots and lots of buyers? You Breakout above an high. This will fill lots of stop losses from the more idiotic retail traders (always remember that a sl on a sell is a buy), and also excite new idiots into buying.

So then what have you got? You have the buy orders beneath you all used up, and you have tons of buy orders to sell to, so you get your bucketload of shorts in with nothing to stop price from falling hard back into the pole

Very simple stuff

Hi, I kinda have been neglecting compression in my trading, mostly focussed at horizontal levels for structure. I've looked at the examples in this thread, this is how I feel CP must be seen, please do correct me if I'm still wrong.

Okay so here goes, compression is used to fill the unfilled orders after LQ has occured. When sellers > buyers and supply is always respected by compression, the drop is still valid. When LQ from sellers fails to advance the drop, this could become demand. Look how buyers react when sellers LQ fails, if there is bulls LQ in return that ENG supply, a change might occur. If the reaction in return also is a weakish CP and still respect the supply, nothing has change, just a minor exhaustion of sellers, but a sign of weakness on the bull's side. Right?

Vice versa when buyers > sellers, showed in the example.

A refill can occur as a FO to the source, or a refill can occur as an FTR, both are strong signs, it add another characteristic to the structure and where price wants to go next.

So for me it's:

CP after LQ in respect to the zone. Or, CP after CP, sign of exhaustion (nothing more) or CP followed by LQ in line of the CP (a drop off a rally due to no interest of the other side)

Is my understand of this correct, please do comment. Thank you.

posts.author: bennygill
posts.text:
I guess it's really easy to do this in hindsight. But I'm hoping by writing it all down it will help me spot it as it's unfolding. I'd also love to get IF's opinion on the engulf you pointed out and whether or not that candle (or the one before?) would have been a sensible time to enter based on his engulf the demand suggestion for trading CP.

This is how I see it all unfolding (from left to right following price and numbers on chart):

1) At this level we see only a small amount of candles in the base and also a large jump away of price. So we had way too many buy orders - price could not stay here for very long and moved away very fast. A sign that pro money has a stack of buy orders here.

2) Price moved up and pro money started taking profits - this shown by the candles with lots of wicks. Since they have open buy orders they need to counter trade with sell orders to exit their positions, this obviously sending the market back down from the highs.

3) All of this profit taking eventually sends price back down. Shown by big red candle.

4) That is the start of the compression. Big money knows they still have a stack of buy orders they need filled (at point 1) so they try and push price down to that level so they can get filled at the best possible price. At the same time they try and remove all resistance to price so that once it reaches 1 it can shoot back up without any supply to slow it down. So begins the slow process of taking out all the decision points on the way down.

5) Because of recent down trend caused by compression, many retail traders will try and follow the trend - "the trend is your friend" mentality. So they sell the continuation of the trend (sell orders placed at lower black line and stops at upper black line). These sell orders helps fill pro money buy orders - when retail sells pro takes their buys. Price also touched their stack of buy orders (from 1) and shot back up.

6) Their massive amount of buy orders at 1 pushed price higher. Once it broke the recent highs everyone who was short at 5 freaked out and exited their position (or got stopped out) creating even more buy orders which pushes price even higher.

7) Once price got back up to acceptable level pro money started taking profits again which sent price back down.

I'm not sure if this is right. Please try and pull this apart. I'd rather be wrong and learn something than people agreeing with me.

It is not in my plan at all to be trading demo or even test trading yet, but I could not resist and wanted to see how I dealt with it.

I hope I can explain this as I saw it, here goes....

I saw on the weekly we were in a Demand buying zone, so I was watching all the other lower time frames for potential P.A set ups.

I finally found quite good P.A on the hourly, first off I saw average CP, the white zones are what I believed to be consumed orders, except he zone in yellow, this was still fresh. Being eager to enter a trade, I decided @ number 1 this was good enough as price seemed to consume most of the sell orders in the yellow zone, and I saw a FL @ number 2 below, so I placed a limit order to enter long and got stopped. I then saw price form a demand base @ number 3 and then the all important engulf happened @ number 4, my entry missed by two pips near number 4. So, price rallied right to my target, the end of the CP zone, and formed a nice-looking cap @ number 5. I thought considering price did not even enter my original demand zone @ 4, I believed there may have been still some buy orders left, so I left my order in place, price triggered me in @ A, and rallied to my target @ B.

A great learning experience for me, and really enjoyed it. I knew it meant nothing and no money was involved, but the nerves got tested and my emotions were still on high.

Cheers

DT

I've been reading through this thread and If's document on post 1. Nice thread.

I keep seeing the acronym CPLQ (Compression followed by liquidity) on charts. Liquidity is all the market is. Liquidity is the reason for the support and resistance lines or supply/demand zones. It is the cause of all retraces and bounces. (I have been heavily influenced by the orderflow camp).

Two things that I have picked up: 1.) Compression in itself eats up bits of liquidity (supply/demand) as it goes along. 2.) Many times it does so into a supply/demand zone (an area of lots of liquidity).

Also, from a noob's perspective, compression looks like it is always moving diagonally (like a finishing triangle) with a slight similarity a very tight ranging price and wicks shooting the opposite direction of the price movement (I'm assuming this is true... can you actually have bullish compression with bullish wicks and or bearish wicks?According to If's document "when price taking out last decision point and the orders that where left there." Sometimes compression doesn't look like a finishing triangle at all. It looks as though price has sort of lost it's structure somewhat. It looks indecisive, but is making decisions at the same time. Is this too vague and simplistic of a description?

If not, this would exclude very tight ranges (areas of indecision). Compression actually tells you the decision that is being made. Am I making sense?

While I'm at it, my perception is that poles are basically price bursts (very long candle bodies in succession and going the same direction) that are typically the origin of a move. Also, flags look like compression between two poles (I'm assuming this is where the term flag comes from). Correct?

posts.author: polymorph
posts.text:
Hello revivalfx, it looks like you're fairly new here so welcome to RTM.

I think what's meant by CPLQ is: compression that leads to heavy liquidity of one type. For instance, price compresses up to a supply zone where sell orders far exceed buy orders - compression leading to sell-side liquidity.

As for your #1 and #2, I think both are correct. Sure, compression eats liquidity from both sides, but in the tight range both buys and sells are fairly evenly matched, and in the above example, price cannot make a parabolic move downward until sells absolutely overtake buys. Compression gets price to that absolute, even if that means the compression enters the zone we've drawn or moves through the zone to a higher supply zone with more sells waiting.

As for the formation, I wouldn't presume to speak for anyone on this site, but it seems like the most experienced among us pay less attention to the look of an individual candle(s) and more to the zones they create, and more specifically the orders behind the zones they create. Does a pinbar matter because of its shape after-the-fact or because demand exceed supply to drive price up where it found supply and dropped back near where price opened that bar's timeframe? In other words, the orders that created the zone that ultimately translated into a pinbar is what's important, not the bar's look/name afterwards. Where the zone occurs is also hugely important, as is who is creating the zone to begin with. These ideas have been (and continue to be) huge learning points for me - what is the smart money trying to hide from everyone else in this zone on the chart? In compression they are removing orders to make it easier to move price through that area of the chart in the future.

As you said in your P.S., if my comments above don't help you process things, it could very well be that I need to study it more. I think a lot of this has been said better elsewhere including these thoughts and charts from some of the experts: readthemarket.com/index.php/forum/journa...-on-course?start=143

posts.author: Kanzler
posts.text:
Hi anneb5,

I think you might be seeing the play backwards. On my chart, you would enter at the demand I'd marked up - entering long to the top of the compression zone. On your chart, while for the most part I agree with how you've highlighted things, there are a few things I'd change from my experience. The first one is that the "H1 Supply" at the top of the compression zone may act like supply but I don't consider it to be supply myself. If you notice, it was spiked just as the other areas were in the compression zone so it should have those orders filled already. What it is, however, is often a take profit area which sometimes starts a selloff. The blue H1 Demand right below the consumed demand zones is an area I'd probably define a little more broadly. See my graphic for where I put the top/proximal line for that demand zone. Now if you were to have missed it because of being more conservative on zones, that's okay too - a friend of mine has a saying, that trades are like a bus. There's always another one coming around the corner!

posts.author: benhur
posts.text:
1. Compression is a signal that price will reverse its direction upon hitting a sd zone. ABSOLUTELY NOT. Compression is not a signal for anything. Compression is a price action the show us all remaining orders are been taken while progressing to a direction. Like you have a Demand or Supply zones defined, compression is a zone where NO Demand or NO Supply left.

2. Lets say price is rising to a supply zone so what happens is a compression zone is IT will push the price down price to a demand zone letting retailers to buy and then IT will again sell the price to a demand zone slowly attracting other buyers until it reached the original supply zone. So once there is no more demand left since all the retailers had filled their buy orders price will easily fall through piercing all the old demand zone. YES.

Compression tells us the is no resisting power. as you well explained, there is no demand left, and price may freely fall to the next demand below.

3. The advantage is for entry purpose we know price is going to reverse. Secondly, as our target to the base of our compression. Third, to hold the trade if we see price engulfed the compression zone we can assume that price will take another level. (this is based from what i read from other members journal, i my self have not put this into practice) Correct, as we know CP is no demand or no supply, we may be more confident to trade against it. Remember we always want to Long in a sutation of Strong Demand against weak Supply / Short in Strong Supply against weak Demand. CP show us the weak side. But never take CP as a signal - it is not a signal its oly a zone that reads a weakness for one of the two parties.

Now with this clarified, go and mark again CP correctly. Add descriptions of how price react when returning to the CP zone/

posts.author: corsica
posts.text: Hi Everyone My compression homework. From what I can understand Cps are a flagging area. In a bullish flag the cp will go down, consuming supply therefore making possible a move up on return. With a bearish flag you can see a CP going up while consuming demand, making it possible for the price to easily go down on return. That's why you will find poles and FLs on the left of a compressed area. Help and comments welcome!

posts.author: staurum
posts.text:
Hi Enlightenme, please see first the first post of this homework and have a good read on the Compression book (Red's work)

Ifmyante wrote: Compression is one of the most important signs that price is getting ready to turn.

As price is rising into Supply, it keeps dropping as it goes, filling the buy orders left at each Demand on the way up, allowing a quick drop through the CP zone when price hits Supply.

The exact opposite is true for Compression into Demand.

Here is a PDF about Compression www.readthemarket.com/media/pdf/Compression.pdf

Homework

Set up a subfolder for CP Homework and get into the charts

Find at least 20 CP setups, at HTF S/D zones, and explain what you see on each chart

Also chart the bigger picture where the CP occurred

While you're looking for CP, take the time to find at least 20 CPLQ (Liquidity) too

If you're not used to these, you can get stopped out of some fantastic trades and deeply regret not knowing why.

Your question: expect price to pass through? in any timeframe? What works or doesnot on CP-ed area is widely discussed here already. Price Action applies to all timeframes. If you have troubles understanding compression, Go over all the posts in this HW section, Pay attention to words/corrections made by the seniors here, and watch CP webinar by IF. Then you may start doing the HW instructions (pay attention too to the instructions). This will take time, please do not expect to grasp just by skimming and looking at the posts. Learning by doing is best.:)

Price was dropping into a Daily level where potential bounce could happen any time and any place. I marked what I believe to be a compression, as I see plenty of indecision point (red circles) but each of them have been tested multiple times as price was making its way down.

posts.author: HCDE
posts.text:
Hi everyone. I watched again the RTMA lite part 1. And i still a problem i can't resolve by myself up to now. In the lesson, a rule is stated -A LFL is a LFL if it broke a UFL and touched the next UFL. Vice versa for UFL. Rules are fine but understanding the inner logic behind it is better. My comprehension is that, in IT's mind, the logic is that before we go touch a zone of free order flow, to take salivan's concept, we'll let ourself some space to create mess and zones we can use on return. Once the mess is created, we go touch the zone and the mess making is over. It makes sense to me. First, we must dissect the kink, and mark all the clean orders in it. Then we watch the approach for distinct stop hunts into these levels. We can trade each and any of them, taking profits to cover trips to the next sets of clean orders.

Say our first minor set of clean orders breaks. Price will, sooner or later get to the next one. It could first retrace for ten pips, or ten thousand. But it will get there. So, essentially, our minor level hasn't turned price.

Can you think of a way to manage a trade taken at a kink which broke, allowing for no loss and the possibility of a giant retrace?

posts.author: staurum
posts.text: had that price not broken that blue LFL and given PA to the upside, then you can consider an entry to long. However as price breaks the blue LFL, PA to the downside is given, it just means you can't consider an entry to long in that FL. No entry to long does not necessarily mean look for shorts. Yes, you can always look for shorts if PA is given. Staying out of the market is part of trading.

The question is: Should we not bear in mind the orange FL as well as this forms over the break of RS also?

I would say that the answer is yes (agreeing with Edge).

However, in the video the issue IF was talking about is "how S/R trader-retailers see S/R or S/R flip" and taught us we should not look to trade at S/R point/level only, but instead look at the FL that is in line with that S/R. RTMers will see price bounce above S/R or below S/R and still see it reacting to S/R flip as long as price is reacting correctly to its FL. In contrast, retailers are so fanatic about price having to react to the exact S/R point to the pip, so if price has not reached S/R level they think price still has not reached its target, or if price pierced beyond S/R level they think price breaks the level out and will go to the next S/R.

If the question is, where are the other FLs, then yes the orange FL need to be considered too, as well as lots of FLs in lower scale as seen in LTF.

Cheers,

posts.author: Edge
posts.text:
Hi EM, A FL occur occurs anytime a barrier is broken, retraces, and advances to hit an opposing TG. Ergo, it also Fails To Return. When price comes back in the opposite direction and takes out the FL, its once the MPL of the opposing FL is taken out that the new FL becomes a UFL or LFL (once it also hits its TG). Its Ping Pong back and forth.

RBDs DBRs Caps etc are exercises for your eyes to see the swings. These swings cannot be relied on to turn price. Nevertheless they are important because we can look at a swing and ask:

Should Price have turned here? Which of course we can answer because FO's can be predicted.

The only time I use a cap RBD/DBR as an actual trade is if its the MPL/LS trick. Which just looks like a little hiccup (FL/kink) on a higher scale but looks like an extreme MPL on the entry scale

posts.author: Kovalenko
posts.text:
HI RTM traders!

I would like to share my experience in journey to business FOREX. This is not a game, by studying the material on this website you can get your real business. I began my journey about 4.5 years ago. Purely by chance, having learned from the Internet, I decided to try it. I visited one-month free courses in my city, but with the obligatory opening of Live account in the broker's club. After the course I opened the account with $ 2,000 on it. As I understand how, I was lucky because a month later I returned $ 2700. It became even more interesting, I realized that I can make money fast and even faster. Two months later, I already had $ 500 on my account, and I stopped trading, knowing that something was missed. My first cognition was the study of indicators. Within 1 year I reviewed 1000 indicators, changed their parameters, and finally I realized that everything was useless and I just spent a year out of window. I didn’t trade for almost a year, so I did not spend my deposit.

Then I accidentally (though nothing happens by chance) came across a book “Trading Chaos” by Bill Williams. I studied the theory, practice, and I realized that since then I was ready to trade successfully. I do not want to criticize this theory and Bill Williams, on many sites is it written that this strategy made his family multimillionaire, but I had no luck, unfortunately or fortunately, but I wasted my deposit.

At that moment I gave up Trading for three months and, honestly, I was ready to forget about the case. Once on the Internet, since the 21 century is a century of the Internet, I ran against an article about the schedule and Elliott wave analysis. I was very inspired and found immediately the books on Wave Analysis, no need to list them here as those, who were fond of the Wave Analysis, know these books well. You know, I was lucky, my second deposit began to grow, and for 6 months I was a profitable trader. I was happy more then ever. I participated at the forums on wave analysis, I began to notice that five Wavers have 5 different versions of market analysis for wave analysis. At first I did not take it seriously, but then I felt uneasy, when the wave analysis began to falter in my analysis. Each proved his case, so did I, and, as it seemed to me, each got a point. I ended in a deadlock... I started to make mistakes, and almost spent second deposit. I realized that although Wave Analysis is really good kind of analysis, I'm probably out of luck. So, 3 years passed.

A friend of mine advised me a well-known site FF, and I got to the Thread J16. I was inspired again, studied, dug and delved. I liked the understanding of the market, but I was not mentally ready to trade, even though I really liked the thread J16 and still like it. I wanted to get something easy that can be fun to use. I remember, when as a child I attended a club of martial arts and the coach said: you need to learn and hone one hold so that you like it and feel yourself the best in it. And then you can learn more advanced techniques, i.e., step by step, and never in a hurry. The comfort will come, but only with practice. I remember these words, which often help me in life - step by step, without a rush.

Purely by chance I met IF on the site FF, and I began to read his thread (read the market). So, I came to the site RTM. Having experience, even segmental, for 2-3 months I swallowed as a machine the journals of Traders... I was so engrossed that I started and ended the day with RTM. It seems intuitively I knew that there I would find what I was looking for.

Then I took a break for two weeks, I did not want to get used to it. Then I started doing homework, as advised on the site. After about 5 months I finally realized that I had found what I was looking for. And I found the following: All the beauty of the market can be read only in terms of pure chart and without any indicators, pure chart only. A thought flashed - it is the same like the doctor reads cardiogram. He can determine the problems with heart, using simple diagram.

It takes about six months to learn the material on this site.

I wrote «Beauty is in the simplicity» at the bottom of my nickname, for the reason that I like to find the simple things that work. I really liked the last posts of Benhur, which confirmed that I am on the right way: look for simple things on the market - this is the main. You have to believe in the main point: the beauty is in the simplicity of the market. And the Grail in this business is Patience. I often say, the grass grows without our efforts. Indeed, our experience, thanks to my favorite site (RTM), is growing itself. And you know, in order to get PATIENCE - you should not wait or demand anything from the market, don’t wait that the market goes towards you. Just hone simple things and use them.

It is very important to create your own journal and put charts in order to improve your skills.

Just wanted to share my experience. Today I'm looking for simple things, and you can see from my posts that I am using the simple things, and they work. Today I am a profitable trader. I do not demand from the market ANYTHING, I just like to look at the chart and have fun as PRO makes money. And one more thing: do not put the goal of making money instantly.

Let the grass grows by itself without your efforts. I hope you understand me. Beauty is in simplicity.

Many thanks to IF and team of Masters-Traders for creating an excellent communication here. This stuff really works.

I hope I helped you a bit on your way to becoming a trader, good luck!!!!!!!

Hi Alex, hope you are doing well!

I couldn't help but revisit this old trade you took. Whether price breaking a FL or FTR results in an engulf vs. a fakeout can be difficult to determine. I've seen advanced traders here on RTM who sometimes get it wrong. Do you purposefully wait for a possible engulf to occur, and watch to see how price interacts with the origin of that possible engulf? If price also breaks the DP/source FL of the original engulf, can you be more sure that the initial move you originally assumed was an engulf, is instead a fakeout?

Adopting this strategy would mean many traders end up missing out on the opportunity to successfully trade the original 'possible' engulf, however I wonder if being patient and waiting for this confirmation drastically increases the odds of a profitable trade...not to mention it forms a basic QM.

posts.text: hi Amit, there a lot of topics, i am confused what to learn? do i have to learn all of these things? i like to stick with S/D with trend lines.. i have practiced on GBPAUD, and i think i am doing not very well but doing good, please tell me should i have to master myself on all topics here on RTM? thanks

posts.author: milkeyway
posts.text:
xetrader wrote: hi Amit, there a lot of topics, i am confused what to learn? do i have to learn all of these things? i like to stick with S/D with trend lines.. i have practiced on GBPAUD, and i think i am doing not very well but doing good, please tell me should i have to master myself on all topics here on RTM? thanks

When I was new, I also thought all the things are difficult to learn. But what i did is I learned these concepts separately then then tried to use them together.

1st understand what is supply and demand (SD). SD is not just where price dropped and raised. There are sub points of SD. like -Fresh (untested) SD, tested (visited 1 or more time) SD (we call it FTB, 2TB, 3TB...)... -Ignored SD, what happens when SD gets ignored, etc.

Take your time to understand the behaviour of price action with supply and demand. Then pick a 1 topic from marketpedia, lets say FTR. Then start learning and locating FTRs and observe how price behaves at these FTRs. Find the max information about FTR as possible as you can. Ask yourself why FTR occurred. Why price failed to return who failed. etc.

Then slowly slowly learn other topic and while learning them keep posting in home work. Watch videos by IF over and over again and notice what reasons he used to enter trade. Every week watch his all videos and read market pedia again and again and keep finding the concepts on your chart and observe how price behaves. This is a slow process but the more time and hardwork you will give to RTM, there more quickly you can learn. It does take time but you can learn it if you keep fighting with it. Read journals of Dr. Swing and Draft's journal. Very nice explanation is given for the entries. But before that learn the concepts separately one by one. Read trading article discussion thread.

posts.author: Jambowlyai
posts.text:
Okay I will try to explain. Lets say that you expect price to turn somewhere in the black box and that once it does you let it run as far as the blue box.

Option A: Enter when price hits the lower edge of the black box. Price doesn't hit SL, exit at blue box. R:R approx 1:1.5 Option B: Hold off on entering as in option A and instead see if price makes a deeper retrace. It does, enter at the lower edge of the red box. Price doesn't hit SL, exit at blue box. R:R approx 1:15

Risking 2% on option A you have made 3% Risking 2% on option B you have made 30%

Following option B will cause you to miss trades, following option A will cause you to enter every trade. I'm not saying that one is better than the other just that both are possibilities worth being aware of. I wouldn't mind missing a few trades if the ones that I got had R:R's in the double digits.

posts.author: milkeyway

posts.author: polymorph
posts.text:
Not to speak for anyone, but what I get from Jambowlyai's comments is that entering at B will give you a smaller SL based on the number of pips so your risk:reward is far greater than entering at A. Waiting to enter at B may cause you to miss some trades because price may not always make it to B but you'll make far more money in a given trade by entering at B than A.

I don't know what the grid lines represent but let's say they are 25 pips. If you enter at: - point A: your risk to the top of the black box is ~5 grid boxes, or 125 pips and your reward to the lower box is ~9 grid boxes or 225 pips, for a risk:reward of 1:1.8. Using 3% risk, you made 5.4%. - point B: your risk to the top of the black box is ~1 grid boxes, or 25 pips and your reward to the lower box is ~13 grid boxes or 325 pips, for a risk:reward of 1:13. Using 3% risk, you made 39%.

A is pretty good, B is FAR better. That's why you often see If enter at the utmost extreme with minuscule SL and huge risk:rewards.

Sorry if that's not what was meant or I confused the issue further.

posts.author: Jambowlyai
posts.text:
No.

I'm simply suggesting that as we reduce the pip difference between entry and stop loss we can increase our position size while still risking the same percentage of our account. As a result we make more, sometimes substantially more from the trade if we are lucky enough to get a deep retrace rather than one that bounces at the periphery of our entry area. But hoping for the deep entry has the drawback of missing entries so I can't say for sure what is best. Sorry if I am not being very clear. To be honest you seem to be doing great so there's no need to think about this kind of stuff until you are ready to go looking for it. I must say though that I am struggling to make sense of your entries. I am very impressed by their precision and consistency.

hi sylntthunder

I am not very familiar with english but I will try to answer you. Win ration is really don't matter (for me). If you have 10 trades, then what if you loose 20 pips in 1 trade and win 2 pip in per remaining trade? Here your win % is 90%. But in fact in total calculation you loose 2 pips. So, win % did really matter here? There are many things that cause for profitable trading and following are highly recommended.

1] Good R:R ratio. with tight SL. (mine is 1: 8 or 1:10 or more) 2] Entries at high probable turning level. 3] Never mess with lot size. Keep the safe lot size according to the balance and increase it according to your profit with the same ratio.

Here what can happen:

No matter if can loose 5-6 of trades out of 10. (Number of loosing trades can be decreased as per increasing your trading skill) and can loos remaining 4 trades. But my good risk reward ration will give me -5 pips per trade i.e. -25 to -30 pips. But due to huge reward my profit will be +200 to +250 pips. So here also did the win ratio really matter? Here my equity curve will look like very weak pullback to downside or side ways. But very strong up move and it will continue making HL and HH with same shape.

So, the matter is the above 3 points I have given. If it is maintained carefully you no need win ratio. So, focus on those points first

This is IF's curve. His win ratio didn't harm him and never harm him due to above 3 points and much more. His drawdown I also very less due to tight SL.

I use 0.10 lot size per trade for $2000 balance. At a time max 3 or 4 trades are opened. Risk max 5 or 8 pips per trade. i.e. risk 2% of the balance (0.5% per trade).

Never mess with lot size means sometimes trader can think to incrase lot size to make his a/c double in just some day because his is profitable trade. He can't control his emotions and uses 1.0 lot size per trade for $2000 a/c. This is not good. This is very aggressive trading.

posts.author: Ifmyante
posts.text:
There can be a lot of comfort in trading one particular lot size, day in, day out.

But, if the trade we're in now demands a stop twice as far as the last trade needed, then really we should halve our position size. If it only needs half the space, then our plan should have us doubling the position size. If we're up 10% from our last trade, and our next trade needs the same stop distance, we should be trading 110% of the last position, so we can compound.

Amit, you asked in my thread lately how far I imagine you've come. Not having studied every trade you've taken, I'm afraid I can't be at all specific about that. But, it seems you know enough to be very profitable, and it seems you now have the confidence in yourself to keep plugging away at the market, so it must follow that very soon you'll be a good enough judge of where you are in your career. When you know it, you KNOW you know it

posts.text:
Ok, Suppose, you are a shopkeeper and you want to sell your product (You want to make a Transaction) but there is no any customer visiting your shop because your shop is at a lonely place.

So, here, what would you do? You would put your shop at the place where there is too much rush of people. i.e where people can make transactions. Those places can be a Street where many people walk everyday or a marketplace where people go to buy their daily needed products. Same as if you want to catch fish, you have to go to the river. River doesn't come to your home. right?

So, here you found "The places where most of the Transactions happens."

The same way, there are specific levels where transactions happens i.e. IT as a Shopkeeper and Retailers are Customers. And those places are where IT can play their tricks because at those levels there is too much rush of retail traders. (People's favorite places / Usual places where they jump into market or out of the market). These levels are like a Marketplace.

So, what you need to know (most of you already know) that the places where People like to trade and because of that IT get chance to play tricks with them.

So, these places (Market places) are:

Support and resistance (horizontal) Support and resistance (Trendline) (I don't use trendline though) Supply and Demand levels Round Numbers (Many times) Important News events Top of the Range Market Bottom of the Range Market Breakout of specific levels. Their stop losses are at nearest high or low.

In my opinion above are the places where IT likes to play with emotions of retailers by tricks with them.

No matter what TF you see. HTF, LTF is like Long term and Short term thing. You need to read the price action story left to right. Price moves from one place to another by consuming orders. You need to see how the orders are consumed and what happens when price comes back to that consumption. If it reacts there then you need to look more back history to know why it reacted there and if not reacted even that you need to look back to know why it didn't reacted. Draw horizontal lines on swing high and low and look left for the reason and see if the reason is repeated. Keep in mind about the consumption, decision and PA story.

Consumption and decision is one of the major cause of price movement. You need to see IF's all videos (again and again) to know how to read price story. Follow the Risk Reward ratio rule. Never break you own rules and discipline. Have a patience. I use at least min 1:8 R:R ratio. Observation is more powerful thing than doing practice. I found many clues by observing than practice trading.

- Amit

You need to know the psychological reasons for the drop and rise of the prices after formation of the flag. Rally-base-Drop has a base which is also a flag. When price consolidate in a side ways within a range for a while and breaks one of the sides some times both the sides by faking out then you need to visualize what happened behind the charts. People look left to see where it reacted but forgets to look left of the left.

1] For me there is no specific and only single reason for the formation of important high (or low). And the things is that each and every high and low is important according to their respective TFs.Here the TFs means the terms, short term, long term, medium term. You should have eye on the these SDs and should watch and IMAGINE what ITs are trying to do at these levels. Then you can see the decision. Ask yourself who bought, who sold around the highs/lows, SDs etc and who failed how & why. If they failed then where the extreme limit of their failure. It can be a decision point as well as QM if price FO.

2] Targets can be the origin of the move. See the beginning posts of FF RTM thread.

3] Video about CAPs by IF is very good to know about how to draw the boxes.

If you are trying to understand PAZ since one year but not understanding then try to change your view to the PAZ. PAZ are the zones where tricks are played and decisions are made (according to my view). You can see gambles journal too as he is doing really good job and now a days active than me. Hi Andrew, just visiting your journal and taking a peep. First of
all, take your time and work at your own pace. Understanding the market
 comes with time. I joined RTM in Sept. 2016 (but have been in the
market for almost 5 years now) and believe me, I have put in thousand of
 hours trying to learn and figure out the market. I went through all
the videos, non-masters and master's journals, and took notes and
review them. After awhile, I was still lost and could not see the
market. One one point, I thought I got it, but then realized that I did
not get it and was more confused than ever. After sometimes, things
begin to click naturally and "aha moments" start to appear. I started
to see the market clearer. This comes with time, constantly learning,
reviewing it over and over again until it clicks, and taking time off to
 let your brain absorb the material. What made my learning process
quicker is through teaching others. When I teach others, I really have
to understand the material otherwise, I will teach people the wrong
thing. Therefore, I had to be certain and confident that my answers
were right before teaching. The one thing that helped me is to"keep it
simple". Don't over complicate and over analyze, keep it simple. Learn
 the fundamentals in Markepedia and try to answer other people's
journals. Make an honest effort to answer your own questions first
using charts and draw out diagrams and post it here in your journal and
IF's journals (for the ones that you really tried to understand but
still struggling with). There will be senior members that will answer
them, only after they know you really tried hard to understand the
material in the first place. There is a saying that "To Master a Skill,
 you need at least 10,000 hours". The market is no different.

posts.author: Edge
posts.text:
Hi Andrew,

Nice journal :)

Take your time and dont burn out!

We can see all over the charts where the IT's start different
manipulative techniques in order to accumulate etc. These are often
Algos programmed at different levels which leave their foot prints. The
foot prints are not left like classic S/D traders claim, in fact most
rbr/dbd, rbd/dbr are mirages.

Also look at IFs blue line, it occurs at an important place where the
IT's made a shift in behavior to achieve desired outcomes.

A great exercise to do is to look on the chart and see these areas,
where they shift behaviors, the edges of these areas can be quite
lucrative at times :)

posts.text:
HI, Every one,it's almost one and a half year I am here.I only can stay here for 7 more day as my registration is going to end on 01 june.

Firstly I am very

blessed that I found this lovely and most probably the only true forex school and would like to thank IF, Edge, H, Salivan and many others for their great contribution to the forum. I learned a lot from here.so I thought why I am only taking and not giving something to the forum?thats why I am trying to give a little contribution to the lovely people here. well this is a very basic thing but we overlook this. we see that in some cases price touch our level but trade not activate..or in some cases we see that price turnd much before our level,in another case we see that price turned after crossing our level,another one is SL hit but price not touched the SL line yet..any of these can make you frustrated or money loss. so to avoid this we have to understand some points.

there are two price,one is ASK price another is BID price

when you BUY (open a long position) you always buy at the ASK Pr ice

when you SELL (open a short position) you always sell at the BID price.

The ASK price is always above the current price(BID price) you see on your chart.

The price you see on your chart is the BID price

[/b]

BUY orders are executed at ASK price, but MT4 charts do not show ASK price by

default. This is why on the chart it looks like the trade was filled too early without price touching the entry level. But ASK price touched the entry price, it’s just not displayed on

the chart anywhere.

Sell orders are executed at BID Prices. That’s why you will see price (BID Price) hit the

entry price level and get activated immediately.

so..what should we do to avoid some loss?remember ITs are always trying to use your order for their benifit..

so we can see in scenario 1 that price crossed our entry line thus trade triggered and hit our SL.but we know that we buy at ASK price and here the ASK price is still with in our FL, but as the SL of buy order will trigger when BID price touche that..thus here we are out from the trade with a loss..to avoid this..we should place buy order SL below our (FL low-spread)...in scenario 2..we see that price crossed our entry level but trade not activated..again the reason is ASK price which is above BID price and here it not touched our entry level thus trade not triggured yet..and from here price can go in the direction of the trade..but you could not enter the trade here and you will get frustrated and will take bad decisions..what actually IT wants..so to avoid this..we should place our pending buy order above (level high line+spread)

in scenario 3..we see a sell limit order..now here how can IT tricks you? we can see the price(BID) is still with in the level but the ASK price crossed your SL and we know that in case of sell..BID price triggers entry and ASK price triggers SL..thus we get entered and get stop out much before our SL in the chart.as we only see BID price..to avoid this..we should place our stop above (upper level+spread).I know that this is a very basic thing,but felt trouble for this so am posting here..THNX everyone for your direct or indirect support

good time for them to do this or that...

posts.text:
I try to stay away from low timeframes but today the Aussie seduced me... here it goes:

AUDUSD reacting strongly to supply edge on H4.

Finding approximate zone where it will move into on same TF as supply. H4 flip + H4 RBR.

VLTF structure gives indication of move lower.

Have missed it on my initial analysis... but spotted it in time. M1 FL limit (gonna make a post about em... later on) was hit to the pip.

Target being the flip with RBR on H4, have to define the target on lower TF. Seems rational to choose another FL limit. We'll see if it goes there or not

Zoomed VLTF picture - TG.

Order triggered. Approach was compressed. Some negative US news hit the wires.... but let's leave news for the analysts after the fact. Been waiting half a day for this.... 2 big cups of coffee.... got edgy. It took quite a while for price to drop. We'll see if it works out or not.

posts.author: Art
posts.text:
a post about flags... There are so many of them. I feel like they are just hanging in the air. Price very often reacts to them... like today on AUDUSD. It is challenging so far to trade these... especially placing SL (yes there is usually some ignored demand/supply to the left).

Anyway, did not trade it but though it should be tradable.

HTF major swing high:

M1/M5 FL

I see many guys from RTM trading these. takes some guts.. Can't explain why but it feels very not natural.. probably due to lack of reference points to place SL. But the lack of reference points is the reason why it works I suppose.

Anyway, have saved this chart that many saw on RTM FF. Named it ¨Grow A Pair 2.2 -26.2¨ of know what. I was left ¨comment'less¨ after seeing this particular chart.

posts.text:
Very nice entry, Art! In fact, that is my dream entry.

It is challenging so far to trade these..." --- It so true! I always wondered about this kind of trade, just haven't taken it for exactly the reason you described below. I feel that it happens in very strong momentum uptrends. At least I have seen it frequently enough in AMZN. Thought about just buying at the limit and place a stop 2ATR of the TF beyond, but never got around to well define the HTF scenarios that allow it to happen. Once defined, take 50 of these charts and do the expectancy calculation to see if it works --- of course this is the robot way, not RTM way.

M1/M5 FL

"Can't explain why but it feels very not natural.. probably due to lack of reference points to place SL. But the lack of reference points is the reason why it works I suppose." --- I guess that is how they play us.

Learning to quote, let's see how it works.

Sean.

posts.author: Art
posts.text:
Trading introduced me to every single devil in my head and it keeps introducing new ones again and again....

It is crazy that mind plays so many games. Every succesful trade I had just appeared on the charts and there were no questions will it work out(or why). They just do. These moments are rather rare experiences, at least for me. It is as if one does truly ¨Reads The Market¨.

Though it is not the market one should worry but yourself and your mind. Market knowledge is essential to prudent trading though it is only half the equation. The other half is in the mind and it has to work for you and not against you.

Enough of rambling.... There is a book called Thinking Fast and Slow by Daniel Kahneman. Basically he describes that brain works in 2 modes: System 1 and System 2. System1 - intuitive (more efficient in the sense of energy required) and System 2 -rational, slow (not efficient, requires more energy). Our bodies are very very efficient so brain prefers to work in Mode 1(system) 24/7... It is a great challenge for most of people out there.

Found a summary online by Eric Johnson. He labeled every certain heuristic so it is simple to follow. I can relate to pretty much every single heuristic he describes in terms of trading (and life).

If you will read it... PLEASE READ IT SLOW! Re-read some parts if necessary. Read it twice... will read it few more times again. When I read I feel like someone picks my brain apart and points out where the errors come from.

I could keep om rambling but one that strucks me most: Heuristic #30: LOSS AVERSION

People will work harder to avoid losses than to achieve gains. People will

work harder to avoid pain than to achieve pleasure.

Just last week: I went BE on a trade. Was it a good decision? NO, of course not. It had no room to breathe and should have used the Supply Cap to hide SL and risk that 0.2R because gain could have been smht like 5R in total. So I decided that risk free is more important than 5R. At that point one might conclude that greatest risk is in hindsight... supply cap was already formed. So I avoided losing 0,2R for 5R gain.. in risk terms, risk was 1 and potential gain 25.

He rambles again.. shut up!

Happy Reading

2. Was the RBD/DBR a source fo anything significant.

i.e. was the RBD/DBD a decision point?

and lastly... seems financial arena works in the same manner as real estate market:

3. Location Location Location.

If price hits HTF supply... would be stupid to expect that DBR would be anything more than best case scenario scalp trade... And vice versus with HTF demand... RBD should cause a tiny reaction or should be consumed.

So one needs to mark quite a few things on a chart. So I got this little tool (indicator developed) that helps me a lot every single day.

Functions:

Show spread:

On/Off Color Font

Extends rectangles:

Extends rectangles to current bar Option to choose how many bars rectangle is extended into the future Option to show rectangle edge prices Show text (it will always be located in the middle of screen/box no matter TF for convenience). Choose text color

Extends and straightens Trendlines:

Extends AND straightens trendlines within deviation to current bar Option to choose how many bars rectangle is extended into the future Exception color (exception color trendline will be straightened out but NOT extended) Deviation (difference in percentage between Start Price to End Price. If above deviation then indicator will not adjust the TL hence you can draw trendlines with the same tool)

Usually deviation 0.3 or 0.4 % solves the issue of using trendlines as horizontal lines and as casual trendlines as well. So one can mark important areas and see the origin easily and still use trendlines to mark other important stuff since we don't use trendlines per say in this nice community

What I do is create a template as you like, add indicator.. adjust all the settings. Then Save template as ¨Default¨ so next time you open any chart it has your layout + indicator set up and you can start doing your thing.

Short video on how it works and do not pay attention what was marked.

www.screencast.com/t/oDZEHOK9

If it helps you - use it, If it does not - delete it;-)

Cheers, Art

posts.text:
Have looked through my trading history since I joined RTM in around April 2015.

My trading has not changed probably even became worse. I pull off these grate trades and then multiple losses follow. I've worked markets but never worked on myself i.e. psychology. All my losses are nidicolous and not within my market understanding framework. I put trades that next day I'm ashamed off since they are so dumb.

The more time I spent looking at the screen - the worse it becomes. Best period were when I just joined RTM after 1 year break from trading, then after decent holiday or another period of time when I have not looked at charts.

I keep running in circles and that has to change.

I understand my losers and the reasons behind them. They are irrational trades that look very rational while in the moment of finding/trading them. Same mistakes happen again and again. Same mental patterns restrain me from being a successful trader.

I've worked my ass off to have the market understanding that I have. I pull off great trades hence it means I know how to do it. What I don't know how to and it boils down to CONSISTENCY. Consistency in trading, consistency in trading patterns.

It does piss me off since I've been doing it for maybe 6-7 years. I do my homework, I do review my trades, I use a LOT of time scrolling charts, preparing my charts for the next week etc etc.

To say the least IT HURTS LIKE HELL. I am my worst enemy. In the beginning I thought I will take a crack at the markets and see how it goes. No it seems I have no option but just to succeed.
