@Art...

I went from 50 to 10/15 trades (sometimes 20 trades per month, it depends..) Just by being very (extremely) picky with my trades. So i end up avoiding many "potential" trades. (in other words, trades that look good but not picture perfect). And like i also said, "patience" is key. And when i say patience, i mean not touching a trade even if it goes against you after being in profit. Not reducing the lot size. (no partial closing, no trailing stops).

Personally speaking i rarely use any targets. (take profits). I sometimes manually move my stop loss, but only if the market sturcture allows it and if price is already distant from my entry. My trades usually last several hours, sometimes days...

Stylistically, i don't have a lot of new things to bring to this forum (but it's always interesting to see how others view the market). I don't trade that much differently than most of you guys. I use a lot of confluences for my trades (even though i could trade them fully "naked" on the chart). I use channels, Pivot points, SD, wait for traps. And occasionally use fibs.Most importantly, i only enter a position if the entry is ridiculously obvious. (That's another way to avoid over-trading).

So patience and discipline are very important. There should be no difference between forextester & a live chart. If you're still struggling on a live chart, (and again, if it's mostly a psychological problem), then change your bad habits. Do a checklist. We often lie to ourselves. People have a hard time admitting it, but it's part of human nature.

I don't know how to help you, i can only talk about my personal experience. What helped me (with my discipline, patience, sticking to my goals, having the mental strength)...Was not trading but losing weight and getting in shape. Losing my belly fat was a real nightmare

Americans, Europeans etc.. Spend billions a year on weight-loss programs. Why? Because 90% of people don't have the discipline or patience to stick to their goals/gameplans. You'll see the same problem with trading....Trading is just a different facet of the same thing...Smokers have the same problem..Alcoholics, drug addicts etc....All have a hard time with their bad habits. Once you've fixed this mental problem, then your live trades will mirror your demo/forextester results. The bad news..... It can take weeks, months, years...Before it happens.

PS: and yes, i have six pack abs now. lol

Next up is USDJPY

Looking at the Monthly chart, I saw price is inside zone (A).

It's not my intention to introduce new strategy, but just to share what I
 have learned elsewhere. Zone (A) is called a 'Breaker' by ICT Traders,
and to them this is the place where place is most likely to bounce. A
'breaker' is a zone that has accomplished the following:

1) It is the DP that broke an opposing zone (B), but this is a fake-out as price quickly reversed back into the DP.

2) As price reversed and returned to this Breaker for the first time, it
 was completely ignored and price pierced through it easily, so in RTM's
 terminology, this is an Ignored level.

3) Now, when price return to it again from the other end, it shall become a high odd area to look for price bounce.

So I am eager to verify this theory. Now let's look at Weekly Chart:

The first thing I noticed is a possible flip area (or swap zone), and
also the double bottom (red circles) which is prone to fake-out. So I
wouldn't be surprised if USDJPY continues to drop until it hit 107.9.

previous bounced fro this area, so there's no reason why it can't repeat

I am going to stop trading for a while until I can figure out how to
draw FL correctly and use FL to plan my trade. I am going to use the
following rules of drawing FL, i.e. combining the classical RTM
definition and also what's proposed by Salivan.

The classical definition calls for a TG to be hit before we can draw FL,
 however, at times, there is no TG in sight, that's when Salivan's
definition comes in handy. I will also include DP in my chart, because
at this moment, I have not been able to figure out how to use FL to
explain all the price movement, so if someone could point to me how to
do without DP, I would be extremely grateful.

First up is the EURCAD chart, the objective is to draw FLs from Monthly
down to H1 so I can use the charts to plan a trade. I start with an
FXTOP chart from 1953 to 1986:

Point 1: Price established a range between the two outer green horizontal lines

Point 2: The upper horizontal line was engulfed, so a signal from ITs that they want price higher.

Point 3: Deepest retracement. I can't really see why price turned at
point 3, not at this scale. I was hoping that price bounced from FL-A,
so I could explain the bounce using the concept of FL but unfortunately
this didn't happen.

Point 4: Price got near the upper limit of broken range, flagged, and
then rallied strongly, making ATH (All Time High). I drew a rectangle
-B, is this a DP or a FL? By definition, B looked more like a DP. It is
not easy for price to make ATH, so B has to be a very strong and
important level. After price left Point 4, we could draw an FL from
Point 2 to Point 3 (orange rectangle), but this is a huge FL, it's
probably too big to be useful?

Point 5: Price returned to B and bounced.

Point 6: Price engulfed previous high, so RTM theory says, if price ever
 return to B again, that will be a safe location to go long.

Point 7: RTM theory is proven right, B indeed held and turned price again.

Point 8: Price broke ATH again, I drew rectangle C around a big kink,
but because it has not held price, according to our definition, this is
an FTR.

Point 9: Another 'kink was created, and it held price, so D is an FL

Point 10: E is a DP that engulfed FL-D

Point 11: F is an FL that engulfed FL-C

Point 12: G is an FL that engulfed B

Point 13: H is an FL that engulfed A.

That's all I have until 1986, there are lots of small kinks, but they
didn't seem to have broken any important levels on this time scale, so I
 don't know what to make of them.

Any feedback/correction, is greatly appreciated.

AK

posts.author: Enkim
posts.text:
When price hit purple zone (it is MPL of PCP) it also hit its target.
So every previous FLs are already completed. So you can draw FL A and FL
 B and you can wait for PA (if you dont like TT purple zone of course).
When price engulfed FL A it must go to its target before it continues
up. They did retrace a little bit and then in your point 4 they hit TG.
At that moment FL C was complete. They chose to respect it, did some BE
hunts with that other bounces and they move up to FL C. After they ENG
FL C price was free to go up and so on
 Blue FL B is the whole blue rectangle and its MPL is the smaller blue
rectangle. Your upper limit and lower limit are just FLs edges. They
where created before it hit purple zone. I hope it makes sense to you

because if you see now, if we look into 5-min chart, we go to the area
where you started drawing your FL, here is what we see:

So here is the thing, when I look closely, in order to justify B
(purple) being an important FL where price engulfed into, we need A
(orange) to be an important FL, but is A an important one based on how
it is created? And how do we justify its creation? On my chart, it did
not break anything, it did not engulf into the CPAZ, but it did one
thing - it held price down twice. So this is perhaps why I see Master
Salivan sometimes use this criteria to draw FL, if you read his journal,
 you will see that some of the FL he drew, did not necessarily broke
something to the left, he drew them because they held price up or held
price down, exactly like the orange FL I drew here.

So at the moment, as I try to follow the FL trails on my chart, I consider the following criteria to draw an FL, that is,

An FL is a 'Kink' that is created AFTER the break of a key barrier, and a key barrier can be one of the following:

- An SR level that has bounced price several times

- A CAP that has held price

- An FL that has held price

- A DP that has broken a key level and/or held price

- The Pre-CP and also the end of the CP of a CPAZ, are both strong barriers too.

AK

posts.text:
I noticed something, when price makes a Rally-Base-Drop, the first
kink you saw on the right shoulder, is often a strong supply zone. I
want to see price drop some significant distance below this kink,
because this will prove to me that this kink is the 'origin' of the down
 move. And hopefully within this kink, we will find a nice, clean DP
that has never been touched before. So when price return to this clean
DP, it will often hold and push price down again. Then it's up to us to
manage our trade properly, do not assume price will travel far, all we
can be sure of is, price is likely to travel to the next opposing kink.

In my chart above, at 1, that pink LSK, I would not short there, because
 I see price didn't drop far enough, it dropped to the blue FL and
immediately bouncing up. So I wouldn't touch trade there at all. But if
price plunged, breaking the blue and the pink FLs below, and then

posts.author: Astrokillah
posts.text:
Just an observation that I would like to share. I have been 'trying
hard' to prove that FL, and ONLY FL, is the answer to unlock the secret
of price movement. But I have failed miserably.

In the diagram above, A, B, C, D are all FLs visibled on H1 timeframe. I wanted to believe that:

1) We should only pay attention to FLs, especially the boundaries of
FLs. When an FL is engulfed, we are promised that price would reach the
next FL in the direction of the engulf.

2) A reaction to an FL is not as important as the FL itself, for example, the peak at Point 1, is a reaction to B.

Well, I was wrong, I have noticed in several instances that after price
engulfed D, it did not get to C, it bounced to the pip at Point 2,
reversed and broke through A. And there's no kink to be found at that
level, not even on M1, there's no visible kink (perhaps we need to go
down to tick chart to see that?)

That makes it very difficult in a way, because the general consensus in the FOREX world is that HTF elements trounces LTF.

So HTF SD zone is stronger than LTF SD zones, HTF SR is stronger than LTF SR.

But in the example I am giving here, it doesn't seem to be the case?

Just saw your post showing the December demo results. 44% return on
capital in a month is phenomenal. You should be very proud of yourself -
 I certainly can't get that kind of return in a month.

For what its worth.. here is my opinion:

There isn't only 'one' way to trade the market. RTM is a way of looking
at order flow in the market..it is a way to trade where the herd isn't.
It's trading with pro money. Everyone has a different strategy, but we
all tend to see the market in a similar way. All the great traders on
RTM have formed their own strategy which is informed by the basic
fundamental principles we all know are true about the market.

Getting 20+ RR trades is exciting and they do happen, but instead of re
working your strategy, I would put $50 bucks in a live account and see
if you can achieve the same monthly return with real money. If you can
do this consistently, stick with what you are doing and make it your
own.

Personally, I spent too much time trying to re create trades based on
what I saw other traders doing here on RTM. While it is important to
learn and expand your horizons by studying other trader's work, you will
 ultimately have to find your own path based on how you best understand
the market and process all that RTM has to offer. It wasn't until
spring/summer of 2017 when I started doing my own thing. And it has been
 amazing.

It is always important to evolve with the market and challenge yourself
to improve your trading.. with risk management and solid trade
psychology being the most important factor to trading success. But if
you are achieving 44% return per month with low drawdown, I wouldn't re
invent the wheel! Basic math shows us how powerful compounding interest
is and if you were achieving 1/3 of that return per month you would be a
 millionaire in no time.

Just a few humble thoughts, sorry for the long winded post....

I am happy for you and I wish you the best in 2018!!

posts.author: Astrokillah
posts.text:
Hi PinkPanter,

I only trade when I can babysit my position. Forex is designed to take
stops, I am not a superman like Master Traders here that can pin-pint
exact entry with 1 pip stop loss. I have given up trying to do that.

I normally trade when there is no red news. I'm a scalper, so when price
 ranges, it will either get to my TP or if it overshoot my 'mental
stop', it will always retrace and let me get out with some minor profit.
 And I like to enter a trade when I see existence of multiple barriers
behind my stop loss. Because I know even when my stop is hit, price will
 get to the next barrier and bounce back towards my entry, allowing me
to get out with minor loss. And more often than not, I split my
positions. So if my full risk is 5 lots, I will split them into 2x2.5
lots, I would enter with 2.5 lot first, if it goes into drawdown, I will
 add the other 2.5 at the next barrier. Most of the time, price would
bounce back towards my entry. This kind of trading can get ugly (so a
hard stop is required beyond the second position), but 90% of the time
it gives amazing return.

On one of my diagram above, I mentioned 'contrarian', this is crucial in
 my trading, it's about knowing where price wants to go (I call this
'juicy' level). Most of the time we focus so much on entry, but
contrarian is target-oriented, I can enter a trade without the best
entry, with a bigger stop loss than I normally use, but I feel good
about it, because I am 99% sure that price would get to where I think it
 will go. So before I take a trade, I need to ask myself, where is the
juiciest level I see on the chart? And where is a logical place for IT
to take stops before they go towards their target. If I see a juicy
level above current price, I would never short. Likewise, I will never
long if there is a juicy level below.

Lots of words, not sure if it helps. I guess what has really made a
difference in my trading is when I put my heart and soul into
understanding price movement on 1-min chart.

 it requires more screen hours per day. There are several rules I
follow:

Rule#1: NO RED NEWS

Rule#2: Understand how Pro Money work.

With regards to Rule#2, there is one paragraph, taken from "The Doctor's Patients" journal, that I hang on my wall:

Remember, for prices to rise they must first fall, why? Unless Pro
Money can get you stopped out, trading in the wrong direction, they will
 not have enough profit margin to start the move and make it pay.

I am going to use a scalp on GBPJPY as an example. Looking at the Weekly
 chart, it shows that we are now at a critical area where heavy tricks
were played in the past. I have no idea what price is going to do, so
entering and holding a trade hoping for 50RR is out of the question for
me.

But scalping is always available.. and is available 24/7. So I look at what price is doing on H4:

Two things to point out:

1) Note the messy area inside red circle. Conventional SD theory says
this is a low quality demand zone, because it's not clean, too many
candles. Well to me, this is utterly nonsense, because I often see such
messy zone acting as very strong support/resistance area. It's very
difficult for price to break such zone.

2) Look at how price bounced from the tip of that zone, this is classic
Pro Money at work, they used RED NEWS to drop the price hard, real hard,
 and made everyone think that the time has come, it's finally turning,
and they sold into the trap set up by Pro Money.

So looking at how price has been moving since it hit that blue
horizontal line, it broke higher high, and now is taking a breather,
that begs the question: do you think Pro-Money are done? Pro-Money
were already up there at 156.44 level, why did they drove price down and
 then drove it back up to the same level?

Next up is 5 min chart, just before I took a scalp. Looking at this, I made up my mind, I'm going to scalp long:

Then I look at 1-min chart and what I see:

The first thing that gave me confidence about taking a long is that
price has broken into CPAZ. This is actually one of the most powerful
concept introduced by Master IF: When a PCP is broken, price would
travel to the end of the CPAZ. So I smelled blood. The question is,
where do I entered? I saw price making a very nice ascending TL, I
remember Doctor's words of wisdom:"Price has to fall before it can rise". So naturally I set my BUY limit order below that dubious TL, and my TP just below the tip of the CPAZ.

And here were the outcome. Not sure if you can see the blue dotted line and the arrows, so I marked my entry/exit manually.

This little scalp pushed me over +62%:

At the moment, price is back to ranging again, it even went lower than
my exit point, so if I hold this trade hoping for bigger RR, I would
have gotten nothing out of it. Do I think Pro Money are done? No, I
don't know.. doesn't look like it. I would follow Doctor's medicine:

A safer way to trade is to wait a few days after the daily/weekly
turn has established a new direction because people have spent a life
time of fortune trying to pick tops and bottoms.

Until that happens, I shall happily remain in scalping mode.

the flags. Sometimes, it would bounce at the first flag (A), but more
often than not, it would break the first flag but bounce from the second
 flag (B). I have been a victim of this many times in the past, because
each time, when I saw the first flag getting engulfed, I thought ok,
seems like it's ready to change direction, so I went short, but then
price gets to the next flag and rallied up strongly. So I have
recently made some adjustment to my trading plan, if I decide to touch
trade, I would enter a smaller lot size at the first flag, if it fails, I
 would enter a larger lot size at the second flag. If both flags fail,
then I would surrender and exit both trades.

Thank you Rinehart, I could never thank you enough for your help.
Since I joined this community, you have always been watching over my

I managed to tripled my account, took 33 trading days (since January 2).

From the equity curve, you can see that I'm a scalper, and honestly, I'm
 not proud of it, because I much prefer to set and forget. I have tried
catching big RR trades but with limited success so far and my impatient
steered me towards the easy path - scalping. So I am determined to fix
this. I am going to stop scalping for a month and only focusing on
taking quality trades: LSK, SRK, First Engulf, First Kink.

Scalping on 1 min may not be for everyone, but it's actually not as
daunting as most people wants you to believe. The most important thing
is to make sure that you have HTF zone in control. And by HTF zone I
mean H4 and above. Start your analysis from Monthly, Weekly, Daily and
H4. Make sure you know where the key levels are. For example, price is
dropping fast, and it eventually hit H4 demand, watch on LTF what price
is doing, when you see bullish engulfing candles, followed by price
making higher-low, higher-low - that's bullish signs. But more
importantly, look at big picture, price do not travel in straight line,
even though the overall picture is bearish, price loves to retrace
upward to shake out weaker hands, look to see if there's a juicy H4
supply above where ITs can use to take stops before dropping the price
majorly again. When all the above conditions are met, now you pay
attention to LTF supplies, these are supplies created when price was
dropping hard, and when you see price engulfing north of a LTF supply,
it's giving you a sign that it's ready to move towards the next LTF
supply. Wait for price to retrace, take long entry at LTF demand,
target next LTF supply.

Sorry, it's too much words, It's time for me to fix my addiction to
scalping. Probably I should stop trading live, go back to demo again and
 only trade set and forget.

calculate your lot size! Also, you need to make sure that there is NO
RED NEWS. I cannot emphasize this enough. NO RED NEWS, NO RED NEWS.

 20 lots if I am 200% sure that the target is going to be hit.

scalp, and it's not about RR. Sometimes I would take profit for $100
(if I see my scalp is going nowhere after sometimes but I'm still in
profit). Scalping is best when price is ranging.

 position in case my first zone fail. Refer to the diagram I posted on
post #262. If my first zone fail, I would enter again the lower demand
zone with 2 x first position size. And I would exit both trades when
price return to my first entry. You have to have the discipline to get
out when both zones fail..

posts.text:
Astro, as much as I've tried to move from scalping to Set and Forget
trading, I've never manage to get it to work nearly as well either. It
sounds ideal, just set these trades..go away and do something more
useful with your time but in real life I find setting limits very
frustrating (when you are constantly watching the charts you can
sometimes make a decision to enter or exit a trade near a level when it
looks like it won't quite make it).

Anyway, my point is this .... look at your equity curve. Nice and smooth
 apart from that hiccup in the middle when you were trying to will
yourself towards Set and Forgets. Look at the difference in profit.
Scalping may seem stressful, but when u have a nice smooth upward slope
with very little drawdown..really..is it THAT stressful? Yes, it takes
up A LOT of your time. I may be wrong but we are all different and from
what I've seen you may be better suited to scalping. I myself just can't
 hold trades to faraway targets enduring huge retraces along the way.

Your results are great. I doubt anyone here will be able to beat those
returns by setting trade limit orders at the beginning of a day and
seeing how it's played out by market end. I would say to you there is NO
 NEED to change what you are doing. You have found WHAT WORKS FOR YOU
and that is the most important thing. If it's a question of stress due
to the amount of time in front of the PC I have a few suggestions...

1) At your current rate of account growth I think it is feasible you
could take more time off. Maybe a monday or friday to extend the
weekend...or a wednesday to break in into 2 days at a time. This is much
 easier to do as an intraday scalper as you can be completely flat with
no trades to even think about on your days off.

2) You could set a target for the week and if you reach it by wednesday then that's fine..rest of week off.

3) You can just trade the most volatile times around data releases.and
if that includes indices then DAX open, DOW open, DAX close, DOW close.
 maybe doing a few hours every day and taking the rest of the day off.

4) If you feel entirely comfortable in your scalping ability then what's
 to stop you doubling the risk on every trade? As long as you have good
control of your drawdown (which you definitely appeared to have before
the Set and Forget hiccup) then it really shouldn't be a problem and you
 could be on the path to making the same percentage growth with far less
 trades.

I'm, sure you are already well aware of the above points, but I just
wanted to encourage you to keep going with the scalping.....If it ain't
broke, don't fix it

My broker has spread between 0.2 to 1 pip. Commission is $7 (round
turn) per lot so this effectively adds another 0.7 pips, essentially, if
 I make 2 pips I will be sure of making money. Just had a quick look,
the spreads are:

AUDUSD 0.3 pip

EURUSD 0.2 pip

GBPUSD 0.5 pip

USDCAD 0.6 pip

USDCHF 0.4 pip

EURJPY 0.6 pip

GBPJPY 0.9 pip

There is really no magic to my scalping. Price move from FL to FL, or
from Supply to Demand (vice versa). I read somewhere (I forgot where),
the best way to learn how to scalp is:

1) Open up 1-min chart

2) Use horizontal line only, draw lines at price levels where you think price will bounce

3) Watch as price hits your line, see how many times you got it right

4) The more you practice, the more accurate your prediction will be

A good place to start (in RTM) is perhaps the 'Finding The Decision" thread (under homework section).

ADUCAD Failed Trade Analysis

I believe we need to be absolutely honest with ourselves. Analyzing
failed trade is painful, especially when it challenges our fundamental
belief/faith.

In my opinion, this AUDCAD is one that is challenging to rationalized, I
 would go through it step by step and welcome any critics/feedback.

This is the basic setup:

As far as I can see, the ONLY thing that 'negated' this short setup is
price bouncing from point 3 (SR swapped level). Master IF has made it
absolutely clear that a valid engulf PA is one that engulf an FL and not
 yet reached next target (i.e. engulf into free space). However, I am
sure you would agree with me if you watch enough chart, yes, we can
often find engulf of FL, the problem is very few are engulf into free
space. 99% of the time, after price has engulfed an FL, it hit some kind
 of FL/SD/DP/SR and bounced from there back towards our entry.

Let's look at Area A in more details:

And we look at how price reacting to these levels. It blasted through
the entry level (LS/SR) easily, paused a bit under the blue FL, and
eventually broke above it.

In chart below, we look at LTF price action inside the red circle, this
is to examine if there is any LTF PA for short (should we decide not to
touch trade):

As you can see, price did engulf a LTF FL, into free space. If we had to
 trade this the RTM way, we should put our stop loss above the blue FL.
However, price went on to break the blue FL and stop us out.

That begs a question: Is this just one of the few instances where Institutional Traders decided NOT to honor the engulf PA?

cheers

AK

posts.author: Astrokillah
posts.text:
This is the exact trick ITs love to play with us...

I got pm and emails, asking how do I know where price is going to turn. My answer: I do not believe ANYONE knows for sure where price is going to turn. Yes, there are structures, patterns to guide you, but be careful, a lot of the times, our eyes only see what I want to see, when you look for QM, it's easy to spot QMs that worked and then said to yourself -this stuff really work! when you see price approaching a supply, you are thinking short, ITs might decide to make it work and you make money this time, but next time, they might fake it out and you lose money, you do not know what they're thinking. You can only do intellectual guess.

It's a constant battle, a cat and mouse game between ITs and retail traders. ITs are ones planning their moves, setting the trap, hiding their true intention. Retailers are forced to guess. Sometimes we are right, sometimes we are wrong. It's normal.

posts.author: einrikr
posts.text:
Granted, what I am writing next is in hindsight, but price just FO'd to the last set of clean orders in the cap it was reacting to, it was not that unexpected was it?

Now, I'm still learning - a lot from you as well - but this is the stuff I'd generally look at. I used to not put my SL beyond the FL price is reacting because I wanted high R trades, but usually, that doesn't work for me. I used to get stopped out a lot. What's your view on this?

posts.author: Astrokillah
posts.text:
It's not unexpected. All those levels you marked on your chart can turn price, how do you know which one would have worked? you can trade all of them, or you can wait at the highest one. If you miss the trade, so be it. My point is not about 'not knowing' where price can bounce from, rather, there are thousands of levels on the chart where price can turn. It's very easy to get sucked into a self-fulfilling prophecy - oh, look at that nice level, right to the pip reaction. Next time, you try to trade the same level and it doesn't work and you wonder why. Price bounce from FL to FL, when it gets to an FL it will decide what to do - remember this quote by Salivan? Most of the time price do get to FL/flag area. But I have seen quite a number of times price just turned in the middle of a pole, no kink, no nothing even on tick chart.

Orders come... orders go... you mentioned about price taking out the 'last set of order'. I can give you plenty of examples where price bounce from the exact same levels multiple times. So a 'non-fresh' level can work again and again.

Oh.. I didn't use SL when I was sitting in front of the chart watching it. So no I didn't get stopped out. Sometimes, (depending on my mood), I enter half position at the first level because I don't want to miss the trade and then if price blast past my first level I would add at the second level.

i'm not a disciplined trader. I used to hate losing, and fear losing. But I found that to make money in this business, you need to have a bit of gambler's mindset. Quite often, I went in with large positions, and tell the market -ok, prove me wrong and I dare you to blow my account! Strange, those were the times when I made the most money. But life is full of uncertainty, one day, I may bust my account, who knows? I just have to constantly remind myself, stay alert, stay vigilant.

Personally, I have found the following understandings useful: - Price do not move in straight line, so do not be afraid of spikes. In fact, spikes makes me a lot of money. - it's easier to grab 10 pips profit 20 times a day, than to grab a 20R trade 1 time a day. - the longer I stay in this business, the more people I know, I have realized that the people who are making a lot of money day-in day-out are mostly scalpers..

first, a very big thanks to your generous sharing of your charts and insights in the forum - your posts have been a real inspiration and eye-opener to a fledging trader like me.

In particular, I think how you approach the market really makes sense - especially the part on LTF confirmation of HTF levels. If you don't mind, I have 2 questions:

1. You mentioned that the levels structure you use most is the QM. Does that mean that you start your analysis by looking for QM levels at significant H4/D1 swing highs or swing lows (which I assume are the extremes)?

2. As for LTF confirmation, are you referring to the LTF structure at the source of the HTF level or LTF entry set-up? Looking at your charts, you based your entry on some LTF entry set-ups when the price returns to the level, but do you also look at the LTF at the source of the HTF level to pinpoint the exact level?

Basically I am scanning for QM levels of HTF. If the level itself is at extreme, I would be more comfortable to take it as is.

There are more QM levels at Mid way of HTF - those offer scalp opportunities.

LTF confirmation would be a newly forming QM structure occurring at logical HTF level and which is also explainable with LTF level at the origin of the HTF level i apply. LTF analysis of the origin provides the necessary resolution for better accuracy. TF are just price wrapped in arbitrary time period, while price is has a definite targets regardless of TF. Therefore MTF analysis is so much important for our work.

posts.author: smimon

Quick question for you pal - am I being overly optimistic in thinking it should be possible to spot the reason for every turn in the market?

I understand that the goal is to focus on only the most significant levels, trade edges etc for high probability, and I'm making some great trades like this. But sometimes, I see what to all intents and purposes appears to be an important FTR get taken out and a PAZ entered, only for price to then turn from a seemingly random place, and no matter how much I try to apply RTM reasoning and methodology to it, it simply doesn't make sense why it turned from where it did. I then get "stuck" with incorrect directional bias, expecting a PAZ to complete, which never does (although sometimes in fairness I've seen an incomplete PAZ move get completed days or even weeks later).

I put this down initially to inexperience, but I'm pretty confident in marking up the correct FLs on the charts now, and 9 times out of 10, even if I get something wrong, I understand why with hindsight. It's the 1 in 10 that's driving me nuts.

Much of what I see that confuses me can be explained if you consider the DP to engulf a FL/FTR an important level in its own right, but I was under the impression that it was only FTRs and the engulfs thereof that mattered in the scheme of things (assuming of course the DP isn't an important FL/FTR itself).

So two questions really - to clarify, is it only the FTR formed after an engulf, and not the DP to engulf that is important? And if so, why do we so often see big turning points take place from engulf DPs, when its corresponding FTR has been taken out?

And also, are there just times you have to shrug your shoulders, and move on? Or is it possible to understand every move?

All the best, thanks for any help.

posts.author: smimon
posts.text:
Apologies for posting again, but a chart always helps in these situations. Here's a chart of recent action on the Dax, M30, which I've annotated to highlight my confusion.

In this case, the DP to engulf was clearly a significant level in its own right, even though its corresponding FTR was engulfed. Things like this happening are the final thing that is preventing me from becoming highly consistent with my trading.

I've dropped down to M1 to see if I could see anything - I marked on the origin of the move down at (1) that was a reaction to the seemingly important FL:

And then zoomed into the area where the big bounce at 3 came from:

I know it's good practice to take profit at the first reasonable target, it's just that when this sort of thing happens it seems to invalidate the FTR theory (to my mind at least - I may well be wrong!) and then makes me second guess taking entries, or whether I should hold a trade or not.

At the moment I'm thinking I need to readjust my thinking - if we have a pole base which engulfed an important FL, and then a FTR which formed thereafter, I should only consider the "whole thing" engulfed if both the FTR and the pole base are taken out. If just the FTR is taken out, and not the pole base which contained the DP to engulf, then the zone is not dead.

Cheers

posts.author: benhur
posts.text:
Hi VT

The moment when things clicked for me in my studies was the moment I realized nothing in the market is technical. Instead I started looking for places where I could find unfilled orders. Today, when I look at the chart I am searching for the ultimate bouncing levels, then I consider if I want to trade these levels.

At decision points there are unfilled orders and you can expect a bounce there. but be aware that a decision level is just the nearby barrier of a PAZ (price Action Zone). The further boundary of that PAZ can react too, because this is the first level that price was balanced with opposing orders, therefor just beyond it you can find unfilled orders. This is why you should consider FTR, FL, DP, CP, QM, DM - these all are variety of formations that unfold imbalanced order flow that you can use in your trading.

To make things more complex, yes you should drill down forever if possible to really fine your level. You should always remember that time is no factor of the market, therefore time frame is just a random necessity to document price. The events of the markets are documented by price only. So our job is harder to extract the finest level to act upon. Yes is no that straight forward, And yes we should be very happy it is like that, only the busy miners get reach the precious rocks.

To be more practical, do what I did for weeks during my initial learning phase; take two lines one for above price one for below market price. stare at one minute charts and place you lines where you know price will give a bounce. Do so for whole sessions with great patience and motivation to really see price in action. If you do so, come back and share with the RTM community your finding. I am sure there are going to be at least few priceless insights you take for life.

The question was related to my definition for Flag-Limits. as some of you know, I tend to breakdown everything to the OF arrays, by doing this I can assume where unfilled orders are located:Think of a Flag-Limit in terms of orderflow balance / imbalance.

The flag area show us where there was balanced OF, while the pole (the approach or the break) is where we assume to find imbalance.

2 really important concepts that I've picked up reading thru various journals of Master traders

1) After engulf, price is free to move to origin of EG in that TF 2) Price likes to go 'coast-to-coast'

So the implication is, if there's an engulf of a H1 level, price is free to move back to the origin of that EG in the H1 TF or the FTR of that DP. Which means don't diddle in the middle of that TF when price hasn't reached its objective yet unless there's another EG which takes precedence

This is from Markepedia..

The CanCan

Very often price will move into, or even better, break out of a zone with strong momentum, creating a pole.

Usually a pole will have a flag on top, gathering orders for price to avance.

But if the flag breaks back into the pole, this is a significant turn in value.

A CanCan can often occur at such an event.

Price moves hard, flags briefly, and moves back quickly with a Liquidity Spike. This liquidity spike will mean there may very well be orders left to be filled at the edge of the flag, so you'll very often see compression back towards it, with extra orders being hidden, so that when price hits the cap, it can shoot back through the compression and on to the base of the pole.

The yellow ellipse is the decision to break into CP, better seen on LTFs.

Looking into M5 and supposing I really still wanted to trade this; one setup was available after the pink line got ENG & price returned to the FTR in the pink rectangle, resulting in a small loss. posts.text:
Where are we going?

How are we going to get there?

How will I know WHEN I'm wrong?

What do I intend to DO when I'm wrong? - Bredin (Four rules of trading)

OK. I have now seen that some of my descriptions are alien to many - this is because I did not have the available "incarnation time" to wade through the amount of chaff at Forex Factory or Baby Pips to find the wheat. But still, by luck, and a lot of good fortune, found my own way through the ocean or sharks that circle our trading business and come out relatively unscathed the other side.

Most terms are learned from others - a few are my own - All my examples are from a trading SHORT perspective - I don't want to type examples needlessly twice

MOMO - a series of candles that together form a big candle in my minds eye - This is the "MOMENTUM " that has the POWER to break a POINTY PLACE (it is not to be confused with a long candle formed by a liquidity gap in the middle of nowhere)

Lets be clear - If momo doesn't break a Pointy Place - It aint MOMO

POINTY PLACE - Posts 29 through 31 save my typing fingers

SHELF - same as above but a different shape - ( so shelfey rather than pointy) - I personally usually stick with just saying Pointy Place - its all part of my charm!

A HOOK - what better term for a pirate - imagine a RBD (Rally Base Drop) - a lovely new targetable supply is often found when the DBD (Drop Base Drop) under that forms a "hook" or if you prefer a "rose thorn" - supply can sometimes be at the top of that;

ZERO LINE This is where traders take a trade, they all see it together and join in a short - they this sit on the trade as they go into profit - price then surprisingly reverses! When price returns to their entry area the feel fear of loss - so wherever they had there stop loss - they move the stops to their entry point - those orders (their profit) are now all in the same place - the market makers can now target the rich pickings all in the same place and buy the original traders good positions off them at a discount - price then carries on down - to the howls of anguish coming from the traders who moved their stops only to see price rush off in there original direction - what fun!

SPACE - my preferred - and imho - The Very Best Money Management System Ever-and I will take some convincing to prove otherwise - if you have the slightest abilty whatsoever you can really do some damage with space - and, for a special treat for all of you here, I might even draw a cool diagram - if I find time.

Why use space for your Money Management? - Well, space acts to protect you against inevitable mistakes - space takes the importance of "winning" out of the equation and at the same time allows you to become aggressive with your held profit to make a killing -for some reason it takes some time to "get it"- but once you do you'll never go back.

As regards using the fib tool overlaid on your space "box" - The fib tool lets you know WHEN you can be aggressive with your space.

You NEVER allow your space to be destroyed with one (or even a run of bad trades) -my mentor has not managed to burn through his space in three years! - and yes he makes many mistakes - this WORKS

FAT CAT - Imagine a cat - happily bouncing away on a trampoline and tapping his head on the ceiling from time to time -

Then he finally gets up enough steam to "really go for it" so he slams up through the ceiling - He is curious about who lives upstairs

Only as soon as he can see into to upstairs room he's so curious about - the owner greets him with an effin great cricket bat, slaps him on the top of his head and sends him straight back where he came from.

The supply demand story for the "fat cat" is the change of supply to demand where price breaks through the ceiling - the cricket bat is BIG supply that send him packing and on the way down the demand he caused on the way up is "broken" and HAS to become supply again at THAT point - after his adventure into the upstairs apartment the cat reaches the trampoline with his head on the sore side - where do you think he will have a good chance bouncing off next time he goes up

I will add bits as I go _ I will chat with wolverine to see if we cant make things complete

.. quote - I've always got confused with MO's description of a pointy place, can you please show me what he/you mean by this please?

To me it is a simple as it says - it is a rejection of price (on any timeframe (but the higher timframe the better))

It looks like a pointy wigwam

But this is NOT a strict rule - if you see price bashing its head on the ceiling - then it breakes through with MOMO - Sort of see that as a pointy place

OK thinking about it - it is price breaking a Supply or Demand level - just work backwards from there - there is a place somewhere before the break of the pointy place that price left you a sign - it is the place where the bloody big order was put on by a bank - it is maybe hidden, within one of the timeframes. - I am very new here but I think you guys call it a Decision Point DP?

It sort of looks like price bashing up and down as the orders are consumed - then one side wins and price takes off - Sam Sieden expains it well

i am working out how to explain "space" atm - I do not use MO's fractional notation - it confuses me - I imagin "space" in my head as a "bucket of money" - with the bucket as tall as i want it to be - the taller the bucket - the less concentrated your cash - a short bucket would have your cash - and therefore your lot size much higher.

you NEVER burn through your space - If it gets chisled away by some losses - you reduce your position size.

Space is a form of trading that involves delayed gratification - you split your account into two -

The big "leverage" side of the ledger, this dictates your maximum lot size - this part of your account is protected and SAFE

The "risk" side of the ledger (the bucket) is to be used agressively - you do NOT put your profit into the main "leverage" side of your account (this rule HAS to be broken on occasion)

The profit is stuffed into your "bucket" - therefore driving up your lot size - this results in so much faster an account growth than the conventional "add your win to your account, and lets see what new tiny lot size increase we have made"

YOU decide when you want to reset your account - ie when you have reached a desired percentage growth. Typically you can cut out 2 to 4 percent of your account as your risk. IMPORTANT - you NEVER use all your risk on a single trade ( imagine nursmaiding a small account within your account)

posts.author: Capn P
posts.text:
MO calls SPACE his sword and shield - Wolverine defines SPACE as a means of defense and aggression - If you learn how to use it.

You NEVER allow your space to be destroyed with one (or even a large run of bad trades) - my mentor has not managed to burn through his space in three years! - and yes he makes many mistakes - this WORKS

This is a simple explanation - I hope - There is more to it - but too much info would cloud the issue

Firstly do not mix MO's method with the way I do it - I still don't properly understand how MO does it. - and I don't have to, as the method I learned achieves the same aim.

OK - here goes

My "initial position" is 4% of my account

I place that position behind a Weekly Extreme - that is usually a minimum of 250 pips away - although it is double that on occasion - My INITIAL entry is the only one i feel I have to get right.

On the GU above - that was an initial entry - my tp should have been at the grey line -but i exited because i was close enough to add 160 pips into my space bucket of cash -this gives my some protection from some inevitable mistakes.

The result! - my spacebox is 160 pips "taller" than it was

Repeat

Repeat

notice I put a fib tool overlaying my box

When the 61 fib is on or just over your green "position line" - you can add lots one step

So if you were 8 lots you could go to 13 lots (the next number on the fib sequence) And you would still be positioned behind the SAME weekly extreme.

My pink lines are IF/THEN lines - meaning if price crosses the line I "DO" something - I would not allow a position to be wicked out by market makers - so only a close over the line on an H4 would tell me my idea was wrong and i exit then -

ER - I would also use a PnF chart for this (close over my pink line) - but don't worry it only shows me where SR lies

You see - my space is so big only a catastrophic event could kill it.

It is delayed gratification - I use the markets money to get aggressive with my lot size

After I strip out my risk - my result can only be $00.00 or $ a LOT of Dollah.

Your Space TARGET is NOT a supply or demand level - it is to add a percentage to your account - MO suggests a multiple of 12.5% - and who am I to argue!

But why go to all this trouble

OK - the bottom line is this - Once your space is big enough -You can trade at Max Lots for ZERO risk - so a move of just 100 pips would double your account - cool huh?

Really good traders such a MO and Bredin do this (and I don't need to tell you there are at least a couple on this forum who could do this easily) - I have not yet achieved this goal.

HEALTH WARNING - do not attempt this in a live account if you have any doubt as to what your doing!

There are a few different methods used in SPACE Money Management

posts.author: Wolverine
posts.text:
If I could summaries my trading education/path. Not in any order of importance.

1. Quality information - Sam Seiden Vid's and Articles (for me). Stay focused I have strayed myself as I love learning but it can be a distraction.

2. Training - Go over old charts find pointy places and ask why did price turn there? Draw a line and change time frames. Be a detective. Take screen shots build up a library. With time you will notice some patterns then you will notice how patterns work together.

Investigate the different elements of a setup, for example study how price approaches a RBD and the effect. Investigate the different elements. If's homework's are spot on here in my opinion. Chris Lori Is also strong here he was an Olympic athlete in one of the toughest sports and he approaches trading in the same way - training for the main event (Essential Qualities of Successful FX Traders Video Series).

3. Build some trading muscle - Expose yourself to the market. Get used to the emotions. Hold trades for a day, 2 days. Wait a week for a setup. Don't look at the screen let your trades run etc. Again a type of exercise for the main event. Read Trading in the zone, trade cold.

4. Money Management - is an art in itself. Phantom of the pits rules 1 and 2. Info on poker players etc etc, will give you ideas. Fxstreet have some good education material on money management.

The recipe for success in anything is pretty much the same. Hard word, dedication, belief in yourself.

The education may take a while so priority one should be to keep yourself in the game whilst you learn:-

1. Demo. --Time--2. Live very low risk. --Time--3. Spank the market.

If you loose your bank role you can't play at the table and learn.

Cheers,

I see youre trying to quantify by what you see, in a measurement perspective.

Understand what length means in the context of S/D trading.

RBD example

the left 'leg' - price has found demand/buyers, and price rises/rallies

the base/top - price has found equilibrium for a relative period of time, but inevitably succumbs to sellers and falls/drops

the right 'leg' - sellers are dropping price, how far depends on price finding a demand that can overcome the sellers.

Now that you are thinking about the ACTUAL MARKET DYNAMICS and not just measuring a leg; if the right leg is in fact longer than the left leg that means the demand that started the whole RBD has been broken and the sellers that dropped that turned price must be pretty powerful. MOMO has been quantified.

SO YES HARSHTHAKR AN RBD WITH A RIGHT LEG LARGER THAN THE LEFT IS SIGNIFICANT AND POWERFUL BUT ALWAYS IN THE CONTEXT OF THE BIG PICTURE.

Good question. I'm a big fan of correlating pairs. I think it serves as a good indicator. First is to realize how one pair correlates to another. Then you watch the levels like you would any other trade. For example, this past Friday, on the GU & EU moved closed together. Watch when one pair reacted at a level then other followed. Also look at the crosses for a good indication. The EURGBP was a good indictor on Friday. AU and NU was also an easier pair to correlate. There's a benefit to trading the pair that slightly lags, just make sure you're trading the levels according to that pair. Meaning that, let's say, demand was 50 pips away on the leading pair and only 25 pips away on the lagging pair, target the 25 pips if trading the lagging pair not the 50 pips as indicated on the leading pair. Hope that helps.

posts.author: @mel
posts.text:
Hi Sunny,

That's a good question!

A decision point in itself is powerfull. The word say it all "Decision", meaning that someone decided if price was too cheap or too expansive at that particular moment in time.

Once a decision has been made, you will always see some kind of follow through however you have to look at the whole picture in order to see where price is likely going to go. Let's say that price is at demand and a decision point was made to take price south. So what happened? Someone decide that price was too "expansive" and they want to see price going down but you should ask yourself where price is likely to go from there... Is there another fresh DP just bellow/above price? Is there enough room for price to move? Could it be that price went down so that they could buy back at a better price?

To answer all this questions, you deffinately have to look at HTF's and see where price is and where it's trading to.

Hope this helps, Mel

posts.author: kaspopsicle
posts.text:
Hi Rosa, so your question is about set ups and stops. As i understand it you prefer to trade off H4....good option for reducing screen time.

Your set ups should be very accurately traced from history on the remaining higher time frames.That would be D1, Weekly and Monthly.

Make note of S/r and S/d static prices levels(horizontal lines). Draw them onto the higher tf...then go down to H4. Most platforms will automatically save what you have drawn. Visually check how your drawn levels relate to H4.and the current pa there.Trend lines are best drawn on the tf that you are trading off....to give a sense of gradient and an additional guide for your stop loss.

Stops are subjective to pa but more importantly to your risk reward ratio. ( please see danandsuecos article on stop losses.)Typically you should only be risking 2-3% on a trade so if you cannot find a trade at that rr you should not take the trade imo.Subjective to pa you should be looking for a stop at next available s/r drawn from higher tf, ideally.

I use same tf levels and/or nearest (to ratio) dp...indecision candles are a favourite of mine.

As mentioned above trend lines can give additional confirmation on setting your s/l, particularly when confluence of static levels occurr ( please read Markepedia on confluence)

I hope this serves to help. Good luck with you trading.

posts.author: Alientrader
posts.text:
Balance occurs when neither sellers nor buyers are motivated to move price beyond a range. We see this balance on our charts in the form of a consolidation or range. These occur on all time frames. Eventually either sellers or buyers will become impatient and move price beyond the range. If there is extreme imbalance as shown here then the breakout will be sudden and violent. These violent moves out of these consolidations or clusters create new demand or supply. In this case new demand was created. So now we are very interested in this area when price moves away for some time then returns.

Hi Rosa.

Regarding the Decision Point. Try to think about the definition of a decision point. I say when One side of Bull or Bears are winning and moving price further in their direction. We spot the DP where we see the last opposing power. Exp.: if Bulls win, we set the DP to where we see the last Seller. Usually that would be at the opening of the opposition bar.

When either side wins a battle, it is called a Decision - a decision to move to the next level. What I think was confusing you, is that the next level did not set new high. it is not suppose to. But the decision was made to move higher.

For the DP not creating new High, it was a hint sent to you, to tell you possible sellers are gaining strength. when last leg DP was broken, they were sending a louder message about their intentions for more selling.

This is how I would look at it.

Hope I am being more clear this time.

posts.author: Alientrader
posts.text:
I know we're beating this to death but I think the discussion is worthy. Plus if we get some of the senior traders to chime in then we all benefit.

When price breaks from a consolidation, range or cluster whether of short or long duration we have the makings of a potential DP. A clear break from a cluster with price moving clearly up or down with follow through is key. If there is no follow through then there really isn't a decision. If price stalls and moves back then IMO no decision was made. Price needs to engulf the previous price action and clearly break away.

I chose this area in the chart below to illustrate something. Notice 1 and 2 are clear areas where price broke up with a bullish engulfing (BE). The first or lower BE broke out of a larger cluster than the one in BE 2. But price IMO did not truly make a decision to go much higher. Price stalled before getting to 3. If price had broken above 3 then that to me is a real decision because price would have engulfed the bearish price action to the left. In this case price did not engulf the bearish price action to the left so no real decision. Now this is in the context of the time frame shown.

Having said all that above if you look at this on LTFs then in the context of LTFs these areas would probably be significant DPs.

Also I want to stress again that DPs occur on all time frames. You may be able to clarify the area on a LTF. Also more DPs will occur on LTFs.

Hi HRT,

If you are new to Supply and Demand than I suggest to just try to trade the fresh zones. Just make sure that you know what the leading directions are from Higher Time Frames zones.

Start your weekly analysis by looking at where price is on the HTF's. For example What is the direction price is trading at the moment on Monthly, Weekly, Daily, 4h. Are we trading towards Supply or Demand? Did we just left Supply or Demand?

Once you become comfortable at trading only fresh zones, you than can start looking at tested zones.

I encourage you to get some screen time too. Draw your zones of intrest and watch how price reacts to it. This is a great way to learn more.

Once you have your zones in place, look at the approach, is price compressing up towards your fresh supply/demand than it's a good thing. Let price show you what it wants to do and then trade in synch with it.

Also, you really want to look at the potential target. If you have a fresh supply zone and there is not a lot of room for price to move, than as a beginner you can skip the opportunity and look for a beter place to trade elswhere.

If you are new, I suggest you don't risk real money while learning. You can learn on a demo accout but yet treat it like it was real money. This is where you will get your discipline from. If you are really serious and dedicated about your future trading career, you got to be disciplined and put a lot of time and dedication to have this working. The good news for you is that you already found out that supply and demand is an important part of trading, this gives you an edge over other traders but like I said earlier there is a lot more to look at than just pure s/d but you'll discover all this set by step.

So try to digest all the above and than make a decision. Are you willing to put the time and effort that is needed to become succesfull or are you not.

Wishing you all the best anyway. Mel

Here's part of a PM I just got:

Hey IF!

You have created one hell of a forum. I have looked the stuff over and am very overwhelmed by the amount that is offered. The only problem is that it seems there are a few different methods at work. Sometimes I see people using supply and demand, others bull flags, and yet others are using caps on price. Is this right, or am I just confused?

Well, what we teach here is the holistic reading of the market. Sure, we give some patterns names, but we're not price pattern traders. We simply get into the mind of the institutional traders. We see their algorithms in action and can read what will in all likelihood happen next.

In essence, we know that if price engulfs South, it wants to move down to the last engulf North. This we teach in 3 easy lessons, and about 180 very difficult ones!

But really, what we do is very simple indeed. It just takes a long time to understand how simple it actually is

posts.author: Ifmyante
posts.text:
Yes, in essence, it would be pretty accurate to say that price is either in consolidation or in a pole. We're certainly safest trading from the extremes of either. Just look at when price breaks an high or low, with an FTR; see the rejection which so very often occurs from the new FL on return. when this FL eventually breaks, price has entered the pole. Some may trade this break, but they must be ready to suffer DD right back through the flag, and sometimes even slightly beyond. Hence, for safety, it's usually best to let price break and form an FTR which we can trade from on return. The tg is usually the base of the pole, but if price starts showing signs of compression through the pole, watch out for possible support/resistance flips along the way, especially if price hadn't hit its target before the flag broke back into the pole.

There are very many variables in this scenario, so to draw a set of charts for it would mean explaining every single PA setup there is. So I urge you to look through your charts and try to make sense of these words.

No matter how I tried I always find a renewed enthusiasm to keep learning more and keep trying and keep working at those things that are rusty. Namely the psychology. It being probably the most difficult part, it is quite comforting to realize that an abstract science (TA) can find a simple model of explanation and execution.

I hope to contribute more to this community and am thankful for those volunteering their time and efforts and their minds.

I've been working for the past 2 years learning about cycle theory and even going as far as studying financial astrology. I have found value from these researches, but even still there is further work to be done in isolating the exact price zone that the turn is likely to occur. So finally I have found the pragmatic approach that I need to qualify my cycle research, and I am quite happy.

Though this may not be the correct thread I figure any place is as good so I will share here now how the simplistic view of price enabled me to pull 670 pips from GJ.

My first trade there is a long in the dashed blue, the level was obvious, even though it penetrated beyond the base of the level. I am still a bit loose with my stops In retrospect if I'd have had a tight stop in there I would've missed the move it happened so fast. My cycle research told me the daily turn was running late. We can see that there is a large compression happening towards the demand level. So knowing this with my cycles helped me to qualify the level even though it broke below the base. Funny thing is I was not aware of the fundamental news to be released for BoJ. The first target would be (IMO) the middle blue rectangle. But it was from a previous level and had plenty of backfilling all around it, and the LQ gap was closed. I interpreted as this level would fail to produce significant bounce, so kept the trade open and instead targeted the higher side of the top rectangle. Target got hit into a nice fresh supply zone, so I shorted that level and traded it back towards the DP at the magenta line for around 120 pips. With the momentum of the market and BoJ pledges to inflate the Yen I decided that supply is CT to the overall trend so am now back long from the DP zone when after the drop was a nice spinner with a drop in the tick volume. Low tick volume spinner tells me not much interest in lower prices. So now am enjoying 304 floating pips from this R/S flip and if you look to the left there is not much supply i am seeing for many more thousands of pips, beyond 160 and 180. Of course this is an ideal scenario for me, and it would take a few years to get there I imagine. But people are talking about the return of the Yen carry trade so I imagine there is large interest and pro money behind it. However the COT report is saying that net Yen shorts have been lessening the past few weeks. However in the smallness of my trading education here to fore as long as the dollar can hold onto some weight I think the trend will march on.

So I will be watching the health of the dollar and other majors and adjust positioning as necessary. I've been up for hours reading this site now and again I am glad to be here. I will go introduce myself in the forum after this post but I was just excited to share because without my current knowledge level of S/D and PA I doubt I would've been a buyer at that level that has been good to me. At any rate when the market opens later I can feel confident that I will let the market take me out of the trade instead of taking profit because now that it's at new multi year highs again, who knows how much further it could go up? I am targeting beyond 150 as it is a nice psych number. And because the trade is def free now I can use the floating profit as margin and lower my trading risk just a little more. Anyways take care everyone looking forward to working with you all honing that edge.

All told the first trade around 670, second one 120, and third is a floater now, we'll see what happens with the open later today, but it's for 300 pips. So around 1090 pips. I also grabbed some positions in UJ and AJ, trading them in a basket fashion. In my trading venture I've given close to 12k pips to the market. I know this is a fluke of intervention but is a powerful testament that you have to keep keeping on and brushing failure and loss aside as lessons. And if you play your cards right losses can be quickly absorbed by trades using this methodolgy. I am a believer and am working that knowledgeable confidence up to make this a career. Now finding this site I am happy because I am making my dream come true. I simply love trading and cannot see myself doing much anything else for a career. Ok enough rambling.

Ifmyante wrote: Yes, in essence, it would be pretty accurate to say that price is either in consolidation or in a pole. We're certainly safest trading from the extremes of either. Just look at when price breaks an high or low, with an FTR; see the rejection which so very often occurs from the new FL on return. when this FL eventually breaks, price has entered the pole. Some may trade this break, but they must be ready to suffer DD right back through the flag, and sometimes even slightly beyond. Hence, for safety, it's usually best to let price break and form an FTR which we can trade from on return. The tg is usually the base of the pole, but if price starts showing signs of compression through the pole, watch out for possible support/resistance flips along the way, especially if price hadn't hit its target before the flag broke back into the pole.

There are very many variables in this scenario, so to draw a set of charts for it would mean explaining every single PA setup there is. So I urge you to look through your charts and try to make sense of these words.

posts.author: extremerrage
posts.text:
this is called whipsaw engulfing. 1. Cluster (where supply and demand are balanced) near supply.

2. Cluster resolves north and becomes demand. Many novice breakout traders go long without knowing that they are going right into supply. 3. Cluster is engulfed south by big sellers in supply. Ignored cluster now becomes supply. 4. Need to go short when/if price retraces to cluster. You may find DBD in Sell Zone in lower timeframe to refine your short entry.

ps; copy it from some where:p

Hiya tradingjedi,

Don't be thanking me just yet - everything I observed might just be irrelevant tosh. just find I learn better through iteration:

1. Do it until I fail 2. Understand the nature of the failure and my part in it 3. Make appropriate changes to my method 4. Repeat

I've never been afraid of my mistakes, they've taught me far more than success ever has. So while I don't exactly invite them in for tea, I won't turn them away at the door. You can still profit from a mistake (if you're willing to admit to what you did wrong), it's just a reward of a different kind than cash.

Recently, I decided that it was time to reboot everything I thought I knew about trading, what I'd observed really wasn't working for me, so I blanked everything. I started by drawing random lines, seeing what happened around them, then deleting them and starting again. Each time I went through the loop I placed them with a bit more thought and care, which I could only do by learning from the good and bad of previous efforts.

I've got to a point where I think I get this subconsciously - some days I can read S / D and PA like a book, most days that book is written in a foreign language. But I need to drag the subconscious knowledge into my conscious so I can take a giant step up. The best way I know to do that is to 'formalise' what I've learned, by keeping on doing what works for me but in a public forum where everyone can point out the obvious stuff that I really can't see for myself, allowing me to ask ever better questions of myself.

The great benefit of a forum such as this is that everyone can accelerate their education, not only by doing their own work and having it assessed (an absolute necessity as you can only learn things your way), but by looking at the work of others and seeing how that is assessed. With momentum South on this chart, you see an effort against the prevailing momentum, which is a sign of strength, so you look for a sign of weakness, that is creating a zone of demand within the range of your Higher High, which would give you the QM level.

But in this case it doesn't provide such level, in return, the HH against the prevailing momentum is encountered by another Lower Low, true, as a Fakeout, it ENG the daily demand level, indicating they want to buy a lot indeed, if price would accelerate down after the ENG, then you know break traders are in play and you shouldn't go against.

So much for the failed QM, at this point you look at a diamond actually, anyway now you know they want to buy, so the cycle for a bully structure continues, strong buying gave you a new HH on top of your previous HH (your qm), so another possible qm. Price had to revisit fresh demand to go higher because it was trapped inside the drop range to your left. A refill of buyers after reppin buying pressure.

Hi tradingjedi - this may not be the answer you are looking for, but may help you understand why price did what it did. In the context of the price action as visible on the 15M chart at that point in time (i.e. ignoring HTF levels etc), this is what I see:

1 and 2 are swing highs (i.e. price too expensive) 3 and 4 are swing lows (i.e. price too cheap) 5 price starts to turn, possibly in response to ignored supply to left - but who cares -because price does not move up and engulf anything 6 price pulls back to whatever tentative demand rests at 5 and then quickly shoots up and engulfs 1 and 2 - i.e. the Decision Point to engulf was in 6. Your initial entry (my blue box) was barely a RBR and not the origin of the decision to engulf - hence why it was ignored on the way back to fill the rest of the orders at 6. At the moment you can see the residual demand created by 5 and 6 being chewed up.

I hope this helps a bit.

posts.author: Alientrader
posts.text: The price action before an engulf is the PAZ. Engulfs seem to occur when price exceeds a previous swing high/low. Price moves back into the PAZ area toward the s/d zones created by the move out of the PAZ. The PAZs are not so discrete.

posts.author: Alientrader
posts.text:
The chart is a H1 and I think it is useful to define PAZs withing the time zone. It may be helpful shift between time zones a bit but you can get confused.

There was a nice downtrend at left with LHs and LLs. Then a QM formed. A new uptrend formed with successive engulfs north. The PA before the engulfs are PAZ. When PA engulfs it returns to s/d zones created by PA that moved out of the PAZ. The s/d zones may be shallow or deep. In this case price trends up and encounters supply on its way up.

posts.text:
There has been some extremely fruitful discussion goin on in this thread...and If's journal. I have had many eureka moments in the last few days. So I dug into the charts to apply what I have been learning to the recent PA on E/U.

I saw the QM on the hourly and was so tempted to buy in, but my new understanding of what you guys have been teaching is in its infancy so I just decided to sit and watch. saw Tradingjedi hopped in on it and am very happy for him because he has been working hard and also gives me hope.

Well onto the charts and questions. I have a couple of questions on the charts themselves, but would also like some confirmation on my reading. I was unsure of the lower 1h FTR because price didnt shoot off strong until after a few candles. Now that I think about it, at that time everyone is still trading the trend, so there is going to be more selling from people who waited too long to begin with, which allows for the big boys to load up even more longs. Plus the fact that it never got tested lends to its strength as well.

File to large, had to break it into 2 parts. A question that didnt make it into my second chart, the supply that I have marked in red on the first chart is a RBD/FTR to a FL on the 4h which would indicate major strength and maybe even the ultimate target of the move up. On the other hand it didnt break the most recent lows and retraced to form another ftr that did break the most recent lows and kept going. I am trying to figure out the ultimate target and has it been reached yet. I just took a look at the daily and it is a FL that has been penetrated pretty deeply. So I would say the target has been reached. Still just watching with my new understanding of price.

The concept of price constantly moving from ftr to ftr is slowly coming to me. My charts display the power of FTRs within the current move. Notice the FTRs as price went up got tested and usually produced a newer high, but also consumed the orders there. The ones that didn't produce newer highs after getting tested usually resulted in price moving through the just consumed FTR down to find the next lower untested FTR which then produced a new high. Then when price hit a HTF FTR on the supply side, price went all the way back to the last untested FTR.

What I am working my way through atm is how does price handle opposing FTRs. I am guessing it just knocks price back to the current trends FTR. So what I am thinking is if price just tested that last untested ftr and reacted, then try to find the next opposing FTR and target that, but if there is a key s/r level between that ftr and current price, then price could form a new ftr before it hits the one you found, and then you would want to exit your position. Hope all that makes sense.

My second chart is the 5M from todays action that I really wanted to get it on, but wanted price to test the newly formed FL which it never did. One problem I dont struggle with is chasing price. I have no problem letting price go. In fact I think I may pass on perfectly acceptable entries while practicing "discipline." That is what this next chart is about. Do you guys see a place to get long once you realize price isn't coming back to your entry?

Hope all this is coherent to everyone, I am on my 4th glass of wine and quicly losing the ability to assess myself.

Oh and addressing the current topic of PAZs. I think instead of trying to box price in. We should identify the last key s/r level price just took out and see if price tested and formed an ftr, and then look for the next opposing key s/r level and watch what happens when price gets to it. Does it push through and test and hold above (hold onto position), does it push through and fall back in(fakeout, exit position), or base and retest(form ftr, exit position).

I was hoping somebody could help with my confusion please..

With an Engulf from my understanding there are 2 possible scenarios: 1. If it touches/breaks a S/D, S/R line it could be consuming all the buys/sells in that area meaning price can then crash through that area as area is failing.. or 2. Ifmyante wrote: I love that chart, and I love that question, so I'd like as many people as possible to find examples of this PA and post them here for discussion

Ok IF, I have recently been pondering this kind of scenario, so it was already something I had planned on digging into. This seems a good time to do it. There is a lot on here and it got kinda cramped, but hopefully its still legible. I just kept finding stuff and wanted to label it. There are still a few things I left off.

In order to convey what I am thinking I used a new term. It should work till you or someone comes up with something better. STR - since price can't just keep going on forever, at some point it has to return back into the PAZ. But this is what really struck me while making this up:

1) Price breaks a high and keeps going till supply hits it and leaves a HH 2) comes back to form an FTR at the old high 3) trades back up and makes a LH 4) falls back down to the FTR, it usually reacts for at least a small move to make another LH, but can fall through the FTR. Just know you may go into DD if your in the market and price fails to make a new high/low. 5) price then returns back into the PAZ that it left at 1. It may react to pockets of demand on the way down, but it ultimately wants the demand that created the HH.

Now here is the kicker for me. If you draw a horizontal line from the high that was origanilly broke at 1, even though there are a bunch of candles now that you had to draw the line through, when price hits that demand and trades up and through the line it leaves an FTR at the line (the old high at 1). Once price fell back into the PAZ and reacted to demand, it tested the PAZ high again, even though there are a bunch of candles there this time, before continuing on the second time. I don't know how often this happens, and I need to do some more studies to make sure, but it happened 3 times on the one chart, all at HTF supply.

Hope this makes as much sense to you guys as it does me.
