This is an edit. When I finished the charts, I had family commitments and couldnt provide a commentary; apologies.

The main focus of this analysis is on identifying where the key zones are in the PA. have been studying a lot of the journals here and pulling it together as best I can.

There are essentially 3 zones here, delineated by the zone in the middle. I have picked up the FTR on the left at the top as being a place where a pause occurs at the edge of a PAZ. An engulf had already taken place and price had capped nicely, and the CP back up to the edge of the zone was a confluence indicator that price might be headed south when it eventually reaches the opposite end of this upper zone. Price moves between the opposite ends of the zones, and then decisions are made. The pause at the top demarks the a decision - price stalled, brielfy, and it could have gone north and returned into the zone and would have been an FO. But it doesnt. Its form manifests as price drops south and this becomes our FTR.

Down in the middle, we have a flag limit and I also pick this up as an FTR. Price hhas halted here, and very well could have reversed back up. But it doesnt. It bases, and then its form again is made manifest, and it is decided it is still too expensive, in the middle of the value curve here. So this is another FTR.

Down at the bottom I marked out what I see as being a key area of price action, and there is a nice FO DBR out and back in from underneath. This movement causes a nice RBR which engulfs the recent high. And in fact the box here could have started higher. After the engulf, one sign prices might be headed higher, the pullback comes back into the zone and bounces of a support level. This itself engulfs the last high that was formed (not shown), but the engulf had already happened, and readying to take a position had already ensued.

Naturally, price makes its way to the opposite end of the zone (flag) and bounces back in from the FL. A few attempts are made, and indeed there are a few short trades here that I havent shown to avoid over cluttering the chart. The nice thing about all of this is that price comes back to where it wants to be - the origin. Within this area an engulf north happens (on the right at the bottom of the chart), and price bounces (naturally) back down from the FL. We have a double bottom and double top. Notice also just to the left, price makes a little CP as it rises, before price plummets. This is a nice movement for the pro money because it allows them to take the liquidity on the way down so that they can load up for the big move up to the top zone that they are look to. So price bounces from that small FL and makes its way back down to the demand zone that was created by the FTR all the way on the left. This double bottom is capped, and for sure this was a place to take an aggressive long position. From here price engulfs the latest high before retreating slightly (FTR). This base at the edge of the zone causes a new makjor move up. Also notice on right at the top edge of the magenta rectangle, a little blip that I point to indicating an FTR. At the edge of this zone, a stall unfolds, but it is decided it is too cheap, and price rises strongly. Nicely, price makes its way all the way to the top, to the FTR that caused the move down right at the left of the chart. A nice TT trade or such like down from this FTB to the FTR could have been taken.

When price falls under the supply at the FTR, where is its target? The FTR that caused the move up - that tiny blip/FL/FTR at the edge of the flag down at the bottom. See the second chart - it shows what happens when price returns to the source.

Hopefully this explains my thinking clearly.

Metta,

MF.

hey all.

working on spotting fake outs at the moment.

i have AUDUSD 4H with explanation, i think i got it right in regard to finding and understanding the dynamics of a fake out to some degree. obviously there are different kinds of fake outs to take into account.

#1 was a previous swing high with DP to take price lower and then a retest with in a short while before taking it lower again.

#2 was another level looks like a flag/DP where most markets participants where waiting to take price lower it retested it 2-3 times. from what i understand, everyone is selling at this level so in order for the pro money to get in, they will look for liquidity. the big blue candle breaking higher @3 is where all the sell stops are triggered and buyers entering while pro taking the other side.

#4 price revisits the previous swing high this is where money are turning price and as price starts moving down all the buy stops are triggered and more sellers getting in thus causing price to shoot down with mom.

this is one example of a fake to my understanding. all i have to say is the pro money are smart but im studying them:D

PS. i also remember reading somewhere that an engulf can mean one of two things. 1. price is in fact heading higher with strong momentum to take price to a new low/high or 2. price is making a strong mom candle to catch everyone getting in that candle before price reversing. thus a fake out candle

rcmacf wrote: Would it be crazy to think that the ECB news would push (spike) this up into the overhead supply?

Well, when I first read this post I took it as if you thought it crazy that news would be used to fill pro money orders. I see now that it was more of a question just to that particular scenario. But I had already made a chart and the rest of this post, so I am posting in case it helps anyone else. Most everyone on this sight probably understands all this and could teach me even more, but it may be helpful to someone. I got it from the Larry Harris book Trading and Exchanges.

Markets exist to find the value of the instrument being traded. In order to do this successfully it needs people who are informed of everything that effects that instrument to buy and sell it. These people are informed traders, pro money. People that are informed are not going to buy and sell against other informed traders. So if there were never any other participants, the market wouldn't function. Price would never move and the value would never be found. In order to function, the market has to have uninformed traders to take the other side of their orders. That is where the news comes in. The most informed traders position themselves in the market first, then their friends, then the people that pay monthly for news data, and then when the data the gets released at the news sites all over the internet the rest of the trading public and most uninformed come into the market and fill the pros profit taking orders. The markets have to function this way or they wouldn't function at all.

I personally believe its all a bunch of B.S. I'll save you all from a diatribe though. I will say I it doesn't bother me one bit to profit from it, and help others who have unwittingly fell prey to their other ways of sucking up all the peoples wealth.

I do have a question about how news effects the dollar. Since the dollar is the reserve currency, when the U.S. economy has good news, then its seen as safe to venture into riskier markets. But since pro money is who does the major investing, I am a little confused as to how to take the movements after news releases. Does the public see good news for the dollar and immediately sell the eur/gpb/aud/nzd/others? Or do they also know that good news for the dollar means good for risk so they buy the risk currencies?

Hi IF-

I think the key here was that price was flagging at a good supply level, after bouncing back up from demand. This was a good place to decide to continue upwards or go lower. The key was to see what PA was telling you. The daily chart shows a clear rejection (or consumption) of the fresh supply, and prices that caused this rally had stepped back down to the edge of the range its been in for the past few months. This is a mid-curve trade on the daily, but the trend is down.

Zooming in, the key is to look for some sort of sign about which way prices will move -ideally you need an engulf south to indicate the reaction to the supply and trend line is solid.

On the M15 chart price reacts nicely to the supply that was fresh on the HTF. The key about the reaction is to see how convincing the move south will actually be. I beloeve this signal comes from the pushing down into the lower PAZ - the edge was breached by the signal bar you pointed to. There are various reasons why price rises from there, but right at the edge of the top was a nice place to follow the double top back down into the lower PAZ.

posts.author: mettafort

Hey DT-

I think you are spot on here. Price moves between decision points until they no longer hold. Price comes down to the FL at 2, and dips below. We say that tells us price wants to go lower, but I think thats indirect, or rather too direct a statement. What really happens is the fresh demand that existed at the FL has now gone, and price dipped lower to the pocket of demand below before heading back up to supply. With that area now cleared, shorting at the top is a high probability/low risk trade because IF price does fall, the next place where demand is is at the origin of the up move - here is just above the P in point 2, where it says 2. Price then...

I dont intend for this to be pedantic DT, sorry if it seems that way. I am just thinking about the mechanics of what is actually going on. I see that dipping down below the FL with 2, bouncing of the pocket of demand to the left - the SR flip. Once the demand there was gone, down it would go. Genius.

MF

aiden wrote: Hello,

i Have a question on engulfing and fakeout for you experienced traders. hope you guys don't mind answering and shed some light on this. so i was reading faldot's journal (but it was also posted a lot by many), and some charts makes me think.

Please correct me if i'm wrong on this: Both fakeout and Engulfing were taking out last low/high, correct? the question i have is, how do we know it was a fakeout and should not be treated as an engulfing or the other way around? or i take it completely wrong and in fact a fakeout is an engulfing?

Thank you.

cheers.

For me there are four types or returns, RT or FTB with normal respect to the zone. FO which engulfs and rejects the zone.

ENG which engulfs and continues in the direction of the engulf. A fourth return is the fail to return.

FO vs ENG When I see an engulf and wonder whether it is a FO or a ENG continuation I'll look for; the strength of the reaction after the FO/ENG 1... cp back to fresh zone (weak reaction), perfect to tighten your SL or if you're confident add another position. 2... lq engulfing fresh zone/dp/fl instantly (strong reaction), you should get out of your trade and wait for your entry signal 3... cplq (wedge... ) continuation after the FO, which should now be named ENG instead of FO. 4.... instead of reacting to the FO/ENG price could also simply form a DP/FL only to advance with strong LQ 5.... price can also cp back to the fresh levels only to consume them and hit you with LQ (hate it when that happens), but most of the time you will see a S level turn D before that happen, vice versa D turns S.

So in general I look at the reaction + where the nearest zones are to counter this reaction (defensive range after effort) and I also base my conclusion on what the HTFs tell me, ofcourse.

BTW good question, hopefully my little explaination helps:)

cheers oz

In a nutshell, FTR's = failed to return. Sounds simple enough? Failed to return to what? Well, I made it simple enough for myself to understand it. Failed to return to the range/flag/SR's AFTER an engulf, and it has to be the first attempt and, a short lived one.

Well, you will see PLENTY PLENTY of FTR's in this case, coz it's the same case as engulfs, you'll see them all over the place. Your job, as a trader, is to pick the significant engulfs, hence the significant FTR's.

I've derived my own answers to this conundrum, but that doesn't mean they are the result of right-thinking, so hopefully this is an opportunity to get better insights!

Hello jogold24,

Thanks for the reply. I had also noticed the base of that Spike you've marked, but I like to try to keep my live charts as clean as possible, otherwise I collect too much contradictory information and I don't need to be more confused than I usually am

Spikes are interesting structures, and my view of them (rightly or wrongly) is that they are only reactions to Supply or Demand areas, not sources of it. That said, Supply or Demand areas can be created in their shadows - where exactly may not always be clear, so we might be best served waiting on what Price Action does in the shadow of the Spike and acting on that. Essentially that's what I did when I marked off the fresh Supply on that H1 chart in post #747.

Unfortunately (or otherwise) I missed the short from that area because I was asleep! It would have yielded profit at TP1 (between 1: 1 and 1.6: 1 according to my way), but perhaps not much more (depending on what happens with Asian open tonight).

The joke is, even though I used the conjunction of brand new H1 Supply as a supposed reaction to 'ancient' D1 Supply as the example for my question, the real reason for posting it is that I had actually favoured the long from that lower Demand area where price turned convincingly north (see one of my H1 charts below and also Spongy's Journal posts #75 and #76for detail). If I had stuck with the original area instead of drilling into it to focus on a smaller area (that failed) I would have been well rewarded for my efforts and willingness to go long into a reaction from longer time-frame Supply, and certainly better off than shorting from either of those D1 or H1 Supply areas. It's because I see this time and again, where PA says one thing but history says another, that I thought clarification should be sought: I think it's a discussion which could benefit many others.

I'm not saying that those areas should be ignored out of hand, but as they become older, perhaps less real attention should be paid to them when compared to what's happening right now. Maybe traders anticipate a turn because of that history, but we are better off awaiting the outcome of that anticipation instead of joining in with it. The fresh liquidity could be just what Pro Money needs to push prices further along if they aren't looking to book profits and turn. We don't know what's on Pro Money's mind until it reveals it, and it only does that in the 'here and now' - once again we are forced to concentrate on the current PA rather than 'back then'. And if that's where our focus should be, how much should we care about the past? posts.author: Vito
posts.text:
Well there are various methods to trade for example touch trades or unfolding PA trades.

In my experience supply and demand zones have higher probability to work out when entries are made in the direction of engulfing waves. When trades are taken against trend, S/D zones are less likely to work out or give just a minor pull back often causing losses. Now if price engulfs down and reaches demand zone which is inside higher time frame demand zone lets say looking at H4 and price enters demand zone of Weekly chart then it becomes a different story. For example on H4 it might appear that price is waving down and engulfing down, but looking at weekly it might actually just retrace to demand zone of waves up and engulfs up. Higher time frames are stronger than lower ones so always need to keep them in mind where price is.

The harder part is to enter a trade right, when waves are rising engulfing prior supply zones they rarely come/retrace back to new created demand zones and price runs away creating feelings of being right but not being in the market.

What I would suggest to try is to go over and study all the information posted here, apply it to charts and see how it works, go over some of major journals see how they have applied that same information to their trading. And then just trade, trade and trade. After gaining experience your method will start to develop.

I think that there is a bit of consufion about this term, because tipically people talk about Fakeout when price breaks a key level or a trendline and then come back inside the level, without specifying what happens next.

As you wrote in your example, the High circled in red is a FO, because price broke high but then engulfed previous low. The low marked in your draw to me is only an engulf at this time. Now, if the price engulfs the previous high, then I consider that low an other Fakeout, if the price bounce below the previous High and then engulfs south, I consider the new LowerHigh a FTR or a pullback.

Hey Joema,

Yeah I definitely have to be more cognizant of these FO levels because, as you stated, it is only logical that if a zone is SOOO obvious that everyone is looking to sell the pro money must look for more liquidity (buys) elsewhere in order to fill their massive sell orders. On a further note, I have been doing some thinking about catching 4HR reversals in general. I usually use the 15 min TF to look for the engulf when price is in a 4HR zone for my entry signal. This works fine when you are taking that trade in the direction of the 4HR trend, but I have noticed that I get burned a lot more when I use this TF ratio to catch a 4HR trend reversal. Since it takes A LOT of money to REVERSE a 4HR trend, using the 4HR zone/ 15 min engulf ratio might be a little too acute. noticed, for this trade in particular, that the 1HR TF for my engulf gave the correct signal for the change in sentiment.

The 15 min bearish engulf

The 1HR bearish engulf

Some say TFs don't manner, but I DO believe that there are golden ratios to look for when going down to smaller TFs to get an early entry. As I stand now, for trend CONTINUATION trades the ratios I use are Daily zone/ 1HR engulf, 4HR zone/ 15 min engulf, 1HR zone/ 5 min engulf, 15 min zone/ 1 min engulf. The ratios I have hypothesized so far for trend REVERSAL trades are 4HR zone/ 1HR engulf and with further testing I will figure out what I want to use for other aggregations.

But to

sum it up, it's all about getting enough of a jump on the entry without having to suffer through a bunch of false signals. There is definitely a 'sweet' spot for doing this.

Hi Andyfx,

I believe you have interpreted and drawn this correctly by showing price going to the bottom FTR (the other side of the PAZ).

Maybe it would be less confusing if IF said: "if price engulfs a FTR south, price has broken into a PAZ and wants the other side of the PAZ, which is the next FTR". In other words, "the last engulf north" is "the next FTR" as you have drawn and the other side of the PAZ.

Naturally, where you have shown the s/r flip line in blue, you would expect price to react as this is now fresh demand (ignored supply) - which I have marked in orange - before moving the other side of the PAZ as per the orange arrows.

posts.author: polymorph
posts.text:
Understanding the words of a new language is critical if you want to speak it, even more so if you want to be able to read it. I want to be able to "read the market" but I confess that I find the lingo confusing sometimes, especially when working through homework (which I will be posting to my own journal shortly.) In this post I'm going TRY to define some of the important words of the language of the market that are used at RTM. I tried to write this for someone with no market knowledge or experience in the hopes that I will learn by thinking through the concepts and taking little to nothing for granted.

Supply (S or SUP): sell orders that put pressure on price to fall. When Supply exceeds Demand, price falls. When Demand exceeds Supply, price rises.

Demand (D or DEM): buy orders that put pressure on price to rise. When Demand exceeds Supply, price rises. When Supply exceeds Demand, price falls.

Rally-Base-Drop (RBD): a 3-step process whereby: 1. demand exceeds supply and causes price to rise (Rally); 2. supply and demand find balance and price stabilizes (Base); 3. supply exceeds demand and causes price to fall (Drop). The return to the base is often tradable.

Drop-Base-Rally (DBR): a 3-step process whereby: 1. supply exceeds demand and causes price to fall (Drop); 2. supply and demand find balance and price stabilizes (Base); 3. demand exceeds supply and causes price to rise (Rally). The return to the base is often tradable.

Support-Resistance Flip (S/R Flip): a price point or zone that limits price's move downward, then breaks and later limits price's move upward.

Resistance-Support Flip (R/S Flip): a price point or zone that limits price's move upward, then breaks and later limits price's move downward.

Cap on Price (CAP): the base of a RBD or DBR. This is where price is limited from further upward movement in a rally or further downward movement in a drop. Source: Caps on Price article, If'd video on Caps, and even the article's name: "... RBD/DBR". Noticing the name alone was actually an aha moment for me last night.

Pole: the sharp rally or drop that precedes a Flag.

Flag: the base of a RBR or DBD. This is where price pauses to "catch its breath" before continuing on in the direction from which it came. Flags are also the "framework" for Flag Limits." Source: previous understand and the Flag Limit article and its name: "...DBD/RBR". This too was an aha moment for me last night.

Flag Limit (FL): the edges of a Flag. Price often rallies from the bottom Flag Limit and drops from the top Flag Limit before eventually breaking outside of the Flag altogether. The Flag Limit that was Engulfed before price left the Flag is often tradable when price returns.

Failure to Return (FTR): the same thing as a Flag Limit. Source: Ifmyante on FF speaking to Les_Paul - link: bit.ly/1pt3VRN I don't understand the "simple" part (yet), but since FTR's = FL's, should we drop using/trying to understand 1 of the 2? Or am I oversimplifying and misunderstanding If and there really is a difference between FL's and FTR's?

Engulf (ENG): two possible definitions: 1. the consumption of a Demand zone when price is coming from a Supply zone. The return to the Supply zone is sellable with the expectation that price will drop beyond the consumed zone that was Demand; 2. the consumption of a Supply zone when price is coming from a Demand zone. The return to the Demand zone is buyable with the expectation that price will rise beyond the consumed zone that was Supply. ** In either case, if there is no Engulf, then there is no Failure to Return. Source: Ifmayante on FF replying to Chica - link: bit.ly/1f9MJxg

Compression (CP): indecision in the market where price ranges between Supply and Demand. With most (if not all) orders removed from the range, price can easily move through it the next time it arrives at the Compression.

Price Action Zone (PAZ): the tradeable range between 2 Failure to Returns. Price moves between Failure to Returns until sufficient orders enter the market to Engulf a Failure to Return. At that point price moves between the Failure to Return that was just Engulfed and the next Failure to Return beyond it, which is another Price Action Zone.

Thanks in advance for your time and thoughts!

posts.text:
As I mentioned in my post of definitions, I find our lingo a bit confusing sometimes so I'm hoping you all can help out. Here are some examples: Chart 1 is an EA H4 with Caps marked in pink and Flags boxed with yellow (I stopped marking Flags part way through because I had enough to ask my questions.) I currently understand Caps to be RBDs and DBRs and Flags to occur in DBDs and RBRs. But it seems that the action that we can take when price returns to either is the exact same.

For instance chart 2 is a zoom in on the green box. Point A is a pause (aka: base) in a DBD. Immediately below it at point B there is a Cap that comes at the bottom of a pole (aka: a drop.) Price then returns to A and a trader could have sold it. The same thing happens between B and C – price poles down from B to C then back up to B where a trader could have sold it back down to and through C. The screenshot below from this post, shows stacked Supply Zones. How do you find them? The same way that you find all supply and demand zones. Higher highs or lower lows will tell you the zones. posts.author: bulbuli

Hi Gigiocean,

I have marked below an example of stacked supply zones. Here, by 'stacked zones' we mean that the Decision Points (Be it Supply or demand or FTRs) are arranged very closed to one another and so prices may ignore the intermediate levels to reach the next or outermost level (the highest supply zone here in example).

posts.author: Cleric
posts.text:
dcabfx wrote: You're absolutely right scoobydoo. FTR/Flags are significant when they break an area of importance and continue in the direction of the break after forming.

I second that. There are tons of zones, levels ENG, FO, FL, FTR etc on each chart on each timeframe Knowing them, spotting them, desribing them is easy for everyone. I think a child could do this after some training. But the thing which separates us from IF and other masters, is their abilities to spot those PAs which are important And only few of them are indeed important. You can spot important ones when you deconstruct master's trades posted here on RTM. But you still will be miles away from them. Because knowing what's important is not enough still.

And what's the most significant thing? It's knowing WHY are those pieces of PA important. Knowing WHAT price is going to do in case you are right, and what is it going to do in case you are wrong. What are you going to do in case you are right, and what are you going to do in case you are wrong is what makes great traders.

After i started asking myself those questions each and every time i see a chart posted, or i take a trade myself, i was amazed how price behaves itself just the way i was expecting. And even if it's a small, tiny reaction, which doesn't even hit a half of a target, i still am statisfied.

Because it's a step. Small one. But heading forward.

I think a lot of ppl here can relate to these words "WHY" is always first, because there is nothing random in this world. Everything happens for a reason.

posts.author: polymorph
posts.text:
Great words, Cleric! About 1.5 years ago I started to realize the difference between support/resistance trading and reading the market is found in the "why". "Why" isn't because there's a line I drew there or just because price bounced before - that doesn't take into account what is really going on, which is buying and selling and not just pretty shapes. Instead, "why" is because supply exceeded demand or demand exceeded supply, which leads to "who", as in whose supply and whose demand. Why did such and such happen? Because the IT's entered their orders and moved the price, and thankfully they tip their hands (FO, ENG, etc.) and often show what is next.

I'm still trying to grasp the simplicity that If talks about but I find things to be much clearer when I contemplate the "why". It sounds like you're in a similar spot. Thanks for your post!

posts.author: rcmacf
posts.text:
Yep, you've got just about every FTR in there. The term "FTR" can be applied to pretty much every swing high in a downtrend (for example). If you can find the key FTRs, those where price has broken something significant prior to forming the FTR, those are the places to look to take trades from the "tip" of the FTR.

I've chosen not to draw in every FTR on this chart, but only those where price has broken something significant (the black lines showing previous lows). At these line, price has the choice to go up, or keep dropping. This gives them their significance -they are previous decision points. In each case, price breaks them, and it's very last effort to go higher is the tip of the FTR. I just roughly marked these in yellow. Each of these area will have significant points of supply in them, and we look to trade down from these, based on price action in a lower time frame.

I like the 3rd one down, it has broken 2 significant levels (the second, more minor level, is not marked in. It's about 1.0932)

Well, and keep in mind I am still not a successful trader, I see it as the engulf in a signal that price will turn. In this USDCAD example, that entry I labeled #1 was the first time any supply had been engulfed on the way down after the 30M FL was engulfed. I see this happen a lot at market turns. I invite you to do the same. Pick a time frame and mark off the turns in the market (not spikes but turns). Often I see one of 3 things

a) something local engulfed, retracement to source and then price leaves never to come back b) something local engulfed, retracement plus fake out and the price leaves and comes back for a QM c) something local engulfed, retracement, plus fake out, price leaves, comes back, QM fails and a diamond happens

Whether it is a, b, or c depends on what is to the left usually. But I do see those scenarios happen all over the place.

Try watching M1 turns for example. At the top of a move, a marker/flag usually appears. When that is engulfed south, that is usually the reverse signal. Time to look for an SR flip, locked in demand or some other structure to reverse on.

An example from USDCAD today. Red lines are levels that get engulfed followed by returns to source. Again, this is just how I see it and I am still learning. I also wanted to add that this does not work everywhere on the chart. M1 levels get broken all the time. But an M1 level that forms in HTF supply, then gets engulfed south, well, that is something to pay attention to (in my opinion).

GJ.

Why is this though? If for example the market fakeouts out to the north (a bull trap), hits into a higher FTR and then drops again, why was it aiming for that FTR? posts.author: ZeeDeveel
posts.text:
I think I discovered my answer to the fakeout question. If we think about a supply zone above the market and price faking out a previous high into that supply zone, we're inclined to think about it in terms of the supply zone relative to the previous high. So we're thinking "Why is the fakeout going to this supply zone above the high?", but if you turn it around and think "Why is this high below this supply zone?" it makes more sense. If when the price was rising initially, before the first high was made, the ITs sell early, before their final destination then they create that high, below our supply (fakeout) zone. So when price fakesout, really it's not reaching some extra supply zone, it's reaching the intended supply zone, but they've structured it in such a way as to deceive traders. Traders think the high is the final destination of price, but price is set up for a final (fake) move up to the supply zone above the high, to be quickly crushed and turned around.

Paul Tudor Jones: "One thing I learned as a floor trader was that if, for example, the old high was at 56.80, there are probably going to be a lot of buy stops at 56.85. If the market is trading 70 aid, 75 offered, the whole trading ring has a vested interest in buying the market, touching off those stops, and liquidating into the stops—that is a very common ring practice. As an upstairs trader, I put that together with what Eli taught me. If I want to cover a position in that type of situation, I will liquidate half at 75, so that I won't have to worry about getting out of the entire position at the point where the stops are being hit. I will always liquidate half my position below new highs or lows and the remaining half beyond that point."

If there are unfilled orders left at the other end of the range (in this case at the top), price need not always go straight to the very MPL (at the bottom). It will very often print ever increasing swings within the larger range, picking up stops and causing confusion along the way.

IMHO, In general Price moves from FL to FL, But specifically, to the pip, price moves from DP to DP. If the DP resides in between the limits of the FL/FTR, even it reacts to that DP, we see it as reacting to the FL (because it is in between the limits of the FL/FTR(upper bound and the lower bound). Exactly.. To find the true FTR/FL, we need to go to the smallest possible TF. I did that too. But later I realized I was making things complicated myself. Lets assume, you found a FTR/FL in tick chart/1MIN (say you have historic tick data) in the past. You will have to find the FL/FTRs once price breaks the current FL/FTR. The ones you find next will also be in the 1 min/tick chart. Searching all those FLs/FTRs made me really tired. After all, we loose the HTF picture, if we are going to find the true FL/FTR in LTF.

For example, Lets say you have found a nice FL in LTF, and you now see it is engulfed(BTW I am still researching if the DP needs to be engulfed or just the FL). So we can assume that the price is going to turn. You have also found a nice FL in HTF. But it has not being engulfed yet. Would you still think that price is going to turn? IMO, I would take the HTF FL into consideration. BTW don't take what I say as it is. These things are what I have seen so far. I am just presenting my observations.

This classroom has become so quiet? So all of us are graduates now? Oh well, it has been quite a journey for me, reading post after post, seeing how people overcame their struggles, confusions, self-doubts, pain inflicted by Market. I honestly think that there are a few loose pieces that needs to be tighten up. Perhaps it's to do with my profession - I am not a perfectionist but I like to be exact and precise about definition. So let's sort out any confusion regarding FTR vs FL once for all, agree?

In case people still wonder what's FTR and what's FL. Let this diagram clear the confusion, and I am not inventing something new, I am just applying what I have learned from the articles in Marketpedia

FTR = Failure to Return. I would actually prefer a more precise technical term. Because Failure to Return can be applied on any Fresh SD zones, i.e. after a zone is created, price has not returned to test it, so arguably any Fresh level = Failure to Return.

The definition of FTR vs FL, according to the Marketpedia articles can be summarized in the following diagram:

So essentially, an FL is created AFTER breaking a key barrier, and FL is drawn from Point 1 to Point 2. Where FTR is the MPL of the FL on this SAME TIMEFRAME.

The next question I see many people have asked is, where do we look for trades? Is it at DP (decision to break), or at FL, or at FTR?

MasterTrader Harry, basically put this to rest. according to him, - If after the creation of FL, price comes back to test the FL within a short period of time, then the FL has a high chance of turning price around. - However, if price does not come back, instead it leaves the area and go on a significant consolidation period, by the time it comes to this area, the FL is no longer a reliable trade location.

So here is my takeaway from Harry's words: if price comes back after a long consolidation period away from the area, I would look at the FL as a FO level, and pay attention to the DP just beyond it as the area that has higher chance of turning price.

I have also seen the word DP (Decision Point) causing confusion, because based on normal English definition, a DP is just Decision Point, and open up any charts, every point on the chart is a decision, every second there are decision to buy and sell by market participants. But in the spirit of RTM, my understanding is that DP is the 'kink' or 'pause' BEFORE the break of a key barrier. Whereas FL is the 'kink' AFTER the break of a barrier.

So DP = Kink, FL = Kink, FTR = Kink but in a lower time scale than the parent FL.

So a 'kink' is one of the most important revelation for me! When I see kinks, I see $$$$, All Hail the KINK! So what is a kink? Perhaps this video can explain better than I do

I feel it's like this, although the term FTR isn't used anymore. - A Kink is a FTR. - A FL is a Kink and therefore a FTR. - A kink/FTR might be a FL, but only if the engulf making it a FTR, hits it's target.

To explain a little bit deeper: a FTR, failure to return, isn't a specific part of the kink or the FL, it's the whole of the kink or FL. Say price moves up, but goes down briefly. There's some sort of barrier and therefore price doesn't retrace any deeper, ergo, fails to return, and goes back up. This whole move is, or rather: was, called the FTR. It's simply not the time yet for price to be turned but these kinks do represent some barriers.

As Edge said, it is of critical essence to have a deep understanding of what the kink and/or FL does and why.

@Trab Trading: I think you are correct in saying that you can also enter a trade a bit deeper into the FL. Doing so, you'll minimise the E to SL part of your trade, making it a higher R trade. I think I'm safe in saying that your SL would stay put at the same place, but your entry point moves closer to it, minimising your risk and maximising your reward. A FL remains a FL and doesn't need any refining when talking about entering a trade. You either do that at the edge of the FL, which is the safest point in terms of probability that your order is getting filled, or at the MPL of it. No need to get more specific than that when explaining a trade, because those are the only two possible points of entry. Strictly speaking, you could enter anywhere of course but we're not being taught that, for good reason

The reason why it didn't get engraved in my mind, was because I thought the old articles that exist in Marketpedia still represents the core principles/concepts of RTM, and when I read discussions among members I wasn't sure if it's just a discussion/sharing of thought, or it's an approved concept by the RTM Masters.

I have taken new notes, and arrived at this new definition of FTR. So FTR is no longer the MPL of FL as presented in the article written by Les_Paul in Markepedia.

Now, FTR is drawn exactly the same way as FL, referring to the diagram below. Point 1 = Furthest Advance AFTER breaking the Key Barrier to the left Point 2 = Deepest Retreat AFTER breaking the Key Barrier to the left Point 3 = Price has to move beyond point 1 in order to have an FTR

The key difference between FTR and FL is: FL = FTR that has hit a TG!

Now, I hear you probably screaming in exhaustion now - why can't you guys just stop talking about FTR!!!?!!!

But there is a reason, because there is a 'gap' in the definition of FL. The rule says we cannot draw a FL until a target is reached (i.e. price reach an opposing FL). So if we cannot draw FL, that means we cannot trade FTB to a level that look like an FL?

So we have seen price reacting to FTR, we have also seen price reacting to DP (i.e. a pause/indecision before the break of a barrier). Now if we scrap the concept of FTR and DP all together, we need a FL concept, comprehensive enough to explain these phenomena we saw on the charts every day.

Therefore I urge you and IF to define the new language of RTM, let there be no confusion when we discuss about FL/DP/FTR in the future, if we have to scrap DP/FTR out of our day to day vocabulary, we need something new to replace them. At the moment, I am spending a lot of time trying to bridge this 'gap' in the my understanding of the FL concept, with little or no success. And I am sure I am not the only one.

Thanks AK

i'd like to give a bit of advice about how you can integrate PAZ concept in your trading:

Regarding the PAZ concept - it is a new dimension added to our analysis to make reading easier - and it was very usefull when you are drawing your trade "arena" using FL's - so basically a PAZ is limited by FL's of the same scale and the way you can trade them is when price doesn't reach it's target -> the other end of PAZ in the same scale. That's why you have to "trade only the edges" When price engulfs into a new PAZ (engulfs the FL that is it's border") and doesn't reach the end of it you can enter a trade on retrace and put your SL above the FL that originated the move (the Think Tank in your charts). A simpler representation of PAZ's you will find in the QM lite course when IF taught us about the space between FL....In the course aren't called PAZ's because it would be another term that would complicate our understanding but that's the concept: The space between FL's. This implies that we have a very good eye when drawing the PAZ's and their FL's (for example in your post your CP PAZ has actually a few important zones in it and it's not really a PAZ, because in a "perfect" CP PAZ price should visit each MPL on the way(pick up the clean orders on the way UP), leaving little or no clean orders behind so that price can travel FREE when it returns to the other end - that's why it's called a PAZ because if price engulfs into it- it travels all the way to the end of it, with or without the necessary retrace that would allow us to join the ride ).

The simplest way to start drawing your PAZ's is to find your CP on the chart and then follow the FL trail. Paz's don't align to the PIP because every time an old FL that was the PAZ border gets Engulfed and a new FL is created -this new FL is a bit higher or lower than the original FL it Engulfed.

In the recent years some of the IT's have changed a bit the way they mess up with the retailers to fill their position and achieve their plans: they use LS and their Kinks for their entries and for their targets and it's pretty hard to find space between FL's (PAZ) ( most of the engulfs reach their target in the same move leaving us with no PA confirmed opportunity to trade). In the Very low time frames there are still PA confirmed entries but they require a lot of patience and wisdom. BUT There are times when LS Kinks align with FL's and you can find clean orders inside them close to the MPL(that's your edge of the PAZ) (that's your sweet spot where you want to trade) That's why you'll see that RTM has shifted focus more material about BSZ and the Traps set by IT and LSK with clean orders inside it in the recent years as it's a more efficient way to extract "safer" pips As traders our main job is to go where the Opportunities will be...and to adapt our styles to our personality and to the market that we have inherited

Stay thirsty,

E.

posts.author: HCDE
posts.text:
I recently made a post saying that some part of the RTM material was confusing. The answer was, more or less: "I don't see any reason for confusion"... Your point is symptomatic of RTM's core problems: it's inefficent, both for those who learn or for those who try to teach. Is it efficient that every student make the fastidious work of compiling every piece of knowledge in the journals? Is it efficient to answer some important questions in everyone journals (pretty much lost in the deep one week later) while it could be done in a centralized place, or gathered once and for all in markepedia?

Then the next question is: how can it remain so inefficient since so many years? To my opinion: because there is no interest to make it efficient for a subscription fee under 600€ in average. I like a lot the RTM concepts IF came up with and i'm very grateful to him for sharing them with us in the first place. I was very happy about RTM re-opening in 2017, i thought it was full of promises and that it would help me succeed in my project of doing another job. But the conclusion of that isn't very fancy. I drained a part of my savings & spent a lot of time studying a lot of useless stuffs, wasting a lot of time like you did, jumping from one vision to another, never finding any consistency. For sure, i'm the first responsible for that. I could & should be more clever, more organized maybe, having a more scientific approach also.... But honestly RTM has a lot of questions to find an answers for. Most people only post their success on the forum, that's human nature, but as a result, IF & RTM team think everyone is fine. But let's be very objective about RTM's achivements: How many people took their shot at cracking it, and how many succeeded to LIVE & CONSISTENT trading? What's the ratio? How good is RTM at making you a real trader? Where are these people who succeeded at RTM (and i mean RTM, not RTMA or with any help from IF)? How many are they? I'm here since several years, i don't have more than 2-3 in mind. How many people have a worst life situation after RTM than before? Obviously, i have my opinion on these questions.

I sincerely hope some of the nice people on that forum will make it, but honestly, i think most of you, like me actually, are wasting their time. That's my humble (& unpleasant) opinion.

Anyway, in everything in life there is a lesson. And the lesson in my case is: When you invest into something, investing into something that has a real reason to make you succeed.

morning dt

..take your time, we are all busy, we reply when we can, no need to sorry.:)

about that trade..read this, is from ifmyante

So here's what we look for on the charts:

General: HTF. Know where price is coming from and going to, and the PA past and present in all the TFs, from the Monthly down.

Specific: At the zones you want to trade, look to

Past. study the zone in all TFs, down to M1 ask yourself Where were the decisions made? Clean S/D? Mark these lines. No clean S/D? -compressed zone Did price really shoot away form the zone, or did it cp away? Did the zone itself react at the right place? Look beyond the zone further into the past. See what it reacted to. Was there a better S/D nearby that price wants to visit? This explains many fakeouts.

Present. Approach. How is price returning to the zone? Where's the nearest flag in the TF you want to trade? This is your tg1 in this TF. Flags in the LTFs? What does PA tell you? Has price tested the last flag on approach? (good sign) Has price compressed into the zone in this TF or LTFs? (good sign) Is there big news on the way? Has there just been big news?

Reaction In LTF, does price react violently to the first decision point? Does it quickly engulf the nearest S/D? (good sign) Does price simply CP away? Maybe it wants to go to the next decision point If the first decision point breaks, watch the signs on approach to the next, and, of course, reaction.

Chew this over for now. Apply it to your chart history. Apply it to as many failed setups as successful ones. Millions of them if possible! Capture and file them all. This will help make it instinctive

so basically rbd and dbr are just one of the things the you have to watch, is like a puzzle, rbd/dbr is one piece, you need others to make the puzzle. That's why we do homeworks, to master all this things togheter and read the price. keep whit homework

posts.author: Doctor
posts.text:
gilben,

You have a good eye and good analysis. As I tell most people, the first part of analysis is being anal, and your attention to detail is good. I will add on a few observations for you.

Above your first compression zone where the C letter is located you have two areas in blue boxes for buying. Technically correct, but dont loose sight of the higher time frames and where the current time frame is, and in this instance the Euro is winding down and the two buying areas wont have the same effect, they will very get blown through. The major selling areas higher up the chart tell you the story.

Compare the other compression zones and the effect of buyers had on the price when it came back down to test them. Virtually all of them provide little impact.

There are times when price runs off quickly such as prior to your 2nd last compression zone, the 2nd compression zone slowly down price and also setup a move back up to collect more sellers where you see your 2 decision areas way over on the left. This also was a resistance area of significance. Those deep pull backs are probably among the most difficult part of trading, in that they throw you for a loop until you can see where the next most obvious resistance is for a continued down move.

Good work!

posts.author: Ifmyante
posts.text:
Every DBR and RBD has its own importance and value, and nearly every one can be traded. For each one that you find, zoom out to the HTFs, and see what historical significance the decision point has. Perhaps it's a failure to get back into an important PA Zone - these ones are special. Perhaps it's within an HTF compression zone to the left - ask yourself would you take this trade, or wait for the tip of the zone?

The bigger picture will always help you decide on the significance of a DBR/RBD

posts.author: Tyoon
posts.text:
justinforex wrote: Question - A Valid RBD

It does not have to break the previous H/L to become a valid base.

What defines a base it that price moves up or down, bases (consolidates, congests, clusters, ect) then moves again either up or down.

Here are the variations. The standard DBD and RBR then the RBR and DBD then RBD during downtrend and DBR during uptrend.

Hopefully this could give you a better understanding. However as you have alluded to, H/L or S/R levels are almost always an intrinsic part to the development of any base. If you can find the levels responsible for the bases it can give you a much holistic picture on the chart.

posts.author: Ifmyante
posts.text: The two charts on the right, in HTF, can often look just like the two charts on the left. It's worth looking into these on your charts, and finding out which tend to perform better on price return - drop/consolidation/drops or drop/RBD/Drops, and the same for rallies

outapips, I believe that when you analyse your charts you must not forget the context in which price finds itself, and by that I mean you must always consider the higher time frames. I can see that you analyse the different TFs of the Euro but I have the feeling you are not connecting the LTFs to the HTFs. Please let me know if I am mistaken.

I'll present to you the way I would do the analysis. It is probably not the only way and certainly not the only 'correct' way but it seems to have been working for me so far.

The first chart is the daily and you can see that price has gone into daily demand, so you are looking for buying opportunities. But beware, though, it is not a fresh demand zone.

In the 4H chart you can see a couple of D/S zones, so you might think: "hmmm, maybe price could move to the upside to at least retest those zones". However, as I said, daily demand is not fresh so price might need to go lower in order to move higher and take them out... PA will let us know.

As you can see on the 1H charts, price has reached a 1H demand level within daily demand. Now this 1H demand zone is fresh and it was reached after price generated a 1H supply zone just above the demand zone. Therefore, I am looking for buying opportunities into the next supply zone.

So we can conclude that price is in an important zone. That's where PA really matters. That's where you must pay attention to PA. If you check out the following link

www.acegazette.com/en/community/ace-foru....html?start=375#8342

posts.author: benhur
posts.text:
I like the idea of collecting probability statistics. I suppose it is good for providing some assurance while trading. I would suggest you to leave collecting numbers at the moment, and invest your efforts in defining good levels, when you'll be comfortable in collecting zones and levels, then your statistics may gain you the confidence for trading.

As for your DBR RBD. Please note that some zones you have marked are RBR/DBD. My idea of this assignment is to locate possible turning points, then see how it reacts when price test these levels.

Some levels that were "ignored" had prior signs. I would suggest you to look for DBR/RDB that are the strongest. you can define strong level by 2 criterias: 1. How strong was the away move >> then >> its a strong level why:: We assume that at the decision point of breaking the balance (among sellers and buyers) are left with stacks of un-filled orders. 2. How Long was the Price at the defined level before it unbalanced > The least is better. why:: As more time given for buyers and seller to negotiate, the more deals the close. The least time they have to negotiate, we assume for having more un-filled orders left at the zone.

There are more ways to define the quality of a level, you will get to learn these with the other HW assignments.

One more thing, if you want to use the conventional terms of SD:

U = untested on this screen >> FRESH R = reaction (normally first) >> TOUCHED B/E = breakeven, i.e. price reacts, but then goes through the level (decision point) often time you may be able to move your theoritical stop loss to breakeven >> SWAP >> although I like the idea of this one... Ig = ignored (at first) >> SWAP

Your observation is correct. When price forms a cluster above demand it is indication that the level will be breached. When price forms a cluster below supply it is indication that the level will be breached. When this happens it is usually the base in a rally-base-rally or drop-base-drop that breaches the level.

If supply is breached and you get a base directly above the supply, then the breach of the supply may be a false break and price may reverse and run back down trapping the buyers. Hi madwt,

This is my take on how new demand/supply levels are created.

Fresh zone are created from an old zone of the opposing type. By that I mean, what was old demand can become fresh supply when price creates a flip zone.

On the chart posted lets assume for the purpose of this example that the left hand side of the chart is a price flip zone which means it was previous supply.

When price broke thru at (1) it cleared out all the supply so only demand was left at that level. We don't know how strong this is (although how price went thru the level and how far it travelled gives us a clue). There was an initial retest of this level a few bars later which showed there was still plenty of demand.

Price came back again at (2) and this is now considered old demand but it was still good enough to hold price again.

At point (3) there was a little reaction up consuming the remaining buy orders and so demand was all used up and price fell thru creating a new supply zone at that level. Price moved well below the level quite strongly so we can determine this is a good level to short next time back.

Point (4) is the first time back to the new supply level so a good place to short. That level is now considered to be old supply.

We don't know if a level will hold or how many times a level will hold so we look to the chart for clues.

Hope this explanation is clear enough to follow.

Outapips This is what I wanted you to see!

Madwt, I saw that you marked s/d on what actually was a retest of the initial s/d zone. You marked highs or lows. Keep in mind that we want to see a base and then a break of the base, take the RBR, DBD as examples.

I remember the time when I first learned about supply and demand... Everyone was talking about fresh zones, so I went to the charts in order to find some zones and everytime I found what I thaught was fresh supply or demand, I saw that it was only a retest of a previous zone... Got lots of headaches from it lol But then I found "broken and engulfed supply and demand, what is also called a swap. This is when I realized that fresh supply can only exists if the demand was cleared and vice versa for demand. Look at it this way... There is a supply zone and then there is a decision to break the supply, so supply is gone and there is only demand left, so now we have fresh demand as long as it doesen't get tested...

I hope that this makes sence.. Mel

posts.text:
Take aways from looking at the DBR and RBD's:

1. When price moves away from a level, it doesnt matter how soon a re-test back into that comes, thats the highest probability trade because of the probability of unfilled orders resting there.

2. When price rallies back into a previous RBD, the supply that came from the D of that previous RBD was cause of a new area of supply to form that is slightly lower than the previous (often). This causes the lower market structure highs to form, because new levels of supply just below the previous market structure highs has formed, capping price from reaching higher levels. This works both ways, and is what seems to happen many times, not always.

3. Price seems clearer to me that it is always moving around to find piles of orders, and depending on the strength of moves away from those piles, we can reason better about what the probabilities are when price revisits and retests.

4. Wicks or tails mean at the point price reached that extent, there were S/D pushing price faster than the opposing direction, but then that move is overwhelmed by the orders that get touched and filled.

5. When resting orders sit at these levels, they only execute when market orders take them out, or other execution mechanics force those orders to move to market orders. It is still liquidity takers that must drive price through these levels.

6. When price breaks out of a recent high or base, it often returns on the other side and re-tests. Re-testing suggests a conscious act for price to go test a previous level. To me it seems like it is more a result of price bouncing away from supply and working its way back to value, but as it hits the demand that was strong enough to break those highs, thats were orders exist to give this level support. This is S/R in action.

I am sure theres much much more I have missed. But here is my next analysis.

Hello tradingjedi,

As well as identifying the RBDs and DBRs, you need to mark out at what level reactions occurred (if any), consider those that failed and what happened at the level afterwards. Maybe not to the same degree that mettafort and I have just done

- we had a

common interest but different perspectives to explore, hopefully to the benefit of everyone.

A long while back I was in a webinar and the speaker made an almost throw-away statement - which I'm sure sailed straight through most people, but which piqued my interest. It was in response to a question I don't recall, but the reply was, "Although we look at the same charts, we see different things". There was more to it than that, but pondering that statement allowed me to form many questions I didn't even know I needed to ask, then answer them to find more questions. It started me on a path of discoveries - still ongoing - that I doubt I would've walked otherwise. I won't expand beyond that, but what is interesting is that three people looked at roughly the same GBPUSD information and applied their logic to it: two of those people had entirely different opinions of the same RBD and one person ignored it altogether on their chart!

So, the benefit comes from the qualitative exercise:

1. What attracted you to this particular RBD or DBR?, what didn't you like? Was your opinion that it would work or not? (Your opinion, mind, not the benefit of 20:20 hindsight 2. What happened when price did return to the Base in each case? If it reacted, where (zoom in to the Base and root around)? If it didn't, is there anything that you can learn about it so you can spot a bad-un in the future (that's why we need to find good and bad examples)?

3. What happened later when price returned to the Base from the other side? Did it react or ignore it again? 4. Zoom out and look back in time, does that change your perception of your chosen examples or help understand why some worked or failed?

By going through this process on your charts you will better train your brain to spot and sort these patterns out, and assess the likely turning point within them so you can successfully reduce your exposure in the market (by this I'm sort of referring to R:R, but I'm also taking time into account). And if you keep hitting a wall in your understanding it will better help everyone else to offer suggestions or guidance.

You don't need to slap everything on the chart, just your main line of reasoning and points of interest, maybe a little bit of filler in the post, but in doing so you will accelerate your understanding.

BTW, why didn't you mark up that RBD?:)

Regards.

Spongy.

Hello mettafort,

Had a few busy days, not least of all because of the fun I had producing the deep dive I put in the classroom.

It is a bit of a nuisance that the upload limit is where it is (I think about 130-150KB) as it means that 1920*1080 sized charts are borderline, depending on how much text you add. I don't know if you had a chance to see those USDCHF H1 charts size-by-side on a PC, I'll put explanatory words here just in case you didn't....

I make reference to concerns about the observations in items A2, A4 and A5. They occur on different time-frames:

1. A2 is on the H4 (first image, lower chart). I draw a tail on the side nearest price so I can check the Price Action history at this level on longer time-frames. The obvious thought is that the more time price spends away from a level, and the greater distance it travels, the more out of balance it is and the more likely that price will react on its return (effectively mean-reversion). I also check reactions to the level, particularly which side price was on just before the zone I'm investigating - I much prefer it to be on the opposite side, indicating that I am looking at a fresh zone (a flip). As I mentioned before I don't like obvious lines of S or R or trend, they are the chart equivalent of the luminescent beacon hanging in front of the Anglerfish's mouth. Here, the last reaction was on the same side, not so attractive 2. A4 is on the H1 chart (second image, upper chart). I check to see how convincingly price moves away from the zone I'm interested in. I like to see long and strong candles with little overlap, and I like to see local opposition levels being taken out easily, preferably to a higher low or a lower high - it shows intent. Here price moves away strongly enough, breaks a small Demand level but turns back at an area that I would consider weak. Again, not so attractive 3. A5 is on the M5 chart (second image, lower chart). As price is leaving the zone for the first time, it spikes it deeply before carrying on. On the retrace, price has to penetrate deeper to find fresh Demand - it does, but that spike was a definite downer

So, in weighing up the pros and cons of my observations, this combination was enough to tip the balance against the zone for me.

Regards.

Spongy.

17) Supply here wasn't as structured as most of the other examples but worked out fine. I notice a demand zone to the right of this area that was embedded in the PA didn't work out so well though being wiped out by the big moves later.

18 ) This demand level I found did some interesting things. First, it bounced as expected. When it broke, it acted as supply as well as resistance trapping PA underneath, in the process forming a broader area of demand itself. Price then broke up through the level again and then danced along the top of the boundary as support before dropping through again, reacting off of the demand just created, and rallying off. posts.author: Spongiform
posts.text:
Hiya Bravo,

The exercise is to identify working and failing RBDs and DBRs, to analyse them on different time-frames, then to watch what happens at those levels in the future, even after they fail. The idea is - by repetition - to get your brain to recognise attributes of each so you can hone your skills to spot their viability in real time, and choose prospective turning points within.

I do this by asking a series of questions to get me to really look at them, and I refine my questions and observations with each pass. I'm not saying my way is the right way or that I even ask the right questions, just that they cause me to take a good look, and think. Hopefully a pattern database is being built somewhere in the dark recesses of my mind as a result.

I wouldn't go so far as to say every peak or trough is RBD or DBR (that's my point of view and I might be entirely wrong, but a spike doesn't necessarily have a base on a shorter time-frame): they can certainly be caps on price, analysis would determine whether they are Supply, Demand or reaction.

Hope this helps.

Spongy.

nichess

Nothing promises that zone will hold price, even at first visit. The zones we mark on the charts are mainly a mapping of decisions in the market. Decision can take price either way. Zones are meant to be broken, and this market decision has its own significance too.

As further you go with your reading skills, you will be able read the hints and clues for zones to hold or to break. Your task at this time, is to train your eyes defining the zones.

Your next step, is to investigate how price is behaving around these zones. there are few things you should bare in mind while you do this work: 1. Be aware of how price had printed the zone you marked, what it was reacting to, and how the decision of price to move further look like. 2. Be aware of how price is approaching the Zones, what is the dynamic. 3. Is price come from a valid opposite zone? Remember that price goes from Demand to Supply and vice versa. 4. Be aware of the reaction of the first touch, how deep it went inside, what had stopped it if any? 5. what are higher or lower TF tell you. SD discipline is a Multi time frame concept. We trade price levels, not candles, so Story may vary on different TF 6. (more Advanced) Look for correlations with Index and other pairs.

it might look intimidating, but actually it's should be very simple. Zones are always a reaction of past Price Action (aka: always look left). As much as you can go back in history, the better your understand be of how price move. there is no randomness for this market, all can be explained with PA reaction, result, decision. just look for reasoning for levels and zones creation.

Best,

posts.text:
OK, so I'm labelling the RBD/DBR/RBR/DBD as Xa, and the reactions as Xb, c, d, etc.

Looking at the M5 (I don't have M1 data back here) we can see that 1a, 2a and 3a are all retests of DPs to go lower (1a DP is from the H1) and are thus FTRs in their own right. 2a, however does not have the significance of the other two, as it is a retest of a minor level.

1a. The internal structure is a bit messy, but as the move away is definite and prolonged, it maintains its significance. The fact it's a good FTR and a break of a flag says to pay attention on the First Time Back. In fact, the more I think about this one, the more it seems that it works because it's an FTR after breaking the three cirlces areas to the left. The lower is a nice flag limit. There is strong move away from level 1a in the end, though.

I can get tied up in knots with this, though, as every candle is an FTR to something!!

2a. This one is a bit choppy, and not such a definite move away. It is more of a reaction to what's going on in 1a than a fresh zone itself, and this is reflected in the weaker reaction at 2b.

3a. This is a nice, clean bit of PA. A strong move down which engulfs the low to the left, retests this break, and a second strong move down.

1b. The reaction is a nice rejection on the H1, but down on the M5 you can see what is likely an M1 QM. Even on the M5 there is a nice bear engulf, followed by a retest.

2b. The reaction is something I have seen a lot - first price bounces off the decision point to go lower, back at 2a, then moves up into the zone itself. It may be worth have one position at the DP, and a second if it returns into the zone. Needs investigating. Probably simpler just to have one at the low of the zone (that DP) unless the zone is a particularly wide one.

3b. The reaction has a couple of good, strong bear engulfs, and a nice rejection after these.

A stop above the zone would have worked in each case.

I would like to have these comments on charts, but MT4 is horrid, and takes ages, and everything else is clunky, too. Would anyone mind me doing this via video posts? It takes me 20 x as long to mark these up and write this, as it does to find the zones and reactions. These 3 have taken me several hours to write up.

Ok, so 4a is actually the reaction to 3a, so is not to be trusted, as it is not a fresh level, and it does fail over to the right. However, the first reaction isn't into the meat of the zone, it's at the DP to go lower, at 4a. This is shown by the red line. The ultimate high at 4b is into a discrete but strong move down that I wouldn't have spotted, but is a flip level, when looking left.

Similar to 1a from the previous post, there is a break of a flag creating the FTR shown which then has a decent reaction, shown in the insert. So this zone did work prior to the fail, but the best (easiest) opportunity for gain would be an entry at the bottom of the H1 zone, with a stop above. That's a big, fat zone, though, and the M5 allows it to be broken into distinct entry levels.

My logic from 1a does not work on the FTR in 4a, however, but 4a is operating over a smaller scale, and is not from such an extreme in price.

6a: DBR

So, we mark in the DBR at 6a, and wait to see what happens. As noted for 5, there is compression down into x (which is a DBR itself) and price has compressed away from x, making some stacked demand, so we shouldn't be surprised to see price move lower and reverse at 6b.

The engulf of 5a tells us that the path to go up is cleared, as 5a is a broken flag limit (I noted the pole earlier). So much easier in hindsight, though.

Now, once again, x is the FTR to 6a.

It's easy to see a pattern emerging, and I'm only at number 6!!!

It's maybe dangerous to go looking for PA in such a tight area, but the M5 shown that price CP'd away from 6a, and the only fresh demand was right at the extreme, which has the looks of a QM about it, too.

posts.text:
7a: RBD

This is interesting, as it shows why moving your stop to BE is a bad idea, and can take you out of a winning trade, especially if you go short at 7b, the retest of the DP to break the highs of the RBD (this will be a flag on a LTF). The drop from the high of 7a made a decent engulf, so a target at least back down to that engulf, around 'x' would be reasonable. That's only about a 1:1 RRR, though.

What I'm learning is that now the DP has been tested, we should watch for shorting opportunities higher into the zone. This setup is also suggesting to me that the retest of the DP (which is 7b) is only likely to be a decent FTR if price has dropped through some strong levels before it returns up to the FTR (I know this is a central teaching of RTM, but this is me now seeing why for myself). If it does not do this, and makes a move back up towards the FTR/meat of the zone, then we should expect price to engulf the FTR upwards, and then turn deeper into the zone. This is another reason the stop should remain above the xone and not be moved to BE until something major is engulfed to the downside.

Also, to the left I have marked some 'kind of' compression. There is some fresh demand in there which 7a and 7b have to fight through, but once price moves up to 7c, it's a clearer path down.

Note the compression leading up to 7b and the LQ/FO sucking in the breakout traders to go long. A consolidation below a level suggests that the level will be broken, so it's important to be able to differentiate CP from simple flat price oscillation (that's what a base is, I guess) and a sinking bull flag or you may be going short at a developing RBR, not an imminent drop. So, we want to see HHs and HLs as we approach a supply zone, if price looks like it's ranging below the zone.

The Blue line at 7a shows the extreme high of the reaction at 7c. When price gets up to 7c, it has already tested the H1 DP to move down at 7a, so we should "expect" it to now move deeper into the zone, and as it has made some nice engulfs downwards, and been away for some time, we can "expect" to now have a more substantial reaction. But where? Well, the extreme high seems to go to the edge of a CP PAZ at 7a (but I haven't focussed on those, yet) but easier to spot is the QM it has made at 7c. The red circle shows why you don't trail your stop near BE, and in fact, you may want to place a short right there.

8a: DBR

This one is messy, but that's no excuse to skip over it. If it's messy, we need to drop down a time frame or two, and now we can see that price has hung around in there for some time, and not made a truly convincing exit from the zone.

There's a lot going on in there, which is maybe a reason in itself to leave this zone alone.

The reaction at 8b comes at the DP/flip to the left, marked with the red line, and so looks like a fakeout of zone x, so I guess it pays to be aware of potential flips for stop placement.

Depending on trade management, you may have got away with this, but is it worth the effort when you can find some cleaner RBD/DBRs all over the place?

8c reacts to something I can't see with my data, but is one of the obvious areas of stronger demand. If you didn't TT this, you would have lost on this one. You would have been taking a TT at a level of stacked demand, which is balsy.

One final point, and another "driving the point home" lesson for me, is that the low marked "Tested, so expect deeper into zone" is the FTR for this H1 zone, despite how tiny it is. It does have a tiny reaction at 'z', but does not give the big move up one would like. Notice that price CP'd away from this FTR, it did not LQ away, so we should not take the First Time Back.

posts.author: rcmacf
posts.text:
9a: RBD

I'm getting more info onto the H1 chart, now that I'm getting things a bit straighter in my head, and can be more concise. That's got to be a good thing.

In this case, the FTR created by the RBD that is 9a has a very strong move away, making it a good candidate for a FTB short, but where should we expect the short to happen? We need to look at the LTF to have an idea, but we can see on the H1 that the DP to go lower has already been tested, this is clearer on the M5, though.

Once more, the the test of the DP to go lower is an FTR in its own right, but right now, I'm picking my FTRs from the H1, and using the M5 for entries. If I pick FTRs off the M5, they are likely to be killed by the H1 action (or at least, it seems that way).

So, looking at 9a on the M5 I can see that the top is stacked supply, which is bad news. However, this looks like a good FTR/RBD on the H1, so it's a-ok to short it, as that must be considered the leading TF. But, as with DBR 8a from my previous example, the CP suggests to expect a reversal at the extreme of the zone. As I go through this homework, the validity of this logic shall prove true, or fail.

In the case of 9b we get the fantastic combo of some CP into the zone and a LQ spike right to the top edge of the zone, which forms a near perfect pin bar. Ooh, that's sexy.

Last thing. On the H1, looking at the big bull candle to the right of 9b, one might expect to see a reaction when price returns to the 9b level, as it looks like ignored supply, that shall become demand, yet that doesn't happen. My first thought was "Well, that would have been a failed trade". No, though, it's not ignored supply, as the supply has been removed by the 3 visits to the supply level, before dropping to the "obvious target" for 9b, so we should not expect price to "see" that level as it passes.

13: RBD

On the hourly there are two obvious rejections, so I'd like to take a look at the inside.

On the M5 we can see a pole up to the first high, which has a pause on the way up - a flag (a RBR on a smaller TF, most likely). Price then moves up to form the first high we see on the H1. On the way dow from this high price compresses a bit, before dropping to break the FL, so we should look for an oportunity to short down to the base of the pole. That opportunity first comes at x, but as we have had the compression at 13a (stacked supply) we should be wary of a move to the edge of the zone - and this happens at y. We than have the move down to the pole base/decision to create the pole, at z.

21: DBD

Now things get interesting, as we see a failure of a zone. On the H1 we can see that price wasn't a strong drop into 21a, but the strong drop away makes it interesting, based on what I have seen in the previous examples.

On the m5, 21a looks like a good move down, with a definite decision point. However, when price returns it cuts right through the zone with no downward engulfs at all. It is interesting to note that it then tests back down into the zone at 21b, but does not break out of the bottom of the zone. When a zone is completely ignored, we know that it is likely to be respected at some point. This can be seen on the M30 chart, where the hourly decision at 21a for price to drop as it was too expensive is ignored upwards, then downwards, then hit to the pip much later.
