posts.text:
There can be a LOT of material to wade through in public forums. I have read through this thread, and although there are lots of good posts, some of them caught my eye more than others. What follows is just a little summary of posts/info/charts I liked while flicking through and for those that may not have the time to read this forum end to end, could serve as a useful summary.

Whiteout: Every RBD/DBR or RBR/DBD is a decision point.

Whiteout: Decision points are a change in value. The bigger the change, the bigger the value.

Benhur: Nice chart showing how to correctly draw a base.

IF: Every DBR and RBD has its own importance and value, and nearly every one can be traded. For each one that you find, zoom out to the HTFs and see what historical significance the decision point has.

> Perhaps it's a failure to get back into an important PA Zone - these ones are special.

> Perhaps it's within an HTF compression zone to the left - ask yourself would you take this trade, or wait for the tip of the zone?

> The bigger picture will always help you decide on the significance of a DBR/RBD.

Tyoon: What defines a base is that price moves up or down, bases (consolidates, congests, clusters, etc.) then moves again either up or down. Here are the variations.

The standard DBD and RBR then the RBR and DBD then RBD during downtrend and DBR during uptrend.

Hopefully this could give you a better understanding. However as you have alluded to, H/L or S/R levels are almost always an intrinsic part to the development of any base. If you can find the levels responsible for the bases it can give you a much holistic picture on the chart.

IF: The two charts on the right, in HTF, can often look just like the two charts on the left. It's worth looking into these on your charts, and finding out which tend to perform better on price return - drop/consolidation/drops or drop/RBD/Drops, and the same for rallies.

Mel: I like Mel’s charts and explanations. I had to add at least one.

IF: IF asks this… but I am not sure what IF is pointing out? If someone knows, please post your thoughts...

IF: Pointing out the significance of the engulf.

Benhur: I thought this was an interesting comment about the lack on convincing buying/demand.

Rufus: To me how price leaves a zone is the way I judge it the most. Another is when the zone was formed and when price returns.

Benhur: Look for DBR/RDB that are the strongest. You can define strong level by 2 criteria:

1. How strong was the away move >> then >> it’s a strong level.

Why: We assume that at the decision point of breaking the balance (among sellers and buyers) are left with stacks of un-filled orders.

2. How Long was the Price at the defined level before it unbalanced > the least is better.

Why: As more time given for buyers and seller to negotiate, the more deals the close. The least amount of time they have to negotiate, we assume the more un-filled orders left at the zone.

IF: One thing which I have mentioned many times before, but not yet in Markepedia (soon to be remedied), is that in a bigger picture range, Supply and Demand zones near the edges may not hold as well as others. Fakeout often occur, because price is attracted to the limits of the range.

Benhur: Nothing promises that zone will hold price, even at first visit. The zones we mark on the charts are mainly a mapping of decisions in the market. Decision can take price either way. Zones are meant to be broken, and this market decision has its own significance too. As further you go with your reading skills, you will be able read the hints and clues for zones to hold or to break. Your task at this time, is to train your eyes defining the zones.Your next step, is to investigate how price is behaving around these zones. There are few things you should bare in mind while you do this work:

1. Be aware of how price had printed the zone you marked, what it was reacting to, and how the decision of price to move further look like.

2. Be aware of how price is approaching the Zones, what is the dynamic.

3. Is price come from a valid opposite zone? Remember that price goes from Demand to Supply and vice versa.

4. Be aware of the reaction of the first touch, how deep it went inside, what had stopped it if any?

5. What are higher or lower TF tell you. SD discipline is a Multi time frame concept. We trade price levels, not candles, so Story may vary on different TF.

6. (More Advanced) Look for correlations with Index and other pairs.

It might look intimidating, but actually it's should be very simple. Zones are always a reaction of past Price Action (aka: always look left). As much as you can go back in history, the better you understand be of how price move. There is no randomness for this market, all can be explained with PA reaction, result, decision. Just look for reasoning for levels and zones creation.

Les_Paul: Interesting post (have not copied content to here).

Rcmacf: My "wow" moment for today is the realisation (whilst very slowly getting through this homework) that every RBR and DBD are, on a LTF, a DBR and a RBD, and are thus valid places to take a trade or set a target. I don't see evidence (so far) that one is any weaker than the other. That may change after going through 200 of the buggers, though.

What I can see, though, is that there is a bigger reaction to the right when the DBD/RBD engulfs something of more significance to the left. The real biggie here is 1a, which as well as being a retest of the decision point to break the flag at the extreme left of this chart, is also an FTR (as are 1a, 2a and 3a) and the source of the entire move lower.

To be more precise, it's when the DBD/RBD is a decision point for that engulf to happen. I guess that's the same thing as the "source" of the engulf?

From here....

There are great posts/charts/observations by rcmacf starting at post 628. A nice reply to the homework by harry in post 636. In fact from there forward to here, there are lots of interesting posts (over the last few pages) which are worth reading, so I will not add them to this summary, though worth a read.

I hope someone finds this summary useful.

Hi CAT,

This is a great question.

I agree this is a valid RBR and on the Daily time frame, you have marked the zone correctly. As to whether the demand will provide a strong buy area when price returns is the million dollar question. The first thing to look at is the higher time frames (Weekly and Monthly).

However, it's still hard to "know". What I find better is to ask the following question... Where can I take a well risk defined trade?" By that I mean a place on the chart where I have a good chance of a bounce for a small risk. This place is a "decision point". In other words, a place where it is decided that price is either too cheap (demand zone) or too expensive (supply zone). When price comes back, it should (but nothing is guaranteed) respect that prior decision.

In essence, this is what RBR, RBD, DBD and DBR are showing. Decisions on price in the market. That is what the first post in this thread is saying.

This is what happened when price returned.

Let's look on the lower time frames to try and understand where the decisions were made. The advantage with this is that is allows for much better risk definition (small stop loss) and better risk-to-reward ratio.

Let's look at the decision for price to break out of the flag (base) on a 1 minute chart.

This time, I have drawn the flag more precisely.

I hope that makes sense.

posts.text:
faridisham wrote: Forgive me this is not a DBR nor RBD setup. I want to ask if this RBR setup is a strong one or will it be ignored on the way down?

If this is a strong buy area, which TF do u suggest i look for PA to buy? H1/M15?

Thanks

CAT

Hi CAT,

Looking back at my reply to your post, I realise that I did not answer the second part of your question, which was...

If this is a strong buy area, which TF do u suggest i look for PA to buy? H1/M15?

Unfortunately, there is no black & white (right or wrong) answer to this question. It depends on your trading experience, your trading time frames and personal style.

I would answer it by suggesting this...

Your should go down time frames until you can clearly identify the decision point that you are expecting to trade a reaction from. If you can see this on a 1 hr chart, than that is suitable. If you can see this on a 15 min chart, than that is suitable. However, the lower the time frame you can pinpoint a decision on, the lower your risk level. In saying that though, lower time frames generally require more time and higher skills.

There are many great RTM traders that trade from 4 hr and 1 hr candles, for example. But, you also have traders like IF that can identify decision points and hence entries on the 1 min chart. I recall a post where a RTM Master was saying that if they cannot identify a clear decision point on the 1 min chart, they will not enter.

Just go down to the time frame that allows you to clearly define your entry and risk. If you zoom down and cannot find this, consider skipping the trade. Instead, see where it reacted and then go down to the lower time frames and try to understand why price reacted where it did. It's better than taking a trade your are not 100% sure about, and you will speed up your learning doing this.

That's about the best answer I can give.

As far was what PA to look for, you can try and use Candle PAbut to be honest, reading Candle PA can be quite difficult to interpret correctly. IFgoes as far to say that he does not care about candles and gives time no importance at all. Rather, IF looks for decisions on price. IFalso says that the best advice he can give you is not to read anything into candles themselves.

The two important things to look at for clues as to what price wants to do is Compression and an Engulf. Of the two, the Engulf is the easiest to see and allows the safest trades. Your chart shows a good example on your supply level. Let's take a look.

Below is your chart of Gold. To understand why I drew a different supply zone, please see this post by benhur. (Note that 'cable' should say 'candle').

Notice that the supply levels lead to two engulfs and two lower highs. In other words, there was a strong move away from that level.

I have marked the zone using a 4 hr chart. Notice the Engulf.

And finally....

Pediniprovides an excellent example in his journal.

Cheers,

Hi guys!

This is my first post here, and immediately with some homework. I will introduce myself in the appropriate topic after.

The last few days I've been reading a lot of the articles in the markepedia, and started with my homework on DBR/RBD as suggested in the welcome mail. I've decided to post 1 DBR/RBD at a time, so that I can really look into them and explain what I see on the charts.

So here it goes:

#1: RBD

Although a bit unclear on the H1 time frame, this is a RBD to me (according to my current knowledge anyway). I've zoomed in using the M5 TF and on the M5 it's a RBD to me.

Thing I've noticed:

- Strong drop, which indicates a big imbalance between buyers and sellers. (Sellers are outnumbering the buyers.) - Price moved away in a strong fashion (momentum), and travelled quite far from the zone. (Zone is approx. 20 pips wide, and moved away for approx. 70 pips)

I would expect a strong reaction when price comes back to the level. When price actually arrives at the level, you can see that price is able to penetrate the zone quite deeply, Which indicates that the level isn't as strong as I thought it would be. We do get an rejection though (long upper wick on the rejection candle) What I've read about stacked orders/zones is that in a supply zone, the higher in the zone the more orders there are. Which would be explainable by looking at this example. Price was able to penetrate the zone, but got rejected in the top of the zone, so there were a lot of sell orders stacked there) Price then spends some time trading somewhat sideways, and then enters the zone again, followed by a big drop, to the demand zone (that I didn't mark) and from there visits the zone for a third and even fourth time, The forth time it penetrated the zone deeply again consuming all the orders that were left and broke the zone.

gxp1 wrote: hi, In presenting the work on RBD &RBD, i have cheated by using zigzag by first scrolling down the chart.The only reason being that its easy to see major turns......

Hi gxp1,

Your homework looks good though I would encourage you not to use the zigzag indicator for the following reasons.

1. It will train your eyes faster and better not using the indicator. Instead, focus on the raw price. It may initially be a little more challenging but you will gain much more from your homework exercises.

2. You will miss the more important and subtle RBDs and DBRs on your chart as the indicator will go straight past them. Some of the more important RBDs and DBRs are small subtle ones as opposed to the obvious ones that catches everyone’s eye.

This post by IF is in this thread is a gem! (I have placed IF's image below.)

The small DBR IF points out towards the bottom of the chart (blue box – the ‘giant omission’) would not be picked up via the indicator and is an important DBR. It’s also an example of how price reading requires us to piece all the individual parts of price action together.

Why is that small DBR important?

The DBR shows where true demand is within the FTR which forms after an engulf of an important barrier. In case it’s not obvious, The following diagram explains the idea.

posts.author: Harry

dcabfx wrote:... I don't see that on my H4. Nothing to worry about though. We work with what we got....

this is a problem when you quickly scan the charts in a HTF. ideally when you identify something important breaking (your SR as i call it in FLs) you have to dig into the LTFs to find its exact limits. you will be amazed how many times you will mark something say in H1, price will come to it and think it engulfed it but then you go and find the exact limits of that FL in the LTF and you see it didnt and your small almost invisible FL worked perfectly well.

it doesnt mean that because something doesnt show up in HTFs it is not significant

This is something I have been meaning to post for a while.... and it seems now is a good time.

Harry makes a great point here and it's very important to grasp.

I have seen many charts marked on the HTF with a FL and then the engulf is shown. Sometimes it looks like the engulf does not work as price continues to charge on. Its worth your time looking at every FL on the LTF and asking yourself where the true limit of the FL is and hence what price level needs to be breached to constitute an engulf. As we are basing our understanding of what price is doing on the engulf of a price level, this is something worth pondering.

Here is an example. It is not a great example as it's the first one I looked, but it's sufficient to illustrate the point, and the question to ask yourself while conducting your homework.

Hi Gian

To understand how to define a SD zone, we must understand what is behind the zone in terms of Order Flow. We expect that the inner boundary of the zone to be the price where remaining stacks of orders are waiting for execution. Since all we have is the chart, we can spot it by a closer look at the candles. There we look where was the last trade before one side overcome the other. Thinking in Order flow terminology, we may suspect that if one side overcome the other, there might be more orders of the winner side which couldent be filled due to less orders of the loosing side.

Understanding this, we can look for this scenario in the chart:

posts.author: PASniper
posts.text:
For all the new ones (like me

), madwt made a recopilation of some important posts:

madwt wrote: There can be a LOT of material to wade through in public forums. I have read through this thread, and although there are lots of good posts, some of them caught my eye more than others. What follows is just a little summary of posts/info/charts I liked while flicking through and for those that may not have the time to read this forum end to end, could serve as a useful summary.

Whiteout: Every RBD/DBR or RBR/DBD is a decision point.

Whiteout: Decision points are a change in value. The bigger the change, the bigger the value.

Benhur: Nice chart showing how to correctly draw a base.

IF: Every DBR and RBD has its own importance and value, and nearly every one can be traded. For each one that you find, zoom out to the HTFs and see what historical significance the decision point has.

> Perhaps it's a failure to get back into an important PA Zone - these ones are special.

> Perhaps it's within an HTF compression zone to the left - ask yourself would you take this trade, or wait for the tip of the zone?

> The bigger picture will always help you decide on the significance of a DBR/RBD.

Tyoon: What defines a base is that price moves up or down, bases (consolidates, congests, clusters, etc.) then moves again either up or down. Here are the variations.

The standard DBD and RBR then the RBR and DBD then RBD during downtrend and DBR during uptrend.

Hopefully this could give you a better understanding. However as you have alluded to, H/L or S/R levels are almost always an intrinsic part to the development of any base. If you can find the levels responsible for the bases it can give you a much holistic picture on the chart.

IF: The two charts on the right, in HTF, can often look just like the two charts on the left. It's worth looking into these on your charts, and finding out which tend to perform better on price return - drop/consolidation/drops or drop/RBD/Drops, and the same for rallies.

Mel: I like Mel’s charts and explanations. I had to add at least one.

IF: IF asks this…

If someone knows,

but I am not sure what IF is pointing out?

please post your thoughts...

IF: Pointing out the significance of the engulf.

Benhur: I thought this was an interesting comment about the lack on convincing buying/demand.

Rufus: To me how price leaves a zone is the way I judge it the most. Another is when the zone was formed and when price returns.

Benhur: Look for DBR/RDB that are the strongest. You can define strong level by 2 criteria:

1. How strong was the away move >> then >> it’s a strong level.

Why: We assume that at the decision point of breaking the balance (among sellers and buyers) are left with stacks of un-filled orders.

2. How Long was the Price at the defined level before it unbalanced > the least is better.

Why: As more time given for buyers and seller to negotiate, the more deals the close. The least amount of time they have to negotiate, we assume the more un-filled orders left at the zone.

IF: One thing which I have mentioned many times before, but not yet in Markepedia (soon to be remedied), is that in a bigger picture range, Supply and Demand zones near the edges may not hold as well as others. Fakeout often occur, because price is attracted to the limits of the range.

Benhur: Nothing promises that zone will hold price, even at first visit. The zones we mark on the charts are mainly a mapping of decisions in the market. Decision can take price either way. Zones are meant to be broken, and this market decision has its own significance too. As further you go with your reading skills, you will be able read the hints and clues for zones to hold or to break. Your task at this time, is to train your eyes defining the zones.Your next step, is to investigate how price is behaving around these zones. There are few things you should bare in mind while you do this work:

1. Be aware of how price had printed the zone you marked, what it was reacting to, and how the decision of price to move further look like.

2. Be aware of how price is approaching the Zones, what is the dynamic.

3. Is price come from a valid opposite zone? Remember that price goes from Demand to Supply and vice versa.

4. Be aware of the reaction of the first touch, how deep it went inside, what had stopped it if any?

5. What are higher or lower TF tell you. SD discipline is a Multi time frame concept. We trade price levels, not candles, so Story may vary on different TF.

6. (More Advanced) Look for correlations with Index and other pairs.

It might look intimidating, but actually it's should be very simple. Zones are always a reaction of past Price Action (aka: always look left). As much as you can go back in history, the better you understand be of how price move. There is no randomness for this market, all can be explained with PA reaction, result, decision. Just look for reasoning for levels and zones creation.

Les_Paul: Interesting post (have not copied content to here).

Rcmacf: My "wow" moment for today is the realisation (whilst very slowly getting through this homework) that every RBR and DBD are, on a LTF, a DBR and a RBD, and are thus valid places to take a trade or set a target. I don't see evidence (so far) that one is any weaker than the other. That may change after going through 200 of the buggers, though.

What I can see, though, is that there is a bigger reaction to the right when the DBD/RBD engulfs something of more significance to the left. The real biggie here is 1a, which as well as being a retest of the decision point to break the flag at the extreme left of this chart, is also an FTR (as are 1a, 2a and 3a) and the source of the entire move lower.

To be more precise, it's when the DBD/RBD is a decision point for that engulf to happen. I guess that's the same thing as the "source" of the engulf?

In fact from there forward to here, there are lots of interesting posts (over the last few pages) which are worth reading, so I will not add them to this summary, though worth a read.

I hope someone finds this summary useful.

posts.author: antraxia
posts.text:
Finally starting my homework, its long overdue.

Don't want to get too crazy with marking all the stuff on the chart so I've only marked what I think are the important ones and noted the reaction with FTB. There are many new FTRs generated upon reaction to the original zones but I'm trying to keep the chart clean and rather than just mark out 200 of these guys I want to try and get 200 important ones.

1)RBD (from the 5M) and small FO which causes a QM level and reacts to the pip on return ( not shown). 2) DBD DP to break into the compression to the left reacts on return. 3) RBD FTR from entrance into compression on the left reacts FTB. 4) DBD formed in the middle of compression to the left not surprising, it gets faked on return (compression is a PAZ so we are interested in the edges of the zone). It ends up being a flip zone. 5) DBR current cap on price strengthened by the engulf of 4. Price reacts on return. 6) DBR 15M base of move up. Price compresses into base forming a nice QM and we are also in H4 demand. 7) this DBR is a point of interest as its the last tiny pocket of demand left before entering the new CP zone. It reacts on FTB (DBD on 5M) is engulfed and then produces a FTR from the other side proving it still holds relevance as a zone on our chart (the boxes are drawn approximately on the 15M). #8 is a very important RBD as it is the top of compression so once engulfed it makes the DBR at 9) worthy of a trade even though it has been tested as we are coming from HTF supply and we have broken into a new zone and will test higher maybe even continue on up to the next H4 supply.

Hey Mohsin,

Here's what I see on the chart.

I have noted a little RBD and DBR within the down trend. I would consider these of lesser importance but if you extend them to the right you can see price reacting off of them as well. I've included them to show you that sometimes we get a longer base in our DBR/RBD. The two of note currently are the top and bottom ones limiting the current flag. I would put the base as the bottom of the candle on this one (the giant pin bar) as the next bar breaks away from it. That pin candle indicates a movement up then down which can also conceal a flag in the LTFs. On this TF I would consider it the base for simplicity's sake.

You can get crazy with drawing every blip on the chart and end up with something that will confuse the hell out of you:). For now the important DBR and RBD are the two that are limiting the flag. I indicated where I would think the FTB would be for those RBD/DBR. I also drew a blue box in with a new DBR that is a reaction to the main one. You could do the same for where I indicated FTB for the top one as well. This doesn't really give you any new info in this case other than that these areas are not fresh and we're waiting for a new decision to break one of the limits.

Does this answer your question? If not I'll try again. Cheers.

posts.author: roqallo
posts.text:
pin bar is more like this

Characteristics of the Pin Bar Formation

• The pin bar should have a long upper or lower tail…the tail is also sometimes called the “wick” or the “shadow”…they all mean the same thing. It’s the “pointy” part of the pin bar that literally looks like a “tail” and that shows rejection or false break of a level.

• The area between the open and close of the pin bar is called the “body” or “real body”. It is typically colored white or another light color when the close was higher than the open and black or another dark color when the close was lower than the open.

• The open and close of the pin bar should be very close together or equal (same price), the closer the better.

• The open and close of the pin bar are near one end of the bar, the closer to the end the better.

• The shadow or tail of the pin bar sticks out (protrudes) from the surrounding price bars, the longer the tail of the pin bar the better.

• A general “rule of thumb” is that you want to see the pin bar tail be two/thirds the total pin bar length or more and the rest of the pin bar should be one/third the total pin bar length or less.

• The end opposite the tail is sometimes referred to as the “nose”

posts.text:
Here is the progress I made

For monthly, I will explain what happens as best as I can

1. The base is formed, after a drop from history. With the limited history I have, I cannot pinpoint, where the price would return at 2nd point, however It is around the area marked in red. There was a possible Fail to return (henceforth FTR) Engulf at 2nd point as well (Cannot be 100% sure, as there are no history beyond this time for me). Regardless, the price turned back down. Where did it come back to? Previous base, marked by 1.

2. The base is formed and possible engulf of previous FTR is made, suggesting price wants to go higher

3. The price returns to the Demand level marked with 1 Forming First time back (Henceforth FTB) previous supply, to pinpoint where it would turn, one could have drawn and FTR level on this Supply. The price then moves to 4th point

4. The price stopped at possible previous Supply level, however because I have limited history, I marked as it broke previous Resistance (Henceforth R) level, therefore is now Demand level, Would look to sell once it retraces back to this level, happens in point 8.

5. The price made lowest low of all time according to the chart, and strongly pushed the price back to Demand turning into Supply level.

6. Looking to short, however not looking to earn many pips, as the price shot back to 1.

If looking only at monthly chart, there was no pinpoint entry. However at point 6 one could have sold to the Support below, as there is now Demand looking at the wick formed making lowest low.

7. The previous Supply has been broken and suggest price wants to go Higher, also FTR is confirmed, therefore looking for Buy on FTB

8. Breaks previous R on 4th point, suggesting price wants to go even higher

9. FTB of FTR formed at 7th point

10. Price engulfs previous high, however Flags right after it creating a Cap. Flag suggests the end of momentum. Therefore we cannot expect price to go much higher

11. Price compresses up, therefore Insitutions (Henceforth IT) are now adding small positions to get ready to go short, however we shall wait for engulf of the Price action zone which happens at 12. Compressed Price action zone is engulfed and the price broke out of CP channel. Now we look to go short on Retracement

12. New demand zone is formed

13. Price goes up to test the last decision point, where the break was made. It bounces

14. Price engulfs the test made in 13th point and reaches the edge of Supply + Channel

15. Short here as planned in step 11.

16. Price reaches the previous FTR made during step 12

17. Then price shoots up, When this kind of move happens, expect the price to compress as market is now confused

18. Price reaches the end of Demand level formed in step 12, and engulfs it, Price wants to go lower. However to break the level, they need buy orders, therefore IT pushes the price back to previous Supply level, which is FTR formed at step 15 19. Price got rejected and is the way down.

Extra. I believe the price will do what marked in Red line because, the price engulfed CP zone at step 12 and at step 18 the price broke previous low, suggesting price wants to go lower. 18-19 Price shot up from CP zone as excepted, however because they made it look bullish like that, there is likely lots of buyers, therefore IT plans to sell as they sent the signal already. Before they sell, they have to re-test the previous level where the decision was made - the rejection at step 19. The price may not go all the way up to the RED box 19, however it will bounce up a little bit, causing more buyers to jump in.

I hope others can give me an insight on my analysis

I hope my analysis is correct

Hi Corsica, what this homework request to do is:

Mark at least 200 caps on your charts - there are so many to see that it won't take long. Draw a box from the cap to where price hit it later. Note how price approached the caps, and how it reacted. If price broke the cap, note what happened next. Was the cap still relevant?

I added RBD to your HW for all the newbie who comes here to look for some suggestion and learn how to complete the HW, as I did in the past.

IMO this HW is important for learn to watch and see the chart in a new way. No one ask us to trade the RBD and DBR here, but if we want there's the classroom thread or our journal.

For your questions.... Start simple, start the clean homework. All will be clearer in the future. Have a nice day

Hi Brox, don't worry, if you are new, just do one step at a time, in this case, focus on RBD and DBR first. We really don't trade those levels directly because this is what classic supply and demand traders do and as we know plain SD trading is just gambling with an (small) edge (IF). The purpose of this homework is to get a feel for basic market structure and to train your eye... And watch out for some tricks too (what happens on ignored levels on return and what happens on stacked levels). Price moves from supply to demand and vice versa. Once you study flag limits you will understand the relationship betweenthe RBD/DBR and FL concept

ps. to your question, it makes sense to mark all RBDs and DBRs strong or weak as long as the basic structure is present. BTW please check also the previous examples in this thread, could be helpful.

posts.author: Enkim
posts.text:
Hi RTM

!

First of all, this is a wonderful experience for me to be with you here and learn all this awesome stuff. Next is my HW about caps on price. I used random charts and random segments of them - different TFs. It is really important for me (and my trading) to be as consistent as possible, so here are my rules how I marked rectangles. According to my understanding (mostly coming from the IFs video about the caps) I marked the most important ones, which I identified by liquidity gaps in them. First edge is of course high/low of the cap, but the second edge is open of the last green candle before drop in RBDs and open of the last red candle before the rally in DBR - that is according to my observations the most precise place, where the decision was made to turn the price (IMHO). (If there is no prior candle of different color befor price goes away i marked whole candle in base of the move).

note: it really depends on how the rectangle is placed. Sometimes price bounce from the very edges of the base, sometimes from the edge of liquidity gap, but mostly, when I don't want rectangles to be too big, rule above can be applied.

note2: red rectangles don't have reaction if I consider both edges of the rectangle. Price react to them though, but not precisely.

note3: it is obvious that RBD/DBR that are reactions to previous caps are much less important to future visits of price (and it was confirmed by IF and others all over the place

), however price tends to bounce from them too.

note4: because I really like statistics, here are the results from 87 reactions to caps -just for fun, of course: 67 was ok for scalp at least, 4 was fine to trade after they break and 16 was bad. Its 77% success rate

This HW was great exercise! Thank you very much IF and all of you in RTM! Best wishes, Enkim

Hi All

I found this diamond on the USDJPY M30. IF indicates that the diamond is one of the most deceptive price structures in the market. I have posted 2 charts, the first is just a markup of the diamond itself, what is interesting to me is that after the diamond plays out it literally shoots through 2 flags and eventually reacts to the 3rd flag.

In my second chart lets look at the PA from a retail traders point of view.

a) Beautiful pin bar at demand this is the reaction retail wants to see so they buy and put their stops just below the low. IT allow them some grace. b) Then IT force price down with vengeance, many retail traders get spooked and close there buy orders only to realize it was a mistake price has turned and is moving up so the buy again, once again putting their stop below the Low. c) Retail is happy we have engulfed up..... but before they can blink IT forces price down this time engulfing the low and picking up all the retail stops. d) We are now at the lower demand level and retail is thinking, ok price should react to this level and once again they buy putting their stops below the new low. IT allows them to enjoy the moment and price moves up, a slight retrace as expected and then the engulf of the H. e) At this point retail is really happy they are already spending their profits. But wait IT is waiting and once again they force price down. f) Retail is still holding on expecting price to bounce off the fresh demand at the QM level. But IT knows this and they push price through this level to take out all the remaining retail stops set at the new low, loading up their orders, and now they can push price up and away.

Scary stuff Note how aggressive the move down are only IT can move price like this.

Hi MudarHM

Ok I'll try put on my IT hat in this example. This is an exercise at looking at a diamond and trying to explain what IT is thinking.

Prelude I know that at the SUPPLY area above (above the white line) a lot of traders will be prepared to invest some money. It’s a good liquidity area, I also know that I’m going to turn price at that level, but I’ve got a lot of sell orders to fill and I can’t fill them all at once. I need to entice traders to buy so I can sell against them.

a) So I start buying hard with a short burst just enough buy orders to get retail traders following me, they think this is the last push up to SUPPLY, I've got my first load of buy orders I can sell against and I start filling my orders, I've got a lot of them so price starts to fall.

b) I need more sell orders so I buy pushing price up just enough to entice retail traders to follow me. I mean the move at (a) was just a retracement wasn't it. I push price up and then sell against the excess buy orders making sure I clear all the orders at demand on the way up (compression). I've accumulated a good number of sell orders in this process, and the sell orders I have are in greater numbers than the buy orders I used to move price.

c) Ok it’s time to mess with these traders, I know lots will buy the break of the high at (a), So I start buying hard but immediately sell against the buying spree (price drops). Strong buy again, retail think this is going higher, I start filling my sell orders and I keep adding more and more.

d) Price drops like a brick. Ahh look the suckers think this is the reaction to the supply zone and are joining me selling and placing there stops above the new high. I could use those stops very effectively, and if I buy now I can still make a small profit on my buy orders when I close them at the fake out level. So I start to buy, slowly at first I must make it look like price is going higher. Buy hard to push price up and as retail try to follow me I sell against their buy orders making sure I’m clearing all the orders left at fresh demand (d).

e) Time to create havoc. I buy hard, It’s aggressive, some retail want In and start following me, others have sell orders which risk being stopped out price breaks the high, more buy orders from retail as they chase the break, other retail stops are hit, sell, sell, sell, against all these orders. In the process I've also closed my buy orders I took at (d) with a small profit, I don’t need them on my books.

f) There are going to be some buy orders left at the flag (g) I need to consume these and open the path down. I start buying using the orders left at the flag (g) to assist me, buy up in a burst, and sell against the retail traders that try following me. I know I have tiered out retail by now and I have enough orders filled, I just make sure to clear any final sell orders left at SUPPLY (e) using them to start the move down.

Regards In2forex

Projectsagana, what I am trying to put across here, is the difference between blindly trading a pattern, and reading price action.

This first chart below would be trading a pattern because it is there. You just see the pattern! The chart below that is about reading price action to understand the location and environment the pattern has formed in.

posts.text:
Studying this next diamond has been very informative to me. I've learnt that when you want to get onboard a trade, you will try to find reasons to justify your trade and convince yourself this is a good one, even if those reasons are totally made up.

I opened my chart and saw this DM setup. Problem is: it wasn't at an important level. So I went left and looked for a level. Couldn't find one. At this point if you trade live and you're a bad trader, you'll get frustrated because you finally found a QM (or a DM) but can't find which level it corresponds to. So you create it. You go find a meaningless FL that has been broken twice in the past and use this as your level. You trade the QM: it fails. But it's ok you say, the QM failed because the real move is a DM! And you will take the DM. What next? If the DM fails, I'll say "oh, it's because it was part of a bigger Gartley", which itself is part of a bigger QM?

This shows the importance of reading the market; seeing is not reading.

posts.author: franc464
posts.text:
Hi Tirnanog, I completely agree with you. Trading from the extremes is key and it is also guarantee for max RR. At the same time I think that trying to figure out what's going on in every (or almost every) area of the chart is important as it gives you the confidence to take the trade at the extreme once price will get there and, even more important, tells you how to manage a trade once you're in it and price approaches the mid-range... We all know that there's 0 chaos in the market so, why not trying to figure out what's happening at every minute, or at every 10 seconds (see Jurij's journal

).

One more thing to think about: Extreme, in my view, is not necessary the very extreme area of the chart, it can be the extreme area of a PAZ that stands in the middle of your screen and so at first look might be considered as mid-range...but it's not.

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
Jurij pointed me this direction last night, and I am going to take a stab at dissecting IF's E/J trade (JuriJ started this E/J trade analysis back on post # 7 of this journal. I apologize in advance if I am repeating analysis that has already been posted...I wanted to try this without looking at the answers

As anyone who reads my journal knows, I tend to post a lot of charts, in step-by-step order. I do this because it is the only way I can keep it straight in my head.

This analysis only covers the "past" analysis for IF's E/J trade and focuses on finding out why he chose this area to trade. I have a total of 12 charts, so it will take two posts.

I start with drawing FL Boxes on the Daily chart. The next chart will show a detailed view of the area labeled "A":

I notice a break up followed by a break down. This looks like an obvious trick.

The next step is determining which is a FO and which is an engulf. To do this, I ask "What did the breakout @ # 1 react to on the left"? Here is a HTF chart showing the focus area on the left.

The chart below is a close-up of the reaction area. As you can see, the breakout in # 1 is a FO to the MPL of this zone. I think this is highly significant. I think it is this FO to a HTF MPL that allows us to focus on the area below this FO or "trick" when price returns.

If # 1 is a FO, #2 is an engulf

The next step is to find the DP to FO, and ID the area where FOF is created when price engulfs the DP to FO. The area in the green circle is where I will zoom in.

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
(Continued from post above)

Here is the DP to FO and the EG of the DP to FO. This is newly created FOF.

On the next chart I zoom in to a 1-min chart too look at the FOF zone in detail. I am looking for more tricks being played so I can refine my potential entry. You can see, the FL Box that contains the FOF also has a similar 'trick' being played...a breakout up followed by a breakout down. Just like before, I will determine which is a FO and which is an engulf.

The breakout to the upside (labeled as # 3) looks to be a FO which is very close to the MPL of a tiny engulf that first created the flag box (it broke the demand zone in the swap zone above). Once again, there is a FO (trick) occurring in a MPL zone followed by an engulf.

This FO to an MPL gives additional confidence to look for a trade at or below this level. But first, like before, I need to identify the DP to FO and the EG of the DP to FO: Once again, I am looking for a more defined area of FOF. The chart below identifies this new FOF:

So at this point, we have two tricks being played, and a clear zone with FOF that also corresponds nicely with the HTF QM level. Next step is to look at what FOF is left over in this area (look to see if it has already been spiked/consumed). We can see that it has been spiked...twice.

We know this is the right location, and since the best FOF has already been consumed, I will look to the next (closest) level where fresh orders exist. I will look for the nearest swap zone.

The new swap zone (located just below spike # 1 and spike # 2 is shown with a red FL Box. This is a perfect location for FOF, and it is still located at the HTF QM.

And the final chart shows a bird's eye view of this tiny FOF zone, located exactly at a HTF QM, formed after two tricks were played.

Thank you to everyone who is taking part in this dissection room. It is very helpful. I will do some additional practice on analyzing the approach, as I know this is incredibly important to executing master level trades.

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
What really stands out to me after dissecting this trade is the concept of price playing 'tricks' in the past. 'Tricks' is really just another way to say fakeout, right?

And we don't want just any fakeout...they happen all the time. We want FO's that occur to the MPL, with a resulting engulf to the opposite side so we know which way price is likely to go (in the direction of the engulf) and we know where price is not likely to FO (back to the MPL, once a FO has already occurred here).

These tricks help us to "zero in" on the important zone of FOF that is likely to react when price returns. The tricks are like road maps that tell us where price has already gone...

Isn't the ultimate goal to find the last available area of FOF within the scope and scale of our trade? Knowing where that last pocket of liquidity exists tells us where price is likely to go before turning..... If we know where price will be attracted (like a magnet to the last pocket of FOF that hasn't been consumed) we know exactly where to enter the market with the least amount of DD.

...And as far as a QM goes...Salivan once wrote he only trades QM's that occur in the right place. Does he mean QM's that have a HH/LL that FO to the MPL? This is the only way to avoid getting stopped out by a Diamond, right?

Am I on the right track conceptually

:?

Some insight into my trade taken today. Hope I figured out this forum software and it doesnt look like a pigeon scrawl.

Below is the eur/usd 4hr chart. The colour bands are supply above and demand below. The 2nd last candle from the far right edge is a close just above an R/S area. Given the candle was long and little retrace towards the end of its life, I considered it strong and worthy of consideration.

Looking at the top left of the chart there are two red arrows, and yes I know my graphic design skills are akin to the great masters of the art world, but I digress.

The two arrows show where two levels had supply removed, but were spiked. It is worth keeping this in mind for future reference when price returns close to these levels. Only price action closer in on the day will tell us if price will push through and then we take more data from the daily/weekly chart.

Next chart is the 30min. A black horizontal line with a red tick mark shows the S/R flip I mentioned earlier and this is a close up view. Note how price broke through, came back, rested the level and took off like a banshee. A clear sign big money was at work here. I hesitated a little before taking the trade long due to the time of day, it was after 3pm London time and who knows if the NY guys will run with this. The lower time frame gave me my entry and this is coming up in the next chart....but to finish off my comments on this chart.....The two red arrows indicate areas where I know price will react, and it did. First reaction was brief enough to pull out some weak hands and give some easy money to the pro's. The second and left most arrow is where price is currently dancing around and where my first take profit target was located. My final target is the upper dotted red line.

My stop is now at entry + the spread. So its a free trade from here on in and no way to loose unless I get a gap down. At this point I offer prayers to any gods that will listen and talk secretly to the lucky rabbits feet that adorn my office. Doesnt sound lucky for the local rabbit population though!

Note, a sense of humor is essential in reading my posts.

And finally a 5min chart showing the gory details. The horizontal black line is the S/R flip zone close up and the retest is clearly visible. Text book stuff but so easy to miss this if you are fixated on very low time frames. My entry was a few candles late after the S/R test, thats what talking on the phone does to your concentration.

posts.author: Doctor
posts.text:
Here is a new chart on Brent crude. It is not an active trade, but a heads up on what to look for next week.

First a little history lesson about the lure of money. In early 2008 it was announced we were in recession, many said, nah, its just a temporary thing cos last year was a boom year just like the last few before. Sure enough in 2008 when the 4th quarter numbers were released we saw the first sign of a slow down, but most still said, nah!

Cast your eyes my friends on this monthly Brent chart. Note the two vertical blue lines. These indicate the entire year of 2007. You will see what is referred to as a parabolic curve in price, it forms a very steep and near vertical climb. These price moves are unsustainable and once they break, you'd better not be anywhere near it. It is obvious (now that has been pointed out) that even though we were in recession there was a massive effort to push oil prices higher for one last money grab. In the last month of 2007 you can see the sell off commence, and this was before the annual figures were made public. Now how could professional money know that the figures for 2007 would mean no more higher oil prices?.....you wont have to think very hard.

Next chart is also of the month but with a upper black line showing where price was capped, a middle blue line showing an important S/R area where on the left most part shows a decision to push price up, then price came back to it for one more hit where some greedy fingers got burned because price pushed through.....right down to a lower S/R line which is the origin of the entire move up. When price touched this line it reacts back up, but with little conviction at first. But where did it go?....right to the middle S/R line. Price stayed at this level for many months where sell orders were absorbed and when it broke, it blew right through resistance and didnt look back. It reached the upper price area where the historic sells were located and it then got lost for a long time before making another attempt to push back up. It once again hit the upper resistance, bounced off, hit the lower line (resistance) to get more buy orders and it now attempting to get back to where the last sells are in the little box. Its not looking good for the bulls on the monthly chart, but we are only half way through that candle so far.

The price structure is looking more and more chaotic and will be so until it breaks the upper or lower lines. Given we all accept we are in recession the likely path is down and lets look lower for some additional intelligence on where the money men are planning.

Onto the weekly. At the bottom is a fresh untested buy area. The ultimate target for this time frame. Look at the middle black S/R line. Price hits this at A, forms two impressive bearish engulfing candles and yes only manages to hit a small lower line which is allowing it take some buys from the arrow at B and it slowly winds up until it hits the resistance line again, pushes through and comes back just a little before the deal is sealed and off it goes, I put in a green tick to show the entry point.

Price continues to the upper black line which is taken from the monthly chart and therefore has major significance and contains sellers as can be seen way to the left of the chart. Price reacts as we expect but takes a long time to reach the previous resistance line where A is, but of course this is now support and price bounces off and is currently heading for the little box I have drawn on. Given we have hit the upper line and my text which says bye bye buyers, means there has already been an attempt to remove the potential for a push through. Look at the arrow and you will see right of it (cant get it pixel perfect on MT$) a bearish candle that tried to form as a bullish candle where it closed on its highs but with no body, the following candle and its partner tells me this is a decision point where price is off to the down side again.

The price now would have to break through the box/sellers and also the decision point in order to make it through the upper resistance line. Also price structure shows the buyers have been taken in as we go up, so no clean demand left below until the resistance line is touched. The near term move to me on this chart is bearish and a weekly candle close so far today says it will indeed be a bearish close and we failed to make it to the sellers box. There is nothing to say early next week there may be a spike into the box, but there is no push happening yet.

The daily is next up. The lower line is our S/R area and the blue line is a new but easy to find S/R area on the daily. Remembered what i mentioned about price failing to get into the sellers box?.....who would have guessed that the S/R area on the daily would have held back price, yet another reason for any bullish moves to be difficult from here and it would take a lot more ummph than what is seen on the chart. The 2nd last candle is a lower close and well towards the bottom on the previous days candle. Note arrow A where price tested its break of the resistance line and headed for the upper resistance line which is from way back. But interestingly at arrow B price blew right through resistance and didnt even come back for a second glance. A sign from the bigger time frames that the move up is over. If price fails to reach the sellers box and buyer shave no interest in coming due to over head resistance, this will eventually fall away. We do have room on the higher frames given the move in 2007 has had only half the value taken back.

And finally the 4hr chart and man am I getting tired from this.

Lower line is S/R from the daily and middle line is a 4hr S/R area and the blue top line comes from our higher time frames as we already saw. The lower and middle lines form a range where price bounces around, nothing interesting in there until we get a break and test. The test came where I have an arrow indicating the entry and the target was the upper blue line, who could have guessed it would go there?....that comment was a combination of sarcasim and quick wit.,,,not to mention a wink from my charming and debonair character....I digress.

The arrow to the upper right shows a gap in price not visible on the higher time frames. So this is the earliest sign of price looking to had back down. Ideally a spike into the sellers box would make me happier about the move. At present on the 1hr price is trying to push through an S/R level. I wont put that chart on cos its easy enough to see.

And there you have it boys n girls. A run down from the monthly to 4hr in glorious colour. A lot more detail could go into the explanations but I would be typing for a week!

My own thoughts as you can see are for a bearish move in Brent crude next week. But like all trades we have to wait for the ideal time to enter and if we have enough factors that show us very clearly that the pro money people are taking it south.

posts.author: Doctor
posts.text:
My last two trades I dont see as breakout trades, they were taken after an area of interest was broken and proof shown the move was continuing. My view of a breakout trade is where a level is broken and you take it immediately on the break. I need more information as a false break is more common place than a break that keeps on going. Look back though some charts and see how many breaks took off without looking back, most dont. Its safer to look for a move back into the area where the break happened.

Rules remind me of a method or a system and these dont work in my opinion, but each to their own. I try and show principles that are based upon fact and are repeatable and proven over time ever since the trading markets began will you see how price reacts off of historic levels. A system, method or set of rules do not take into account how price goes back to an old area of interest and how it left the old area. All these are very important to the kind of trading style I show.

I do not use any indicator other than price itself. A candle body and its wick and tail all have importance to me, especially when they are in important areas.

My stops are not always shown on the charts and most are mental and putting a line on the screen is good enough for me. I want to keep the charts as clean as a I can so people can see whats going on and not look at all the stuff I got in the way of price structure and price action. Stops also subjective to the individual trader and you might feel comfortable with a wider stop than the next guy. You decide before you place the trade how much heat (loss) you are willing to take if the trade were to go bad, and you also place your stop either a hard fixed stop with your broker or a mental stop. All new traders are better prepared to use hard stops as discipline is not something everyone exercises equally.

The last two trades I took and posted charts of are both lower position size than I typically take. My reasons are two fold. The time of day was getting late and any move is unlikely to hit the ultimate target shown on my charts. I put the target on the chart so that it will concentrate your eye on where to look and the other important time frames are all shown for reference and how I go about finding those areas. The other reason is the trade is in a place where most day traders wont feel comfortable and many will say its trading within a range and this is not ideal, I agree. But my entry and reaaons for taking the trade were based on solid facts and my first target on both was hit. Taking such trades as these mean the risk reward is not as good as I prefer, but its profit and a relatively short term move to reach the target. I would not suggest anyone try trades like that until they get a few years of watching screens in real time.

If I had rules, one rule would have been dont trade in the middle of a range. Now you see why I dont have rules and your eye will eventually focus on where opportunities prop up.

If you use a mental stop you will need to watch the charts all the time and not be hesitant to close the trade when the line is hit and not wait and hope it will go back from the line. This is a good way to loose an account. On occasion I will use a fixed stop with my broker if the area has been spiked or tested multiple time already, there is nothing worse than getting taken out and see the trade go in the direction you had decided on. If you were to use a mental stop on a 1hr+ time frame where either supply or demand was present historically and the pro money decided...no, we are taking it the other way, thats when a mental stop will test your nerve. A hard stop there is safer and by all means scale into a position slowly as price action shows you there is no desire of price to not go where you think it will go.

Most of my trades are from 30 minutes in duration to a few hours in duration. I rarely take trades longer than a day in duration because the width of a stop loss and the time taken for the trade to end means I miss other more profitable trades on lower time frames, and there are tons of these to be had. One exception last year was a 8 month trade on the Aussie dollar, a nice earner and the pull backs didnt take me out and I stepped along with it.

My preference is to take trade signals off the 4hr and higher time frames where I see supply and demand about to be hit, then I drop down to lower time frames and look for trades in the direction given to me by the 4hr or daily etc. If the market is slow I will take trades off lower time frames down to the 5 min and grab anything from 15 to 30 points.

I am delighted to see you and others benefit from these posts.

Price made a second attempt to break 1 hourly supply or at least push deeper into the top, which is did with a spike and there was no clean supply for quite a ways up after that and price drifted back down and spiked old supply from the 15th at 11:00am, it reacted back up and closed with an engulfing candle.

Your analysis is good and my only comment is to ensure that you keep an eye on whats going on higher up. In the London session we have an 11am and 3pm 4 hour candle close and both need careful attention. Lower down you will often find the last few seconds of an hourly candle close is met with furious anger, watch them during London and be entertained. A 1 hr candle close is traded as much as a daily candle, and this is all big bucks that take action on both candles.

If nobody has said it before, only look for a candle close and do nothing while its forming.

I attached a chart of eur/usd 5 min just to give you a closer view of the action.

The two boxes are supply. There is what looks like a minor support and resistance zone. But if you plot the same line and go all the way out to the daily, you will see the same line was pinned to the point, highly significant and bring the time frames lower you will see it formed more and more of an important S/R flip.

Back to the 5 min chart again, the most current S and R are shown on the left and minor supply is below. I call it minor as it is close to the upper supply with respect to the time frame. One attempt is made to spike the supply and fails, we eventually hit supply and close at S...you could split hairs as to whether it closed above or below the pixel, but the 15min does show a strong candle and it spiked supply and closed at the top of the box, maybe a touch above it if I took more time to tweak the lines.

posts.author: Doctor
posts.text:
A whole heap of time goes into producing these charts and I dont have time to proof read them as I would like. Please point out any erros/typos and I will fix them. While the instrument traded on these charts is a commodity it has no significance other than to show all financial markets and all time frames are traded off the same principles.

What we have here is a monthly chart of the Dax30 index.

The horizontal blue lines are areas of major support, resistance, supply and demand and in some cases the areas where the market made a decided about face.

Starting on the left we have our blue line showing the upper end of a price consolidation area and the bottom line is now visible and is below the screen. Price pushed up through the blue where a decision was made, price returned to the line where resistance is now support and this also brings us to an important principle. When such a decision is made and resistance becomes support, it also tells us what was old supply becomes new demand, thus we have a new demand area. Many many traders miss this entirely. In fact in my previous post where I replied to a trade I took on the eur/usd last Friday, you can see the same thing happening on a lower time frame. Where you must place more importance to your trading decisions, it must be from the monthly time frame and lower. The first break we have here happened and the entry as shows where I have 'S' for support would have been taken at its close.

Those who use indicators would wait much longer for confirmation, and confirmation will take much profit from a move. You are getting into trades that no books or courses will tell you about. These areas we look for are not obvious and your eye and brain will take a while to see what is going on.

We have our entry and price moves up, and now I have a question for you all. In box A, what do all those green candles tell you?.....I will answer this later in the week. Think hard, the answer is not obvious at first.

My data feed only goes back to the early 1990's and I cant say why price stopped at the R above box A. But for the sake of education lets say its an old resistance area, and we mark the area with an R to show it is resistance over head. After box A price made a parabolic move up, terminated with a candle that has a long wick. This most of you will call rejection of higher prices, this is only partially correct. What it should also tell you is that in order for such a long wick to appear it means serious selling was taking place, and taking place right into retail buyers who were buying at the top where they felt comfortable buying and they had the 'confirmation' thing going on as the books will tell you. All lies!

Who do you think were the sellers up there?.....yes, the people I call pro money, professional money. And I dont consider pension funds and small banks i.e regional to be pro money. We know otherwise and know there is over head resistance and there has just been a parabolic move into resistance so the likely outcome is a sell off. And indeed the sell comes and it heads for where price wants to go, which is back into old demand and the origin of the move where I have the tick, jez, who would have guessed!

I wont labour the chart too much and will press on to box B. I now have the same question as box A. What do all those red candles tell you?

The answer I will give you is something I doubt anyone here will know and you wont find it in any books and you wont hear it mentioned at expensive trading courses. But it will make you think differently to the herd i.e retail trader.

Onwards...

Now we have hit the origin on the move past box B and we reach support. Another decision is made here in the green candle with tiny body not to bounce off, we then push through strongly and two attempts were made to reach the overall origin of the move up, but we do get there and end with a nice lot of buying into very old demand. We get a close above support and there is plenty evidence even for the most skeptic to go long. A second chance was given on the seond green candle where it showed a fake bearish move, but given we know for fact we are in monthly demand we would hold tough for at least the next resistance above, which is formed from two red pins and the decision point. Another 'who would have thought it would happen in there moment'.

Price breaks through resistance, comes back to test it, and now resistance becomes support and the supply we also just broke becomes......yep, new demand, a new area to look for in the future. We break easily break through the consolidation to our left because we know price has to move up from there to at least the next area of resistance or supply. We get a hiccup at old supply at the top of box B, but push even higher where the next target is....yes more old supply or resistance. In fact we hit both, and we being sensible traders take full profits due to hitting resistance, and supply and weak price action. Price falls back onto the top of old supply which now forms support. Look carefully at the X. What do you see?.....for most traders this is a pull back within a large range from the overall high on the top left, to the first test of the low where I have an S. The two candles form a valid setup for a long trade due to the fact that major buying is visible where the tails formed, plus it happens at support and at old supply which we now know becomes new demand. Nice huh?

Do I paint a picture in your mind yet?....this is not complex material to soak in. Trading is not complex.

Ok, now we are at support so price once again heads up look for more supply to take it back down. We push through the resistance and old supply that kept us down for a while, now the path is only one way, up. Given the price action left of where we now are, we do see very strong large bodied candles which means price will hit hard the top of old supply, which it does and in fact tried twice to push even higher. At this stage we are at historic highs. I would not take this higher at this point for all the tea in China. I will skip onwards a little to save some of you from total brain over load.

Price eventual works down to the box where I have text below it stating......1st higher high, heads up! What this signifies is on the monthly chart we now have a higher low and a sign price is unlikely to come back to this low for a long time. We also happen to hit on an old resistance area which again acted as support and where major buying came in because it is also a fresh and untested area. Also note the line I have on the bottom of the candle body close prices. Both are equal, but the tail is where the deal was sealed. That help hit support perfectly.

Skipping to the end as I am sure you will by now be able to read the chart on your own, the last three candles tells us we are looking into strong buying. The 3rd last candle closed above support, its tail not only spiked support but it also took all the buyers with it when it went deep into the last place where buyers came in. The other two candles done the same thing by taking the buyers with it, this can only mean we will likely go higher and the last candle while not yet fully formed suggests from lower time frame action we will see supply to the left ignored and we push into at least the supply in the very top box. After all, when you look for new fresh supply to the left, how far back to do have to look?.....The very top box. Another 'who would have thought' moment.

Weekly chart next up.

The two blue lines from the monthly are retained and have not be adjusted to clean them up and get a more accurate picture, but you should. This is just me working quickly on a Sunday. By now you know S means support and R means resistance. Look at the top two arrows, both show attempts to take out supply quickly, given both look like rather weak efforts I doubt they will be valid, but time will tell.

I have a thin black horizontal line where A and B show what most traders will say is mid range, which is is in the greater scheme of things. A is also resistance from price consolidation to its left. Remember, resistance when broken becomes support and when supply is broken is becomes demand. The opposite applies when come down, you can work that part out yourself.

Look at arrow A. It is a red candle with tiny body and long tail and closes at the high of the previous green candle. Of significance is this happens also on the monthly close candle, major buying here but not a trade that can be taken off the weekly. Given we have monthly and weekly buying price has to go up and we eventually hit weekly supply where I have the tick mark. Now that we are in weekly supply we sell off slowly, but we do hit the origin of the last move up as seen by the wick of the green candle to the left of arrow B where it hits the base of the candle following arrow A's candle.

Arrow C also shows us monthly and weekly buying, we are taking the buyers as we go up, a sign of strength. Arrow D, exactly the same thing, we keep the buying going and from the weekly chart the old supply to the left looks like it will be exceeded as the last few candles from arrow b are all, bar one strong bullish candles.

Now are are onto the daily and something more people will be looking at, but never forget what is going on higher up because those higher time frames show the major turning places.

The same blue lines are left in tact even though they are lower on the chart because we have zoomed in considerably from the monthly where those blue lines have been drawn.

The Z and Y are the same as A and B mentioned on the weekly. Keeping the same convention would have been more useful, oh well. Next time. To the left of Z you will see one red candle pin the Z line, there is our long entry and its taken off broken resistance which is now support and off of broken supply which is now demand. Can you see how the higher time frame entries and lower time frames all behave in the same manner?

At the top of the chart is our supply box and again you see the first spike hit the bottom of the box. There is little there in my view that shows all supply taken out. Where I have an X we see our first gap in price that happened at an interesting area where previously we also had a gap up, can you see the other gap?...I have not marked it and its up to you to find it. No difficulty there. This gap is support broken, we test the break later on and fall away as expected. We push through the Z line to the lower blue line and got support there, bounced off, hit upper resistance, fell back through support and stopped at our weekly buying area which on this chart looks like no mans land, but now you know better as there is always a reason why price stops and why it changes direction. It is not haphazard or chaotic as most people think it is, there is an order to ALL of this.

In my own mind I am thinking here aloud that I am starting to labour these points. But lets finish up this chart anyway. The arrows B, C and D are taken from the higher time frames and transposed here to aid clarity. Can you see here how some people will call the higher time frames reaction at these price levels to be pivot points?......they are not pivot points when you look deeper, the reason priced reacted with apparent magic higher up is clearly show on those arrows as valid places. Do not trade these on high time frames, let price action show you lower down that there is a clear reason to take a trade.

Finally look at the daily close from last Friday. We see a strong bullish candle that broke out and closed above obvious resistance where I have a black line. Here is a question, where does price now go and what can it do before it reaches the next target?.....there are four possible outcomes, they are for you to figure out.

The last chart is of the 4hr and a typical chart we will use every day.... i.e you WILL USE this chart every day from now on. Doctor's orders:)

The blue line is long term support and resistance and the most obvious, there are others here and you can pick those out by now. Below the line look at arrow B, this comes from way out on the weekly and see how cleaner the entry becomes and you should also see how its taken off of support which was formed after old resistance broke and also into old demand now. I didnt draw a line to show this, maybe somebody will take that up and draw in the line?

The red R doesnt make a lot of sense here does it?.....look back to the daily and you will see it closed above support and then we gapped up on the open. If you need more evidence to determine what a candle means, look at least one time frame above and one below. This tends to solve the mystery.

On to arrow C, once again this comes from way back and again it is at support, at demand, and deeper into demand than the previous shot down. The entry is better taken on a lower time frame than this, getting a clean entry is important.

On to arrow D and this is also mid range to most traders, look to its left and you see a decision/support/demand area.

The move from arrow D reaches its target of old supply and closes about the old high close, and not to be confused with the overall high. The next candle does close about the overall high and a decision is taken to move higher but there is not enough interest and price consolidates into a small trading range for some days. On the last few candles we see a break out of the top through resistance, we come back into the top of the range which again turns old resistance into new support and also create a new area of demand. So now do you think my earlier comments of the likely path of price being up is more likely than down?

Look once more at the daily and compare the 4hr to it and see where over head supply is located within the box. The near term target is in there, but weekly and monthly still have some ways to go.

There is no value in looking at the lower time frames yet, we need a new week to set us going and see can we pick out a direction.

Time for me to take a break and relax from all these charts and typing. If this post was useful do let me know, if anything confuses, please say so. Also remember, if you are an absolute beginner this stuff can take years to get in your head, if you came from the indicator school of trading, you will feel lost trading naked with no comforting indicators to guide you anymore. If indicators were your thing you should now see how they misguide you and waste time.

Hi Homerus,

The 4hr candle close was the first sign I wanted to see, first because it is the most powerful candle for intraday trading, when that candle closed it had a long tail and the only thing that causes a long tail, is buying. Some say its a rejection of lower prices in this instance but think like pro money does, they dont reject any price but they will defend an area if it hurts their bottom line. If the battle between pro money from bulls and bears is pretty much agreed, then it will form a nice neat tail like this one. If not, what you will see are more chaotic and sometimes it will stretch out into patterns people call flags or consolidation etc. This 4hr candle took buys from old 4hr demand meaning more buyers were willing to go long there.

The close gave us new support as shown on my 30min chart and you also get a better look at some 30 min tails which confirmed the 4hr tail in greater detail.

On my 15min chart I have a tick mark below a green candle close where you see buying, and it closed above support on the 15min time frame. It also closed a above the old decision point back at the first area of supported where I placed a large 'S'. Can you see a long tailed red candle there that touched the support line and closed very high and with a tiny body?....a clue of whats come follow, a big clue.

I always take a trade where possible on a high time frame signal and look for an entry on a lower time frame, typically the 5 minute. That trade was not taken solely on the 4hr candle, that would have been nuts.

Aha, I also see you think the 4hr candle as bearish. It is in fact bullish. If I put all the candles the same colour on a chart could you pick out bullish and bearish candles if they are all the same?

Its almost a contradiction in terms to say my red candles that are meant to signify bearish activity can actually be bullish, and vice versa. This will be hard for many to get, explaining it might be equally as hard.

As if that is not enough, depending on where within a price range a candle forms, it also be have the opposite meaning. This is very hard to type and screen time is what will show you, if you are new to this it will take you years, I am not joking when I say that. Part of the problem understanding how trading really works means you can to forget all the books, all the courses and what the media say. You are being cleverly guided in a particular direction with the imparted thought process which is why most retail traders fail and the professional money wins (most of the time).

When you look at probably all my trades any new person to trading will say this guy is going long when the market is clearly dropping. Correct, clearly dropping in their eyes because they have been told to do it like that....rubbish such as the trend if your friend, and buy the dips in a rally. Total and utter tripe!

That particular 4hr candle I mentioned looks bearish to you, but my reasons to say its bullish are summed up like this.

It touched an area of support. It formed a long tail. It was at long term lows on even higher time frames than the 4hr.

If you get that in your head it will really help you. If its mid range, well, lets not go there just yet because I dont want your head trying to understand conflicting information on when a candle is bullish or bearish and how the so called rules change depending on where it forms. The truth kinda hurts huh?

A lot of looking at candles is in your future my friend, if you can put up with the boredom and frustration.
