posts.text:
Today I just want to thank you all who makes this community to the nicest gem:s of all! Ifmyante Ive never met you but Ive downloaded almost all charts from you that is ever posted here on rtm and on ff. For me they are like small pieces of a big jigsaw puzzle. You must learn how they fit together to solve it.

I want to quote one of IF:s posts from his journal about a quiz asking where the price was expected to move next. The answer of this from IF was a real eyeopener for me realising this is just a big game or scam from the IT:s trying to trick and lure the retailers. To survive this you must think like the IT:s. Thats what IF is trying to teach us. Ty so much IF for sharing your knowledge with us

1. The leading IT engulfed price back up into the range (engulfed V), showing he was taking price up to the last FL above (U)

2. The other ITs, who had been short from high above, saw that price had turned, and wanted out of their shorts and into long positions. So they sold against the retail breakout long trades They will have Faked Out below a ltf demand (not visible in this tf), scaring the BO buyers into selling at a loss, and enticing BO sellers, giving them lots to buy against and go net long.

3. A marker was set for future use

4. They turned price before the target, creating a supply which could be broken later

5. Price had been dropping for some time, attracting lots of retail sellers; the IT's were eating these up bit by bit. It was obvious to the more savvy of the retailers that price was heading for W. So the natural thing to do was turn price before the tg, creating a demand to be faked later. They buy heavily, taking all the herd's sells and shooting price back up.

6. They removed their pending orders at 4, allowing price to break supply. All the short retailers freak out and start closing by buying. This allows the ITs to sell to them, beginning the process of going from long to short.

7. They begin to flag price downwards, adding little shorts as they create LLs and LHs. This of course means a downtrend to the retailers, so the retailers begin selling too

8. The Its want to be the only sellers, so they buy heavy into Supply (U) shaking out the retail sellers and enticing BO buyers, all giving them more to sell to

The retailers are getting frustrated by now. In the chop, there are lots of losers buying and selling all over the place, taking revenge trade after revenge trade. With prices still making HHs and HLs though, very many are still buying

Savvy SD retailers, however, are selling at 8, putting their stops above (U) (poor beggars!). As price rises through supply, these SD retailers are adding to their shorts, delighted to get even better prices, and the ITs are happy to let them do so, because at

9. The ITs have either once again removed their pending short orders in Supply, or have used them to tentatively buy against. By adding different sizes of orders, they can now feel, by how price reacts to their orders, who's in the market with them. They feel when the selling pressure has dropped, and take this opportunity to buy just enough to break the supply.

This hits the savvy SD retailers' stops and entices tons of BO buys, giving them masses of buyers for the sells they're ready to make. They're now heavily short.

10. They take some profit, creating a demand to be broken later

11. It's important that they bewilder every retailer out there; tire them out completely so they have no idea what they're doing. So they retrace price back up, breaking LTF supplies as they go, attracting more buyers. Price hasn't engulfed anything south yet, so the once savvy SD retailers are buying too, trying to reclaim their losses. The ITs are selling to them in bits, until they feel the buyers have dwindled enough for them to put in their next set of big shorts, breaking 10 at 12.

They buyers stops have hit, and the remaining BO sellers are getting in, giving the ITs a breather. They're heavily short, and happy.

13. We're at the SR of 4. ITs take a little profit, bouncing price up a bit, breaking a LTF supply. This gets the retail sellers out, offering more buys for the IT to sell to

14. It's the same story as 6 and 9

15. The FO to the Demand of the FL. It would be remiss of any IT not to take full advantage of all the shorts on offer here, and cause some midrange mayhem!

16. The engulf - time to flag

17. Create Supply before tg to be broken later

18. Inverse of 17

19. Chop for some confusion now and levels to be broken later

20. Sell to the BO buyers and SD sellers' stops

21. Lots more easy BO and stop orders to be snatched up. This is real fun for the ITs, and is having little effect on their overall position size in the big picture, until they want it to!

22. Catches lots more of the usual losers and fills the range

When you want to buy, add in the price you want to buy + spread. Ifmyante Ive never met you but Ive downloaded almost all charts from you that is ever posted here on rtm and on ff. For me they are like small pieces of a big jigsaw puzzle. You must learn how they fit together to solve it.

I want to quote one of IF:s posts from his journal about a quiz asking where the price was expected to move next. The answer of this from IF was a real eyeopener for me realising this is just a big game or scam from the IT:s trying to trick and lure the retailers. To survive this you must think like the IT:s. Thats what IF is trying to teach us. Ty so much IF for sharing your knowledge with us

1. The leading IT engulfed price back up into the range (engulfed V), showing he was taking price up to the last FL above (U)

2. The other ITs, who had been short from high above, saw that price had turned, and wanted out of their shorts and into long positions. So they sold against the retail breakout long trades They will have Faked Out below a ltf demand (not visible in this tf), scaring the BO buyers into selling at a loss, and enticing BO sellers, giving them lots to buy against and go net long.

3. A marker was set for future use

4. They turned price before the target, creating a supply which could be broken later

5. Price had been dropping for some time, attracting lots of retail sellers; the IT's were eating these up bit by bit. It was obvious to the more savvy of the retailers that price was heading for W. So the natural thing to do was turn price before the tg, creating a demand to be faked later. They buy heavily, taking all the herd's sells and shooting price back up.

6. They removed their pending orders at 4, allowing price to break supply. All the short retailers freak out and start closing by buying. This allows the ITs to sell to them, beginning the process of going from long to short.

7. They begin to flag price downwards, adding little shorts as they create LLs and LHs. This of course means a downtrend to the retailers, so the retailers begin selling too

8. The Its want to be the only sellers, so they buy heavy into Supply (U) shaking out the retail sellers and enticing BO buyers, all giving them more to sell to

The retailers are getting frustrated by now. In the chop, there are lots of losers buying and selling all over the place, taking revenge trade after revenge trade. With prices still making HHs and HLs though, very many are still buying

Savvy SD retailers, however, are selling at 8, putting their stops above (U) (poor beggars!). As price rises through supply, these SD retailers are adding to their shorts, delighted to get even better prices, and the ITs are happy to let them do so, because at

9. The ITs have either once again removed their pending short orders in Supply, or have used them to tentatively buy against. By adding different sizes of orders, they can now feel, by how price reacts to their orders, who's in the market with them. They feel when the selling pressure has dropped, and take this opportunity to buy just enough to break the supply.

This hits the savvy SD retailers' stops and entices tons of BO buys, giving them masses of buyers for the sells they're ready to make. They're now heavily short.

10. They take some profit, creating a demand to be broken later

11. It's important that they bewilder every retailer out there; tire them out completely so they have no idea what they're doing. So they retrace price back up, breaking LTF supplies as they go, attracting more buyers. Price hasn't engulfed anything south yet, so the once savvy SD retailers are buying too, trying to reclaim their losses. The ITs are selling to them in bits, until they feel the buyers have dwindled enough for them to put in their next set of big shorts, breaking 10 at 12.

They buyers stops have hit, and the remaining BO sellers are getting in, giving the ITs a breather. They're heavily short, and happy.

13. We're at the SR of 4. ITs take a little profit, bouncing price up a bit, breaking a LTF supply. This gets the retail sellers out, offering more buys for the IT to sell to

14. It's the same story as 6 and 9

15. The FO to the Demand of the FL. It would be remiss of any IT not to take full advantage of all the shorts on offer here, and cause some midrange mayhem!

16. The engulf - time to flag

17. Create Supply before tg to be broken later

18. Inverse of 17

19. Chop for some confusion now and levels to be broken later

20. Sell to the BO buyers and SD sellers' stops

21. Lots more easy BO and stop orders to be snatched up. This is real fun for the ITs, and is having little effect on their overall position size in the big picture, until they want it to!

22. Catches lots more of the usual losers and fills the range

posts.text:
Price spends more time in consolidation ranges than moving and trending. Until recently i would wait 'til price breaks out of these ranges and i would wait for a retest of the break. But these ranges are tradeable, so why not benefit?

A few months back Ifmyante posted an image of a BEFL and he said price should bounce at this area and he pointed at a DBD hiccup in the way down. I said i have noticed a lot of these and asked what is the name, he said "we don’t have a name for it, just a decision point". I told him "i think i found me some new homework, i'll go find many examples of it and report back." I guess this is it now.

So here is a short article of what is a "Flag Limit" since it is widely used lately. It should help avoid confusion. As Ifmyante said a while back: "If there's an area of indecision, it manifests itself as a flag. The limits of this flag then become the new zones." He also said that "the Flag Limit represents the end of the momentum". All credit goes to him, for bringing it to my attention.

Below are some graphic representations to simplify things before we go on real examples.

and some real examples follow

Some of course are more messy than others, the trick here is to take the best shaped and clear ones. The whole Flag area has a lot more plays than the FTB alone. Its your job, if you like, to take this basic setup and expand on it. I don’t list any other plays here because it will only confuse you for now and miss the basic point. Discussion will continue in your blogs, if you have questions post in the school room. Best of luck to everyone.

by Harry

Homework: Find and chart 20 flag limits that bounced price on return Find and chart 20 flag limits that bounced price on susequent returns -note the PA Find and chart 20 flag limits that failed to hold price on first or subsequent return - note the PA, and where price then went Discuss this article HERE

I wonder whether my thoughts are correct. To me flags (I mean flag limit + indecision area - flag, without a pole) looks like that they are places where pro money are doing one of the two things: - distribute orders: in this situation we have a flag which means trend reversal - accumulate orders: in this situation we have a flag which means trend continuation

posts.author: Springger
posts.text:
Something Wulfgar and Harry pointed out,

1. When ever a S/D zone is broken or consumed, it becomes the opposite, the strength of which is determined by the speed at which the zone was broken. This translates to the faster a zone was broken, the stronger it is. 2. The major reason for this is that it didn't stay long enough for orders to get fulfilled as large institutions need both time and liquidity to offload positions. 3. Trapped traders reversing their positions and getting out at break even is also part of it.

This roughly translates to (what can be seen on a chart):

1. Well respected SR flip, 2. Broken by a momentum candle in a LTF (M5, M15) so that Institutions did not have time to enter their positions. 3. Price takes a bit of time to filter back to the D turned S or vice versa.

Any takers on this??

Hi Hoto,

For me a broken FL is just Broke... If I understand the FTR concept correctly, after price engulfs something important like a FL, it tries to return to origin of the drop/rally and fails. I may not have the best definition of FTR, but for me, if that area that failed does not print a new low/high then it is no FTR and I will steer away from it. Also an FTR can relate to any other important area, be it SR, SD, Swap, another FTR or even a FL. But... IMHO an FTR to a FL has to happen before that FL breaks. FTR should highlight bullish/bearish strength, so it has to happen before the opponent takes control.

Now as far as my diagram above is concerned, I was just trying to highlight the relationship of price (after a break of FL) to the limits of that same FL once price retraces back into it in the future. It was just an observation I wanted to share with everyone. It was not meant to confuse anyone... Here is the chart I was tearing apart at the time...

posts.author: rcmacf
posts.text:
My head has had "All flags are FTRs, but not all FTRs are flags" going round and round in it. I've been trying to get straight when we should expect price to reverse at a flag, and when it might reverse at an FTR above. all I can really determine as yet is that a "quick" return to the flag is better, and a more drawn out return is better for an FTR (that's one of the "odds enhancers" for an FTR, in fact). So, this came into my head.

I shall speak my brains....

1. Here's the pole, big buying 2. Price flags on the way up - we should look for a long entry on the FTB to this 3. Price makes a more local flag, here - likewise, could be a long on the return. Price creates a high from here. 4. Here we have the FTB to the local flag - long opportunity 5. The target for the long is back up into the previous high. Now we don't know what's going to happen. Price could break the previous highs, or it may drop to break the lows created by 3. We don't know, we have to wait (on this time frame, anyway). 6. Price returns to the flag, but we don't get a signal to do anything - we trade from the edges of flags/ranges, not the middle. 7. Oh, come on! I'm getting bored, now... Ok, arguably we broke the high at 5, but not the high before that. Was that a fakeout on a lower time frame, into the high before 5? I dunno, but it looks like it might have been. 8. OK, so now we know it was a fakeout, as the IT selling has now engulfed the flag at 3, and is now also the FTB to the flag at 2. Wow. So, we take a long here, targeting the high at 7. 9. The ITs are protecting their position at 7 (where they made the fakeout) and sell right through the flags at 2 and 3, and the low at 8. That's a strong engulf, and now 9 becomes a pretty good FTR. 10. Price flags just under the engulfed area, as it decides what to do next 11. Price breaks down, but does not reach the base of the pole (Aaron

)

and so we should look for a short on the FTB to the flag at 10. 12. here's the FTB to that flag. 13. Our target for the short is the low made at 11 14. Errr, it's usually 13 that's missing from airliner rows, etc. Oops. 15. Price has cut right through the supply at 10, and has become demand -we should look to take a long at the top of the zone created by 10. 16. The target for that long is the superb FTR created at 9. We also look to take a short at 16, aiming for the base of the pole. 17. We need to be careful (maybe take some profit) as price returns down to the demand at the 15 flag. In this case it cuts right through. It might even give chance for another short from the underside of the flag 18. The engulf of 2 and 10 by the move to 11 gives us the confidence to aim for 18 as the ultimate target.

If I can ever do this (or 50% of it) in reality, I'll be the happiest guy on this site (or any other).

This is hopelessly idealised, and I may have some concepts a bit off, so lend a hand!!

posts.author: dcabfx
posts.text:
you read my mind Harry. My goal was to spike some interest in this discussion on FL's and not only draw lines at SR's and boxes around FL.

Here are some comments.

Where to enter in a FLAG? Look for a decision within its limits where price broke the extreme. Sometimes this is easy to spot moving lower in TFs. Look for fresh S/D within the FL zone.

What happens when a FL is engulfed? Engulfed FL is a good sign Price wants to fill the base of the FL pole. This is something I like to use as criteria for an FTR trade setup.

Why do some FTB trades at FL's work and others don't? A FLAG should break a key level/area to be considered significant. When a bases pole has momentum coming out of a significant price level, SD Zone, SR Flip, etc, and the FL engulfs a key level/area (SR, SD, FL), this is criteria that is important when considering entering on RT to the FL area.

posts.author: Mike1
posts.text:
dcabfx wrote: Some questions when considering oppurtunities on the FL play: Why do some FTB trades at FL's work and others don't? Where in the FLAG ZONE should we enter? What happen's when a FL is engulfed?

1 - it depends how strong is the S/D zone that holds it, PA should tell us when to enter 2 - look for LTF DP in the FTR 3 - price enters new PAZ, trade continuation ENG at the RT. This RT will usually be an ENG of a LTF FTR in an opposite direction new FL that will overlap the original FL. Or could be a FO, you'll know if price keeps engulfing away of the FO

Just a quick write up I did on what Flag Limits are prompted by a discussion I had today with someone who introduced me to a local Trading School. First attempt on analyzing a FL that bounced price on subsequent returns. Unfortunately couldn't add my comments onto the chart because it would've gotten too messy imo.

Well price broke the SR, and forms a nice and tidy FL. Price moves away from the FL with some nice momentum and takes out the minor FL to the left and forms a new one (not marked tough). After that price reaches some level of resistance, and decline a little to the place where price was too cheap for the last time (the local FL). After that price engulfed the high to the far left, declines again back to the local FL and breaks it but there's another one below. Then pice rallies up and forms a RBD. This one is actually a reaction to the FL that isn't visible in this chart, but it's there. It's the FTB.

The FTB to the FL that I marked on this chart gives us an opportunity to take the trade, with a small stop loss below the FL. I would trade the FTB to the RBD that formed just before the FTB. I've also marked the 2TB to the FL, but from what I've read it's not recommendable to trade a second return to a FL, so I won't even bother. Quickly after that the FL gets engulfed, showing us the intention that price is free to go lower. The candle that engulfed the FL is actually a big wick, showing some buying pressure, which can be seen by price moving up again. Well, I have to look into this first, but something to think about is: is it possible to sell after price engulfed the FL and moved back to the supply zone? I mean, I do have a clear target on this occasion: the base of the pole.

posts.author: rungodrungo
posts.text: @piphop As I understand it a FL is a decision point that confines a larger flag/range/rectangle. Depending on the time frame, the larger flag represents accumulation or distribution by larger entities (or just fluctuation in a range on HTFs), which by its very nature means a pause in the "trend," so the momentum of a larger movement is, at that point, considered lost (as you saw, price changed direction, though it is common for momentum to pick up in the same direction again) Also, I understand that what distinguishes a RBR/DBR/etc. from a FL is price's tendency to form a flag adjacent to that level so the term FL cant really be used until a FTB. Flags happen when price pulls over on the side of the road to look at its map. p=m*v where v=0, if you will As always, if I'm wrong, someone please correct me for pophop's sake.

milkeyway wrote: What I understood is when price breaks the swing low/high, it creates FL at the break. and if price engulfs it back, we should look for entry in the direction of the engulf. right?

Yes, but in this case those spikes are Fake Outs, with the FO they (ITs) make retail traders to buy, so they will have people to sell. Remember, to buy you need to have a seller, and to sell you need someone to buy.

So they pull the price a little bit higher to the other flag that I show you, to:

1. take the pending orders in the flag. 2. take the stop loss of the traders that went short. 3. take the SL of the traders that trade the breakout.

By this FO they found the liquidity to heavily sell, it’s a trap.

That’s why I tell you to remember your quote, price didn’t respect the FL, because there were the ITs pulling the price a little bit higher to start selling. Some say this is manipulation, but I think that manipulation is part of the Price Action and Order Flow, in the end they are the ones that move the market, not us.

I hope I have answered your question or at least part of it.

If I am wrong, we should wait some master to explain it to us, I am learning just like you.:P

akifusenet,

You're asking some very good questions which I was asking myself a month or so ago!! I don't have all the solutions but hopefully what I've learned is of some help. First, about the significance of flag limits...some of them are more "localized" flag limits. For example, FL1 is an engulf of a local high, while FL2 is more of an engulf of the flag area to the left (where we see price meandering around without any new poles). To me that tells me FL2 is probably the more significant than FL1 since we're engulfing a larger zone. FL3 is another story of price engulfing a smaller flag area, but it did work nicely several times as you see.

Now onto the more difficult question which I've been searching for as well...FL2 - was it engulfed or not? I don't think so. First, I'm not entirely sure that FL2 is the actual flag limit or not. On the M1 chart where you can't zoom much farther unless you have a tick chart, it's possible that the actual FL extends closer to the "SR" area. If it doesn't and price did move below it, I still see this as an FTR which would show up on higher time frames as a FL in its own right (they are the same thing). Note how price broke above the S/R, tried to get back in, and then moved above the original breakout high, confirming an FTR. Where would I place the stop? Well, I wouldn't have been completely comfortable with that original FL2 zone for previously mentioned reasons, but if I were, I would have placed it a pip or so below the base of it given this is an M1 chart. If I were stopped out, I would have probably given the FTR a try as well since it's valid too. Others might put it beyond the S/R but that isn't something I care to do. Note how in your bottom center graphic that FL2 may have been exceeded by a pip or so but if you use the FTR area it would have stayed within bounds.

Significance of FL/FTR has nothing to do with time but with what kind of flag area was engulfed. Are we looking at a strong engulf of a huge daily flag area or are we looking at price engulfing a local flag on the M1? That's what makes the difference in my experience.

Keep in mind this is just my two cents, but I hope it helps. This is an area of interest for me as well.

Hey toti,

Welcome to the forum! I'll do a quick critique from left to right. Thank you for including the engulfs!

The first one probably has a FL there, but I'm not sure how important it really is. It looks like the low 6 bars left probably wasn't broken on the first attempt down, so I'd take a closer look at the M1 to investigate further. A FL I'd have watched for, depending on how discrete the flag was to the left, was that other more prominent low. Keep in mind, that breaks of entire flags themselves have a higher importance.:)

The second flag limit breaks that swing low; a logical place to watch. That said, look closely at the first candle to break that swing low. It drops, and then spikes up - the FTR/FL has to be somewhere within those two candles. The FL you marked up may be a second time back, although I'm not entirely sure of my analysis here as I imagine that area you marked up shows as its own RBD on the M1. Perhaps a cap on price as a reaction to the true flag limit?

Your third area has a good swing high as the basis for the engulf, but I'd look again at the lower time frame and see if something shows up, even a very small half pip break and pullback, when it was crossing the first time. The FL you marked up is probably a reaction to such an area, which makes the FTB the second time back.

The third one has a good local engulf, but the flag limit can't be right. You have it starting and being based on the candle right before it broke the area. I can't tell from this time frame if price initially rose before breaking the zone or if it broke the zone, ran price up, and then fell again before the period ended. You'll need to dig into the M1 to take a closer look and check.

Just my two cents, hope it helps.:)

Hi Guys,

here is my homework on FL. More screenshots will follow in next posts.

I have concentrated on FL which built on the broken S/R level as I saw them working best and being the most obvius ones. There are a lot FL building far away from the S/R level, especially in strong trending conditions. They tend to not work as good as the ones situated at the broken S/R.

What I have ebserved so far: - Going with the trend will produce the best FLs and increase the odds of working - The immediate FTB is usually the best chance to suceed - Price will very often bounce from the S/R level which got broken creating the FL - Tighter FL seem to work better than wider once - Once the FL gets engulfed/broken, price tends to go to the next swing low/high (FTR). Sometimes it goes there directly but most of the time it retraces first

Hi John,

this question is bothering many of us, including me. The problem is, we are looking for perfection, for something what works 100% of the time. I think, one is only wasting the time doing it. How many weeks, months, years are we wasting looking for answers in forums with clear rules wich work 100% of the time? This is a process oriented approach and you have some very good rules here which you have to build on. But to do, you have to do your own research. There is no way around it. No short cuts. If you take one rule from marketpedia and and go over charts and use the rule in a consistent manner (you use this rule the same way every time), you will get results in terms of if it works or not, in which circumstances etc. You then come to the conclusion, how to trade it. If it for example doesn't work 80% of the time, that's perfect, because you know that when you do the opposite, it will work What I am trying to say is, stop wasting the time searching for perfection and start working on your own unique style, which will work for you and which you will understand because you have built it from the scratch. The process counts.

The other thing which is stopping us from improving is the endless searching for 100% accuracy, when there simply is no need for 100% accuracy. We have to accept that we won't be right every time and that is fine because we can still make money.

Take something what you think you understand or what you like and do as detailed research on it as you can, then build on it. That's really it:)

posts.author: smimon
posts.text:
Whilst it is true that a FL is formed after the break of any high or low, it does not necessarily make it an important FL. The important ones are the ones that form after the break of important opposing levels

In your chart - what is the significance of the green box? What important opposing level was broken that led to its formation? I see you've drawn on a small box that it broke - presumably off something on M1 - but do you think that the break of a small M1 level is as important as the break of the highs to the left, at which price spent a long time? Not trying to be patronising, forgive me if it comes off that way, but just trying to get you to think about it. "Look left, and then look left again" is a great IF quote.

Here's the AU move as I see it:

Remember, spotting important levels is only half of the battle. Reading the movement of price as well is what gives us the context on which to base decisions. Just a zone by itself is only half of the equation.

Try not to get too hung up on "needing" to always find exact single tiny FLs on M1. You will drive yourself mad. Instead, find the big obvious ones on higher timeframes, draw a box around the whole FL, and try to focus on just reading the movement of price as it approaches, and look for any surges that give us a clue to when the big boys have entered the market.

How did it approach the zone? Did it surge into it? Did it CP? What was the direction of the last large surge in price, bullish or bearish? Have we reached the best level to turn price from, and therefore can we expect a FO? Have we reached the base of the move yet? Is the FL we are looking at inside daily supply/demand? H4? Weekly?

Remember the RTM method is pieces of a jigsaw which all must be pieced together to make full sense of price movement. Focusing exclusively on just one part will cause you to miss the bigger picture. Quite often if we are patient, price will tell us what it wants to do, and we can just get along for the ride.

grownupchild wrote: I try to answer my own question. Flag limits we do find at strong areas, like major S/R. Price breaks out, makes the hiccup and goes higher. FTRs are simply failed returns. No strong areas are needed. So take an FTR and gear up (outbreak from a strong area, hiccup) and it will become an FL! Well, it is not easy to express with words what I mean. Here is it on a chart.

It can be confusing at first, hopefully this will clear it up for you. Plus it won't hurt to re-read the FTR article

FLs are not exactly FTRs. FL's contain FTRs. FL's ecompass the whole range of hesitation after engulf. FTR's are decision points within FL to continue.

FTR's are decision points that happen either before or after engulf. So, for FLs we are interested in DP to continue after engulf.

Naturally, when there is an engulf, we can find an FTR (a DP to engulf), and then we can find a FL, that contains a DP to continue (which is also an FTR, but we say it's an FL to point out the difference). Sometimes we can't find an FL, because we have a fakeout and price reverses.

2. Price tried to retrace back into the range but it went off further. Hence Failure-To-Return.

There is no flag without FTR (IF). FTR is the ¨official¨ point in time/price where new ¨trend¨ started. The word TREND is not entirely true but serves the purpose. Probably we could say new directional movement.

karlo wrote:

grownupchild wrote: I try to answer my own question. Flag limits we do find at strong areas, like major S/R. Price breaks out, makes the hiccup and goes higher. FTRs are simply failed returns. No strong areas are needed. So take an FTR and gear up (outbreak from a strong area, hiccup) and it will become an FL! Well, it is not easy to express with words what I mean. Here is it on a chart.

It can be confusing at first, hopefully this will clear it up for you. Plus it won't hurt to re-read the FTR article

FLs are not exactly FTRs. FL's contain FTRs. FL's ecompass the whole range of hesitation after engulf. FTR's are decision points within FL to continue.

FTR's are decision points that happen either before or after engulf. So, for FLs we are interested in DP to continue after engulf.

Naturally, when there is an engulf, we can find an FTR (a DP to engulf), and then we can find a FL, that contains a DP to continue (which is also an FTR, but we say it's an FL to point out the difference). Sometimes we can't find an FL, because we have a fakeout and price reverses.

posts.text: We don't have many important FL in a given TF/scale but we have many SR but not all are important. We have to focus on most important. Let consider that a FL has a max value and min value and that values are SR itself, so when we talk about the eng of a FL we're talking about the break of its SR too, isn't so? If we consider a FL that hold price up we're interested in the ENG down of this FL, meaning the ENG of its support. Salivan wrote a nice post about how he select important SR due to FTRs: he starts from important FTR than look for SR the FTR broke. The post should be in Hoeschec journal. That is his way to spot them, you can feel comfortable with it or find your way, but you must find your personal way studing charts. Hope it helps.

Hi Edge, I enjoy thinking about these things too, so thought I would chime in - even though my experience with this is still in it's infancy.. who doesn't like a good poll?

My thoughts coincide with 2) - "we don't actually know which set of orders in the flag limit may turn price. It could either be the mouth, body or MPL".

Of course as is mentioned the MPL is absolutely the best trade, and I mostly prefer to wait for these orders as well, but we have no guarantees that price will reach the last remaining orders there. If I am to take a trade at the mouth of a FL, it will depend on the size of the FL; with good space provided by PA to allow a trade down to a first target, and a tight FL, we have the luxury of a smaller stop loss, - since whatever the scenario, one thing is certain, my stop must go above the FL we're reacting to. For larger FLs, I'd much rather wait for the MPL of the FL. This is mainly for trade management, and keeping my stops tighter. With nothing to the left, I don't yet see a reason why we can assume that price will necessarily want the MPL, when the ITs may well have all their orders filled by the time price hits the kink to the mouth of the FL, or any possible free pockets of liquidity in the body on the way to the MPL..

This is where I am at with my thinking on this, and of course welcome more thoughts and opinions to build a solid framework for all of this!

Hi mate, its best to discuss these issues here which go to the core of the methodology as opposed to the other place.

The terms kink/ftr/fl get used a lot. I simplify it by looking at it like this (we all need to take the teachings and use them how we see it). Harry recently said the articles were written so you can train your eyes (or similar) as opposed to a play by play, which we dont want anyway.

I hope this helps. I would ask any other member to also share their view. But after hundreds of hours looking at kinks/FTRs/Kinks in the charts this is what I believe to be true

1. the kink is the actual bump or hiccup itself. (at the very pip or tick price crosses a barrier) -Once I sense there could be a kink. I go looking for it. Sometimes its on that same TF other times it will be on the 1 min or ticks. 2.the kink retraces fails to return and passes the mouth in the direction it was heading after the break. Ergo,. The FTR is formed; 3. Once the above conditions are met the FL is only confirmed once the opposing TG is hit.

If any of what I said gels or makes sense, draw up some charts and post here so we can all discuss. Remember there will be times where you will NOT be able to find the above FTR/FL. Its been said before, if we are not there watching price as it breaks the decision could be anyhwere in the entire candle that breaks the area. This is something THAT is so important, because thats how the IT's hide their foot prints and a new high or low forms. I have seen many students draw this hook as the FTR when in fact its the FTB to the FTR/FL and it can take your stop!

Up to you buy mark up some charts if you like and we can discuss further. I know that a few of my good friends here like Staurum, Gregg Hoeschec have a sound understanding of this. So hopefully a few of us can comment on what you come up with.

Lets all remember, the best way for us to develop is to put these ideas out there warts and all, its important that we come up with our own answers through screen time and research. I dont know about you, but I dont want the teachers like IF Harry and Martin,giving us everything word for word. Passing on our own research and understanding is a much better way to grow. I think that the misinterpretation of the term FL is this one:

The orange rectangle is a FLAG which has got 2 Flag Limits (FL). What I found is that in a Flag you'll find only one FTR, in this case the FTR is the one marked in lime. And, as you see, it bounced price 2 times:

The FTR is also a FL but there's also the upper flag limit which is represented by the upper side of the orange rectangle. And this is a zone to be watched when approached by a compression or a 3 drives because there are may orders (long in this case) and price could reverse prior to reaching the lower Flag Limit or the FTR. That's why on the first time back to a flag you see the upper and the lower Flag Limits as a Reaction Zone This are only my 2 cents of course, but that's the conclusion I came to by watching how price reacts to zones and where price reacts to!

Please Staurum or Master Harry, correct me if I'm wrong.

Hi everyone, Continuing down the path now with PAZs From the markepedia: PAZ P: The PAZ article is about getting an idea of where price is going to go so you will be able to pick a trade direction with a higher probability of success.

W: By practicing and doing your PAZ homework you will be able to identify the direction of price with a much higher success rate. Once you are able to identify the direction you can then focus on the best My current understanding of PAZs: - Essentially, from my understanding,PAZ is simply the space between FLs.

- To use this for our trading, we should just remember that when price enters a new PAZ from one side, price would then want to continue to go to the other side of the new PAZ. - To enter a new PAZ, price need to engulf the previous PAZ's FL. In RTM, we are taught that after price engulfs into a new PAZ without hitting the other side of the new PAZ, we can enter on the retrace to the FL that caused the engulf (many call this the DP/Decision Point, which, from what I understand, is also a FL).

- Since PAZs are defined as the space between FLs, then naturally there would be PAZ between PCP MPL and base of CP MPL, between two ends of a pole (LQ gap or wide range bars), and between the top and bottom of flags. The best trades should be taken at the edges of these PAZs, i.e.not inside a PAZ. - With the above logic, then we should be able to classify the regions on the chart as either a FL or a PAZ. - PAZs, like price movement, are fractal in nature as well. What looks like a single PAZ in one timeframe can have many FLs and smaller PAZs inside of it. The choice on how we should define our PAZs is ours to make according to which timeframe/scale we want to trade. - This part is if I didn't misunderstood bro Staurum and bro Enkim: Something that I learned from bro Staurum is that we should always look at the higher scale picture for any possible sign of FO that could happen to the lower scale price movement. Here is the post that hinted on this issue. The clue is to look at the HTF picture. Always make sure that the price movement in the HTF has already cleared the MPL of that HTF FL before trying to trade LTF FLs because if the HTF MPL hasn't been hit, price could fake past all of the LTF FLs and go for the HTF MPL, even if there was a valid engulf to the next PAZ edge. Bro Enkim wrote a note (here) that I understood only a few days ago. Thank you bro Staurum and bro Enkim - If price directly hits the other edge of a PAZ, then all trades are off until there is another engulf into another PAZ or if there is a LTF PA telling us to stay within the PAZ (this case, I believe is what we call flagging).

Apologies for the lack of charts, but I think the concept of "spaces between FLs" should be a clear picture if FLs has been properly understood.

As always, I appreciate any comments, hints, and corrections on this matter. Thank you everyone

I will start with the Engulf and Fakeout.

From the markepedia: Engulf: P: "There is no Price Action without an Engulf" and it is what defines our trading. It is our leading "indicator" regarding price intentions. W: Forget about candle engulfs/engulfing patterns. What we look for is Flag Limit Engulfs. Through homework and experience you will learn which FL engulfs are real PA. Once a FL is engulfed price will want to go to the next, but we always have to be mindful of how much it can retrace.

My current understanding of Engulfs: - Real engulfs or PAs are defined as the consumption of all orders inside FLs, i.e. Engulfs arenot simply breaks of local SR, highs and lows, FTRs which are not FLs, or random supply demand zones. I always try to keep this one simple:If I can't find the FL that I think a price movement engulfs, just find the next clear FLs to see the engulf from and scratch the previous mentioned engulf interpretation.

- I always try to remember to draw FLs properly first before assessing engulfs from them. The markepedia gave us a hint on this:Through homework and experience you will learn which FL engulfs are real PA. What looks like a PA/engulf, could be a reaction off the real FL or true supply/demand which is obscured inside a large candle in the tick chart. Please see the following example for a real chart example: - The only useful engulf is the one that hasn't reached its target. We should only look for these types of engulfs. Engulfs that has reached its target is non-tradeable - About this part in the markepedia:Once a FL is engulfed price will want to go to the next, but we always have to be mindful of how much it can retrace, through screen time, I concluded that this has to do with the HTF FL that we want to trade from. The important question to ask about an engulf is:Did the engulf came from the last clean sets of orders, i.e. from the MPL? I would be very careful of trying to trade from a FL if previous price movement didn't clear the HTF FL MPL first beforehand, since a DM of the HTF price action could form after an engulf of a LTF FL if the ITs decide to clear all the orders in the HTF FL. This was my first question in thispostand the answer to that question is summed up in the previous sentences. In short:Always be mindful of the HTF picture, particularly their MPLs - A personal recipe of master Salivan's engulf, which can be read from the FOF Articlestates that the ITs can show their intention by engulfing LTF FL, while at the same time, not engulfing the HTF FL. Personally, for a noob trader such as myself, I believe it is best to leave this advanced master class concept for when we understand all other RTM puzzle pieces. I have not proven this concept myself, but I believe it is safer to wait for whole FL engulfs because there might be clean orders inside an even lower chart than the 1 minute chart, e.g. 10-second or tick charts, above or below the given 1-minute FL.

- An important article from master Salivan is theEngulf/Retrace Article. The conclusion that, I think, we should understand from this article is that: an engulf which didn't reach its' target, would surely have left a set or more clean orders from the FL it came from. It is the retrace to this price level with clean orders (FOF) that we should trade from.

- Also from the engulf/retrace article, the depth of retrace after an engulf depends on whether the target is an important FL or not (i.e. FTR).

Important FLs, from my studies, would have FOs in the form of QM levels that hasn't been touched. Master Mertch's charts show what these FOs look like. If the target is a FL with QM levels that are still clean, then a deeper retrace should be expected as these are ITs' price targets and they would want to get their last orders from the other side of the market to be closed in the FL with clean orders mentioned previously.

- Master Staurum created a helpful, three partposton FLs, Engulfs, and Targets with Master Salivan's answer in his journal that is very beneficial for everyone here.

- Also important from Master Harry:If you want to find good bouncy places you have to follow the order flow and see where it failed, where there are people (or robots) trapped.

- To sum up the wordy, mind-dumping words above:The useful engulf is the one that hasn't reached its target, which signals us to trade in the direction of the engulf from the source FL of the engulf, i.e. from places where people/robots are trapped, while keeping in mind the HTF picture for possible DM/FO scenario As usual, this is what I have learned and not necessarily the truth. The charts, and not my or anyone's words, would provide the ultimate truth.

Also, I would extremely appreciate any corrections in any of my flaws of thinking in any of the above points as I am still studying.

Hopefully nothing is way off the mark Thank you all in advance!

Next up would be the Fakeout and how to distinguish FO from engulf.

Next up is the FO and what distinguishes them from engulfs Markepedia doesn't have an entry on this, but I believe it is important to understand them and differentiate them from engulfs.

My current understanding of Fakeouts, Origins/Targets, Ignored Levels, QM, and DM: - To distinguish between FO and engulf, we should look to the FL they are reacting to. While an engulf consumes the FL they are reacting to, an FO stays within the confines of the FL. Please see this modified diagram from IF for my understanding of FOs: - A great explanation from Master Mertch's journal can be seenhere - FO's purpose is to create liquidity. They serve as targets and origins for ITs. These are the "tricks being played" part of the price action puzzle.

- A DM should be expected if FO level doesn't quite touch the MPL of the FL price is reacting to. A DM is essentially, Imho, a FO of a FO level.

- Targets and origins naturally has a double role. They both are one of the same thing. A long origin/source's target is a short origin/source and a short origin/source's target is a long origin/source. These are essentially LS kink / QM levels inside FLs.

- We should check LTF for each QM levels inside the FL we are interested in if we are entering our positions as they may be spiked on the way away from the FL. Do not trade the second and subsequent touches to a QM level if we do not have engulf away from the particular QM level. 1st time back has the most chance of a bounce.

- Quote:"Look for tricks being played on approach into places where tricks were played". My understanding of this quote:"Look for tricks being played on approach (BSZ, CP, CPLQ) into places where tricks were played (QM levels or LS kinks inside FLs). All should be done with proper PA/engulf in the right direction.

- As for Ignored levels, after many hours of studies, I would stick to just iQM levels that was inside a FL, like in my homework above. My current understanding is that the FO level should be inside the FL to validate the iQM, if the QM level doesn't get respected on the way back. iQM levels that wasn't created inside a FL, I would personally pass. iQM levels would create the next swap FL. Ignored CPs and SRs are left out at the moment.

I want to master a few things first at a time.

- For QM and DM understanding, at this point in my education, I understand it all comes down to finding pockets of trapped traders and robots, i.e. clean sets of orders. These can be seen through a LS level that hasn't been touched on the way away and, preferably, create some sort of BSZ or CP on the way to the true supply or demand. If we were to zoom in on LTF, at the tip of a DM, we would likely see a miniature QM formation.

DM and QM is a byproduct of the IT manipulation, imho. If MPL was taken by the QM's HH/LL, then QM level or LS kink will work. If MPL didn't get taken by the QM's HH/LL, then expect a DM to form.

Risk Management & Correlation Considerations Risk management is one thing that I rarely read about in RTM. Probably because this topic seems like a common sense for everybody, but I would like to hear your opinion on this as well since it doesn’t seem like a common sense to me. I apologize in advance if this topic is too basic to post as I want to understand all aspects of trading, not just the technical side of things.

To start, I have understood this one thing that everyone should do:we should never risk everything on a single trade. I understand that we should have many bullets, i.e. capital, to spread the risk for all of our trades, unless we are the IT themselves, which would know where price is going to be next.

Throughout my studies of the markets, there are many money management systems/methods that I have learned, but three in particular stood out. But they each have their own weaknesses as well. These three methods are: 1. Fixed dollar risk 2. Fixed percentage risk 3. Fixed lot size with a defined number of pips for stop loss Fixed Dollar Risk Method If we are using this method, we would set from the beginning a maximum fixed amount of dollars for each trade and we would adjust our lot size according to the fixed dollar amount that we have set at the beginning.

For example, if we have a $10.000 account, we could set that we want to risk $100 maximum on each trade. Given that we would be getting a margin call from our broker when our account equity reaches $2.000, we would need to lose 80 times in a row before getting one. The important part here is that the dollar amount doesn’t change for each successive trade.

To calculate the lot size, we would use the formula below: Lot size= ($ Amount Risk Maximum)/(Lot pip x Amount of pip risk)

For example, for a 100 pip risk on EUR/USD where the lot pip is 10 and $100 maximum risk, we would obtain 0.1 lots as our lot size. By using this lot size, we would ensure that the $100 maximum risk for the trade is fulfilled.

The strength of this fixed dollar risk method is we would know in advance the dollar risk we are risking for each trade, considering there are no gaps or slippage. In the above example, we would know that if we lost 80 consecutive trades, then we would be down to $2.000. If this seems like a small or large dollar amount than expected, we could easily adjust the maximum dollar amount that we would be risking. Increasing the maximum dollar risk would leave us with smaller number of consecutive losses buffer until margin call, and the opposite is also logical.

The weakness for this method is we would have fewer consecutive loss buffers than using the fixed percentage risk, which would have more consecutive losses buffer since the top part of the equation is always changing depending on the account balance.

Fixed Percentage Risk Method If we are using this method, we would set a fixed percentage of the account balance that we would risk for each trade. The lot size would also naturally adjust to the dollars being risked.

To calculate the lot size using this method, we would use the formula below: Lot size= (Percentage risk in decimal x $ Account balance)/(Lot pip x Amount of pip risk)

For example, for a 100 pip risk on EUR/USD where the lot pip is 10 and 1% maximum risk on a $10.000 account, we would also obtain 0.1 lots as our lot size. By using this lot size, we would ensure that the 1% maximum risk for the trade is fulfilled.

If we took a loss on the previous trade, then our account balance would be $9.900. The next trade we take would have $99 as the top part of the equation. Taking the same trade with the same risk parameter as above would obtain 0.09 lots (rounded down).

The strength of this method is that we would automatically lower our risk the more losses we get. We would have a larger number of consecutive losses buffer. Also the size of our wins get larger the more wins we get.

The weakness of this method comes when we have multiple positions across many different markets at the same time. It would be a hassle to re- calculate the lot sizes for all other pairs (assuming they are still pending orders) each time a loss on one trade occurs. The orders that are still open would have a relatively “higher” risk since the account balance would have changed by the time the loss occurred. So while this method has its big strength, it seems impractical from the strategy execution point of view.

Another weakness also comes from the fact that we are using smaller lot sizes each time losses occur. The size of our wins would decrease significantly if we are relatively deep in drawdown (We shouldn't worry about this though if we understand RTM materials properly)

Fixed Lot Size with a Defined Number of Pips for Stop Loss Method If we are using this method, we would set a definite number of lots and a defined number of pips for stop loss. For example we could set to trade 0.1 lots and define the stop loss at 10 pips from our entry. The potential trades that don’t fit into the 10 pip stop loss parameter is automatically discarded.

The strength of this method is we wouldn’t need to calculate the lot sizes and the stop loss pips each time we would want to enter a trade. If a potential trade fits the criteria, we enter the trade. If not, we pass. Decision making would be efficient if we are using this method.

The weakness of this method comes from the changing value of the lot pip for non-base pairs. For example, the lot pip for AUD/USD would not be exactly 10 if we are using a CAD account, while AUD/CAD would be. Essentially, this would vary our risk from time to time, depending on the value of the lot pip.

What I Personally Use I personally use the fixed percentage method for risk management, but I do not strictly adhere to the percentage risk parameter. What I mean by this is at any given time, whenever I want to open a position, I calculate the lot size depending on the present account balance (not equity).

If a loss or a win occurs, I don’t cancel the other pending orders and re- enter the positions according to the new risk percentage parameters. The percentage risk would not be fixed, but in a relatively safe range around the base percentage risk, which, personally, is 0.5% of account balance per trade. This simplifies my lot size calculations a lot.

Correlation Considerations As an additional risk management method, I also use correlation considerations. I would limit my exposure to any given currency to a maximum of 3 at any given time to avoid overexposure, and hence imho, increasing the same type of currency risk.

I would also limit the number of correlated markets to a maximum to 2 at any given time. Examples of correlated markets are, to my knowledge: Gold and silver, AUD/USD and NZD/USD, USD/CAD and CAD/JPY, EUR/USD and USD/CHF, one stock index with another stock index, and many more that I haven't listed here. The concept behind this is also not to increase the same type of currency risks or cancel trades out due to strong negative correlations.

I don’t have experience with this concept, though, and would appreciate any comments or guidance regarding this topic. I could be way off here as this is basically what I think I should do from information around the web and previous trading courses. Hoping to hear your opinions on this matter I apologize for the lengthy post

Hi Frosty, I find it best to combine the fixed dollar amount method with the fixed percent method. Easiest way to show it is with an example: A 10 000$ account, risking 1% per trade. That would mean that as long as the account balance is between 10 000 and 10 999, you risk 100$ per trade. Between 11 000 and 11 999 you risk 110$, so on...

I think this gives you the best of both methods. If you have a loss or two, but you are still in your range you don't need to lower your risk and make more than your losses just to be break even. But if you keep trading bad, you will need to lower your risk. On the other hand if you trade well, you have the power of compounding on your side. Also simplifies calculation, although if you use MT4, a simple script can take care of that for you.

As for the correlation, 3 for any given currency at the same time still seems too much for me, unless you actually divide your risk among them. If you get a decent momentum on a major, it's unlikely that the others would move differently. Think of a Brexit news nowdays, and having positions on GBPUSD, GBPAUD and GBPJPY. But that's just my opinion on this.

After engulf X, previously I would expect FL B to hold because what I understand is that price would need to reach its target first before breaking the source FL. Basically the question was:why did B break? Shouldn’t the source FL of engulf not break?

According to the Litevideo #1, we know that FL A – D are FLs due to the fact that they were defined after reaching their respective targets, but only A and D are the true FLs (in this specific diagram) because price movement picked up the leftover orders in FL A and D, but in FLs B and C, price failed to do so.

Walkthrough of my understanding of the price movement process: 1. Break of blue FL down, immediate target is FL B. EDIT: the next immediate target is next LFL not shown here, but there is a high chance of price filling down to FL B (just to avoid confusion) 2. At B, ITs would make a decision to break B or to bounce from B.

Decision is needed because price has reached its target. We would need to look for PA again at Z.

3. In either case, price would be attracted to (but not guaranteed) the true FL at D, specifically its MPL, because B and C are weaker levels due to the fact they failed to return to pick up the orders. 4. posts.author: Astrokillah
posts.text:
Hi all, An FL is created when an important barrier is broken. This so-called important barrier can be any of the following: opposing FL, important SR, PCP, end of CP, and QM level.

When it comes to classifying the scale of an FL, we really only need to use two criteria: 1) It's accomplishment - what time scale does the broken barrier belong to?

2) It's visibility - On what time scale is the FL visible?

Now, I see many people still get confused on the issue of scale. When we call something an H4 FL, what do we mean by that, what is an H4 FL? I have not yet come across a definitely guideline on this. Some people call it an H4 FL because it is visible on H4 time frame, but I have recently ask Master IF about this, and he seemed to imply that it's not about visibility, it's more about its accomplishment: So let's say we have a clear swing high/low on H4 being broken/engulfed by a long extended candle (a pole) on H4 timeframe, so we are not going to see a kink on that long candle, but we will find a kink on 1-min chart that coincide with the swing high/low, so this kink visible only on 1-min chart, is actually a H4 kink. And if you can recall, IF has said it several times that we absolutely must go down to the lowest possible timeframe to find our kink.

However, a subsequent post by Master IF confused me Because he seemed to imply in the above post that visibility is what we should use to classify the scale of an FL.

Hence, the quest for the ultimate truth is still on-going....

cheers AK

It is easily copied and will take a short amount of time to be understood and processed to be re-sold elsewhere, but I've found that inherently lazy people won't even read words that looks too lengthy and heavy. They just want things explained and served to them and you can see their intentions from how they ask questions. I think by placing important posts in a single thread to be put together will not put RTM under more threat as it is already in now (the lurkers and copiers threat). It is already been proven to be unsafe from robbers/thieves as is anyways.

To solve this, I'm proposing the important posts to be placed in this centralized knowledge thread. This would reduce the post count and unnecessary repeating around the forum. For example, if the question has already been answered somewhere from a post in the "centralized knowledge thread", then the person giving the guidance would be able to just say: "see post #xxx in knowledge bank thread". Further reducing unnecessary word count.

Of course, the lazy people won't even read what is being said by anyone.

This could be just me and nobody here in RTM feels the way I do. posts.text:
the 3-D is closer to compression approach, which often couples well with QM/DM reaction.

DM is basically a trick to trap QM traders (incl. SnD & S/R traders) because QMers think that the the Head of the left shoulder has touched a true supply (MPL), whereas in reality the head just touched the RS or SR of the true supply FL.

The main problem i do have is: often times, when we read the market wrong, i.e. thinking the head is a important FL not seen in that momentary TF chart), QM/DM trade should not work & often dont work but they sometimes do, only to miss my tg and hit SL turning my trades into losses.

Just be really careful. it has something to do with what Edge & Gregg is prepping atm.

In the meantime, i'd suggest you find the ones that we'd think would work well had we been in the moment to trade it, but then lost/failed. I'd found these exercises to be most challenging, because the reasons for failures could be numerous and sometimes bring you to the point of overcomplication. just be careful and stick to the most obvious reasons, dont try to make sense out of something unconfirmed/unproven, because it did burn me out into exhaustion a few times.

I've found DM to be the true essence of many of IF's trades.

many call it Fake-Out, too. so Aaron's work: Engulf vs Fake-out should bring u up to speed in conjunction with this one.

:)

FTR Homework #10: Another FTR homework and what I think I have learned more about is that FTRs that gets tested and bounced more than a few times are places where ITs are either buying or selling. When these FTRs are engulfed, price then will try to reach the target, which, in my current opinion & understanding, the next origin of a move on the opposite side. For example, an FTR where price bounced down (short) from a few times, when engulfed, will create an FTR and now this FTR will become the new place where the ITs will load up on longs until the most extreme sets of orders in the next origin of move on the previous down leg has been touched. The logic applies in reverse for shorts.

From the 3 charts from FTR homework #9, I learned that the target for long orders are short orders, and vice versa. After much thinking then the extreme sets of clean orders in the origin DBR/RBD of the previous move up or down must have been the target because this is where the ITs started either buying or selling, i.e. shows their decision. This extreme sets of orders, I believe, is the MPL, which can be seen as a QM level that has not been touched yet.

Bro Staurum actually pointed this out on the CHF/JPY chart onpost #29 marked with "g". When there is no more orders left there, a new set of orders is coming in.

HW - Flag Limits 14 This attempt at in-depth analysis of FLs was done in just above 2 hours. I know some of you can draw this up in seconds By far, this is the hardest RTM material, personally, for me to grasp.

When I was finishing the HW, I tried my best not to look at the right side and try to mark things off after moving bar-by-bar. I do this to avoid positive outcome bias (if this is the right term for it), i.e. not looking for the results first and then finding the reason why. What I did was the reverse, i.e. mark the zones first and then look at the reactions later.

When drawing up FLs, I remember what bro Staurum said: without FTR, there is no FL without break there is no FTR without a zone or price barrier, there is no break without price movement, there is no zone or price barrier What I understand the progression of thought is:price movement - barriers/zones - break of barriers - FTR - FL The logical step from that, then, would be:find important barriers, look for their breaks, draw FTRs, assess which are the FLs I will document the steps and thought process that I use in this HW. If it is not too much to ask, I would love to hear any opinions from all of you regarding my thought process when looking for FLs. I might be doing the wrong things and, therefore, over/undercomplicating this. A simple yes/no will suffice, if you all have the time and will to comment, that is Monthly Chart: Find the clearest important barrier starts from this TF for best / largest amounts of pips reaction. This one clearly has an important SR flip level at a BRN at 1.37000 (purple line). I then mark this off in the Monthly chart. I start analyzing at the region of the big bearish candle that breaks the important SR flip from above (shown on the chart)

Weekly Chart: I drew the red thick FL from the break of the important SR flip. This also coincides with the break of a local low (blue line). I trace the chart to the right and found a trick level below (blue box). That was all that I marked the first time.

Daily Chart: After the above two charts are done, I went down to the D1 TF. Here, I marked FTB, 2TB, and 3TB.

H4 Chart #1: In the H4 TF, I mark the FTR after the break of an important barrier in the LTF (two highs that lines up). Looking back on the D1 chart, I can clearly see now that the level is a FL since it held price up a couple of times before the LQ described on the previous D1 chart.

H4 Chart #2: I mark FTB and 2TB to the upper green FL. I can clearly see the LQ base (Pre-CP) and I marked this on the chart. I also marked the swap FL (purple box) from engulfing the top green FL.

I can see FTB and 2TB to the purple FL but I didn't mark these on the chart.

The LS kink (bottom green box) is then drawn after looking at the H1 chart, which also coincides with the engulfing of a CPPAZ on H1.

I then mark the engulf that hasn't reached its target (the pre-CP MPL).

Then lastly, the potential BSZ because of the 2 similar lows. This 2 lows touches the mouth of the LS kink and the previous moves haven't touched the LS kink level. I guessed that this would be used for future fakeout to the MPL of the LS kink.

H4 Chart #3: I marked the reaction further on the right side of the LS kink.

PA clearly shows the DM forming to touch the exact LS kink level (thin blue box).

Personally, the SL for any trade I will take should be placed beyond the trick zone (thin blue box)

The target for the long is the pre-CP MPL, which clearly is hit later on.

That was a long explanation, lol. I hope I get some things right this time. I really tried to keep things in the simplest manner I could.

Thank you everyone for your continued guidance and comments. I appreciate them as always

There are 6 pairs that I'll be using for this studying purpose: AUD/JPY, EUR/GBP, NZD/USD, USD/CAD, NOK/SEK, XAU/USD The only reason why I chose these pairs: they seem to have weak correlation with each other (....and because I love Canada and Scandinavia ) I personally dislike CHF for some reason, so I think I'll leave CHF pairs for the future Money management rule for risk is 1% of total account balance per trade or 0.5% if I feel less confident about a setup. I'll be treating this account as real money account. Still trying to find a way on how to adjust the % if there are many open trades but I'll get there in the future.

The main purpose, to be honest, is to get feedback on analysis of trades, whether it is correct or incorrect. The second major reason is to train my chicken mentality of not placing trades due to the fear of losses. If I did my analysis, I should have the confidence to trade it. Bro Staurum also mentioned this once in reply to one of my post:If we are always second guessing, we cannot trade.

If the trade is a win, great, I'll learn from those and that means some or all of my analysis is correct or mostly correct. If it is a loss, all the better, I will learn from those more than I learn from the winning trades, then use the lesson as a feedback for the next trades so I don't make the same mistakes. And most of all, I believe all of you here will guide me through my losing trades when you have the time. Account balance curve should be the last thing I should worry about because I understand that if I focus on the process of trading the right way, account balance curve will take care of itself.

After watching the "curing perfectionism" video on bro Staurum's journal, I now somehow understand the reason why I can't make progress is really mainly because of the fear of failure and I expect RTM method to work ALL THE TIME (100% accuracy) right from the very first time I place an order until the time to exit.

Mastery takes thousands of hours of practice, but I can't even start the first second of the journey just because I'm too afraid the trades will have many losses. I realized I was expecting a PERFECT, FLAWLESS method that can't lose 100% of the time, which I should understand by now that this expectation is just unrealistic. I also re-read Edge's markepedia article and that stands out in #1 (not surprising after understanding my own thought process)

If I find some trade setup that don't work, I keep scouring the charts endlessly for ways to optimize the trade and how to make them work out so no losses occur. Usually by widening the zones, changing the level i thought the entries should be in, curve fitting targets so the trades work out before reversing to SL level, etc.

My INTJ nature doesn't help in this case as well as I always beat myself up extra hard if something goes wrong or if I perceive something can go wrong (in my mind, those are losing trades). Bad self-talk happens or will happen inside my mind that says something along the lines of: "You're still not qualified to trade!", "You're still a noob, read everything again!", "You can never be a trader", "Your trade reasoning is crap!", etc.

So for me, the plan for the rest of this week is to finish up on reading and to understand each of the puzzle piece down to its sub-atomic particles as best as I can (while realizing that I can't truly understand it in one sitting and that understanding will improve through screen time and analysis time). Tomorrow, I'll open a perpetual demo account ready for next week, when I will start to analyze charts in real-time and place demo trades to start the training process.

Believe me, I'm not looking for any sympathy by typing up these words. The purpose is that I want to declare my fears out in the open so I can vanquish it and kill it down to its roots. Starting today, I will try my hardest to have faith in my abilities to improve. I will not blame outside circumstances for my current psychological condition, because if I blame external factors, I will never be able to control myself. I will focus on things that I can change first and that is myself.

I apologize for this rambling. I'll get back on track starting next post. Thank you all for taking the time to visit my journal Thank you all for your continued guidance.

Another kink marking exercise as in Lite Video 2. Since bitcoin was mentioned in IF's journal, I'll use that as an exercise.

Not all kinks are marked. I've marked only the ones relevant to the current price from the daily scale and looked at where the "to-the-pip" kinks are in the LTF. Corrections and comments are more than welcomed This week and last week I've been repeatedly watching and analyzing Lite video 1 and 2 to learn something new.

Paused trading for a while to get more education since lots of hints were and are being thrown around RTM This time around, what sticks to my brain was something along the lines of "clean orders that are not picked up on the way away from a zone are very magnetic for price". Time to work this brain harder.

The way I understand that statement is that these orders are left for targets for the future retrace after HTF FL engulf, which is when the LTF price wiggles have been completed and all LTF targets have been met and the ITs want to take price into a new HTF playing field (PAZ).

So how I understand price movement is that inside a given flag, if all LTF orders are taken (except a clean one on one side) and their LTF targets have been met, ITs will engulf the HTF FL (that has all its orders taken by the LTF wiggle) and price will retrace to collect the clean order that was left on the other side before the engulf happened (provided engulf didn't reach its target yet).

A retrace does three things, imho: 1. Shake out weak correct position holders - because ITs are greedy and they want to be the only ones in the correct direction 2. Create more LQ for the ITs (read: retail stop losses) by creating tricks that generate opposite orders to further increase their profits - Greed again 3. Take the very best set of clean order that they left behind to take it to the next target after the engulf - Greed again By reading bro Salivan's Engulf/Retrace article, I also learned that after an engulf, if the next target also has a clean order, the possibility of existing clean orders in the FL price came from before the engulf is very high, which, to my understanding, is a candidate for a higher scale trade since it will fill a greater range/symmetry.

Also I concluded FOF = the best set of clean order = clean MPL = untested MPL. Again, need instant slap on the head if this isn't right I'll try to put my ramblings into chart form next, hopefully soon. Day job is always hectic in the 2nd half of the year for the industry I work in.

Imho, this homework naturally overlaps with caps on price so I guess it is safe to say that I am understanding two things at once from this homework.

Not all of SD zones are marked as the chart would be incredibly messy. I mostly marked caps on price (which is itself a SD zone) that looks significant. By that I mean caps that are created after the break of other caps and also caps that held price down or up at least once.

My current understanding on SD zones and Caps on Price: - Price swings from balance to imbalance and back to balance of buyers and sellers repeatedly.

- The rallies and the drops are where the imbalance occurs. A rally is an imbalance on the buy side and a drop is an imbalance on the sell side. - The base is where the balance of transactions between buyers and sellers occur. - The base looks like a square or box. Price finds equilibrium inside the base. The amount of sell vs. buy orders are mostly evenly matched. - The zone between the bottom limit and the top limit of the base is what we call a flag. - SD Zones are decisions whether price is too cheap or too expensive.

- Not all SD zones are created equal, i.e. most are reactions to important DBR/RBD we call Flag Limits.

- RBR and DBD is, in essence, can be reduced to LTF RBDs or DBRs. In my opinion, it is safe to assume that we will not need to concern ourselves with these two things. - Inside a given HTF SD zone, there are many smaller SD zones that can be drawn. This is due to the fractal nature of the markets. Examples inside A and B on the chart.

- When important SD zones (i.e. flag limits) break, we look for the opposite SD zone to be created after their break. This would be the decision that price was not going back inside the base and it is the relevant important one for the next approach.

- Ignored SD zones most of the time would be important when price is coming back from the other side.

- From my studies, I believe the important caps on price held price up or down at least once. The break of such caps on price will create an important caps on price on the reverse side, which we used to call FTR. - Caps on price are safe to trade if we get CP on approach back to the cap.

It is even better to wait for PA/engulf first though for added layer of safety. - Most SD zones are extensively used to create tricks that would provide liquidity for the ITs and, therefore, unreliable as a basis for trades by itself.

S/D Article: Prologue/why this article is here: Although the article briefly discusses Supply & Demand, what we are most interested in, is when it breaks.

What you should learn by practicing: After finishing your homework you should now be able to answer the question “what are the supply/demand levels themselves reactions to?"

My answer: SD levels are reactions to flag limits and it is these flag limits that we should focus our attentions to.
