@ Master Salivan and Corsica, Thank you for visiting my journal and checking my understanding I really appreciate it!

Next up on the list is Support Resistance Levels (SR)

From the markepedia roadmap: S/R Article: P: A S/R level holding so many times in the past must be strong, right? Well.. think again. W: Again our interest here is to train the eye for where these “infamous” S/R levels break. Later on, in the BSZ article you will see how to take advantage of these stop-loss stacked places.

Now I'll post what I have learnedbefore coming to RTM first.

Start with the highest TF we can find. For our case, 99.9% of the time it is the Monthly TF (unless somebody has yearly charts)

I marked the closest important MN SR levels relevant to the D1 chart that I was analyzing from the SD homework.

The criteria for "important" is: the level should hold price up or down many times, i.e. the SR level should be used a lot of time from both sides.

Then I dropped one TF lower on W1 TF. Repeat the same thing again with a different color (red)

Again, dropped one TF lower on D1 TF. Repeat the same thing again with another unused color (violet)

I used to think SR levels were all that I need to start trading properly. Mostly the strategy was the usual rejection-type candlestick forming on SR levels.

Surely this leads to eventual frustration due to inconsistencies in the setup. And the thing I hated most of all, which I remembered clearly, was that the levels need to be estimated, i.e. not exact to the pip rejection would occur every time.

Some days, the rejection candle would print above a support line and some days it would print the candle below the support line.

I'm sure you all have tried this type of trading as well at some point before After coming to RTM and reading many materials in this community, I understood (and saw on the charts to prove it myself) that SR is fake propaganda. And the objective of that propaganda is to create liquidity for the ITs.

Let me copy paste this definition of "liquidity" from investopedia: Liquidity describes the degree to which an asset or security can be quickly bought or sold in the market without affecting the asset's price.

Market liquidity refers to the extent to which a market, such as a country's stock market or a city's real estate market, allows assets to be bought and sold at stable prices. Cash is the most liquid asset, while real estate, fine art and collectibles are all relatively illiquid.

Now when I think about the statement "create liquidity", that, in simple terms, would literally mean "create the opposite orders to trade into as not to move price too much" To create liquidity for a truckload of "sell" positions, we would need a truckload of "buy" positions. The reverse applies.

Also, by now, it is a public secret that the ITs want to be the only sellers or buyers at every particular time and market.

To achieve this maximum greed type of trade, they would need to create price movements that builds up a lot of "stop orders" on price levels they would love to maximize their profits on their positions from.

We know that price changes simply when there are imbalance of orders on the bid or offer side (which was summed up previously on the SD zone and caps HW) Why do the ITs need lots of stops to trade into? Simple: it is because they don't want price to move too much away from their best entry point (hence the need for liquidity at their price levels of interest). If the price level they are going to trade in has only a small pool of stop orders, when they place their large orders, even chunks of it, would immediately cause an imbalance and price would move too much away and eat their potential profits.

In order to achieve their goals, i.e. massive amounts of stop orders at desirable price levels, the easiest trick they could do is line up two or three highs/lows. Retailers will see this as an opportunity to fade the SR level once again and place their stops beyond them, where ITs would be the happiest to take these stops. BSZ trade is one of the setups in RTM to exploit this phenomenon.

So with the above explanation (and the hint from the markepedia roadmap -Stop loss stacked places), the types of SR manipulations like in these two charts is what I think we should focus on regarding the topic of SR: FXyogi's chart is at the top of my list for this demonstration of how to trade QM using SR levels to FO My current understanding of SR Levels: - SR levels, by itself, are also unreliable to base our trades upon. Just like SD zones.

- Retail SR levels, through my observation from the 3 topmost charts, usually forms at round numbers (decimals ending with 00s and 50s). From previous studies I learned that retailers are basically taught to place stops at the next 20s for shorts and at the next 80s for longs. In my opinion that is why we usually see some form of reaction at the vicinity of BRNs (big, round numbers). This shouldn't be a basis for trade confluence though (from what I concluded from studying charts). - SR levels, especially clean looking ones with identical highs or lows, are mostly traps for retailers to provide liquidity to the ITs. - The only reliable SR levels that I can think of is the SR levels at the highs of UFL and lows of LFL (including the FL from PCP and MPL of CP) along with LS levels, where we would like to look for their kinks/FLs at the rightmost edge of the chart. Of course we are looking at other confluence of factors as well rather than the SR levels themselves. Kink and LS takes the most precedence. - The higher the TF, the more the stops are going to be above/below the fake SR level. - Personally, I would use SR only to find the stops beyond like the bottom two examples.

Please excuse the lengthy post. I gave the topic of SR every single thought I can think of. Hopefully I got this topic cleared already.

If anything is missing, i appreciate any guidance. All comments and guidance are more than welcomed Thank you everyone!

I can't seem to keep things less wordy because I think everything is important, so I apologize in advance if this is too wordy and confusing to read I appreciate your inputs and corrections on the matter of CP below.

From the markepedia roadmap: Compression: P: Often a sign of reversal, compression is used by ITs to pave the way while hiding their true intentions. W: Combined with a valid entry place, it can be a powerful “indicator” for our trade result. You will also see how it is often used as a trap for S/D traders, especially in CPLQ form.

This is the SD zones from CAD/JPY previously with the CPs marked. The light blue boxes are the PCP and the MPL of the CP (not all are marked though as my kid wants to dine out like... ASAP!)

My current understanding of compression: - Compression (CP) does two things for the ITs: 1. Swapping out their orders from net long to net short or vice versa for their last trade position at the true supply or demand respectively, which, from what I understand, is the MPL. I believe Master Salivan calls this Free Order Flow (Please correct me if I am wrong about your concept of FOF, brother Salivan).

How the ITs achieve this swapping of orders is by creating a series of HHs and HLs, in the case of CP to supply, or a series of LHs and LLs in the case of CP to demand. Retailers love to use these definitions of a “trend” as a base for their “trading systems”. HHs and HLs would create buy stops above the last highs. What the ITs do is they will push price above the previous high and consume all the buy stops sitting there with their sell positions, which would drop price again due to the absence of bids. ITs are essentially reducing their exposure to their long positions. Retailers would believe that this drop is a “retrace” and place more buy stops above the new high and the cycle repeats until the ITs are satisfied with their now net short position. The same logic applies for downwards-sloping CP to true demand.

2. Clearing out any pockets of supply or demand in the way of their desired net position. As an example, if ITs desire a net short position from the true supply as in the case of upwards-sloping CP, it would make their lives much more easier if they clear out the pockets of demand during the CP process for ease of movement through the CP zone.

What I understand by “clearing out pockets of demand” is to take every last sets of orders in the demand zone, which is also the MPL of the demand zone, on the way up. In a perfectly ideal world, every last sets of opposing orders inside a CP (like MPLs of the demand zones in the previous example) would already be cleared on the way to the true supply or demand. Below is IF’s diagram of a perfect CP which I think we all should always keep in mind.

- At the end of CP, we would often see an LQ spike. I personally see this as an odd-enhancer as it is effectively used to create euphoria (in the case of breakout traders) and misery (in the case of the last SD or SR fader). As a side note for myself, I personally prefer to use the term “Liquidity Gap” instead of LQ since I believe there would be a shortage of either bids or offers in an LQ, but that is just me being foolishly over-technical.

This final LQ push to the true zone would create massive opposite orders for the ITs to add to their positions, e.g. lots more of buy orders for ITs to short into in the case of CP to true supply.

- I have also found that some bases of LQ, if aligned with LS levels, could be a nice place to look for bounces, like the below NOK/SEK example. This is already mentioned by IF in the Lite Video #2, which is the Pre-CP (PCP). The other place to look for bounces in price is the MPL of the CP. The area between the MPL of CP and PCP is a flag and we wouldn’t want to trade inside there, unless we are trading a lower TF.

- CP in the direction of the ITs desired final net position can also be used for providing a push to the true zone, as we can best see it from IF’s example below.

- Another thing we should look out for is a HTF level that runs through CPs. IF said (I think it was from the homework analysis section in Lite Video #1)

that when we have a HTF SR running through the middle CP, we should divide the CP into two distinct CPs on each sides of the HTF kink, i.e. one CP above with its MPL and PCP, and the other CP below with its MPL and PCP. The way I understood this is that the HTF kink from the HTF SR level has the potential to turn price in the middle of the CP.

- Last thing that I can include regarding the concept of CP is that we can look for CP to form after price has hit our zone of interest. The Price Reading Article gave out a clue for this: Reaction In LTF, does price react violently to the first decision point? Does it quickly engulf the nearest S/D? (good sign). Does price simply CP away? Maybe it wants to go to the next decision point.

If the reaction from our zone of interest is a CP instead of a liquidity spike in our intended direction of trade, the trade could potentially be in trouble.

Continuing with the D1 CAD/JPY chart from the previous homework with the important SD zones and caps on price marked, I have marked three chart sections that demonstrate BSZ scenario. I removed the CP markings for this homework since I don’t want to extremely clutter the chart.

HTF Chart: CAD/JPY D1 Chart LTF Chart A: LTF Chart B: LTF Chart C: My current understanding of BSZ: - BSZs are traps that provide liquidity for the ITs in the form of opposite stop orders from the retailers.

- BSZs are formed by multiple highs (or lows) that exactly or almost line up together right below the true supply (or right above true demand). From my observations, it is not necessary to have exact highs or lows that line up at the perfectly same price, but they would need to be close together.

- The key important point about BSZs is that we should understand where the retailers’ stops are clustered by understanding retail SR and trend trading methods, and, therefore, where is the best price level beyond them to trigger all of their stops for the benefit of the ITs.

- Another thing from Bro Edge that deserves a mention is that the BSZ is best formed outside the true supply or demand zone. I believe the reason for this is because of two things. One reason is for RR considerations, i.e. more space between the trap zones’ highs/lows and the true supply/demand would equal to more profit potential. The second reason is the more important one, which is that we can’t be sure if what looks like a BSZ might already hit the best set of orders in the true supply/demand. By having the BSZ forming outside the kink, we can be absolutely sure that the MPL hasn’t been hit yet. I believe this is what bro Edge shared with us in thispost - To trade a purely BSZ setup, we would only trade from the true supply/demand, i.e. MPL of the Flag Limit, down/up to the Flag Limit that were created after the break of the BSZ barrier and expect no more than that.

That is what I have on BSZ. It looks relatively straightforward and there seems to be no ambiguity in the concept as well, so I think this is one of the easier puzzle pieces to understand. I believe I got the main idea down from the above points, but I’m very open to additional guidance and corrections Thank you all!

Hi everyone, Continuing the RTM path after another hectic week of work. Seems like I'm part of the slowest learner here in RTM, but as usual, I keep reminding myself every time to go at my own pace.

Now onwards to FTRs. I know FTR article is removed, but it was a great exercise during my first time around to understand what a price bounce was a reaction to.

From the markepedia: FTRs: P: The charts are full of FTRs, learn what it is and how to identify it.

W: Flag limits and FTRs are the same, but not every FTR is a Flag Limit. Practice and learn how to use them in your trading.

From previous homeworks, bro Staurum actually gave out a nice hint on this already: without FTR, there is no FL without break there is no FTR without a zone or price barrier, there is no break without price movement, there is no zone or price barrier So I started with SRs that seems obvious up to the monthly level and worked my FTRs from those.

I marked all FTRs from the weekly timeframe and moved on to the daily timeframe.

The most important part of this exercise is to find the important barrier and the resulting FTR that would be created after.

Below is what I have marked for this exercise. Please note that not all FTRs are marked to prevent a mess of colors.

I just marked the important ones that are created after a break of significant SR or after a break of previous FTR.

My current understanding of FTRs: - FTRs can be seen all over the chart. To eliminate the worst ones, immediately remove the ones that broke local SRs, i.e. the ones created after the break of a previous highs or lows in the same swing. - FTRs can be created by a break of any barrier, but the most important ones are the FTR after the break of FTRs that held price up or down previously, which we all know as Flag Limits.

- FTRs are created by the ITs to either: trap retailers by creating false SD zones or mark their and their IT friends' PAZs.

- For the fake SD FTR, from IF's recent diagram explaining FTRs and FLs, these can be seen in FTRs thatdid not retrace to pick up the orders in the previous kink/FL. ITs create these FTRs to create liquidity from the SD traders, i.e. their stop losses for ITs to trade in the true SD. BSZ concept also comes from this fake SD concept of FTRs - For the true PAZ marker / PAZ delimiter type of FTR, I think there was a different concept in the beginning years of RTM, which causes a lot of confusion in the past. The new concept is that the more hidden the delimiter FTR, the better. as the retailers can't see them. This is what I understand currently: - The way we use FTRs now is to use them as fake SD zones to expect FO from. The most common way of tricking the retailers are where price reacted off the mouth of an important FTR (the FL), creating a fake SD zone (the FTR of the FL) and then on the next visit fakes to the MPL of the important FTR. Bro H recently wrote a lovely piece on thishere.

- Remember that all FLs are FTRs, but not all FTRs are FLs. Again, the distinction should be clear from IF's diagram above.

- After reading many of bro Salivan's journal, I also believe that FTRs that held price up or down many times are the important ones to look out for.

These would be saved later for the FL homework. Orderflow-wise, as in everyday buying and selling in any market, I think it makes the most sense for ITs to open their positions in roughly the same price level or only a few pips off rather than scattering their orders for a certain direction in a wider zone.

Thank you all for any corrections and comments. Have a lovely weekend

Sorry for the busy charts there. I wrote every observation down in the neatest possible arrangement I'd love to hear any comments and corrections on it if you all have the time to check whether I'm on the right trackThank you in advance!

My current understanding of FLs: - The best FLs are ones that clearly holds price up or down as these show the price level that ITs use to accumulate their positions, either long or short. - ITs can't create tangible goods or services like normal people and businesses. They create their "goods", i.e. liquidity, by creatingtricks. These tricks, if I understood correctly, are basically fakeouts of expected retail behaviors (mostly breakout traders)within the confines of FLs. Master Mertch gave a clear explanation about this concept for us in his journal:When I see peace of PA inside a flag, then for me it became LIMIT.. Thank you Master Mertch - The MPL of FLs are where ITs want to be the only buyer or seller in the market. Movements above or below the MPL, for demand or supply FLs respectively, are only tricks to build up liquidity for the ITs' massive buy or sell orders respectively.

- With the above logic, it makes the most sense for us to enter only at MPLs for the highest probability trades. Remember that nothing works 100% of the time. Even trades at MPL could incur losses, possibly due to the taking of clean orders down in the tick charts on the way away from the MPL the first time. Money management should always be kept in check. Unrealistic expectations are the bane of traders.

- Also from the above logic, stops for our trades shouldalways be beyond the MPL of the FL we are trading from.

- If an FL is engulfed and hasn't reached its target, then the ITs would retrace to pick up orders from the FL that price is coming from. This is how we should trade as taught in RTM: enter on the retrace. - What I learned from Master Salivan (if I didn't misinterpret what he is saying): If the target for an engulf is the origin of the previous move and isn't hit yet, then a deep retrace is required to collect the orders from the MPL (FOF) of the FL we are coming from. - Another thing that I learned from Master Salivan (again, if I didn't misinterpret): An engulf of LTF ORFL, preferably 1-Minute ORFL, is a sign of an engulf, even if the HTF FL is not engulfed yet. Personally for me currently, I think it would be best for beginners like me to keep this concept on the sidelines at the moment and go with the original engulf definition first before moving to advanced Master class concepts.

Apologies for the lengthy post. Hopefully I got the concept behind FLs clearly understood there Have a great weekend everyone!

posts.text:
What I have found and learned about CPs are as follows: - Upward-sloping CP to a supply zone = price more likely to go down from the supply zone (provided the last demand in CP PAZ is engulfed down)

- Downward-sloping CP from a supply zone = price more likely to go up through the supply zone (provided there is an engulf up of the last supply in CP PAZ and the last demand after CP holds price up)

- Downward-sloping CP to a demand zone = price more likely to go up from the demand zone (provided the last supply in CP PAZ is engulfed up)

- Upward-sloping CP from a demand zone = price more likely to go down through the demand zone (provided there is an engulf down of the last demand in CP PAZ and the last supply after CP holds price down)

- CP followed by LQ without engulf of the approach flag = potential bounce later on from base of LQ - CP that didn't activate immediately, i.e. price didn't engulf the last approach flag in the CP, will still be effective at a later date - The best way to trade a CP is to let price engulf the last approach flag, i.e. the last demand or supply in the CP PAZ, and enter on a RT to a previous DP - If price engulfs the last approach flag in the CP PAZ, then price will slide through to the base of CP PAZ - CP can be used by ITs to push price in the direction of a DP if there is not enough order to reach the DP (easier to explain with a charthere)

- CP away from a demand or a supply level can be used later on to create LQ spikes that could trap retail traders into selling or buying into a demand or supply level, respectively, for the ITs to fill in opposite orders (seehere for example)

Please correct any incorrect interpretations of CPThank you all for your comments and criticism P. S. Sorry for double posting this also on the CP homework since I think this is very important for my understanding of the subject and should also belong in the journal

There are a few types of PAZ: CP PAZ, Stacked SD PAZ, the space between 2 FTRs 4. True engulfs are those that engulfs FTRs. Some engulfs are fake engulfs to trick retail traders into taking opposite orders that the ITs want to trade against. This fake engulf (FO), usually stops at the FTR, where the ITs' orders lie 5. Engulf of an FTR, price wants to go to the next FTR in the direction of the engulf Questions that I have not yet found the answer to: 1. I did some deep thinking about order flow and what the retailers have been taught (outside of RTM, of course, lol).

Specifically, I really wondered why IF mentioned LS and LS Kinks to be extremely important. I want to see behind the definition and thought about the things I have been taught previously in other sites and books. What I have thought about and come up with is summed up below. I might look stupid in the process if this isn't correct, but I will definitely learn from you all and what you have to say. Please do correct this reasoning if anything or everything is all wrong as I don't want to dwell on false ideas and beliefs This explanation is for inverted LS (L-H-LL-HH-HL). For a LS (H-L-HH-LL- LH), same thing but in reverse.

Below a LS, there are trapped sellers, maybe primarily from breakout strategies (I've traded one myself called the Ross Hook). When price rises above H to make HH, these trapped sellers want to get out with as minimal loss as possible, so they sell as close to the initial L (which is the LS) to minimize losses.

This closing of sell orders from the previous break of low of LS comes in near the LS for an obvious reason, i.e. to get as close to breakeven as possible, but since every trapped sellers are doing the same thing, there are naturally some buy orders that are left unfilled. This is because to close a sell order, we need buy orders and the buy orders, in this case, is injected to the market at almost the same price are, which is the LS price level or somewhere close to it. There simply aren't many sell orders around that price area to fill all those incoming buy orders. This created the LS kink, which can be seen as a demand zone in the LTFs.

These unfilled buy orders, assuming the ITs' target, i.e. the next important FTR, hasn't been reached, we can safely assume that the ITs will pick up these unfilled buy orders and, afterwards, head for their target.

This will be the basis of my 6th FTR homework here. I put this example forward since I think this example shows what I'm trying to explain in the above paragraphs. Here's how I am marking in the PAZs, based on my current understanding. I'm leaving out cpPAZ until I've got a handle on the FTR PAZ. I'm using the same chart area as above, so we've consistency. Peds, am I getting there?

1. First I mark in the FTRs I see. These I take to be an engulf (a new high in this case) showing intent to go higher, then the fail to go lower. It does not become a true FTR until price then moves higher than the initial higher high. So, for example, z does not qualify as an FTR as y is a few pips lower than x. (it is a cpPAZ edge, but I'm not going near those yet). I've used a little red ellipse to show the tips of the FTRs.

2. I then mark in the demand zones (or supply if moving down) which the FTRs represent. My indi marks those created above current price blue, and those below as pink). These are going to become the targets on the way down - the FTB to the FTR, essentially.

3. Then it's a case of watching what price does:

The engulf at 1 means expect price to go to 2 (engulf 1 also engulfs an FL to the left of the top elipse, and should have you primed and ready for point A to happen - it is ignored demand becoming supply - an SR flip).

The engulf at 3 means expect price to go to 4

The engulf at 5 means expect price to go to 6, whichever PAZ edge that leads to next. If you were sharp, you could maybe get in at B.

And see how the influence continues..

In my view a FTR is created when something (a previous High/Low, a Key Level, a previous FTR, a previous SD zone like RBR/DBD) gets engulfed and there is a pullback.

I think that most of the FLs are FTR too, because they form when a SR level gets engulfed and in the flag there is actually a pullback, an attempt to return to the origin of the move, so we can call it FTR.

But why not all FL are FTR? Well, if I understand FLs, most of the times a flag forms after a SR level gets engulfed, so we can call it FTR, but in some FLs the flag forms BEFORE the SR gets engulfed, so this flag has not yet engulfed something right now, so we can't call it FTR, in this case the real FTR is the FTB to the flag limit. Look at the draw below.

Decision points are FTR? Same as I said about FLs, most DP are FTR too, but not all. Imagine a Rally-Base-Rally that forms in the middle of nowhere and there is no engulf of previous things, is this a decision point? Yes, when the flag breaks there is the decision to go higher. Is this a FTR? No, because no engulf.

Makes sense?

posts.author: Les_Paul
posts.text:
1. Introduction Before solving the puzzle of price action and before being able to read it successfully, one must discover and understand the individual pieces the puzzle is made of. After all, every eye-catching building is made of individual bricks and stones. For most of us at RTM, the beauty of price action is just as stunning a structure as the cathedral of Chartres or Sagrada Familia in Barcelona. The only difference is that bricks and stones of real buildings are represented by price caps, FTRs, engulfs, fakeouts, quasimodos, diamonds etc. Of the building blocks of the price structure nothing is more important than engulfs and FTRs! In my article I am going to explain one of the two most important pieces of price action – FTR. Together we will explore what is looks like, where it can be found and what is its role in the structure of price action. FTR must be learned properly before one can advance further. Please take your time, don’t rush; learning price action is an amazing journey, so enjoy it. 2. What is FTR? So, what actually is FTR? FTR means ‘Failure to Return’. But wait… Who wants to return? Where do they want to return? And why on earth do they fail? These three important questions must be answered, so let’s do it. It’s a well known fact that price, once it reaches a certain barrier, either bounces of it or breaks it. Once it breaks it, two possible scenarios occur: it either returns back below/above the barrier and goes on in the direction against the break or fails to return and keeps going in the direction of the break. In the latter scenario, a FTR is made. ALWAYS! And it is of vital importance to be able to identify it! Why? Well, there is such a strong buying or selling pressure aka supply / demand at the FTR that the price just cannot return, it must go on in the direction of the break. Hint 1: the selling / buying pressure always remains at FTR after price has left. Can you see the implication? J Now let’s take a look at the anatomy of FTRs. In the following picture you can see a diagram showing some basic variations of FTRs. Look at them carefully, you will see that they may look a bit different but remember: they are absolutely the same in terms of the structure.

The red line (a) represents a barrier. It can be a SUPPORT / RESISTANCE, a FTR in opposite direction (will be explained later) or limit of a PAZ (Price Action Zone). Price action breaks the barrier (1) and retraces (2). It is irrelevant whether price action crosses the barrier again or not (as in examples (ii and iv above). At the extreme of the retrace a base is very often made (b). Then, price action continues in the direction of the break (3). FTR is confirmed after price action breaks the high / low (c) which formed after the break of the barrier. Only after the break of (c) we can say that price action indeed failed to return. Now, when the FTR is confirmed, we draw a rectangle at the base (b) and protract it to the right. Hint 2: for information how to draw the blue rectangles see the article Caps on Price at RTM Marketpedia. Now that we have studied the diagrams above, we can look at real life examples of FTRs.

3. FTR after the break of SUPPORT / RESISTANCE FTRs after the break of support / resistance are very common. They are simply everywhere in the chart and you will learn to spot them. You certainly know that there are major support resistance lines as well as minor ones… the more important the S/R line is, the more significance we must assign to the FTR that follows.

Major S/R line Ok, let’s start with the major ones. I assume that you already know how to distinguish a major SR from minor SR... In the following chart you can see the brown RESISTANCE line. The RESISTANCE is a major one, it has been respected many times in the past (not just those two touches seen in the picture). Suddenly, the R line is broken. Is it just a fakeout or genuine break? How will we know it? Yes, right! We will wait for a FTR to be formed. And voila, a spectacular FTR is made! The price then rushes away from the R line. Now it’s going to be interesting! Such FTR is an amazing place to trade on the first visit. The first visit occurred in approximately one week. And look at the reaction! The first visit to an FTR is called FTB (First Time Back).

Hint 3: Upon return to the FTR the price is falling in a free fall, everyone is happily jumping into trend because “it’s going to go on and on…” but beware, predators are patiently waiting in FTR level, and so should you…! For your convenience, there are two more examples:

Now open your trading platform or Forex Tester and see for yourself how often this works! Minor S/R line It’s important to know that the FTRs in the above three charts are actually not the only FTRs that can be spotted. Far from it! Every time price breaks a minor support/resistance, fails to return and goes on, a new FTR is made!

In real life, however, the chart seldom looks so neat and clean as in the above diagram. In the following chart you can see the above principle in a real chart (in a down trend).

Please take your time and study the above chart, you may notice that I haven’t marked absolutely ALL FTRs because the chart would be very messy. Open a chart in your platform and mark all FTRs. Practise! Mark a swing high/low, find where it was engulfed, then find the FTR. Repeat with next high/low. Remember, the purpose of the article is not to tell you that each and every FTR is tradable but to teach you how to spot FTRs and how to mark them. Let me repeat: it is of paramount importance!

4. FTR after the break of a FTR in opposite direction FTRs are formed after engulfing of a barrier. We already know this. One of such barriers is an FTR in opposite direction. Look at the diagram below, I think it is self-explanatory. FTR d is engulfed and FTR 1 is made, and so on.

And a real life example.

Hint 4: FTR 1 is a great confirmation of a reversal. For more information on this see my journal starting with post 304 on page 13 (sweet FTRs).

5. FTR after the break of a PAZ limit The limit of a PAZ is another barrier, the break of which results in extremely important FTRs! This is, however, rather advanced and it goes beyond the scope of this article on the FTR basics.

6. Conclusion In my article I tried to introduce a very important building block of price structure – FTR. We have learned that FTRs are formed after the break of a price barrier. It is important to realise that FTRs are places where institutional traders open / close their positions. This makes them ideal places for looking for trade setups or targets. However, it must be stressed that FTRs on their own are not enough for trading, one must master other important building blocks, engulfing being the most important one. Les_Paul

Thank you for your clarification

Hey, Mr L. The easiest way to differentiate is that price exiting an FTR must engulf something significant in the past - this is represented by the red lines on the original article's FTR diagrams. RBRs and DBDs only engulf themselves, if you get me.

The FTR's move away engulfing something tells you that it had a strong SD imbalance, and so is a good opportunity on the return. The DBD/RBR on the other hand does not, and so is better as a target than an entry point.

Now, the place where I need to have more understanding is where we have a flag occur after breaking an SR area. It's a RBR/DBD more than an FTR, and yet is a good place to take an entry on the return, the teaching states (flag limit article) but I beleive that a flag forming prior to the break should be more meaningful, as it also holds the decision point to break the SR area, and thus holds a greater S/D imbalance.

posts.author: antraxia
posts.text:
Hey Pauga! Great to have you here.

After you read for a while you will find that (at least to my current knowledge) they are the same thing. A failed to return FTR limits the resulting price action until it is engulfed thus it usually becomes a flag limit FL. In your chart you have a special type of FL. The one that forms after a significant pole base has been engulfed or the first one that forms after a change in trend (after the last swing has been engulfed and a new FTR is formed). We look for important swings to be engulfed, form a FL and then look for PA on return to that FL or take a Touch Trade (TT) if the conditions are right. Hope this helps some as there was some confusion in the threads as to whether they were the same thing or not. Cheers.

Hey,

I do not think that FTR and FTB are the exact same thing. As far as I know, the FTR happens after a break, through a resistance for example. Thereby it is not important if the FTR is after or before the Support, as it is in this case (also see Markepedia article about FTRs). On the chart price breaks (engulfs) the Support, then retraces. The end of the retrace is the FTR. Price then engulfs the first breakout, which is a confiramtion of the breakthrough. When price then returns to the FTR and reacts, it is called FTB.

Would be nice, if an expert could confirm.

posts.author: MaxxAstral
posts.text:
This is one of the best place in this whole Forum, esp article #1 which explains all about FTR. I want to thank Les_Paul for explaining this intrinsic and fundamental element of Price Action.

To sum it up, FTR is simply price Failing to Return to its old Price Action Zone after price Engulf the Limit of the Zone which is denoted by Flag Limits. So naturally the FTR is a decision point that indicates that price is either too expensive or too cheap in that old Price Action Zone hence it must move in the direction of the Engulf ( the hidden signal ), in search for its value. Now in that FTR decision point there are always clusters of unfilled orders left, so when price returns to that FTR and the approach/pressure is not strong then that place is an excellent place to take a position at that FTB.

Thanks

Staurum wrote: mm.... ok.. here is a note from my studies. Like a sequence of creation:

posts.author: Kohai
posts.text:
I want to try this little exercise to identify FTRs, analyzing them and seeing where they bounce price when they get engulfed.

In the next screen there's a nice action. Price is trapped between two FTRs, but we know that 5 has been engulfed which could be a signal that ITs are putting their shorts in.

FTRs are structures highly respected by price and they are important if they are respected, because they can be traded with a very nice R:R, but they are also important when they are broken because they signal us that price wants to go to the next FTR. So it is important to see how price reacts to these levels and see how price is approaching the level: is it compressing towards it? Is it compressing and then a huge liquidity spike appears and reach the level?

I think that this is an important point.

So, as Staurum suggested, I re-read the FTR article and found many new information which I did not see previously.

For example, an FTR is made after a break of these barriers:

1. An SR line which are two or more highs/lows lined, in this case, the higher the number of highs/lows, the stronger the FTR that is generated when the level breaks 2. Another FTR in the opposite direction 3. A PAZ limit

OK, let's find some FTRs of the first type. (As always, correct me if I'm wrong)

posts.author: Astrokillah
posts.text:
Hey man, good stuff there, I'm looking at the same thing! I like your
 level because it aligns with a very distinctive low to the left (See my
 thick orange line 1)

However, I must admit that since I went back to demo, trying to 'set and
 forget' my trades, the results had baaadddd! But ok, granted, I
looked at my losers, actually none of them fully meet the criteria I set
 out in my trading plan, I just took them because I was bored waiting
for valid setups.

RTM teaches us to find our trade at LTF levels. I normally look for kink in as low as 1 min.

For the LTF kink I want to trade, the criteria I set out are the following:

1. The kink must sit inside a HTF FL, and my HTF starts at H1 and above

2. The kink must align with a distinct LS or SR of HTF.

3. The HTF FL must have caused a valid engulf PA (with a clear TG not
reached). If not, I have to wait for engulf PA by the LTF kink I want to
 trade.

4. The approach back to the level of interest must have one of the following (compression, BSZ, 3Drive)

Oh well, as I'm finding out, setting rules are easy, but having the
patience to wait for the setup is another thing. And too often, the
setup occurred when I'm not in front of the PC!

So back to this USDCAD, it fulfills my rules #1 and #2, but not yet
fulfilled #3 and #4. So yes, I'm extremely eager to set PO there, but at
 the same time I'm hesitant!

What should I do???! Help!

AK

Is it a matter of probability?

See this part of the chart (in red circle)

First, the blue zone is an important zone as you can see:

Now we zoom into the red circle:

Here, I have seen price engulfed south, breaking 3 demand levels before retracing up to FTR at point 4.

If we follow RTM's engulf rule, then this is not a valid engulf because
engulf of 3 is not enough, price hit and bounced upwards from the end of
 compression.

But if we follow an alternative rule - which is engulf of a low (or multiple engulf of low), then this would be a valid PA.

posts.author: fxeyes
posts.text:
Just learned about BSZ last week. Interesting that's its the first
thing I see on the open. Didn't recognize it at first, so i missed the
trade. Reacted to a great s/r level, m5 kink.

posts.author: fxeyes
posts.text: definitely need to do more homework

posts.author: fxeyes
posts.text: Missed trade, need to be faster with my reads

posts.author: fxeyes
posts.text:
Was able to still get in on UC. QM formed within PAZ, zone starting
at one PCP + qm lvl, ending at a higher PCP. Very conservative TG1 at
PAZ level, looking for symmetry to complete the trade.

posts.author: fxeyes
posts.text: Result from previous trade. Incredible reaction, gotta shake the short bias. iLS was a great entry zone

posts.author: fxeyes
posts.text:
EU hit a nice mpl level on H4. Got a LTF confirmation (pole cm) but
engulf hit a FL so kinda risky, took tg1 asap. Gonna SAS this one and
gamble a bit (no PA for a bigger up move yet, but I like the pole up and
 move down on H4), ftg at the QM level to complete symmetry. If it
starts to compress into the H4 pole it's in now, might get out early.

posts.author: fxeyes
posts.text:
Price hit nice H4 mpl zone, with LS lining up with H4 lvl. Hesitated
at 1 when it hit level and started compressing into zone. Hesitated
again at 2 after an engulf and retrace back to LS. Finally got in on
the 3rd try, QM lvl + PCP. Got out half at tg1, not sure what to do
about the other half yet, probably should have just closed it (no HTF
engulf on that big move down)

posts.author: fxeyes
posts.text:
Update on post #8 EU

Saw that there was a really strong level to react on LTF, S/R + Mo lvl +
 kink, exited manually when it didn't look like it was going to break
through. Price retreated but then make the next move up. This meant i

Reminder to follow rules: trade tactics

Although i got out of this mistrade relatively unscathed, its a reminder
 to follow rules, as one rule broken leads to other rules broken.

Entry 1 was at a supply level, but no tricks played so I should have
played it tight on TT. Got good entry, but reaction was compression back
 to untouched zone. Instead of exiting half at flag, I held on just a
little longer trying to get a perfect 1:1 for BE. But of course, PA
reacted as you expected and it breaks my zone, turning a (near) BE to a
loss. Next zone was the one I was really gunning for. Price shoots
into it, but i hesitate because of the mistake earlier, so i get a not
so good entry, and exit the entire trade on s/r, instead of selling just
 half, and holding on to HTF trade.

Lessons:

- Follow PA for BE, don't try to pull 1:1 or more if PA is not telling
you that you can. (Or don't take trade if 1:1 isn't there for BE).

- Broken rules and mistakes leads to more broken rules and mistakes.
Instead of a slight gain with an opportunity for a HTF trade, i end with
 a small loss.

posts.author: Ifmyante
posts.text:
In words:

Draw the line from the LS.

Go to the right hand side of the swing high/low.

Find where price, coming from the H/L, broke the line.

Draw LSK from the deepest retrace after the break, back to the furthest advance before the retrace.

Should there be smaller kinks in LTF on the right edge of this kink,
mark them too, as clean orders here are what allow us to get to the pip
entries, right at the LS price.

Lots of words, I know, but try to apply them literally to a couple of
charts, noting all the steps, and you will never forget the technique

happen to line up with an LS, FL, CM, or some other price structure,

When we draw left shoulder kinks, it is always better to draw the whole
kink in that scale, not just a part of it. Then you can clearly see
which point first reacted to the kink and then decide if it is a QM or a
 DM. The trick you marked actually reacted to the original LS kink if
you carefully see. Then engulfed into compression. Then retraced back up
 and came down.

too non-specific for me. From whatever little success I had with LS

this fact that left me sleepless for nights on end, how could I just

got activated because price crossed them on the way down. Below the blue
 lines, you would have to use red lines from previous highs and lows as

obvious stuff for you, but for me, I am a bit slow I guess.

different trading methodologies. I'm not primarily looking at these
lines for kinks to trade; I try to look at price as a whole, and use
s/r, ls, rs, kinks, etc.. as factors for areas of entry. I have a lot
of lines on my chart but i naturally ignore a lot of em (and I'm
reconsidering how/when to draw them), so whether i draw a line
'correctly' is less important.

Maybe you should simplify things for now and just look for upcoming LS
(MPLs), using rectangles. Then you can look for a kink at the inner
line of the rectangle.

Oh one more note, you picked a chart that is pretty congested, which makes it harder to pick apart for learning purposes.

Here's an example of a recent trade idea. Notice how the s/r lines
don't come into play until later in my read. And notice how it's only
one factor in my decision making. So that's just one way I use lines,
and you can see why i don't make such a big deal about drawing the right
 lines (which makes it hard for me to give you a good answer).
Sometimes price sets itself up so that the lines are more obvious, which

lines in congestion. Maybe there are others on here that know how to do

think your trouble is mixing up the lines between different time frames.
 Im reiterating stuff being said in the video and video forum (i
rewatched em), but I'll try to re-interpret it in a way that'll
hopefully help you.

Starting with a blank chart:

1. Drawing your major lines, at the extremes, where price has crossed it
 at least once. These are the lines that cut across all the way the
charts. The obvious stuff. Use judgement call of how far to go back as
 your TFs get smaller. There shouldn't be too many of these.

2. This one is trickier and you'll just have to practice and find a way
that works for you. The tops and bottoms of FLs that broke an important
 FL are important. But when price crosses price alot, it's leads to a
lot of lines. So if it looks important, draw a line across the chart.
If you're unsure, maybe only if it's been crossed recently.

3. Include the rest: PCP, Cm breaks, etc...Again same as two, maybe only
 include recently crossed ones, unless it looks really important.

4. Any other areas that seem to stand out, given what price is currently doing.

5*. I'll also throw in areas where price swings are at least semi-major
 and tends to swing a lot, if it hasn't been picked up by any of the
above (which is unlikely). The area will need more 'touches' the lower
the timeframe. So for example, in Mn it needs at least 3 touches. In
Wk it needs at least 5 touches. etc... These numbers can change
relative to the chart (charts that whipsaw back and forth will naturally
 have alot of touches. For example USDJPY vs USDCAD in Mn chart.

These should be all your major lines. For lines that you are not sure
about, just leave it out for now. I'll naturally be picked up in a lower
 tf. Then go and find your kinks. If you're not sure about something,
just use a judgement call. Don't worry too much about being wrong.
Here's an example from a chart that crosses alot

4

I dont feel like I'm an expert at this, but i think you might be over
complicating things trying to be perfect. I kinda feel like i've over
done it already, and a number of the lines was better left to the lower
time frame, but its no worries. Maybe I'll dive into the LTF and adjust
 if needed. You just have to make a judgement call when you;re not
sure. Do you want to be more cautious so you won't miss a trade (but
will make your reading more difficult because you have so many lines),
or do you want a clean chart so the reading becomes easier?

Thank you for the insight IF! Between Sali's achievement of figuring
out the market through the same resources we have (probably less since
he doesn't appear to use the video concepts), and Ysbail's recent
improvements through study, I'm inspired to use your teachings to look
behind the covers of price and see what's going on underneath. I have
an odd way of learning; i need to know all the pieces, play with them
and see how they all work individually, before I can put them all
together. I've played with enough of the pieces and seen them in action
 in live trading to have a good idea of what they're about. But there
are some questions and uncertainty about them that i think is causing
hesitation and second guessing. I also have a theory of how the market
works. I seems like a good time to stop and do some intense studying to
 answer these questions. I'm going to list them out here for myself as a
 guide for my study, but feel free to offer any guidance where you see
fit =)

Flag Limits

1. How do I correctly identify FLs, so I can find the correct engulfs
and targets? I've been confused by a couple of styles:[/li]

a. Finding the kinks through major S/R lines.

i. If i'm trying to follow the FL breaks, how do i identify with FL to 'start' with?

ii. Or do I just find the last FL that breaks on the right side? If so,
 how do I draw the FL when price is choppy through the line?

b. I've also seen people draw FLs based on the last FL that's been holding price, then trace through it, which seems more local.

i. In this case, was there already an engulf somewhere that's offering guidance for the trade?

ii. Were they tying it in with a major s/r further to the left?

2.

PAZs

1. I understand there are PAZs in between the spaces of MPLs, but the
PAZs that stand out to me are the ones through symmetry, which seems to
be through s/r. I need further study of PAZs through MPLs (and I assume
FLs)

2. Do those concepts already naturally intermix?

2. How do i identify trades within a PAZ? Lets say a PAZ engulfs one
way, how far can price retrace (within the context of the last FL)
before going to the next FL?

Engulfs

1. I guess I need to a better understanding of FLs and targets first.

2. Sali had an interesting concept of FLs engulfing within an engulf, not necessarily always at the edge of it.

3. I think i need to train myself to look for these engulfs first for trade ideas.

Entries

1. Instead of looking at all the possible sets of orders and trading
each as price approaches, there seems to be a of figuring out where the
last set of orders are before price turning (and this may not always be
the last set of untouched orders, i think).

2. Should i only enter at mpls/qm/ls? If so, what makes them tradable,
do they have a particular structure? If seen price bounce at really odd
 looking patterns. Were they 'valid' or were they simply just noise
between the true mpls?

QM

1. Too often I've missed great QM trades because I was waiting it to
the neckline, but price turns before then. Why? Was it left there for
later? If so, how was it used later? Maybe this ties into the concept
of last orders for a given scale.

2. Should I even chase entries below the neckline? If so what should I
be looking for? Is it just down to MM or are there clues in price that I
 should be following?

 orders, order flow and transactions

1. Some concepts that seem to be at the core of Sali's trading. Interesting, need more study.

Scale

1. Heh, what else can I say. It's hard, need deliberate practice.

And the theory. Its been said many times that price simply goes from FL
 to FL. Engulfs of these FLs (whatever these engulf signals are)
indicate the ITs are ready to move price to the next level. Footprints
are left behind in the form of mpl/qm/ls levels of remaining orders and
ultimately, where price will turn. Reversal signals and tricks will be
played as we approach these orders. The more orders they have to fill,
the more tricks will have to be played. And we tie these signals
through scale to get the complete picture. That seems to be pretty much
 it, no? But the trick is to accurately identify these signals,
especially in real time. And that's where I think I need to go back and
 fully understand FLs, how they're engulfed, the footprints left behind,
 and targets, as they seem to be the fundamental framework for what we
do.

Wow that was a lot more questions than i thought I had. Probably left a
 few out too. I feel like before I've been frustrating with not trading
 because that's where 'true' learning happens. But now I feel like true
 learning happens when you have full grasp of the concepts, and using
the market to test out your theories. You, Sali and many others before
us has showed us you can read the market to the pip, so that is now my
goal, and the material is all here. Whether i reach it or not, I will
become better through it's journey. As always, thanks for everything
you've provided us IF! Now time to get

news week (US FOMC meting, GBP major events, etc..), where when i got
loose (trading areas of interest without confirmation) and was getting
killed. Where that strategy sometimes works well in previous days.

I did some analysis of old trades, and watching the charts today, price
is moving pretty much exactly as expected now! Completely different
than earlier in the week! And of course, its a slow day! News has run
its course. HTF S/D is being respected, kinks are being respected,
price is at least bouncing on all PA (compression, LS/RS). Damn easy to
 trade in the LTFs. and the HTF stuff is easier to read and playing out
 as expected as well. No surprises. Of course, I'm gun shy today
because of the poor performance from yesterday. Frustrating watching
all the predictions come true, almost to a fault.

So I guess the question is, do you guys have any tips or tricks for
recognizing these days? Its tricky sometimes because price seems to set
 up for big news days before the event. Sometimes there's no news on
the calendar and price still does crazy stuff (maybe its news from other
 countries, like China, that can move Asia markets). This concept seems
 SO incredibly important, especially if hanging out in the LTFs, and
explains a lot of why I sometimes have incredibly bad days, and
incredibly good days.

Notes for myself, but feel free to comment:

1. Higher TF compression seems to be key. The big boys are around when we see it.

2. On these slow days, we can be aggressive with scalping. Most action
seems to be respected. Kinks, important s/d, flipped transactions,,
compression fades, ltf engulfs, etc...

3. On trending days, the scales seem to change to the Highest time
frames. Dont trust things to give significant or even minor bounces in
the lowest tfs. Sometimes even the higher TFs. Probably prudent to
follow the larger trend in the LTF (pole into direction of trend,
compression back), and recognize where price is coming from and going to
 in the highest tfs.

4. So understanding which scales are most important for a given day is
also important. The bigger the news impact, the higher the TF we have to
 go. Which also begs the question, what type of news applies to which
scales? I'm especially thinking about news that fundamentally changes
direction for months (although I guess we'd also be able to see this by
reading the charts in the HTFs).

5. Do certain pairs tend to move like this more than others? Such as the minor crosses? Need to research.

Anyways, just some thoughts for now. Need to do some research. Any comments are appreciated!

posts.author: fxeyes
posts.text:
I realize I'm overloading my brain by constantly being sucked into the
 LTF looking for trades, trying to trade both sides. Scalping and
mixing TFs. So by the time price does get to my HTF zone, I'm exhausted
 and a bit confused, losing sight of the HTF trade. Even when I catch
the HTF, I cut my TG short because of the scalping. This is a
continuous habit, and when I get into this 'mode', I always do poorly.
 On the opposite end, I tend to be very tentative getting into my first
couple of trades. Then I see trades go by that I was suppose to get in,
 and start 'chasing'. Need to fix these bad habits. Reminders:

1. Stick to HTF for your trading day m15+. Find a direction and stick
with it. Let the trade come to you. Patience. If you don't have a
read for a pair, don't trade it. Be careful fading big trends without
confirmation.

2. Trust your HTF read. Entry and Target. Need to train myself to just
 enter when I see an entry, and stop reanalyzing. See entry, execute.
See entry, execute. Unless you are at the best orders, look for
approach or confirmation.

3. Trust your read. Let them run to your identified TG, unless you see bad PA (CM reaction, reversal at the right TF).

Remember that you make good trades when you have a HTF read of the
story. Scalping has always caused you trouble. Focus on fixing the bad
 habits, and creating good ones.

Go back and look at your trade plan. What are you following, what are
you not? What do you need to change behaviorally to follow your trade
plan?

/rant over

posts.author: fxeyes
posts.text:
Ok I think I know what's causing inconsistent runs in my trading.
There are periods when I really focus on FLs and engulfs (good!) and
other periods where I focus on the orders and not paying enough
attention to the FLs and engulfs (bad!). I think this is when I get
lazy and not doing through analysis through all the TFs. Ultimately it
means i'm not following my rules.

Rule #1 - If trading in the direction of a HTF engulf, you can TT your
zones. Be conservative with tg1 until you are at the last set of orders
 (mpl, original fl, last set of orders). Sometimes I'm not reading
engulfs right, so need more studying. Can't be frustrated if I'm
following the rules. This rule keeps me out of trouble on trending
days.

Rule #2 - If you don't have a clear engulf, but see a nice set of orders, you can only trade it if:

1. You have approach (mostly *good* CP, sometimes its just building the order and not really CP for a turn)

2. You have LTF verification.

3. If it's something really strong (LSK + nicely formed kink or other PA around kink). I think this one gets me in trouble.

I'm not doing a good job of just taking what I can get here, always
hoping for a reversal. I really need to take profit at tg, and re-enter
 on engulf. Need to pay special attention to reaction, get out if it's
CPing away.

Problem areas

1. I also need to stay out of the m1 unless looking for a zone or entry. m1 engulfs can lie in the context of a bigger move.

2. Mixing scalping with HTF trades makes me forget the bigger picture. I get sucked in a miss the big move.

3. Give more weight when I see CP. Too many times I see price CPing
against me, thinking I should get out and don't, but rather *hoping*
that price will continue on. CP wasn't lying about 90% of the time. I
 probably need to zoom out and re-evaluate the HTF picture when this
happens. Although having a HTF read will probably prevent alot of this
from happening in the first place.

That'll be the focus for the next 30 days, train these new behaviors until they're second nature.

For some reason, I have a hard time trusting my overall reads, although they tend to be right a majority of the time.

Instead I'll do stupid stuff like:

1. Fading strong trends without good confirmation.

2. Trading kinks and mpls and disregarding PA (direction of engulf, HTF
trend, etc..). As if the kinks and MPLs will magically hold (its the PA
 that tells us what price is going to do stupid, kinks and mpls are
areas of interest).

3. Getting sucked in LTF and forgetting the bigger trade.

4. Not believing the PA I see and trusting the kinks and mpls more. Applies to entries and reactions.

I dont know why I just don't trust my reads. Maybe some deep
psychological issues or bad habits i'm still not shaking. I think it
also means my rules arn't being followed. Gotta think of a way to
re-train myself. Something I'll sleep on for the rest of the night. So
 what should have been like a 20x day ended up being a 2x day. I marked
 up my thought process throughout the day, and all the signals that i
simply ignored. Ah maybe that's it, spending a week or 2 just
executing, get it into muscle memory... hmm.. How did some of you
overcome this?

What I do (read I try to do) is two have kind of two different trading
plans, two mind sets. One for long term HTF trading, the other one just
for scalping. Well that's whenever I have time to sit down and spend
some time trading.

So for HTF I only go down to LTF in order to look for entry points, and find kinks in the past, set SL, PA, ...

I don't mix this process with scalping LTF trading.

I came to this because I don't have to much time to trade due to my
work. Maybe an hour or two a day, and not everyday. Of course I still
struggle a bit, missing trades, or being impatience if I haven't traded
in a while.

Well that's how I am trying to handle it.

Hope this helps.

posts.text:
Hey bro,

Can I ask what do you mean when you are saying "watching PA" at the zone of interest ( let's make it short - ZOI )? is PA an engulf of opposite direction from where price coming from?

Something like when price getting close/touch/inside the ZOI, you'll want to wait for engulf down (your 4 ZOIs)?

What would it need to engulf that counts as a real engulf (Not FO)? breaking/engulfing last flag? There are flags in all LTFs (M1, M5, M15), which one that you would weight more? Very often I saw that an engulf of M1 flag failed to flip price, and engulf of M15 flag has put price too far and entering will be in the mid way, which is no good (IF said entry should be at extreme).

Also, what happen when price break the first of your ZOI? will you take a trade on the retrace to the DP, and TP at your second ZOI (from bottom up)?

Sorry to ask a lot of questions at once, because I think it's all tightly related...

posts.text:
Good trading pal. Some of those are unconfirmed trades - you just going off PA around the zones? Lose many like this (if you don't mind me asking)?

I resolved last week to try take nothing but confirmed trades from now on (unless I'm already well clear of my profit target for the day, then I don't mind SAS style) - I was hitting some awesome winners, but losing a load too, and I can't cope with going live in those sort of circumstances. 16 trades now since I lost one - some of those are b/e, but that was something I also needed to improve on - reading when price wasn't going the right way off my entry, because I'd read something wrong, and getting out without a loss.

By the way - 23 pip spread on GU? I guess you're not on an ECN broker? It's about 3 or 4 pips usually on mine - it makes all the difference for getting in tight and being able to take quick profit.

Cheers

posts.author: ShadowPit
posts.text:
HTF and down...always, before you place a trade, when you're managing a trade, when you close a trade. Don't give yourself tunnel vision on M1 charts.

EURCAD M30 Strong push into M30 supply. All eyes on the FL.

EURCAD M5FL Engulfed. No real nice supply though. So we must watch PA at a point of interest. In this case we can see the distribution of sell orders quite clearly during Asia and now in hindsight during London.

EURCAD M1 M1 - push into area of interest. Price comes down and engulfs the base of compression, what more confirmation does one need? The doubt will kick in at this point. Could a diamond form and stop us out? Yes. Could price shoot higher 20+ pips and find higher supply? Yes. Is it likely? No, because we keep our rules simple and repeatable. Risk - 8 pip SL.

posts.text: What about busted QM's too? They can be highly reactive on return. Things I've notice about em ----1. There is quite often one on the LTF right before a major turn, like a final IT trick. 2. The reaction level (first shoulder) can still be valid well into the future after prices crosses many time....maybe because of point 3 3. There's quite often a quick move away when QM breaks... and normally a fast drop/ rise to return. This creates nice R/S flip at first shoulder level (which can be nice buy/sell level after change in trend.

ShadowPit

Form your analysis around interesting and obvious levels, a single chart mark up could involve the following 7 step process: Step 1: Draw a horizontal line along support or resistance. Step 2: Label the engulfs (ENG) of this line when they occur. Step 3: Label the decision points (DP) of those ENG. Step 4: Label the FTRs that form AT or AFTER the DP has formed. Step 5: Observe when price is capped by a DP or FTR...this will give you an idea who is in control, buyers or sellers, whilst keeping you out of bad trades. Step 6: Observe when price engulfs a DP or FTR you have labelled. Step 7: Label the NEW DP. Rinse and repeat.

Now imagine the power when you combine this with multi-timeframe analysis and when you wait for the price action to confirm your bias.

nice article.. qoute from ALPHA OMEGA, is it true?

AlphaOmega said: "Some people here are just wrong in their understanding and theories. The whole assumption that only the buyers and sellers (traders) move the price is just wrong! The fx market in the way it exist today is not pure auction. It's a little bit more complicated. Think of the market as two sides. 1. The SELL side - these are the Liquidity providers and the market makers. 2. The BUY side - these are the liquidity consumers. (all traders, large and small, hedge funds, and all other market participants who trade in order to exchange currency for business/corporate transactions). Over 98% of the fx liquidity is provided by 15-20 banks, and about about 80% that liquidity comes from just the biggest 5-8 banks. The SELL side not only controls the market - they ARE the market, they own it! This is THEIR game. Not the game of the traders(regardless of size). If for some reason the market makers want to move the price 1000 pips in 5 min. - they can do that! The traders CANNOT! When you see the price suddenly jumping like crazy and creating this long big single bars on your chart(usually just after news release), what do you think happened there? You think this a result from huge volumes ( traders buying/selling)?? NO it is NOT!. There is very little volume done during these moment. What actually happens, is market makers pulling/removing their limit orders. (They reduce their risk by providing less liquidity on the risk side of the market). Of course the buy side( the traders) have some influence, but nothing significant. When the news hits the wires, the liquidity providers will be the first to react. That's their job. Then, when there is no news and no risk events, this is the other side of the game called price manipulation and stop hunting - take the lows, take the highs, creating fake breakouts and squeezing traders on both sides. Why market makers doing all this? Because volume = profits for them. If price doesn't move, nobody trades. No volume from the buy side = no profits for the market makers. So they will do anything they can to provoke the traders to trade. They will move the price all day long searching for the buy side. Less than half of the price movement is actual buying/selling from traders".

Also BIS (Bank for International Settlements) where countries like Switzerland can make deals in the market with some kind of incognito, no one knows who ordered money transactions made by BIS. Okay, I'm going to start a journal.

As anyone who knows me would expect, it is going to be different than most. That's why I choose the name "Black Sheep". I am the "Black Sheep" of the Supply/Demand trading flock here at RTM.

If you are new to Supply/Demand trading, I urge you to read the wonderful journal here like. I wont mention any names simply because I do not want to leave any out. Which is another way of saying you can't go wrong with any of them. My journal is different.

I am going to attempt to do two things:

(1) Show open Supply/Demand Delta Zones on various 60 minute (or higher) charts. These zones are not trade signals (more on this later). (2) Show trades taken on the 5 minute time frame for the EUR/USD and JPY/USD currencies. These trades will primarily be shown in hindsight, but I will include information from my trading station for verification. If you saw my old journal at FF, then you know what I mean.

Here are two recent charts of Gold (XAU/USD cdf). BTW as an American, I can not trade this cdf. I could of course trade the futures contract, but I would never do that on such a large time frame which could mean holding overnight.

Again, no prognostications are being made here. We simply see open Supply or Demand Zones. These Zones are ideal places to look for either shorts or longs respectively. I believe that these zones are not trade signals in and of themselves. Therefore, I need to see some type of entry signal within them to get into the market. That is why another name for these zones is Entry Signal Zone.

The basis for my zones is the concept of AGGRESSION. I want to get into that concept in the next post.

posts.author: HiddenGap
posts.text:
A lot of well meaning people often make a huge mistake when trying to explain why the market did what it did at any given time. They say things like, " the market went up today because there were more buyers than sellers". Or they say," the market went down due to a 'seller's' strike". These are completely wrong. The market's sole purpose is to bring a buyer and a seller together. Every price where a transaction takes place MUST have a buyer and a seller.

WHAT MOVES THE MARKETS, IS THE RELATIVE ENTHUSIASM OR AGGRESSION OF EITHER THE BUYER(S) OR THE SELLER(S).

Let's take a simplified example.

Suppose you want to buy a car. The price you are willing to pay is 50,000. The seller of the car is asking for 100,000. Now let's suppose we can't just split the difference and make a transaction at 75,000.

The car will sit there and no transaction will happen unless one of you is willing to move. Suppose you as a buyer see three more potential buyers coming. You may now have incentive to raise your price to 100,000. You are now willing to hit the ASK. This willingness is enthusiasm or aggression. The opposite could be true as well. Suppose the Seller becomes aware that another sellers of the same car is coming and is willing to take 45,000. The first seller would have incentive to quickly lower his price to 50,000. That is, the seller needs to hit the BID and make a transaction happen before the buyers gets word of the other car on the market.

This is what actually moves the market. Buyers willingly hitting the ASK will raise price and Sellers willingly hitting the BID will cause price to fall. Therefore, If we want to determine where a key change in the supply/demand dynamic as taken place, we look for where the sellers have been more aggressive (hitting the BID), which we call supply. Or we look for where the buyers have been more aggressive (hitting the ASK), which we call demand.

There are a few more things that go into the definition of an Aggression bar. The main point is that for every buyer there is a seller. A transaction takes place when one side moves aggressively to accept the price from the other.

posts.text:
So, how do we interpret aggression on a price chart?

There are some basic elements we are looking at:

(1) Volume

(2) Range (3) Effort (4) MidPoint trend (5) Open/Close percentages (6) Hidden Gaps (7) Facilitation

" Green (+ tick volume and + MFI) A Green signifies three things:

1. More players are entering the market (+ volume); 2. The arriving players are biased in the direction the bar is moving; 3. The price movement is picking up speed as it goes (+ MFI)." Bill Williams

This is a key concept for understanding an aggression bar. We want to see a bar that has an increasing range on increasing volume. And we want to see volume proportional to the range.

Another very key factor is "MidPoint trend". If the midpoint of the current bar is greater than or equal to the high of the previous bar, the immediate trend is UP. If the midpoint of the current bar is less than or equal to the low of the previous bar, the immediate trend is DOWN. If buyers are being more aggressive than sellers, then one would expect to see the midpoint trend to be UP. If sellers are being more aggressive than buyers, then one would expect to see the midpoint trend to be DOWN.

We are also looking at volatility. We are measuring this in two ways. We are looking for candle bodies that are greater than the previous 3 intervals. Thus making the interval the largest candle body in 4 intervals (inclusive). This is the candle definition of a WRB, where B stands for body. We go one step further. We also look for the range to be the largest range (H-L) in 4 intervals (inclusive). This is the bar definition of a WRB, where B stands for bar.

To determine if an aggression bar is a key change in the supply/demand dynamic in the market, we will need to look at the price action following it. But before we do that, there is one element of the subsequent price action we need to see to determine if a true aggression bar occurred. All aggression bars form Hidden Gaps. Take a look at the chart above. Notice that the low of the candle after the "Climber" is greater than the high of the candle prior to the "Climber". This area is a Hidden Gap. If we were to erase the middle interval we would have an actual gap. We know actual gaps are valid supply/demand delta zones. These Hidden Gaps may be signaling a valid zone as well.

posts.author: HiddenGap
posts.text:
My last post to Romano83 got me thinking.

Actually, it brought up an issue that I have been struggling with for a long time: what is the best "Entry Signal Method" to use. In trading as in life, there are trade offs. No one method is perfect all the time.

Supply/Demand Zone trading seems to offer a unique situation with respect to entries. As I have stated before, I am not a "limit order" proponent. The main reason being I do not believe that a Supply or a Demand Zone is a trade signal in and of itself. I also believe this to be the case with Support and Resistance, which are not the same things as Supply and Demand.

Now I know that a the market can't always respect a zone (supply or demand), but it is the respecting of these zones that tends to give belief and trust in them. Yet, suppose the market respected the zones 90% of the time. However each time it did, it failed to give an entry signal. Where's the profit in that?

There are many times when the market respects my Supply/Demand Zones and no trade signal is given. This begs the question are the entry signal patterns lacking? Do I need less strict patters or more patterns in general? Although there are VSA patterns, I look at VSA as the alternative to a price pattern based entry signal. On the surface, VSA would seem to make more sense with Aggression Bars.

This is not a VSA thread, so I do not want to get too much into it. This is an example from Friday of the Yen.

Point A. is a wide spread down interval on increasing volume. However, note that the volume is less than average. The volume is also disproportionally small compared to the range of the interval. Of course note that this down interval is into an area where the buyers were previously aggressive.

Point B. is an Squat. The range of this interval is small than the previous interval, but the volume is greater. And although the interval makes a lower low than the previous interval it actually closes on its high. From a VSA perspective, this can only mean buying. This is a possible entry point. It's a bit "aggressive", but it tells the story you would want to hear. In an area where buyers were previously aggressive, we see increased activity( volume=activity) on an interval that is closing on the high after a wide spread down interval that was lacking in activity.

Point C. This is your basic No Supply. This down interval has volume less than the previous two intervals. In fact, it is colored grey because it is the lowest volume in the last 20 intervals. Volume is activity of the professional trader. Therefore if volume is this low, we can conclude that the professional traders are not interested in lower prices. If they are not interested in lower prices, it must be because they expect prices to rise. Again, buyers have already demonstrated that they were the more aggressive ones in area of the price chart. It should be of no surprise that as price falls back into this area the sellers are not aggressive and are in fact withdrawing.

Anyway, Point B is not a true hammer so I don't have a valid Hammer pattern for entry. None of the other patterns I look for are there either. So if I use VSA, I can get into this trade. If not, I can only take satisfaction in seeing the Supply/Demand Zone respected. Just seeing the Zone(s) respected is nice, but leaves your account the same. And lest I forget, there are certainly times when the VSA does not give an entry signal but a price pattern appears.

It's late and I am just rambling now. Forgive me. I would like to hear from some others who went through this struggle and how they came to reconcile it.

posts.text:
Once we have an Aggression bar that forms a hidden gap, we know we have a change in the Supply/Demand Dynamic in the market. However, not all changes are key changes. Only key changes in the Supply/Demand Dynamic become our Supply/Demand Zones.

In order to determine if a key change has occurred, we want to look at the price action following the appearance of the Aggression Bar. What we want to see is strong continuation. There are a couple of definitions of strong continuation. below is an example of one.

Notice that after the Aggression interval we see two consecutive white (close>open) that are making higher highs and not lower lows and are closing higher. Also not that both close higher than the close of the Aggression bar.

Basically, we are defining what Sam asks when he asks, "how does the market leave the (would-be) zone"?

posts.author: HiddenGap
posts.text:
Another example of the type of price action we want to see to confirm a key change in the Supply/Demand Dynamic has taken place involves Fractals. Fractal highs or lows are reaction points. They are also decision points.

If after the appearance of an Aggression bar, we see price move back into the range of the bar but fails to close the Hidden Gap before moving back out and forms a fractal, the market is telling us that this is in fact a Key change in the market.

Closing the Hidden Gap is very important. We never want to see price action close the HG prior to meeting a definiton that tells us a zone is created. Once the zone is created, the HG portion does not matter. A zone is open until price shows conviction above or below the zone..........
