posts.text:
pres78 wrote: HG the bar before the one marked engulf fills the hidden gap. Does that now void this zone for you for any future trading?

Hello my friend.

The simple answer is no.

The Hidden Gap alerts us that there has been a change in the Supply/Demand Dynamic in the market. Once the market has shown that the change was KEY (via strong continuation for example) a Supply/Demand Zone is created. At this time, the Hidden Gap portion of the zone does not really matter much. Trade signals are valid as long as the Zone remains open.

There are some traders who only use the Hidden Gap as the Zone. If that were the case, this zone would still be valid for future trading because the interval that closed the Hidden Gap is involved in a valid trading pattern.

HiddenGap

Here's a good example of what the Hidden Gap can be telling us.

Notice in this example that we have a Drifter (interval where the aggression is by the sellers) that forms a hidden gap. We don't know if we have a KEY change in the Supply/Demand Dynamic, but we know we have had a change in it. We also note that the recent fractal low is within the range of the Hidden Gap. If the fractal low is some sort of decision point, then for this interval to be "gapping" through it must be of some importance.

Still, we don't know for sure until we see the subsequent price action. In this case we do get strong continuation. The definition of strong continuation in this case is, three dark (close<open) intervals with lower highs and lower lows closing lower than the close of the Aggression bar prior to then next swing. Where one of the three dark intervals is an Aggression bar that forms a Hidden Gap.

At the bottom we see an valid "fakie" long trade signal. It closes the gap but it does not close the zone. I like to see conviction to close a zone. Conviction would be a full (non doji) candle body below the zone, where said body's interval is not involved in a valid trade signal pattern.

Please don't stay quiet my friend. You always bring something to the table with your insights and questions.

In a nutshell, the reason the second WRB Hidden Gap does not create a zone is because of cause and effect. Although we don't know that the first WRB is a S/D zone until it meets the strong continuation definition, we do have an idea it will be when we see the second WRB. The reason being the range of the this second WRB is within the range and specifically the body of the first. Therefore, I consider the first to be the origin of the second. Or as two old VSAers might speak, the first Aggression bar is the effort and the second is the result.

When there are two consecutive Aggression Bars that are Hidden Gaps, the first one potentially becomes the zone. Here again, the first is the effort and the second is the result.

Basically, we don't want overlapping zones. Therefore if any portion of an Aggression bar is on or within an existing zone, said Aggression bar cannot create its one zone. The zone it is touching/ within is always seen as the true origin of the movement.

Just the type of question I would expect from you. Keep 'em coming.

Hello. I want to answer these questions if I may.

First, let's look at the question/comment in the upper right hand corner. There is no Supply/Demand Delta Zone there. Why? Because we do not see any type of strong continuation before price fills the hidden gap.

The second question/comment is a bit more complex. You are correct that I said the aggression candle should be a WRB using both definitions. Definition 1 defines a WRB as Wide Range Body (open-close) greater then the previous three bodies. This definition is primarily associated with candles. Definition 2 defines a WRB as Wide Range Bar (High-low) greater than the previous three bar's ranges. This definition is primarily associated with bar charts. If you think about it, you can see that it is possible to have an interval meet the definition of a Wide Range Body and not be a Wide Range Bar, and vice versa. By combining the two no matter what type of chart was used, the aggression bars would always be the same. But if one was to choose to only look at candle charts and therefore only focus on the body, it would not be wrong.

If one does focus only on the body to define an aggression interval, however, the interval in question should still be on an increasing range. No matter what one chooses, the key is to stay consistant.

Hello.

This is another case that tells us that we are likely dealing with an aggression bar could be a key change in the Supply/Demand Dynamic. The main thing is how you draw the Supply/Demand Delta Zone. In the chart below you can see two examples. In the one on the left, we see the normal way to draw the Zone. We are drawing the zone from the high and the low of the Aggression interval. The hidden gap is defined as the area between the high of the interval previous to the aggression bar and the low of the interval after the aggression bar.

In the example on the right, there is an actual gap that occurs prior to the Aggression bar. If we get the required strong continuation that tells us a key change has occurred, we will draw the Supply/Demand Delta Zone a bit different. We will include the gap as part of the zone. Notice that the low of the zone is not the low of the Aggression bar, but rather the high of the previous interval prior to the actual gap. Basically, we want to include the actual gap in the Zone. Note how the hidden gap is defined as the area from the low of the Aggression bar to the low of the interval proceeding it.

The easy answer is that I found WRB Analysis first and after looking through that prism it's hard to change to Sam's SD method.

The harder, and truer, answer has to do with how and why I was attracted to WRB analysis in the first place. I came to WRB analysis after I started my journey into Volume Spread Analysis (VSA). Tom Williams would talk a lot about looking for a low volume narrow spread (range) interval within the spread(range) of a high volume interval. After looking at numerous charts, I was able to see the validity of his claim. Many good trade set-ups were indeed occurring in the range of a wide spread high volume interval. As I was seeing this phenomenon, I came across a post by Mark where he mentioned WRBs. While Mark did not use VSA, I immediately thought that there must be some connection. Or at the very least, they would be compatible. Despite the fact that Mark was originally dealing with the body of a candle and VSA does not look at the open, WRB (Wide Range Body) analysis proved to be very usable with VSA.

By the time I was introduced to Sam's work, I was already a firm believer in the power of the concept of a WRB hidden gap. I also have a problem with one aspect of Sam's method highlighted by your second picture. I do not believe that a Supply/Demand Zone is a trade signal in and of itself. Nor do I believe that Supply/Demand Zones can change polarity. Actually, I should say that in all the videos I have watched, Sam never mentions that zones can reverse polarity. Yet in all the threads I read about SD, the concept of supply becoming demand and vice versa is used.

I don't think this is accurate. If a demand zone is created by a rally base rally pattern and a supply zone is created by a drop base drop pattern, then the only way a demand zone can become a supply zone is if there is a drop base drop at the exact same place. In other words, merely cutting through a demand zone and then finding support (a totally different concept than supply and demand) does not in my opinion constitute a change in polarity. I like the fact that all zones close in WRB analysis. There is no concept of reversing polarity. Which is really a concept of support and resistance.

Hello my friend. The Fakie (or Fakey) is a price action pattern that comes from Nial Fuller's site. There are a few FREE videos on his site or youtube showing it with a bit more detail than follows.

Basically, the Fakie (or Fakey) is a price action pattern that requires there to be a false-break of an inside bar setup. So, once you have an inside bar setup, you can watch for a false-break of the inside bar and the mother bar.

Take a look at the chart below.

A. Is called the Mother candle. We only know it is the Mother candle after we see B. B. Inside interval. That means this interval does not make a higher high or a lower low than the previous candle. C. This interval makes a false break of the high of both the inside bar and the Mother candle, but it closes back within the range of the Mother candle.

Note that the intervals between X and Y also form a fakie. However, this would never be taken because no part of any interval in the pattern is occurring within a valid Supply/Demand Zone.

The false break must be on the first interval that trades outside the range of the Mother candle.

Hello Gristar.

Lots of questions there. Awesome!

I want to first focus on the issue of a zone closing. Take a look at the chart. There are three (3) possible ways a zone can be considered closed. That is to say, each individual can choose which method he or she prefers and then stick to that one for consistency.

Methods

#1. One can consider the zone closed, after price action has filled the zone.

#2. One can consider the zone closed, after price action closes above the zone (for a Supply Zone).

#3. One can consider the zone closed, after a full candle body (white for a Supply Zone) is formed above the the Zone. This body should not be a doji.

I prefer #3. If the interval in question is involved in an entry signal pattern, the zone would remain open. For example, #3 on this chart could have turned out to be part of a valid Fakie pattern. If it did turn out to be a valid Fakie Pattern, then the trade would be taken and the zone would be considered still open.

Also note that one can take trades anywhere within the zone. In fact, there really only needs to be on tick/pip of an entry signal touching some part of the zone for the signal to be considered. So if there are 5 candles in your entry signal pattern, only one tick or pip of one of the intervals has to be touching the zone.

We first need to define an Aggression on bar. All Aggression bars will represent changes in the Supply/Demand dynamic in the market. However, not all Aggression bars will represent KEY changes in the Supply/Demand dynamic in the market. Only those that represent KEY changes will be used to determine a Supply/Demand Delta Zone.

One of the most important requirements for a Aggression bar, is that it forms a Hidden Gap. This particular element is not part of my " Aggression bar finder indicator", so you will see an indication of an Aggression bar on some bars that do not form Hidden Gaps. In reality, they are not Aggression bars and are immediately disregarded.

The other elements that Constitute and Aggression bar are as follows:

1. For a Climber, the open is in the lower 25% of the interval's range, while the close is in the upper 75% of the interval's range. For a Drifter, the open is in the upper 75% of the interval's range, and the close is in the lower 25% of the interval's range.

2. The range of the interval (open -close) is greater than the previous interval's range.

3. Volume is increasing.

4. The interval is a

ide

ange

ody (WRB).

5. The midpoint of the range is greater than the high of the previous range for a Climber. The midpoint of the range is less than the low of the previous interval for a Drifter.

6. For a Climber, the low of the interval is greater than or equal to the low of the previous interval. That makes it a "Buying bar". For a Drifter, the high of the interval is less than or equal to the high of the previous interval. That makes it a "Selling bar". In other words, a Climber will make a higher high but not a lower low than the previous interval. And a Drifter will make a lower low and not a higher high than the previous interval.

Once you have an Aggression bar, you have a change in the Supply/Demand dynamic in the market. To determine if it is a KEY change, we look at how the market reacts to it. We look for strong continuation to verify that a change has taken place.

First I would start out by saying losses happen in trading. They are the cost of doing business. In fact, some call trading a loser's game. Where he who loses best, wins.

Personally, I do not see that as an engulfing pattern. Based on the chart, it looks like the body of candle #5 does not fully engulf the body of candle #4. It looks like the open is equal to the close. So it's not engulfing. In such a case, I would at least like to see the range of candle # 5 engulfing the range of candle #4 and the close of #5 greater than the high of #4. So #5 would have to be an OUTSIDE bar.

There is an entry signal that I have been flirting with that appears hear. It is not perfect, but let's assume it is for discussion. The entry signal is the "confirmation entry" signal. You can find information on it at YouTube or on the PIE II thread at FF.

From this point on unless otherwise stated, when I refer to a number it will be the numbers in black which I have labeled.

#1 is our "stop run candle". I don't like the fact that the upper wick is equal in size to the body of this candle. If the upper wick was bigger than the body, then I would not consider this our start point or "stop run candle".

#2 meets the requirements for the "confirmation interval". It closes higher than the body of the previous candle and it closes in the upper 66 percentile of the range.

At this point, we have a maximum of 3 intervals for price to retrace back into the wick of our "stop run candle". The idea being, that we want to place a stop a few pips below the low of the "stop run candle". Therefore, we would like to minimize our risk by entering as low as possible. One can choose to wait for a 50% retracement of that lower wick to enter. In this case that did not happen. But let's assume a more aggressive style. So we are simply waiting for a retrace that is lower than the low of candle #2 and back into the lower wick of candle #1.

We get this at #4. Now we are in the market. Our risk is defined as the shaded area.

Ultimately, we take a loss on this trade. But take a look at the yellow arrow. The arrow points to a down WRB that closes lower then the low of the candle that triggered us into the market. This could have served as an early warning that the trade was not going to work. So an early exit could be contemplated at this time. One key here is that the WRB occurs within 1-5 intervals after the trigger bar.

More examples with the modifications.

The rules:

1. There may be a variation that does not include a WRB, but as of this time the first requirement is the appearance of a WRB

2. After the appearance of a WRB, we need to see the "Stop run" candle(#1) within 1-3 intervals. Rather than thinking of this interval as a "Stop run" candle, it may be more appropriate to think of it as Supply Swamping Demand (SSD) for shorts or Demand Swamping Supply (DSS) for longs. In the case of SSD, the candle's upper shadow must be greater than the combination of the body and the lower shadow. The SSD candle must also make a higher high than the previous candle.

3. The confirmation candle must close lower than the body of the previous candle (for shorts) and higher than the body of the previous candle for longs. The other requirement is that the body of the confirmation candle is larger than the body of the previous candle.

4. After the confirmation candle (#2), price must retrace to within the range of the upper shadow (for short) within 3 intervals. Excluding the WRB, this is a minimum 3 interval pattern and a maximum 5 interval pattern.

The first modification for me is that an entry signal is "valid" as long as at least one tick/pip of the pattern is in or one a Buying or Selling Aggression Zone.

Most definitely, they have an arbitrary number just to have a rule. Many of their rules are like that actually. Price entering or hitting a zone is enough.

Another modification is that the "Stop run" candle should: (1) make a higher high (for shorts) or a lower low (for longs) than the previous interval. (2) The Upper/lower shadow of the "Stop run" candle should be larger than the combination of the body and the opposite shadow. (3) The initial "Stop run" candle needs to appear 1-3 intervals after a WRB.

Yes, and we should keep in mind this is only one type of the many reversal patterns and possibilities at our areas of interest. We have 2 bar reversal, which is what was in that picture I posted, hangman(for short), inverted hammer(for long) as well as combinations of the above (I have rules being formulated for these as well). I also think whether the high probability zone in question is via a HG/WRB zone or a S&D zone must be taken into account. Low volume test reversals happen more in HG areas and high volume rejections happen at S&D zones. I think one important rule is if price confirms the reversal pattern and you're waiting for pullback, price shouldn't ever open and close above (or below) the stop run candle more than once (maybe not at all?). Also, since we are volume specialists, particular attention should be paid to the intervals after the stop run candle (and of course all of the candles really). Many times wicks to the upside on a shorting reversal trade (these wicks maybe being our pullback we're waiting for) can be low volume tests and/or inverted hammers on top (out of place), absorbing supply for a further push up. That's one place where the confirming entry pullback can get one in trouble. If the pullback was actually on low volume and the next candle closes up, its basically a failed test and price has a high probability of going up further and same for longs.

Another modification under review has to do with the confirmation candle. While it still needs to close below the body of the previous candle (for shorts), instead of having to close in its lower 33%, it only has to have a larger body than the previous interval.

I like this change also. I think I'm going to take the day off trading Friday and I can expand upon what I wrote here and add charts, and study more. I just wanted to get some thoughts down before I forgot what I was thinking: ) Long night and just got back from a show, I usually never stay up this late! Please feel free to correct my mistakes and tell me if I'm completely off base with this.

posts.text:
There is so much to go over I'm not sure where to start. The DTFL confirming entry is actually an aggressive entry and that's why there are so many rules to go along with it, they don't worry about why price moves how it does, they kind of believe that it is rather futile to try and understand why. We know why price moves why it does, S&D. One thing on my mind is the retrace. It's not like one wants price to retrace against the reversal for any reason than for it to be a test for supply or demand and then for it to confirm in the direction of their trade the following candle. DTFL guys have no idea why price retraces (I've talked to Sterling about it), yet they take that retrace (they take it at 15 ticks at least usually 12 ticks from the high/low of stop run candle, it doesn't have to retrace into the wick for them). This is fine, it really gives one a great price to enter the trade. Like I said in the previous post, the following intervals just have to be monitored for failed tests and for price opening and closing above the level one is using. Another thing is the "stop run". For them, the stop run is because "SM" is searching for the liquidity to help them move price in the direction they want it to go (opposite of the stop run). We know price doesn't need a "stop run" to move in a direction. A stop run is a juicy bonus but it's not the reason price turns direction 30+ ticks. Supply sitting at an upper level is more of the reason price turns and goes down than stops being triggered at said level. We know every buyer is really a seller and vice versa which would help "SM" absorb their selling for instance if they ran prices up to actually desire for price to go down. Everyone who was short would become a buyer at that level, buying what "SM" was selling. This line of thinking gets rather convoluted though because said scenario should also trigger an up move according to other philosophies. What I'm getting at is there should be rules for non "stop run" reversals also, which happen a lot of the time. One example from today, I'll show the 3m and 1m chart, they both have examples of non stop run reversals at the same spot. Here is 3m overview chart: 3m

3m. 1. Enters an area that was previously a VHV WRW(wick) area of resistance and now support. 2. Price rejects on UHV, closing on the high but not above body of previous candle. This is alright, we just need it to close above the body of candle #1 within

number of

intervals (1 or 2?) 3. Closes above interval 1, also on its highs. 4. I realize this doesn't retrace into the wick, I'm not sure how I feel about retracing all the way into the wick. Retraces within 8 ticks of the low of interval 1 (I have no set number of ticks yet that it should retrace, DTFL uses 15, that's too much for me, I'm thinking 10 at least). This is where it can get messy. This retrace is also a LVT (lowest volume in prev 6 candles), that does confirm the next interval, even though that interval has a huge upper wick. Taking the trade at the bottom end of interval 4, would allow one to have a stop of 15 say, if the rule was 10 tick retrace at least (10 ticks to bottom of wick and 5 for cushion). One more thing about the LVT too, this last 2 weeks more than half my trades have been on them alone. That makes for some really easy rules. The stop run/2bar reversal/hangman or whatever, can end up doing whatever it does at the area of interest. We don't care because we don't enter until we see a LVT that confirms, within number of candles. That's Sebastian Manby style entry. You miss out on ticks, but are able to have a stop loss of 1-5 ticks at most. Just another idea I suppose.

Now for the 1m and the inverted hammer type entry. This is the same entry spot as 3m. For me the Inverted hammer at an area such as this offers the best risk to reward. One can have a very small stop because if price goes lower it is really then a test (for demand here) on high or low volume, that has passed. The only other reason would be a stop run candle like a hammer after it. A hammer > inverted hammer is a better setup. 1. Inverted hammer on UUHV, right at the demand zone in blue. The interval before it is basically a hammer type stop run as well on UHV with UUHV IH as result. 2. Confirms up above IH. 3. A LVT 4. LVT confirmation candle. For me on an IH type entry its just long after price crosses IH body with 2-5 tick stop in case price goes a bit below again. Waiting for the LVT here still gives a great entry.

HiddenGap wrote: The rules:

1. There may be a variation that does not include a WRB, but as of this time the first requirement is the appearance of a WRB What makes you need a WRB within 3 candles? I've noticed a lot of times its a good sign of reversal when there is a WRB say going up, and then contracting volatility for a good amount of bars slowly going up into a stop run candle at an area of interest.

2. After the appearance of a WRB, we need to see the "Stop run" candle(#1) within 1-3 intervals. Rather than thinking of this interval as a "Stop run" candle, it may be more appropriate to think of it as Supply Swamping Demand (SSD) for shorts or Demand Swamping Supply (DSS) for longs. In the case of SSD, the candle's upper shadow must be greater than the combination of the body and the lower shadow. The SSD candle must also make a higher high than the previous candle.

SSD and DSS is a great way of thinking of it, especially if other candle patterns are used instead of just stop run, big wick candle.

3. The confirmation candle must close lower than the body of the previous candle (for shorts) and higher than the body of the previous candle for longs. The other requirement is that the body of the confirmation candle is larger than the body of the previous candle.

I like this, I also like the progression of candles type of outlook. Say the confirmation candle doesn't completely confirm, as long as the next one finally closes below/above it etc.

4. After the confirmation candle (#2), price must retrace to within the range of the upper shadow (for short) within 3 intervals. Excluding the WRB, this is a minimum 3 interval pattern and a maximum 5 interval pattern.

That's what we have so far............

[/b]

Just a few ideas, I have a lot more to write about this. I hope this isn't too disjointed. The girlfriend is making me do more normal human things so got to go for awhile: )

Here's an example of the flexibility this entry "pattern" can allow. What I want to create is a rule based entry that is specific in nature, yet general enough to allow for a wide range of possibilities.

We begin with the appearance of a WRB. There are a couple of ways to do this. We wait for the appearance of the WRB and then focus on the next 1-3 intervals for our Start Point Candle. Or, we can identify the Start Point Candle first, and look back 1-3 intervals to see if there is a WRB

I think it is easier to identify the WRB and see it as an alert that a signal might be coming.

1': This is our Start Point. It is making a higher high than the previous candle and its upper shadow is greater than the combination of its lower shadow and its body.

2': This candle does not confirm. It does not close lower than the body of the previous candle (the Start Point Candle) and its body is not large than the body of the previous candle.

At this point there is no trade signal.

But wait.

The next candle makes a higher high than the previous candle and has an upper shadow greater than the combination of its lower shadow and body. And it is within 1-3 intervals of the WRB. We have a valid Start Point Candle. A new #1.

: This candle does close lower than the body of the Start Point Candle and also has a body greater than the body of the Start Point Candle.

: We can look to enter as price retraces into the area of the Upper Shadow of our Start Point Candle.

So this is a "Valid" signal, but it does not appear in a Zone. Therefore, no trade would be taken,

There is indeed a Progression of Candles in this pattern, at least with respect to our Start Point.

In this schematic, I have drawn what a Progression of the Start Point can look like.

After the WRB, we have our first Start Point. A Start Point must make a higher high than the previous interval and the upper shadow must be larger than the combination of its lower shadow and its body. This is the candle we start our count on. The next candle should confirm the possible shift in the Supply/Demand dynamic that our Start Candle represents.

In this case, the next candle does not confirm 1A. But it is by definition another Start Point. So we begin our count anew. We can continue to restart our count as long as we are getting consecutive Start Points. Note at 1D we are now beyond 3 intervals after a WRB. Since the initial Start Point was within the 1-3 interval requirement, we are able to continue.

In this example,

is our confirmation candle. The confirmation candle must close lower

than the body of the previous candle and it must have a large body than the body of the previous candle.

Suppose that 2 did not appear, but we got 1F instead. This would be the LAST time we could restart our count. Typically a Zone closes with a close above/below unless the interval that closes above/below is part of a entry signal pattern. In this case not only does this interval close above the zone, but its entire range is above the zone. So the very next candle would have to be a confirmation candle or we would not have the possibility of an entry.

In general, we want to see price retrace into the shadow of the Start Point. As this represents the area where the change in the Supply/Demand dynamic has likely occurred. To enter not only do we need to see a retracement into the shadow, but we need to see that retracement be 10 pips deep.

Update on the Yen.

This one poses more questions than it gives answers.

Ultimately, this one gets into trade management. Remember that the reason we want to see an retracement, is so that we can minimize our risk. We want to place our stop x pips/ticks below the low of the Stop Run (SR) candle. Therefore, the lower price pulls back into the lower shadow, the less our risk will be. Simply put, a pull back into the lower shadow is needed to validate the signal. How much of a pull back into the lower shadow is based on an individual's risk tolerance.

One question that arises is, are we only going to exit with a loss if our stop is hit? If we are only getting out when our stop is hit, we could actually still be long at this moment. Depending on profit targets and position size of course.

Which brings up another issue. As previously stated, we can minimize risk by requiring greater retracements into the lower shadow. Another option is to wait for less of a pull back, but to decrease position size instead.

Now we are starting to get into trade management at this point. So let's come back to this once we have establish what constitutes a valid entry signal............

I believe we can call the modifications set.

The new modifications are: A. There must be a WRB in the sequence. This isn't so much a new rule as it is making the appearance of a WRB definitive.

B. The initial Start Point (SP) must appear 1-

intervals after the WRB. We've gone

from 1-3 to 1-4. Therefore, there can be 3 intervals after the WRB before we see the SP.

C. The Long Lower Shadow (for longs) of the initial Start Point (SP) must be greater than the lower shadows of all the intervals after the WRB and the 3 intervals prior to the WRB. And the Long Lower Shadow must be larger than the bodies of said intervals as well. But the Long Lower Shadow does not have to be larger than the combination of the lower shadow and the body of any interval except its own.

While there will always be losing trades, let's take a closer look at these here.

A1: I am not sure that this is in fact a valid SP. The long lower shadow does not look larger than the body of the candle before it. Nor does it look larger than the lower shadow of the candle before it. The Confirmation Entry is a VISUAL ENTRY. That means the better set-ups tend to be those that you can tell meet the requirements visually with ease. Now, you may do the actual math and conclude that lower shadow is larger than the body of the previous candle. But when you can make that determination easily with the naked eye, the set-up tends to be better.

B1: This is more of an obvious valid SP. A valid signal is produced, which results in a loss.

Let's take a closer look at B5. This is a White (open<close) WRB that appears 1-3 intervals after our entry candle and closes higher than the high of the entry candle. That is a Nullification Candle (NC). In this case, the NC stops us out. But if it had not stopped us out, we would want to be exiting, or at the very least, moving our stop closer to our entry price. A true "contingency" plan would have us stop and reverse our position. Especially since the WRB preceded a doji candle line.

The other place where an NC can appear is after the SP but before confirmation. This NC would tell us not to enter the trade at all.

Note that our NC could be the interval that both enters us into the trade during its creation and tells us to exit once it is complete. Which is the case here.

2. If we are in a short trade, a white (open<close) WRB 1-3 intervals after our entry candle that closes higher than the high of said candle, is a NC.

While we call this the CE pattern in part because it was already called that, we mainly call this the CE pattern because the Entry signal Confirms what the pattern signifies. Ultimately, our pattern is thought to represent a change in the Supply/Demand Dynamic in the market. At the heart of this change, is either the

emand

wamping

upply

DSS) inverval or the Supply

wamping

emand (SSD) interval.

The CC:

1. For a long, the CC must close higher than the previous candle. And for a short, the CC must close lower than the previous candle. 2. The body (ABS(Open-Close)) of the CC must be larger than the body (ABS(Open-Close)) of the previous candle. Where, ABS stands for absolute value. 3. For a long, the close of the CC must be greater than the midpoint of the Long Shadow of the DSS interval. For a short, the close of the CC must be less than the midpoint of the Long Shadow of the SSD interval.

Note: Based on the above rules, the CC can be the same interval as the SSD/DSS interval.

4. Progression. The maximum number of intervals that can appear after the SSD/DSS interval and the CC interval is three (3). Which is to say, if the SSD/DSS interval is not also the CC interval, the CC interval must occur within 4 intervals.

This shows the "full" progression of the CC interval. While I did not mention the NC, you can see a White (Open<Close) WRB among the intervals after the SSD. But it does not close above the high of the SSD's Long Shadow. Also note that this CE did not occur in a Zone, but it does create a Zone.

This visual nature is a benefit as one goes down in time frames. The lower the time frame, the less time one has to do the calculations. It also is beneficial if one is trading multiple markets. What signal should be taken? The signal that is visually apparent rather than the signal that needs to be calculated.

I have shaded one of the intervals yellow to simulate a dark interval, so we can think of the pattern as valid.

Notice at SSD' we have "valid" signal. Again, it is not actually valid, as there is no dark interval among the three (3) intervals prior to the Dark WRB. But we are pretending that the shaded yellow candle is a dark (close>open) interval.

After we see SSD', our thoughts go to finding the CC by the next 4 intervals. While it is not a rule, we would like to see our CC close lower than the close of our SSD' interval. (The actual rule only requires it to close lower than the midpoint of the Long Shadow (LS) of the SSD interval)

The next interval turns out to be a SSD interval itself.

1. Its high is greater than the high of the privous three (3) intervals. 2. Its Long Upper Shadow is greater than the combination of its lower shadow and its body. 3. Its Long Upper Shadow is greater than the upper shadows of all the intervals in the pattern, including the upper shadow of the White WRB 4. Its Long Upper Shadow is greater than the bodies of all intervals in the pattern, excluding the White WRB 5. Its body is smaller than the body of at least one (1) interval of the three (3) intervals prior to the White WRB 6. There are no more than three (3) intervals after the appearance of the White WRB and the appearance of the SSD interval. **Note**: this rule does not need to be true for the progression. Only the firstSSD interval must meet this requirement.

After we see this new SSD interval, we would now begin looking for the CC interval again. Our "count" is set back to zero. Again, notice two intervals later when the CC does appear, it closes lower than the close of the SSD

Also keep in mind that this progression requires the new SSD/DSS intervals to be consecutive, or back to back.

akifusenet wrote: Hi HG,

Amazing additions. CE is evolving very nicely in my opinion. I am just wondering what is the rationale behind the dark body interval requirement? (even for shorts) Akif,

Yes, I too think it is evolving nicely.

That's a great question about the rationale behind the dark body interval requirement.

It is true that the overall concept behind the CE entry could be described as, "a signal pattern manifested by a change in the Supply/Demand Dynamic", with three (3) intervals in particular, the Dark/White WRB, the SSD/DSS, and the CC being necessary elements of that change.

The rationale behind the dark body interval is much more utilitarian.

In looking at many successful CE pattern signals, I have found the that the vast majority of them have at least one dark interval among the three(3) intervals prior to the Dark/White WRB. This of course does not mean the existence of a dark interval guarantees a "winning" pattern. Which brings me to the next point. Among those patterns that "fail", I have noticed more of them do not have a dark interval among the three (3) intervals prior to the Dark/White WRB

There is another reason, which I touched on briefly when this project began. Take a look at the chart below.

This is one of my favorite types of CE entry. The DSS interval appears immediately after the Dark WRB, and the CC interval appears directly after the DSS interval. The DSS interval also happens to be a Doji. What we also have here is a valid "High Close Doji pattern". One of the requirements of the "High Close Doji Pattern", is a dark interval with its close higher than the close of the Doji, So by simply incorporating the need for a dark interval among the three(3) intervals prior to the Dark WRB, I have increased the possibility that a valid "High Close Doji Pattern" would be picked up. Therefore, instead of looking for both the CE entry and the "High Close Doji Pattern", I can focus on the CE entry. With the knowledge that most valid "High Close Doji Pattern signals will also be CE entry signals.

I wanted the CE to be broad enough to encompass a wide range of Price Action and yet be specific enough to incorporate some already known reliable Long Shadow family subgroups.

posts.text:
Should we have a contingency plan?

To say that the introduction of a contingency plan is a game changer, might be a bit hyperbolic. Yet, the addition of a contingency plan would take us to a new dimension as Price Action traders.

So what is a contingency plan

A dictionary definition would be: a course of action to be followed if a preferred plan fails or an existing situation changes.

This valid CE (long) leads us to our preferred plan- As we are in a Demand Zone, to enter on the buy side after the appearance of the CC. And then to ride price movement up using successively higher closing WRBs as profit targets, or as trailing stops, or using unfilled opposing Zones as profit targets. There is more to the plan of course, but for now we need only focus on "the riding price up" part.

Trading is about probabilities, not certainties. So there will be times, perhaps many times, when price does not go up, it goes down. This is why we always want to use a stop. But do we necessarily need our stop to be hit to know that our preferred plan is failing/has failed, or that the existing situation is changing/has changed? Obviously, we do not. So if we can use the available information to tell us we do not want to be long before our stop is hit, can we take that information one step further and deduce that the best course of action is to actually get short?

Before we delve into the rules of the contingency plan, we should note a few important things. First, before you can have a valid contingency plan entry, you must have a validCE. Second, we will be getting short in a Demand Zone and long in a Supply Zone. This is not the same thing as the zones "flipping" (more on this later).

It's late. I will finish this soon. I hope your appetite has been peaked.............

I did want to note that the Supply Zone is yellow, not because it is part of the contingency plan, but because it is the first WRB Hidden GAP with continuation after the FOMC minutes were released at 2 pm on 10/8. If you're saying to yourself, knowing that makes the likelihood of the contingency plan succeeding even greater, move to the head of the class. You're not just trading patterns, you're trading market context.

Hey HG, I can't remember if I thanked you for answering my last question so thanks!

I came to RTM via Wyckoff and VSA.. as you may or may not remember from threads elsewhere. Now that I've internalized SD PA trading, I've taken volume off my charts because I found it unnecessary in trading successfully... For various reasons, which, what the heck, let's get into briefly:

1) VSAers get caught up with looking for high volume and miss a lot of trades. The market turns round on low, medium and high volume at different times. 2) NS/ND can be observed in real time by observing the candle being formed, you can see if there is high or low volume by the amount of activity and often the range/spread. When you see a succession of tiny bars, you know the volume was low, especially on a LTF. 3) On a LTF the volume doesn't seem necessary because it can be inferred from the candle with some degree of accuracy.. and on a HTF the tick volume profile tends to be rather flat. 4) If SD/PA is enough, then adding volume risks giving conflicting signals - if it aint broke, why fix it.

I'm sure there are other reasons, but those are some thoughts. My question is, for Forex trading, do you think there'd likely be much value in delving back into volume and VSA and trying to supercharge my trading with it, or do you think it would likely be unnecessary and a potential point of distraction and confusion?

Cheers man!

Hello ZeeDeveel and thank you for the question.

I have to be honest, I waffle back and forth on the use of volume all the time now. The only thing I know for sure, is that adding volume in another pane on the chart diminishes the amount of space available for PRICE.

You're right. From an entry signal standpoint, low volume is more important than high volume. Of course those with a deeper understanding of VSA would say, its that low volume occurring where once volume was high that is the real key.

If you like how things are going without volume, then there is no reason to add it to the mix. If you do add it, you will miss some trades you would have gotten before. However, the real key is, you will stay out of some bad trades you would have gotten into before.

In fact, many successful traders would argue that the question to ask about any new tool/methodology is not, "What will this get me in to?", but rather, "What will this keep me out of?".

I hope we can get some discussion going on this, because I am struggling with it myself.

Hey guys, just a small lesson on how to trade candle PA!

Infact, candlesticks are great to find out the Kinks. But which candle we should look for?

I personally like to look for Swing High Candle or Swing Low Candle. Break of Swing High candle is like breaking some kind of RS in LTF which might exist on left. But if CAPS forms near SHC (Swing High Candle) or SLC (Swing Low Candle) that is even great as it is FTB to MPL!

But if we have LS below or nearby to SHC (or SLC) then the low of that candle again becomes important RS Flip. But if there is QM on LS with just 2 candles then that QM is also need to pay attention.

Yes, MPL’s are great placed to trade for FO when they are just near to Kink or what my friend Sali named ORFL.

If you look for every candle, it means less but when you look for SHC and SLC along with PA and Kink it will definitely help you out to take to the pip entries!

What inspired me to look for candle PA?

RTM’s old article which is now locked kept ditching my mind every time that IF started candle PA means there must be something there to look for candle. But then many time I lost looking for old terms all over internet. But then suddenly I got surprised when I was looking for engulf of candle. Then I got my eureka moment and sharp bounce to next level of trading.

Thanks to my curiosity to take me to RTM, and thanks to all Masters and specially IF for educating peoples for free and giving me 2nd chance!

posts.author: Kavya
posts.text:
If the signal is given by the market mover (an engulf into a new zone), then price is very unlikely to break the extreme of the zone it just came from. So, if you have the patience to wait at the last remaining set of unfilled orders in the origin, you can be almost certain that, that price will be respected. Look for tricks being played on approach to a place where a trick was played, and you'll find where price will turn. If you can look beyond S/D, you'll see that the Flag Limit is the only true place to look for PA for a trade. Trade these levels and you're taking gambling out of your method. All we can ever hope for is a bounce at these levels, unless we are certain that this level is the deepest possible point of retrace after a previous engulf. Without that, we must watch PA as it develops, both before and during the trade. Set and Forget trades can only be taken once the signal is given and the target is clear.

Has price tested the last flag on approach? (good sign)

Trend lines — How trend lines are best intrument for ITs to trap retail traders? ➡

Most of the (I must say all of the) retail traders look for trend lines as potential supply

demand areas! as they find price sticking to trend lines herd get confidence in putting there orders at trend lines. And as soon as they see break to those trend lines (but less to see engulf of zone) they tries to trade opposite (breakout orders) at nearest supply demand areas or support resistance areas! But when bunch of retail orders coming into market ITs have really great chance to have big profit against those orders. They won't trade immediate zones(LTF zones) in most of the cases,but they will setup good looking Higher High's or Lower Low's trend formation {again on smaller scales (this might be Weekly w.r.t. Monthly)}. ℹ )So what's the point we should bear in mind in this case? ➡

Whenever price closes near trend line, it indicates that trend is slowing down. So

we can look for potential opportunity to go against those orders! Orders might be sitting on Monthly, where price failed to reach or clean orders immediate to Swing Highs or Lows which could setup traps for herds as well as for fund managers!

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
I have been a silent reader of this forum for several months and decided to start a Journal and begin contributing to this wonderful community. I'd like to thank IF for offering this place to those of us who are committed to understanding how and why the market moves like it does. I am immensely thankful for the time and continued efforts all associate and master traders who take the time to respond to those of us who are still in the beginning stages of our journey to becoming competent traders.

I found this website in August 2014 and joined November 2014. Despite not posting any content to date, I have spent at least an hour a day going through the homework assignments and member journals in my quest to understand price movement. Previous to finding RTM last year I spent two arduous years trading Forex with little success. This community has helped tremendously.

I have read through all of the materials posted under the Marketpedia section (multiple times) and after reading through various Journals over several months I feel the following concepts are most important when it comes to truly understanding how everything fits together: It has something to do with the relationship between:

1. How to accurately draw all price action zones and understand the difference between an engulf and a fakeout. 2. Proficiency in using multiple time frames to utilize the fractal nature of the market to pinpoint critical reaction levels and decision points.

Aaron's 'Homework Room' topic titled 'Engulf or Fakeout?' has been a great resource that has helped me see the difference between an engulf/fakeout. Many thanks to him for starting that thread!

For me, drawing the PAZ is the most challenging concept to understand and draw accurately. My goal is to finally take each article from the Marketpedia section and begin combining the concepts together to see the bigger picture behind price movement. This journal will be a great place to begin this journey, post my charts, and track my progress.

I plan on posting both historical chart analysis (hindsight) for conceptual purposes as well as live trades taken on a demo account for practical application and accountability. I will perform a 'trade autopsy' on any live trades I take that fail so I can identify the mistakes and eliminate bad habits.

First chart posted here is just for practice to make sure I am inserting the picture correctly. I am using Gyazo to snap screenshots.

More posts to follow...

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
Trade Setup – Hindsight: I found a nice example of an AUD/USD FTB reaction that took place back on 6/2/15. This is not a trade I caught in real time but one I researched in hindsight to see if I could identify why price reacted like it did.

HTF Analysis: This is a good area to look for a reaction on the FTB because the associated FTR is significant. There is a clear decision made that price is too expensive and a resulting price cap is formed. There is a strong bearish move out of the FTR showing a significant imbalance where more orders may exist when price returns to this area. Because of these factors, I will watch the 4-hour chart until price reaches the FTR zone, at which point I will drop down to a LTF to look for specific price action to make an entry.

LTF Analysis: Price moves up through the lower limit of the FTR. Since I know price is returning for the first time, I am looking for a reason to short. Primarily, I am focused on price forming an engulf to the downside before considering any entry. This is not a situation where I would risk a TT.

In this example, price does end up engulfing and in doing so also forms the LL of the QM.

I labeled the source of the engulf as the location where I would have executed a short trade. I would have placed a stop just above the upper limit of the FTR (around.78420). Target is shown on chart. My target might be a little aggressive, and there’s a good chance I would have taken ½ of the position off around.76940 just to be safe.

Fakeout vs Engulf: It’s my understanding that price will fakeout when IT’s needs orders. Fakeouts are used to push price in to a specific zone that will contain orders. Engulfs and fakeouts both have the same effect on retail traders (tricks), but the engulf is really just indicative of future price direction. Because of this, engulfs usually don’t engulf in to a significant level. That is why I think this example shows an engulf and not a F/O.

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
This is an example on EUR/GBP (4-HR Chart) where compression exists between two FTR’s. My focus is on the location of the engulf and the subsequent final bullish push through the CP in to the FTR zone above (by the large black arrow).

Was there a way I could have predicted that price would reach the upper FTR following the bearish engulf?

I am not entirely sure how to read this chart accurately. On one hand, the engulf on the 4-hour chart could be read as a clear intention for price to drop. In this were case, the IT’s would need to fill lots of short orders. Since the lower FTR zone is depleted (three times price has visited this FTR), it would make logical sense that price would need to find the next real level of Supply to fill short orders. The push through the CP to the upper FTR could be seen as a FTB, but it also looks like a great place to FO and load up on short orders.

Maybe this is both a FTB and a FO?

IF’s trades often occur at levels where he experiences very little (if any) drawdown. After breaking down some of those amazing trades I notice many times he is able to predict in advance and place a PO at the exact area where price turns.

I could be wrong, but it seems like he knows where the fakeouts will occur by looking left of the engulf to see what the RBD/ DBR (supply/demand) is reacting to (usually an important FTR) and determining whether there are any extreme orders left to fill in that FTR. If so, price will likely FO to a specific decision point within this FTR. That is why he often drop down to a 5 minute or 1 minute chart to plot his entry….he is looking for the most accurate decision point.

This is what I need to work on because trading at these extreme levels offers the highest R:R.

posts.text:
One of my worst habits is being overly anxious to get in a trade out of fear that I'll miss an opportunity. It's a completely irrational fear, as any trader knows there are dozens of prime setups that occur every day. That said, I still regularly fall victim to this and it happened this evening on a trade I took on the Cable. Here are the charts (1-HR and 1-Min)

I saw price bounce from a HTF FTR, so I dropped down to a 1-minute chart to see price action. The 1-minute chat showed a nice engulf and bearish QM setup so I waited for price to retrace to the origin of the engulf and took a short trade. My stop was a couple of pips above the swing high and my target was the base of the pole.

Here is why it went wrong:

Almost as soon as I executed the short trade I began having doubts. I looked at the 4-HR chart and saw a bullish reaction out of demand which made me question my reasons for taking short. Even though the short position was a quick scalp, I was concerned the QM was going to fail. Because of this, I closed the trade with a minimal 2.5 pip gain (barely enough to cover the spread).

Of course, within a few short minutes of closing my position, price ended up dropping to easily hit my original target. I tried to jump back in when I saw price take a dive, but was only able to pick up another 4 or 5 pips.

I am embarrassed to admit that after three years of trading I still make these kind of mistakes.

Looking forward to kicking this bad habit.

posts.text:
Thanks for the reality check and encouragement Ptp!! Maybe I am getting caught up on insignificant details (I have a tendency to obsess on details and miss the main point). Where I often struggle is stop placement - either the trades get run through or the stop gets hit just before price reverses. The difference between a winning trade and a losing trade can be stop placement.

Knowing price is going to F/O allows a trader to widen their stop and keeps them on the right side of R:R. It's amazing to see how bad timing on an otherwise excellent trade setup can take a major winner and turn it in to a loser. I am actually embarrassed at how often my stops get hit...

To improve on my past errors, I have started closely watching price to understand why price changes when it does. That's why I was surprised to see price break the extreme orders of the FTR by ten pips (AUD/USD).

IF has mentioned many times that predicting a F/O should be easy. I agree that an engulf or a F/O have basically the same effect on retail traders as far as trapping them on the wrong side of the trade (and in that context the difference between them really doesn't matter). Of course, the difference between the engulf and F/O is the engulf dictates future price direction. And I would suggest (from what I know as a beginner) that it is incredibly important to distinguish between the two from a practical perspective.

I suppose the other aspect of this that I need to work on is the PAZ. It seems simple enough in theory...PAZ is just the space between FTR's. For some reason, once I open a live chart, I start getting all mixed up on how to draw them, how to not leave any out, and how to understand price's reaction to them.

Enough of my rambling...I really appreciate that you and D took the time to leave a comment here and I will try to stay focused on the bigger picture and get really competent at specific setups that I can duplicate over and over.

You have the right attitude which is more important than any price structure. In the trade of #19, my advice is to try to avoid looking for the exact reason. Is price at a key supply/SR zone? Check. First time back? Check. If you want to, was there an engulf? Check. Now decide where to get in. If you see the RBD between the doji and the red candle, theres a clear little pullback in there - one of those "ftr" things. Its simply a pullback before the drop, and theres a level in it. That little ftr is NO DIFFERENT to a fakeout, its just within the price curve it was part of in the up move. I dont even know whats left but that push up had to react at the most obvious next reaction point, which is the FTR or whatver its called.....and to be clear, I would have been in on the RBD, not the retest, around 27722 or even around 277738. This was a really easy trade H - so if it feels like it is hard, you are possibly looking for something thats not there, or really not relevant. This trade is at major supply, and it rotates. Jump in on the rotation or wait for the engulf. If you look at the M1 chart at the PA left of the entry, what I see as being more predictive is a nice SR level around the entry. If you look at M1 the entry higher, simple SR, was a much better price. In either case you still dont know if price will rip north...thats the uncertainty principle. I personally dont like the entry that was taken - it looks good on a H1.

Nick.

You have a good read on price, thats clear to see. I dont like how you use the word "trick" in some of your charts - for me that sets me up emotionally to think there are these douche bags playing the rest of retail. I have worked in the depths of the financial markets since 2006, and I have never come across this. I even looked very deeply into the notion of big players pushing price around. Price does get pushed around by big players, the shops that have the money are often huge institutions, and they arent half as clever as we are made to believe. The smarts in trading comes from the smaller places, and often they have strict risk controls. One reason prop trading is a double-edged sword is that often the way to make good money due to the split involves leverage, but it can take a long long time before the company will give you that leverage. I was offered a role at ITG as a prop trader - to learn it - and it ws impossible to survive due to the risk. Ignoring the recent big-sell side bullshit around chatting each other in FX, I do not believe that exists in the futures world....yet the same patterns unfold.

Its not a trick, its a normal manifestation of price action. It is behavioral finance made-manifest. If you see things as tricks, its difficult to not feel an emotional response when oyu are on the wrong side. I lost a lot of money on the wrong side of a spoofing in the russell 2000 last year, and it was hard not to get angry. Trading in my view is 20% setup, 80% psychology, and this is where my problems lie today. I can read price. know how to manage my trades to makea lot of money. I struggle with emotions...a common problem when trying to move into full time day trading I read.

Regardless, you will work it out, but question everything, including what you read as being "the situation" of what you are reading in price. I just see it as price doing what it does. Its helped me a lot, and I avoid anthropomorphic projections as best that I can.

In Market Wizards, the stop run and the understanding of placing stops at better locations to avoid getting hit by a stop run, imply the act of searching for stops. Whats not clear is, is it one program or institute, or many, and are they collaborating or not. Furthermore, when you move to the edge of a price curve, there will be a lot more emotional response/activity there than mid-curve for example, and the ability to control how far price moves can be a tricky problem. FX brokers know where your orders are and nefarious acts by them to force bad fills is a known worry of the FX space - wild wild west - certainly on the smaller timeframes. But there are many reasons why price may run past a level, all of which could be a mixture of program/retail/whoever.

Nevertheless, I play this from the perspective of these areas are merely key places where more emotion plays out and the location is less a price lvel and more a zone.

It seems clear to me that people know where stops are - pick up any book on retail trading and you can see the advice given about placing a stop at the high of an entry candle + 1 tick or so. A single candle can have breakout traders and range traders all playing out their own views of the market price action. When price reaches an extreme, a key decision has to be made, and that really in my view comes from the larger market, with some nudging from size. If price FO's the highs, the question for the bulls is, will this hold or not. If they get any indication they could be wrong, they will close the trade - there will be a panic often at the extremes, more so in more volatile instruments. Crude is a great example. It is actually pretty easy to spot the emotion watching the tape at the extremes. It might well be that "its" push price beyond a level and then they wait for the response of the market to see if price snaps back. Or they could be trying to drive price up and then back down. I can see how that would go, but market manipulation is illegal. Spoofing, a major tactic that was known/is known to exist, is illegal. Its illegal because its market manipulation.

For me at least, its better to think about emotions at various places, agnostic of nefarious activities, because I actually think regardless of the programs/bad practices that may go on, the price action would look much the same. I could be wrong, but I find that outlook allows me to at least not feel like I am being taken from behind by the investment oligarchy.

I have lost a lot of money being on the wrong side of a range play where price snaps back into the range. I once took a short on TF, the Russell 2000, and I was so cock-sure of myself I loaded up - it was a surety price was going lower. I shorted the FTB from underneath, and I remember clearly the moment time slowed down as I saw the tape explode and price was many points away from my entry. I didnt have a stop. Best trading experience I ever had - I watch for that all of the time and make sure I am on the right side of it now. Explosive moves from such places. All I do now is look for similar locations for explosive moves - places I fondly refer to as High Probability Reversal Zones.

My intention is day trading, and so I am looking for how to extract money on a daily basis. I look for D1 and H4 levels, but then I use other techniques to look for zones that I think could have a reaction based on simple price movement. If I see a key pullback, regardless of origins or breaks of more important places, I still watch them. I have found some of the most non-obvious areas can turn price, so I have learnt to be adaptive. In fact I developed my own method to embody uncertainty at its core and still have positive expectancy. Trading Crude and Gold for many months last year, I constantly had my @ss handed to me for making assumptions or sitting at the charts with a bias.

I should also mention I use tape, order flow, tick charts, volume charts and in some cases volume profile. I use no indicators.

I marked out some key areas that I gravitate too. I would be reading what the larger timeframe direction is and look to trade only in that direction until price hits a reversal zone. That is, never counter-trade until its in an area to be tested. It might seem boring, but after you have your live account handed back to you empty, I am ok going for uncool with-trend trades and riding them than getting the kick of choosing the right turning point for a contrarian trade. So in this daily chart I marked out key areas I would definitely have in my sights. The daily FTR you point out falls on a key SR level, and I would be all over that when price returns.

There are many more opportunities here on the H4. Right now price has pushed into the highs, and it even looks like its rolling over. As price nears the higher part of a curve, towards a new level, thats the time to look for markers that price could fall. You dont have volume in FX AFAIK and that can be a huge marker. I WOULD HIGHLY RECOMMEND GETTING YOUR ACCOUNT TO A LEVEL TO PLAY FUTURES. I have no idea why people do FX apart from the smaller lot size....futures have mini lot sizes too, though they are still more expensive than the micro lots in FX. But you get to trade cleaner PA (my judgement).

From the comments you make in your post, I can see how you are approaching the charts and my only advice would be to try not to worry too much about whether price will turn or not. If you want to touch trade, you can spend hundreds of hours trying to perfect your ability to spot the exact turning point....maybe thats doable I dont know. was pretty good at spotting amazing turning points, when price turned, and I quickly overlooked the many more times I failed at it. Theres nothing great about selling into a zone due to an expectation of a fall only to see price rip right past your SL. The touch trade technique can work and can be easy, as long as the math works out. I found for me my ability to forecast was forever failing me. It is only made harder when you see a fantastic equity curve from an academy student, whether or not that student already had excellent success before the course or not...fear and greed....it gets us all.

My style is profoundly adaptive. I have learnt to read the market at the zones - that is where my market reading kicks in. Until then I merely mark areas I *think* will react. In your charts, if you only want to trade the higher timeframes then the locations you put out there are those that I would monitor, looking for key SR lines. SR helps me zone in, and then I will look for pullbacks on tick charts. Almost every pullback will get a reaction, but some will be deeper, and some will be reversals, while others will involve a stop out if you dont bother to listen to what the market is telling you. As long as you factor in MM into the process, the stop outs should be irrelevant. For me I can often get in on every reaction of a rotation in price at a key level, and I never know which one will be "the one" that will cause the best/true reversal. I factor this into my approach so that I frankly dont give a damn. I can mark the levels up in a matter of minutes, because to me my edge comes from rolling my sleeves up as price approaches them. Sr levels are debunked in the academy, but they offer a much simpler mechanism in my view. Theres nothing more disappointing than spending hours at the charts marking out all of the constructs based on the "rules", only to see all of them fail. My emotional constitution isnt mature enough for that.

I would conclude with this - it is a well known fact that a method that is complex is most probably riddled with a number of emotional problems. For example, when a trader who gets off with indicators takes a big hit in the market, he/she will go in search of a better indicator that will give more edge, and they will add that to their system ad nauseum, creating a more complex system. Someone else with price aciton might create a colorful and complicated way to read price action, full of all and sundry. Most of the constructs added are products of emotional distress - loss avoidance techniques. They dont exist because they are necessary to trade, but because they offer the ability for the creator to feel less emotional pain (hope for). The cosmic joke for traders is that it is profoundly simpler than we make it out to be, often because its always about trying to avoid the innate fear of loss. Most often the person who has a complicated way of trading trades little - an phenomena I found myself doing whenever I get wrapped up in complexity. My experience now is that it is simple.

I openly admit my issue is not one of price reading any longer. I struggle with the emotional/psychology side and I have a coach helping. In fact I have a bit of the Jonah Complex going on which I never thought I would have. I mention this only to highlight that my approach is extremely simple, and when I trade now I make more money than I ever thought I could. The gravity of that has been a cause for my recent need to grow psychology....but I approach the markets extremely and profoundly simply...

HTH

This was also enlightening for me because I didn't realize engulfs always had a target... I just usually placed a target after getting in to a trade at the base of a pole of an important S/R level.

#1 – Is an FTR which occurs after engulf “A”, and is the origin of the engulf “B”. #2- Is an FTR which occurs after the engulf “B” and is the origin of the engulf “C”. “D” is an engulf of FTR “2”, and is a FTB to FTR “1” #3 is an FTR, but it is also the target of traders who took a Long trade on price’s FTB to FTR “1”. Doing some studying this weekend on PAZ and FTR.

One question I've been having regarding the FTR:

I usually see multiple FTR's when watching price. They are everywhere. There are obvious FTR's that jump out at me & are easy to draw, but there are many situations where technically I see a FTR formed, but it isn't a very good one and I become confused on how to draw them. The whole problem with the PAZ, is that the PAZ concept exploits even the smallest amount of confusion one has with any of the other parts of the RTM method. If you aren't 100% comfortable with all of the components of RTM's Marketpedia section, the PAZ is going to be impossible to totally understand and trade with regularity. That's why IF has it last on the list...it's the component that binds everything together.

Here is a chart example of what I'm trying to describe about FTR's:

In this chart I drew all the FTR's from Left to Right (only the ones that appeared on this time frame). The way I see this, there is really only a couple major FTR's that break major S/R zones and form a nice retrace. The problem: what about all the minor FTR's? There are FTR's within FTR's within FTR's in every fractal time frame. When I apply this to the FTR PAZ concept, the space between these FTR's isn't really clear space between the FTR's. There is always something else in the way if you change the time frame. At some point don't all the minor FTR's together form a compression area? Is that when I should start looking to draw a compression PAZ?

The more I think about the PAZ the more my brain gets tied in knots.

My charts get too messy with all the rectangles and zones. I've seen some charts that are so filled up with boxes and arrows and text etc.. that I can't even see price anymore (no offense to anyone of course, as I am the least qualified to judge anyone here!!)...but in my opinion, It's just as bad as compiling a bunch of indicators on a chart because its information overload. It's too much and it detracts from really being able to see what is truly important.

....This is what I struggle with. I can mark up a chart too, make myself feel insanely "smart" that I can "see" so much going on with price. I can draw dozens of zones, lines, circles, arrows, text boxes, lines, etc... all on one time frame. What's genuinely difficult (in my opinion) is being skilled enough so that you don't have to do this. It is being able to see only what you need to see in order to take an accurate trade. All the Masters charts are clean, and they only point out what is most important and relevant to their trade. The same is true for the associate traders... they know what to look for and their charts reflect that knowledge clearly. I get frustrated with myself that I can't see what is important. I can't see the PAZ without ending up with a crazy chart that is so busy it's unreadable. I look through Pedini's journal and wonder why I can't see the simplicity that he sees. He (and other like him here at RTM) make it look so damn easy! But then I open the live charts and shit starts getting confusing.

My apologies for the ranting. I guess I am feeling frustrated at the end of what was a really bad week of trading.

After nearly year of reading here at RTM (and three years trading in general) I should be doing much better than this.

No worries,

Try checking the tick chart if possible to see the DP. You know it definitely exists as it broke the highs/supply. Don't forget that S/R doesn't always align perfectly as the DP is a kink which offsets it one way or another. IF explains this somewhere in a post, but I saved time and made a new screenshot instead of finding it.

So the only way to see the DP exactly in real-time is to be looking at a tick chart. However if we cannot check it; as the screenshot shows we assume the whole thing is a DP to break the highs and price can turn anywhere within this kink, so basically we wouldn't trade it if we didn't have a tick chart as our R:R would be bad.

In regards to economic news release, I believe its the other way around. The news helps price get to where SD is faster to help fill orders.

Cheers, Muffles

Hi H,

Well yes, there are multiple engulfs, DPs, etc using multiple timeframes. That's where screen time comes in

Another thing, don't try to collect huge puzzle in 1 attempt. I.e. if you are studying engulfs then start with swing low and swing high engulfs. Forget the PAZ, CP, FL etc. Focus on 1 thing and learn it. There are definitely setups only with key ingredient -engulf of swing extreme (it applied to any RTM concept).

EJ trade was taken not too low. it was taken higher in HTF. Then your setups was very strong. Your targets were scalp level. So it worked out very fine since you traded within market conditions and within what price was doing. AUDUSD was a forced trade IMO.

Nonetheless, every trader needs to finds his/her own style. If you like scalps... good for you. Just take them in good locations.

Regarding HTF... HTF concept is relative IMO. I.e. If you are taking a trade on M30/H1 then HTF could be H4 and Daily. If you take a scalp on M1... not sure the Daily is so relevant. At least not at this stage. IF looks at everything from what I see therefore he gets great entries... but it's better to learn this stuff than trying to do what he does

On the last note, give yourself a break. Literally, don't look at charts. I can give you some studies but in short it boils down to this:

- Overload Brain (lots of new info, you are doing HM, market analysis etc) - Short Release (break from trading, so everything could fall into the right places in your mind. If you won't it does not matter matter how much you work - you will not be able to use the learned stuff in efficient way) - Amazing High. (That's when everything makes sense. All the concepts you studies just makes sense and you seem them everywhere.) - Recovery (the is crucial. Post-High you might feel depressed, like nothing makes sense, etc. That's natural way the brain deals with highs. You need a longer break so your brain regroups, chemistry is adjusted etc. In these stages usually I can't even look at charts... felt bad about it for years. But since finding this stuff out my learning curve improved).

Then you will feel ready again and start new cycle. That is the formula for great performance, mental or physical;-)

Best, Art

P.S. sorry for the spelling. Am rushing a bit.
