Hi Art!

Thanks for the info. That very well may be an engulf that I missed. I have been ignoring the individual candles for the past few months as well, after reading similar advice from other RTM journals that the candles aren't as important as understanding the zones (flags, FTR's, PAZ etc...) and the engulfs or F/O that occur at these levels.

So far, the engulf/PAZ concepts are not working out for me so I have wandered a bit off course to the Doc's Journal

Here's my reasoning:

I know it may not be popular to admit this here, but I am beginning to question the engulf being defined as a 'secret signal' that the institutional funds use to hint at future price directional. Of course, I say this as a humble trader who is really in the beginning stages of understanding how to trade, so I am totally open to the possibility that I am dead wrong. I mean absolutely no disrespect to anyone here, as every time I get someone to post on my Journal, I am both excited and honored.

There is something very refreshing about the Doc's Journal that keeps me intrigued. He states that there are no secret signals and nobody knows where price is going to move. His strategy is simply based on S/R flip zones and watching price to find areas where professional money is at work..actively accumulating positions.

What you see on my Journal lately is a feeble attempt at applying his lessons.

Doc's philosophy is relatively straightforward and he takes the time to post step by step charts (Weekly through LTF) showing how he reads the charts and why he takes trades when he does. There are no secrets to his philosophy or ambiguity (like sometimes I find in the mainstream RTM PAZ concepts) and it is this complete (and repeated) process really helps me train my eye to see the important areas.

In come cases, I have been pleasantly surprised to notice some overlapping in how the Doc and IF view the market. What IF sees as an engulf, is described by Doc as being analogous to a ice fisherman 'testing' the ice to make sure it is thick enough to support his weight. It is 'testing' that often results in the long wicked candles, and is done to test how the market will respond. A similar type of testing is the fakeout, and it manifests in a similar way...for example (at least this is how I am understanding it) Professional money wants to move the market up, but wants to see how many bears/bulls are left in the market before doing so. I like Doc's philosophy because it offers a logical reason instead of a belief that there is a secret engulf signal for no other purposes than communicating with the institutions. I can't see a logical reason for the RTM's definition of an engulf other than it is a signal. I need to understand the logical reasons why something happens if I am going to understand how and why to trade it.

The more I study, the more I think there are so many players in the market it's impossible to think there are secret signals being given. Too many different banks, governments, funds, private high net worth clients, etc... to know for sure. There are big players clashing on the open market...there has to be, right? After all, the retailers don't posses enough capital to make it worth the institutional banker's while to trick. Retailers make up a minuscule part of the market. I think even the big dogs win and lose sometimes.

I agree that candlestick patterns are worthless (and the Doc touches on this many times in his Journal).It isn't so much the candle patterns (doji, evening star, etc...) as what the HTF candles are telling you about the order flow of pro money at these critical S/R levels. I am trying to think like a pro money trader "where can I enter the market at the least risk for the highest return, and who am I buying/selling to?" & "When I exit the trade, who am I going to be buying/selling to?".

I must conclude this posting with a disclaimer that I am only a few dozen pages in to Doc's huge journal and I may very well be making a fool of myself by mis-interpreting Doc's strategy. I am such a beginner that I feel inadequate posting on here, because there are so many traders here on RTM (You, IF, RDK, Alex, Milkeyway,PTP etc...) that seem to understand these concepts and log amazing trades with consistency. Nobody can deny IF's abilities are super human and his zero draw down trades are honestly one of the most incredible things I have ever seen. The freedom one could achieve with his ability is endless

For me....I am still drowning a bit, and trying to find a life jacket to keep me afloat!

Thank you for your continued guidance and help Art!

And then there is the further complication (once you determine which FL needs to be broken to signal the engulf) of judging whether the price break is really an engulf or just a fakeout. posts.author: HotRod
posts.text:
Hey hoeschec here are a few things to consider regarding your loss. We always have to be aware of what price is doing in all TFs. While price can certainly move up from the point you took your trade you should realize that price is coming down from supply, and the best place to buy is at a fresh demand FTR. No matter what TF you use for entry it should be backed up by and at HTF FL/FTR. Your trade was in "no mans land" on the HTF.

I certainly see your reason for the trade and it does look enticing. Price did engulf an FTR, but unfortunately it also immediately hit an important FL and the target. Its important because it is supply that engulfed and formed at the last demand. You found a place that would bounce price, but the move away from price tells you whether to keep it and discard it and try again at a better place. In this case price cp'd away which leaves no demand levels left to "guard" your entry. What you want to see is an engulf of the immediate supply/demand. Price ended up forming a QM against you. You can't see this in real time, but can see the environment in which one can form if you keep in mind all TFs and what FLs are in play on each.

This is my take.

Hi Peter,

This is a relatively new concept for me, so hopefully a more experienced trader can step in and correct me if I am wrong...but here is my understanding of what I mean by 'source' engulf.

When price is reaching an important HTF supply or demand zone, I drop down to a lower time frame to see how price forms as it reaches in to the area of importance. On its way in to the zone, price will FL many times (base-pole-flag...etc). FTR's will also form & I watch for these as well. What I look for is the original FL or FTR that acts as the source of the major push up in to the HTF zone. I also look for major S/R levels to mark the FTR that forms after the break of the S/R level. Basically, I want to find the FL or FTR that is important...not just FL's that form as a result of the important FL's. It is critical to find out which FL/FTR is the origin of the move in to the HTF zone because it is this FL/FTR that matters when it comes to a possible. engulf.

Previously, I would be watching the charts and point out what I thought was an engulf, when in reality all I was looking at was price breaking the high/low of a reactionary FL or (meaning nothing of importance happened). Here is a illustration I made a few pages back in my journal that I think is correct (nobody corrected me on it) and it does a decent job of illustrating this point.

As you can see on the illustrated chart, the original FL/FTR (arrow 1) is the one that occurred on the very Left.This is the FL/FTR that formed after a break of an important S/R level...because of this, I would deem this FTR/FL as being important and the 'source/original' FL/FTR. You can see from this drawing that price attempts to break the original FL/FTR (arrow 2) but isn't able to. Look at Arrow 3: This arrow breaks the top limit of the RBD that formed at arrow 2 making it appear that an engulf has occurred when it hasn't.

The true engulf only occurs when price is able to break the top limit of the FL/FTR show at arrow #1. The engulf happens at arrow # 4. This is confirmation that the last orders have been taken from the initial source FL/FTR and price will move to the north after (hopefully) retracing to the origin of the engulf.

This is my best understanding of the concept, and although it is hard to put in to words, I hope this drawing helps. For anyone who reads this and finds flaws in my response to Peter: please let me know! I'd hate to lead another trader down the wrong path!

Hope this help Peter, please let me know if you still don't understand that concept and I'll draw a new diagram with more examples

I think the key is first drawing all of the important S/R levels or opposing FTR's and see when one of these important zones are broken and price flags or creates a new FTR. It is this newly created FL/FTR (after an important level breaks) that we should keep an eye on. It's a FL or FTR that served a specific purpose and these FL's contain decision points that will often bounce price. That is why an engulf of these important zones is so important... the engulf clears out those remaining orders and allows price to move freely to the next important level. Price wants the path of least resistance (I heard this quote from someone here on RTM, but I can't remember who it was that coined the phrase).

Since I'm sitting here bored as my Broker has temporarily closed out the platform for maintenance, I spent some time to draw out a recent concept I've been working on. Here is my interpretation of what it looks like:

1. Find a Base-Pole-Flag: where the Flag portion forms in a HTF supply or demand zone (the HTF confirmation is very important)

2. Once price starts flagging, drop down to a lower time frame and start marking out the FL's and FTR's that price makes as it spends time in your HTF supply or demand zone.

3. Mark the important FL or FTR that supports price's move in to the HTF zone and marks the end of the 'Pole' and starts the FL (this is the important FL that you want to see price engulf before looking for a place to get short).

4. Price will move sideways for a while while it consolidates. Just be patient...wait for the engulf.

5. After the engulf has occurred, start looking for a place to get short.

6. Find the high limit of the FL that formed within the HTF supply zone and watch for the area in the FL where the last orders (most extreme orders) could possibly exist. This is the MPL (I think).

7. Wait for the deep retrace to this MPL and get short with a tight stop. These entries are the ones that can be 1:10 R:R or more.

I am not sure if my drawing is 100% accurate, but I will use this idea in my trading next week to refine my entries and find trading opportunities that have a higher R:R.

Hi Niekumaty,

I marked up the chart with how I see that area...hopefully this is what you are looking for

A QM is only valid if the HH or LL is a true engulf. So in the case of GBP-AUD 15M chart, price would have to follow the path of the orange line in order to make the area you pointed out a valid QM location. Price needed to engulf and return back to the source/QM Level (dark blue rectangle).

In this example, it did end up engulfing (if you look at the chart) but this occurred late on a Friday when many traders were closing out their positions, so it wouldn't have been a good time to trade the QM. Many traders close out all positions before heading in to the weekend...especially these days where the market is so unpredictable.

Feel free to let me know if you are still confused. No need to apologize, I am still pretty new to this as well and I am more than happy to share what I've learned here!

Here is an issue I need to study more: Stop placement.

A good example of this is currently AUD-USD (15M Chart). I expect price to RT to the origin of the move, however in this case (and many like it) there is quite a bit of downside that I need to cover with respect to stop placement. If I have a tight stop (Stop "A") by R:R is terrific, but I stand a good chance of getting stopped out by a couple of pips.

I could put a stop as low as "B" or "C"...but is that a smart thing to do in this situation? Any PA below stop "A" is basically moving in to a compression area...so if price enters this CP it is likely to fall all the way through. Is it best to keep a tight stop at the level "A" and get out of the trade if price breaks in to the CP below?

I am thankful that I've gotten to a point in my trading career were I am able to see opportunities like the AUD-USD example above. It has taken a lot of time but some of the most obvious setups are starting to 'stand out' to me. When they work, they are beautifully simple.

My next major hurdle to contend with: weeding out the bad trades...the ones I take that fail because of the following reasons:

1. I am tired in the morning, turn on the computer, and immediately think I see PA developing so I quickly open a trade for fear of 'missing out'.

2. Over complicating the concepts and looking too hard to find a trade.

3. Emotional trading (too many lots opened out of greed, trading while frustrated or angry etc...)

4. Sloppy and lazy trading - not doing a full top-down analysis

5. Lack of patience....Instead, I need to determine the EXACT setup I am looking for and wait for the right time to trade it.

If I can start eliminating these bad habits, I will become profitable...very profitable. I must eliminate those bad trades that wipe out a week's worth of profitability.

3. Emotional trading (too many lots opened out of greed, trading while frustrated or angry etc...)

4. Sloppy and lazy trading - not doing a full top-down analysis

5. Lack of patience....Instead, I need to determine the EXACT setup I am looking for and wait for the right time to trade it.

If I can start eliminating these bad habits, I will become profitable...very profitable. I must eliminate those bad trades that wipe out a week's worth of profitability.

Maybe someone reading this can offer me a little direction on a problem I've been trying to figure out:

The picture below shows IF's webinar example about price reversing/bouncing off areas where tricks have been played in the past. I can find tons of locations where tricks occur in a chart of any time frame. The hard part seems to be finding the ones that are actually going to bonce and timing the entry accordingly. It is actually pretty hard to execute these trades in real time- for example, on IF's recent example, I find many locations where price approached the level where price played a trick.

How did IF know to wait for the exact approach to the level where he went short? (there were many touches at this level previous to his entry, as shown by my arrows).

Also, why would there still be short orders waiting at this level after price repeatedly spiked this zone? Wouldn't all the price spikes have zeroed out any remaining short orders that originated as a result of the original "trick"?

The only explanation I can think of is IF waited for the engulf to occur (I labeled it on the chart) before taking the touch trade. Anyone have any ideas? thanks!

Here is an example I found while practicing. Price reacted nicely, but it did not reach the highest point of sell orders. To me, it looks like it bounced off of the RBD decision (LTF chart) point that occurred after the "trick" originally happened. I did not see any tricks occurring or a QM/Diamond forming as price returned to the level. I am pretty confused....

Here is another example - this one shows an area where a trick occurred but there were no clean orders left over to give price a bounce. Instead, a Diamond formed and bounced off a different location altogether. How could I have predicted the diamond bounce at the highs shown on the chart below? This type of pattern recognition is easy when looking at historic price action, but doing this in real time as price is unfolding seems really hard.... any advice?

Another question: what if price's RT to an area where a trick previously occurred includes a trick of its own while it bounces? If a reaction to a previous trick includes a trick, would it be a valid starting off point for price even further down the road? (This is hard to explain using words so look below at the chart IF used)...I added the black lines and labeled the three important areas as 1,2, and 3. Technically, #2 is a reaction to the trick played at #1. Let's assume for this example that there is a spike that occurs on a LTF chart as #2 forms which creates another "trick". When price moves up to #3 (where price "tricked" at #2), is that a valid area to once again look for PA to justify another bounce, or is #2 just a reaction to #1? I know when it comes to engulfs, you can't count it as legitimate if it is "engulfing" a flag that is simply a reaction to another flag. Is that the same concept when we are looking for these types of "tricks"? My apologies if I am doing a bad job of asking this question...it is hard to explain these concepts. If this is indeed true, it might explain why some of these setups appear to look like they will work but fail miserably.

althoufx- thanks for the reply and charts.

I have been trying to figure this one out for a couple days now...I am still inexperienced when it comes to trading, and I have a hard time deciphering the intricacies of finding engulfs vs. fake-outs on multiple time frames. The time frames are fractal, so it seems to me there is always an engulf/fake-out that could suggest the opposite of how I am viewing a particular trade opportunity.

The more I look, the more I see. The more I see the harder it is to keep it all straight in my mind.

Here is an example of how I would analyze this chart in real time (I am referring to your M1 chart and drew colored circles over the areas of interest for clarity).

Yes, there is seemingly an engulf at the blue circle (as you have pointed out). Bu the only reason we see that as an engulf is because it broke the high of the FL in the orange circle. In order for an engulf to be valid, price must engulf an original FL or FTR - not simply a FL/FTR that forms as a result of a reaction to a different FL or FTR further to the left. So technically, we would have to look left to determine if the engulf was legitimate.

Also, price action can form what appears to be an engulf when price is really only bouncing off a S/R flip level. This is where it gets tricky and I get confused...How could we have known the price spike shown in the black circle was a F/O and not a valid engulf to the downside? In retrospect we can decipher that it was indeed a F/O, but I'm not seeing a way to know that during the live formation of price action.

The complication gets even worse when I start reviewing different time frames- it is really hard to know where to start looking since price continues to bounce and react to previous historic levels. I suppose we would have to look left and see why price engulfed to the upside in the red circle to find out if the break of that high ended in a critical location where orders were remaining. I think the engulf tends to take place in areas of low significance, whereas fake outs are essentially the IT's searching for LQ by triggering stops and finding pockets where orders reside.

Sorry if this is hard to follow, I'm not good at describing this using words.

Thanks for your help and contribution!

Spending some time practicing engulfs this weekend. Here is a chart on EUR/JPY.

I am doing these on a 30 min-5 min time scale. Looking for areas on the 30-min where price is likely to react and using a 5-min chart find entries based on engulfs.

Here is an example of one that didn't work out well due to a lack of a RT:

EUR-JPY 30 Min: I notice stacked zones, and I think price will likely bounce from one of these two levels on RT.

I will drop down to a 5 min chart to look for engulfs of important flags on approach to these stacked supply zones. I see an engulf on a 5 min chart but there is no retrace.

But....if I look closer, there looks to be a mini engulf just before the obvious engulf I marked. See my next chart:

Is this 'mini engulf' valid as being an engulf of the first red rectangle, or is this price action just a reaction/bounce from the second red rectangle? It is clear to see retrospectively that this was an engulf but in real time I would have had a tough time determining the validity of this engulf.

My understanding is that an engulf might not be a true engulf if the following situations exist:

1. The potential engulf occurs at a flag that is a reaction to the original flag. 2. The potential engulf occurs at a S/R level 3. The Engulf hits its target straightaway (easy to miss if you don't look closely)

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
Here is another example: EUR-JPY

Here, I see a strong S/R area (30 min chart) where price has lots of history. I see a nice FTR with fresh demand, and watch as price shoots down to hit the level on its FTB.

This is an area I would expect to see price bounce, and would drop down to a 5 min chart to look at price as it approaches this level.

On the 5 min chart, I see what looks like a bullish QM forming and an engulf (the HH portion of the bullish QM). My question: is that HH a true engulf or is price just reacting off the supply level? In real time, it would have been tough to determine. This is what I really struggle with, and I believe it is the source of many of my failed trades. Conceptually the engulf is easy to understand. In reality, they are very tricky.

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
Another example E/J:

Here is a 5 min chart that shows lots of compression on approach to a HTF supply zone. I have drawn the flags on approach, most of which are in the CP zone (not sure if I drew it correctly with the blue rectangle). It looks like price engulfs in to this zone at the red circle, but is this an engulf or just a reaction/bounce off of the flag it ends in? Or, should I see this as a break in to a CPPAZ? If it is a break in to a CPPAZ, does it matter that the engulf ends up in the middle of a flag?

Or, should the CPPAZ be drawn like the chart below shows? Even this scenario shows the engulf breaking in to a demand area to the left....which raises the same question: how to determine a legitimate engulf from a illegitimate one? Looking at PA, it seems that this was an engulf, but in real time I would have seen price engulfing the low of the flag that formed as a result of its reaction to the flag below it...making the EG invalid. There are many situations where engulfs looking very similar to the example on this chart end up not following through and the reason (in retrospect, from most traders) is "the engulf didn't occur because price didn't engulf an original flag, it engulfed a flag that formed as a result of a reaction to the original flag". Wouldn't almost any break into a CPPAZ engulf a flag that ultimately formed as a result of price's reaction to the flag below it? CPPAZ are basically stacked flags with price returning to the MPL to clear any remaining buy/sell orders right? I am confused

Here is a 30 min chart that shows the bigger picture as price moves in to the two stacked supply levels (both are fresh as price approaches). On the 30 Min chart I see price break in to a CP zone (between the two stacked supply zones) but it fails to reach the upper fresh supply. If I had been watching this live, I would have expected price to engulf on the LTF chart (as it did on the 5 min chart) but instead of RT to the origin of the EG, F/O to the other end of the compression to get all of the sell orders waiting at the fresh upper supply level.This never happened, but it's another factor to consider when studying engulfs. Even in a scenario where a valid engulf occurs, price may not RT to the origin of the engulf and continue on to the target....PA might form a fakeout (diamond) to reach the MPL, triggering stop losses and trapping breakout traders to give IT's liquidity.... In this example, it seems odd that price didn't fakeout to the upper supply level- especially considering there was nothing but compression between the two supply levels, and once price broke in to the CP, I would have expected it to freely travel to the end of the CP and take the sell orders waiting at the supply zone. Any ideas on why this didn't happen? I must be missing something...

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
Here is an example on EUR-JPY where there is an engulf, and a nice QM short opportunity.

I notice however, that if I look at where the EG ended up, price stops at a S/R level that had quite a bit of history. In real time, had I looked at this location, I would have seen this PA as an invalid engulf and assumed price was simply bouncing off an old S/R level (which is often does, and doesn't mean an engulf occurred).

Here is the chart, with the vertical dotted red line showing the location of the engulf. How should I read this when I am live trading? It seems like the engulf concept works when it works, and there is always a reason why it doesn't work when it doesn't work. But many times, I feel that engulfs don't work when they should, and they do work when they shouldn't. What am I missing?

And here is a close up of the PA - it would have been a really nice trade. I wouldn't have taken it based on price engulfing into a S/R level with history.

I am not trying to be pessimistic...but sometimes we share too many situations where engulfs work out and fail to take a hard look at the ones that don't, or assume that an engulf is valid just because price followed through the way we suspected it would. Lately, I've been challenging myself to look objectively at these trades and avoid a type of 'confirmation bias' where I only see the winning trades as proof that I'm understanding a concept while discounting all the evidence that points to the contrary.I am not challenging the RTM concepts, I am questioning whether I understand the concepts as well as I think I do.

It seems that everything at RTM revolves around the engulf, so it is worth the time to really practice and understand how and why they form, and how to spot them in real time - not just in retrospect looking at historic charts.

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
E/J Example - nice price structure with an engulf that looks pretty straightforward and clean to me...no S/R levels or reactionary flags to worry about. I see two consecutive downside engulfs, which (in my experience) increases the odds that price will follow through accordingly.

Something I have been noticing, is price often times does not RT to the origin of the engulf - many times it only retraces to the S/R flip directly above the engulf. This chart is a perfect example of the PA I see on a regular basis.

In this case, two trades could be taken: one at the S/R flip and another at the origin of the engulf (in case price does return). The downside to this strategy is the location of the stop loss - it hurts the R:R ratio substantially. Has anyone else noticed price is not returning to the origin of the engulf as frequently as it used to?

Would I be right in saying the following:

Every Flag that forms must have have two flag limits. Those flag limits are formed when an engulf happens and an FTR is formed. The FTR's that are formed are decision points and areas of true supply/demand (where price often fakes out to gather orders for liquidity). The flag contains all the PA that exists within the flag limits. The Flag is the PAZ - the portion below and above the flag/PAZ are the flag limits which "box in" the area where price bounces around until it has the ability to engulf one of the two flag limits. These flag limits represent the furthest (most extreme) set of orders remaining. This is true supply/demand (within the context of the Flag it's currently in), and this is where the MPL's are located.

Just some drawing's about concepts I've been thinking about lately.....

Fakeouts:

Here is a HTF chart showing a typical QM setup. I circled three critical areas that I will detail in future pictures.

More detailed:

My explanation:

These are good places to look for a low risk high return trade. I've noticed Salivan takes these frequently. I think the whole setup essentially revolves around two major pieces of PA: a fakeout followed by an engulf within the scope of a QM. For a bullish setup, we look on the higher time frames for a recent fakeout (to the downside) followed by an engulf into a PAZ (above). The fakeout forms the LL portion of the QM. The HH portion of the QM is the engulf into a PAZ above. This engulf is only valuable if it hasn't hit it's target yet. An engulf that hits it's target before retracing wouldn't be useful.

Let's go back to the fakeout for second....the fakeout is where all of the detail begins for the actual entry when price returns later on. I notice there are three areas that matter within the scope price forming a fakeout:

1. The decision point where price breaks down to form the fakeout (this is an FTR, a DP, and a FL). 2. The engulf of the DP to FO (price breaks the upper level of the FL that acted as the DP for price to EG) 3. The FL that forms as a result of the engulf of the previous FL that acted as the DP for price to fakeout. This new FL is the true demand and origin of the move up. It is within this FL that price will bounce on return. The lowest level of this FL is the MPL and price will often fakeout to this extreme set of orders. We can anticipate this by setting an entry order with a very tight stop loss. Nice R:R.

The reason I am getting into this is because if we have the sequence of flag limits wrong then everything else will be wrong.

What I've taken in so far about flag limits is the following: ( I might be completely wrong) 1- The most important FLs are those that are created after engulfing an opposite FL. 2- The last FL in a rally (b4 RBD is established) is the most important one... the last FL in a drop (b4 DBR is established) is the most important one. 3- The first FL coming out of a new zone i.e. RBD/DBR that takes out another opposite FL (2-) or an important swing high/low (that gave the lowest low/highest high) has great value.

4- Sometime FL cannot be well seen defined as per breaking an important SR or another opposite FL, but often we can tell of their existence by looking at where price held several times in a row. 5- Flipped FLs are important as they may at times of non visibility of the new ones define the new zone for us. 6- The best trades to be taken are the FTBs to FLs. 7- Price will often FO in the zone between the the first FL that come out of a RBD/DBR and the RBD/DBR itself. 8- A FL may have other FLs inside it, an important one would be an opposite one that got faked out, then flipped. 9- The decision to break out of an FL is often tradable. 10- A FL is a RBR/DBD and often defined as one candle - the whole range of that candle.

Good points, Lucien. It is definitely making me think harder...

Salivan and IF both are confident in the trades they take...they have tight stops with large limits. They trade in the direction of an engulf that hasn't hit its target. Trading with such tight stops requires knowing exactly where the last extreme set of orders/liquidity lies within a FL. You are right to say that we should look for trades in areas where tricks were played in the past. In every one of Salivan's trades there is a fakeout that recently occurred and his entries occur near these fakeouts.

An analogy I think of: The fakeout is like a tornado that destroys a town and everyone in it. There is nothing good left for the survivors so most people pack up and leave town looking for a new place to live. A few people end up going back to this town a few days later in a last ditch effort to grab any money/gold/valuables left behind. Everyone left in such a hurry that inevitably there were some valuables left behind.These people gather up all the valuables they can find and hop on the last train leaving town. Salivan is always one of the people who go back to grab whatever valuables they can find

If the point of a fakeout is to grab liquidity by trapping traders into taking the wrong position and/or triggering stop loss orders, it would make sense that a fakeout would happen in an extreme area of a FL - the extreme opposite of the engulf and target. If this is true, we can conclude that fakeouts occur in an extreme part of a flag. If a fakeout takes all liquidity in its path, it would logically make sense that no orders would be left in the area where the fakeout occurred.

We know fakeouts tend to spike in to areas of liquidity - which is usually an extreme part of a FL or FTR. Maybe the goal is to look for the last place where orders exist after the fakeout has cleared out the extreme set of orders in the flag it broke in to. I would say the last fresh set of orders would be found in the extreme portion of the FL that forms after the first engulf of the base/decision to fakeout. The FL/FTR that forms after the engulf of the DP to FO would be the last place for price to return to and get orders before continuing on to its target.

As opportunists who want to gather up value easily, we start looking around for other towns where tornadoes have recently destroyed everything. We wait for everyone to start migrating out of the town looking for a better place to live and that's when we show up to grab what is left. This is what we should be doing in these charts - looking for places where tornadoes have touched down but nobody has come back yet.

Not sure if this is right though...

posts.text:
The market moves depending on order flow. We focus mainly on engulfs of important FL's in to a PAZ for an indication of where price is preparing to go next. The engulf is only valid if its target hasn't been hit, and IF says "every engulf has a specific target".

Lets assume a bearish engulf happens:

If there is a bearish engulf on a HTF chart, there will be an associated target (the origin of the last move up?). Until that target is hit we would be taking a big risk taking any long position...even if we found a bullish engulf into a different PAZ in a lower time frame.Until the HTF engulf hits its intended target, the prevailing momentum of the market won't change. We wouldn't feel safe getting in to a trade if we were in the middle of a PAZ in the HTF...IF also tells us to trade only the edges of these zones.

Just because there is an engulf on a LTF at an extreme edge of a flag doesn't mean we are at an extreme area on the higher time frame. We might still be stuck in the middle of a PAZ. Maybe the missing piece is knowing when the HTF and LTF engulfs and final orders/liquidity line up with each other...? Wouldn't we anticipate the largest volume of orders be located in these target areas?

Maybe that is why Salivan and IF and other experienced traders on RTM always say "look left, and look left again". Maybe we have to first track all of the engulfs and their targets before knowing if the trade we are about to take is being executed in a low risk/high return area. Not sure, but its worth thinking about

posts.text:
The difference between en engulf and a fakeout (based on my understanding) depends on the location of the engulf/fakeout. A engulf happens in to an area of no significance (no important OF). A fakeout has a specific purpose - to get liquidity. So fakeouts occur in to areas with substantial OF.

The areas of a chart that have the most OF or liquidity is FTR's/FL's.

Flag limits are also FTR's - and these areas of price structure contain important decision points. These Fl's/FTR's also represent the extreme levels of a particular flag and mark the upper/lower boundaries of price action zones (PAZ).

Maybe the key to finding the best areas for a reaction/bounce is focusing more on what the initial fakeout is reacting to (look further left).

Are all HH/LL in a QM a fakeout? Is it possible to have a QM form without a fakeout?

Is a Diamond made up of two fakeouts? One of the HH/LL portion of the QM and another for the diamond formation (which fakeouts the initial fakeout).

More diagrams - can both of these be true? If price breaks in to a PAZ it is supposed to be en engulf - but what if price breaks in to a PAZ while forming a QM? Is the HH portion of the QM a fakeout even through it happened in an area without important OF?

As you mention, OF is found in FL's/FTR's. I see OF the same as liquidity...it is an area where ample orders exist. There are FL's everywhere, and not all of them hold the same level of importance. I am focusing on finding FL's that form (as an FTR) after an engulf of a swap zone. You want to focus on finding swap zones of importance - I would suggest going out to a higher time frame chart and looking for times when price made a bold decision to engulf a swap zone. The more times price has tested a swap zone and bounced, the more significant this zone is. Look at the engulf, then watch as price RT to form a FTR. The FTR that forms is also a FL, and this is an area with strong OF because it formed after a very important engulf.

Another place to find FL's with strong OF:

1. Find a fakeout 2. Find the decision point to Fake out 3. Wait for price to engulf this DP 4. The FL that forms after the engulf of the DP to Fake out has substantial OF and will likely be a good place to trade when price returns on its FTB.

Not all of these FL's bounce price really far, and I am still in the middle of trying to figure out why this is.

Here is a chart that I found that seems to illustrate this concept. I apologize for the messy labels...they are all important in explaining the PA. I will do my best to explain (in words) what his happening in the chart. Hopefully Salivan will tell me if I am still wrong...as always, I don't want to mislead anyone here

The deep retrace happens in a PAZ - between two FTR's which form the upper and lower limits of the PAZ. These FTR's also include FL's which act as the origin of the move down and the origin of the move up.

If you look at the chart, you will see the origin of the move down (also target for longs). Price falls from this level, and bounces briefly before faking out (labeled fakeout # 1) below the low of the swap zone confirmation FL Box (red rectangle) where new order flow was created. We identify the decision to fakeout, and wait for price to engulf this DP and form a FTR/FL. This FL/FTR is also the origin of the move up, and will be the target of future shorts (this is very important to remember).

Now that the origin of the move up/target for shorts is formed, we have a completed PAZ (the space between both of the origins). I labeled that in yellow.

Price continues up to the origin of the move down (like Salivan says, these origins act as magnets attracting price). When price reaches this origin, it creates another fakeout to the upside (labeled fakeout # 2). Wait for price to come back down and engulf to the downside (the engulf on the chart is labeled & occurs below the blue rectangle FL Box. This engulf is important because we know the target for that engulf is the origin of the move up (it has not been hit yet, so price will be attracted to it).

Price begins to fall towards the origin of the move up/ target for shorts but does not make it before reversing back to fakeout #2. Price is reversing to gather the remaining OF before continuing on to hit the target. This is good for us, because we will have a very tight stop loss and a wide target (as usual, we zoom in to find the DP to FO, and wait for an engulf of the DP to FO. The FTR/FL that forms after the EG is the best place to wait for an entry. In this case, the short was about 1:13 RR.

I don't know if I am 100% correct but hopefully someone will correct me if I am wrong. The hard part will be finding these live.... but with practice it will be possible.

Incredible potential for building a trading account with a R:R like this.

I want to spend some time better understanding 'true supply' and 'true demand'. It's my understanding that the MPL is located at the extreme edge of the true supply/demand zone. If we can get good at identifying and labeling these zones, we will have an excellent chance of trading price as it returns to the level. Ideally, we will draw these zones, check every scale/TF, and wait for a QM to setup near the zone.

Everything else falls in to place from that point forward....QM's that form too far from true supply/demand end up turning in to diamonds.

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
Here is a simple drawing that explains how I see true supply.

Usually, I look for a rally in price and wait for an engulf (to the downside) to occur, which indicates the direction of PA is changing. The FTR that forms after the first engulf is true supply/demand...but I am not sure that is always correct.What exactly is true supply, and how does it differ from regular supply?

**What specific factors must be present in order for supply/demand to be qualified as "True"?

For example: My drawing shows true supply, but it also shows a RBD "A" which is also supply. RBD "A" formed after an engulf & is located within a FTR. Why is RBD "A" just regular supply and not "True supply"? What specific factors make the red rectangle "true"? Does it have something to do with the importance of the zone engulfed prior to the supply/demand level being formed?

More Questions to Investigate:

1. Does true supply/demand exist in the same FTR as the origin of the move down? 2. Is the MPL always located at the extreme edge of the true supply/demand zone? 3. Is True Supply always the target for future longs? 4. How does scale effect true supply/demand zones? Can you have LTF zones of true supply/demand within the HTF true supply/demand zones? 5. When do we know true supply/demand has formed? Do we know as soon as the FTR has formed (after the engulf), or do we need additional confirmation? 6. How does Order Flow fit in with our understanding of true supply/demand/Origin? Is true supply/demand the first time price engulfs an opposing zone and creates fresh orders?

It is easy to get comfortable with the RTM terms and concepts without actually understanding how to define these terms. Trading is highly visual, and I notice over time I am finding & labeling "origin" and "true supply" without really knowing why... It just "looks right" based on the PA. I am probably right some of the time (and that is when my trades are successful) but I am wrong frequently...and that is reflected in my failed trades. These failed trades stem from my lack of understanding.

A good test: being able to explain why a certain area is a origin/true supply or demand/ MPL etc... AND being able to explain why other areas (that may look similar) are not origin/true supply or demand/MPL, etc..

Using scale in our analysis exponentially complicates everything - which is why having a true understanding of these intricate concepts is so critical for sustainable success.

I will start with finding the origin of the move up- the origin of the Rally.

The origin of the rally would be the first time where new free order flow was established. It is the place where bears were defeated by bulls. This defeat would manifest itself in the form of a swap zone. We need an engulf and a RT in order to create new free OF...but there are many engulfs. We need to find the most important engulf. Since we are looking for the beginning of a rally, we are looking for an engulf to the upside. We need to find the most important bullish engulf to give us a starting point. But we can't use just any bullish engulf - the only one that matters (for the purpose of finding the origin of the move up) is the upside engulf of a previously established bearish swap zone to the left. We want to find the last time a bearish swap zone was established, tested, and held price down. I want to find an engulf of this final zone.

When I say "established, tested, and held price down" I am looking for the last place a bearish swap zone was established, bulls pushed up into this zone and were rejected and price formed a new low as a result. Price bounces off levels all the time - I am only looking for a bounce AND a new low.

I analyzed the PA located to the left of the beginning of the rally to ID all swap zones. See the chart below: I only drew zones that held price down, and price made a new low/high as a result of the bounce. The arrows show where those bounces occurred.

Here is a different view, with the labels deleted for simplicity & clarity:

Hopefully someone will correct me if I'm wrong, but I think the FTR that forms in the lower extreme RT of the engulf of the last Bearish-controlled FL is:

1. FTR 2. FL 3. Origin of the move up 4. Future target for shorts 5. True Demand 6. MPL is located at the extreme low of the FTR

Here is a chart to illustrate:

Is there anything I have labeled (so far) that is wrong or dependent on something to the left that I haven't seen? This is where I get confused. Often times, a diamond will occur when a QM setup occurs to early and there are still orders at the MPL (true supply or demand). If you look closely at my analysis of price and the swap zones I drew, you will see two different bullish QM's forming:

Typically, in IF & Salivan's trades, the MPL is located in true demand and it is the furthest place price will RT before turning. In this AUD-USD example, anyone going long at the MPL of "true demand" would have been stopped out. This must mean I have improperly labeled the area as true demand and the MPL must exist elsewhere. Where am I going wrong?

I think the answer might be found in the swap zone that forms just prior to true supply/true demand.

Drawing:

1. FTR forms and Buyers are in control. Price bounces many times. 2. Price forms a RBD as it breaks the low of FTR 1. This is also the origin of the engulf 3. Engulf of 1 4. Price RT to DP to EG on its FTB 5. Price falls and a decision is made to break the low of the engulf (# 3) 6. New low is made

The last decision made (5) is the origin of the last move that makes the swap zone confirmed. Until a new low is made at 6, price could have kept rising. Instead, the sellers were in control when price tested the first DP...that test is the FTB (4). Sellers are too strong and push price down to form a new low (6). Now any RT to the origin of the new low is the final DP before the confirmation of the swap zone. It is where the first level of fresh sell orders lies - true supply.

Price won't fakeout above the true supply until it makes a decision to make a new swap zone. A fakeout above # 5 wouldn't net the IT's any more liquidity anyway as all the OF above # 5 was accumulated/distributed in order to form the bearish controlled swap zone. The first area where fresh order flow exists would be at #5.

Is this correct?

Here is a drawing, and a real life example:

At some point, the swap zone could itself be engulfed and a new swap zone could form. I think we are safe to trade the true supply in this zone so long as one of two things are happening:

1. Price has not yet hit the target of its engulf (in this case, the target for shorts) 2. The target for shorts is itself engulfed (target hit, but low extreme of the target is engulfed, indicating price wants lower...)

In this example, as long as there is a current valid bearish engulf (meaning an engulf with a target that has not been hit) we can feel safe trading the true supply area in the bear-controlled swap zone. Once the target for shorts is hit, and no downside engulf of this target occurs, we will wait to see where the new swap zone is formed.

Once a new swap zone is confirmed, we start the same process all over again.

I could be totally wrong about this....

If you disagree, feel free to tell me.

Drawing below to illustrate:

Example where target is hit: we would wait to see what price does before trusting the true supply zone.

Example where TG for shorts is itself engulfed, Supply zone can still be trusted to hold price down.

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
I've been reading through Marketpedia and looking at my old posts, trying to conceptualize the MPL and true supply/demand.

We know FTR's and engulfs are everywhere on a chart...there are so many of them it would be overwhelming to draw each and every FTR/FL and engulf in every time frame on the chart. We know not every engulf and FTR/FL are created equal...some are much more important than others. We focus on the most important engulfs- specifically, engulfs of established swap zones.

If True supply/demand is formed after an engulf of an important swap zone, we know the true supply/demand level is also a FTR/FL. The MPL (as Jurij helped me understand with his post last night...refer to post # 953) is always located in a FTR.

If everything I've said is true so far, then it makes sense that not all MPL's are created equal - some are much stronger than others. The term "MPL" isn't inherently special in any way...it isn't a 'magic' area where price won't break. It is simply the most extreme set of order flow left in a FL. The MPL is only as strong as the FTR/FL in which it resides. Not all FTR's are important, and not all FTR's will bounce price. Some FTR's are weaker than others. Similarly, not every MPL is going to hold price the way we might want. There is no guarantee an MPL will hold price at any given time.

When price easily engulfs FL/FTR, it was able to break the MPL included within. Easy breaking of MPL = imbalance of order flow. Example - a FTR that forms after a bearish engulf that fails to hold price down doesn't have enough sell orders to compete against the buy orders that push price back up. The stronger a FL/FTR, the stronger its MPL will be. Strong MPL's will bounce price, and we can feel comfortable trading fakeouts to these MPL's.

If we find critical areas where an engulf of a swap zone occurs, we can be relatively confident that the resulting formation of a FL/FTR (and the MPL included within the FTR) will be strong. Strong FTR = MPL that is likely to bounce price. MPL's that bounce price have a lot of order flow ready to protect its position.

As always, I could be wrong, but I want to keep track of my thoughts.

I've been practicing lately on understanding scale. Here are some quick notes about my findings so far:

This is conceptual....I will be posting charts as I become more comfortable with the basics.

Price begins a new move by engulfing a swap zone. A FTR usually forms after an engulf and this zone is:

1. True supply/demand 2. FTR/FL 3. MPL 4. Origin of the move up/down 5. Target for future buys/sells

This is true regardless of the scale. 1 minute chart or monthly chart...the structure and fluidity of how price moves does not change. It is the dynamic behind how orders are filled and how price moves. PA doesn't exist because we say it does, or because we name the individual components. PA forms the formations we see because that is how price moves...

Analogy: we've all heard the comparison that the market is like a Russian 'nesting doll' (also referred to as Matryoshka Doll). It is a good analogy. Each smaller scale is nested in with the higher time frame that proceeds it. The higher the time frame, the more data is included (even if it is hard to see). We often have to drop down to lower time frames to see the details of PA on lower time frames. Every engulf/FTR/FL/PAZ/target/MPL etc.... exists in various scales within the market.

As with the market, each smaller doll fits inside of a bigger doll.

Assume all the dolls are put together: Even though you can't see all the individual dolls when they are assembled together, you know all the individual dolls exists within the largest doll. You also know (regardless of what size the doll is) the following:

1. Every doll has a head

2. Every doll has two eyes

3. Every doll has two arms

4. Every doll is painted and made of the same material etc...

5. ** You can't properly put the dolls all together without starting with the smallest doll and placing larger dolls over it consecutively. The entire doll's assemblage requires all dolls to work together** ( I am not suggesting you always start a top-down analysis by beginning on a 1-min chart, but I use this example to emphasize each part's contribution to the 'whole'. The smallest doll gets put away first, the largest doll gets assembled last (over the top of all the smaller dolls)

Similar to a Russian doll, the market has its version of heads, eyes, arms, etc...Each time new orders are transacted (regardless of scale), we have a new 'doll' with fresh order flow.

We know this following is also true:

1. Price engulfs to indicate future directional flow of price

2. FTR/FL formed after important engulfs are origins and future targets

3. Every engulf has a target - regardless of which scale it forms on

4. Engulfs are valid and important until its target is hit.

5. The MPL is important as last place of free order flow until price fakes out to consume the orders

6. You have to pay close attention to all time frames, at all times.

More to follow in next post...

Here is AUD-USD Daily Chart:

I labeled the chart according to which zones were the largest, and which were smaller. There are many smaller zones located to the right of 'Medium Doll B'.

Notice that every RBD has an engulf of its own - and an associated Origin and TG for shorts. These engulfs are valid and so are the targets...it just so happens that they are occurring within the large origin/target (PAZ) of the main original zone (labeled as "Bigger Doll A")

As price bounces around in the large PAZ created between the two FL's (and two origins) of 'bigger doll A', it forms numerous RBD reactions. Each of these RBD reactions that their own engulfs, fakeouts, and origins/targets. Each of these RBD's have PAZ too.

Salivan took the AUD-USD short trade last week, and if you refer to his chart, he writes " last pocket of demand is consumed"...this happened after a confirmed downside engulf. (you can see the chart on his journal post # 692). That demand pocket was medium time frame origin 'up' and the future target for shorts. The shorts that pushed price in to the zone consumed the buy orders...clearing the way for price to drop down to the next target of 'Medium Doll B'. The smaller time frame targets have to be cleared before price can be free to move down and hit the original target for shorts - which originated at 'Bigger Doll A".

Once a target is hit, the engulf that preceded the target is satisfied, and price can move on to take out the next closest target... once that target is hit, price can drop to the next largest target etc... Price will satisfy all the lower time frame engulfs/targets first because they have to....these smaller targets/origins were formed inside the HTF PAZ.

I think this is how you can keep track of price on multiple time frames- know all of the EG's and Targets and identify them as they become satisfied. Always know where your main PAZ is located.

as always, I could be wrong about this, so please don't take this as 100% true until an associate or master trader agrees

posts.text:
The more I study charts the more I question that there is any difference between a FO and an EG.

To me, its entirely dependent on the scale.

For example, what looks like a FO on a smaller scale may be just a reaction to a HTF true supply/demand level, or it may be an engulf in to a new PAZ of a HTF chart. Depending on the scale, a FO may very well be a fake out...but it may also be an engulf.

How we deal with the FO depends on the scale we are trading on, and what target/origin is next in line to be satisfied.

Maybe it all comes down to asking "what engulf is currently in control"?

The lower time frame engulfs matter more (if we are looking for exact entries and targets) because it is the LTF engulfs that have targets which will be hit first. Each engulf has:

1. Engulf 2. RT, with new Origin 3. Future target

Here is a simple drawing:

It seems to me that every time a new engulf happens this 1-2-3 system is established. It works from the LTF out to the HTF (like the Russian stacking dolls).

In order to know where to take a TT (virtually no stop loss) you have to know which engulf is in control (which 1-2-3 system is in control). As Salivan puts it, you have to ask "where is price coming from?" (at least this is my interpretation of why he asks this question.... I definitely could be wrong)

This is my greatest weakness - keeping track of where the most important EG (and its associated origin/target) in relation to the entire chart.

These origins and targets are important because they represent true supply/demand...which means they represent areas with free order flow. If we are going to take a trade, we have to know that there isn't any untapped area of free order flow opposite our entry (within our scale) or else, price will have a reason to take the order flow. I think this is why so many of my trades get stopped out...there is still free order flow existing in a pocket above/below my stop loss.

Assume this drawing is a HTF - Daily or weekly chart.

Assume the drawing starts with a downside engulf of a PAZ.

This is the "Biggest Doll":

System has three main points:

1. Engulf 2. RT to form Origin 3. Engulf has a Target

The PAZ is everything between the two FL's

The ultimate target for the engulf is to hit its target - which is the last HTF origin of the move up (at point # 3). Of course we know it isn't going to hit its target right away...a lot will happen in the PAZ. It may take weeks/months/years for the HTF target to actually get hit (depends on the time frame). Price is free to move around within the PAZ until it breaks one of the two FL's that establish the top and bottom of the PAZ.

Every engulf of a swap zone has the same '1-2-3 system' with its own engulf, RT to form Origin, and target for engulf. Imagine if there are 3,4,5 or 10 of these 'systems' all located within the largest time frame....it would get very confusing unless you had it labeled perfectly.

If the EG hits its TG right away, it means it hit an origin (the target is an opposing origin)...which is a FTR/FL. FTR/FL = FOF, and FO's occur in areas of FOF.

Engulfs occur in areas with little FOF significance.

EUR-AUD - Sample trade with full analysis:

Start with HTF FL Boxes that form opposing swap zone. Fl Box B forms after an engulf, and the target for that HTF engulf is shown as well. I will be focusing almost exclusively on FL Box B for the other charts.

Fl Box B is formed by three main data points:

1. Data Point 1: HTF Engulf 2. Data Point 2: FTR/FL (only confirmed when price makes new low at Data Point # ) 3. Data Point #3: makes a new low, which confirms the entire HTF FL Box B. This is a confirmed RBD.

Data Point 4 shows the target of the engulf at Data Point 1. It is important that this target has not been met yet.

A closer look at Data Point 2: This is the furthest area of the RT after the HTF engulf at Data Point 1. This FTR/FL contains the true supply level & MPL. This is FOF.

This is a 1-minute chart focused on Data Point 2. This shows the exact area of true supply. Price will react at this level when price returns at a later date. This is this is the most extreme area of FOF in FL Box B. Price will want to get this liquidity before prices moves on to hit the HTF target of the HTF engulf (located at Data Point 1).

This is also the area of the MPL

This chart shows the entry. Notice the entry is also located at a LTF QM level. Again, I want to stress the importance of the HTF engulf not yet hitting the HTF target. This is how we know price still wants to drop. Price returns all the way to get all extreme orders within FL Box B. If the TG of the EG at Data Point 1 had already hit the target, I wouldn't feel comfortable shorting at this MPL.

Lastly, I want to focus on Data Point 3. This LTF PA forms a LTF bullish QM, with a LTF upside engulf. The target of this LTF engulf is also our entry point...the origin of the move down. The best short entries are found in an area that is also target for longs,. Price drops all the way down to the target of the HTF engulf that first occurred at Data point 1.

I am learning that knowing the target of an engulf is as important (if not more important) than knowing EG VS FO.

An engulf is only useful/valid/ if it's target is unmet.

I found a really good example on EUR-JPY

This is a really long example, because I am going step by step for identifying the target. I don't think we spend enough time stressing the importance of finding targets

There are 12 charts posted total (over the next two posts) and it is step by step to show the phases of analysis. I hope this is organized enough to follow...if not, please don't hesitate to ask for clarifications

First chart shows the initial FL Boxes that got me interested in this area. FL Box C engulfs the low of FL Box A, and as a result, forms a swap zone.

Before analyzing the details of FL Box C to find a place to get short, I must find out where the target is located for this engulf. I need to find the target for shorts. I look left and see an area with lots of PA that exists before FL Box A. This is an area of consolidation where price eventually broke to the upside and formed FL Box A.

If I am looking for a target for shorts, I need to find the last opposing bullish controlled swap zone....

This next chart zooms in to this area (previously inside the neon colored circle in the chart above). Start drawing FL Boxes - only the important ones that held price AND as a result price made a new low/high. We only want the strongest zones. I found two main zones: the blue rectangle shows an area of bullish/buyer control, and the long black rectangle shows an area of very strong seller control.

Look how well price respects the upper level of the black rectangle....it takes a while to break this high. This is good - it means this is a strong bearish controlled zone. When price breaks this upper level, it will be significant.

When looking for a target for shorts, we want to find the swap zone that gives us true demand...remember on my previous posts I said "The best place to sell is in an area that is a target for longs".It works the other way too "The best place to buy is in an area that is also a target for sells". This true demand is the origin of the move up, and it is the 'magnet' that is attracting price from above. This 'magnet attraction' concept is something Salivan came up with and it makes a lot of sense.

Wait for the break of the strong bearish controlled rectangle. Here is when details matter...don't be sloppy/lazy with your analysis.

Just because price breaks the upper level of the strong bear-controlled rectangle (FL Box), doesn't mean it is the best place to draw your new Fl Box. Look for the following:

** Wait for price to break your important zone. After the break, label the breaks and the corresponding lows that form.

Look at these breaks and corresponding Lows: Pick the lowest low that forms and find the high that preceded the lowest low. These two points make up you new FL Box..the important Fl Box that holds the true demand and origin of the move up. You want to choose the high the corresponds to the last low that forms because you want to origin of the move up...it has to be the last demand zone before price moves up.

The chart below shows this new FL Box D. This Fl Box holds the origin of the move up.

Here is a clean chart showing all of the important components of finding the target for this EUR-JPY trade:

This is a continuation from a long post that started above (post # 1101). You might want to read post #1101 first, as it will be easier to follow along with this post. These concepts are really hard to explain using words, so hopefully it isn't too confusing...

Referring to FL Box D: We know this FL Box holds to origin of the move up, therefore it is our target for shorts. Of course, we need to refine the target to an exact FL.Here is how I did that:

If you read my posts last night on post #1094 and #1096, you will see I use the same 3 data point method for identifying the important areas within FL Box D. Whether you are looking for a place to enter the market, or for a place to exit the market, the analysis is the same. We want true supply/demand areas that are origins and targets.

I use this analysis in FL Box D to find true demand...true demand = origin of the move up = the target for my shorts.

Target Data Point 1: Is the engulf of the strong bearish controlled FL Box

Target Data Point 2: Is the FTR/FL that forms the extreme end of FL Box D. True demand is located here as well as the MPL

Target Data Point 3: This is where price makes a new high, which confirms FL Box D. This is a DBR.

The next chart shows a zoomed in view of Fl Box D. To ID the true demand zone, we start drawing LTF swap zones...only the most important ones. Find the first swap zone that forms that still has FOF.

You can see where this LTF swap zone first occurs. This level is strengthened by also containing a perfect looking DP. True demand with a nicely formed DP = great place to attract sellers. I drew FL Box E (within FL Box D) to narrow the target down. I copied a neon greed dotted line (the line runs horizontally through FL Box E) to show the exact location where price bounced later on. You can see exactly where the confirmed target was...it reacted exactly in this area.

The next chart shows a bird's eye view of the entire trade, with the target extended along the bottom of the chart so you can see how price reacts to it, as it falls from FL Box C after the major engulf of FL Box A.

Now I will focus on the entry... the PA located inside Fl Box C will give us true supply & the origin of the move down. You don't start looking for an entry until you identify the target of your engulf and determine that the target is still unmet.

There is an important distinction to make (regarding this specific example) about the target being hit before price returns to the true supply level in FL Box C, but i'll discuss that towards the end

Here is the same three point analysis:

Data Point 1: Price engulfs Fl Box A - this is a major engulf and is the reason we are even looking at this EUR-JPY example. The target we just found is the target of this engulf.

Data Point 2: This is the extreme edge of FL Box C and is also the FTR/FL and true supply. MPL is located here too.

Data Point 3: Price makes a lower low which confirms FL Box C. This is a RBD.

The next chart shows a zoomed in view if FL Box C. We are looking for the first swap zone that forms that still has FOF. LTF FL Boxes are drawn and you can see a nice supply zone with another perfect DP. This zone is also the origin of the move down. You can see how well price reacts to this level on its FTB. Finding nicely formed DP's in your true supply/demand level really increases the odds that price will be attracted.

Now..for the most important part of this whole example: As you can see in the chart below, price broke out of FL Box C and hit the target straightaway without returning to true supply. In a situation like this, you would want to be very careful about shorting at the FTB to true supply, because the engulf has already hit its target. If you weren't aware that the target had already been hit, you might go short and place a stop above the MPL of true supply....depending on where your limit order was placed you would be stopped out (see the big red circle). Often times, I think failed trades are a result of not knowing where your target is located, after an engulf occurs. This becomes even more important when you start looking at higher time frames and drilling down on many different scales and time frames.

Getting in on a trade, in the right scale, because of an engulf that has an unmet target, will drastically increase the odds that your trade works out.

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
With regard to price faking out past true supply to a DP located above (see my last post for a chart example and the drawing below for reference)

What I am trying to understand:

In a scenario where price forms a FO to the DP above true supply:

Does a DP located above true supply negate the the true supply zone itself with regard to FOF, or do we view it as price skipping over true supply? If true supply = FOF, and we know FOF bounces price, how can price just "jump" over this important zone to hit a DP above? It makes no sense to me.... Doesn't price have to pass through this zone of fresh orders? The only way to blow through an important area of FOF to a DP above would be to flood the market with so many buy orders that the FOF (sell orders in this example) doesn't turn price. What would be the point of doing that, if the goal is to drop price? If you want to drop price, you want someone else to start buying from you...by pushing price through an area of FOF short orders you absorb the liquidity at that level by buying more orders than actually exist at the level (that would be the only way to physically push through that level...right?). Only IT's have the financial power to push price on such a huge scale, and it would be a very expensive move to make to hit a DP.

The only way this becomes profitable for the IT is if there are so many sell orders/liquidity/FOF in the DP above, it warrants the buying that is necessary to push price to this level. There would have to be more FOF in the DP than exists in the true supply zone below it. Under what circumstances does a DP have more FOF than a true supply level below it, and how can we identify this on a chart? Is this the key to predicting when a FO will occur?

EUR-AUD - Continued from post above:

Taking a closer look at this RBD to ID more important swap zones....

B engulfs A

D engulfs C

So which of these boxes represents the origin of the move down? Sometimes it is hard to know, but it is really important because origins are also future targets. Not knowing the future target means you don't know an ORFL when you see one. Not knowing a target/ORFL = not knowing if an engulf is valid and how far price may RT before hitting the target.

It can be hard to ID an origin, because often times there are multiple origins within different time scales.

What process do we use to identify an origin? Generally, they occur after an engulf of an important swap zone...but there has to more to it...especially when there are multiple engulfs of swap zones all located in close proximity together (as in this EUR-AUD example. It is easy to look back in hindsight and label origins and targets, because history gives us a complete view of price reaction. The difficulty is in identifying these origins/targets in real time. I would refine that statement by adding: the difficulty is in identifying the relevant origins/targets in real time, within the proper scale of the engulf you are using to begin your trade.

Every engulf has a target. Valid (actionable) engulfs have unmet targets

If every engulf has a target, we can safely assume there are many engulfs and many targets all existing in relatively close proximity to each other. How do we go about keeping it all straight?

Here are some of my ideas on this - I have been spending a lot of time on this question because I am convinced this is the key to success in trading.

Firstly: as intimidating as the issue of scale is, I think it is actually a major benefit to us traders...if we can learn how to use scale to improve and normalize our analysis. I am still very new to this, so I am also learning how to "use" scale to my benefit.

Scale offers us a chance to focus on one engulf/target at a time. LTF engulfs and targets will get satisfied first (by first, I mean the lower scale time frame engulfs/targets get met before HTF targets) This happens because PA is fractal, and in order for price to move long distances to satisfy a HTF target, it must pass through countless smaller zones full of LTF engulfs and targets. This is also where the PAZ concept comes in.

As confusing as the PAZ is, I think its intention is actually to simplify trading.

A PAZ is defined as the space between two FTR's/FL's. Regardless of the scale, a PAZ exists between two very important decision points (the areas of true supply and true demand exist within the FTR's that contain the PAZ. In order to break out of a PAZ, price must break through one of these important FTR's. Until this happens, price will bounce around within the PAZ.

How does price move out of a PAZ? I think it all goes back to FOF. Strong orders must exist to break previously important levels within a FTR. Strong orders means the bulls and bear fight it out, the team with the most liquidity wins.

Breaking a strong demand zone requires ample sell orders, and breaking a strong supply zone requires ample buy orders.

Continued from my post starting on # Post 1130:

Let's keep analyzing this concept of targets/origins and scale...

Since the issue of scale adds complexity, I will begin by listing all components of PA that occur regardless of scale. Instead of 'laws of physics' it is my version of 'laws of price movement'

Please don't hesitate to tell me if I am wrong about any of this... I

am still very new to this

We know the following is always true, regardless of scale:

Each PAZ is bordered by a FTR/True supply/demand/associated MPL: Regardless of scale, a PAZ is only a PAZ when bordered by two controlling FTR's (one is bear controlled, the other is bull controlled). The PAZ contained between these two FTR's is essentially a PA battleground aimed at obtaining enough FOF to break one of the opposing FTR's.

The concept of a PAZ is true in a tick chart, and it is true on a monthly chart.The only difference between a HTF PAZ and a LTF PAZ is there are a lot more subsequent PAZ's within the HTF PAZ. The PAZ's all form for the same reason, and they all break for the same reason: order flow.

Analogy: the laws of gravity effect you whether you fall off a skyscraper or fall off a ladder...the only difference is how far you fall from the time you lose balance until the time you hit the ground. You pass through a lot more space on your way down from the roof of the skyscraper. There are more objects you must pass through before hitting the ground (trees, awnings, shrubs, birds, people walking along the sidewalk below, etc....)

But.. the inevitable consequence of gravity is you fall & hit the ground regardless.

I think the same can be said for price movement inside and throughout PAZ's.

In fact, a HTF chart will all of the origins and targets of various scaled (marked out with rectangles) sort of resembles a high rise building with each rectangle representing a floor of the building.

If we know origins and targets are formed after an engulf, we have to determine what qualifies as an important engulf.

How do we determine the importance of an engulf? The importance of an engulf is directly correlated to the importance of the zone it engulfed (to the left of the engulf). But... is this the only factor we should consider when identifying an origin?

What about looking at which engulf and subsequent FTR occurred first? Does the origin always come after the first engulf of a swap zone (after a new high/low is formed)? Is there a difference between finding an important engulf and finding the origin of a move? Can a very important engulf occur and not be an origin of a move?

For example:

Here is a drawing with two FTR's that may contain the origin of the move down. Which one do we choose? Do we choose the origin that was formed as a result of an engulf that happened first, or do we choose the origin that was formed after an engulf of a very important zone to the left?

This situation happens all the time-

I am thinking the answer may be related to what is happening to the left of this PA (on a higher time frame). Is the PA reacting to a HTF origin? If so, maybe the key is looking at the zone it is reacting to... Maybe analyzing the relevancy of the engulf that precedes the origin in our example depends on which price structure is engulfed in the true supply to the left....

Here is a chart example of EUR-AUD: there are many possible origins of the move down. If you look on a HTF chart, you can see this entire area is just a reaction to a HTF zone. Maybe the origin of the move down in our scale is somehow dependent on the PA occurring in the HTF FL its reacting to.

Another question: can an area be correctly labeled 'origin of a move down', but have all its FOF spiked before price returns to hit it as a target from an earlier engulf?If a target has no remaining FOF, do we still name is as a target, or do we look for the closest area that hasn't been spiked yet?

Here is what I came up with - not sure if its right, but it seems logical.

To find the origin of a move down:

Start your analysis when price enters the reactive zone. The green rectangle below is extended from an important swap zone to the left. What we are seeing is price reacting to an important level on its FTB.

If we want to find the origin of the move down, we want to find the place where new opposite orders are executed (FOF). We want to find where the sellers controlled the buyers.

I see two important HTF FL Boxes:

Box A: Forms as price enters the reactive zone Box B: forms as price engulfs the low of Box A. The PA that forms Fl Box B is a RBD

The engulf of Box A's low is the beginning of Sellers taking control...it is the first major step (see data point 1). What follows after the engulf is a retrace to form an FTR/FL (data point 2), and then price continues down to make another new low (a low below the original engulf of FL Box A @ data point 3).

The origin forms somewhere between the furthest RT of FL Box B and the new low (between data point 2 and data point 3).

I labeled all of the possible zones for the origin of the move down (within FL Box B, between data point 2 and data point 3) A-D:

A: Reacts to "X" - not originally created FOF

B: Looks like good supply, but it was not formed immediately after an important engulf

C: First supply formed after engulf. I think this is the important supply

D: Formed after reacting to Supply C, and is the closest zone with remaining FOF (supply C already spiked when price returns later)

Result of the reaction - major bounce (this happened because this origin's target was hit (below) prior to price returning.

Hi H, I like this question since it is all about targets.

It is hard because I think there's no fixed rule. The origin is a level where an important decision was made (new transaction, new decision, FL). And to asses the importance of a DP I think we have to consider multiple things as swap zones (or S/R flips), previous FLs and symmetry (including QMs). I also think there's no fixed rule like "first engulf of a move up" because in the end what moves or holds the market are orders and if there's a wall of orders before a LTF origin FTR, price won't get there unless this barrier (important area like swap) is broken. But could be wrong, it is just what I observed from the charts. I'm coming more and more to the conclusion that there's really one origin and it is the true supply/demand FL after a swap zone break (aligned aka swapped FL).

But if anyone is seeing an easy fixed rule about origins then I'd love to hear about it and the way to identify it
