How do we know when these DP's matter and when they don't (often times price bounces from the DP's but often times it doesn't).

There always seems to be a complication or reason why an MPL will break... a DP located just outside the MPL for example. But it is hard to learn the concepts when there is always a reason why price doesn't respect the MPL. It is highly ambiguous and price is almost always reacting to something on a smaller scale...so where does it stop? It leads to over analyzing and constant second guessing of one's own analysis.

Origins are difficult to ID, and there are a dozen exceptions to every rule (at least it seems that way) so they are hard to identify. Engulfs and fakeouts can be very tricky as well. Even if you ID the origin and target and engulf correctly, you still have to nail the entry on RT...which involves the highly complex work of finding the MPL. All of this is hard, but becomes exponentially harder when the issue of scale is introduced. Even if 99.9% of the analysis is correct, you also have to be 100% to-the-pip correct about the exit (which is a whole other level of complexity). If you miss the exit by a pip you can lose an entire trade that was otherwise a winner.

All of these complex factors must be analyzed by the trader with 100% perfection or else the trade will fail. It seems, even when all of these factors are analysed correctly, the trade still sometimes fails.

I was reading through the RBD and DBR article on Marketpedia. I have a question about the concept of engulfs as it relates to the base of these price structures. Here is the link for anyone who wants to review the material on Marketpedia:

www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/education/markepedia

It is really challenging to ask/propose such a complex question on a forum like this, so I will post everything as clearly as possible in a step - by -step format. Hopefully it isn't too boring or difficult to follow, because I think this is an important question to answer....

IF uses an example of a RBD, and this is a screenshot of the chart he uses to illustrate his point:

In this example, we see a rally that forms the pole, a base which is a flag, and a drop which occurs as a result of an engulf of the flag. This RBD can be drawn like this (drawing I made):

In order for price to form the "drop" part of a RBD, there must be an engulf of the flag (base part of the RBD) and a FTR is formed. The engulf (regardless of scale) has a specific target...in this case, it is the base of the pole/rally. The base of the pole/rally is made up of a lot of PA, but the important PA is the DP that occurs just prior to the emergence of the pole/rally. The origin of the move down occurs somewhere inside the flag, after the engulf, in the area marked as # 3 in the chart below. This engulf + origin down + target hit is all occurring within the RBD in its own LTF scale. All we see from a higher scale is a RBD.

Here is an example I found:

1: DP to rally (pole) 2. Engulf 3. FTR & Origin Down 4. Target of engulf hit at base of pole/rally

Now...going back to my question: IF makes it seem as through price must engulf the low of the entire flag that forms at the base of the pole/rally in order to be valid. Here is a chart he posts that shows this engulf occurring. Take a look at the picture below (I added my writing to it for clarification)

He later goes on to show how this engulf of the base of the pole (rally) is a good indication that price will hold at the cap formed previously on RT...here is his chart showing this (the chart below is a higher time frame from the one previously posted, but it is the same currency pair)

The example IF uses looks great, and it is useful for beginners to understand the basic concepts. That said, It isn't the best example to use for a real life scenario.I rarely see PA this clean and predictable. Price is nasty and it deceives constantly. Firstly, the massive engulf that is shown on IF's example entirely engulfs the whole flag relatively quickly and decisively. Usually, I find that the engulf is not as clear, and usually doesn't break an entire base to obviously. I find it more typical to see PA that acts something like this:

Here is the last chart I posted:

You can see I marked a relatively specific area as the base of the pole/rally (labeled on chart below as # 1). I chose to identify the DP to start the rally/pole...good DP's are precise. I did not include all the other PA that makes up the larger 'base' that forms around the DP. I circled the entire 'base' on the chart below... to me, it looks mostly like compression anyway.

When price forms the 'drop' part of the rally base drop, it engulfs the important decision point that acted as the origin of the pole/rally/move up. To me, this is a very significant piece of PA.

Going back to IF's example, he shows a scenario where price blows right through everything...the DP and all the other PA that formed the base. Which scenario is the correct way to label an engulf of the base/origin of a move up? Does price have to engulf the entire base or just the important DP? I think this is a really important distinction to make and the lack of specificity (oversimplification) in the Marketpedia example causes ambiguity. This question is important because it is directly related to the correct drawing of the MPL. Where do we draw the MPL? If the DP is also an origin of the move up and the target for shorts, it is clearly very important and true demand must also exist in this area. If we don't know the true demand and MPL, we can't be sure of the exact price structure that must be engulfed in order to have a valid (actionable) engulf.

It is a vicious circle of confusion

If I was to take IF's example literally, I would be waiting for price to engulf the low of the flag that contains the DP to rally/pole up. In the USD-CHF scenario, I wouldn't see an engulf at all.

I am especially focused on this issue because it seems like all the market consists of (in its simplest form) are DP's that lead to RBD and DBR (depending on the scale, it might look like a DBD or RBR). Price just seems to bounce around from important DP to important DP. Whether a DP is important depends on the PA that occurs after it and whether it leads to a FTR/FL that holds price up or down. Price breaches levels through engulfs, and IT's obtain liquidity through FO. We have to know these DP's and we have to know (to the exact pip) where the engulfs must occur in order to be actionable (usable).

(Continuation....starting all the way back on post # 1195)

Now for the next set of questions. We use a lot of terminology... sometimes it can get confusing when it comes to drawing the charts correctly. For example:

We use the following terms to label the area where price engulfs an important swap zone to the upside:

Demand True demand FOF FTR MPL FL FTR ORFL DP Origin of the move up Target for shorts Base

This is a lot of terminology and I understand all of it conceptually. Drawing it on a chart and knowing which levels are where is difficult. In theory (like IF's simple example of a RBD engulf on Marketpedia) the concept is somewhat easy to understand. When trading on a live chart however, it can get very confusing. These areas have to be drawn exactly right or else the trade will fail. There is very little information on Marketpedia about these terms, and it is hard to find concrete answers for the common situations where PA is less than clear.

I will start by posting some examples:

Question 1: How to find and properly draw an origin

I don't know of any resource on RTM that explicitly defines this. There are lots of postings with traders using origins and labeling them, but most traders are still learning and you can't just take everyone's word for it. Too often I see mistakes go unchecked in people's journals and I wonder how many novice traders are led astray by this. I know for a fact I am frequently wrong in my journal, and it bothers me to think I might be leading other traders down the wrong path. Can we come up with some concrete rules for identifying and properly drawing an origin? No abstract or vague 'half' answers but actual firm answers that we can use as the basis of all our analysis. I understand we won't be given a perfect step by step manual for how to do this, masters and associates shouldn't be asked to spoon feed us

, but even a couple of verified

and clearly explained pointers would be incredibly helpful.

Let's start by asking how the DP and the origin of a move are related. Maybe a better question is: "with specific regard to FOF, is it the origin that makes the DP or the DP that makes the origin?"

-- Every origin of a move is the beginning of price going up or down after an important engulf of a swap zone. There is a point in every single important FL Box (just prior to the rally/pole) where a decision is made to make this move. But for some reason it seems the origin and the DP are separate...but are still both equally important. What is the decision point? Isn't a decision point on a chart just represent just a specific price when the balance of buys/sells became so uneven that a major move occurs? If so, is the decision point of an origin the same regardless of what time frame/scale we are looking at? If so, we shouldn't we be able to go all the way down to a 1-min chart (or lower) for every single decision point to find the exact price that represents the exact moment when the decision took place?

If I follow this to its logical/conceptual conclusion, wouldn't it have to be true that the origin is wherever the DP occurs? The DP is the whole reason the origin is important, right?

If we can agree that the DP is what makes the origin important, and the DP is the source of the FOF that occurs at these critical levels, we have to understand that the actual fresh FOF always exists(and is formed) at a very specific point in time...we can drop down to the lowest scale possible to identify exactly when this FOF is executed. If this is all accurate, we can say true supply/demand is also located exactly at the time and price FOF is executed.

* FOF/True supply/demand/origin of a move is not dependent on scale. It all exists together at a specific time and price, and finding the exact zone becomes possible the lower you look on the time frames.

If everything I have written so far is accurate (and I am not sure it is) then the next logical question is..how do we go about locating this "special moment in time when FOF is born". This is where we move away from conceptual ideas and focus more on actual execution on a live chart.

How does this 'magical' zone manifest itself physically on a chart?

Let's start with an example EUR-AUD. The chart below shows three FL Boxes that form an important swap zone.

(I chose this example for a reason...FL Box 3 ends up not holding price and I want to investigate why this happens)

If we were trading this chart live we would be focusing on Box 3. This box represents the place where FOF was created after an engulf of an important swap zone.

As you can see, price comes back to this areas and completely ignores FL Box 3.

Clearly, even if I had found the DP and origin located inside FL Box 3, I would have been stopped out almost immediately.

Why did this happen?

Isn't there an origin located in Box 3 with FOF? There is an important DP in FL Box 3 that acted as the source of a very large move up...so why did price blow through this FL Box? What specific mistake did I make in my analysis that led to this (would-be) failed trade?

1. The FL Boxes look accurate. Each box was formed and held price down. 2. Price was held down and it made a new low/new high as a result in each of the three boxes 3. Price went from buyer control to seller control to buyer control.... swapped completely and FOF was formed as a result 4. There is a clear origin/DP located in FL Box 3

So...what happened? What specific step do I need to add in my analysis to 'filter' out situations like this? This example is not a rarity...these fail ALL THE TIME

There must be more to the analysis.

First, we have to realize the following:

1. Not every origin and DP is going to bounce price. 2. Not every swap zone will lead to a FL Box that contains the DP/Origin to bounce price (even if the FL Boxes are drawn correctly like mine

If these two factors are true, we have to look beyond the FL Boxes and the swap zone to understand the context of what is happening around this area.

Maybe the answer lies in the context of price in and around this area

Let's look at the context:

Hourly chart...zoomed out for reference. I circled the area where price missed FL Box 3.

As you can see from the hourly chart, FL Box 3 was actually pretty close to the area where price ended up bouncing....it missed by a nasty FO. Unfortunately when it comes to trading, 'pretty close' is worthless. I need to be exact.

Here is what I see on the hourly chart:I will circle and number all of the lows that may be relevant to this trade.

I suspect someone is likely to tell me that the FO which occurred at # 7 happened as a reaction to the low made at # 6. To that person, I would ask the following questions:

1. Specifically what DP was price reacting to in low # 6 and how could we have known price was going to FO to that level? What makes the OF in that area so important?

2. If price FO (at #7) because it was reacting off of Low # 6, what kept price from FO even further to react off of Low #4

Under what specific context will price FO to a neighboring high/low? Why does this happen, and when do we know we have reached a place where price will not fake out any lower? As you can see from this chart (and virtually every other chart) there is always a lower low or higher high that price could FO to. We have to place our stop loss somewhere.... There must be an answer to this or associate and master traders would be unable to take the trades they do with such low draw down.

It is usually at this point that someone mentions the issue of true supply/demand & the issue of scale. This is something I have studied a lot yet I struggle to devise a clear methodology for applying it to finding the right location for taking these types of TT.

It is obvious (from all my failed trades) that we can't just trade any swap zone...even if the swap zone is formed nicely with perfectly drawn FL Boxes. The swap zone must occur in a specific location within the scope of all the PA surrounding it. It is this "elusive" location that I have yet to find. Nobody seems to directly disclose what they look for in a location to start drawing swap zones. When the question is asked, the answers are generally equivocal.

This may be because answering the question of 'context' and location of swap zones exposes a great deal of the strategy behind successfully executing these types of trades. If this is true, it is good new because it means we are asking the right questions....

I may be wrong, but I think we can narrow the reasons for the failed trade at Box # 3 as a fakeout forming at circle # 7, as a reaction off something is the low represented by circle # 6.

Fakeouts occur in areas of liquidity - usually to true supply/demand. A FO always has a specific purpose. Anytime we draw swap zones and identify the DP/origin where we expect price to react, we must be sure there are no remaining pockets of FOF remaining below our entry (or above our entry if we are attempting a short trade). I have heard Salivan mention this many times in his posts.

How do we go about making sure there are no pockets of FOF below or above our targeted entry? Isn't there always an area of liquidity below or above our entry if we look hard enough? The answer is yes, of course. Depending on the scale, there might be a hundred areas with FOF located somewhere above or below the targeted entry....knowing that alone doesn't help us at all. The real question is one that involves refining our definition of "areas where pockets of FOF remain". This is technically a true statement, but it is much too general and pretty unhelpful if we don't understand more context and detail.

A more clever question would be:"under what specific circumstances is a pocket of FOF located above/below our targeted entry relevant with regard to a potential FO?

Fakeouts aren't random - they are calculated moves to obtain liquidity. They occur all the time, but I don't think they are as random as they might seem (although I must admit they seem very random at times...

)

Then there is the issue of reactive vs. original price action. Often times when we look at a chart like the USD-CHF example used in this posting, we see multiple lows and think they are all independently formed, when in reality they are often just a reaction off a different zone...it might be a reaction from a HTF area of true supply/demand but it also might just be a reaction of another reaction that is a reaction off a HTF area of true supply/demand.

To complicate this further, even in a situation where price is just reacting off a different level, the reaction itself is forming an independent true supply/demand level on a LTF chart. It is just in a different scale. So essentially, what we have is a whole bunch of reactions off other reactions that create new reactions. All these newly created reactions include smaller areas of true supply/demand (original supply/demand that is formed independent of any reaction) and within their smaller scales price will react to these levels accordingly. All of these originally formed areas of true supply/demand have their own MPL's which dictate how far price is likely to FO. How do we know which scales are relevant and which ones are not relevant when it comes to our trade setups? Again, I repeat the question I asked above: "under what specific circumstances is a pocket of FOF located above/below our targeted entry relevant with regard to a potential FO?

I think the answer to many of our failed trades can be found in answering these questions. We need to know which pockets of FOF (another way of saying this is "we need to know which areas of true supply/demand") are relevant to a possible FO occurring at our entry point.

Hi H, I see from your latest posts that you put in a lot of work and determination to understand the market and RTM. I also sense a bit of frustration which I totally understand. IMHO you are fine with market structure ie. identifying FL (true S/D) and FO vs eng.

The next part which helps to stick it all together is the psychology of ITs. In my opinion, we can't know which level is likely to hold unless we consider this, because ITs or smart money decides which level they want to sell/buy at. Remember we look for tricks into a zone where a trick was played. If there are no tricks on approach including manipulation of hope and fear then there's simply no trade because there are no signs a level is going to hold. Sometimes a level is fine to TT because of past tricks played at a zone which in itself is a very good place, for example an MPL or FTRFO within a FL aligned with a HTF QM level (FO/trick level), but then unless PA kicks in to let us hold that trade we must get out at first trouble area or cover enough for a possible stop as there are no clues for further IT intentions.

I'm no master at this, I lose too, but understanding this helps to filter out a lot of losing trades. Check the dissection thread, all setups have something in common, the manipulation of retailers (approach and/or history).

For example recent GU trade you took. It was a solid FL with CP on approach, could work and wasn't really a bad trade. The thing is the context of what happened before it. Price approached an origin and then engulfed up, after the eng up, price FO into the lowest possible QM in that zone and respected it with buying signs. Knowing this means a trick was played into a past trick zone (QM), so the intention of ITs are likely long than short although we have still a previous eng to the downside in play and price might still follow this but we also know the market doesn't move in straight lines and a RT is always possible. BTW when an origin is respected and an eng happens this is a big warning sign for a possible RT, independently of HTF engulf cycles.

Another aha moment I had recently was to not follow strictly the rules about higher/lower scale FL boxes and engulfs but instead trying to see the orders (true S/D) and the context in which they happen.

Wish you good luck and I hope someone more experienced can help you with some important questions you asked above

Something I have been noticing...I wonder if anyone else sees this too:

First, I think there is a difference between "true supply/demand (FOF) (origin up/down)" and the extreme end of a FTR that forms the edge of a FL Box. The True supply/demand doesn't always form in the FTR.

We draw Fl Boxes based on the break of swap levels, therefore we draw FL boxes based on the break of FTR's.

Example:

This becomes important when we look to ID an engulf....are we looking for an engulf of a FL Box or an engulf of the "true supply/demand/FOF/Origin up down" within the FL Box?

Both seem important...

So I started looking at areas of historical charts and I noticed some of the best reactions came from areas where there was an engulf of both the origin of a move up/down (FOF) and the top/bottom of its associated FL Box. Why is this especially important?

1. The engulf of a FL Box indicates an engulf of a swap zone (and the potential forming of a new opposing one) 2. An engulf of Origin up/down (FOF) indicates consumption of all opposing order flow, and newly executed FOF exists as a result.

We can draw lots of FL Boxes, but not every FL Box holds an important origin up/down. When an important FL Box (with an origin up/down located within it) is engulfed, the new zone formed is highly likely to react when price returns.

I've noticed an EG of the origin (FOF) is followed by a FTR, but it often turns into a confirmed FL once price continues on to break the extreme of the FL Box as well, and comes back to test the FTR. This ends up looking like a DP located just under a newly formed FL Box. The big bounce happens later on, when price returns to this area, and forms a FO to the 'DP' below the new FL Box (the DP is just the FL formed after engulfing the opposing origin. While the new FL Box is important to establish a new swap zone formation, the new FOF that is formed after the engulf of the opposing origin is where all the new orders exist. When they combine, the result is a very strong level with potential to bounce price quite far. (or at least this is what i have noticed recently, as always I could be wrong

).

Here is a drawing: This is how I normally draw FL Boxes

Next I will post a real life chart example:

USD-CAD:

Here, FL Box B is formed when price engulf the True Supply located within FL Box A. Then, price RT a little bit before engulfing the extreme high of FL Box A (making FL Box C).

We are left with two closely related FL Boxes...one created a new swap level by engulfing the opposing one (this is FL Box C) and the other engulfed opposing True Supply and is the location for newly executed FOF (Buy orders). Even though FL Box B looks like a DP below FL Box C, it is very important as the area of true FOF.

When price returns later on, it bounces very strongly off the newly formed FOF - as you can see, FL Box B and FL Box C work together (like a 'special' combined FL Box) to create extra strength. This is also a ORFL...

And..here is a simplified version showing the special combined FL Box/ORFL & the reaction that happened when price returns to it.

Very low risk...incredibly high return.

Here are the 4 important areas: I will draw each one, starting from # 4 and working my way to the reaction:

Next, look for the exact candle that breaks the low of FL Box B...this is the start of a new swap zone and "True Supply" level. True Supply "C" is especially important because it formed after an engulf of a previous Decision to FO...that DP to FO was also the DP to engulf a previous TS zone (TS A).

Price Reacts @ point X to the MPL of True Supply C. Point "X" is not originally formed...it was a reaction to an originally formed Supply zone.

FL Box "D" is still Seller-controlled...the balance of power has not changed to Bulls, so this is a reaction. How do we know if we can trade the fractal TS level formed in Box D? We have to look left and see if price has already visited the MPL of the original TS zone.

Reaction X has already hit the extreme set of orders in the FL contained within TS "C"...we are safe to sell when price RT to the fractal TS level created within FL Box D. That is why price reacts so nicely...

In theory, this is a relatively easy concept to understand. The challenging part is executing the trade...

(assuming a short trade setup...it would be the exact opposite for a long trade setup)

The main components you must know for this trade:

1. Find an original true supply/demand zone with good history of price reaction (FL)

2. Watch for a FO above this level (RBD)

3. Draw the FL Box that forms as a result of the engulf of the original true supply zone

4. Draw the DP to FO

5. Draw the EG of the DP to FO

6. Determine the target for the EG of the DP to FO

7. If price returns to the newly created FOF (New TS) prior to hitting the target of the engulf, it is a high probability trade.

Making a mistake on any of the 7 main components above will probably result in a lost trade. I will be keeping track of all my losing trades to find out which of the 7 main steps I need the most practice on.

I understand the concept of FL Boxes better now (before, I was drawing FL Boxes on areas that were not FL's...)

All FL Boxes hold price (or else they wouldn't be FL Boxes). The trick seems to be understanding which FTR's will bounce price...and trading that bounce. Or, you can wait until a FL has been formed, but the key would be knowing that the FL will bounce price a second time. Not all FL Boxes bounce price more than once before breaking.

Why do some FL Boxes bonce price more than once, and how can we predict these bounces? It must have something to do with order flow

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
More Questions to Ponder:

1. Why does price RT deeply inside a FL Box sometimes (before bouncing) and why does price bounce closer to the start of the FL Box? And how does this fit with the concept of FOF and tricks being played?

2. Is there a connection between tricks (FO's) and the FOF that is created as a result, that could indicate the location of a price bounce within a FL Box?

For example, let's look closer at the FL Box below. As you can see, price bounces many times in this zone. I labeled 6 of the most obvious areas of reaction. We see price react for the first time very deep inside the FL Box.. This RT looks like a QM level as well. I can understand why price bounced here.

Here is where the PA gets tricky, and seems a bit random:

You can see price bouncing from #2 - # 5 at the beginning of the FL Box. Each time price bounces from a different level. Sometimes it bounces deeper, then shallow, then a bit deeper, then a little more shallow etc.... With regard to FOF, why does this happen? How can we possible trade these reactions if they are occurring so randomly? The most interesting bounce is at # 6. How are there still orders left here after # 1 already visited the QM level? How can a trader every be able to predict multiple bounces at or near the same level?

More visits to a level = less orders left behind. The more a level has been tested the more likely it is to fail, right

Is our goal to find the most likely area within the FL Box for price to bounce with the lowest risk and highest return (and ignore the other reactions in the scale?) The deeper we look in the FL Box, the lowest the risk and the highest the return.

Another important Question:

At what point do we ID this as a FL Box? Do we have to wait for the new high @ A-4 to form in order to say this is a valid FL Box that bounced price, or can we go to a lower time frame and verify the big FL Box by watching price engulf, RT, and bounce on a 1-min chart somewhere within the wick of the candle at A-1?

If we have to wait for price to bounce at A-3 or A-4 for confirmation of a FL Box, we wouldn't be able to trade the first deep RT in to the box (the first deep RT would be the first test of price entering the FTR, and until it bounced to make a new high, we wouldn't be able to confirm the FL Box.

I know it may seem like I am over complicating things, but I think these are important questions to understand. This is why it is easier to look at historic charts...when the market is live we have to make decisions based on how price is unfolding. We don't have the benefit of hindsight.

When I practice, I always try to look at the chart as if I didn't know how price will end up reacting. I always pretend I am analyzing a live chart (I cover part of the computer screen). These are the questions that come up

First step is learning how to draw the FL Boxes. That part is relatively easy. The next part is knowing which ones are going to bounce price multiple times. As you can see from the chart below, Box A is important and price bounces many times. Box B and Box C are much smaller FL Boxes that bounce price comparatively fewer times. Then, Box D forms and price bounces many times.

Is there a way to know which Boxes will bounce price more than others? Does it have something with the process of swapping from bear-controlled to bull-controlled?

It seems like Box A (Bear Control) and Box D (Bull Control) contain the most FOF. Box B and Box C look like the swapping process that takes Box A and swaps the power to the Bulls controlling Box D. Is this a pattern that is common on different time scales? If so, is there such a thing as 'major FL Boxes" as opposed to 'transitional FL Boxes"?

The more I practice the more I see FO and EG as the same thing...the only difference is scale & time.

Here is an example:

Look at the area is red:

NZD-USD Weekly

Clearly this is a FO, and if you saw it as an engulf in 2001 you probably lost some money

For the purposes of this scale though, it's a FO.

Here is the uncompleted FL Box for this PA:

The low is set....bu the highs of the FL Box are not set until a new low is made (engulf). Then any break above the 'set' highs is a FO.

You can't determine if a break above the highs is a FO until you confirm an engulf has occurred below. Until a new low occurs, this is an incomplete FL Box.

Although this is a very HTF example, this exact same concept occurs over and over again in every scale.

If you refer back to Salivan's post on my journal (#1306) you will see a chart he edited for me. I am posting it below for quick reference. You can see he is referring to the same concept...The FO can't be confirmed until a new low engulfs the old to completed the FL Box in this scale. This how to keep the FO vs. EG straight.

1. Know your scale 2. Know your important completed FL Boxes 3. Be carefully watching incomplete FL Boxes 4. Know ahead of time what your target will be for a valid engulf 5. Know ahead of time where your MPL is for a confirmed FO

Hi Staurum

I have found that learning how to draw the FL Boxes has helped quite a bit when it comes to identifying engulf vs. fakeout. I used to open a chart and look for fakeouts and engulfs and try to piece together a trade from that perspective. Lately, I have been opening a fresh chart...usually in the middle time frame (hourly is good). I put everything else completely out of my mind..no thoughts about compression or engulfs or PAZ or fakeouts etc.... All I look for are areas where price was held down and I draw the FL Box responsible for holding down price. I do this until I have several levels drawn. When uncertainty arises I will refer to 4-hour or daily time frames. I usually look at the weekly time frame analysis too.. sometimes it helps to see the big picture when drawing the FL Boxes.

I avoid drawing any LTF FL Boxes at first.

Once have the HTF and middle time frame FL Boxes drawn, I begin to focus on other aspects of trading. Specifically, I start rating the FL Boxes according to their importance. How many times did they bounce price, were they formed as a result of an engulf of a very important zone? Was the FL formed after engulfing a ORFL?

With this focus, I identify two or three main FL Boxes that hold special importance and then drop down and look at the PA within the boxes. I draw the major swap zones inside the FL Box. I focus specifically on the three data points that make up a FL Box: the engulf, the RT/FTR, and the breakout (new HH or LL which confirms the FL Box). I find the origin and the fakeouts within the FL Boxes and make note of what levels they are a reaction to. Of course, the MPL is a critical part of this as well. I mark all the MPL's within the targeted FL Boxes.

Most recently, I have been focused on learning more about how these zones react with each other. How price moves from zone to zone...

I have a hard time keeping track of everything too..I like the triangle picture you posted...it is a good analogy. Your process for identifying and analyzing a chart is just as important as understanding the concepts that RTM teaches. Consistency in the process and steps taken to analyze a chart is critical, and I am still working to find a niche 'focus' when it comes to trading. Everyone processes this information differently, and everyone seems to have their own style of trading.

There is no shortage of valuable info on this forum, and it is all important. That said, I think it can be overwhelming at times to focus on too many applications for this knowledge...I am challenging myself to be a more disciplined trader and need to specialize in a particular type of setup that can be replicated over and over again with precise consistency....like a computer.

I am still looking for that area of 'specialty'. A good example is Mertch. He knows all the RTM concepts, but he is laser focused on specific QM setups. All his trades are remarkably similar. He has become a master of one type of setup and most likely has executed thousands of trades over the years. I believe this is part of the reason he is such a good trader.

I know I didn't offer any solutions to your frustrations, but just know you aren't alone. We will figure this out, and we will succeed

Thanks Jurij

I've gotten better managing my emotions when it comes to trading, but I gotta admit EUR-AUD had smoke coming from my ears yesterday

Juri, you hit the 'nail on the head' when you wrote " If so, there must be a way to know which level the ITs are targetting for the final reversal? Or are we supposed to guess the level by taking a few losses on the way? There's always a better level above/below."

I don't know the answer to this, but here is something I've been pondering for quite some time now.

I look at many successful trades where price reacts exactly as I predict, and my target is hit. Even in these trades, there are MPL's that haven't been hit above my entry. There is always a better level above/below an entry. We can't put a 500+ pip stop on every trade to account for the possibility that price will do some crap like this.

What I am coming to believe: The market is reasonably easy to predict if you have the right understanding of why price moves from level to level. I must admit, as unpopular as this viewpoint may be, I don't believe anyone can predict the market 100% of the time...even 90% of time. There are too many external factors that contribute to the global markets to say that there is a secret that will give us 90+ success rate in taking trades.

What I think RTM does best is teach a method to analyze the market in a way the cracks the code on how the algorithms work on the super computers that trade most of the IT's capital. The algorithms are predictable because they operate consistently...until they are adjusted/changed. There are so many big players in the market, sometimes an infusion of orders will enter the market and blow through setups that worked in the past. I don't think it is always our fault (sometimes it is) but it may be worth accepting there will be losses...our success depends on how we handle our losses. I don't think we spend enough time taking about this on RTM and it needs to change. All traders lose...and they lose on a regular basis. It his how they handle the losses that determines whether they are successful.

I do believe there is chaos (at times) in the market. There is unpredictability (at times) in the market. That is OK...we shouldn't try to over analyze why every trade goes against us. It is important to autopsy every loss to determine if there was a mistake in the analysis (this is critical) but it's OK to come to the conclusion that the trade failed...there isn't always a reason.

Once we can free ourselves from internalizing every loss as 'our fault' we can move past the losses and re focus our efforts on the next setup.

EUR-AUD is a good example...I should have been out after the ten pip loss. Instead I got back in and tried to get the next open level of FOF...which got blown through again and again and again. The trade I took yesterday has worked in the past (with regard to my analysis and execution). This time something else occurred, I was wrong, and that is OK.

If the market stops out a position, I need to accept it and move on. Tight stops, wide targets. Emotionless trading.

If I could sum up RTM and its concepts in a simple way I would say: RTM doesn't contain a special secret or 'holy grail' of trading. It teaches you to understand the market in such a way that you can get in to the market with very limited risk and very wide targets. In my opinion, this is the inherent beauty of the RTM forum and the education here. We trade at the best moments when FOF is likely to exist and reverse price.

It doesn't mean we are right all the time...and that is OK. I think it is a waste of time trying to be right 100% of the time. It is impossible.

With the right application and through hard work, RTM teaches a method of understanding PA in a way that ensures you will still be wildly successful...even if you are wrong half the time

Just my opinion, and I hope I didn't offend anyone!

If we see price EG in to a seemingly unimportant area, and we drop down to a LTF, we may see that it was a significant area for a LTF chart.

posts.text:
(Continuation of investigation in to True supply/demand)

So...the question I have to ask is: What is the differences between these reactions?

The main difference appears to be the issue of a FL Box creation after an engulf.

In the drawing below, there is an engulf and price retraces and FTR is formed. Price reacts to this zone many times. The reactions are easy to see, and they are bouncing from the FTR...not as a result of an engulf.

Does TS and TD have something to do with an engulf and FTR/FL being formed?

Could the difference between original (true) SD and reactive SD be how, when, and where it is created?

Here is the main difference I see:

If I continue down this path of analysis...would it be accurate to say every FTR contains a true supply/demand level? If yes, then the following must be true:

1. Every FTR has TS/TD 2. Every FTR has an MPL 3. Every FL Box contains an FTR 4. Every FL Box contains true supply/demand 5. Every FL Box contains an MPL associated with the true supply/demand zone

Assuming all of this is accurate (and I am not sure it is..) My next questions involves the Origin/ORFL.

- We know an origin is also a FTR. We know an origin has not been tested and has not bounced price. Once an origin is tested and bounces price, we consider it an ORFL.

- The only difference between a FTR and a FL is a FL has been tested and bounces price.

- Not every FTR is a FL but every FL is also an FTR.

- Like I mentioned above, every FTR has true supply/demand and an associated MPL.

- If this is true, then every FL has supply/demand and an associated MPL.

If this is true, we have to say every ORFL has an area of true supply/demand that is created, along with an associated MPL.

Let's look at a real chart: GBP-AUD:

Basics first... reaction creates reactive supply. Price reacts to reactive supply and an origin is created. This origin is immediately tested and bounces price. This Origin is now a ORFL - Down.

This ORFL is also an FTR...so if my analysis (above) is correct, then there must be an area of true supply located within this ORFL.

I think 'zone' is PAZ, and I think the PAZ has something to do with the FL Boxes. In this case, the QM level is formed within a 'Origin up' that was created as the result of price engulfing an ORFL (origin down). This new 'origin up' is at the edge of the zone....so price can RT to this extreme before going higher (in the direction of the engulf) There just so happens to be a really nice QM level at this extreme...perfect place to bounce price. Seeing a LTF DM form just above the QM level would be even more perfect.

All that being said, it would have been nicer if price had made a new high to break the previous high that forms the top of the blue box I drew....that hasn't happened yet. Still, Salivan says the only true engulf is an engulf of TS/TD...so technically we do have a valid HTF engulf indicating price wants higher...

If we ask "where is price coming from" we can say it is coming from a unmet target for longs...which tells us three things:

1. We need to look for buys 2. We need to expect tricks to occur when price RT 3. The RT will occur to the extreme set of orders left in the zone

If you were an IT, you would want to make the engulf of TS look like a FO so traders would be focused on shorting. You would be gradually buying in to all those shorts. They would see the engulf of TS as a FO and the FO of the QM below as an engulf...You would trick everyone to taking the wrong side, leaving yourself the only one with buys.

This is something I have been focusing on lately:

Simply looking for a DM to occur at TS/TD.

Price engulfs TD, showing clear intentions to move price lower. This is when we look for a way to get short...with as little risk as possible. The main question is always 'how far will price RT?'

You can see the three green lines as they cross in to this area..these are all areas of consumption of FOF. I notice a couple of things:

First, there is no upside engulf of this TS zone...which means no intention for price to go any higher (this is why there is no concern that price will hit the ORFL Down as a target).

Second, the last reaction (the one we are looking at) is the third reaction to this TS level... it is clearly consumed. Because of this, IT's don't benefit from another FO...orders are already cleared out.

We can feel confident in looking for shorts, knowing we have a 'backstop' supporting us from a possible FO.

Back to the trade... we can now safely look for a short at TS

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
The more I practice trading, the more I feel like the only truly important areas of PA are TS and TD.

Engulfs are worthless if you don't know which zone to focus on. FO is also worthless without context.

TS and TD gives us context...it is what helps us understand scale.

If I could offer one bit of advice to struggling traders...focus on drawing TS and TD. Everything else tends to fall in to place once you have the zones properly drawn in the correct scales. This is the advice i am giving myself.

Regardless of where price is traveling, it has to pass through many TS and TD zones along the way. The method for passing through these levels is the same regardless of scale. They are either engulfed straightway, or you have something that resembles a 1-2 test...all the important tricks tend to happen in these true zones with FOF.

Test 1 - at the SR of the TS or TD area. Supply/demand created on reaction and the trap is set for price to FO deeper in to the TS/TD zone at a later time. Test 2 - Price retraces deeper in to the zone and price turns. The trick is complete and the IT's have filled all the orders they need to hit the intended target.

I am amazed at how frequently this happens...so predictable once you see what's happening

A drawing I made this morning...

Is it the FTR that forms after the break of a new high that is important, or is it the decision to engulf that is important?

We focus on the FTR, but the FTR is FO'd all the time to the DP below...there are two scenarios I can think of:

1. The FTR that forms on the break of the high retraces down to the DP...so the DP is a tiny FL after it bounces price.

2. The FTR does not reach the DP to EG, and the DP is an FTR that price can FO to in the future. It is a trap being set.

This is an important concept because we want to predict possible FO, but it is also important when deciding whether an engulf has occured or not. Omid's drawing shows this exact situation...the DP located below the FTR that forms after the break of an important level. The FTB to this zone is a FO unless it breaks the low of the DP

If price visits the DP while forming a FTR, the break of the FTR is an engulf. If price does not reach the DP when the FTR forms, then we have to wait for price to break the low of the DP (not the low of the FTR) before determining if an engulf has happened.

Engulf Vs. FO:

Decision points are the areas we look for engulfs/FO's. If the only true engulf is an engulf of trues supply/true demand, we can say:

Hi H, maybe it is confusing because of mixing it with other things and the way you draw it. So for the basics of the MPL concept let's forget about true S/D, ORFL and reactive S/D. First, the MPL is the most extreme zone (not a line) of the FL or FTR you are looking at.

Here is an excellent example of trading psych and stop loss management: The pair is EUR-JPY:

This trade could have gone one of three ways:

1. Winning trade (modest) 2. Break even (no loss, no significant gain) 3. Stopped out with a loss

I will post the charts in order first, then I will explain how to analyze (my opinion on how to analyze

)

HTF:

Lower TF to show the FTR/FL/Kink

Close up view of the reaction:

Option 1: Wait for price to hit the MPL and short to the first modest target (target shown as dotted rectangle). This is straightforward, but would take discipline.

Option 2: Getting out with no loss/minimal profit: Clearly, we can see that this was not the best setup for a reaction. With that said, as soon as price engulfed the MPL...GET OUT! There is almost always a decent RT after an MPL is broken. This is out chance to bail without taking a loss. In some cases we can even come out ahead by a couple of pips. The key: knowing the exact moment when your trade plan is shot and having the discipline to shut it down.

My # 1 motto for trading: I focus on capital preservation.

Option 3: Taking a loss. If price was allowed to run, it would have eventually stopped out. As we can see, the bounce at this FL was weak. Try to avoid this..be an active trader who manages their open positions. It will cut down on the losses. Imagine if you could control a majority of your losing trades at BE? All you would need is a couple winners from time to time and your account would grow exponentially.

It is important to review every losing trade...we need to know why the trade didn't work out. That said, the more I trade, the more I am convinced there is far more value in being able to contain the losses as opposed to bashing my head against the wall trying to find out what I did wrong. Sometimes the market does something we weren't anticipating...that is OK. I'd rather become an expert of slipping out of a losing trade at BE

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
One Idea i am experimenting with (to get out of a losing trade without taking a loss), is scaling in to the position.

If I get in on a trade at the SR of a FL (where we tend to see a supply/demand reaction), I can execute a trade of "X" size. Assuming the MPL of this FL is still fresh (orders remaining in the extreme end of the FTR) I can add a second entry order in this area. The size trade I place in the MPL will be approximately 3X the size of the first entry.

Here is my reasoning: When the MPL is engulfed we tend to see a RT back in to the FL. Sometimes the RT is not deep enough to cover the initial SR trade (especially if the FL is wide). To mitigate for this problem, I place a 3X trade almost at the edge of the zone. There is very little draw down on this trade, and if price does engulf the MPL, all it has to do is RT far enough to bring the second trade to BE, then travel 1/3 of the distance towards the first entry before the entire cumulative trade is net zero or slightly positive.

This dramatically increases the odds that I get out of trouble since I don;t need as deep of a RT to cancel out my first entry.

On the upside, if the MPL holds, the R:R will be incredible.

Anyone think about doing it this way? Any drawbacks I might be overlooking

Drawings:

Here is a good example that just happened on EUR-GBP:

First chart shows the basics:

You can see where my first entry was (beginning of FL). I added a final position at the edge of the MPL approximately 4X the size of my initial entry. As soon as the FL broke to the downside, I was watching my net P&L calculator to wait for a deep enough RT back to the FL to cover all losses and spread/commission. As you can see, within a few mins there was a decent RT back to the FL. I was able to close the entire position for a slight profit (basically break even).

No loss incurred... of course I still had a protective emergency stop at approximately 1:1 RR on the inital entry in case price takes off and never comes back to RT.

I have been pondering a new theory lately...nothing too spectacular...just been experimenting with session highs/lows. I know this strays away from the core RTM strategy, so if this is too off topic please let me know and I will delete the post.

I think session highs/lows are important to consider. Not because they hold significance based on theory...but they hold significance because many traders think of them as being important. They have all kinds of indicators that trade based on a break of a previous sessions high/low. Breakout traders love these trades..especially if the session high/low happens at round number. We want to trade where the herd's stop losses are located.

It makes logical sense to choose areas on the chart where the highest number of traders are likely to get caught on the wrong side of the trade.

What better place to look than at a FO of a session high or low? So many traders would get in on the breakout and get caught on the FO.

Here is an example: EUR-USD:

Red shading is NY green is London

1. LS that holds as the high of both the London AND NY Session. 2. LTF shows this as the first break and retest of the LS. This is the LS Kink.

3. The break above # 1 is a false break and many traders are caught trying to unload long positions. This is a RBD FO. 4. Price drops considerably making a new low 5. Price works its way back to the old Kink and there is a nice reaction that occurs at the FTR.

Note the downside engulf that forms just before the spike @ # 5

Here is another example on USD-CHF: same 1-5 labels.

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
In reference to my previous post (post # 1696)

I am trying to filter out weaker trade opps by thinking about "why" price reacts the way it does at certain levels.

It reminds me of high school math.

You can take and pass a calculus course relatively easily...by simply memorizing how to solve math problems. Math is systematic...it is exact and the process to solve the problems are well-defined and consistent. You can get an A in calculus by memorizing the steps. The harder part is understanding why...the application is the hard part.

So in terms of trading, I want to think about why price moves the way it does. Not just memorize terms and abbreviations and boxes. But understand the context behind what all of this means.

Price capping out at the London and NY session high is a good place to look for a FO but it isn't the only place. Any area of the charts where the herd is caught on the wrong side of a trade is a good place to look for a bounce/reaction.

I was doing some simulation trading this evening and made a an incredible trade...50% return my fake money account with one trade! This is a good example because it raises some important questions/issues.

~ 50:R Trade

USD-JPY this trade occurred back around September 2015 if you are wanting to follow along

__________________________________________________________________________

I will start with the chart that caught my eye: I am looking on an hourly chart for momentum an find a very strong bullish candle that significantly engulfs a previous range of highs that forme over a few days. Here is what that chart looked like, and I put an arrow on the chart that show the candle that caught my eye.

So far...easy and straightforward

Now that I am looking for a possible bounce when price returns to the decision to break to the upside, I am focused on finding a likely location ripe for a trick. This next chart shows a few zones that I find are potentially important. There are many areas that could be a goof location a LTF kink. There are several left shoulders, QM levels, IQM, etc...and that is just on this hou time frame...imagine all the potentials levels we would ID if we dropped down to a lower time frame!

This is an ongoing problem for me, and I am trying to find a good answer. In this simulation tr I ended up picking the right zone (and I will explain my reasoning behind that soon) but I don; feel comfortable in my ability to explain why the level I chose was superior to the other levels it relates to order flow. I feel lucky that I did well on this trade...and I don't like that feeling. I should be able to do two things as it relates to every trade:

1. Explain why I chose this specific level 2. Explain why I did not choose the other levels

It is very easy to explain (in hindsight) why price bounced at a certain level... but the harder question is why wasn't a different level chosen? In my opinion, being able to adequately answ this question is where the true understanding exists.

Here is the chart that identifies all of the levels I was considering:

Going back to my simulation trade: I ended up choosing the LS below (see chart below). My reasoning for choosing this LS is overly simplified (and I don't think it is a good explanation)

I chose this LS because it was the last high that formed prior to the big bullish engulfin candle

...if I am being completely honest, I can't explain why price didn't bounce from the other level marked. This bothers me...it is a weak point in my skill set and I need to work diligently on this Just because my simulation trade was a success doesn't mean my analysis was correct...it m just be that I got lucky.

It is my humble opinion that often times traders make the reckless assumption that if their trad was a success, the analysis for that trade was correct and well applied...I don't agree with this mentality. A winning trade doesn't necessarily mean your analysis was correct and your application of the RTM principles was applied accurately. Sometimes we win trades out of luck...if you trade enough you will eventually end up with some winning trades.... Even a brok clock is right twice a day

I think it is important to honestly take a step back and assess every trade (winner or loser) ba on how well you understood the 'story' of price....regardless of whether or not you made a pro fro the trade

This is one of my biggest weaknesses... I use the term 'confirmation bias' to explain this phenomenon.

OK...moving on. Now that I've Identified my LS I need to start thinking like an IT. If I want to bounce price I need to start stockpiling long positions without making it too obvious. I do this gradually by making the market look bearish so the herd will load up on short orders. I start looking for areas where I know the herd will start selling. I am focused on the three areas labe below:

A: S/R Level will be a magnet for retail traders who want to trade the bounce. If I am the IT I don't want to compete against he herd...I must shake out the buyers at this SR level to take them from net long to net short. I do this by creating fear. Let price drop below the SR line to p pressure on them. I know where their predictable stop losses are located...so FO to the LS below will stop most of them out of their long positions. Triggering a SL for a long position is a short order. I am more than happy to buy their desperate attempts to get out from a 'failing' trade.

B: Supply and demand traders will look at this level as a good place to buy. They will see the (A) as a additional confluence. Their stops will be located in the same general area as the FL the SR traders at "A".

C: Many traders and computer algos/indicators for retailers will buy/sell based on price break a previous sessions high or low. If you look at "C" on my chart below you will see the demand level "B" is also the session low for both the London & NY session for 9/8/15. Many BO trade and trading indicators will be selling on a downside break of this level. Those who get short w be sadly mistaken, and those who think the level will hold will feel greedy when it breaks and they will get short. Playing with fear and greed gives the IT an advantage to get everyone on wrong side of the trade.

The next step is for me to refine my entry by looking at a lower time frame I want to find the exact FTR/DBR that forms as price crosses over the LS line. I will drop down to a 5 -min char see how clear this FTR is. If needed I will drop down to a 1-min chart or a 10-second chart. It important that this FTR be accurately drawn as 'tight' as possible.

Here is what I see on a 5-min chart. I am encouraged by how clear and tight this kink is. The kink is only 15 pips wide, based on a LS that formed on an hourly chart. My target is quite som distance away from this kink, so 15 pips is an excellent range.

5-Min Kink

Lets look at this on a 30M, 15M, and 1M chart respectively. Keep in mind how the kink's high/ may change based on the time frame. Of course, the higher time frames show a more generalized view of the kink and the LTF will show a refined FTR.

So...after looking at the LS kink multiple time frames, it is clear that the range of the kink depends on the time frame. It would make sense to drop down to the lowest time frame possible to get the most accurate entry. I am finding that price does not always respect the LTF kinks...price will often times bounce somewhere within the larger time frame kink - often times just a few pips below the extreme low of the LTF kink. I think its good to find the exact entry, but equally important to give the trade enough room by placing a SL at the correct spot.

The problem with placing the stop wide enough to match the extreme low/high of the Kink, is it will usually hurt the RR. While I don't have the best answer for this, I think it is reasonable to simply wait for price to RT further in to the Kink before an entry is taken. This will inevitably result in many missed opportunities, but the trades that do occur will be amazing RR. The closer the entry is to the MPL of the Kink/FTR, the higher the return and the lower the risk.

Using the 5-Min kink, I looked for a good entry point. I saw two main lines located inside of the kink that caught my eye. Th chart below labels these areas as # 1 and # 2.

#1: This is a Bearish IQM level #2: This is a Bullish QM Level

The space between these two lines is the sweet spot - this is where i placed my entry.

Here is my entry - I drew the low extreme of the Kink as shown on the 30-min and hourly chart. Technically I think the SL should be located just under this level...but this is way too much risk for me. Instead, I placed a stop loss a couple of pips under the 5-min FL/kink where my 'sweet spot' entry was located (the space between the bearish IQM and bullish QM). I should have a better method for placing my stop..this is something I need to work on.

As you can see, price bounced almost exactly where my sweet spot was located and the bounce was huge...over 100 pips. My stop loss was only spread/commission plus a couple of pips. This was just a simulation trade, but it is a very good example of how powerful these spots can be for bouncing price. 50% return on one trade! Incredible...

Hoeschec, First let me clarify that a FTR = FL = Kink. They are all the same. It all depends on the time frame and what you want to call it. We look at 4 areas for a trade, LS, Pre-CP, RS, and break into CP. Your chart is a RS, so if falls into the one of the 4 areas where we look for a trade. You did the right thing by drilling down to the M1 to find the kink. That kink you found on the M1 chart is spot on. We need to drill down as further as possible to find the kink. You M1 chart shows the kink clearly and that is where we wait for PA. find the lowest time frame kink gives us the best risk to reward if we are trading from a higher time frame chart. In the kink, we always should look for the clean set of orders that are left behind. That is where you are likely going to get a reaction. In video 3 you will be shown about order flow of a QM. Once you have an understanding of the order flow, then you will understand where price will bounce and if the bounce will be strong or weak.

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
A good question to start asking myself when looking for a good LS kink:

Where is the bait for the herd?

Fishermen use bait to attract fish to their pole.....it is the same for IT's. IT's need to entice traders to get on the wrong side of the trade.

The best LS is probably located somewhere below the bait level on a bullish setup and just above the bait level on a bearish setup.

I want to revisit this post from Gslao:

The first engulf:

The low of the engulf and the extent of the RT creates the Upper Flag Limit (UFL).

The Upper flag limit line was broken twice...the first time it was broken (labeled as the Head in Gslao's drawing) there was no trade on its RT to the LS kink (see blue circle in chart below). How did you know not to trade the RT to the kink after the first break of the LS? Do we always wait for a 'head' to form on the first break of a LS?

The second time price breaks the LS and the head of the H&S pattern. When price RT to the kink the trade is taken: See the orange circle:

So, it seems to me the following steps must be taken in order:

(for a bullish kink bounce)

1. Find a strong opposing FL that is broken. Mark low and high of the break. The high of the break is the UFL.

2. This UFL is the LS

3. Wait for this UFL (LS) to be broken to the upside. This break forms the head (RS)

4. Wait for price to RT to the LS line after breaking and forming the Head/RS.

5. We would expect a reaction at the LS (to fulfill the H&S pattern). Wait for this H&S to be ignored

6. Ignoring of the HS pattern creates a new high...this time breaking above the original LS and the Head/RS

7. Draw the Kink for the LS and prepare for price to return to this kink

8. We expect residual order flow to exist in this kink after price ignores the HS pattern, and we buy when price returns to this kink

I am going to show this in a drawing step by step in the next post.

Hopefully I am understanding the order of events...Feel free to tell me if I am wrong...thanks for everyone's help

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
Step by step drawing - bullish kink setup:

Step 1: Price engulfs an opposing FL

Step 2: Mark the low of the engulf and the furthest extent of the RT before a new low is made. This is the Upper FL:

Step 3:: Wait for a new high to form above the UFL/LS. This is the 'head' of our HS Pattern and it is also the RS level that will act as bait for retailers trying to buy the bullish swap level.

Step 4: Price approaches the LS of the H&S but does not react... it ignores this level.

Step 5: Price makes a new high after ignoring the H&S Pattern. This is when we really want to start preparing for an entry. Watch price as it returns to the LS below...

Step 6: Look at the LS and the IHSP (Ignored H&S pattern). Go to LTF and draw the most accurate kink possible. Use tick chart data if needed. Look for last place where price crossed this important line. Draw the kink/FTR and look to make sure it has fresh order flow (make sure orders haven't been consumed already).

Step 7: Look for PA as price approaches the kink. Ideally there will be some kind of compression or Diamond setup on LTF to indicate IT's are preparing to buy. We buy when price RT to the kink.

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
By far the most challenging part of trading: knowing where the relevant targets are located.

* You will not buy if price is coming from a reached target for buyers

* You will not sell if price is coming from a reached target for sellers

* You buy if price is coming from an unreached target for buyers

* You sell if price is coming from an unreached target for sellers

Logically this makes total sense.

The hard part is drawing the relevant targets correctly...

Also, knowing if the target has been met. For example: if targets are FL they have an MPL. Is a target met if price reaches the FL but has not consumed the extreme set of orders in its MPL

IQM or IHS (Ignored Head and Shoulders) are great places to look for a trade when price returns to the LS kink.

Major questions to ask when determining whether or not to trade the bounce:

(not sure this is accurate, but I want to write it down anyway)

posts.text:
Lately I have been wondering what the statistical analysis of the 2-touch trade would be.

(RS = Touch 1) (MPL - Touch 2)

It would be interesting to find a hundred of these and see the average win/loses, RR, DD, etc.. Just keep it this simple (don't add complications and confusion). Only trade strong FL's that are located in important areas and swap zones.

Also, any losing trade would mean price engulfed the MPL..we almost always get a brief RT (back in to the FL) after breaking an MPL. It is reasonable to assume you could have many BE trades as a result of good stop loss management.

If losses can be minimized by getting out @ BE my trading account will grow like crazy. You would only need a couple wins per week (maybe less). Managing loss is just as important as executing profitable trades.

Here is an example on GBP-AUD:

Decent FL setup @ swap area. Price doesn't RS and bounce from the edge, but the MPL was still fresh. The approach wasn't compelling, but even if you did go short at the MPL, price broke out and then RT back in. See second chart below for detail on how I would try to get out of this losing trade at BE.

And here is my trade management: entry about 1/2 way through the zone. This allows makes my entry easier to access if price does break out and briefly RT back in...this way it only has to RT 1/2 the width of the FL.

You can see the exact place (on 1-min chart) where price broke the MPL. As soon as this occurs, look for a way to get out. In this case (and many others) price does come back briefly and there was ample opportunity to close out the position at BE.

Incredible way to approach trading! Minimizing losses by closing a majority of bad trades at BE....

There are two ways to build huge equity as a trader: make more profit or reduce loss.

Thinking a lot about IQM's lately.

How does an IQM happen? How can IT's ignore levels?

Do they place huge orders over a short amount of time to cause a gap in pricing?

Where do they place these orders?

Let's assume $100M of sell orders exists here. When price reaches the QM level it will bounce as long as there is less than $100M worth of buyers at that moment. If there is more than $100M of buyers price will consume the sell orders and price will rise. Price must consume the short orders before it can move beyond the level, right?

How are IT's able to 'skip over' these areas?

If IT's want to skip the level they need to create more buy orders. This causes price to move up. The theory behind trading the IQM (as I understand it) is price bounces at a previously ignored level because residual orders exist. But how can there be residual orders...aren't those orders consumed when price moves through the zone?

Maybe IT's create huge Buy orders to cause a gap to occur? If price changes rapidly there will be gap...trapping traders who can't execute quick enough.

To me, it seems like an IQM really just a liquidity gap that fills at a later date?

How do we define an IQM? What is the difference between a DM and an IQM? What if price comes close to the QM level but falls just short of the level. Does this count as a IQM? Often times price will miss the QM level by a few pips...do we still count this as an IQM?

During IF's video, he mentions "IQM" when there is no valid QM...I think there is a difference between an IQM and a IHS (Ignored head and shoulders). QM's have an engulf whereas H&S does not.

Which one of the drawings below depicts a valid IQM?

"is the kink located within a PAZ? If so, is it located in the middle of the PAZ or at the edge of the PAZ?"

PAZ in a scale/range/size is limited by a Flag Limit or Kink or "King" Once we get this, we need to zoom in (or peek) where the "King" is hiding the "Queen Majesty" / QM / Quasimodo / the "King's Maximum Pain Level MPL". lol... sorry for the jokes, i just played cards with kids going crazy not knowing the difference between King cards and Queen cards.

Anyway, back to chart. I was looking for poles essentially (remember CP = Pole), because i want to know there is the FL that ends the pole so that i know when that FL is broken, it will target the polebase. Otherwise, the FL that ends the pole will be met with another FL from the opposite direction to ping-pong the price within the FLAG / PAZ. rest is finding out if price is trying to bounce at the FLAG limits by watching an Engulf PA. Or when it breaks the FL, which polebase it's trying to target. Therefore, to sum up again. FL is always at PAZ edge.

Regarding the little blue kink, yes it's one, but i would prefer watching the kink that engulfs the whole CPPAZ and fails to return to it (it be CPPAZ).

Simulation on AUD-USD:

I used a free version of simulation software from FXCM, and it is useful but has a lot of bugs. One of the bugs happens when my entry order doesn't get triggered despite getting reached. That happened in this scenario, but I wanted to show the top down analysis of the trade anyway..it is a great example.

Like my oil trade above, I began by finding a HTF IQM.

Next, drop down to LTF and look for another IQM or other important PA that supports a possible long trade.

My main focus at this point is setting up the best trade with the lowest risk and highest return. I look at the last candle to cross the HTF IQM and I draw the range of that candle. As you can see from the chart below, the candle has a large range (44 pips). I look at every scale from 1-min to 30-min to draw a conservative candle...I place my stop loss just below the low of the candle on the 30 min scale... (In this example, the 30-min candle's low and the 1-min candle's low is the same)

The ideal place to go long is at the yellow shaded area where the black and red horizontal lines exist. But here is where MM and trade psychology comes in: I have to be aware of the necessary location of my stop loss. This stop loss has to be located below the low of the black box - and if I set an entry order to buy at the yellow shaded region, my SL is approximately 20 pips. This is too wide of a stop loss for my trading strategy. I am looking for a minimum 1:3 RR - but would rather see closer to 1:4 RR. In keeping consistent with my MM goal, an entry at the yellow zone requires a target to be located 60-80 pips from my entry - too ambitious. I want low risk high return trades. The only way to manage this trade properly (under my MM requirements) is to set my entry order no more than 11 pips from the SL. I do this specifically because my target for this trade is approx 35 pips away from the proposed entry. I accept the possibility that price will bounce at the yellow zone and leave me in the dust. I am OK with missing out on trades.

An important point regarding the target: I don't know my target until price unfolds and comes very close to my entry point. This can be complicated, since the entry is dependent on the SL but the SL is somewhat dependent on my proposed target. This is why it is important to watch trades as they unfold as opposed to setting a limit order and walking away. As price unfolds, I see a nice supply zone forming just before price takes a dive to my entry.

The chart below shows where my entry, SL, and target is located. As you can see, my simulation software didn't trigger like it should have..that said, it is easy to see how the trade would have turned out.

I know the entry above looks too good to be true...It is my humble opinion that predicting exact areas where price will turn is not always possible. I simply got lucky on this entry...price could have easily missed my entry by a couple of pips and there are times when this happens. In my opinion, this is why trading psychology is so important: the fear of missing out on a trade shouldn't cause a trader to execute a trade that is beyond the scope of their MM requirements. It takes practice but over time a trader can train themselves to shut off their emotions. I still struggle with this, but I am getting a lot better at it.

I currently have a buy order set for GBP-USD. Here is a top down analysis of the current setup.

HTF:

LTF confirmation of IQM. There are two areas of interest shown by yellow circles.

The range of the blue rectangle is too large...at approximately (21 pips). I need to reduce the risk, especially depending on where I expect the target to be located

My stop loss is shown on the chart below - the stop loss is located just beneath the low of the last 30 min candle to cross the HTF IQM line (black horizontal) and the LTF IQM (solid red line). Notes on the chart reiterate the issue with setting my entry order at the top of the yellow shaded rectangle.

The target (and the entry) is not set in stone at this point - the reason for this is I cannot set my entry unless I feel confident where my target is located, and I can't feel comfortable about the location of my target until I see more PA unfold. Specifically, I want to see PA as it approaches my entry. At this stage, I see the future downside break of the "FL" labeled on the chart below as the most likely area where my long position will encounter a substantial set of sell orders that could bounce price lower. Depending on how the PA develops as price approached my entry, the target may shorten. If so, my entry will likely be adjusted lower as well - to decrease the risk between my entry and the stop loss. My current entry order is set in an area that requires a 14-pip stop loss. This is a high stop loss for me - usually I like my stop loss to be at or under 10 pips. My requirement for a target is minimum 3X risk. In this case, the target is located approximately 64 pips from the entry (roughly 4.5 R). If my target drops, my entry will drop accordingly. My stop loss will not change.

A quick note regarding my methodology for entry (I am still in the process of refining my standard approach to setting an entry order): I understand price may bounce prior to price reaching my entry - in fact, this happens on a regular basis. I have decided to sacrifice good trading opportunities for a strict risk management plan. I am OK with missing out on trades but I am not OK with taking on too much risk Years ago I lost a very large live account over the course of a few short months. That is NEVER happening again. The main reason I don't adjust my positioning size instead (as opposed to adjusting my entry to control risk) is the issue of my target - wide stop losses require an equally wide target in order to meet my 3X risk/return requirement. My core specialty will be executing low risk short-term 'opportunity' trades. Once the SL exceeds 10 pips, my target requirement exceeds 30-40 pips, and it takes longer for the trade to complete, which exposes my trade to increased external risk.

I want to share some insights I've been working on recently regarding trading around a FO.

We all know why a FO is an ideal place to look for a bounce. Not ever FO will react nicely however, and after many hours of simulated trading I am beginning to see certain patterns that drastically increase the likelihood of a bounce. In my opinion, knowing if price will bounce at a a FO level depends mainly on the PA to the left of the FO itself. The best FO bounces occur when price forms a FO after establishing a range, between two FL's (upper and lower FL).

In the case of my trade below, the upper FL is formed as the result of an engulf of a Flag to its left.. this is important, and it makes the future FO of this FL very important. Once the correct FL is identified and faked out, the rest is super easy. In this case, I knew I had a runner because of the engulf in to compression below, with price missing the main demand zone by just a few pips. Price forms a deep RT to gather enough bearish LQ to fuel the move down. They have to shake loose all sellers first, so they have ample LQ to sell in to. The result is a whole lot of trapped buyers...and plenty of LQ for the push down.

I know everyone here is aware of this kind of setup.. I am not discussing anything new...but many failed trades (as I see in my trading and other's trading) is the result of picking a weak LS/starting point. In the case of this EU trade below, the starting point was the FL that formed after price broke out of Box 1. That new FL is labeled as FL "A", and it is highly significant because it is the FL that contains the range where price faked out to the upside. When price returns to the important decision points, the entry is easy, the SL is easy, and the target is the demand zone below where price engulfed in to compression.

Hope these are some useful thoughts to ponder

This trade was about 13:R (my SL was under 5 pips)
