posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
The hard part of trading these FO bounces is knowing where price will bounce when the kink is wide. The wider the kink, the higher the risk. The best way to refine an entry when a kink is wide, is looking for a LTF 'inner kink'. Often times, price will bounce from the inner kink, inside of the larger scale kink. This is a big part of understanding how to use scale to your advantage.

In the case of the simulation below, there was no inner kink because my charting package only goes to 1-min candles and there was not enough detail. In this case, I drew the mouth of the kink & waited for a reaction there. But...here is where it gets tricky. When I trade, I want very little draw down. I usually like to keep my SL at or below 15 pips. If I had waited to short price deeper in the FL Box (as opposed to shorting the mouth), I would have been stopped out. The first two touches of the mouth took all of the short orders, leaving plenty of room for buyers to break through and establish control & a new high.

The rule I am currently working with when it comes to these setups:

1. If the setup is too confusing, just skip it and look for something else. If it doesn't 'jump out' at me right away, I look for a different trade.

2. If I want to trade it however, I will look to trade the mouth first, with a tight SL. (this is assuming the kink is wide and there is not inner kink to use as reference).

3. Each FO is a RBD or a DBR. In the chart below, the FO was a RBD. Look where the "drop" is... you can see that is a base. When price reacts to the mouth of the kink, it RT to the base. To me, that is a sign that price is ready to move higher. It did not engulf that base to the downside... i would be very cautious shorting a 3rd visit deeper in to the blue FL box.

These are the details that make or break a trade. It gets hard, because the intricacies of trading are somewhat subjective and it is almost impossible to teach this. I'm sure there is a better way to trade these setups, but this is my current take on it.

In reference to my post # 1937:

It is always hard to decide whether a lost trade is simply a fluke of the market (which happens) or if it was an error on my part. Post # 1937 is a perfect example. At first, I wrote it off as a 'fluke'. but after seeing the perfect reaction on the EA trade on post # 1938, I think I am still missing a piece of critical analysis.

My hunch is that the 'missing piece' has everything to do with the relationship between a swap zone & a FO. It is important to see where the FO occurs... I remember Salivan mentioning something about looking for a FO that occurs in to another FL. He might mean that the FO needs to dip through the FL in to the opposite swap zone to clear out all residual LQ.

If you refer back to my EUR-AUD trade on Post # 1938, you will see a great entry point with very little DD. If you look to the left of my entry, you will see a clear FO that occurs below the distal edge of the black box. That FO and subsequent high is drawn using the blue box. I am pretty sure the false move to the downside (in to a PAZ below) is key in getting the right bounce when price returns for the FOF that remains at that level.

My apologies if I am doing a bad job of explaining this... there concepts are notoriously difficult to describe using words

But for those who are struggling....start looking left and spend more time understanding what price is doing as it forms prior to the main FL where you start looking for an entry. Left side data is crucial, and I am still learning how to read it properly.

Confluence of the following factors is important as well:

1. Swap Zone

2. FO/False moves 3. Clean orders 4. Squaring up 5. Drawing FL Boxes & decisions in the right FL to prepare for an entry 6. ** False supply/demand zones that set up just above/below true supply or true demand. 5. Opposing targets (aka opposing tricks)

This is what I will continue working on.

Here is a simple version of the EA trade that worked out well in my post above.

If you look at the chart below, you will see I labeled FL "A" for reference. There is a tiny LTF kink that forms after price breaks the top of FL "A", but price forms a FO below that kink as well. The FO drops all the way back in to FL "A" (imagine if I extended FL "A" all the way to the right...). I think this holds importance because it is clearing residual LQ, making it much more likely that price will bounce bullish when price RT to the yellow box I drew.

We always want to make sure the last pocket of short orders is taken if we are looking to get long, otherwise, price is likely to do whatever is necessary to absorb that LQ. Clearing the last pocket of sell orders loads the buyers, and we can proceed to mark up the correct FL to find where the opposite orders are executed and FOF is created. [/b]

Hey Hansma,

It is good to hear from you

This way of looking at the market is still pretty new to me.. but I am looking specifically for a swap zone to start the analysis. The swap zone has to include a FL that holds price up, and a FL that holds price down (I think the terminology is LFL and UFL). If drawn correctly, this should create space between these FL's. It is in this 'space' that I want to see a FO occur.

I mark all of these zones as they form...then I start looking closer to see if there is an opportunity to make a trade. I treat each UFL/LFL combination as a 'system'.

Here is a drawing:

There isn't always space between the FL's, but if there is not space, then there is always an overlap. Here is a drawing that shows overlap, but no 'open space'.

I haven't done enough testing to find out which scenario is better, but so far, I prefer the situation where there is space between the two (usually you can see a very LTF kink in the space). The key is the FO... I want to see 'clean orders' in the form of a false move to trap LQ on the wrong side. It is the FO that occurs between the two FL's that form the swap zone that seems to clear out all residual LQ..making a bounce trade perfect.

If the FO forms and clean orders are left behind, I can trade along side the IT's when they square up their positions. It is the 'squaring up' that causes the bounce.

There are some exceptions to this.. most notably situations that incorporate compression. Compression creates atypical PA and usually I set my order just at the beginning of compression (or at the very least I will place my stop beyond the compression area). When I get stopped out using this method it is almost always because I misread compression.

Looking at your example on AUD-USD, I didn't quite see the swap zone. I do see your methodology however, and I think you are on the right track.

I formulated this way of looking at the market after revisiting Salivan's trades... he regularly took trades at the last possible pocket of supply/demand near a swap zone. It almost always happened near a FO/trick. I am curious if other traders see the same opportunity as I do!

Thanks for stopping by my journal!

Hi GGJJ,

Not entirely sure if I am correct, but the way I understand the 'last pocket of orders' is being the last place where buyers/seller took control of the market. There are two important pieces of information:

1. The decision to FO 2. the FTR/FL that forms after the engulf of the decision to FO.

The FTR/FL that forms after the engulf of the decision to FO is the last place where sell orders took control of the market, following the FO. When price returns to that last pocket of LQ, price bounces. That is also where price returns to 'square up' after the trick occurs ($$$ is spent to move the market in the wrong direction, and those who invest in this false move need to eventually exit their position, as it remains a constant drag on their balance sheet until the position is closed.

This is my understanding of why this 'last pocket' of LQ is so important.

Specifically for the AUD-USD trade, the decision to FO is drawn, and the engulf of the Decision to FO is also drawn. That FTR/FL is where I took the trade. In my opinion, the 'last pocket' is the FL labeled 'X" below. Technically, you could have chosen the first red box, or either of the purple boxes as the 'decision to FO' and you would still end up with the same FL "X". It is in the FL "X" that price bounces.

In reference to my post above (Post # 2007)

Something I noticed about that USD-CAD Short:

There were two scales involved with this trade. The First scale has a UFL and LFL and FO, and the lower scale has the same structure: UFL, LFL, and FO. The reasons I call it the "second scale" is because it forms as a result of it's reaction to the first scale.

What ends up forming, are two FO's.

Not sure how useful this is in trading these zones, but it might be a good idea to find multiple scale FO's occurring in close proximity together, because it decreases the likelihood that price will FO above your entry (If the space above your entry is just a higher TF scale with its own FO).

Great entry, but I still got stopped out on this EUR-USD Simulation.

It's a good reminder to be reasonable about targets. In this case, I kept my SL very tight, but my target was too wide. If I widened my SL to just above the FO, my original TG would have been hit nicely.

My Lesson:

If you take a trade with a very tight SL, make sure your target is reasonable (specifically, make sure your TG is placed at the first possible place where price might encounter resistance.). If you want a wider target, keep in mind that your SL may need to be widened to give price a little breathing room.

USD-CAD Trade Closed

This one started on Aug 1st.

My 1st target was a 15 R Trade My 2nd target was a 26 R Trade

The reason for taking a long was the FO shown at the bottom of the screen in the red circle.

I will start with the 30-min chart showing the entry and both targets. The 1st target was relatively straightforward, but the reason for staying in the trade after closing a portion of the position was the engulf located in the yellow circle... the target of that engulf gave me the 2nd Target of my buy trade @ the MPL. The MPL area of that FL is shown by the green rectangular box at the top of the screen. I exited the trade just before that MPL area (in case price bounced from a LTF "mouth" kink instead of making it all of the way into the MPL itself).

The next chart shows a detailed view of my entry on a LTF 1-minute chart. My exact entry was at the LTF QM level of the UFL formed after price engulfed the LFL. In this case, since I don't have data below a 1-minute chart, I had to use the entire 1-min candle as my LFL. While not shown on this chart, my SL was placed directly below the the fakeout itself. The SL was located 6 pips from my entry point.

The hourly chart below shows the reason I noticed this area to begin with. Basically, saw several consecutive lower lows, with one big move up just prior to the final lower low push. I saw this as an excellent bear trap. Specifically, I see that everyone starts buying at Point # 1 after several lower lows and higher lows. Traders see this as the end of the downward trend and start buying. Shorty thereafter, price cannot sustain this bullish push and price crashes down scaring everyone who got long and catching all of their stops at Point # 2. When Low # 4 forms, breakout traders get short and everyone who was long has closed out their positions and are looking to go short. Bearish traders are placing their stop losses above.

If you look at the green flag limit I drew, you can see Point # 3 is a FO below the box. This is the exact location of the trick. It is in this location where I will be looking to Buy (on a lower TF) when price returns.Those who were short at the FO are caught when price snaps back up. No major dips back in to this zone, so clean orders are formed at Point # 4 (they don't have a chance to get out in time). IT's have short orders trapped here as well. They have to square up eventually, and when they come back, I will be waiting. Eventually, price does return and I buy at Point # 5.

Hope this helps share my process!

Hey Enkim,

I don't have any specific rules when it comes to drawing FL's. I remember someone asking Salivan the same question a few months ago (over on his journal "Art of War") and he answered that drawing FL's comes down to intuition in some cases. I remember hating that reply because it seemed so unhelpful

But...there

is some truth to that.

I don't think you can draw FL's by using a strict, mechanical process every time. Sometimes it requires seeing the whole picture. I know, that's a crappy answer!

I'll do my best to explain exactly why I drew that red FL instead of the blue one...They are both legitimate FL's, but there are two main reasons why I chose mine over yours.

First Reason: Engulfs

I chose my box because I was looking for an engulf that could get me better R:R. The reason I drew my box instead of your box: the engulf of your box pretty much hit its target immediately...it was of no use to me. It wasn't until price engulfed out of that LTF FL (my box) that I had an engulf with an unmet target.

So, in summary, I chose the FL who's engulf pushed price in to a pole, with an unmet target above. You could sum it up in one word: Scale.

Second Reason: Proximity to LTF trick above:

Salivan had a concept which he referred to as 'magnetic attraction' as it referred to to price being attracted to certain areas of the chart based on the LQ that exists at that particular level. In my experience, price is attracted to areas where previous fakeouts have happened... and we know the best FO's are the ones that leave no room for trapped traders to get out in time.. simply put, the best FO's are proceeded with a sharp move away (pole). In this case, there was a mini trick, and price shot away very quickly, forming a pole in its wake.

If you keep the chart on the this TF, you can see price shot down quickly and didn't hesitate until it formed the first FL/FTR (this is my box). It was the first time price stopped to "catch its breath" after a trick and sharp pole-down. So, this FL/FTR is important to me. When my box bounces price and a new low is formed (the formation of your box), I give even more weight to my box. It is the "final northern frontier" before getting back on that 'highway' that leads directly back to the trick above. It is the last stop before that 'magnetc attraction' starts pulling price back in.

Hope this is at least a little useful to you. I hate ambiguity, so I try to make sure my answers are as direct as possible.

If anyone disagrees with me, please feel free to say so! I am wrong all the time.

Please refer back to my Post # 2073 above:

Here is a recent drawing I made to explain my updated strategy for trading price's RT to a previous FO.

Something interesting I just thought of: the FO of the LFL in the drawing and subsequent low confirms the original LFL as an "inner FL" or "inner kink".

This ties in nicely with what I was practicing yesterday when I said price engulfs, then forms FO

If applied to this drawing, the LFL or "inner kink" is also and engulf, which precedes the FO.

The tricky part is verifying that the "engulf" has a valid unmet target. If so, you are clear to trade price's RT to the FO that forms as part of the 'outer kink'. But, if the target of the engulf (inner kink) is already met, the "FO" of the inner kink is actually an engulf. Why? Because price has no reason to FO if price is coming from a met target. Any breach of a level (if price is coming from a met target) is indicative of future price direction (it's not a trick; it's an engulf). When price is coming from an unmet target the breached levels are FO's...tricks are needed because there is an unmet target. If you miss this detail, the trade will fail. This is a new concept for me, so please don't accept this as being 100% accurate....but it's certainly worth thinking about.

Here is a Drawing to illustrate:

The next drawing is similar to the one I just posted above, but this time I am showing a progression where a FO forms along with a new low, confirming the formation of an outer FL/kink. Notice, the FO is a "FO" only because it forms while the preceding engulf has yet to meet its target.

OK, the drawing below shows a situation where the engulf hits its target before the "FO forms". If this happens, I would label the area in the brown circle as an engulf...not a FO.

I want to refer back to a trade call I made last week on EUR-AUD (You can see it on my post # 2096).

I am detailing this trade because it is a setup that works almost all of the time...with tremendous reliability. The hard part is understanding the methodology and having the ability to apply it properly to a live chart.

Please feel free to challenge me if I say anything incorrect

First, here is a copied chart from post # 2096:

But here is more detail as to why I took this trade:

Take a look at point # 1 and point # 2: they are both fakeouts. The important part of trading these accurately is taking the time to carefully analyze where the perspective FO forms. I have a bad tendency to get sloppy when it comes to carefully analyzing the exact location of the FO. This is the reason for many of my losing trades (I went through a bunch of losing trades from 2017 this year and noticed many losses happen as a result of sloppy mistakes on my end).

It starts with drawing FL Boxes at the right locations: in close proximity to swap zones. Once the boxes are carefully drawn, it is much easier to see how price reacts to them. But it's not always clear.

In this example, look at FO # 1. Despite missing my main FL Boxes, FO # 1 ends up forming at a very important area: pre compression. Price came just shy of engulfing in to compression. This makes FO # 1 important. Not all valid FO's will bounce price because they aren't created equal...all FO's have varying degrees of strength. Pre-compression is one of the strongest.

When price forms FO # 2 you can see price does not engulf any LTF FL's...and once again there is an important FO. The rest is easy...finding that exact entry becomes pretty simple once the FO's are drawn and verified as being strong. Specifically, I extended the red 'inner kink' over to the right and used that as my detailed entry point (since it is located within a larger HTF kink). Look how perfectly price respected that red inner kink.

Hi Pinkpanter,

You have some good questions...I might be the wrong person to ask when it comes to kinks and engulfs.

Lately, I have been focusing my attention on trading the return to an important fakeout. Ideally, there will be two fakeouts happening- each in their own scale.

I want a high time frame fakeout, followed by a slightly lower scale FO... then I trade the RT to the that smaller FO. A good example of this is in Post # 2127 above.

You can see I went short on EU at the second FO. These FO were on the same scale, but it still looked good because FO # 1 did not engulf anything important on the LTF. This is why I felt comfortable shorting at the second FO.

Also, and maybe most importantly, I need to see a valid FO AND clean orders to take a trade.

To me: Clean orders = trapped traders = LQ waiting on price's RT

If I was looking at your chart, and I had no other TF to look at, this is how I would analyze it:

I would look at the area I marked FO # 1 on LTF to see exactly what it was reacting to. Was there an engulf on LTF? If so, avoid a trade on FO 2. I am not impressed by FO #1...there isn't much of a FO happening here, although it does happen near a swap zone, so it is worth looking at on LTF. The FO has to occur in to an important area without engulfing.

If there is no EG on FO #1, then FO 2 is possibly in play...but there must be clean orders (trapped traders with LQ) at the FO # 2 area. From what I see on this chart, there are not any clean orders..price meandered away. No trap means I am not trading it. I would look at a new chart.

But don't be discouraged

... I am working on a very specific type of strategy. There

are countless ways to apply RTM theory and add your own strategic influence to specialize in a specific type of setup.

Maybe someone else can do a better job of answering your question. I hope my response was somewhat useful!

Hi GGJJ,

It is always hard to find the place where price will bounce once you find the right FO to trade from. Usually, I look for that last FL or decision point before price fakes out....but I also look at that potential entry point in relation to the size of the FO and the FL Boxes around it to see (visually) if my entry is reasonable. I always ask: Is my entry too far below the place where the FO eventually stops? If so, the risk is pretty high and I may adjust my entry.

I wish I had a concrete answer for exactly how to find the perfect entry every time... but the closest I can get to that is:

Use the last FTR/FL that formed before the FO occurs...you want the last place where price hesitated before shooting up (or down) to form the FO You want the place right before the trick happened...where all the traders got stopped and BO traders got in on the wrong side. You want the "calm" before the storm.

Hope this is useful

I think the general concept is remaining LQ is left over from trapped orders occurring when price fakes out before turning abruptly. All this type of trade is: taking advantage of the 'bounce' from left over orders at a level where there was some previous carnage.

The stronger the false move, and the stronger the move away from that false move, the greater likelihood of a a bounce when price returns to that area.

I believe you are spot on in your thinking about residual orders on these types of scenarios. The way I think about it, perhaps incorrectly, is that IT create a false breakout where they trick uninformed traders into buying. The better the trick the more orders they have to overcome to reverse the market. So I figure if they build a really great level that draws lots and lots of interest that means they have to dump more sells to overcome the buyers and drop the market. If they dumped lots of sells onto the market chances are those orders were not all filled because the market moved too fast. So when we come back to revisit the area, those leftover orders are often sitting there waiting to be filled.

The only way this wouldn't be the case is if they pull the unfilled orders. Which I imagine they would only do if the market extended down to their target and it was some type of substantial bullish set-up like a QM or DM on HTF.

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
I totally agree!

Gregg mentioned a concept to me a few months ago which I have applied to my trading... he uses the term 'square up'. I interpret 'squaring up' as the trapped LQ left over after the main event has occurred... tremendous capital is spent to push price in that false direction, and those open orders remain on their balance sheet as the trade progresses. Since banks and institutional funds don't use SL, they have to 'square up' or clear the orders open and dragging on their balance sheet. When price RT to that false breakout, they get out of these positions...and that is the bounce I trade.

It all seems quite logical to me... and it explains (in part) why these areas are so reactive when price returns.

Therefore price will go to higher Supply level to search for more Sell orders. Once there is no more Supply. what happens is, they need to create the Fake Supply and hide their intention of wanting to Buy, therefore they will make it looks like Sell is going on, enticing sellers and breakout sellers in. Why not? =) They want the best possible price, which is this case is MPL, because that Demand has not been taken yet

In the drawing below, the price has not hit its target yet, therefore ITs are not satisfied. They will want to hit Target, before they make new decision. The risk of trading this kind of setups are, you don't know what will happen to the price as it is still in the space and anything can happen, while they play tricks. In this case, the price can go all the way up to MPL of UFL before hitting their target, CP to their level or shoot straight down to their level, if they suddenly want long. Too many options:D, therefore it will be guess work what they will do...Oh and you will not know if the LFL will hold the price or not in this case

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
Just a quick reminder to traders when it comes to drawing FL's. There are often multiple scales with different boxes. Quite frequently there are tiny low TF scale FL's that occur but aren't visible in your other time frames.

It is really easy to overlook these tiny FL's (I have a bad habit of doing it), but properly drawing them gives you a HUGE edge on the market. I recently went back through my losing trades to see what I did wrong. More than 50% of my losses were due to sloppy HTF drawing if FL's. It is amazing actually when you start practicing because you see how relevant those tiny FL's are.

posts.author: Rinehart
posts.text:
My answer is it depends on the importance of E:

If zone E is what the MPL of D reacted off of to form zone D. Then, we don't have an engulf / trade. If zone E is just a hiccup between the HTF zones, I think D is engulfed and I'm looking for a trade. If zone E was the actual FL formed right after the break of C and zone D is really more of a DBD decision point, I'm not looking for a trade because we have hit the next target.

I said hiccup to mean kink but imply it is not important.

From what you have written about wanting E to be THE FL. I would say you have no trade here.

Word of advice --- examine every FL on the lowest possible time frame to get the proper boundaries.

Wouldn't a HTF FL be a LTF Flag?

The other thing is this is one of those questions you kind of have to figure out yourself. If you put a chart in front of us, we can answer it case by case. On the other hand, if you are talking about an abstract situation, it depends because each situation is a little different. A break of support on weekly will create a FL. That HTF FL is still comprised of LTF zones. When I'm examining price to put on a trade, I examine my FL on the lowest time frame available to get he boundaries right. Your job is to find the important ones.

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
Here is an analysis of my USD-JPY trade today: I'll start by posting the final chart, and then I will attach each of the charts showing my analysis that led up to taking the trade.

Part 1:Look left to draw the order flow as price engulfs, retraces, and forms a swap zone.

Notice how Box 3 was drawn... paying close attention to the inner FL (lower scale).

"A" shows where buyers entered the market to push price up to "B", where price took the remaining supply in Box 3 (which is a swap zone). I used the low @ "A" as the basis for Box 4, which ends up being the reason for my trade. Point C & D was confirmation that a FO would happen in to Box 4 (B&C is a RS bounce from the edge of Box 4). But, I only took the trade because of what happened in the PA between "A" and "B", specifically that B took the LQ in Box 3, which is a swap zone. No engulf happened above Box 3, which tells me all of the seller LQ was taken.

As you can see, once I complete the order flow analysis to the left, the entry is really easy. In this case, my SL was tiny.

This trade is not my typical setup, as the primary reason for taking the short was not a return to a fakeout. That said, the methodology is very similar. In my opinion, the most important part of this trade, and the reason there was sufficient order flow to bounce price, was because of how price reacted to Box 3, a swap zone. It is the same scenario for FO trades... I want to see the FO happen to a specific area of LQ at a swap zone without engulfing

Interesting Trade that I took last night on USD-CHF... great example to share. This was 17:R

I tried to clearly show where my entry and exit was. For some reason, my platform places arrows in odd places. The dotted red line is more accurate to show my entry/exit. I closed out the trade in the red circle area. My SL was about 3 pips.

Something I want to share...I have been making some changes to my strategy lately. I am becoming MUCH more interested in the approach price takes before it reaches my entry. I am learning that is more important than finding the bounce points. For example: the yellow box is pretty easy to find/draw. It's just carefully drawing FL boxes... simple.

We find areas like this all over the charts, and often they bounce price. But, we also see these FL's fail.

I am learning that whether a FL will hold depends on prices approach to the level. I want to see a structured attempt at creating supply/demand just below/above my FL box (my entry of interest). I want to see how price approaches my box, but I want price to FAIL to hit the zone. Then, I want to see a deep retrace back to some strong pocket of Liquidity before price begins to rise/drop to the entry point. These supply/demand created levels that fail to hit the entry target act as a perfect trap for traders to get in on the "breakout".

This takes some time to find on the charts... I am still practicing it. But, this USD-CHF is a perfect example. I would not have taken this trade if price hadn't formed that supply level to the immediate left of my actual entry. When I saw that false supply form, I added my limit orders and woke up to a 17:R trade!

Focus on thinking like a predator... rewire your brain to see the tricks for LQ and trading gets easier.

Hope this helps!!e

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
I just want to share an update with you guys about my recent progress in trading. I have been challenging myself to move away from terminology and patterns... and shift towards understanding why price often fakes out certain levels. I am learning to shift my strategy to look for opportunities to trap traders.

If you train your eyes to see the Fakeouts, you will notice they tend to occur in to areas of importance in terms of order flow.

The fakeout usually tends to serve three primary functions:

1. It spikes to areas of LQ already existing on the chart 2. It creates LQ not existing on the chart through bull traps/bear traps 3. It creates LQ pending on the chart by taking stop losses (which is LQ in the form of limit orders)

With this in mind, I shift my focus. I ask myself:

1. Which FL's are MOST likely to convince traders that the supply/demand located within is significant enough to bounce price? 2. Which FL's (or important highs or lows) are most likely to entice breakout traders when price breaches the level? 3. Which FL's are located directly above/below an area of significant LQ?

With these three questions in mind, I begin looking for a combination of these events to occur in the chart. Ideally, I want a setup in which I can say the answer to all three questions is YES

This a step-by-step analysis of the simulation trade I took in Post # 2273 above.

Starting with the basics: Finding a swing low/high that includes a false break and strong follow through. I labeled this as "A". This is a HTF FL, with a false break down and a strong follow through to the upside. The false break down was the origin of the move, trapping bearish LQ to fill the longs that preceded that strong push up. A retest of that false break (bear trap) occurs, but price does not make a new low. You can see this retest in the red circle. This is important.

The next step is to identify the location where sell orders were executed at the beginning of the false move to the downside. This order flow is critically important. As you can see, in the hourly chart we are unable to discern the exact location where the bear trap originates. We need to drop down to a 15-Minute chart to see the actual FL that occurs at the break. The bets trade opportunities occur when LQ is sought by trapping LQ in the wrong direction AND when the exact break is hidden in a HTF candle. The chart below shows the execution of orders that formed the trap. That FL is labeled as "B".

After identifying the exact execution of orders forming the bear trap (B), the FL is extended to the right... all the way to the right. The details of this zone are relevant to everything we do to set up the trade.

My attention now shifts to the RT that price made to this trap, when it bounced without making a new low (I showed this reaction in the red circle on the first chart I posted in this journal entry). I am going to shift my attention to this RT. I want to draw the areas where price interacts with the "B". There will be two versions of this step... and the distinction between these two charts is really important. I will label these charts as version 1 and version 2. Take a look at Version 1 below:. I drew the FL's formed as price engulfed "B"... and labeled that FL as 'C". When "C" is engulfed, I labeled that FL "D".

The next chart is Version 2.... it is the correct way to draw this. Version 1 is drawn too broadly. When you drop to a 5-min chart, you will see the boxes are different, based on the exact location where box "B" is engulfed. The distinction is really important... and the existence of a trade setup where this occurs is good news because it increases the likelihood of your trade working. The details matter, and drawing exact FL boxes is incredibly important...I just recently realized this over the past couple of months. Look how Box C and Box D differ based on drawing the LTF boxes properly... Version 1 shows the incorrect way to draw the boxes, and Version 2 shows the correct way to draw the boxes.

I am running out of space, so I will continue this on the next post. For clarity, I am shading "D" in yellow since it is my execution box (where I will be placing my buy orders). Here is a clean chart for reference: See next post for a continuation of this trade analysis.

(response to Dengaima from yesterday's question)

You asked why I didn't re-draw my yellow box after price broke the LTF FL. I used to do this, but the more I practice the more I am seeing the importance of the lowest TF FL that forms after price engulfs an important area. The higher scale FL's are useful for positioning, but the real orders seem to exist in the hidden 'inner' FL's that form when price first engulfs an important zone.

This is important because the size of the FL determines when/where you draw the next engulf. That is why I prefer drawing the LTF FL first...then see what other FL's set up in the vicinity that could be used to form a FO to grab some added LQ. The LTF FL (the yellow box used in this example) is my starting point for seeing what LQ traps might set up in the area.

Two great opportunities to buy. Notice the green lines prior to each trade... the line sets up a demand zone which is taken out.

If you are looking to take a long trade, look for a false demand zone. If you are looking to take a short trade, look for a false supply zone. Price is drawn to origins and important FL's at swap zones because they contain large amounts of orders. When price comes really close to one of these zones of magnetic attraction, but fails to actually hit the zone, we have a possible 'false' zone setting up.

posts.author: hoeschec
posts.text:
Referring back to Post # 2349:

Here is a re-post of the chart I made:

My philosophy is an off-shoot of the main concepts taught here on RTM. Several weeks ago I began a study in to understanding why price bounces and fakes out. If you remember back to my old posts for 2016/2017 you will see I focused almost exclusively on trading the return to a fakeout that already occurred in the past. That is still a good strategy & approach to trading the market, but I always wondered how difficult it would be to trade the FO as is occurred instead of trading the return to the FO.

Trading the FO as it forms has its own benefits: mainly better RR and quick trades. Also, it's REALLY fun!

I've noticed that traders tend to form their own strategies over time as they gravitate towards a certain 'type' of trading style or methodology.

I strongly believe that price moves because of order flow. Price moves in the direction of liquidity. It is always bouncing around as the war between bears and bulls rages on. Finding where the true or 'free' or 'fresh' order flow exists is key to knowing which direction price is headed. As I mentioned yesterday, I believe true order flow exists in the tiny FL formed when price engulfs an important levels (ORFL, SWAP, FL's etc...).

Most traders on RTM know how to draw the FL boxes. They are fun to draw, and they do an excellent job of framing the market in a visual structure that draws our eyes towards the important decisions and the relevant areas of order flow.

Lately, I have been studying how to draw the FL Boxes properly. Often times, price will engulf a level and form a new FL on a LTF but price will form multiple iterations as it passes above and below that initial FL to form a HTF FL. I've heard others refer to this as an 'inner' FL and an 'outer' FL.

In my opinion (and I admit i'm still learning as I explore chart after chart after chart...) the first engulf and FL formed after price breaks an important level is the most important FL in terms of order flow. The HTF FL's that form outside of the inner FL is like a 'shell' and it's important too... but not as important the tiny inner FL.

This distinction of the inner vs outer FL is very important because we draw the boxes based on engulfs of previous boxes. Once these start getting drawn in multiple scales (fractals) we see a type of divergence or "deviation" exists between the fractals. This divergence/deviation looks like a gap of space where the distal boundaries of one FL (in one TF) are different from the distal boundaries of another FL (in a different TF). Why does this matter to us? Because if we are looking on the higher TF scale we might expect price to bounce in a particular FL where this gap exists...and price will overrun the FL making it look like price engulfed in the wrong direction when in reality it was just bouncing from the lower scale FL. Usually, these Lower scale FL's are accompanied by a false supply/demand level to create a bear/bull trap as well.

Since each new FL box depend on engulfs of preceding FL boxes, finding the exact starting point is CRITICAL. If the first FL box is incorrectly drawn, or is based on an engulf of a wrong level (or an engulf of the wrong scale) the proceeding boxes will all be wrong. Identifying the right starting point is my main focus right now...this is what I am currently working on. I will post more info when I find good examples to share.

I know this is a really hard concept to explain using words... hopefully I can find some good examples to post in my next few posts. I am still figuring this out as I go too. I am feeling highly motivated and I am excited to find out where these new discoveries will lead. Hopefully, if I am on the right track (and I think I am), I can post this information on my journal to help others as well!

posts.author: Ifmyante
posts.text:
Hi C-12

There certainly is more that fear and greed to get over in this
business. There's also the balance between chart life and real life to
be set and maintained.

If you don't have the complete support of your loved ones, you may find yourself living in some very dark days.

It's a long and sometimes lonely road we must walk. To an observer we
simply look like we're sitting passively at the screen, but in reality,
we're fighting demons daily, living through great victories and crushing
 defeats, on our way to mastering the market.

We must make our partners aware of every step we take, and also listen
to their concerns. We are making a journey into the unknown, but at
least we are choosing the route. They have no such control, and this can
 make them panic if they're not kept fully up to speed on progress.

So, communication is key. Always let your loved ones know where you are
with it, and always listen to their concerns. When listening, really
listen. Switch off those charts that forever seem to tick away in your
head, and SEE the person before you. Their feelings and opinions really
count in your life, so heed them, and find a way to make a balance
between the great future you're making and the great present you could
be missing out on

posts.author: Ifmyante
posts.text:
This perhaps should be the first thing that anybody ever reads regarding trading:

We're always looking for signs of what the big guys are doing at
significant areas, and if we don't see what they're doing, there's no
trade

So, on approach, if we see the big guys trying to hide their orders in
the market, we see compression, and can feel pretty sure of their
intentions - to get in as many orders as they can before the turn

If we don't see this, we can be pretty sure that it won't just turn
immediately, as there usually won't be enough orders against them to
fill all the orders they must fill.

This is why we wait for an engulf. This shows their intention to reverse
 price. Then we watch them trying to hide their orders in the market on a
 retrace, ready to take price to the origin of the move

after the engulfing or can we enter as soon as the euro prints the
rejection bar?

When price doesn't compress to, let's say, supply, then we will need
some kind of signal that reveals big money's intentions. The signal is
the engulf.

Then we wait for a retest of left over supply, or break of flag or resistance.

Below is a chart of what I think we are supposed to be doing. Its a
chart of the EUR/USD. FIrst off lets start with the flags. I think the
definition of a flag is when the top and bottom are liquidity gaps. In
other words you find the area on the bottom that was broken with strong
demand and the area on the top that was broken with strong demand. The
area in the middle is your flag or CP. Right? My flags on here are
marked with blue rectangles. The red lines are the extremes that we
would look for price action and the middle is where we don't want to
diddle! In other words there is either really clean ignored/broken SD
above and below the CP or its just a flag. This is why the other areas
that I marked with trend lines are not flags. These areas are just CP,
thats why price moved through them. I don't know however why price
stopped at the yellow line. That demand was spiked.

If you look at the flag at the top with the red arrow, that is where I
would look to short. Its an engulf from the area just to the left of it.
 For now it looks like price is compressing back up to the flag that did
 the engulfing. This means that I would look at the red lines of that
flag on lower time frames for a sign. This could be a swap level, QM,
engulf, or it might CP into the edge. Is this right?

Thanks,

H

posts.author: mettafort
posts.text:
To Harsh (I hope you dont mind IF):

Hey Harsh-

This is how I see it. RBR/DBR are formations, as well as metaphors.
These formations are what I see as canonical examples of something more
subtle - disequilibrium. The base of DBR is the area of focus, for it
has within it an area of equilibrium - the base. Price bounces tightly
in a state of balance, and then eventually price rises, fast or slow.
The way in which price leaves an area is what the focus is in the end as
 far as I see it - if price leaves slowly, the probability of orders
being left at the base area is lower than if price shoots away.

In IF's diagram the base is at the bottom of the PAZ. That is a DBR for
 sure, and the R piece engulfs the upper supply. The source of this
move then is the move away from the base. But notice also that price
pulls back and makes an FTR, which itself is a variant of a DBR. Again,
 when price leaves the FTR, if it moves well, it becomes an area of
significance when price revisits.

When price is seemingly stable, and then moves quickly away, this is
place to focus on. It is the Balance->Imbalance cycle. You can spot
 this all over a chart. A good example is at the extremes. Imagine
price breaking to new highs, and then struggle to get higher. Then a
ledge is formed as price falls - a type of base with perhaps the highs
falling but the lows remaining at the same level for 5 bars or so. Then
 price plummets, confirming supply is up here - this is one version of
what some refer to as a hook. The point being that price might not look
 like a canonical base, RBR, DBR, RBD, etc....the key is to look beyond
that, IMHO.

HTH,

MF.

posts.author: Hotochin
posts.text:
Jam,

I don't think IF will mind if I answer some of your questions. I was
actually talking about this with someone else one this forum. Think of
FTR's as the flag limits. I have attached a chart with engulfs and the
following flag limits marked with purple arrows. Notice how price "stair
 steps its way up?" When one of the limits gets engulfed that is your
clue as to where price wants to go! When a whole zone gets engulfed you
will be amazed at how price will respect them on the way down. Notice
how price is compressed while in the zones? I think the trick is to
watch the extremes of these zones and look for PA on smaller time frames
 for confirmation.

Good luck,

H

posts.author: Ifmyante
posts.text:
Hi all

I've been doing lots of deliberating lately about my place in the world of trading.

When I first saw a chart, I thought "Yes!! I'll solve that puzzle and make a fortune from it!!!"

I should've known at the time that all I really wanted to do was simply solve the puzzle.

As you have probably guessed already, I love to teach what I have
learned. Many of you have also found that I've given out all the
information necessary to work out the entire market. Sure, you had to
put in a lot of work to make the lessons your own, but all the signposts
 and pitstops were there to help you on your journey.

If I teach any more, I think I'd be taking everyone straight to the finish line.

The problem for me is, I still want to teach it.

I've been looking at the other analysis schools and awarding bodies, and
 none of them come even close to reading the market fully. The teachings
 of RTM blow them all out of the water.

I believe that an RTM Degree should be THE most prestigious qualification in trading.

So I'm considering running an online trading university, with a complete
 syllabus, teaching everything that needs to be learned - a complete
course in analysis, and also a complete course in trading methods, with
 dedicated teachers helping the students all the way to the final exams
and graduation.

Some say that those who can, do, and those who can't, teach. Well, we've
 made enough great traders that I certainly have no need to trade for
myself, so perhaps I should just keep doing what I love to do - teach

Let me know what you guys think about this

Best

If

If,

When I first came across the PIE thread, what really grabbed my
attention was one of your videos which had been linked. You have a way
of teaching which really gets the point across and without the arrogance
 and chest thumping which is often the case with people who are very

slope one day and they were having a free concert and you could see that
 tons of people were just totally into the music and really in the zone.
 What makes a person listen to music like that or be a rock climber or
do any specific activity that they have a passion for? I believe that

most. We are meant to BE, actually live, in this moment. For you,

have everything planned and are open to something new it's often amazing
 to see what the Universe delivers...

DT

posts.author: rcmacf
posts.text:
I miss my days of teaching (instructing adults in some oilfiled
operations and data analysis) and take opportunities wherever I can to
pass on my knowledge, so I understand the drive to do so in others. So,
 I say go for it, as it won't leave you, and will burn away until you
find an outlet.

For RTM specifics, I'd like to mirror the thoughts of a few others, that
 I'm off down rabbit holes with walls at the end (PAZ, anyone? I'm
almost embarrassed to ask for direct help with this, so long have I been
 trying to make it work in my head, without subjectivity) and I can feel
 an internal struggle starting, pushing me back to the comfort of old
ways. My desire to master this RTM way is strong, however, and it shall
 win through.

On the other hand, there are so many sheisters in trading that I feel
uncomfortable with the 'cost' option being used to exclude people from
knowledge. I know of "elite" groups charging $25,000 for membership yet
 giving no more knowledge or profit than I've gleaned from a week with
youtube. Also, the people who would like to take your proposed course
are more than likely (like me) those who have struggled to make trading
work for them, even though success is right there - look,
right......there......just out of reach, and so a big financial
commitment has the potential to be yet another market related kick in
the balls. I have been involved in groups, for example, where your
happy, free, trading helper starts pushing more and more products your
way, until you suddenly realise that their methods don't work for them,
either, and the products are their bread and butter (and more often than
 not somebody else's, just repackaged). Yuck.

I've given much time to the markets, and have even been passing on the
knowledge I have to others for concepts that I know inside out so it
would be great if this was my last rabbit hole, and I could stop
chasing, chasing, chasing.

Forums can take you so far, but as this one grows, so do the rabbit
holes. They may lead somewhere good, but how to know when you start at
the top?

My approach, perhaps, has been unfocussed, and this is where a course
would be of the most use to me. I have not completed all the homework,
and so perhaps this is where I am failing, although I think I have a
good enough grasp on the concepts. However, there is a purity to how
you see the markets, IF, and that is diluted (you could say enhanced) by
 all the others teaching on this site. You can't police it all, and so
there chance of the new going down the wrong hole is always there.

Anyhoo, I put together videos as it's always a struggle for me to get my
 point over effectively via a keyboard without about 45mins per
sentence. Ok, about 10 words per minute, but all the same.

I'm gonna take a leaf from Rufus' journal and post a poem.

I wrote it some time ago, while quite poor. Reading it now, I'm glad I did!

Nevermore

I hear the distant echo

of a song I knew before,

it hovers o'er the river

I swam in days of yore,

when enclosed me only sunshine

and all the world was mine,

'fore penury got its grip on me

in the dark'ning veil of time

I hear the distant echo

of a song I knew before,

it plays in attic treasure chests

my mind loved to explore,

when diamond chips and pirate ships

abounded on the main,

'fore my childhood dreams cried mutiny

now no mystery remains

I hear the distant echo

of a song I knew before,

it swings on oak tree pendulums

I tied before the war

'tween a young boy's dreams of flying

and an old man's hopes of dying,

and with time's speed multiplying

'til the clock tic tocs no more

I hear the distant echo

of a song I knew before,

so I'll ramble on

and sing my song

and regard not nevermore

posts.author: Ifmyante
posts.text:
oneday wrote: At the risk of being flamed...will this not need a little editing?...

"We won't charge for these lessons; we intend to give them all for
free. It is my intention (Hi, I'm Ifmyante, by the way) to write the
most comprehensive and no BS Wiki course on trading that has ever been
written, and put it in the site for free."

Flamed? Not at all! I'm delighted this came up in such a polite and considerate manner :)

The article doesn't need editing at all.

RTM has the most comprehensive and no BS Wiki course on trading that has ever been written, and it's all on the site for free!

The paid course is a luxury rather than a necessity. Anybody who puts in
 the work to make the free lessons their own, has just as much chance of
 making it as those who pay for the course. The course is just a
shortcut. No more, no less.

It was implicit that the first rung of RTM was all about reading the
market. Learning to trade it was to be a personal journey, aided by
seniors as one climbs the ladder. But there'll be a module on the course
 dedicated to trading, and making trade plans to suit each lifestyle and
 personality. So yes, in this case, there IS a difference.

It may seem that I started RTM for altruistic reasons, but that's not
the case. Sure, I stop to help people who've broken down or are in some
other trouble, but I do that because it makes ME feel good. I started
RTM to make an army of great traders who'll work with me in the future.
No altruism there. I'm delighted I did, as we already have our first
fund traders lined up and ready to go.

So why don't I now hand out ALL I know for free to everybody? I steal
orders from the big institutions, but not so many that they lose out.
The more people I tell how to do this, the more of their orders will be
taken. Once they can't get their orders filled, they'll need to change
their methods - methods that have been very secret for a very long time.
 This would render the information I have sold obsolete.

I'm so proud that so many have earned the keys to the kingdom through
hard work and perseverance. To then just give the keys away would be
truly irresponsible.

So, in essence, this course will be a luxury, absolutely not a necessity!

posts.author: Ifmyante
posts.text:
Scipio wrote:

Hi If lets talk about the course...I have a question:

How the course will be structured?

Hi Scipio

As I see it, I'll be remaking all the material that's already here on
RTM, relating it all to the revelations I got over the last year. I also
 have other revelations to add (let me stress once again, that all these
 revelations I got were based on the lessons I already gave, and can be
had by anybody who ties all the lessons together!)

The lessons will be structured in such a way that each makes a strong foundation for the next

Students would be given homework assignments on the lessons, and once
we're satisfied they know the material, they'd get access to the next
lessons.

There'll be regular tutorial webinars intended to tie the lessons together.

As I see it, there will probably be two modules to the course - one for reading price, and one for trading.

Access to the trading section would be granted to those who've graduated from the reading module

In it I'd be explaining everything about chart setup, trade selection, trade management, and trading plan construction.

There are a number of types of trade, and a myriad of trader lifestyles,
 temperaments and time limitations, so this section will give the
students the trading rules which will work best for them. These trading
 plans will take much of the emotion out of trading, making their job
mechanical.

There'll be a lot of personal attention put into each student, but for
those who want to book extra one on one time, there may be packages on
offer to cover this

There'll be final exams for each of the modules, and qualifications awarded to the graduates.

There will be a forum for students, and a forum for alumni

I'm sure I'm leaving loads out here, but this is the essence of it

posts.author: Springger
posts.text:
Guys, the course hasn't been out as yet, but so far RTM has been able
to crank out consistent winners. Look at Pedini, Harry, Sunnytrader,
Infest (my personal hero.) Eurotrash, 2OZ. The list can go on and on.
They took the time, they made the effort, they went the distance and it
paid off. That goes to show, the magic isn't in the course, its already
in the forums. You just need to sift through and find the nuggets of
gold hidden here there and everywhere.

To the naysayers, I ask (you know who you are!! )

1. How many of you did the homework that was asked?

2. How many of you watched the videos that were posted in the Education
Section of the website over and over, at least until you got an AHA
moment?

3. How many of your tried learning, then reading, then trading?

Try that first. Then make judgements and assumptions. Take 1 step at a
time. Eat the elephant one bite at a time. (sorry vegetarians!!)

Think this is something you can pick up in 1 month? HA... Think again.
If making money consistently was easy, wouldn't everyone be doing it?

The course is a luxury, not a necessity. Its been said over and over.

To the other detractors....

1. Can you give me an estimate of the cost of operating a website such
as this with related bandwidth and what not? Yet we take for free and
not give anything back. Why is this?

2. Forex traders want everything for free. 90% of us use MT4 as a
platform as its free. Backed by some shoddy broker. I'm not saying that
they all are. But most of them are some type of bucket shop operation.
Thats why they can do as they want, when they want. I'm sure we have all
 heard about broker horror stories. How many forex traders have a
proper data feed and trading account? Backed by reliable names in the
industry? Nothing based in Cyprus, some back corner in Russia, etc. Its
 a very small percentage.

We want everything and we want it for free, with minimal work. Isn't that another definition for LAZINESS? Why is that?

I'm starting to sound like a cranky old man from somewhere we might remember
 . IF, Mods, Seniors, you know the drill. If I have said anything that
doesn't belong in the thread, feel free to edit. I'm pretty sure I might
 have offended someone. But in my point of view, it has to be said.

The easy access to quality information we now have is slowly but surely changing many businesses.

 to a BMW specialist, because he was the only person who knew it well.

posts.author: Ifmyante
posts.text:
Hi Forethan

I abhor discussing money, so I shan't.

As many of you already know, I lost my family due to all the time I spent helping people for free.

I had locked myself away day and night for so long working out how the
market works, that of course it depleted the patience of my love. Then
what did I do once I had learned enough to make us very rich? I opened a
 website, where I spent day and night teaching people what I'd laboured
over for so long.

After such a cost in time and money (yes, I was trading live from the start ), I was now giving it all away for free! Well, of course I was asking for trouble!

I had the opportunity to fix it, by not opening RTM, and focusing solely
 on family and trading. But instead, I went ahead with it, and by the
time RTM went live, I was in my third day of homelessness. I'll never
forget New Years Day, 2013, I can assure you.

It's now exactly seven months since RTM opened (7 mths 2 days since I
lost my home), and I'm about to start giving focused lessons on all I've
 learned, spending alot of time on each student who comes with me.

But now I know the value (and the cost to me) of what it is I'm giving,
and if the students are in any doubt about it before we begin, they'll
know it once we're done.

Now, should I do this for free? Should I make deals over my time and
experience? Should I devalue myself and all I've been through?

It's simply in my nature to learn and to share what I've learned. But
it's also in my nature to live with my family, whom I miss more than
most can ever imagine,

Is it wrong to hope, that if I can show that all the time and effort
I've put into teaching has actually been of some benefit to my family,
that I may actually get them back? Maybe even regain the respect of the
one person I most want the respect of?

I'm sorry Forethan, this rant wasn't in any way directed at you. It's
just that I have no filter on which parts of the truth I should leave
unsaid

So, back to business:

Regarding guaranteeing success; All I can do is guarantee that I'll
teach how the market works, and will help each student choose the
trading plans that'll work best for them. All that's important, and none
 of what's unimportant will be in the course, and if the students take
this to heart, and follow their plans with patience and understanding,
they will have every possible chance of getting to the top of this
business.

I cannot guarantee that students will stick to the plans. I cannot
guarantee that students won't get the sudden urge to try an MA crossover
 system ten minutes after graduation, and blow their accounts in a week!
 I cannot guarantee that some students won't do exactly the opposite of
what they've been advised.There are so many variables within each
student that it's impossible for me to guarantee their actions.

Best

If

I'm no elite, I'm a cadet. I'm proud of it, and to be honest, there
are people here that have shaped me and touched me and we havent even
shared directly a single word. But I know my future can never not have
that experience of that persons knowledge be within my mind; any
progress I might make in new associations would be because of the input
of the many people I have learnt from already; the shoulders of giants.
 We are all giants here, because we joined here because of a common
theme, and it is deeper than Traders Helping Traders; its even more
human than that. We want to help each other, because together as
brothers and sisters, we can all float higher together, knowing we not
only *took* to rise, but *gave* to push out.

My dreams of what I want out of life have this year have become more
solid because of the existence of RTM and the mentors here. Before I
found RTM I was lost, and had spent more than I should have on stuff
that offered nothing in return. Ironically, my most profitable trade,
after spending a lot of money on signals and professional trading
strategies, was one that I discovered myself through many long hours on
the computer, deep into the depth of night. Sometimes I would have
realizations but more often, I just grew cold from the darkness of not
being able to see something, just something. And then one day I saw
something, and it worked repeatedly, and it was my first time that I
actually got to understand more about money management - before this I
had heard about it, but I still wasnt clued up. I was just early on in
the journey, thats all. Yet I moved forward, I learnt what was good
about my pattern and what was bad about it. I even began to see how if,
 I could spot this pattern n times, and x times where profitable at a
ratio of at least 2x the risk, then I potentially hold in my hands
something that could truly change the course of my life forever. And
while this is further on the journey, it is nowhere near where it needs
to be. But now, at this stage where I have at least held in my hand the
hope that I could change my destiny by taking control of my career and
finances in this way, then that is powerful.

But it should never be about the price, it is ultimately ever only about
 the goal...that reward. If it doesnt magnify well the risk, then
theres no trade. Simple economics. And if you think doing a course
would be false economics, thats perfect. If you think doing a course
would be a life changer; thats perfect. There is no destination without
 the source; kill the source and the destination is gone.

Namaste.

MF

posts.author: Ifmyante
posts.text:
I got a PM, probably today, from a member who's been trying for many
years to trade well. He admits he's still not got it, and gave me a list
 of his ideas for my advice

This is good stuff, and I want to share it

If you would be kind enough to advise me if I am at least close to the Golden Egg it would be appreciated.

1: There is no such system that is a "Holy Grail" ...full stop.

Wrong! The market is run by people who know what they're doing. They use
 a finite number of tools to trick retailers into offering orders up to
them. They use a finite number of algorithms to do their work for them.
In order to avoid chaos, they have rules they abide by (honour amongst
thieves)

Once you learn these tricks, how to spot these algorithms, and the rules
 they obey, you will be in the mind of the market makers, and you can
trade just as they do

2: I have played with indicators until I have worn them out, they are lagging in price and can not either predict or work.

Absolutely! The Market Movers know these indicators too!

3: PA together with Supply and Demand is king.

PA at important S/D S/R levels is key. Price history tells you which are important

4: Money Management is a top priority. No one can out run, predict or me smarter than the market.

Money management IS key. But it's not difficult to out run, predict and be smarter than the market

5: Always respect higher time frames in respect of placing trades on lower time frames.

Very true

6: If an acceptable set up is seen calculate the risk to reward ratio (this should be 3:1 at a minimum)

3:1 is a very very low number, but it's OK to begin with

7: Before entering in any trade make sure there is a bullish or bearish candle confirmation present.

Forget about candles. It's engulfs that are important

8: Place stop losses accordingly and and move to break even at the earliest opportunity.

This is a massive subject. But in essence: If you're not at the screen,
do put your stop losses beyond true S or D. But know that price will so
very often retrace to pick up extra orders. This leads on to your next
problem - the retrace is there to take out your break even. If you fear
the BE hunt, get out at TG1 and take the trade there again if the setup
looks good

9: Patience is a virtue (one area I fail in badly)

Amen to that!!!!

move price. They must also get massive amounts of orders filled in order

false signals, which could ultimately cause chaos for everybody.

Think of these things as you study, and you'll be able to get into the mind of the market mover

Hello Ifmyante, harshrthakkar,

I hope you don't mind me dropping in on this.

Harsh, perhaps try to think about who is doing what to whom, rather than
 what the patterns are - if you understand the mechanism behind the
movement of price you'll realise that the patterns themselves aren't as
important as what they convey. ITs need liquidity to enter and exit the
market, and they have the wealth to 'send signals' that manipulate
beliefs in retail traders and herd them into areas where they
effectively trade against the ITs... . Yes patterns do repeat and can be
 used as short-hand, and brains are great at spotting patterns, and ITs
know this, and that's why patterns repeat... .

(And just to misquote Mark Twain, "Patterns do not repeat themselves, but they sure do rhyme.".)

Here's my attempt at If's quiz, I'm not saying my observations are
correct (and they may even be completely wrong), but they show how I try
 to think when I'm looking at a chart. It is much much easier to give
reasons why price should have turned at an area when you already know
that it did, it's not so easy on the hard right edge (at least not for
me!), and we don't know what was going on before we see these patterns
(they may be reactions to Supply and Demand areas).

The notes are a bit jumbled but read them in numerical order:

Caveat lector!

Here's a PM I got this morning

Hey IF , got a little question I
was wondering about : "do you look at charts differently now than you
did back during your forexfactory times", meaning do you use new aspects
 now or did you always use the stuff you learned us ?

Since my first days at FF, I've been adding to my understanding of market dynamics.

Support and resistance was a great start, and then Supply and Demand added to it nicely.

Price action patterns became the next great tool.

By the time I wrote the Price Reading article, I had finished learning
all the technical aspects of the market, and was ready for the most
important part of Price Reading - understanding the mind and needs of
the IT.

This was the quantum leap that got me totally at one with the market.

I was no longer looking at the market in any technical manner, but,
having learned the rules the ITs live by, and the tricks they play on
retail traders, was able to simply trade as one of them.

So, to answer your question - when I look at the charts, I look at
exactly the same things I have taught in the fora, but I see them
through the eyes of the people who created them, rather than in the
abstract manner of a technical analyst.

The leap from analyst to Price Reader is a very simple one, and in RTM I've brought everyone right to the edge.

What I haven't taught publicly is that which I want you to understand for yourselves: the psychology behind price movement.

Some of you have taken that leap, and have landed right on top of the market. This has made me very happy and proud! :)

Hi Buddy, "I understand that an engulf involves price making a lower
low on reaction to Supply, or higher high on reaction to Demand" - This
can be correct, but it certainly is not always correct, actually most of
 the time it isn't correct. You need to find the important engulfs of
flags, it is when these happen that an engulf becomes meaningful. Simply
 making a higher high or lower low will not show you any intent.

Also understand that an engulf will achieve the same thing as a FO (in
terms of retailer trading behaviour) but it is the signal that price
wants to go to the next important level in the direction of the engulf. A
 FO is simply a ploy to trap traders once the signal engulf has already
happened.

Study up on flag limits, there has been some very good posting on them
recently, understanding the FL and the engulfs of the FL's along with a
HTF analysis and you will be able to tell the FO from the Engulf.

Sorry if that was a little bit of a mouthful,

Peds

It's a very long time since I posted my quiz.

On the topic for tonight's management meeting is why I haven't resolved
it yet, so I'd better get in here and answer it before I get a
rollicking :)

So let's get to it:

1. The leading IT engulfed price back up into the range (engulfed V), showing he was taking price up to the last FL above (U)

2. The other ITs, who had been short from high above, saw that price had
 turned, and wanted out of their shorts and into long positions.

So they sold against the retail breakout long trades

They will have Faked Out below a ltf demand (not visible in this tf),
scaring the BO buyers into selling at a loss, and enticing BO sellers,
giving them lots to buy

against and go net long.

3. A marker was set for future use

4. They turned price before the target, creating a supply which could be broken later

5. Price had been dropping for some time, attracting lots of retail
sellers; the IT's were eating these up bit by bit. It was obvious to the
 more savvy of the retailers that price was heading for W.
 So the natural thing to do was turn price before the tg, creating a
demand to be faked later. They buy heavily, taking all the herd's sells
and shooting price back up.

6. They removed their pending orders at 4, allowing price to break
supply. All the short retailers freak out and start closing by buying.
This allows the ITs to sell to them, beginning the process of going from
 long to short.

7. They begin to flag price downwards, adding little shorts as they
create LLs and LHs. This of course means a downtrend to the retailers,
so the retailers begin selling too

8. The Its want to be the only sellers, so they buy heavy into Supply
(U) shaking out the retail sellers and enticing BO buyers, all giving
them more to sell to

The retailers are getting frustrated by now. In the chop, there are lots
 of losers buying and selling all over the place, taking revenge trade
after revenge trade. With prices still making HHs and HLs though, very
many are still buying

Savvy SD retailers, however, are selling at 8, putting their stops above
 (U) (poor beggars!). As price rises through supply, these SD retailers
are adding to their shorts, delighted to get even better prices, and the
 ITs are happy to let them do so, because at

9. The ITs have either once again removed their pending short orders in
Supply, or have used them to tentatively buy against. By adding
different sizes of orders, they can now feel, by how price reacts to
their orders, who's in the market with them. They feel when the selling
pressure has dropped, and take this opportunity to buy just enough to
break the supply.

This hits the savvy SD retailers' stops and entices tons of BO buys,
giving them masses of buyers for the sells they're ready to make.
They're now heavily short.

10. They take some profit, creating a demand to be broken later

11. It's important that they bewilder every retailer out there; tire
them out completely so they have no idea what they're doing. So they
retrace price back up, breaking LTF supplies as they go, attracting more
 buyers. Price hasn't engulfed anything south yet, so the once savvy SD
retailers are buying too, trying to reclaim their losses. The ITs are
selling to them in bits, until they feel the buyers have dwindled enough
 for them to put in their next set of big shorts, breaking 10 at 12.

They buyers stops have hit, and the remaining BO sellers are getting in,
 giving the ITs a breather. They're heavily short, and happy.

13. We're at the SR of 4. ITs take a little profit, bouncing price up a
bit, breaking a LTF supply. This gets the retail sellers out, offering
more buys for the IT to sell to

14. It's the same story as 6 and 9

15. The FO to the Demand of the FL. It would be remiss of any IT not to
take full advantage of all the shorts on offer here, and cause some
midrange mayhem!

16. The engulf - time to flag

17. Create Supply before tg to be broken later

18. Inverse of 17

19. Chop for some confusion now and levels to be broken later

20. Sell to the BO buyers and SD sellers' stops

21. Lots more easy BO and stop orders to be snatched up. This is real
fun for the ITs, and is having little effect on their overall position
size in the big picture, until they want it to!

22. Catches lots more of the usual losers and fills the range

with, and constant support (there'll be support through all stages, of
course).

Should they thrive, that account will be doubled, and doubled again once ready, etc.

For the sake of our investors, our focus will be on preparing and
maintaining the most confident and most profitable traders imaginable.

posts.author: Ifmyante
posts.text:
I've been doing a lot of thinking about people who give up everything
to focus their lives on becoming traders, and have come to a very firm
conclusion:

A future in trading can be greatly compromised in the learning stage by needing to win to survive.

I'd advise everybody who's learning to trade to have a source of income
all the way through the process, and not to trade live until you're at
one with the market.

It's only once you're truly at one with the market that stress doesn't
come into your trading. You CAN become one with the markets by learning
in your free time.

A dead-end job is the perfect companion for a trading student. It pays
the bills, but once your shift is over, can be instantly forgotten. If
it's menial, all the better; you can daydream of your studies while you
work.

There's no stigma to be attached to it - it's an easy way to support yourself while you improve your life immeasurably.

Amit, I think technical analysis or Price action itself means that we
are following Institutional Investors. We are analyzing zones and
patterns (like QMs and diamonds) of the past ,which itself were created

Thanks IF,

But this brings about a couple more questions regarding PA and
stops. Now when it comes to levels and stops, I was always under the
belief that if a new level was created during active market hours within
 your zone, then that becomes your new trade/ risk area. A little
unwritten rule of thumb that I have myself is that at least a new 1hr,
30 min, or 15 min embedded zone has to be created for me to make that my
 NEW trade/ risk area upon revisit since higher TFs are more reliable.
Here is an example of a trade I took yesterday on the CADCHF.

1hr

4hr

As you can see, the trade I took was a plane jane trade that was simply
based off of the 4hr zone that cause the consumption of upper supply.
Since we were still clearly in an uptrend with a plausible 4hr target
overhead yet to be hit, I figured I would go for it even though we
didn't get the full engulf. The trade worked out fine, but in the LTFs,
 I watched the action develop, and a setup that I have always considered
 valid came up.

Here is the setup I'm talking about as previously mentioned in the first two paragraphs,

1hr

As you can see, there was a new 1hr demand zone that was created WITHIN
my 4hr zone during the active market hours. In my mind, this was a high
 probability trade which I would have probably taken on the retest if I
wasn't already in the trade. My logic for this is if a NEW 1hr demand
zone was created when pro money was active, then why have my stop beyond
 the original 4hr zone? Whey not enter on the retrace to the newly
created 1hr demand and have your stop below that? That is the same
logic I had in my EURGBP trade, so assuming we did get the proper PA and
 engulfed the 1min FO level, why would my stop still need to be below
the original zone you showed since this would have been a NEW 1hr demand
 zone within the 4hr demand??

The way I have always looked at it, playing PA to the right like this
increases RR and I have seen it work a hundred times before in my
studies. As for the TP, it would have stayed the same for me (the
'ultimate profit target' in the 4hr chart) since this was a new 30 min
or greater embedded demand zone. If this were just a newly created 15
min demand zone, I would have switched to 'intraday' mode and my
ultimate TP would have been more conservatively based upon the lower
4hr zone that caused the retrace.

Also, with regard to PA, I personally have a problem with
zooming all the way down to the 1min to check for the limits to be
engulfed because when you get down that low, it seems you can always
make a case (or a least most times) as to whey 'this' or 'that' 1min
zone is the reason price is being held down. It can just get very
messy, confusing, and paralyzing when you go down that low to look for
confirmation because there are rarely places in the chart where one will
 have a complete liquidity gap/ pole down to the 1 min. If I were to
scrutinize every trade I took to this level, well, I don't think I would
 ever take a trade because this is a perfect setup and the market rarely
 provides those in my eyes, which is why we have stops in the first
place.

Sorry for these long drawn out questions, but I feel these are key
issues I have been battling with for a while now without avail.

Long ago I gave up on the idea that the orders have literally been lying there since the move was made.

In the short term, sure it may be the case, but in the very long term, I think probably not.

That point is moot, however, as the orders tend to get put there before price arrives again.

When the ITs make trade plans, they look for levels to work from and to.
 They don't just target the middle of space to take profits and turn;
they look for a place with history.

Any IT worth his salt will always know where the main mover is taking price to.

It's simply a club. Don't forget that!
