posts.text:
I tried to take the exercise on and began to elaborate some scenarios.

NB: i had to reproduce IF's drawing and made a clean version of it i
join to the post in case other people want to use it for their scenarios

It made me realize something important that i missed.

I tried many times to spot engulfs into a FL (opposed to engulf of a
FL). But when doing that i was considering in the same way a break in
between two targets Inside the FL than a break in between the S/R kink
of the FL and the first iLS. This is a mistake, because by breaking S/R
kink and reaching first iLS, price reaches it's TG and therefore
validates a new UFL

Any break of that UFL is actually PA UP... So in that situation we
shouldn't expect price to retrace to the UFL we came from and then get
further into the LFL...

Lesson learned.

I have small question. When you have time, let me know your thoughts.

We usually mark our UFL/LFLs when price breaks a important level to the
left and then price its target. But sometimes price bounces at these FLs
 when it comes back to them or sometimes breaks FLs ignoring them. So we
 do not know exactly what FLs are with an importance which holds price
until price actually bounce at such FLs. May be we can guess the
important ones by looking at the approach.

Is it safe to consider a kink which hold a price up or down as a FL
without considering the levels it broke to the left(given that it hits
the target) I have shown these two cases below.

Image 1. shows where we consider a High(X) as an important level.
Breaking that and hitting the top HTF red FL will make the FL1. Then we
follow breaking of that FL and mark the FLs to the right and so on.

Image 2 shoes where we simply mark a kink(FL1) which held price up,
which hits target(Red HTF FL), then breaking these FL will create the
other FLs to the right. If we follow these two approaches, we will not
end up with the same set of FLs.

Another question is that, What is the important level in the first image
 X or what X is reacting to? So based on that, the FL1 in the first
image will be a different one too.

EURUSD

PinkPanther, Ysbail, dkd11, I am taking the risk of being accused of 'curve-fitting'.
 There is a saying that hindsight is always perfect, and if you look
hard enough, you will always find the exact reason that causes price to
turn.

I start with this visible swing low on H4, see point 1 on chart below:

you may argue that 1 is a reaction to FL-A, but most traders who doesn't
 understand FL would look at 1 and think that's a support and therefore
place buy orders there, therefore to break this swing low, it would
still require a significantly large sell order. That's why I went
searching for the FL that broke this swing low.

In chart below, I found the FL-B that broke below the swing low from
point 1. But I have also found several interesting elements:

I saw a smaller FL-C which breaks into the CPAZ, so this can be an important FL.

Then I saw a DP (green box) which delineated the upper edge of FL-B, and
 from my observations so far, in order to confirm PA to the north, we
need price to engulf not only FL-B, but also the DP that defined the
edge of it. If you think about it, even though we call FL-B a flag
limit, but on smaller scale it's actually a flag, and then the DP became
 the flag limit of Flag-B!.

Then I also saw a QM level inside FL-B, and I want to see what was responsible for breaking this QM level too.

Fast forward to 14 November 2017, where all of these elements were broken.

I see FL-C being engulfed by FL-D

QM-level being engulfed by FL-E

DP being engulfed by FL-F

So we now see how price reacting to each of these FLs.

Chart below showed price reacting to the upper edge of FL-F and bounced upwards

Then on 19 November, price plunged into FL-E and bounced upwards strongly

Then on 21 November, price hit FL-D twice, and the second time it 'almost' engulfed it.

posts.author: bobyv87
posts.text:
Its very difficult, if not impossible to give signals using RTM
reading way. Why? Because even the right level can be FOed. So, knowing
that, we always should have hard stops somewhere, but we don't wait for
the hard stop to be hit, instead, after price break our level (fail
level), we exit right at the next chance, when price bounce back to our
fail level so we can exit without loss. Now, imagine that every level
could have inside a few fresh orders. Would you wait always for MPLs
inside each levels? If yes, you will miss a lot of opportunities. Would
you wait lower than MPL? Maybe you wouldn't have the chance to exit at
BE if your level fails. So, you have to take quick decisions, even if
you have a good level and a good signal. At the same LSK IF can take a
BE or a small profit, but in the same time others can take losses.
Because of these multiple factors, its very difficult to do that. And
imagine how much pressure you can put on IF with that. However, i'm
planning to create a group of traders soon on the whatsapp, formed with
those who can participate at meetings daily and share our setups for
the day together so we can all benefit of our setups. :)

posts.author: Atari
posts.text:
We are our greatest enemy. The inner voice that is between our ears
manages to take over all the time, bombarding us with excuses, with
negative thoughts, shoot us down, telling us we cannot make
it....etc..... Unless, we are aware that it is the inner voice talking
and not us, then we can conquer and shut it up for the time being. It
will want to come back and it is our job to notice it and shut it up
again. When you catch it and shut it up, eventually, it will lose its
grip on your mind. It is not gone, but it loses its power over you.

Yes, RTM is a puzzle and you will have to put the puzzle together
yourself here. Trading is not easy, but it is simple, once you get it.
 If trading is easy, then your garbage collector will be doing it too
and you will not have anyone to pick up your garbage every week or day
from your house.

If Thomas Edison gave up on the 100th trial of creating a light bulb, do
 you think we will have a light bulb today? Thomas Edison had more than
 1000 trial and error before you was able to invent the light bulb. If
 Steve Job and his team decided it was too difficult to create an
Ipod/Ipad after months working on it, do you think we will have an
Ipod/Ipad today.

Success takes hard work and a spirit not to quit, no matter what
obstacles are in front of us. You fall down, you get up, you fall down,
 you get up, you fall down you get up. We all forget that we are all
champions when we were a baby. We all forgot that. Remember, when you
were a baby learning how to stand and walk. When you fell down, you got
 right back up and try again and again and again, until you were able to
 walk and then run after. You did not tell yourself then, when you were
 a baby that it was too hard to learn to walk. You just got right back
up and went at it until you got it. What makes you any difference now?
 It is your inner voice that is between your ears. You are listening
to the negative messages it is feeding you. That is the difference.

If you truly want to become a trader, then you must realize that and
conquer it. Here is a question for you to ponder at. "If trading is
the only thing I am committed to do, what would I do differently today?"

Let me give you a story... A long time ago, there was a war between 2
countries. The captain was given 100 men to sail on his wooden ship to
the enemy shores and take over that area. The enemy had 1000 men
waiting for them. As soon as the captain landed and his men disembarked
the wooden ship, the captain burned the ship. His men were left with
the message, 'you can either choose to die here or defeat your enemy and
 live. His men did not have the comfort of retreating back to their
ship for it has been burned. So either die at the enemy shore or defeat
the 1000 men and take over and live. His 100 men at the end defeated
the 1000.enemies.

So if you come to RTM with that kind of mentality, your chances of success is much greater.

You all know that we do have RTM Academy, which we put the puzzle
together for you so that you don't have to spend thousands of hours
trying to figure it out yourself. Even inside the academy, the students
 there have to roll up their sleeves and work hard on the lessons and
assignments and learn how to think critically and apply their analytical
 skills. While the price tag may cause some of you to shy away from it, I
 can for certain say that the value you will get from the Academy will
easily overshadow the price tag once you graduate from the Academy.

I look forward to hearing from the Masters but my opinion is the reaction from D's failing to reach E creates a brand new pocket of IT orders. We know there are orders down at B (or E). When price revisits a little deeper into B in the first chart, it is reacting from the orders in that zone and that zone proves to have enough demand to break FL A.

Because the move was strong enough to break D, we know there are leftover orders at this new Decision Point. This DP also sets up a really good FO zone to trick retail. I think the leftover orders and of course the ability to catch retail stops is what makes price go deeper than FL F.

A broken level does not mean an ignored level Just because a level breaks it does not mean it has been ignored. Sorry to jump like this into discussion, Astro. I had the same problem understanding the ignored levels but i think right now i know the answer to this one. Some masters can confirm, of course.

Before you go looking

for every LS/QM or whatever it is, you have to look into what that LS is a reaction to. If your point 1 is a reaction to something like 2, then your point A ( the iQM) it is very insignificant. If you don't get your scale right in cases like this, i think you can't expect running trades, but only just small bounces and that is alright for scalping. Another thing: you want for your bigger scale LS to ties in with lower scale MPLS. These are the best levels to trade from on a touch trade, so basically, that point 2 which is HTF thing, it could align perfectly with an MPL inside your B zone. In this case, if you want to TT your first target would be inside B, and after that you will hope to fill the symmetry with B and maybe with my bigger grey box. However, that bigger grey box could be a FL in making, but it have to reach a target first, so basically the retrace could go even lower, and there is a lot to ask if you want a symmetry with the entire box. Now lets say you want a trade at your point A, and that point is reaction to my point 2, could you TT on it? Well, it could be possible, but you have to manage your expectation, because you are in the middle of things. posts.author: Spongiform

Hello in2forex,

When you hit some stumbling blocks it can actually be more productive to just walk away and do something else. Not focusing on a problem directly moves it from conscious to subconscious and that can be a more powerful and creative tool for problem solving. Scientists have even proven (finally) that walking helps problem solving - the issue at hand is there, but it's not prioritised - the chains are off that wonderful subconscious....

It seems that trading is full of stumbling blocks, no matter how far along the road you think you are! Matters aren't helped by the fact that it's based on probabilities - you can be right and lose money, and you can be wrong but make money. The contrary feedback from these two entirely different scenarios doesn't help you when you are trying to learn what is right-thinking and what is wrong-thinking.

Even if you spend many hours investigating Price Action on the left (an absolute must), it doesn't necessarily convert into success at the hard right edge. But it is definitely one of the building blocks of success. If you're having trouble at the hard right edge now it might pay you to go back to the left.

I don't know how you think through or solve problems, but it's usually best to identify them, state them, and break them down bite sized chunks to be solved. You will have noticed that this is a major part of how I approach things - it's got me this far, but I really am struggling with the next bit right now

. I also don't know what draws your

attention when you look at a chart: if several people look at the same chart, they will all see different things! For instance:

1. Do you notice the peaks and troughs as price zigs and zags or do you just notice the general direction that price takes over time? 2. Do you notice horizontal levels where price reacts or do you notice diagonal lines? 3. Do you notice spikes from levels or clusters at levels?

Knowing what you automatically key in to might be the first step in working through your stumbling block. When reading others' journals remember that although everyone is pretty much doing the same thing here, they may describe it differently, and each may arrive at the same point by different paths: that is a reflection of those different thought processes we each have. You might find one person's way confusing because you just don't see things their way and you might gel with another's because you do! It might be that as your experience and knowledge grow the first person's way becomes more obvious! There is no right or wrong to this (all views are valid if they are long-term profitable) you just have to find and stick with what works for you and grow from there -another of those building blocks for success.

If you don't know what you key in to try what I did way way back. I took charts and drew 'random' lines on them (knowing I would necessarily apply some element of judgment: brains aren't good at random, they are pattern seekers). I looked at what converged on those lines. I rinsed and repeated this several times until I confirmed that I was generally identifying the same things each time. Then I built from that.

Hopefully there's something of use here, but good luck and good hunting.

Regards.

Spongy.

Hello in2forex,

I thought I might pitch in seeing as you mentioned you were struggling with Compression. This is my take on it so it probably isn't "according to Hoyle", keep your pinches of salt to hand

Compression usually happens at the end of a Momentum Move (or some sort of main move). Buyers or sellers have thrust price - unopposed - in their chosen direction (either because they had the strength to overwhelm the opposition or the opposition was sorely lacking (each can have different implications)). Eventually they reach an area where opposition slowly increases - the Momentum Move is over but inertia (read late buying or selling) sees price continue in the same direction. The strength is slowly sapped out of this incursive move until there is none left and the opposition can now push price in their direction....

Compression should be self-defeating, that's why it's thought of as a leading 'indicator' as price approaches Supply or Demand. What you see is the law of diminishing returns in effect: each successive thrust depletes orders to support the move, sees less distance covered for the same effort, and drives price deeper into opposition, perhaps even convinces opposition they are witnessing increasing weakness so attracting more of the same. The very shape (wedge-like) expresses Compression!

But it is not really Compression (in the sense it is meant in RTM) until price can close within its confines - that is, we do not know whether it is consumption of orders or rejection of 'cheap' prices, until we know

. That is, price could just as easily

'compress' into Supply or Demand and then drive straight through it (there are many variables at play here).

Also, that price is likely to be turned back at the last place of strength (i.e. the transition from Momo to Compression) implies the beginning of ranging and perhaps a continuation of price in the same direction as Momo, but as with all things it doesn't have to be this way.

Compression examples (please note that a little poetic licence was used

):

What you were seeing on EURUSD is a Flag. There are some similarities and many differences between a Flag and Compression:

1. Both occur at the end of Momo (or some form of main move)

2. Compression continues with the Momo whereas the Flag goes against it, because... 3. Compression occurs going into opposition Supply or Demand whereas a Flag occurs after hitting it 4. This also means that when Compression eventually hits Supply or Demand it is still fresh whereas the Flag has already started depleting it, so... 5. On retracing through Compression price is likely to be turned back at the last place where strength was shown whereas once a Flag has completed its pull back (to a source from which the Momo or main move can continue) it is likely to drive through its own extreme and continue with the main move 6. But, the transition from Momo to Compression is a base of strength which might lead to support ranging, and that might lead to a continuation of the main move, so in the end the outcome might be the same for both Compression and Flag even though the mechanism is different 7. Both deplete orders within their structures, removing obstacles to any move through them 8. Oh, and Compression is generally wedge-shaped whereas Flags form equidistant channels

EURUSD Flag:

Remember: learner driver, so caveat lector! But I hope this helps all the same.

Regards.

Spongy.

Hello in2forex,

Unfortunately there always seems to be fun when it comes to interpreting patterns, or even naming them. Mine is my way based on what I saw in the Compression Homework section when I first visited, reinforced by my many visits to Redsword11's PIE forum on Forex Factory (950 pages and still going...).

I haven't been into the Compression Homework section for a long while but I noticed there is now a PDF at its start, it's instructional:)

Compression.pdf

There are several examples that agree with your definition, but there's one specific one (on page 19, showing both structures on one chart, but you might want to start reading the text from page 16 as well) which highlights all the difference for me - it's from Redsword11.

As I say, there are several similarities between Compression and Flags, not least that as each rises to Supply (or falls to Demand) it absorbs buy (sell) orders, creating weakness within its structure, allowing price to move through it with relative ease (if that is the direction that price then takes). But there are important differences which prepare us to anticipate different Price Action after we see them: after Compression price might range in a PAZ before making its next move (possibly continuing in the same direction as the main move); after a Flag price might just shoot through and continue on in what's called a measured move (the first 'CP' example in your chart above shows this, so does Redsword11's example on page 19).

It's a shame that Redsword11's example doesn't capture what happened after the CP, but there are other examples from page 20 onwards which not only blur the definition of Compression but show price ranging after it. None of these things is set in concrete, and anything can and will happen - it's all about the next candle! And, of course, reference time-frame is important, so while your H1 example shows two Flags (as I would call them), they are part of a larger structure on H4 and D1 (in this case a range). It's sometimes difficult to decide what you're seeing and what you should pay most attention to....

In the end, as long as you know what you mean by Compression, and what you anticipate could happen after, that's what matters most.:)

Putting all that to one side, I'm not entirely sure I understand what you mean when you say your "main challenge is very often what looks like compression to me on the HTF doesn't translate to compression in the LTF". If I've understood the challenge correctly (and I'm probably very wide of the mark), then if you see Compression on some HTF (spiking into Demand as price rises, for instance), all you do on LTF is check whether ever higher Demand areas are being created in the shadows of those HTF spikes and that all these stacked Demands have been tested. There will be a lot of other detail down here, but your focus should be on the structure you saw on HTF.

So:

Regards.

Spongy.

posts.author: Spongiform
posts.text:
Hello in2forex,

One thing I've learned as time passes, is don't sweat the detail too much (a terrible thing for an engineer to contemplate, let alone say). Price Action is rarely going to be perfect, so if you have a directional bias and you see a road block, that will be your TP1. If you can't get good R: R to this from your chosen opportunity to enter, then it's failed your quality filters - drop it and move on.

The occasional fresh Demand is an occupational hazard of Compression, and we don't know whether it will be respected or disregarded when price gets there. For the EURUSD example - if you could have found an area to get in with good R: R - that fresh Demand level was an obvious point for TP1.

When I saw that particular Demand area print I thought it would be a great area to get long at (which is why it was an obvious TP1 if you were looking to short), but because it was in a Flag I was only thinking of shorts. When I step back and take in the D1, that whole structure is not much in the grand scheme of things - of course it was going to go up....

Regards.

Spongy.

posts.author: in2forex
posts.text:
Hi KBG

Very valid question, it shows me that you are really looking at the market in total. Concentrating on entries and exits are both as important as the other, the only difference for me is that when in a trade different aspects of emotions start to play on your mind. Learning to control these, is as important as choosing a good entry or exit. Enough rambling.

To answer your question, i'm going to run through the process I went through in making the trade As I have mentioned previously in my journal, I have had to change the way I trade due to other commitments which have reduced my chart time to almost zero.

This trade was based on a total of about 5 minutes of screen time.

Entry: On Friday morning I open about 5 pairs of charts all HTF and flicked through them looking for something to jump out at me. On the GBPJPY I saw the Cap and compression (A good looking can can in development). I drew in some rectangles noticing the ENG (1) and the FL(3) set my PO at that level and my stop loss above a higher FTR which you can see in the LTF). At this point I was only interested in a reaction and price falling through the CP. I didn't set a TP. I thought I'll check on the trade later during the day just before NFP new which was due out at about 14h30 my time. As it worked out I never got a chance to look at the chart again until after the market had closed on Friday night. When I did open the chart I notice the PO had been triggered and the reaction to my entry was perfect, price had reached the FTR you mention in your chart. I would have loved to exit then and I was kicking myself for not setting a TP. I couldn't do anything as the market was closed. Exit:: I thought of waiting for the market to open and then exit the trade but this was a demo trade (sleep was a reasonable priority) so I thought let me let it run. When I woke up I check the chart, price had engulfed up. I then did something I try avoid, I looked at the trade profit and that was a good enough reason to exit considering I wasn't able to manage the trade on a real time bases.

So in conclusion the exit of this trade was based on emotion and not PA. In the past my general strategy has been to exit a trade when I'm confident to take a trade in the opposite direction based on PA. Due to my current screen time limitations I can't do this now. So I'm having to change how I trade. This is just another learning curve on the journey to success.. I'm still struggling with the emotional stress when in a trade and often find myself looking at the profit, hence why I'm trying to avoid this.

Sorry for the long post, hope it helped. Now I need to get back to work.

posts.text:
Hi,

Below is the 4hr chart, and the supply zone that I will be using – the year is 2004 for anyone interested in looking at this on their own platforms.

Below is the 30 min TF and this is the chart that I will be looking to see how the ITS played/manipulated P.A to suit their accounts.

1. Price heavily broke the RN collecting lots of buy orders from stopping traders out who were attempting to fade the RN. The ITS not happy with the RN LQ they decided to engulf the small FTR that can be seen in history. This would have given the ITS not only a ton of buy orders to see into from stopping out traders who were fading the upper FTR, it would have also enticed BO traders on the LTFs to go long, once they were nicely long, the ITS reversed price and stopped them out also collecting a load of sell orders to help push price down.

2. Where would I have thought price will react, the next demand… The ITS know this, so with me having my order placed neatly at the demand zone and the stop just beneath, the ITS sell into this demand completely engulfing it collecting mine and probably millions of others stops which gives the IT’S A nice load of sell orders to buy into.

So as Harry suggested, here is my understanding of order flow and topics connected to it. It is more of a simple explanation, than an article. But i hope i can help someone with it. Everyone are welcome to criticize, or add something i forgot.

In trading we use two types of order. Market orders and limit orders. Market orders move the price, while limit orders provide liquidity. Lower is a table, which i will use for explanation of movement in the markets. Prices are taken from EUR/JPY. Size of orders is in lots. In real time there are a lot more limit orders and the difference between the prices and orders is smaller, but i simplified it, so it is easier to explain. In the orange part of the table we have offers(sell limit orders), in green part we have bids(buy limit orders). Two prices with gray background are best offer and best bid. You can see this information in upper left corner of MT4, if u have one click trading enabled. As we can see, in this example our spread is 2 pips.

As i mentioned market orders move the market. So for the price to move up to 140.10, a trader(or more of them) have to enter the market with market order at the size of 50 lot. If we want lower prices, we need sell market orders with the size of 80 lots, for a move to 139.90 and 90 lots, for a move to 139.75(in this case we would sell 80 lots at 139.90 and 10 lots at 139.90).

Example 1: If someone with big pockets would buy 300 lots of EJ, price would go up to 141.15(first 50 lots would get a fill at 140.02, next 20 at 140.10, next 80 lots at 140.25 and so on, all the way to the top) and only 5 lots would be left at that level.

So from this understading we get explanation why liquidity gaps happen. For example IT(institutional traders) are entering the market with HUGE sell market order. So price moves down, consuming all buy limit orders, until all positions of ITs are filled and price settles.

Us, the retail traders have one big advantage comparing to professional money. We get a fill at every price we desire to enter. So even if i enter with big position(our big position is nothing comparing to ITs), i will get a fill at the price i enterted, no matter what. That is not true for ITs, what makes their job a little trickier, which takes me to our next topic.

FAKEOUT

There is a topic about FO in the forum, if someone wants to see many examples on how FO looks. Bellow i have random illustration of price movement. In green square we have a FO. Many times we see it as a spike, but it can also look like illustration in purple square(just imagine that instead of green square, there would be purple), or any other shape.

So lets take a deeper look, what is happening and why on the provided image. Price is getting closer to supply in blue square and comes to supply at 1. ITs want to sell huge volume here, but they have 2 problems. First is the lack of liquidty, so if they would just enter the market with all the orders, they would cause liquidty gap, and not all the orders would get a fill at the price where supply is, but at a lot worse prices. Second problem is that many other retail traders also want to sell here with them, since we are in supply. So what is the solution for this problem? They let other traders to sell(many of them put stop loss just above previous high). Then ITs drive the price up(no.2 on the chart). Here price hits SL from the traders i mentioned before, transforming their sell positions to market buy orders. Also the breakout traders start buying. But if there is so many buy orders, why it doesn't cause liquidty gap up? Because ITs are waiting with their sell limit orders, so they get a fill at good price. If FO would look like the one in the purple square, also trend following traders would start to buy, because of higer lows(no.4) and the traders who have a feeling, they will miss the move, also come on board. Here is also perfect place for ITs to unload buy orders from lower levels. After this, they push the price down(no. 3). Price hits SL of many long traders creating even more sell orders, adding more fuel to the fire, so price falls even harder.

posts.text:
Ok, I think a definition of ITs is in order. Some call it Pro Money, I like to call it Big Money. Now I could be wrong about what the Official RTM definition of an IT is. But in my view is that all these different names are the same. Now to the important point.

Who are they? Or better yet who is THE biggest FX player in the world? The answer is quite obvious if you think about it. It is the United States Federal Reserve Bank. Yes, the same people that issue the FOMC reports and such that create large FX volatility. They basically own the market along with all the other Government banks around the world. These are the top tier Institutional FX players. Below them are the other large banks around the world. They in turn help facilitate large corporate and private institution transactions. And below all of this is the Retail Market. (My view of all this may not be 100% correct so feel free to correct me)

The important thing to remember is that WE in the retail market have ZERO visibility as to what they are doing. EXCEPT for PRICE. They are the ONLY significant movers of price. The retail brokers mark their rates and spreads based upon the feeds that they get from above. There is no visibility of volume sizes above the retail market. The volume information, Bid ASK order sizes that we can get are only retail and specific to a brokers capability.

In my Journal posts #64 and #66 I attempted to describe the actions of the BIG Money or ITs.

I hope that this helps this discussion.

Onwards and upwards!

Before I start trying to attempt to describe the numbered sections, I just want to point out that I pre-marked the FL on the chart, there is not description as it is what it is.

1. If we look across to the right, we should see the RN figure.3400, now look what P.A did when it arrived there, we had a nice spike, the ITs clearly wanted the stops waiting just above the RN. Now these stops were not just from traders who were trying to fade the level, thus giving the ITs buy orders which to sell into, there were also BO buyers around this level too, who would have been unaware of the HTF supply above, this would give the ITs more LQ, sell orders which enabled the ITs to push price up more into HTF supply.

2. Number 2 we see a nice pin bar again in HTF supply, a nice short, and again would have worked if one had the balls to hold through the chop! Ok, depending on where the retail traders entered, be it the pin or a little lower waiting for the confirmation part of the pin bar (the next bar), we will see what happens @ 3.

3. The pin bar traders would have been happily short FOR A WHILE. Don’t forget though we have the RN just below the pin also. The ITs here have clearly decided to kill two birds with one stone, fake the RN and collect the buy orders from trader who were short on the LTFs at the RN and also distort the original traders who were short at the pin bar @ supply. The traders who were short @ the pin may be experienced and know where we are in the HTFs and expect some pull back, but the traders who are unaware will start panicking and as most know, panic is not a trader’s best attribute! What do we do when we panic, we get scared! Once we are scared, we do things we would not do when we are thinking rational and using logic, the ITs here are playing with this! Thus a ton of traders are closing their trades at a small win/B.E or even worse a small loss. So from this small move the ITs have not only collected buy stops from the original shorts at the pin bar, but also all those poor souls shorting the RN on the LTFs.

4. Once the ITs have manipulated enough traders, a bigger move happens south, and where does it go to? The next fresh demand, we know this is the most fresh demand left as we have seen all the smaller demands spiked. This move would have attracted a lot of retailers seeing the momentum south on the LTFs, some or most of them were probably unaware of the FL below which would need to be consumed before going any lower. The ITs sold into this FL knowing full well a lot of people would follow suit. Also, please don’t forget about the RN in all of this. So, the ITs buy, and buy quite hard collecting all of the buy stops off of all those LTF traders short the momentum, and again on the LTFs traders would have seen the RN break, and I am betting they would try to short the return as I would do before, the ITs clearly know this will happen too, so there buying took out not only the momentum sellers’ stops, but also all the LTF stops at the RN, superb if you’re an IT! Not so good if you’re one of the retailers getting thrown left, right and centre.

5. All the ITs work is done, they have enough LQ now to short this pair, and on a personal note, this would have been an even better entry if @ number 4 we engulfed that FL, but all we did was consume some of the orders. Do you see what happened though, look at the arrow, notice the tail, this was finishing the job of the consumption of buys there.

For me there was no trade here, would anyone of traded this type of P.A and if so, how?

Right above the pin bar, because for us who have studied pin bars where are we taught to put our stops??? A few pips above the wick! Beautiful. So with all those traders now stopped out, and a ton of buy stops are available for them to sell into, the ITs can go to the next demand.

My next example.

Something I have noticed a lot with my logs is that the ITs really like to use the RNs around HTF levels for a LQ boost to move price around.

4hr chart below, I have chosen a swap zone this time.

And below is the 30 min TF

A quick observation, price did not actually even reach the swap zone, it was shy a few pips, but I will still continue to analyze.

1. ITs are buying hard here, and like a few of my other logs, it is no surprise as to why. Strong buying into a HTF level, meaning a lot of LTF traders will be following suit, what I mean by this is plenty of traders would see the momentum and buy, the ITs know this. The ITs have also engulfed the RN.1900 which would contain a lot of buy stops, notice the wicks above the candles at the top of the move; I presume this is the ITs beginning to sell into all those buys.

2. Now we have nearly touched the HTF swap level and the selling begins, soaking up all those buy orders and stopping out some of the retail who were following closely with a stop collecting some sell stops in the process. As before in my previous logs we see price manipulating the RN around the HTF level, stopping out a load of traders who were going long on the retest, this gives the it’s a load of sell stops to sell into for the push up

3. Price rallies through the RN again stopping out a load of LTF traders shorting the retest of the RN, this gives the the ITs buy stops to once again sell into for the push down, by now the ITs have loaded quite a few short orders in the market, whilst confusing a ton of retail in the process.

4. The ITs can see a small demand below that will need to be consumed before taking it further south, so they push price into demand, once again trapping a lot of BO sellers, and traders selling because of the HTF swap. What do we retailers do? We place our stops where the ITs know, just above the high. So with this in mind the ITs push price back up using the BO sellers buy stops to help the process.

Look at that FO above where all of us retailers would have our stops, that wick has stopped so many traders out, and given the it’s a lot of buy stops to sell into for the final load of orders they put on the market. posts.author: HotRod
posts.text:
We are told the reason the markets exist is to give value to an instrument. All the market participants with interest in an instrument come together to give the correct value to that instrument. This may have been true in the 1600s, but now this is a bunch of BS and assumes everyone obeys the law and follows exchange rules.

If everyone had the same access to the same information, then the market would truly be random because price could then only reflect all the differing opinions about that information. But what about information that would have an obvious effect on price? If everyone had the same opinion then the market would be "broken" because no one would want to take the other side of the trade. But where is the profit in that? If the true reason the markets exist is to find value, then they would make information freely available. They don't do that because the markets wouldn't work. The markets only exist so the people at the top of the money chain stay on top.

Information is the most valuable commodity in this world and is kept in the closest of circles until it can be used for profit. The people who have it are the ones at the top of the worlds industries, and the banks that hold and loan them their money. You also have to include top governmental positions (financial) since the people who hold them are usually "experts" that were CEOs and such. These people have relationships with each other and we would be extremely naive (American public) to believe they don't use that for their own gain.

One of biggest things I took away from the book Trading and Exchanges is the concept of informative prices. Prices become informative when informed traders trade. Now this doesn't really help us take a position because there is no way of knowing when these traders are trading. But the concept does allow us to form a better view of the markets participants.

There are 3 types of traders: informed traders, uninformed traders, and uninformed traders who believe they are informed.

Informed traders: These traders have information that will effect the real world supply and demand, and are able to take positions in the instrument's market before the information has its effect. In the forex market it would be things like interest rates and policies, or major changes in a country's leading industry. This can also be the banks holding the order book, friends and family who were given tips, or people who are able to use a chart to see where these informed traders are taking positions.

Uninformed traders: People who just trade as a hobby, gamblers, News traders, people who only watch the right edge of the chart and trade off emotions.

Uninformed who believe they are informed: Pretty much anyone who gets their "education" from a book. You know, indicator traders, system traders. would throw people who subscribe to these news agencies here as well since they usually end up getting fleeced. Some of these people probably make money, but most don't.

The idea here is that if the market was only made up of informed traders, then they would never be able to take a position. If all the informed traders know the same bullish information, then none of them are going to sell. This is where uninformed traders come in. So, how do they entice enough people to take the other side of their trades? First they put the perception out there that there is all kinds of money to be made in the stock market. (Economics class anyone? Ok that may be too far, but i doubt it. I'd say they have connections to the gov. positions that develop the curriculum) Then they herd us like a bunch of cattle. They know humans feel safer when in groups, and if they can get enough people following a certain way of thought, then others will follow.

So what do they use to herd us into groups so they can profit from us?

Scheduled news releases with the CNBCs of the world to make people feel informed is probably the biggest. I'm going to guess the second biggest way is with all the "education" out there. I believe the material constantly being put out there comes from these same informed traders, either through straight up funding for it or some other way. But even if not, its out there, and can be used to fill their orders. How long has S/R been out there? Since Wyckoff in the 30s? Earlier? What about trend? Trend lines? All the different patterns that are taught and where to enter on them? And lots more. The stronger the following each "herding tactic" has the more profitable it is for the informed traders. The market mechanics of S/R is there yes, but it isn't going to have that strong of effect on the market, when it works its because the informed ITs are behind it. Yes it all works sometimes, until it doesn't. It serves two purposes, first to fill their orders and then to save them money when moving price to their take profit positions. What do all the educators preach? You have to trade it EVERYTIME and use good money management. All of this is herding. And don't forget that evil little ticker on the hard right edge for all the emotions. That gets manipulated as well, and always right into informed traders orders.

Informed traders are always going to stick together. They are out to make as much money as they can. And they aren't going to make much money by battling each other. They want the easiest prey possible, and the prey will always be uninformed. Whether they use their "herding tactics", or whether they want to "eat" their own and feed them some bad information, either way they are uninformed. There is always a battle, but the informed will always know they are going to win.

Vogon, on your chart the sellers were informed, and the buyers weren't. Simple I know, but its best that way. Any thing else and your head will become clouded with unneeded thoughts which will lead to frustration. We can paint any picture really, because there is honestly no way of knowing. And being on the weekly chart it coulda been a central bank with bad information, or maybe some uninformed ITs. This was back in 07/08 when all the economic trouble began. Look where it peaked. It peaked in Nov of 07, so whoever it was had their info at that time and started selling. Any bullish info put out between that peak and the drop was all manipulation to fill their orders and trap the buyers.

If you have ever read reminiscences of a stock operator, then you know Jesse Livermore made a killing off of the drop that caused the great depression. He traded by being able to read the ticker tape and knowing when the market was being manipulated, then jumping in with the manipulators. We would be very naive to think that it no longer gets manipulated.

So how can we profit from all this? I'm still working on that

Knowing all

this is great, but on the hard right edge the informed traders and uninformed traders are ever evolving and changing. The market environment is never the same with there being times when there are tons of news coming out, and other times when there is a news drought. Especially in forex since there isn't as many news events. This is why its seen as being a more technical market, they need someone to fill their orders. There is also the issue of time frames. The informed traders on the HTFs may or may not be the same ones on the LTFs.

In times of news droughts and on the LTFs the only real informed traders I can think of are the market makers. The people who can see the limit order book and know where the big orders are is the LTF uninformed traders enemy. But even he has weaknesses because he can only see limit orders, he doesnt know what market orders are going to come in and endanger his position. There could be a large IT out there who hits the market with a big market order to test a price level to see how dense the orders are there.(i believe this is one explanation for the engulf.) There are multiple market makers in the forex market in each instrument. They compete to provide liquidity to the uninformed traders. They don't have to provide liquidity if they don't feel they will make money on it. (only the NYSE specialists have to provide when they don't want to, and they can just widen the spread to protect themselves.) So if the market makers believe they have an informed trader entering the market they will just sit on the sidelines. If they were wrong the worse that happens is a competitor makes money and they don't. If they believe there are uninformed traders entering the market they will happily provide liquidity because they know chances are they will be in profit very shortly. I don't know the tactics the market makers use to discern the difference, but that is our job as well. I would say they can tell by how the orders come in or maybe make deals to get info.

Just by thinking about the tactics that uninformed traders use, and knowing how the informed traders use those tactics against them should give us a way to piece together the story of price. If we know where uninformed traders are going to put their orders, and we know that informed traders need those orders to trade, then we know where the battle is going to take place. If price doesn't do what the uninformed trader expected and he lost then there is a good chance an informed trader was active there, and then we just use the tools that IF and the gang have taught us and that will tell us to take action or stay on the sidelines. If price does do what the uninformed trader expected, then the informed trader sees an opportunity for more profit.

When I get time I want make a chart showing how I see it, but its late and im tired. GL trading today everyone!!!

Ifmyante wrote: We will, however, battle with the monsters, and we will win, without darkening our souls a shade

I definitely agree that for ITs using algo's, programmed by their intentions and rules definitely relieves them of time and imprecision. Though i would just like to point out, basing on my recent research, using algo's doesn't necessarily mean HFT (High Frequency Trading) as it is very commonly believed now a-days. A light speed trading they call it, and the ones that have planted their asses the closest to the trading terminal, have the fastest execution. Why would you fight for nano seconds?

As i see, most of these highly technically educated people are very brilliant at working out the best codes for taking the profit out of the market. Though from what i have read and understood, their mindsets ONLY understand the markets microstructure and mostly just opt to gain return with tactical tricks.

Common practice is them offering liquidity to other manual traders, entering with a market order. Once the HFT's pending order is filled, they close it in a split of a second, just to profit on the spread the retailer has paid to get into the trade. Ofcourse there are psychological tricks that go around these liquidity offering twists, but nothing is intended for a longer period of investing.

That is where the tight spreads come from! HFTs competing between each other and getting fees just for supplying liquidity to dealers.

Simply put, there is no long term strategy HFTs live by. A tactic is hardly successful if it isn't sufficiently applied within some bigger/higher-picture plan. Plan being the engulfing signals and other.

Now, if u get a trader that understands the basics of HFT codes and the strategy, you get a golden boy, who can program and hugely lessen all the needed work and especially the risk. ~~~

Imagine: We hava a buying range. creting compression and a consistent buying in small lots is requiered,before we give a signal to break out and advance to next level. Doing it manually, well...:P Its exhausting, to say the least. I know i would program the algo, tu buy small lots with market orders on the way up of the range, and just let the algo put pending longs, while price is retracing within a move. (If there is a scenario to break long.)

Big orders don't get a fill, and even more, you dont want to bust open the range, and bring confusion to other ITs faces, while they are happily loading their cargo. (I believe there are even upper lot limits for market orders, with some brokers.

~~~ This is very interisting article that sheds light on alot of what HFTs are considered to be! www.forbes.com/sites/richardfinger/2013/...aders-and-investors/

These topic has been hot since 2010 the FLASH crash. Contemplating wether these algos are of risk to the stability of market! From what i read, people kept unplugging their sweet HFTs algos as they in horror observed DOW plunging. That way they created volatility, price droped presumeablly to a targeted level and resumed back up! (I havent checked since i got no DOW with my broker.)

Those in-the-moment-profit guys, considered it risky since they had no clue what was going on, and with such speed of price droping, their light speed pending longs would not get the return either. They dont even want to think about the loss scenario, due to over laveraging....

From my understanding, price has simply pushed to target and retraced. Driven by the IT traders (or algos), that were fully aware of the target for retrace. Long term strategy won again.:D

Morning Everyone,

For a while now already I have been obsessed to get myself to think like an IT. Yesterday after I called it a day and especially due to IF’s comment on the charts; “think like an IT, think like an IT, think like an IT…” was playing over and over in my head even when I was asleep!

This morning, while I was preparing to start analyzing Area 5 (In my Journal), my mind asked a set of questions:

1- Is it possible that a five year old area would still hold left over orders?

2- If I were an IT, would I have left pending orders there for so long? Especially that the framework in the mix of fundamental, geopolitical, economical, financial… etc... climate was surely different?

3- If the answer to the above questions is yes, wouldn’t brokers, market makers, liquidity providers and what have you, make a killing by just charging for those pending orders? (Just imagine the accumulated returns on a certain five year old level)

4- Wouldn’t we know about such interest payment requirements?

Certainly after more such questions we come to the conclusion that it has to be a definite “NO” for the first two above.

Ok…. So hypothetically, why would a five year old level react the way it does? It must be NEW orders there then. But what’s there? Older levels… hmmmm

Now at this point and due to my previous career, I shifted my thought process back into the corporate world. Isn’t that what ITs are really? So they must think in terms of Daily, Weekly, Monthly, quarterly, semiannually & annually…. With cycles in between, some longer others shorter.

Now let’s step out of our trading shoes for a while and think in terms of consumerism. Imagine I was an avid car collector and Bugatti was giving away free Veyrons, with the only requirement to get one being to stand in line and waiting your turn. How long do you think the Q will be by the time I get there? Will there be enough cars left by the time I get there? Will the plant have enough cars to satisfy all the demand? At what point will the manufacturer start pricing the product again? On the other hand imagine if that same product was priced at 1 trillion, would there be any demand for it? Supply? Parts? After Sale Customer service?

So there is a tipping point isn’t there i.e. a shift from when something is considered a bargain to when it becomes a rip-off. But between these two points are more stages such as, too cheap, cheap, average, expensive and too expensive.

The same applies to our charts. The charts show us how the buyers and sellers behaved at a certain time in the past. This is translated through price action and does not mean that because there were lots of buyers at a certain base or level that that pattern will repeat. It just means there is high probability of a reaction in the buyers’ favor.

Our study here at RTM is not about picking tops and bottoms, it is about following along the path of the ITs once the signs are there, staying flexible to change and acting accordingly.

Now back to area 5:)

Well can you guys be a little bit specific? What are you interested in my management?

Roughly I don't have any strategy. I have some points I want to follow, but they are only in my head and this is not like 3x profit means end of trading this day. My rulez are more about the feelings. My favourite T-shirt has a logo "dont think...feel" and it's because of the markets. Every day is different so maybe you can, but I can not, to write conventional rulez and than follow. I have made this last 3 years and there were only problems, that no one knows if rulez I have written are ok, even I don't know, no Idea if they making sense, if they take me on the right way. Just rulez and follow:) And this has led to problems with discipline, frustration that I can not follow any rulezz and that I'm realy dummy....BUT wait a minute....It's the same like a painter, artist... he can not have rulez to, 3cm with light yellow and than switch to blue and continue 5cm on the paper:) it's funny for me now to think about it this way, sry for that:)

I hope you understand, that by cooking your dinner you can not say "I'll put away 30% of the ham from left and 30% from right and the midle, the rest 30% I'll cook on the pan, because this is how my mom do it" Do you know this story? The husband came to his wife and ask why is she doing that and the answer was "because my mom do the same" So the husband went to the mother and ask again, Why 30+30% of the ham into the trash and cook only the rest, making no sense. The answer was again the same "because my mom do it like this" so he went to grandmother and ask again why are you doing this? And now the answer was " because I have a small pan":)

Do you understand? Everything is changing and you can not follow the way of someone else, make rulezz because you should? go to the school because you should? have a wife because you should? buy a car or house? have a daily job? blow out 60% of a ham because your parrents do it like this...

I do not like this way

So if you want to get some specific Info, please let me know have a nice day J.

Well this is exactly as you said. In the begining I took 18pips on risk 1%. After some time it was 36pips on 1% of account. So this is now my TOP risk level, according this I know for example that my highest lotsize could be 1,0 lot and this is my maximum for any trade. So if the setup looks good, than I trade 1,0lot a if it didn't than I trade it with 0,1 lot and doesn't matter how much pips I give to the SL.

So it's not the best way in progress, because if I need SL only 15 pips, that mean I can easily risk 2,0 lot because of the lower pips needed to reach the risk 35pips = 1,0 lot, but I'am not doing that. Just trade fixed risk and make no calculations during the day

This maximum I set every morning, so on monday TOP risk level is 50pips with 1,0 lot and if I make some money, than Thuesday can be 50pips with 1,5lot etc...not weekly or monthly basis, just daily

Well, I obviously had a long bias on Yen pairs, which was why I held the runner to run from 96.97. Well, i don't think it's a mistake of what you did. But you've got to have a plan, of where and when you should exit, or move ur stops.

There're 2 types of traders: 1. Let the trade run, with full positions, and don't mind being stopped out and giving the pips back. 2. Take partial profits along the way, and don't mind "missed profits" when final TP is hit.

I'm type 2, and it seems like what you're doing now = type 1. There's no right or wrong, just personal preference, and whichever suits the personality of the trader.

timos wrote: How did you made 4k pips in one day? Care to explain please? Tim

I'll tell you. Suppose we have a USDJPY demand zone 30 pips wide. Now, you set limit buy order for every pip in that zone. So, that gives you 30 buy limit orders. Next, you choose a currency that has a high correlation coefficient with the USDJPY - GBPJPY for example. Demand zone for GBPJPY zone is 35 pips wide. You use the same procedure of placing buy limit orders as in the USDJPY. That gives you 35 buy limit orders. Market begins to move, demand level has been hit and penetrated 90% on both pairs. So you end up with 27 buy orders on USDJPY, and 32 orders on GBPJPY. Demand levels holds and the market begins to move in your direction. Finaly, USDJPY is 80 pips up and GBPJPY 120 pips up. And voilà... you made 80x27+120*32= 2.160+3.840 = 5.960 pips in one day. Publicly, you don't talk about the losses in the same manner or about aggressive scaling method so people think you are a superman and they start to buy your "know how" for just $30 like creazy.

I have one point to make about the snowball effect, and it's the other side of the coin

I have vivid memories of adding to positions that were going against me, as your chart shows. and I must say, it's absolutely not for everybody.

Our stops are what they feed off. So I must advocate having the patience to wait until the stop hunt occurs before entering a trade - the best price - where one can go in heavy, with just one trade, and win big or lose small from there

posts.author: josh1125
posts.text:
Hello RTM, I've decided to finally take control of my trading. I'm 25 years old, and I've been trading (or trying to trade) for about 3 years, and my rate of success isn't the best. When I began trading, like many people I got caught up in the indicators and systems. For a while I did well, then everything started to fall apart. Then I began my search. I then moved on to trying to read candles. I discovered Steve Nison's "Beyond the Candlesticks", and I thought I had found everything I needed. I began trading every candlestick pattern he taught, but still something was missing. I would identify the patterns, but price would go the opposite way. Then one day, I came across the thread "PA by Julexo" on forexfactory. and Paraipan. The rest I hope will be history.

I am starting this journal to log my journey to hopefully becoming a great trader. I've spent quite a while reading DrSwing's journal and what an inspiration and learning experience it was. Feel free to be as hard and critical as possible on me during my endeavor. I must succeed, I will succeed.

Thank you all in advance.

josh1125

So I decided to start with compression, below are some markings on a few charts, that shows what I understand compression to be. Compression is when price moves from one level to another, clearing out pockets of supply and demand so when price hits a key level, (Supply or Demand) orders have been cleared allowing price to easily move from Decision Point. Please feel fee to correct me, and help me, and please be as critical as possible.

posts.author: Oedipus
posts.text:
I don't know if this will help but I've found the great thing about flags is that so much can be done after the fact. My favorite trades are those that return to a flag after it's been established. So first you can look left to see what the high of the flag is reacting to. Then you can wait for the flag to be fully formed. Then wait for price to leave the flag and then return to it, or not as the case may be (FTR). Even returning to it a second time is often very good. (FTB).

So look to see where price failed to get back into a flag and you can guess there are still sell orders there. Does this make any sense at all?

posts.text:
So I've been studying really hard

trying to figure out how everything ties together.

After reading markepedia and the articles several times and several journals, I still struggled with how to it all fits together. Individually, I could identify everything, but putting the puzzle pieces together was difficult. Well today I had what I think was my biggest ahah moment. Something finally clicked after reading once again one of IF's article on Past, Approach and Reaction.

1. Price first has to create a zone. We use FL (RBR and DBD), FTR, S/D(RBD, DBR), and S/R -. These zones happen in the past, and we want to identify those zones as areas of interest. 2. As price approaches the zone, we pay attention to whether or not price shows compression or if it gives a the 3 Drive pattern. -. This is important, because price this gives us clues on whether or not that zone will hold. 3. The Reaction. This is where we watch the PA in or around the already established zone. In order to achieve our maximum R:R we would switch to a LTF to watch the PA play out. This is where we look for Engulf, QM, Diamond, and Can Can. - This comes AFTER our HTF zone has been established and price has come back.

Please feel free to correct me wherever you see error in my thinking.

I typically try to see the chart in flags. Base, flag, pole. The base and the flag are two different zones. The space between the base and flag which is the pole is what I use for my PAZ. Once price engulfs either the flag or the base, price then is free to move to the opposite side. There aren't really any orders inside the pole. So when price starts in one direction, it won't stop until it runs into more orders.

Think it looks good pal.

Practising my analysis if you don't mind, here's my interpretation of a slightly longer term possibility...

Because we've engulfed the source of engulf of important FTR (A), and also the FTR formed from the engulf of (B), the level we're coming long off currently looks "insignificant" by comparison.

Another possible nice play could be to take the short from the fresh FTR (D) (being mindful it could also go slightly higher) - which was the FTR formed after the engulf of the FTR formed after level (A) was taken out - down to the very strong FTR formed from the engulf of the engulf level at (C) (which is also the origin of the move), and then look for a big long move from there.

I could of course be completely wrong, still very much learning myself

but since

we've had a nice initial reaction off the daily FTR, taking out a decent opposing FTR in the process, I'd think if the ITs wanted to really push it higher in the long term, they'd want level (C) for the buy orders.

posts.author: josh1125
posts.text:
Charles, There are two possible scenarios that I see here. (A) price will compress to our zone, or (B) which is shown below, price will turn before we enter the zone and begin to flag. If (A) occurs, I will look for PA on the LTF engulf, because price can compress through our zone into the next one. If (B) occurs, we know that there is heavy selling in that zone, so if I want an aggressive entry, and I know I wouldn't be around to watch what happens, I would TT. If I am able to watch the charts, I would wait for an entry with what should form a QM.

The safest trades are the ones where you engulf in to a pole where price clearly did not reach any significant target or last remaining orders in a zone. and then wait for the last remaining orders in the zone price came from. This set up would have been perfect to go long to that QM level then switch 180 degrees and short it all the wat to the 0.66590 area.

I draw the CP on after, the CP tells us a lot about what is happening and give us a good indication where the next big set of orders are.

Orders are always on the edges of any PAZ. Whether it be a FL, stacked FTRs, or CPAZ. We never trade midrange. I stopped out of this trade, but it was totally my fault. I have to continue to tell myself, "ONLY TAKE TRADES AFTER AN ENGULF." After going through many of my trades, I noticed that I only lose when I anticipate a retrace when I think price is ranging. Waiting for the engulf takes the guesswork out, and it leads us in the right direction. Yes they're orders on the edges of these PAZs, and we will get a bounce, but without an engulf, anything could happen. I just have to remind myself of that very thing.

posts.text: Filoyell, Hey, thanks for stopping by. It would be very difficult to take a trade based on the information provided on your chart. We have to look further left to know what the low marked in the chart below is a reaction to. That low could very well have been the end of a retrace that hadn't yet hit a target, it could be a break into a PAZ, and it is also possible that it is an engulf of an entire zone. When I began RTM, I thought I could pick any random low or high, and a break of that level automatically means the FTR following that break was important. It is always important to look "left and then left again" to know what that low or high is a reaction to. Remember we are reading the entire market.

posts.author: josh1125
posts.text:

posts.author: Atari
posts.text:
Hi Josh and Hoeschec, First of all, let me say that you both are doing great! You are learning more and more each day and getting better and better and reading price. In our learning curve, we will come to a time where we are learning quickly, and then come to a halt, and then once we figure it out, we are learning quickly again. Keep on at it and you will start to see which LS to use and which one to ignore.

There is a lot to IF's teaching and it takes time to absorb. As I mentioned to Hoeschec I believe, I had to review video #2 four times before I understood the fake PA in the large kink that broke the support on the Gbp/Cad pair. That part skimmed over my head on the 1st 3 times I watched the video, but on the 4th time, I was looking for an answer to price bouncing off a FL, especially a very large FL and that it when the light bulb went on. Eureka, I understand.

To answer your question and frustration about which LS to use and which one is important, I do have a better understanding now than before when I first took the course. I was frustrated like you, wondering which one will bounce price and which one won't. Here is what I found. We look for LS of a FL that broke another FL to the left, just like a QM. For example, your trend is up and now you form a LS. That LS needs to break a UFL to the left for it to become important. Once we have that, then we marke the high and low of that FL and look for the kink on the right side for PA when price returns to it. Now, we don't know if the kink (on the right side) will hold price or if price will break thru...... hence that is the reason we want to see the the ENG (then the QM/DM) before taking the trade. I find higher time frame LS especially on the Day/Week/Month to be stronger than the lower time frame. The other thing that we must look for in the kink is that have price come up to take the orders in the kink. If it did, then that kink is less likely to hold price. If there are clean orders in the quick, then you are likely to get a bounce. Hopes this helps..

Sorry for such a late reply, things have been really hectic lately. For me, decision points are important, but then again they aren't. I've noticed that most decision points are going to give a bounce in price, but FL's are where the real orders lay. Many times, decision points are used to create BSZs. They are normally extremely visible to every trader, and normally happens somewhere near a FL. I very rarely will take a trade from a decision point. When taking trades, only decision points that matter are the ones that occur inside of FLs. For me, decision points are good levels to use for targets.

Thanks IF.

Yes, which level is going to hold, the only trading question that matters.

The journey for me to answer that question starts here and from the basics.

So let's begin

Disclaimer for this and all future posts: the following contents come
 from my own understanding of the original teachings by IF and other
members, so always be aware that I could be totally wrong and that each
unit of knowledge is subject to my own interpretation, filtering and may
 not reflect the original concepts as intended by IF

Caps on price

Every S/D trader knows them in and out, yet the best, strongest and perfect looking ones still fail.

I can conclude from my own experience that the shape of the base and
departure strength from a level have only limited influence on the
overall outcome.

What really matters, as RTM teaches, is the context.

But before I get into that. There are some important clues that I
consider to determine the quality of the base, I'm sure someone else
here at RTM pointed them out.

An interesting fact is that many traders think that consolidation (bases
 in RBD/RBD/RBR/DBD) means low activity (volume) and that momentum bars
happen due to high volume. Sure, sometimes this is right, but most of
the time momentum bars (liquidity gaps) are thin market moves (low
volume) because price has to move in one direction once the last
unfilled order is filled and ready to move to the next liquidity zone
(base), where enough opposing orders get filled to stop price for some
time, until again the balance gets broken one way or the other.

This is also the reason why price bounces from those bases, because of unfilled orders left over from the last battle.

S/D traders say that those orders at the bases are left there for undefined time, even for years.

But it was a real revelation to me what RTM teaches about targets (PAZ).

Another common reason for RBD/DBR failures is also explained by RTM.

Just by knowing this and the above, we should be able to filter out many losses.

Now to what really matters, the context where caps happen.

Target 1 was there because of the past history:

I see that in the last part I'm already ahead with FTRs, engulfs and targets.

I will try to get in those in my next series of posts.

And it is also clear from the above, that one concept taken in isolation
 (in this case price caps) is not enough to decipher price.

posts.text:
My EU trade ended up at B.E. but what a great lesson.

First the charts

As you can see price stopped at the first opposing FL of that scale (good for 1st profit tg).

Then the pivot low 30m FL base, was not a good point for the full reversal.

Reasons:

1. the base was a pivot low, which means a reaction to a previous base,
in this case a 30m FTR (which itself is the top of a small CP)

2. the sharp arrival and departure makes this more a stop hunt/fake out
than a full reversal, also because most reversals have larger tops with
QM/diamond levels

I have to correct my previous understanding of the FTR and FL.

In one of the first post I wrote that for me a FL is a FTR of a previous FTR (something like an important FTR).

Then I had a lot of trouble because of the markepedia FL page which
shows FLs before a zone break (ie. FL without FTR). I would call those
decision points rather than FLs.

But now it is clear to me that there is no FL without FTR.

And to clear that confusion, here is now my newest understanding.

As I already wrote this in the classroom thread few days ago:

The FTR is a structure that forms only AFTER a break of a level/zone.

The FTR can become a FL when price bounces from it, hence the name (it limits the flag).

The flag limit is just a property of the FTR.

Here a drawing from IF posted on FF

posts.text:
Hey Jurij, wanted to give my take on what happened to your trade.
That was an engulf where price DID move to the next FL, but that's all
you can reasonably expect since you were on such a low time frame. I
think the mistake was expecting price to KEEP going down on such a low
time frame move. Usually I try to only use the M1 to validate a higher
time frame move. I marked up your chart looking at it more
holistically.

1. You see price engulfed what looks to be a fairly significant FL. And
 it engulfed it with a bull candle (2), which would suggest price wants
to go up. At this point I would be looking for an area to enter a long
trade.

3. Now price did engulf downward, but it was in the context of a larger
move. Price was compressing into the bull candle. At the end of the
compression, you would expect price to continue going up. Rather than
go short here I would read price is just retracing before continuing its
 move up.

4. And you see the compression ended right at the s/r flip level, and price continued its move up.

The s/r flip level and base of the pole are possible areas to look for a
 long entry, depending on your risk profile. When starting off, try to
stick to the higher time frames for analysis. I bet if you were looking
 at the m5 or m15, it would have been easier to see that price wanted to
 move up.

claudiuschan wrote:
Jurij wrote: Psychology of stop hunting

Hi Jurij,

first of all thanks for the post, it really make me have more understanding on the market direction.

Just a quick question, how you know which is the retailer stop?

You know all retailers who follow trend put their stop below the last
newly formed high/low in expectation for a trend continuation (new
high/low). So retailer stops are just beyond pivot highs/lows, but here
at RTM we know that the true orders are at the FTRs and those highs/lows
 are made sometimes to build traps so that ITs take the stops from
retailers to get some extra liquidity.

In that way, even if they are right on the direction, they lose.

The idea with that chart is, once you know the new direction and target
price wants to follow, when you see some highs or lows just above/below a
 fresh FTR then it is likely that price fakes out to the fresh zone.

That's because those are 2 different types of PAZs.

Check out these two posts from Les_paul:
	post1
 and
	post2

I think the SPAZ type works only if there is nothing important on the left, like a broken key level.

Because the break of a key level makes it an FTR/FL.

Also the reason for ITs creating stacked S/D is to pick up orders on the
 way and on return to fake out all classic S/D and S/R traders.

Think about it this way, if ITs created those stacked demand/supply
bases to fill their orders on the way, this means that on return there
is little possibility of unfilled orders still left there. This is
especially true for compression PAZs.

That's why price needs to break only the last/first demand just before the CPAZ or SPAZ to make it through the entire zone.

So if there are still unfilled orders then they are likely there at the tip (entrance of PAZ) and not inside that consumed zone.

Right, PAZs are just a piece of the puzzle like everything else.

This is something that I think is the key to understand:

1. Some FL/FTRs work but many don't, so this concept is not enough on its own

2. Some engulfs work but many don't, so this concept is not enough on its own

3. PAZs (all types) work but many don't, so this concept is not enough on its own

4. QM/Diamond patterns work but many don't, so this concept is not enough on its own

5. Compression is sometimes a reversal sign but not always (LQ after compression is common)

6. S/D levels work but many don't

7. FO levels sometimes work but many don't

... I think it is clear where this is leading to.

Perhaps this is exactly what IF means by saying that we need to make
that final juxtaposition, where we see those concepts all at the same
time. Often there is this common question in the homework section: "Why
did that or this FTR/FL/CP/... fail?" Because it was never meant to work
 that way.

Looking at the charts, there are almost dead sure setups that present
itself only if multiple of the above RTM concepts appear together in the
 same setup.

For example: at HTF supply, a trick is played (FO) then at the right
shoulder of the trick level price forms an FTR/FL which happens to be a
QM level also. Price meanwhile broke a lower FL and starts to retrace to
 the QM level. On approach price is starting to compress (making a
CPAZ). Once price hits the QM FTR level at the FO key level at HTF
supply price bounces and breaks into the CPAZ. If price now retraces
back to the origin for a second chance entry then you have one of those
almost dead sure trades

Something like this past setup:

Jurij wrote: CADJPY

30m Had a limit sell order not triggered, too high

5m LTF second chance (missed this one too)

I think those setups are really nice and clear, that's what I want to trade more.

I guess the difficulty in all this is to have the patience to wait and take only that kind of setups.

In the dissection room we talked about targets and origins.

The big question was whether price, after an eng, wants the origin, intended as the first engulf in a move up/down (extreme origin) or just the next obvious FL?

Many times IF wrote on his charts after an eng "FTR - easy traget" looking like the sure target is always the first engulf up/down after trend change.

This works only if there's nothing in the way (important level) before the origin.

I think without this past SR structure price would have gone to the origin.

So my little aha moment was that the assumption that price just wants the extreme origin is too simple and not always true (if there's a swap level). I think we must always look for symmetry and swap zones to make sure to not miss an important target.

Jurij wrote: NZDCAD DM in play?

4H

30m

initial QM spotted by a trading mate, so not all my credit

Looking back at this, at that time it was a solid looking setup to me.

The problem and the error I've been doing is to consider scales, making everything more complicated than it is, especially mixing smaller and higher scale FTR/FL boxes.

But the market doesn't care about boxes with fixed rules (for ex. 4H box is stronger than 5m box and an eng is a signal...).

If a 4H FTR/FL box is made as a reaction to a 1m FL it is because of these orders sitting there.

Orders have not time frames because they are just orders.

There are levels that are stronger than others, not because of time frame but because of orders and decisions of greater or lesser importance (swap levels vs simple barriers...)

Thanks to Salivan and Omid I began to focus on the real orders (true supply/demand aka FL) and this was a big missing piece in my analysis
