Each time I listen again (4th time now) to this webinar something new comes to my attention.

It really is one of the best and most important videos, in my opinion.

Surprising how easily our brain overhears little details and the extend of lack of focus.

So, the new detail I noticed this time was the clue IF gave about the change ITs made.

I'm not going to spoil it, as I respect IF's work.

Really he actually says it in the webinar and then once someone ask about it specifically he gives a hint.

Basically, if I'm not mistaken (always possible), the change affects greatly S/R traders by letting them miss their targets and hit their stops. Before the change, S/R trading was easier, but as soon as everyone started to trade this way more and more, the market had to change, as only a few can win and the masses must be always on the other losing side.

There's good news though, if you follow IF's teachings you are already aware of it and should not fall for this trick.

I'm pretty sure that those who have put in many charting hours probably already noticed this kind of trick, so nothing really special.

Other key questions answered in the webinar above:

1. What is an MPL?

2. What is a scale and how to trade the PA in the right scale?

3. What is the origin of the move?

5. What is PA and when do we have PA?

6. And more....

Just a reminder to watch these videos over and over (while our general understanding progresses) as each time there's a possibility of noticing something new.

Salivan explained nicely FOF in his jorunal.

Basically unfilled orders are one thing but FOF is different.

For example if we have unfilled orders we can expect only a bounce.

If we have PA (signal/intention) then the last set of unfilled orders becomes FOF as there are no orders beyond that FOF level.

Without the signal, we have just the last set of unfilled orders but no guarantee that the level holds.

If the ITs filled all their orders beyond a certain level, it doesn't make sense to fake out past it, they must hate drawdown too...

That last level will have all limit orders of the ITs to make sure it doesn't break.

Once tg is hit, those orders are removed.

And price is allowed to break that level.

That's my understanding of FOF as of now and since I'm new to FOF as well, I'm not really sure about it yet.

Hope it helps.

harshrthakkar wrote: Hi Kruger, Have read it,but still would be happy if you can tell me what is it that has to be seen in the patterns of RBD/DBR.. Iis candle colours or candle count etc.

There are no strict rules in terms of candle count or colour for defining RBD/DBR. In addition, it is dependent on time frame in which you observe pattern.

As the name suggests, there must be three components to create RBD/DBR: 1. rally, strong price movement (momentum) in south or north direction 2. base, time of price consolidation in defined range 3. rally, strong price movement in opposite direction than in point 1

OK, my eyes and hands are on charts now, so I will try to show my view about this trade.

Let's start from daily. We can clearly see blue support line which was tested to the pip two times (blue arrows) and after each test price went north strong. If you zoom out to monthly you will find other clear reactions confirming importance of this support. These two rides are reaction to demand ( 1) created after highs from 20.06.2012 and 27.07.2012 were broken. Third visit resulted in three-day battle between bulls and bears ( 2). For three days bears wasn't able to close below blue line and bulls were fighting drawing strength from demand ( 1). On the fourth day support is broken and days closes below blue line ( 3). Immediately after the break we see retest of support line ( 4) but price wasn't able to go higher which suggests the possibility of sellers sitting above.

H4 chart shows nice supply ( 5) with origin of move below blue line ( 6). Price returned with strong move ( 7) which could suggest further run. After candle ( 8) I expected flag to demand area ( 9) and next bull run but ( 10) candle blew this scenario. Could we expect this? It was hard from H4 perspective so let's go to H1.

On H1 we can see that this wasn't bull flag scenario at all but rather compression/3 drive to supply ( 11). When S/R flip ( 12) was cleared breas colud take full advantage of compression and price fall to demand ( 13). Fall was hard and it created big juicy pole. Next three hours was and example of bear flag in the making (blue) and when price went toS/R ( 12) bulls just gave up.

As a digression I want to add (and we all know that) that no chart will show our thoughts, mental and physical state, environment that we are in, and lots of other stuff affecting our trading.
Very nicely explained Kruger!

Hi Naughtypip, in normal market conditions (without important news releases) if setup is perfect I just take it because there will be no second chance.

In case of news, perfect setups usually works as well, but you have to be prepared for spikes and fast moves. To avoid this, It's better to wait for new post-news S/D zones and than trade them.

Even when scalping, I'm still watching all TF up to 4H/D1 to be aware of potential obstacles. In addition I like to check every new closed candle and how it looks in whole picture.

But say it was a typical flag w/ the pole reaching close to the top, would you expect a coast to coast run if the bottom got faked out?.... I may have just thought of some homework. HotRod wrote: Hey Kruger... Always following your trades. Great job.

HotRod wrote: I shorted about where you did as well. The structure had a nice rounding look to it at a good place so I figured why not. You obviously targeted lower than I did. I was basically scalping.

HotRod wrote: I thought about leaving it on for lower but was weary of that engulf on the hourly.

But instead it based nicely and engulfed. I actually took a long there that I got out of because it didn't go anywhere.

Very well noticed! H1 engulf was significant - created flag pole (2) and after that price was capped (3) and base for any bull movement was engulfed (4). These things have helped to create flag with origin at (1) where my target was. Also notice that market was quiet as it was during Asia ranging session (5).

What was important while pole (2) was created? Fake move through (6) - stop losses - to (7) for extra long orders - trapped sellers. This mixture gave us really nice QM level - target.

HotRod wrote: I don't know why but it will not let me post my chart here. Anyway, if you look on the hourly you'll see a base and an engulf that lead up to the cluster where your entry is. My target was at the engulf point of that base.

Nothing wrong with that from H1 perspective Targeting lower than (1) was like flipping the coin IMO and we don't want to do that, but let's assume we are holding short. In this case, we should be especially careful because of London session open and big boys tricks. So we had strong move ( 8) to QM level (1) where buyers were found. But those buyers had to fight with ignored demand (9) and it was only one chance for bears to push price lower. And that's what happened but thing is that big boys used the news to do the trick (10). It was last call to get out because of decision point marked by Cosmo Can you imagine all sellers trapped by this move? Yes, big boys need them...

HotRod wrote: Also, just a general question. When do you expect price to go coase to coast? I ask because of the current position that eur/usd is in at the moment. Although it seems to be heavily supplied, much of the supply above has been consumed. I don't know if you could call what I have squared off a flag or not, but whatever it is we are at the bottom of it. It seems more like a rounding reversal, so I would expect the large 4h bar to be consumption. But say it was a typical flag w/ the pole reaching close to the top, would you expect a coast to coast run if the bottom got faked out?.... I may have just thought of some homework. Hopefully this expresses what I mean to ask.

Well, we should always expect coast to coast moves because this is how the market works. It's just a matter of time.

The question is if your coast is marked well:) Your target is reasonable at H4 time frame but optimistic from LTFs point of view. Watch price @ the top of consumptions you have marked.

posts.author: Kruger
posts.text:
bcho018 wrote: Hi Kruger thanks for your posts. I've been following your post for a while now.

Hi Bcho018, you're welcome and it's good to know.

bcho018 wrote: I just want to ask you something. Since you day trade and scalp(in my books) I assume that you sit the whole day in front of the screen..

May I know how do you cope with things like boredom, tiredness or distraction?

Not the whole day but most of the time... I just like to know what's going on with the market. My professional life gives me this possibility.

My concentration is greatest when I'm in the early stages of the trade and there is no room for the boredom and distraction at that time. When setup developing in my way and executing plan I can relax and move on to other things or just watch price. It is never boring to me and I'm still trading in my head without real orders to practice and to have good feeling of the pair.

If I'm distracted or without full trade plan, there is no trade. Taking such is simply a waste of money. In this situation, I try to stay focused and looking for further opportunities. Distraction is not a problem when the plan was prepared in advance.

There are no negotiations with tiredness. When I feel tired, trading platform goes down.

bcho018 wrote: I mean how do sit there the whole day waiting and waiting like a cold blooded crocodile in the river? (Since I assume you are warm blooded)

When scalping even crocodile would turn into the warm blooded because M1 setups occurs all the time and just as quickly come to an end. During trading day I take a lot more trades than posting.

bcho018 wrote: I use to scalp not too long ago and I felt burnt out after a while.

There is nothing wrong with that. Maybe you just have to move to higher time frames and start to use alerter or smsnotification.

its because when such an area gets engulfed cleanly, orders remain there that are filled when price returns.

so at ignored supply engulfed north, all the sell orders were consumed
for price to go through and engulf, but not all the buy orders got
filled.

so when price returns from above.. these get filled and you get a bounce

Great start, Les_Paul.

I will also post a few more setups of this weeks trading session -
mostly homework at entries that would have been good to enter but I
didnt because I was not around or not aware of the setup.

This can also be used for trend continuation. It is kind of quasimodo
within the trend. Works best if the the countertrend-swing bounced off
unimportant levels, so the probability to enter at the setup level is
the highest because the trend is always your friend ;-) But a trend also
 ends at some point, and most of the time this happens at HTF levels.

But since I also like to trade countertrend on HTF, it is a good method
to get in when an engulf happens at M30 or higher at a HTF supply or
demand zone. Thats a good sign that pro money is active and they want to
 retest a decision point to confirm the trend reversal. If you look
through your examples, you see that most of the time, a touch trade just
 doesn't make sense, because price ITSELF tells you time is right to
step on the train when it engulfs previous swing levels. So instead of
trying to catch tops and bottoms, it's better to wait for this setup to
happen so that we can enter on the retest of a broken level. Also
important. If you look through your examples, you see that the REAL move
 in the opposite direction happens AFTER the retest. So there is no
reason to be nervous to miss the move. Price itself will tell you when
it's time to change direction. This is something very important I have
learned in the last weeks and months. For me, there is only one level I
would enter with a pending order right now: If the level is a) a HTF
level, b) the turning point of a big swing, c) lots of time went past
and d) the level is fresh and has a clear decision point (S/R flip) to
enter at. Especially midlevels, such as DBD or RBR on HTF always need
this kind of setup confirmation first in order to trade the reversals. I
 just got stopped out too many times and this prevented me from growing
my account.

posts.author: mettafort

Hi Les_Paul and Hotochin,

I just wanted to add something which I dont think is always obvious.
When price breaks out and then retraces but holds under new demand that
has formed, out from the top of the PAZ, like the first example in the
chart LeS_Paul put togther, thats the failure-to-return - it tells us it
 couldnt return down because sitting here is fresh demand. When price
breaks out of PAZ 2, there is a clear RBR - the B is the FL, and then
price retraces, only for a bar. This bounces right above the FL - this
is the FTR as far as I understand it, because its major purpose for
being identified as a concept on the chart, is that it is a marker that
supply or demand is now imbalanced in the opposing direction - it is
another place that allows us to reason about order flow. And more
subtely, to me an FTR is the marker that price failed to get back to the
 origin of the move when it retraced, because of order flow.

I am sure you understand this actually, but thought maybe using some different verbiage might add to it.

MF.

Dear Hotochin,

I will try to explain my way of identifying PAZ's. I by no means claim
that the way I do it is right cause I am still working hard on it. I
must admit that I am doing this in hindsight, in real time I find it
much harder.

SCREEN 1

In the SCREEN 1 you can see that price makes low, turns, engulfs FL
(dotted line) and makes FTR. Then it starts travelling. north. The newly
 formed FTR is now lower edge of my PAZ.

Above, you can see an FTR that was mede on the previous way down. This
upper FTR is my top edge of PAZ. Will price bounce or go through? Only
PA in LTF can tell me.

SCREEN 2

In SCREEN 2 you can see the price shot through the FTR, which means that
 its supply becomes demand. It is now my lower edge of the new PAZ. As
far as the upper edge is concerned, it is formed by the nex FTR in line.
 What is PA going to do now? I don't know, I must wait and see.

SCREEN 3

In SCREEN 3 we can see that PA raced to the upper edge, engulfed it a
bit and got back into the PAZ. The bias is long after 2 engulfed levels
in a couple of minutes. PA starts flagging.

In this situation I took the failed EU trade. Had I done this analysis before? Well, no...
 If I had done it, I would have never taken the trade in the place I
did. In M5 it can be nicely seen that PA engulfed Flag Limit and
retraced to the origin of the move - upper edge of PAZ. Now it was
apparent that price wanted to go down to that SUPPLY TURNED DEMAND level
 (lower edge of PAZ). In my opinion this was the moment for taking a
scalp south.

But I was not aware of the situation. Due to my stupidity I did not
check the overal situation and took that trade - in the middle of that
flag / range / whatever we call it. It was nobody's land - no trade
should have been taken...

Well I hope that what I have just written makes some sense.

Les_Paul

Hi!

I want to show two setups here: in conventional terminology it is Demand-turned-supply zone (SWAP ZONE).

However, behind this technocratic term there are novice traders who are trapped in losing positions:

1 - demand is created and people unaware of the fact that price just left HTF RBD zone buy.

2 - demand is engulfed and these people suddenly have losing positions

3 - price revisits zone and people liquidate losing positions at BE.

Big money use these trick very often and it's tradable nicely.

a) find trapped traders

b) find DP within the swap zone - DP to engulf demand

c) open position upon retest of the DP (SL above DP or above zone)

Les_Paul

EDIT: according to my observation, the setups appear mostly after leaving HTF S/D to add to buying / selling pressure

they are good "with trend" setups

Hotochin, my friend!

I hear a lot of frustration in your voice. The frustration is
understandable, I have been through a LOT of FX frustration even after
joining RTM! However, the frustration is not necessary. If we look to
other sucessful traders here, we can be sure that it can be done!

Concerning what you have written: I got your point! But imagine it as a
menu in such a kind of restaurant where you can set up your menu on your
 own from available ingredients. You can decide what side dish, what
kind of meat, etc etc etc. Here it is the same. You have individual
components and it is up to you what dish you will create.

So, let's choose one setup! In the following picture you can see my PL curve from Forex Tester 1. Looks good, doesn't it?

I concentrated only on one setup:

1: I identified H4 FTR's and price caps (all of them).

2: I waited for price to engulf a level and return to one below
above.(here, the main difference between FT1 and real time trading
shows: in FT1 you can fast forward PA so you don't have to wait days...
and it is also the main reason I cannot reach such success in real life:
 I AM IMPATIENT!!!! )

3: So once PA got into a H4 level, I switched to M15 and waited for a QM or break and retest of M15 S/R line.

4: TP - opposite H4 level, SL - some 15 - 20 pips below/above pivot

Of course, the PL curve shown above is UNREALISTIC for me in real life
due to my lack of patience.... but I am working on it! Also, well, I
knew there would be a big drop in 2008 in advance... so I could act
accordingly and concentrate on shorts mainly!

So my dear Hotochin, if you find the setup interesting, try to find some
 examples and you can put them here in my journal or in yours... Let's
work on it together mate!

LP

posts.text:
So my personal EURECA moment is something which has been repeated here
 many times by IF and other kind teachers. I am 100% sure that all of
you have heard this and many of you have already incorporated this basic
 truth in your trading. I finaly realised this only after countless
hours spent with Forex Tester. I asked myself a question:

How is it, George, that you can rock in Forex TEster (see my fancy PL
curve in one of above posts) but you rather suck in live trading?

And the Almighty gave me the answer: It is because in Forex Tester you need to wait for the ideal setup only a couple of minutes but in real life you often have to wait a couple of days...
 (I am sure that you are aware of the function in FT that you can FAST
FORWARD the market, so for example one week in H4 TF lasts only a couple
 of minutes).

In real life I am very impatient (I have been working on this issue of
mine for a couple of years now and must admit that I have made a
substantial progress, but still, I am far from ideal state), so I hardly
 ever wait for a proper setup...

SO, the answer to my personal struggle is: ALWAYS WAIT FOR THE PRICE ACTION TO SHOW YOU THE WAY (universal RTM rule),

and ALWAYS WAIT FOR YOUR SWEET FTR!!!!! (my personal extremely englightening rule)

I hope I haven't disappointed you very much - I know it's nothing new, but for me it is a huge leap forward....

Les_Paul

posts.author: Spongiform
posts.text:
Hello Les_Paul,

I love what you're doing with 'sweet FTRs'. I've been following a
similar line of thought for a while, what I call 'trading in the shadow
of the reaction to longer time-frame Supply or Demand'. I seem to keep
mangling this on the hard right edge: I think it's been down to a lack
of direction, and spending too much time in the detail rather than
stepping back and watching the big picture.

I'm a little late to the party, but I was particularly interested in an
FTR you pointed out (in post #317) in response to a question from Daft
trader 1 (in post #316). Fxyogi sort of picked up on it in post #340.

Here's your chart with the FTR in orange:

 Warning: Spoiler!

 [ Click to expand ]

 [ Click to hide ]

I'm sure it's a matter of what your rules say, but why did you pick that
 one over the lower one? I preferred the lower FTR but the reasoning is
discretionary. The difference between our choices is the difference
between viewing that spike down as an EG of one FTR or a reaction to the
 other (and thereby directional bias for potential trades). This is not
to say I made the better choice etc (and a visit to my journal shows my
preference for making the wrong choice as often as humanly possible ), but to understand the different philosophies and to learn... .

For comparison, here are some charts explaining how I thought both FTRs
(hindsight being 20 : 20 and all that, but I would have been attracted
to the one I've marked regardless).

 Warning: Spoiler!

 [ Click to expand ]

 [ Click to hide ]

H4 - first up, ancient history to give context to the PA of interest:

H4 - two views of the PA of interest. It shows your higher FTR and my
lower FTR. Mine occurs as a result of most recent PA, (to me) yours
seems to occur at an area from ancient history rather than a break above
 recent Supply (there are no orders from that time in the market, and
information quality degrades over time).

That higher FTR occurs at an interesting area. Market orders (Buy Stops
and breakout trader buys) are triggered right into that ancient Supply:
this would have been a great place for an FO if Pro Money wanted to move
 price down (having plundered liquidity to fill short orders) but
instead we see price grind higher (CP) immediately after. That CP
suggests hard work being done, and that suggests orders being filled.
This combined with my thoughts that this is a reaction to ancient
history (i.e. questionable) makes the upper FTR (which I thought of as
more of a DP, but I'm sure that's semantics) less utile than the lower
(in my opinion!). By comparison that lower one looks like it had an easy
 life:

H4 - for fun, a reminder that it's always advisable to look to the left for Stop placement on FTRs

W1 - and for more fun, stepping back would have shown a Flag in the
making, a pullback into Demand for a move higher (again, with the joy of
 20 : 20 hindsight):

Thanks in advance.

Spongy.

If price engulfs the limit and retraces, entry is at DP to engulf, and target is the base of the pole.

Hope this helps.

Hi, Les Paul

Sorry to post this in your journal.

But because this was your posting which i have some queries, i thought
it would be better to post it here , hoping to get some feedback from
anyone.

In posting 174, you have shared your knowledge of PAZ - compression, stacked supply/demand and zone between PAZ.

I couldn't understand the concept of stacked supply/ demand PAZ and how to really spot them.

And for another reason i do not understand is that unlike compression
where supply/demand was already consumed while on the way up or down to
the the next DP, ity was said that stacked supply and demand still has
its unfilled order left behind. So i do not understand the rationale
that when the the edge of the SPAZ was engulfed, how is it that we can
be so sure it will reach the other end of the PAZ? I mean since there
are unfilled orders at every stacked supply/demand, shouldn't we be
expecting reaction at one of the stack that could possibly bring price
back to the original direction?

I have this thinking because since stacked supply and demand has
unfilled orders and they carry on to move lower /higher, aren't they
considered as FTR and if they are considered as FTR, that's the more i
feel that price would have reaction when they retraced to the stacks
rather than engulfing every one of them all the way to the other end.

Then on this example Les Paul shown in his post 174, he showed this chart as an example of a SPAZ and how it was engulfed.

Hi Supreme,

I personally subscribe to the VIP data package, and update the data
almost on a daily basis. You can use the ECNfeed option to get good
quality tick data up to something like 2013 (which I found to be the
best), and then I just use FXCM data from then on whenever I update the
data. Alternatively, I know people who get their data from a service
like Dukascopy and import data into Forex Tester themselves.

Everyone has their own way of learning along with the tools that they use, and FT is by no means a necessity.

distant past, and if I spot an interesting chart someone posted from
2012-2013 for example, I can go and investigate and play through it
without any issue, whatever the time frame may be!

posts.author: danandsueco
posts.text:
Luska wrote: My Vessel delayed for 14 hrs...Managed to locked in 35 pips and counting... In this ping pong range just sell the high and buy the low until either one breaks and re-entry at retest...

Your statement here is near perfect. When a pair is rangebound buying the lower demand levels and selling the higher supply levels targeting the next nearest fresh zone will allow a trader to increase their risk/reward ratio as well as increasing their potential to hit targets. If the range breaks, waiting on that retest is a high probabilty winner. Key point in all, let the market come to you and if you're willing to wait... it always comes knocking. Keep locking those pips!

Something i wanna touch on my entries and stops... Usually i dont use stop loss... The entry is important to me... Ok if u have been following my thread, i did mentioned somewhere that ur entry is supposed to be where ur sl is... This recent move will be explained why. This is Gbp/Usd... first i start by watching the calender. Yes i trade the news. But only when there is significance entry point nearby. Else i will just leave behind pending orders and forget about it.

See how the chart shows you the possible entries for the news... I dont even know what the news or what the bullsh*t its talking about but i know its RED News a major one and something is gonna happen. As a technical trader, i trade solely on what the chart is telling me... Gonna need experience for it. Only God knows how hard i fell... See that a Marabuzo or railroad track watever you call it. This shows when the bulls are happily buying, someone ( you know who, the ones who controlled the market) wiped out those buyers. What happen is, this will result a psychology of the massive to induce sell. SO the bulls were either stopped out or holding to their losses. Then more sellers comes in. The mindset is now diverted to Selling.The people who trade against you doesnt want to lose out when they are selling and retails are selling too. so they need to bring in more sellers before they reverse the market. What happen is, they need to clear the leftover sell orders from that marabuzo. And they did. So no more sellers there. When the trend exhausted, they reverse the market drastically to wipe clean the open sell orders of the retailers who was a buyer and then change to a seller. These are the traders who trade the weather. They didnt know wat the hell is going on..More grey hairs will grow here. Next pic is how the return of the price to a level where the resistance change to support. I bet the retailers will place their stop loss just below that RBR. They know where you will put your stop loss.

So how the hell they wanna profit with so many buyers in the market? Simple... NEWS!!!! if you were on ur station while the news is happening, u will see that the price drops like theres no tomorrow.... Now the buyers before was stopped out. The psychology is changed to selling again. More retailers chase the sell. But we SND traders will wait at the demand... But did u noticed that you will be stopped out by that spike and if u place a sellstop orders like some does will get triggered. Then it reversed... See how these bastards stop your buy orders and triggers your sell stops before they reverse... SHould be enough forr them to profit both ways... And the cycle continues again and again.... So remember, if you wanna do pending, make sure you have ample space for your stop loss. Always think the reversed way... although it might not work everytime as proven by my number of losses.It does helps you to profit more than your losses. Now you have to decide, either place your entry at the start of the base but place your stoploss slightly further to get filled OR Place your entry where the stoploss is supposed to be but you wont get your orders triggered most of the time but when it does, your reward is far more greater than you imagined.

You dont need to learn so much about the chart but if you can spot the emotions on the chart, you will be trading just like these bastards and profit like them.

Happy profiting Guys.. Hopes my blabbers helps..

Dont trade anything in those boxes... Look for trade from 1am to 4am NY time above or below the blue box which is the asian session which is also outside the box, this is the time they hunt stops. Evryone was taught to trade breakout. So since the massive are trading breakout, if i were the market, i would trigger their entries and reverse. Then the next trade for continuation or reversal happens from 7:30am to 11am NY time. the reason i use m15 is for entries and its my trading frame. SND bases i look in H1 and above. They wont trade the same direction for 3 consecutive sessions. Unless the higher tf permits a direction then you may hold the trade. Else just end the trade earlier before 5pm NY as and intraday trade. Do note that timing are just guidelines and not fixed, else the percentage of winners will be 95% instead of 5%. The market rewards the 95% 1 out of the 3 attempt in order for them to stay in the market. With such mindset when a breakout trader wins, will make him feel that his methods works and continue to do what he does. Thats why we are taught to trade 1 to 3% of our equity. Its all about emotions which is 60% of the time. Strategy is only 10% and money management is 30%....

If you can understand stop hunts on a daily basis, you will be able to capture 50 pips almost everyday and by compounding only 3% per trade, you can turn a $5k account to $225k in 50 trades or lets say 10 weeks.try to measure your daily candle from wick to wick and see if you are able to get 50 pips or more. So who says picking tops and bottom is impossible? You just need to learn how its being made and capture it.

Mark your Yesterday high and yesterday low, weekly high and low, monthly high and low and asian session high and low everyday and u will be able to see how price reacts to these as stop hunts.

posts.author: MarkG
posts.text:
Take this with a pinch of salt as I'm new around here. I've always believed the MPL to be the lower limit of the FO zone when price changed direction.

So there will be outstanding orders at that price and it will be the last place for price to turn when it comes back to that area. It sometimes turns below the MPL, but to get the best price you wait for it to reach the MPL. It doesn't always happen, so you get fewer trades that way. The trades you do get will have a higher R.

posts.author: Edge
posts.text: The MPL will always be the last set of orders. This can be right down to the tick. Lower scales in a flag will show you where the smallest order blocks may reside to cause the maximum pain.

posts.author: sev87
posts.text: is it MPL?

posts.author: moneydeep
posts.text: What you have drawn are caps. An MPL is the maximum pain level which the IT can give to retailers before turning price. As Edge said, the last set of orders inside a flag. Look at in terms of fractals. Draw flags on the TF you wish to trade then dig down to the lowest tf you can go and find the last set of orders inside that area you wish to trade. An easy way to start understanding how it works is draw Flags on the lowest timeframe inside the larger flag which you are looking to trade and you will find pockets of unfilled orders ready to be taken. the last set of such orders is the MPL.

 the rest were winners for a few pips. Making this week a +8 pip week
for me :huh:

winners or return but in term of pschycology! I haven't felt like that
in a long time.

I had the feeling that I was fighting the market ! I made everything complicated, I was overthinking!

I was just stupid!Periode!

In fact, I made a plan on sunday and saw that we were at weekly demand
on the eur. I saw that this level had already been tested several times.
 Since the Monthly demand was not that far away under the weekly demand,
 I thaught that the Monthly demand could be revisited soon! I had this
idea in my head and it made me look for shorts when the charts were
screaming to long! Why did I do that? Normally, I know that a supply or
demand area remains a supply or demand area untill it gets broken! Why
was I stubborn to think that a Weekly level would break instead of
waiting for it to prove it to me?

posts.author: Tyoon
posts.text:
@mel wrote: I had the feeling that I was fighting the market ! I made everything complicated, I was overthinking!

I was just stupid!Periode!

Yup, there is a big difference between fighting price and following it.
For me, the best way to follow price is by chunking it down and trying
to see it as simply as I can. Watching the Hs, Ls, the ranges that form
from them and the movement in and around those ranges. For me boxes are
the foundation to my trading as they put a frame to what I am viewing.

What most learn about trading is levels and PA. The bigger piece of the
picture is how price MOVES. To get a feel for this, open up any chart on
 the 1h and get a pen and paper out. Draw out the main Hs and Ls. Then
draw out boxes to chunk it into individual bits. Look at how price moves
 in and around those Hs / Ls and the boxes. You will see that price has a
 few standard characteristics and they are incredibly simple. Usually
when price does 'A' it then does 'B'. For example, if price establishes a
 H/L with a retest, it will usually fill the range back or beyond the
previous H/L. These things are not patterns, they are dynamics.

Hs and Ls are the most essential part of the chart. Every day there is a
 H and L that is formed and there are many Hs and Ls that form in
between them.

Again with your pen and paper, divide the price out in time periods and
see how they move during different sessions and days of the week. Get
curious.. why does it do that?

It took me a few weeks of doing this to get to grips with it.

Trading Plan:

Why am I a Trader?

I have been introduced to trading in 2008, didn't had any succes in the first years.

I didn't want to become a Trader when I was a little girl, in fact I
didn't even know that this kind of activity existed before. I guess, it
was the lack of succes that I had in the first years that was what kept
me going. This is what triggered my intrest to get to know more about
the market. I had this feeling that it was possible to become succesfull
 in trading and to learn everything about how the market worked, inside
 out. It has been a long journey since then, as I tested so many
different things that did not worked. In fact, it was me, that did not
knew how to read the market. Eventually, after so many years I found a
way, I finally discovered the true beauty of the market and now that I
know,I am certainly not going to give up and stop trading.... :)

Trading Style & Strategy

I consider myslef to be a Day/Swing Trader but I also take some scalps here and there if a good opportunity present itself.

I am a supply and demand trader but I also look at PA. I do a weekly
analysis every sunday for the coming week and I also adjust or modify my
 plan if needed every day, before London open.

I like to trader higher TF supply and demand zones but I do like to look for lower TF fresh zones within the higher TF ones.

I mainly trade the EU but I may also check other pairs once in awhile.

I do not trade the Asian session. I prefer to trade from London open untill London close.

Money Management:

I will never risk more then 2% per trade. If I do have 3 losses in a
row, I will stop trading for the day and I will analyze why the trades
failed.

-My r:r per trade need to be at least 1/1 , otherwise I will not take
the trade. If I take a trade at a supply zone, I would prefer to exit at
 the demand zone and vice versa.

-For my stop loss, I use 2% risk but I will look at LTF charts to look
for the last 2 decision points, if thos are broken (against me) then I
will exit the trade manually and I will take the loss.

-My main focus is to preserve my capital.

-In terms of return, my daily minimum goal is 20 pips gain. I normally
do not want to set a fix minimum return in terms of pips because I want
to take what the market wants to give me (if it's more fine, if less
fine too) but since I have to set some goals for myself, I won't go for
too much pips. 20 pips seems to be fair enough.

Points to be careful about :

-Don't trade what you think, but trade what you see. Buy at demand and sell at supply!

-Pay attention to higher TF zones, as those are more powerfull than LTF ones.

-Always try to improve yourself!

Explain how you do your analysis and what you look for.

1)Look at where price is NOW, go ahead and mark all the supply zones
that are above current price and all the demand zones that are under
current price on 1h up to a monthly chart.

2) Mark in a specific color which of this higher TF zones are Fresh ones.

3) Find lower TF fresh supply and demand zones that are located in the higher TF zones from point 1 & 2.

4)Now that you have the zones marked take another chart and mark last day, week and month highs and lows.

5) Back to point 1, 2 & 3. On a lower TF, identify where price is
now and try to locate where the previous decision points are (to the
upside and to the downside).

6) Pre-entry, when price does approach the zones that you have marked,
look at how it approches exactly. Is it compressing towards the supply
or demand zone? If yes, then this is a plus point.

7) Look at point 6, if we are approaching a supply for example, look at
where you first "problem area " can be. Is the distance between the
supply and the "problem area" at least 1/1 rr? If yes, then ok, if not
pass the trade. Look also at decision point for your stops, make sure it
 fits your stop size.

 About the entry,I want to look at PA. My prefered entry is this:

Let's assume we are in a higher TF supply zone, I like to nr 1 see price
 cp towards it at least on a LTF chart, then usually price start to flag
 under this supply ( on a LTF) , what I like to see is a move away from
this flag, then a break a minor demand base (on a LTF) and a retest of
the fresh formed supply flag.

Let's assume I took a similar trade, the next thing I want to do in
order to stay in the trade is to look for break of the next minor demand
 lows/decision point.If price is unable to break the lows, then it might
 move in the opposite direction, so I'll look to exit the trade.

I think that this is it. I will update this post if somthing changes in my trading plan.

Mel

EDIT August 16 2012

Adding a Rule to my plan

-Identify swap levels From 15 min TF and higher.

What I want to see is a break of a supply and then a well defined base,(RBR)and vice versa for demand (DBD).

If there is a break of a supply/demand zone without any clear base
around the break, then I won't trade the first visit of the level.

The base, if there is one, would have to be a well defined one wich will
 not be tested with any wicks and the move away from it will will have
to be clear and strong.

If I find a potential good swap level that fits the above "rules" I'll
look at the chart to see where my first area of "trouble" is (DP, S/D).
The distance between the Swap and any potential "trouble" area should be
 at leat 1:1 rr , otherwise I'll pass the trade and move on dot com.

The market's action these past weeks might have felt a little odd to
lots of traders including myself but I took the time to make a detailed
analysis on the Euro wich is my favorite pair as you might know by now.
 :)

The Euro can act like a charm when it trades in a clear direction but a
few times per year it can act really "strangly" and fool lots of
traders. However all this can be explained imo.

The chart below is a monthly chart. The blue line on it is a significant
 level , it acted as as s/d and last action there was a bull action.
This line is now demand and last month candle closed above it.

Following chart is the Weekly chart, On this chart you'll see the
Monthly demand aswell (thin blue line) but if we look at this TF, we see
 the lower black line wich is a clear demand too.

So, to resume everything so far , we have had a reaction of Monthly
Demand , price then traded , we also have a weekly close (last week's
candle) that closed below another weekly demand wich now turned Supply.

So far I'm thinking that a revisit of Demand might therefore be an option.

Next chart is the Daily one, I added an upper blue dahed line wich is

Cheers guys, thanks a lot.

HR,

Ok, I have marked a chart for you, hopefully I could help you out with it.

Don't forget that price already bounced from HTF demand here and we saw sign of buying off demand.

There are 2 types of engulfing that I'm aware off, Engulfing candles and Engulfing of a zone/Flag/Supply-Demand

Engulfings of zones are very powerfull, they happen for different reasons:

1) To consume the remaining supply (short orders) or demand (long orders)

2) Clear the path for the future, like Red used to say, Price thinks ahead of time

3) Fake traders out and get them envolved in a wrong direction and take their stops.

As you can see from the example below, price engulfed the Supply and price came back to a demand level within the range.

Btw, If has a video about engulfings, I highly recommend you to watch it.

I hope this helps,

Mel

posts.author: Ifmyante
posts.text:
OK.

Start with getting to understand the PAZ. There's tons of info about it around lately.

Think about where to look for trades - At the edge of the PAZ and nowhere else

Understand what you need to see to know that the PAZ edge has been respected or broken - an engulf

Learn the PA setups based on the engulf, and don't forget the Cancan!

That's it

There's no more to it

Nothing!

posts.text:
Hi everyone

I'm happy to be back and thank you IF for putting me on the list.

I decided to start a new journal here, but this time it will be more
results oriented. I'm going to post my statements regularly regardless
of how good/bad it is. The reason for that is that I want to be honest
about my performance in order to not create unrealistic expectations for
 new members - that can happen when winning trades are posted (mostly)
and great setups explained. It all looks logical and easy in hindsight
but even though I have a good understanding, in real time I have doubts
all the time and it is difficult to make a good decision.

So I'm going to talk about ways/techniques I will use to improve my
performance and whether it worked or not, and if I managed to apply it
correctly. I am also going to post a lot of setups with detailed
explanations and commentary, as I used to in my old journal.

Here goes my first statement. I started trading this account 25th of
January - it is demo, because there is a lot of things I can improve,
and losing a lot of real money had a really bad effect on my psyche and I
 had to take a break from trading... Trading live is no time for
improvements - all bad habits can be changed while trading on demo and
that is what I intend to do. I will continue this until I can see
consistent results on weekly basis for the period of 2 months at least.

The number of trades is much higher than a number of setups I traded. It
 is something I need to work on - I enjoy too much pressing these
buttons. Also, there is a ton of breakeven/small loss/small profit
trades - this is where I make an impulsive decision, or bad decision and
 realize it - then I close trades to avoid further losses. Overtrading
is something I struggle with for a long time now, also respecting
trading rules etc.

I don't know if there is a hope in trading career for people like me,
but I'm not going to give up... I think that I slightly improve over
time even though I'm nowhere near to overcoming all psychological
challenges of trading. The current result may seem pretty decent right
now but the real challenge will come when I'll have next losing streak. I
 had one already - I survived, but suffered 10% drawdown. It was
basically 2 setups where I entered too many times breaking MM rules.
Another big issue is entering after a reaction to a level - RR is worse
and bounce already happened - pointless. I'll work on that as well and
I'll post updates on my progress in this journal.

Where do I look for trades?

What I aim to do is to take touch trades in the direction of the trend.
But by trend, I mean situation when the price is coming from a valid
zone and didn't reach the target yet. I basically try to find places for
 a touch trade after continuation engulfs. I do this when ITs have
positions open and add on retraces by stopping traders out. When I see
that price is reacting to valid target and there is some kind of
reversal I assume ITs are short (for example) and then I look for
opportunities to join the move. So even though most of my trades can be
classified as continuation trades, all of them are reversal trades at
the same time - because if I sell, I sell against strong (usually)
bullish move on smaller scale, and vice versa.

It is important to analyze all scales and to make sure that you are not
trading against direction signaled by engulf on a higher scale.

I'll quickly mark EUR/USD charts to show what I mean:

This quasimodo is beautiful you can see how clever ITs are. Look how
long price was going up. As price moves up more and more people are
biased long and then big push happens. The way I think about this is as
follows: ITs don't have to do much here. People are biased long and ITs
"add fuel to the fire" to make the move look strong/scary/exciting,
whatever. The point is that now price is where they want to sell at and
people keep buying this thinking that price will go up forever . Btw. there is a big daily "marubozu" candle after pin bar - some people consider this an excellent buy signal.

Countertrend moves are usually strong and it may be counter-intuitive to
 trade against but that is what we do. Here is nice examples of moves
like that. I marked them with arrows. Red lines show where people got
stopped out recently. So I think that ITs are still short and there is
potential for continuation as there is a lot of space below.

Of course, it is easy to mark this stuff in hindsight - much harder to
do it real time because it often seems that move is genuine and it will
stop you out, but you need to pay attention to bigger picture and trade
against moves like these fearlessly.

posts.author: Michal238
posts.text:
I have currently one trade open on eurusd, that I didn't explain in my
 last post. It is a nice example of continuation trade. I noticed some
time ago that there are a lot of continuation opportunities after
breaking QM levels. And there is a good reason for that so this setup
gives me a nice opportunity to elaborate on that.

I try to look at price more in terms of orders opened by ITs. So at this
 point, we can say that there was a quasimodo, and then more shorts were
 opened on the way down (see my last post). The idea for continuation or
 at least bounce from broken QM lvl seems logical to me. Because I ask
myself this - what needs to happen for QM lvl to be broken? We know that
 people get trapped and orders remain at the level - in this case, buy
orders. If ITs want to push the price down they need to sell against buy
 orders. So they have shorts orders open at the level. If price goes
above this price level then it means that they will get into drawdown on
 these positions. They don't want drawdown, so they will protect this
level by adding shorts and pushing price down.

There are also other things to consider, for example - had ITs have a
chance to reverse positions already? or is there a better place for
retrace? You can see on my chart that there is no obvious better place
for retrace (CP).

This eurusd chart is beautiful, setups are rarely this clean. Its still
possible that I am wrong of course. But thinking about orders in this
way will allow for great trades when your read is correct.

So what I learned is that compression is a great indicator of where you
can expect short retrace. Sometimes price moves from a target area, and
didn't reach the opposite target, and there is "no space" for deep
retraces - so you can get in on the move on short RT.

posts.text:
I took a lot of trades this week, too much to post in real time so I'm
 going to post them in bulk. As I go forward with this journal I'll work
 on reducing the number of entries and posting them more often. I
unintentionally developed a habit of entering many times with small lots
 instead of picking one entry point. There are a lot of reasons for
that, for example:

- entering before FL (fear of missing out), and then adding more when the price gets closer to MPL

- being afraid to enter with full risk before price reacts to a level
and. Seeing price bounce gives me a feeling of being correct, so I
enter. But this feeling is not really based on my knowledge. We need to anticipate and not react
 to what price is doing. So the best moment to buy is before any signs
of price rising occur, and same goes for shorts. I think that most of
traders experience this - when the price is moving up it feels like it
will countinue, and vice versa. Sometimes even direction of the last M1
 candle influences how I feel about my trade. I need to learn to ignore
this feeling.

- not being prepared for entry beforehand. When this happens I see price
 reacting to something, then I do analysis, I find out that price is
reacting to a MPL of some important level and then I try to enter

I think that using only pending orders is the way to go. Using
pending orders means that I was prepared for entry and I anticipate what
 will happen, and I was completely prepared with my analysis beforehand
instead of reacting to what price is currently doing.

Here is my statement. This week was a fail, biggest drawdown so far. But
 it shed some light at biggest mistakes that I make in trading.

Last week only:

So, as you can see at the beginning of the week I had a lot of winners
and I took partial profits regularly. But then after a couple of losers
instead of trading the bounces, I tried to catch swings and holding
trades until it hits final TP to make up for losses. Trying to catch a
swing is probably the biggest mistakes I make in trading. And it happens
 because I try to recover from losses. Of course, it doesn't happen and I
 only lose more. This happens when I am strongly convinced that price
didn't hit the TG yet, and I am often right, but the problem with
catching swings is that:

- I ignore good entry points - because I don't want to miss the obvious move

- I don't take partial profits

- I move my stops because there is still valid engulf signal that didn't play out yet or I enter soon after being stopped out

- I don't wait for deepest possible RT

This big drawdown is the result of doing that on two correlated pairs at the same time, and this was a break of MM rules.

The red circle is where I took the biggest loss - I not only moved my SL
 but also added at the next level. Around the same time, I was trying to
 catch a move on GU, and I lost a lot. I am still convicted that EU and
GU will go down, I will write why in my next post with the trades that I
 have currently open.

It was okay to short EU, but I did it incorrectly. I didn't wait for
best prices with my entries and I didn't take partial TPs. Look at these
 left shoulder levels, and how embarrassing my trades look now:

The correct way to trade is to take touch trades in direction of the
trend, and the trend is down on EU (because it is coming from a valid
level and TG for shorts is not hit yet). Entry from PO, then TP1 after
the bounce at 1-2R, so that after SL overall result is small profit or
BE.

So the goal for next week is put more time into analyzing charts in the
evening and in the morning and finding places where I can set POs. I'll enter only from POs and take TP1 after the bounce. If I failed to take TP1 after the bounce, I'll close my trade at BE.

engulf before price reached this level, but compression on approach told

 next FTR below.

posts.author: Michal238
posts.text:
Hi guys.

naascott

There are few things I want to see when I'm looking for good DP:

- it can be located on swap zone

- FO zone can be created below it ( short scenario)

- also I like to see CP above strong DP - if price is compressed above,
then it is more likely that price will be reversed on this DP - it is
only fresh DP in the area

DP is a barrier to ITs, because another sellers are waiting on this
level (short scenario), so they need to do their manipulations before
price reaches it - they need to create LQ and when they do that we see
reversal patterns, FO zones etc.

bobyv87

FL and PAZ between them work in every TF, therefore some FLs are more
important than others, smaller or bigger FLs. There are diffrent
cycles.

It's quite difficult to learn spot all of this correctly but with a lot
of practice it will become clear. And don't forget to look left:

Markers are usually small FLs - ITs use them to reverse price before DP.
 I like to see when price bouces from this level few times - it creates
FO zone below DP which provides LQ for ITs. I enter on FO to DP after
confirmation - in this case it was eng into CPPAZ on approach. I thik
that after this reversal PA SL can be above DP (grey box - because it is
 FL in itself - you can see this on m1 chart). But if situation is not
very clear then you may use wider SL.

To define cycles you have to evaluate importance of FL. I'm not an
expert at this yet, because I still have some things to learn about PAZ,

on chart. I find it difficult to explain though. You have to think
about space between FL's. When you find space that is limited from both

direction of eng. Befere this happens price creates Fls as it retraces,
but these FLs don't affect main move. They work in different cycles.

is high that didn't engulf anything. Price engulfed FL at 3 and FL was
made at 4.

This folder contains everything related to trading, but majority of charts is FL analysis.

Number of folders is so big, because I have many setups saved in
separate folders, and I make new folder for every session on FT2

I realized recently that I'm pretty bad at decision making, I'm not
patient enough on live charts, and I tend to make the same mistakes many
 times due to loose analysis.

So I set some rules regarding my analysis during practise on FT2:

I test one pair at a time and I have 3 separate charts. One is for
general HTF view and I mark most important lvls and FLs on it.

Second chart is for LTF FL analysis - sometimes it gets messy and that is why I need more than one chart.

On third chart I mark S/R flips, swaps lvls - it is easy to miss them when chart is not neat and clean.

Doing this I'm sure that I used propely my best analysis tools, and I wont do mistakes that could easily been avoided.

And this is how I'm going to improve my decision making:

- I take screenshots with my analysis and mark best places to look for PA

- as price is approaching my lvl, I make decision - do I wait for
confirmation or can I TT? why? I write this on screenshot. Decision is
made.

- let's say that I took TT. At this point I have marked on chart
different sized FL that were formed on approach - I decide where is my
TP1 and where

are potential trouble areas

- I make screen after TP1 , and then after every continuation ENG, or reversal ENG.

- reversal ENG - I close my trade

- continuation ENG - I make decision - where I'll let price retrace to, before closing my trade? where in next FL?

As price is moving away (or towards) my entry I mark new FLs that are
created, I mark CP, and strong SD lvls / ignored SD lvls, using always

the same colors. I don't want to miss/ forget anything. Also I do this to develop habists:

strong SD lvls formed against me ----> look for exit

CP between my entry, and current price ----> I move my SL above last fresh SD lvl

FL not engulfed --> exit

etc.

I know that this is basic stuff, but sometimes I ignored important
information, because I wanted my FL analysis to be correct every single
time.

Its stupid, I know, but I have done this in the past on live account

Every trade is narrated, and I also try to think like IT - what they want to accomplish, where is LQ for them

- what are doing trend followers?

- what are doing BO traders?

- what are doing savy SD traders?

In the next month I will continue practising in this way, and what is
most important - I also want to apply this method to live charts.

In this way I will have everything propely analysed, and decisions will be made only once - I wont stay undecided at any time.

Analysis is made ---> its time to make decisions and write it down.

New piece of PA created --> make analysis marking FLs, SD, CPs ---> make decision, just like on FT2

I described briefly how my perfect price reading session looks like.
Probably I will post here example of this on real charts soon.

It is easy to just fast-forward charts not thinking much about it. Its
tempting as well - because there is a part of me that enjoys gambling.

What I want to achieve in my every single price reading session is
called "deliberate practice" - it takes big ammount of effort,

but I believe that in this way I can get great results.

Thought I would take a crack at this, as it was a good exercise for me as well. Here's my take, which include some adaptations I've made for my own trading: 1) First FTR: Validly identified. However I look for the RBR that every DBR reacts to (The DBR in this case being your FTR). This RBR was not engulfed where you marked, so I wouldn't consider the next level an FTR. And the RBR bounced price nicely to the next supply on this timeframe.

2) If you follow/agree with the logic of #1, then the 2nd FTR marked is not an actual FTR. And it also seems as part of a compression, so I wouldnt look to trade it, nor would I look for an engulf of the level to ID the next FTR. 3) 3rd FTR identified not valid as per my rules because of statements in #2. But when the compression is broken a little higher, I see a nice FL created which bounces price a couple of times in that flag (above where you marked your 3rd ftr). Thats a nice trade.

Also looking to the right, when that FL breaks, looks like a new FL is formed and a nice bounce from it when revisited.

4) Your fourth FTR would not be an FTR, even if the first 3 were valid, because a lower low was not made.

5) Because of #4, your 5th FTR was not valid.

It really is a pain in the A because if you identify one thing wrong, it can lead to a series of incorrect levels.

Also - assuming all were identified correctly, it also pays to look at the quality of the level. So each FTR is pretty much a RBD or DBR. Look at each on your timeframe, and see which of these you see a clear drop, basing, then rally (or vice versa). It's really only the 3rd FTR which could meet this criteria. Alot of them CP into or out of the base which isnt great. And the 3rd one likely didnt react because it wasnt actually an FTR.

Hope this helps! This is just my take, though. Would love to hear others' input.

The FTR setup starts with "some important barrier" being engulfed to start off the process. For me, identifying this barrier regularly is my main challenge.

Just my two cents!

3rd last arrow from the right is demand and the second from the right is ignored demand. See how if marked the box? He marked between decisions and high = PAZ.

Not sure what your analysis was trying to say, but here's my take on the important elements and what i'm expecting price to do: a. First major trend points down so i'm looking for a short entry. 1. H1 demand (not supply) broke as you identified, but i wouldn't call that a decision. It gives you a clue that price wants turn continue down at some point. 2. Price is stepping up and engulfs the first FL to the left, signifying it wants to continue higher to Supply above. 3. Price retraces and starts bouncing up from the newly created FL to the left, as expected. 4. I'm anticipating price will reach Supply at 4 before turning down past 1.

and here's what actually happened...

1. Price does not engulf the previous high before turning, which tells me it might not reach Supply above before contining its trend down.

2. Price engulfs previous low. This tells me price is ready to continue down.

3. Price hits the FTR and goes down past our initial H1 demand engulf.

So price didn't react exactly as we expected, but pretty close. Gotta be ready to change plans based on what price actually does.

You will hit walls but keep going you will soon see the truth!

posts.author: moneydeep
posts.text:
First I would like to start with a very heartfelt thanks to IF for RTM and even more to Salivan who showed me the way. and his posts really fast tracked my learning. "There is zero chaos in the Market" FOF is the Key.

I have been here around 3 months and after going through marketpedia I
started reading the various Journals starting with IF's and Salivan's.
All the answers have been provided by Salivan and looking at it now I
understand but even a month ago I would read his words and would still
not get it. I then took a small holiday and came back and started
studying the charts again and I have to agree with him when he says
screen time is key. Now When I look at a blank chart unfilled orders pop
 out like sore thums.

I would read Salivan's posts then go to traders gym and trade. (Trade
interceptor is basically a free version of forex tester. You can log in
to Traders gym in there and trade the historical data. It has upto 5
years worth hourly charts and 20 years or so of daily history data) I
would draw FL and see where price would react.

As salivan says there are so many FL in the chart but what makes one
bounce price and another not is FOF. What we need to find is where the
IT still has orders left and the level hasn't been hit yet on the way
up. And a FL will still have orders until the mpl has been hit to the
pip. If not then the IT want lower/higher prices. Study ORFL those are
very important and are always good for a bounce. I will not get more
into this as it is all there in Salivan's posts. I would suggest you
study that.

I guess what I am trying to say is even after being taught the basics
once you start looking at the charts and think what the IT want thats
when things will become much more clear. And as IF and Salivan have
both constantly reiterated, look from the higher time frame down.

Where is the nearest monthly demand FL and monthly supply FL targets?

Based on current price what are IT doing buying or selling to the target?

Drill down to weekly and repeat

Down to daiy and repeat

Down to hourly repeat

Now you will start seeing eg. IT are accumulating on monthly FL and the
most recent supply FL has been engulfed so now you know the next target
FL. You now drill down lower and you find the FTR in the DP of an hourly
 swing which in turn is a monthly FL and now you have a potential 5 pip
risk trade with a 500-700 pip monthly FL target.

All the tools needed are here in RTM. There are various ways to trade RTM but what stuck with me was FOF. Thanks again Salivan.

I have been busy with a full time job but I am very satisfied with what I have learnt and can hopefully start trading soon.

I would like to share a chart which should fast track your learning.

FIND THE DP OF THE BREAK This is just scratching the surface but when you dig deeper things should start becoming more clear.

posts.author: moneydeep
posts.text:
I would like to post these quotes of IF which I have copied from
Salivan's journal. I looked at them recently and realised I understand a
 lot of things which IF is saying which I didn't understand when I
started RTM. I know that I will understand more of it when I read it
again a month later. Hope this helps some of you too.

• If the signal is given by the market mover (an engulf into a new
zone), then price is very unlikely to break the extreme of the zone it
just came from. So, if you have the patience to wait at the last
remaining set of unfilled orders in the origin, you can be almost
certain that that price will be respected.

• There is absolute order in the market. Nothing at all there happens by
 chance. That's why it's so easy to read what's going to happen next.
There are rules which are strictly followed; so much so you'd imagine
it's all run by algorithms, up to the moment when the signal is decided
upon, and straight away thereafter. There is zero chaos in the market.
It's elegantly designed; a beauty to behold.

• Fakeouts are extremely easy to predict. Most SD traders still look
directly left, which is the big shortcoming of Supply/Demand trading.
It's further left again we should be looking.

• Say price is coming up to a supply. The only way we can be sure that
supply will hold price down is if that supply has already visited the
extreme set of orders in the flag limit to its left. If the supply fell
short of that, we can anticipate a FO to those extreme orders. Extremely
 simple stuff.

• We always look to what S or D are reactions to, rather than just S or D themselves.

• Look for tricks being played on approach to a place where a trick was played, and you'll find where price will turn.

• If you can look beyond S/D, you'll see that the Flag Limit is the only
 true place to look for PA for a trade. Trade these levels and you're
taking gambling out of your method.

• All we can ever hope for is a bounce at these levels, unless we are
certain that this level is the deepest possible point of retrace after a
 previous engulf. Without that, we must watch PA as it develops, both
before and during the trade. Set and Forget trades can only be taken
once the signal is given and the target is clear.

• Being patient is absolutely vital for making giant trades. We must
wait for the very best possible places before we enter; the places where
 you'd expect great PA to react.

• If you're around to watch the PA unfold, it's rare your stop should
get hit. Price will so very often retrace enough for you to get out
without a loss. That's why I wait for the very best price to TT - it
tends to keep me in the black.

• I'm not even a part time trader now, so I miss nearly every piece of
action there is. If I ever open the charts and see a trade opp right in
front of me, I take it. However, I usually get between 10R and 25R per
trade. If I lose, it's usually no more than the spread and commission.
There are between 5 and 20 such confirmed trades available every day.

• First of all, we need to understand that time has no place in any read
 of the market. The only way to be completely sure of where a FL is, is
to be there when the break occurs, and mark the highs and lows as they
occur. Within a minute they can be obscured by a candle, but we'll know
exactly where they are. If we're not there to watch and mark, we must
use the full candle as a FL.

• If we've had an engulf and are getting in on a RT, we must always be
ready for a diamond to occur, especially if price hasn't yet hit MPL of
the zone the original bounce was a reaction to. So, if we're not going
to be around to watch PA, our stop must be beyond the original FL.

• Funny you should say that, as I teach to always and only trade within a
 flag. Sometimes the flag will already have developed, and sometimes the
 flag is to be made while you're in the trade. Either way, always trade
within a flag.

• Attune yourself to what the buggers are doing, and don't let them fool
 you. Just know they've got orders to fill at a level, watch them fill
some on approach (CP), see the momentum, and watch them come back to
fill more orders 'til they've had their fill.

• This perhaps should be the first thing that anybody ever reads
regarding trading: We're always looking for signs of what the big guys
are doing at significant areas, and if we don't see what they're doing,
there's no trade. So, on approach, if we see the big guys trying to hide
 their orders in the market, we see compression, and can feel pretty
sure of their intentions - to get in as many orders as they can before
the turn If we don't see this, we can be pretty sure that it won't just
turn immediately, as there usually won't be enough orders against them
to fill all the orders they must fill. This is why we wait for an
engulf. This shows their intention to reverse price. Then we watch them
trying to hide their orders in the market on a retrace, ready to take
price to the origin of the move.

• When we see decent CP coming into the base of a pole, we are very
often safe to touch trade the base. The safest thing to do however is to
 await the first engulf into the cp zone as confirmation.

• Very often a zone will break strongly and price will retrace but fail
to retouch it. This is still the FTR - the confirmation of a new trend
(do a study of how price reacts and how far it goes after hitting this
spot). So an FTR can be first time back, but doesn't need to be.

• During holidays, volume in the market is often greatly diminished.
This would lead some to imagine that price hardly moves. But. Say
someone decided to put a truckload of orders into the market. If there's
 nobody else in the market to oppose these orders, price can do nothing
but shoot away. So remember. Low Volume can = High Volatility.

• Until now I have been so unfocused on the charts that my exits have
been very sloppy. My trade plan now has a couple of variables, but
essentially I'll let price travel back to the other edge of the last PAZ
 in the TF I'm trading. If it engulfs, I'll exit on a RT or a break of
the next LTF FL. If it rejects, I'll let the trade run and await exit
PA.

• It's all about getting into the mind of the market makers and trading as they do. Nothing special.

• Most of my analysis comes in after the trade is entered. Before taking
 the trade, I do as you said - simple - it's really easy to find pockets
 of orders which will bounce price, and if they happen to be at great
htf levels, even better - there's the highest chance of them giving
maximum pips. What I do certainly looks like touch trading - picking
tops and bottoms, but what you said belies that. These are not tops and
bottoms, but retraces to the best price to re enter. Once I'm in though,
 I'm never guaranteed massive returns - sure price will bounce where I
enter, but I'm never complacent until I've seen the engulf. In fact, I'm
 never really complacent at all. If PA tells me to get out, I must get
out!

• Many might misconstrue us as pattern recognition traders - we're not.
Certainly while learning we look for recurring patterns in the market.
But once we understand them, what becomes most important is WHY the ITs
made them. It's paramount to understand that it's not enough for the ITs
 to simply move price. They must also get massive amounts of orders
filled in order to make maximum gains. They must also refrain from
giving other ITs false signals, which could ultimately cause chaos for
everybody. Think of these things as you study, and you'll be able to get
 into the mind of the market mover.

• Here are just a few targets for price, and the QM level is a big one.
Certainly we need to get PA for entry before or once it's hit. If it
breaks, then the same level can have the opposite effect on return.

• Once price engulfs a level, all that's important is how far it
retraces before hitting its target. While the pockets of orders remain
in this RT, it remains strong. If price totally compresses (picking up
all orders) forward from the tip of the RT, then we will look primarily
for the orders at the entrance to said CP.

• To the ITs, candle closes don't mean a damned thing, so please don't use them in your own analysis.

• A line is not the answer. Certainly, you may draw a line, but you must
 then go into the LTF to find a DBR/RBD on the right side of the LL/HH
swing which covers that line. That RBD/DBR will be your box. You can
scalp from each of these, knowing that it may only be a scalp. If you're
 simply setting a PO, then you must set your stop beyond the FL the
HH/LL is a reaction to.

• The usable engulf is the one which hasn't hit its target. Every engulf
 has a very specific target. Apply that statement to your charts and
eventually you'll see what I mean.

• Being only a sporadic trader (I really couldn't sit and watch the
charts all day anymore!), I tend to open the charts from time to time
and ask myself what's coming up in the next few minutes for me to take.
If I'm lucky, I'll open the charts when we're at an HTF level. If not,
I'll gladly take whatever high R M1 or whatever is there for the
picking. 30 pips with a 3 pip stop is exactly the same as 150 pips with a
 15. If there's nothing decent to take, I shut the charts.

• If I were asked where to trade, in one word, I'd say: Stops

• I'm way too disorganised to use limit orders! I just open the charts
from time to time, and if I see the ITs scaring the retailers into
closing good trades at a good level, I enter. I'll take off some of the
position at the first target, so if my stop gets taken I can profit
overall, then watch PA level by level. If price doesn't get into a big
zone quickly, I'll usually get bored and go flat, having made enough to
cover my next week's expenses. If I were truly meticulous, I'd treat my
exits the same as my entries, and trade up and down all day, but trading
 is usually way down on my to-do list.

• Certainly there's an awful lot to learn here. But if I were to
summarise what I think is most important, I'd say look to an engulf into
 free space that hasn't yet hit the origin (tg). Very often it will
retrace deeply before advancing to the origin. Learn to spot these, and
you'll be better equipped than most other traders out there.

• Price moves from PAZ to PAZ. The clear target for any trade after an
engulf is the other end of the PAZ in that TF. If you zoom out to HTFs,
you may find the TG is even further, but if not, stick to the TF you're
in.

• I just want to warn you though that watching candles is an absolute
waste of time. It distracts you from reading the story of price. The
chart is a page, and a candle is a word. A word in itself has little
meaning; it can be taken out of context. Sure, a sentence can be very
powerful, as can a group of candles. But to get a real sense of the
story, we need to view it all as a whole - be aware of how this
paragraph relates to one many chapters back, and get a sense of where
the story will lead in the future.

• In essence, we know that if price engulfs South, it wants to move down to the last engulf North.

• We want to read the story of price, and believe me, price has a story!
 You'll need to go further left to get your analysis right. Yes, you've
marked levels well, but what are those levels a reaction to? Without
knowing this, you're just gambling. So, look left, read the story, and
be better equipped to predict what'll come next.

• Ask yourself "Why did price shoot up from there?" You'll answer
"Because someone wanted to buy a lorryload, but there was nobody willing
 to sell at that price, so price shot up to find sellers." The next
question you'll ask yourself is "Will he have left orders to buy again
at that price?" The answer is usually "yes". Next question is "will
price reverse from there?" The answer is, "Well, it may well bounce form
 there, but we won't know if it'll reverse until an engulf tells us it's
 reversed"

• Of course, the extremes in one TF can be midrange in another TF, which
 is why it's vital to manage your adds in the lower TF until they break
into HTF trades.

• Okay! One giant clue: If something which should have been important got ignored, then it will be given great import on return.

• Personally, I love to dissect the HTF zone, in LTF, and look for a DBR
 or RBD within it, where price had broken out of a box and failed to get
 back in.

• Whipsaw engulfing - a fakeout followed by a quick return breaking the last zone. It's great PA.

• An excellent Supply or Demand zone is one where the future has already
 been written. Having done some study of the markets, we know that once
we have an engulf of a zone, price will want to go to the origin. So we
look to where the trend change was confirmed - FTR.

• You must study the zone which is being reacted to just as much as the reaction itself.

• Just consider the manipulation of hope and fear at turning points, and you'll have a very valuable eureka moment.

• When you begin to see the symmetry in the market, you're making one of the final steps in reading and predicting it.

• High R is High R, and these trades happen with great frequency. I
applaud this easy way of making good money. If you're at the MPL of an
HTF level, however, think about taking enough at LTF tg1 to cover the
HTF stop, and letting the trade run.

• A bit of simple advice, to avoid overtrading and impulse trading: Draw
 up the most important looking zones, and look for trades only there.

• We absolutely must have an hard stop, always. But if we don't have an
engulf before entry, we don't put it directly above the high or below
the low, where all the retail stops lie. Instead, we find a lovely LTF
RBD/DBR just beyond, and put it on the other side of that, so that we
have the best chance to get out at BE or in big profit from the usual
RT.

• There's no indication that a demand has been respected until the source above has been engulfed.
