Area 2

So now that I analyzed Area 1 and know that price broke into new historical highs, I am going to recap the move up from Area 1 into the new highs and what would have been the requirements to trade along the way.

First chart up is the monthly:

Here we clearly see that the up move started from Area 1 which was a FO to a monthly low as well as to a previous swing low on to its left. The confirmation that it was a FO came on this TF once we broke above the swing high between points 1 &2.

1- Here is the DBR, FO, QM & FTR, this will in the future be an excellent area to buy off of as is indicated by the arrow down pointing to Area 5. 2- After price broke the swing high (SH1) between 1 & 2, it flagged, broke the flag up into an FTR where it reacted creating another flag that also broke higher into the tip of the swing high 2 (SH2). There it retraced down to the local FL of the last break up before engulfing the SH2, it retraces creating another FL @ 3 & up it went. 3- This is the FL of the break of SH2 also some clear demand left there on this TF. Price between 3 & 2 is compressed and the only demand left is at the edges i.e. pts 3 & 2. 4- Price reaches prior highest historical high of the time & cuts right through that resistance creating the final FL of this TF before the RBD higher up. The supply below resistance @ 1.45350 was clearly consumed & if you notice that top is quite compressed. Also an important note is noticing the long wicked candles inside the yellow FL. They also imply lots of consumption of buy orders, not a great sign in case we wanted to buy that zone when price came back. 5- This is the area in focus and up till here in this TF I would want to see an engulf of the yellow FL for any shorts to take place. However, we know that as price moves it keeps on creating FLs and there’s one more I can see in here which is between the two bullish bars right under Area 2. It is marked with a “?” as we need to make sure it is a FL and also we need to define it.

Next chart is the D1, W1 didn’t show me much… So here I want to investigate and see first if the FL I pointed out to earlier with a “?” is in fact one. From the looks of it is.

But I want to look into its build up… So here is M30

This zone has seen many FOs as it was being constructed. I am guessing that whenever something like this happens it only stretches the boundaries of a flag. Now we know that this area should hold price up when it comes back to it & if it breaks it would also be a great place to trade since it would flip polarities. So this becomes out next FL in line on the MN chart for a trade short after the break.

Back to daily

Here after we have defined our higher new MN FL in yellow we get a D1 local FL from which we could take the FTB which was also into D1 demand up to its origin at the last RBD supply.

Even thought a lot of seniors don’t advise to trade a FL area more than its FTB, I think they’ve mentioned that other setups in the zone are valid if PA confirms. So here I’ll show one other long setup from the same D1 FL but on H4

Finally before price moves out of our monthly/weekly base we get a very important heads up on what might be going on. A D1 FTR gets engulfed and unfortunately I do not see any opportunity to enter on smaller TFs… here’s the FTR

Area 3

The relevance of the broken lows at points 1, 2, & 3 are respectively associated with the breaks at A, B & C. Therefor on this TF they hold lots of weight compared to other ones that can be mostly considered local breaks.

Point 4 is as was discussed earlier the last FL before the big drop, thus the most important zone in this rally into Area 2.

The SR shows great history in several areas in the past, the most prominent one being the last time it acted as resistance before the big bullish candle that broke A (at X). The SR also shows lots of importance if we were to see it on a line chart.

When price broke down through all of 4, 3, 2, & 1, big NEW decisions were made along the way.

Now, I think there are two types of decisions in the market, prime & secondary. The former would be the break of something important like FL, FTR, Swing, SR, SD etc… & the latter the decision to either respect that initial decision (with a FL/FTR) or to reject it (with an Engulf of the primary in the opposite direction). Our job here at RTM is to follow in the footsteps of the last primary decision made until proven wrong (I think!!!), of course while bearing in mind all of what we have so generously been taught i.e. knowing where we are in terms of HTFs S/D and acting in our best interest.

As human beings first and traders second I believe our attention is drawn to chaos over harmony & clutter over order. The reason I say this is because I always seem to pick the wrong areas to trade from and suffer the consequences of this visual incompetence. In the following chart is an example;

In this chart we have the base of our previously discussed Area 2. In it I have highlighted the two most important FLs (IMHO) that were responsible for holding price up throughout this zone of balance. The upper green one bounced price back up 8 times as is seen on this TF. Now we know that the more a zone is visited the more orders get depleted from it especially if no newer orders are placed there. What I mean by that last part is, if you look at point A, this candle went really deep into the zone and must have picked up a lot of the remaining orders in the zone if not all of them. I for one would have definitely thought it would break down on the next visit after A… but it does not… why??? Because newer orders were placed there again. Be they limit or market orders… doesn’t matter… ITs bought there on two other occasions before finally breaking the green zone. So in other words, a zone is not broke b4 it is broke.

After the green price cuts through the yellow. Look at that beauty of a WRB! Nice! Had this been real time I am not even sure I would have given the yellow importance over the green… I know I wouldn’t have! Why look at all the action that took place in the green, isn’t this the area to look for a juicy short for when & if price comes back… surely! …. WRONG!!! First price doesn’t make it there, second, hell if I was an IT why would I want to sell in an obvious place such as the green? So I’m slowly coming to the conclusion that the most important areas could be those we pay very little attention to like the yellow one.

Here’s the return to it

Excuse my delay on the initial analysis of Area 3… back into it now… So the last thing we were discussing was the new decisions made on the way down. Here they are;

Price breaks A & B retraces at 1 & goes lower making 1 a W1 FTR

Price then breaks C retraces up to 2 where it reacts very strongly because of 1 and continues down to D. In the process the continuation of price through point X makes 2 another W1 FTR.

Down to daily for a clearer view on the rest

Price breaks D makes a low at Z retraces up to Y and then it’s back on the way down through Z into E. Making 3 a FL with an FTR at Y. Price halts at the SR back from the first chart. Now we also see that the latest FL gets engulfed north signaling opposition. This one goes back to 3 as an FTB and we could have traded the return into confirmed demand in 4 once price came back targeting Y. Entering is one thing, holding is another… I don’t think I would have had the patience before starting to second guess myself as this is often the case.

Price then engulfs the FL at 3 & the FTR at Y, reaches ultimate target which is the second W1 FTR and drops as expected. Let’s see if I could get an entry…

Price engulfs the last FL on the way up, creates a flag (around our previous low C from chart 4) and breaks another important zone before returning to give a chance at 1. The approach into 1 is a weak one as is evident.

Stop would be above the zone of the flipped FL

This would be target… next zone in line on H4

Entry would be on M15 after the ENG and on RT to line C (previous SR)

We then make it to target and beyond into the source of the move that rallied all the way up to the second W1 FTR… A second visit to Area 3 (to be continued in a while…. Sorry I need a break

Ok a little recap on the target…

Had I looked better Target should have been lower. Here is the chart;

On the left we have the FL from post #34 Chart # 5 with an upper limit (FTR) Y & a lower limit Z. Zone A was the decision that was made to break the lower limit. And when price came back there it gave us the FTB to the FL at B. Then at C price broke through that decision “A” creating another FL. This should have been target! important, E is very important because it broke the yellow FL on the left & FTR Y. So now a break of E and or C becomes significant... They both break and result in the creation of new important prime and secondary decisions.

Here we clearly see both breaks of E & C with their respective FTRs marked as FTR1 & FTR2 followed by their FTBs pointed to in white arrows. Now when price broke through FL C it got to the upper part of the base of the last DBR and started to react to demand there. It came to FTR2 and went back down consuming more long orders from previous untested demand zones. As it was dipping into the base it was also removing lots of sell orders as is evident in the compressed tops. It reaches the final untested demand before curling up and heading into FTR1.

For some the CP action is enough to get them in a position, I’d rather get it confirmed…

There are three ways a position could have been entered as I see it

1- Based on a FO of a D1 low with a PO at the green horizontal line after the candle “a” breaks the low & closes above. A fill would have come in the following day at “b” with stops below the zone of the untested demand. BUT that is an entry for the brave and since I am not I drop lower…

2- A second option would be once price came back to the source of the ENG move on H4, which was a FTR on H1 entry.

3- The final option which I would chose, the FTR setup on H4 with a white arrow pointing to where I’d try to get in. In all three cases the stop would be the same below the zone of the untested demand.

Area 5

Because I made my homework I knew I should expect some kind of reaction at this level. I couldn’t know that for sure until it did react (that is something I am drilling into my head).

Just look at the history of this SR/QM level! Notice the orange arrows in the past there. There was some serious buying.

Point A is the low of 2008 i.e. the lowest point price got to during the crash of that year.

Point B is the low of 2009, and as is clear during the beginning of that year when price came into the zone of the low of A, there were buyers. Why? Because it was last year’s low zone from which point price rallied, so people bought again. Isn’t’ that text book herd behavior? When price visits those levels again what is the expectation of the ITs? They’ll know that there surely will be buyers around those levels following the “buy low, sell high” advice no? Also wouldn’t there be break out traders salivating over price going down to hell? Surely…

What happens next is buyers & sellers get tripped for their stops, the ITs fill their huge orders and price rallies. This can be clearly seen through the candles 1,2 & 3.

On this TF we also see that the drop in A cleared all the demand down to A, engulfing the previous FTR at X which implies that SHOULD (not a necessity) price ever cross below A it will go down to the next FTR in line. I like to look for clean, clear, untested preferably non-local FTRs.

Now price keeps going until it hits a wall of buyers around our QM level. If I were to be strictly trading this TF I would need C to get taken out of the way before considering buying.

Here are the FTRs in line and they all fall inside our bigger zone from weekly. The middle one I did not project it into the future as it had already been tested pointed to with an orange arrow. So watching PA there on nothing less than D1 TF is the safest since a lot of chop can happen before a decision is taken. Once a decision has been made on D1 and I can clearly see that only then will I start going lower.

Here we see price cuts through the previous yearly lows B & A, hesitates a little then drops into FTR1, bounces from there up to the supply where the decision (also a FL area) was made to break into B & A, creates area C now also a FTR (same C from previous chart) and goes back down to FTR1 where again a lot of buy and sell orders are being exchanged (In another life I would be stuck in this chop!). After the ENG it was decided that price will in fact go lower. The deciding factors here are the move beyond the lower limit of the ENG, the break of FTR1 and the close of that WRB below the level. The following day price drops into FTR2 (which is also a combinations of other things pointed to in the first chart) and starts a slow move up. At this point I still don’t know anything for sure but by just looking four days into the touch of FTR2 the story says a lot. The first two candles show the sellers lost the upper hand (maybe just for a short while), on the third day the demand in the second candle was revisited (look at the lower wick) also it had a long upper wick and a small body (green none the less). That upper wick indicates that at some point during the day there was buyer power and lots of it only to get overcome by sellers. Could the following day continue lower then… possibly… but no the fourth day confirms the presence of big buyers and that the previous day’s high wick was consumption of sellers.

At this point I am still not interested in touching this; I want to see a break of the yellow FL. And it comes a few days later… great now lower!

Inside the daily FL the decision “Y” that had been taken to break out of the lower limit and FTR1 is now very clear. Y was also the lowest high on the curve before the lowest low. When price got back there on the way up it flagged, then decided to break into the zone of Y & out of it. There wasn’t really any respect shown to such a big decision. After that price created a FL/FTR @ Z.

The plan is the following: IF and when price comes back into the zone of Z or lower into the Demand that broke the lower flag up I will watch for buyers.

Buyers do show and I set a PO at the QM with a SL behind the rectangle at Y & a TP1 at T1 & T. Knowing full well that if the trade ever makes it that far it could go beyond into C from weekly.

Price comes close no fill for me but the QM worked from its demand, price goes to T1(FTR by the way). I’m upset for sure! Ok… I remove order and wait again…

Price comes back and strong, goes deep into the area of Y even breaks Z now, I’m starting to think I might be wanting to long when in fact maybe we’re going much lower. Price broke Swing Low 2 (SL2), SL1 & Z. So unless I see some sign of buying there will be not buying before the Green rectangles & even then I want proof (Engulfing or CP).

THERE IS BUYING! The last two seller decisions have been countered and I go on to place a PO. This time it will be around the top edge of rectangle Y at 1.22130… it just looks like a good SR… SL & TP1 will still be the same as before except now that point T1 has had so many tests T is first in line.

Price reaches TP1 I take 2/3 out. The next sign will be an engulf in the opposite direction on H1. That comes in around C from weekly and a strong drop happens, I just close and run… RR were app 3.2 & 5.7… not bad

Will wait out the chop to see what happens… back higher

And I will also be writing less and annotating charts more. So if there is anything you’d like to ask please don’t hesitate.

Morning Robbie,

Well I started out trading a very long time ago and had mixed results. Of course over the years I made and busted accounts. Throughout all of that there were days where I just thought I should just give up; but I did not. Then a few years back I read one of Cloggie's posts on FF where he recomended Red's PIE thread. That's where I came accross IF and the older gang and followed him to AG and then here. What RTM teaches are the nuts and bolts of trading but it is up to the individual to make it their own.

A few months ago I read two books that have totally changed my perspective. One is "Trading in the Zone" and the other is "Flash boys".

IMHO, having expectations while trading is the most dangerous minset of all. Micheal Douglas explains it all in his book. If you haven't read it, I reccomend you do. Even if all you gather from it is miniscule, it will reinforce proper trading behavior.

In the previous post I mentioned my average was 18%, I've had days where I was making almost 100% while never risking more than 1% per trade. Many trades were also taken with a 0.25% risk. I had many off days as well, so yeah I'm content with the results.

I have come to realize that pending orders are not for me. I want to be there while everyone else is working, and finish my day without any running trades. I just sleep better that way. My typical trading day is 13hrs, except for the days when I am satisfied with a certain return and there's lots of news coming up, I will shut down early. Yes I don't trade the actual event, I might get into something a few minutes after the dust settles but that's it.

Don't stress yourself with expectation percentages, dollar ammounts or otherwise. They will only block your potential. Find what works for you and what doesn't. Trust yourself fully and treat each trade individually. If your stop hits, don't upset yourself and revenge trade. When you enter a trade you know that there is a probability that the SL can hit, that's why you placed it there in the first place. In the market, anything can happen at anytime.

Hope this helps,

Cheers

Hi Robbie,

Yes those were big decision areas. There is no "Price should or shouldn't" (IMHO) in trading. The only thing there is, is that price will do as it pleases. Our job is to try and tag along for the ride. Our signals come from all that is here on RTM. Each one of us trades these brilliant set of works differently. I for example am a true believer in "The Now"; i.e. I adapt to the current flow while paying attention to where we are. We could be in an amazing looking supply zone, I won't sell unless I see bigger fish biting first. Then it is all a matter of probability and MM. No two signals/opportunities are ever the same, they might be similar but never identical. Therefore; we are to keep an open/flexible mind and always be ready to change our orders with the current changes that are happening. For instance, I was scalping heavy buys in the first half of yesterday until the tide changed and I started selling. Granted, I am trading a lot of contracts during the day and closing at first or second TP on STFs. It's working for me for now and if a day comes where I'll need to tweak that, I will.

Hope that helps, Cheers

Hello Robbie,

All of the trades I take are either FTR setups or reverse FTRs. The latter is nothing but an ignored higher low or lower high. The trick here is to give the trades enough room to breath while it may go against you a bit, and more importantly to close out early. A lot of times my RR is not really a good one per RR rules. That's because I will mostly close at the first area of opposition. I have deleted from my system the notion of "Price will/should break" because we are coming from HTF SD or what have you. In the event it does break I will re-enter. It is indeed tiresome to be watching and micromanaging entries and exist. But the advantage is really no more than a couple of hours work per day. I often trade until London closes but that is not really necessary as most days I make my quota even before London opens. For example, today I made 12% in two hours. I could call it a day or maybe not, we'll see. Below is the P&L chart of this morning:

In the past year I must have sat in front of FT2 over 18hrs a day. Sometimes I'd get no sleep whatsoever. I must be thicker than all the rest on here cause there was always something I couldn't apply. Then it dawned on me to focus on one setup, and that's exactly what I did. Now I do recognize all the different ones as well, but I don't' necessarily trade them. I stick with my setup in thick and thin. Yes I do get stopped out like anyone else in this business but it usually is nothing more than a tiny scratch. As you mentioned, patience is the key. So is trading every one of your setups religiously, whether they get stopped out or not. I am in no way affiliated or trying to promote Michael Douglas' book Trading in the Zone, but it was a game changer for me. It might not have the same effect on everyone else. It benefited me greatly and this is why I am mentioning it again.

I hope I answered everything you meant to ask.

Have a great day,

I have found that with qm's the location is paramount to its probable effectiveness. I also think that with any pattern if you have to stand on one leg and squint your eyes then the pattern is not obvious. So, to me the pattern needs to be obvious and in a good location.

QM is a reversal pattern if used in the right locations.

The best place (as always) to really assess it's potential is to look at your charts. You'll learn more by looking at your charts than you will any book or forum - get the basics from here and then go and spend hours pouring over your charts until spotting QM's etc and where / how to trade them are part of your subconscious.

In terms of the 'why' they work, let's take a short QM setup...

1. When it forms the 2nd high this is where the professional money is shorting - this is also where novice sellers / weak hands have placed there stops and breakout / trend traders have placed long orders.

2. Price making the 2nd low is in affect the tip off that a reversal is coming - a seasoned trader spots this and is looking to short. If this new low also happens to trigger a break of a significant level / TL then all the better - the more noticeable the location the more likely clever traders are looking to enter the market with shorts.

Of course the new low also trips some stops and encourages novice shorts on board who look to bail out as price retraces - breakout traders are weak players who don't hold for long - this helps the 'distribution' process and allows the Pro's to load up shorts on the retrace to form the RS - you should be able to predict where this RS 'should' form.

3. The process is complete - Pro traders are fully loaded on shorts, weak hands have been had their orders utilised for liquidity and now the reversal can play out.

No access to charts right now but look over a chart and think about who is participating and why at each 'leg' and what their orders are doing to price and it should become clear...have a go at annotating a chart and I'll review over the weekend when I get some time.

posts.author: okami
posts.text:
I have yet to dig deeper on QM, but I tell you my view on it.

I use to consider QM when the HH and LL just break a little the previous H and L. As I understand, and as I said, I can't talk too loudly about my QM knowledge, what a bullish QM does is:

1) to cheat the sellers with the LL, that inmediatly goes up, getting fuel for the way up. 2) to cheat the buyers with the HH, that inmediatly goes down, cleaning the supply zone of orders, and letting free way for the up movement. But the HH also tell us that the downtrend probably has finish

3) Then price go back to the next demand zone, from where goes up, completing the QM.

posts.author: okami
posts.text:
Of course, I was trying to point out many things.

What I meant was that I would not qualify what you're showing as a QM, because the Higher High has gone too far away, on a unproportioned way respect of the rest of the QM. That was my impression when I show also this other chartyou shared. The LL is unproportioned to the rest of the QM.

But this oneI would consider a proper QM. It is proportioned. It makes a HH, but then a LL that shows the trend is changing. It has not a HH or LL that gets over a lot of previous H or L.

In the chart we are discussing, although, there is what I would consider a proper QM, as I signal the yellow HH, that just gets over the previous H, showing bull intentions. Then price came back to demand, and then shoots up.

So one of the interpretations we could do of a QM is that price is taking out orders on both sides with the HH and LL. Why? Because over the Highs and Lows there use to be clusters of orders. As breakout trading and SL over the Highs and Lows is one of the most extended ways of trading ("if resistance is broken, then buy, and put SL under the last low"), there use to be a lot of orders. This order positions are well known, so when price goes over a H or L they trigger a lot of orders. But what happen if price inmediately goes the other way? panic and SL triggering that add fuel to the movement. In this charts, a lot of sellers were trapped on the LL, that became buyers when their SL were triggered, adding fuel to the bull movement. At the same time the retail uninformed sellers were being the counterpart of the big money buyers, that need a lot of sellers to fulfill their orders. On this chart we could read that then price arrives to a Supply level, doing a HH. There were yet sell orders, so price came back to the next demand where the QM completed. When price did the HH it shows the bull strength, and consumed the few Sell orders that were left on the level. So the level was cleaned, and the sellers that were trapped on the LL that started triggering their SL, the way to the highs was ready, and as it happens, it shoots up.

IF explainswhat I'm trying to say much better than me. Read the first explanation slowly...I just did it and understand it much better than when I read it for the first time

Hope this clarify what I was trying to say. Please, ask anything you want, so I could focus better on what I'm not explaining well.

Hi AdamH,

In regards to AUDUSD and the area you question.

pros: Daily level which has shown to be quite strong in the past. Last reaction from this level was very strong indicating that more sell orders are possibly waiting to be filled. There is also level on levels which makes the area more prone to a reaction.

Cons: The main one it that this area has been tested a few times already so how likely is it to hold next time? We are not sure but it does indicate caution required. The quasi that you have identified while valid and conforms to the definition is not one that I would give a lot of attention to. The Quasi should be showing signs of order flow and this one doesn't do that for me as the highs are too close together and the LL doesn't give me a sense of power or strong move to the downside when compared to the prior L.

Summary: I would watch this area but be cautious and only trade it if I saw A+ PA.

That's my take and I welcome other comments

posts.text: I read several times the Marketpedia but still the QM dynamic is not very clear to me. While a QM is forming, the engulf of previous demand for us is a strong signal that price wants to go lower, so we wait the FTR to sell at Supply of Higher High (Head) or previous High (left Shoulder). My question is: why the big market players let engulfing previous demand, wich tells us that price wants to reverse? If they need to fill their sell order, isn't enough waiting for people buyng at a pullback of the trend (higher low in an uptrend) and suddenly push the price lower without any warning? What kind of benefit do they have from engulfing previous demand and not simply consume it to prepare the sell off? Probably I don't understand the market dynamic behind the QM and why it occours the way it does, but I can't figure out why. What do you think?

Great work DT, nothing to say

How do you manage entry and stop loss at QM left shoulder level and Head Cap?

Usually I perfer Entry at Head level, because stop loss is well defined, many times I miss trade at left shoulder level because not enough RR if stop loss is beyond head level.

Some basic options are: - if head and shoulder levels are not too far entry at shoulder with stop beyond head - if they are a bit far half position at shoulder and half at head, both SL beyond head level - if they are far: entry at shoulder with tight stop loss beyond shoulder level DP, and if price comes to head taking that little stop loss and re-enter at head level.

What do you think?

posts.author: Aaron
posts.text:
Hi all,

I have just finished testing pure supply and demand on the daily charts, and it worked out profitable even with a few minor hiccups. However, I want better results if I am ever to make this into a full-time or even a part-time endeavor. My aim is to attain a nice monthly or even quarterly salary without being at the computer for too long burning my eyeballs, I am a guy who can sit down for too long. This is me, and I am very relieved to have finally realized MY WAY.

I have just began a full study of QMs, inspired by Kruger and some fantastic posting I have seen over the last week or so, big shout out to Madwt, you’re really nailing it, and putting in the work, I love seeing this! The AHA moments must be flying in!!

Anyway, below I have created a fictional chart, I will use this to describe how exactly I see QMs and how I believe the ITs utilize this pattern to their benefit. I am not saying I will only use this pattern solely, if I see CP, a possible FO within the QM setup, all the better.

1. Aware traders see the oncoming HTF supply, the ITs know this, so just before the HTF supply they turn price creating a nice area to be faked for later on, confusing a lot of traders who were long and using the HTF supply as their targets, this would cause a lot of traders to panic and exit their longs early and cause a drop in price assisting the ITs with their intentions, which is to create a low which can be faked later on.

2. The ITs have joined in selling with the retail, this would entice traders who were aware of the HTF supply to go short now, thinking that price has turned before the supply creating panic and fear of missing the move AKA: trigger-happy sellers. The ITs know this, and know there are millions of buy stops to be had, to assist them in reaching HTF supply.

3. This is where it gets fun! Notice the high above (Marked with a line), there will no doubt be a lot of sellers there attempting to fade the high with their stops just above, this gives the ITs and incentive to smash this level and take the LQ for the push up in to supply, this attracts BO buyers, and on this account they would have been ok, if they were not greedy, however not the brightest move buying into supply, but they would have been ok in this case for a little while, and are currently enjoying the free ride up.

Putting them aside for one moment; we are now in HTF supply, and who waits at HTF supply??? Sellers and lots of them. The ITs know this and where are we taught to put our stops?? Just outside of the zone, the ITs know this, and in this case they engulf the zone collecting all of those buy stops to sell into. But hold on, engulfed the zone, should price not go higher??? Yes it should, if it was an engulf, more than likely there was a supply just above this zone that the ITs used to FO into, a clever move created by the ITs on unsuspecting traders.

4. With all the buy stops for the ITs to sell into, they have enough LQ to drop this baby!! And this is exactly what they do. This will create panic for the BO buyers from earlier and encourage them to sell adding fuel to the move, also this will attract sellers that were short at supply originally to short again, what do we call this?? Oh yes, CHASING PRICE, NOT A RECOMMENDED PRACTICE. We have now arrived at an S/R flip area, and as most of us know, these areas attract traders attempting to fade the area even though we’ve just come out of supply, BO sellers in the anticipation price will break the support level. What price does in this instance is collect more LQ, faking up and down, collecting more LQ from all these small FOs for the push down, this forms a nice supply zone, lining neatly with our QM level. Think about this for a moment, these levels attract BO sellers, and also traders who are attempting to fade, with all these short up and down moves (price Faking out) this would have triggered in most of the BO sellers and stopped them out collecting their buy stops, also doing the same for the traders trying to fade the level, triggering them in and stopping them out. A nice way to get short would you not agree?

5. The ITs have pushed price down, and pushed it hard, this again will attract more BO selling, but don’t forget the LTF traders getting stopped out who are going long at minor demand zones, this all adds to the ITs LQ. We now have reached the low (2) Do we see a break of this level and a continuation or do we see a FO, we wait for the ITs to make their move. They FO the area this stops a load of traders who were fading the low again giving sell stops for the ITs to buy into, and this would be our Lower low of the QM formation. With all this LQ and remembering the BO sellers will begin panicking once they see price reverse and will begin thinking of closing their position i.e. buying. This will cause confusion among traders, and encourage revenge trade after revenge trade taking loss after loss, filling the accounts of the big cats as they’re smiling all the way to the bank.

6. The ITs work is done, once price reaches the supply created by them, and confused enough traders, and making sure they are the only, or should I say the main traders short, they enjoy a nice drop to their target.

This is definitely not the only way of looking at a QM formation and I am sure there are many more experienced traders who could paint a clearer view, however this is how I see it for now, and it is definitely working to my advantage in testing.

posts.author: projectsagana
posts.text:
This is how I understand QMs

They appear at the end of a bullish or bearish trends, so it's a reversal trade set up.

Price action needs these things to happen for Bearish QMs: 1. Pre-existing up trend with HLs + HHs 2. Price makes HH into HTF Supply 3. Price makes a bearish engulf or a newly formed RBD/DBD inside HTF Supply 4. Price drops breaking most recent demand, support, or previous low. Makes LL 5. Price then rallies up to the origin of the bearish engulf or the newly formed RBD/DBD inside the HTF Supply 6. Price is then expected to significantly drop into a new downtrend. Money

Here's for the Bullish QMs: 1. Pre-existing down trend with LHs + LLs 2. Price makes LL into HTF Demand 3. Price makes a bullish engulf or a newly formed DBR/RBR inside HTF Demand 4. Price rallies breaking most recent supply, resistance, or previous high. Makes HH 5. Price then drops down to the origin of the bullish engulf or the newly formed DBR/RBR inside the HTF Demand 6. Price is then expected to significantly rally into a new uptrend. Money

Ok, I'll take a stab at this. I can't tell from the where the previous areas of supply and demand are, but after a large swing down I'm presuming we might be at an area of HTF demand. If that's the case...and I wanted to take a QM "IN THE HTF", then I'd be looking preferably for a bullish QM.

I've marked the purple bullish QM at the bottom of the swing. YES, the price doesn't return to a low enough area to buy from. BUT, price goes on to engulf the high u mark as QM (and more significantly the HH too). If u had taken the bearish QM setup as u indicate, then I think there's some lovely PA here to at least let u out of the trade with minimal damage limitation and maybe even flip the trade for profit. The engulf of HH is a warning. It may well take your stops if they are pretty tight, but if not then there's a good chance of a return to the source of the engulf (green box). The price shot up strongly from here, so there's a good chance of buy orders still sitting ( it's also an indication that's as low a buying point as the purple bullish QM watchers are going to get). It would be wise to exit the bearish QM trade here and might also be a good scalp long.

I guess the price structure u labelled turned out to be more of a diamond, but regardless of what price pattern we call it, it's the IT's job to shake us out of positions and I think in this instance they did their jobs pretty well. I think it's important to keep in mind that these patterns do fail from time to time. the IT's HAVE to make them fail otherwise it would be all too easy to read their intentions, but I think what I'm learning from RTM is the fact that although these patterns do fail from time to time, there is quite a clue develops about it's failure which allows us to get out with minimal damage...or indeed reverse our trade.

posts.author: astro
posts.text:
Great idea Benhur. Here goes for me...

Please refer to the QM article, and lets gather a list of price events that qualifies a valid Quasimodo:

1. A swing high forms at a S/R zone - Big Money places their 1st round of Sell Orders here. Novices join in the selling. 2. Price creates a swing low - Big Money starts buying here 3. A new Swing High forms - Big money pushes price thru the previous swing high to a new supply level, taking out stops to help fill their sell orders. 4. Price drops rapidly creating a lower low - big money sell orders are filled and price drops rapidly taking out previous demand. Stops are triggered causing prices to rise. 5. Price creates a new swing high in the zone of the 1st swing high. QM level. Big money piles on more sell orders which allows price to drop from here and confuses traders..

Hi guys, havent posted for a while but been working away. As soon as I've got everything sorted in my head I'll resume my journal. I've read this whole thread and I have a few questions that I dont think have been asked before.

So I'm watching price as it approaches the zone waiting for it to make a lower low, followed by a higher high (which breaches the high preceding the low) which it eventually does. so I think I'm looking at teh start of a QM. But where to place an order? Usually you have some visual looking H+S level that normally works but its not that clear here. Should I be placing an order at the first "low" on the left? It seems that from reading other parts of the forum that if I do this, then I still need to have my stop below the zone rather than the low in case PA turns into a diamond. The problem here is that the HTF demand I'm seeing comes from hourly/4hour, yet this QM I'm looking at is 5 minute so the zone is enormous compared to the relative 5 min PA.

So for this I'm thinking that if its hourly demand zone, I should probably only consider a 15/30min QM, if its a 30 minute demand zone then 5/15 QM is ok, but if I'm looking at 1min PA, there needs to be a 5/15minute demand/supply zone.

There's obviously no point on looking at a 1 min QM setup as a way to trade a daily demand zone but does anyone have any rules as to what timeframe a QM is acceptable to consider vs a relative s/d zone? Any feedback on this train of thought would be much appreciated!

I'm afraid those are not QMs from my point of view. Take another look at the QM article, and read this thread.

Also, before going to find more QMs, maybe consider what they are. They are an effort by somebody to take the weaker players out of the market, so they can more easily move price in the direction they choose. A QM is used to fake out people in both directions. So, the extreme of the QM should look like it faked something, ideally.

posts.author: prosenjitghosh
posts.text: Hi Forexlit, This could be the answer you are looking for. This is a reverse Diamond formation, which is a Bullish Pattern, The price wanted to complete the diamond formation, so it went up touched the flag Limit (C) taking out all the pending sell orders there, then came down sharply breaking the demand (1) to attract novice seller's or Breakout seller's and from diamond demand flag Limit (Swap) (2), it went up sharply, changing the trend to up. So what you thought was a Quasimodo is actually a trap laid down by the institutions. And hence your target was not achieved and price hit your stop loss.

posts.author: staurum
posts.text:
by IF: Fakeouts are extremely easy to predict. Most SD traders still look directly left, which is the big shortcoming of Supply/Demand trading. It's further left again we should be looking. Say price is coming up to a supply. The only way we can be sure that supply will hold price down is if that supply has already visited the extreme set of orders in the flag limit to its left. If the supply fell short of that, we can anticipate a FO to those extreme orders. Extremely simple stuff. We always look to what S or D are reactions to, rather than just S or D themselves.

one more from Pedini: www.readthemarket.com/index.php/en/forum...tups? start=325#22279

Since I'm active during the NY session I've been looking at the possibility of trading futures in addition to forex since things seem to go quiet in forex after the London close. I was looking back at the movements in crude and came across this setup. I decided to post it as a reminder that there are great trades to be had even when we miss the initial move out of HTF S/D.

With this setup we have a spike down into a fresh 4H demand zone. We then get a QM formation on the 1H and have a lengthy CP on the 15M which brings us to the 50% fib and an ignored demand zone.

Given the compression it would have been reasonable to set a limit at the top of the 1H ignored demand which also corresponds with a decision area on the 15M. Stop would be below the 1H demand which is also the QM area (about 35 pips). Expected return would be the top of the CP area which is 100 pips.

Often when I look at a chart and see that a big move has occurred I will say, Oh well, I missed that one and move on. I tend to focus too much on the LTF and this is a good reminder to keep the HTF in focus and look for the opportunity that comes as a result of that big move that I missed.

My 2c - the move from the lows is not a false break - if you zoom in you should see where price reacted and why - it was not a typical false break IMO.

The more obvious false break was at the start of the down move - price reacted at the DBD in the process tripping stops enticing breakout trades above that previous significant swing high.

Remember that just because price has tested a demand or supply zone once doesn't mean that supply/demand it fully consumed.

Also remember to zoom in, higher timeframe charts hide information that can be shown on the lower time frames.

Don't think like the herd in terms of LH, LL - this is how technical traders think - use that to your advantage - i.e. if you know how the technical traders think, then you know what they will be doing at certain scenarios but learn to just follow what price is telling you right now and LH, LL is irrelevant to that.

Lastly, if you have any grasp of fundamentals, you'd realise that it was FOMC last night. What does that mean, it means price is very unlikely to break well defined ranges prior to a big news event.

posts.author: Josh
posts.text:
kruger wrote:

Josh wrote: My 2c - the move from the lows is not a false break -if you zoom in you should see where price reacted and why - it was not a typical false break IMO.

I agree but isn't every false break seek for DP? In other words are false break turns back without reaction to DP?

A false break involves big players using liquidity from novice traders (liquidity they know is present) to their advantage i.e. to offload their large orders.

This is of course very likely to happen at an already identified demand / supply zone (not always) - like the short setup in UCHF - i.e. from that DBD which is proven supply.

But there has to be a trap element otherwise it's not a false break and you don't get the order-flow that typically follows with a false break. For the trap element to be present we need to conclude that the area being broken is an area where novice traders are likely to have cluster of orders and I don't see that low as a big area relative to the high - but that's how I view false breaks - I look for obvious areas where novice traders will have clusters of orders and look to find a close supply / demand zone that can 'cause' the trap.

posts.text:
The W1 supply area was more than likely going to provoke some sort of reaction but when it came the reaction was rather meagre. The result was a consolidated range that lasted the best part of two days. Suffice to say that one day I hope to feel qualified enough to offer an explanation of why price consolidated here but for now I’ll proffer that it has something to do with profit taking and repositioning.

Experienced scalpers will have made some very nice trades in this zone. But the well-defined demand and supply levels shaded in white and the aggressive pin bar reaction to them ensured that I remained a market spectator for the first half of the week.

The first signs that pro money was preparing to move price came in the CP zone. The initial long tails indicate strong selling and after a further period of consolidation the break of support finally came at point 1.

Some of the more experienced AG traders sold into the break for the neat intraday target of local support, which I have annotated with the white dashed line. The more I observe these zones the more sense they make. Hopefully the more sense they make the more I’ll feel confident to trade them.

What I have referred to as Local Demand established local support and comes into play again to lift price to the origin of the break at 2. This move seems to serve two purposes:

1. Allows big money to test that the demand at the base of the large consolidated area has been absorbed.

2. Creates a fresh market of buyers along the way that big money can sell to.

After all the orders are filled at 2, supply exceeds demand and price falls. The long tails on the second and third red candle indicate the final grab of buyers to sell into before price falls off sharply.

Interesting here is the target for this phase of the move. The W1 RS zone confluences beautifully with a local demand level and closing profits for the short from 2 with an immediate reversal of position for the long at 3 formed the basis of If’s “No Brainer” trade, which he posted up shortly thereafter.

Things get even more interesting at 4. With the sustained period of selling (albeit weak) this is the first big money response that I can see to the institutional shakeout zone shaded blue and subsequent support area labelled Shakeout Support.

I think it’s important to add a note here. Until the shakeout support actually held I was not confident enough to take a trade from the area. I have deliberately presented a H1 chart here to illustrate the red high/low candle penultimate to the breakout. On my M30 chart this candle is actually coloured green. With what seemed to me like mixed signals I erred on the side of caution and sat out and watched.

While I was napping Doctor was buying the head (!!) of a reverse H/S. In retrospect I would have been happy to buy the right shoulder. The LTF charts exhibited all the right signals and it was my mistake to sit out. But as I keep on saying, one of the major benefits of doing one’s homework during the live market sessions seems to be that this stuff sticks.

The subsequent CP up climaxes in big money aggressively marking down price such that they are able to fill their last buy orders. Demand exceeds Supply and the resulting LQ is explosive.

Friday’s fun and games was a cakewalk for those guys who have reached the level of confidence in their trading to which students like me aspire. And so I close this homework by paying homage to Josh. What is it they say about imitation being the biggest form of flattery?

I have marked an area on the chart, which I call the Josh Trade. Apologies Josh if you ever get to read this but I first happened upon this type of very low risk high probability setup in your thread. I’ll leave it to you guys to search out the specifics of the trade suffice to say that Josh’s thread contains many examples that will point you in the right direction. Ironically, on Friday it was actually Kruger who bagged this one! Hats off to Kruger:)

posts.author: Rufus
posts.text:
Oedipus99 wrote: I'd love to get into this homework but I'm having real trouble figuring out what the difference between a bull/bear flag and compression looks like. If anyone wants to chime in I'd be grateful.

For the sake of understanding lets keep with an uptrend.

Compression price is moving up while at the same time spiking south taking out multiple demand zones at times. Olive triangle on chart. As a result when price heads south it just falls right through (usually).

Now a bull flag dips south to pickup more demand to continue north. As you can see on the chart. The dip south is often caused by a supply area to the left. Often times this makes a new demand area when price returns as you can also see on the chart. With compression demand is often used up throughout the whole compression zone.

Now I have to post this then edit it to add the chart. Two different computers.

One more thing. BUFL are often tradeable to add to a position in a strong trend whereas compression can chew your account up.

Hope this helps.

Harry is also right about having compression withen a flag and visa versa. This is where multiple time frame analtsis comes into play. What one trader trades on a 1m chart could be awfully confusing to a trader who is sticking with an 1h chart

posts.author: @mel
posts.text:
Nice Oz, you mentioned 2 important things: The engulfing of the

demand and the FO at Supply. The third thing that I marked on your chart is the previous Supply that was ignored and became demand. I know you marked this as demand but the fact that this area wasn't respected will usually act as a "magnet" once price comes back.

Look on your chart, at nr 2, Price engulfes the demand, what happens?

The black doted line is also a support line 1) S/R trades go long with there stop just below it 2) Breakout traders go short So, there was some stop hunt going on untill price reached the demand and that's why price was accelerating south. Once price reached demand, there was some long orders waiting there so price went up and the breakout traders from nr 2 suddenly see price coming against them and hit there stops...

Once there is an engulfing as it was the case here, price will usually retrace deeply and FO (IF copyright

), and this is exactly what happened.

You see the demand was engulfed and price went up, we would look for a place to short and the FO was absolutely beautiful, becaue it was another trap. Price is at Supply, resistance traders go short and what happened price fakes out and take the stops out, this creates more sell orders....

IF, drew a diagram some time ago about the engulfing & FO, I will add it here as an attachment. This was about the engulfing of Supply but the same happens when Demand is engulfed like it was the case on your chart.

Hope this helps, Mel

posts.author: Oz
posts.text:
Thank you Mel, Funny tho, I was looking at that diagram a few hours ago;/

"Once there is an engulfing as it was the case here, price will usually retrace deeply and FO, and this is exactly what happened."

Yes, I've suffered a few times from this kind of scenario, having a perfect sell, price eng the demand, so I start thinking, great this looks strong, so I BE my trades, ignoring the strong reaction after the demand eng... that is so wrong yea,.... even if I know it landed in the swapped level, again very wrong thinking,.. yes this level which I marked as demand, is indeed ignored supply, when going to a 1M chart you see it's ignored supply, so swapped it. I see those as BUFL's.

After I observe a break of demand like this, I usually start BE these high sell positions, plus what I do is I start thinking that supply now is very strong, so I enter another sell at the best looking supply level, so in these cases, my BE trade's profit is being eaten away + the new sell is in DD. BAD. But that's what trending is, demand broken, so sellers are strong, BUT you cannot start thinking like this when it's the FIRST break of the prevailing "trend". That is the mistake I make A LOT of times.

So this huge retrace resulting as a FO, only/mostly happens after a first time eng of the prevailing trend Ok. Typical stop loss hunting yes.

So vital lesson, you cannot let a trade // against the prevailing 'trend' // run for a longer time before observing the reaction of the eng (base of prevailing trend)

I'll try find some more example like this. Once again thank you for the help

Looking at some of my recent trades which failed, I've noticed I'm falling for a similar trick over and over...

A mistake I've been making regularly is setting up trade plans but not
considering when there is a zone of liquidity right past my stop loss. I
 think this is probably going back to overconfidence and some
overtrading. I've been so bloody excited to finally have something
profitable with a high win rate, I've been trying to be part of every
trade on every pair. I've been taking trades that have PA and LS lining
 up with clean orders, but often I've been ignoring the need for there
to be a trick. The need for a BSZ, DM, compression on approach, or a
FO, etc.

Every trade doesn't have to have a trick of course. However, most of
the really good trades do. Most of my trades are entered overnight
while I'm asleep during the EUR session. I don't have the benefit of
watching the approach on LTF most times due to work. Emotionally this
is good, lol. But it is bad if I'm trying to trade these trades that
lack a trick. Moving forward I'm going to work harder on thinking like
Staurum....if this trade doesn't play out like I expect, what are other
likely scenarios?

I used to have a saying before I found RTM. I would say, "It is best to
 wait for someone to get F___ed before entering a trade." At the time I
 didn't realize how right I was! Now that I've joined RTM, I'm trying
to enter while they are getting screwed instead of after, lol.

In nature we see lovely examples of fractals. We can see a plant or
shell that looks the same on smaller scales as it does on bigger scales.
 The market is structured the same way. The smaller pieces combine to
form the bigger pieces.

posts.author: Rinehart
posts.text:
When we trade, we are interested in trading around HTF boundaries but on LTF.
 A FL on Weekly will contain at least 2 or 3 FLs on 4hr. It will
contain many more on a 1 minute chart. However, only a few of those 1
or 5 min FLs would be near the HTF boundary, have fresh orders, proper
LS, etc. It is our job to identify which one(s) to trade after we get
an engulf.

posts.author: Rinehart
posts.text:
I used Weekly, 4hr and 15 min charts to breakdown important areas. If
 I wanted to go to even smaller time frames, I would probably use 4hr,
15 min and 1 min. I'm sure it is possible to go from Monthly to 1min.
But your charts would be unreadable.

I haven't talked about Eng in these charts because I wanted to impress
on you the importance of playing "important FLs." The ones around the
boundaries. It is our job to find the good ones. We also of course
need PA to tell us where ITs want to go.

Now to think a little bit about Eng. If we have an Eng of of a 1 min FL
 without engulfing any HTF FLs. Well, that is PA and we can expect
price to reach the next 1 min FL before breaking the FL behind us. You
can play it and place targets based on the 1 min chart. On the other
hand, if you have an engulf on daily chart, then you can use daily
targets. Now think about the video IF made showing GBPUSD Daily. The
QM video where he showed a 50R trade. This was a LS kink QM trade. Now
 imagine that you dropped from daily down to 15 min to sharpen your SL.
 It is as simple as that.

posts.text:
Considering Frosty's recent journal posts as well as some PMs from
newer members asking for advice about learning RTM and trading in
general, I'd like to give a little perspective:

Learning the materials taught at RTM does not mean you have to trade the way IF trades. In trading the only thing that truly counts is having a positive equity curve! IF is able to nail near zero drawdown, high R trades. That is something to strive for but it is not the main goal.

I think some members get so caught up trying to learn how to nail
perfect RTM trades, they lose sight of the most important goal. Your
purpose with RTM has to be to find a way to read the market better.
Armed with a better understanding of where price wants to go and where
it will not violate, you can find ways to trade that match your
personality and situation.

AK is a 1 min scalper. I trade larger time frames mostly set and forget
 due to work. This works fine for both of us. On the other hand, I am
not a scalper and AK isn't comfortable with set and forget. The fact is
 both of us have incorporated RTM into what works for us and we use it
to grow our equity. Could AK learn to set and forget or could I learn
to be a scalper? Possibly, but we don't have to. We have found
something that works for us. We can stay in our lane, rinse and repeat.
 With RTM, you don't need to learn how to nail a 5 pip SL 150 R/R
trade. You achieve your goals by growing your equity curve.

Case in point, here is a trade I took on Gold today. My entry was
absolutely not a RTM entry. This is not a trade I would normally post
on RTM because it doesn't fit with the way members are taught to trade.
 We are taught to sell at supply yet this was a breakout trade. I took
the trade because I knew where price wanted to go. RTM gave me
knowledge of the engulf and I used that knowledge to trade what was
given.

FOCUS ON GROWING YOUR EQUITY, PERIOD. Take from RTM what you need to become profitable, period.

posts.author: Rinehart
posts.text:
Astrokillah wrote: Hey Rinehart, Great work; you're miles ahead of me when it comes to applying FLs! Quick question regarding this statement, "A FL needs to hit its target to be considered a FL" - does the target have to be another FL? or can it be SR, SD area, DP or CAP?

Thanks man! AK.

Hi Astrokillah, Thank you for the kind words. I too find (and still do at times) FLs the most confusing part of RTM. But obviously also the most important part lol. IF talked about FLs, FTRs, DPs etc before. But now we call them all FLs because people get caught up in terminology.

It is our job to identify the good FLs. The ones that were formed from breaking a significant barrier like S/R or a past FL of significance (or sometimes the ones that preceded the breaking of the significant level--DPs). If we accept that all these DPs, FTR, FL,etc can all be called FLs. Then the only other thing is what is in between the FLs which are the PAZs. So the market is really just FL, PAZ, FL, PAZ, FL, PAZ, FL.

To answer your question. We don't consider a FL a FL until it passes through the PAZ to the next FL and hits it. SR alone is not a target (though it usually is formed from a past FL). If price hits an important DP (that led to the breaking of a SR), then I call that DP a FL and say price has hit its target. If it hits a CAP, that CAP was usually formed from a previous FL and I say it has hit its target.

The times we don't consider price hitting its target is when price engulfs a FL but doesn't quite make it all the way through the PAZ. These are the engulfs, FOs, BSZs etc. These are great because they are a sign of where to start looking for a trade. Other times price will engulf a FL, for example engulf a FL and pull back a lot and then eventually push to the target. These are the times were you end up with a much bigger FL. The ones that were formed from price will bounce, annihilation of mentality etc.

Lots of thinking going on right now. Few more penny's dropping. Still lots of questions though.

This is where I'm at right now; I think if we engulf a FL/RBR/BDR we want to go to the next FL, this could be another DBD/RBR but we would be targeting the RBD/DBR within the DBD/RBR. Or we could be heading for the origin of the whole move down, we could just draw a box around the cap on price and make that our target, or we could look for the source, the FL/FTR, the real beginning of our move up or down.

I hope this makes sense. I'm just typing the things running around my head at the minute.

Where I am struggling when trying to prove this concept is in the lower time frames. I know it is irrelevant as long as we keep an eye on the bigger picture but it's knowing when to stop, knowing when to say, these are my targets, I know there are more FL's further down the time frames but these are the FL's I'm going to trade.

What importance do we put on an FTR that isn't a FL? The FTR to the FL has caught my attention so far. I from what I have seen a reaction should be expected there and it should be trade able as long as you look at the bigger picture.

People like to trade the same things in different ways. Dissecting IF's trades really helped me learn a lot, I hope I'm learning the correct things. IF seems to just go straight for the source as long as he has confirmation PA, and he then exits at the source of a move when he has confirmation that source will be the turning point for a move in the opposite direction. I think this is just part of IF's trading plan. Others look at the same area but take the trade after more confirmation.

That brings me nicely on to creating my own trading plan, how can I possibly think about becoming a trading without a plan.

1. Money management, the key. What am I willing to risk per trade? 2. What am I going to trade? Just FL's? FTR's? Only certain FTR's. Will I take multiple trades on the what I consider to be one move if I get additional confirmation PA that allows for another entry? 3. How many trades will I have open at any one time? 4. How many pairs/commodities will I monitor? I can't monitor them all, which ones will I chose? etc

What I've been looking for are basic rules, rules to follow the market, rules to put on top of my foundation of money management. If I have an engulf, I look for an entry. Looking at the charts this morning I'm realized I need more time in front of the charts to train myself and make this second nature, or close to.

I really believe price will go back to the source of a move if an engulf occurs, it's keeping an eye on what else has been engulfed.

Anyway, I've rambled far too much, I just had a lot of thoughts I needed to get out of my head. Hopefully at least one person can learn from my struggles, and if I might be heading in the wrong direction please just let me know.

In IF's chart I believe the first blue box is the FLAG, the red box isn't the FL of this FLAG, this is an important point to remember. A FL in the past held that flag up and the break of the FL in the past creates a new FL holding price down. Bearing this in mind, the last blue box is our new FL, holding price up.

So, we've left our FLAG with an engulf, before carrying on towards the FL below (we're in a FL PAZ so we want the other side) but before we can carry on we need to go back to the source of our engulf, the RBD that caused the drop. After returning to our source we then engulf the previous low, creating the FL/FTR.

Jumping ahead, we engulf the upper limit of the red box, our FL FTR. It's no surprise we've looking for the same simple thing, we've engulfed so price wants to go back to the source of the move, the decision.

Why had price hit it's target? When we engulfed the engulf of our red FL we created a new FL. The decision to engulf and create this new FL and enter the PAZ above was the source of the move and was where the orders were as strong upward movement from the source shows.

There were other things to indicate we were going to return to this point. Price move in to CP above and then broke the source(FL) of the move in to the CP making our blue FL the target.

Is the FL Stacked FTRs? when happens if price pierces into these stacked FTRS? when does it go next? retrace to the last supply/demand then on to the origin of the move within the major FL? Is this seen as a FO or is it just where price really wants to go?

Are the real lines of S/R being blurred by the ITs to make life harder for us? I believe they are, I believe they're trying to give us false readings, fooling us in to thinking our FLs are higher/lower than we think.

Are zones defined by the real decision and not the fake one, is this the essence of the QM? Price is respecting the real boundary to the zone it has just engulfed?

Are all FLAGS FLs to another FLAG? Are all FL's price actions zones in their own right? Is the origin the last set of orders in a ZONE or is it just the boundary to the last Flag/decision in a zone, the last line of defense?

How do stacked zones interact? lower and higher limits CP? Engulf, retrace then move to bottom of last stacked zone like CP?

Lots of questions, and a lot of the answers are in the charts. Will confirm with demo trading over the coming weeks.

Moving to a demo account full time as of next week to nail down my trading plan and make any adjustments and to give me the confidence to trade with real money. Wish me luck.

Morning mate, so the PAZ article states this;

'So what is a Price Action Zone? A PAZ is exactly what it says; it’s a zone on your charts that show a distinct type of Price Action! These distinct zones include poles, flags, stacked supply/demand and compression. Once we are able to accurately determine where these zones are, there is one rule. ONLY trade the edges!'

The most important part, when you've identified a PAZ, You wait for an engulf, this is the signal to trade the edge. A nice place to look is an area where there has been a pssible FO, you want to look for the engulf that confirms the FO. On this picture the red box, or PAZ is basically boxing up a swing high and low. After the FO we engulf the decison that took us above the swing high, sellers are now in control, best bet is to wait for a good op to sell, there was a quick scalp straight away but I'm going to cover that later.

We then engulf the swing low, and more importantly, the decision holding it up.

We now look to the extreme of the PAZ. Our sell point just happens to be a QM level, ever wonder why they're such good places to sell? I would say that they're probably always the edge of a PAZ.

I'd go and look for some examples of that and mark everything up, they key thing I think, is to remember this is a market place and decisions are being made on price, so the most important thing to remember is to look to where the decisions were made.

This is the GBDUSD M1 from last night.

Hope that helps,

Robbie

EDIT: I forgot to add, this PAZ is essentially the space between to FLs.

For me, the key decision, is one that exerts momentum and breaks a key level, I would call this a FL and I would call the first time back to this (after the subsequent engulf of where the FL took price) an important FTR. If I create the FTR without returning to my important FL, I will expect a FO with momentum towards my FL and most definately away, if price stalled too much at the FL when I'm expecting a FO to it I would thnk twice about the situation.

I don't think I would ever use an FTR as a place to trade to be honest, not without considering the FL it is reacting off i.e. the FTR fully consumed the FL.

One massive barrier to get over (and then fully understand, which is where I'm at now) is that it's all about scale. Our FL is an imbalance within balance. We're told a FLAG is consolidation, prices are bouncing around in an area where there are no overwhelming buyers of selling to take it beyond the FLAG. Our FL is the first sign of imbalance, so the greater the momentum from our FL the better. A strong imbalance indicates too many orders which means we have orders left to be filled.

I'll show you something else that from one of my charts yesterday that also give me faith that price will not only hold but will exert strong buying pressure. Hi Robbie,

even not being an expert too, I would like to give all the possible support as well, as I think we are all rowing in the same direction. I may be of course wrong, so we can discuss our opinions.

First of all my thought about FLs: they ARE a decision.

But not to Engulf. They are a decision that an EG is a real EG and not a FO! Therefore important.

Let's think about a rally: Price EG the last Supply level (SR or Supply) and searches for the next higher Balance (it is all a matter of Lots in both directions). As soon as it finds it, it stops (that's the balance). Then Supply takes over again, using all Buy Orders and looking for below further balance.

In case of a FO, there is no Demand there anymore, so it still drops.

In case of Real EG the Buy orders take over again at a certain point, and the rally starts again - Taking over all the above Supply. That's the Battle Won! That's the DP and the FTR and the end (Limit) of the F.L.

About not receiving any feedback, I think we cannot expect any Master stopping by in all the posts. But what I am trying to do is to get the only real feedback from the charts. In other words: you have a theory about reading price, look at it in some charts. If you don't get the imagined reaction, then it sounds like some Master said: "you are wrong, look at our Journals again".

Perhaps (and here I fully agree with Distinction) we all sometimes want too much. To may see any singular reason of any singular move in price. That's Greedy: one of Trading's Devils.

Or we are impatient and want to see all possible setup for not waiting any longer and TRADE!

My suggestion (and my point of this Journey too): try to Master one Set Up only. Forget about PAZ for a while, and look at SR of HTF. EG => FL => FTR => FTB.

I am of the opinion too, that mastering those we could make enough to have no need of further investigating. May be we will want. Then we will study why and when they fail, and price goes further to look for the DP to EG (the origin of Supply).

But till then I would suggest: clear your mind from TOO MUCH (I say to myself as first of course) and learn to WAIT. Psichology will be trained, Focus will be trained and with high probability Balance will grow

Sorry for the long post and do not hesitate to critic or reply: mine is not the absolute Truth Just some thoughts after some experience.

For instance, in the diagram in the last post, lets assume A came back and consumed all of the orders in B, we would then have a mini compression PAZ. we would be well within our rights to take a trade at A but we would have to have our stop below B. In essence, this is when the FTR in A is at it's strongest, because it has consumed the orders in the FL below, it then becomes the last line of defense, this doesn't mean a reaction is going to take the price in to space, but we should get a reaction at least, to the last decision.

We get in to confusing territory when multiple decisions have not been revisited and they are stacked, I believe this to be a PAZ as well but I'm unsure how to approach it. What I mean by this is every decision is reacting to a decision, If the first decision that started the ball rolling hasn't been consumed we have to expect price to get back there. This is very hard to explain, but think of a small decision, this decison decides to engulf something, the FTB to this decision forms a flag, this flag is then a decision to engulf something else, the FTB to this Flag then forms a flag, if the momentum leaving the flag continues in the same direction again and engulfs something else, we have another decision

It's CP if it's consumed the last orders in each decision, I believe it's stacked demand if it hasn't, either way, from what I've seen they both work in a similar way.

Hope that makes sense,

The flag limit is the feature which defines the flag. As Robbie stated previously, where the flag goes to beyond the limit is not relevant. (Well, it is relevant in so much as where the areas of S/D are within the flag - as this is where price will react on return, once the flag limit is broken.

So, the diagram you've posted above does not show the flag limit, it shows where the flag was (maybe) broken. The full story would be something like I've marked here, where the blue box is the flag limit, defined by the points noted in the green circles ( the FL as the abbreviation). So, what's marked as B is the Decision Point (DP) to break the flag and A is the FTR created after that break.

What I see is that the FTR was the price point the ITs used to be aiming for in the past, and would FO to the DP (B) but nowadays, they aim for B, and what was once the FO zone, has become the new target.

Hello V,

I'll give this my best shot. I'm still not 100% on IF's reasoning but I'll give it ago.

1. Price engulfs the high to the left and returns to the decision to engulf below, notice the nice RBR below? well this forms the rally of the bigger RBR. 2. Price FTRs off the decision below (demand) and shoots away, we now have our FL upon the engulf of the new high. 3. Price exhausts itself at 3 and hits the supply at the FO to the left.. 4. We then move slowly down to 4 where we have our FTB to the FL, notice of the way down we removed all of the supply? 5. 3 and 4 define the limits of our flag, at 5 we engulf the upper limit as well as the FO to the left. 6. we try to get back in to the flag at 6 but hit demand at the decision to leave the FLAG. We CP away from 6 removing all of the buy orders. we eventually break 5 and form our FL/FTR. 7. Price then rallies up to 7 where we hit some S/R from the past.

8. At 8 we have our FTB to our FL and we remove the last of the supply. This area shouldn't cause to much of an issue in the future. I believe 8 then becomes the limit of our CPPAZ. 9. at 9 we engulf 7. 10, we fail to return at 10. 11. At 11 we engulf the FL low at 10. 12, we rally and try to get back in to the flag above at 12 then we get rejected by supply at the cap on price. 13. We then start making lower lows and lower highs towards the base of the blue flag we have just entered. 12 is now an important FTR. we are aiming for the supply at the edge of the CPPAZ at 8 where we should get a small reaction at least. 14. we retrace back to the supply above at 14 which is a nice cap on price. 15 At 15 we engulf in to the CPPAZ, and want the other side, we retrace back to the last supply at 14, the origin of the move/decision to engulf. we drop through the CPPAZ and through the other side to the base of the pole at 4 where the sells overwhelmed the little demand that was left it that area.

Now, I'm unsure whether the engulf in to the CPPAZ meant we could expect to drop all the way to the bottom of the blue flag because the CP had effectively removed all of the orders from the FL and this was the barrier to the Blue flag below. Maybe IF can confirm this one to us?

16. So at 16 we engulf the lower limit of the blue flag and also the FL holding it up. 17. price retraces to 17 where there is a strong s/r flip right on the edge of the FTR which was created after engulfing in to the CPPAZ. I don't know why IF put the red box around the swing high? Maybe because it was stacked supply? With the FTR and the CAP? 18. so, we hit of the S/r flip and the FTR which was the edge of the previous zone, which makes sense as we just engulfed in to a new zone at 16. and 15 is the edge of the last FL. 19. From 17 we can take a trade knowing that price wants to go down to the FL at 18 because of the engulf in to the FLAG.

So, to answer your question, i think IF means we should follow the key engulfs of these flags especially when they are forming either side of key s/r levels. as we cross one of these levels and FTR we are flipping sentiment on the value, what was once a great place to buy, is now a great place to sell.

OK so, this is where things aren't straight forward, so how do we define a FLAG? How do we know the limits? after leaving a flag limit, lets say it's a demand FL, how do we know where the high is? is it the point reached before we come back to the demand of the FL, I say this because often we will only hit the s/r of the FL, engulf the high and then come back down to the body/demand of the FL. so would the high of the FLAG in that scenario be define by the high reached upon leaving the FL or the HIGH reached before returning to the body/demand of the FL? I think this is very important for us to nail down, If there is a flag then there is a way of defining it.

IF, can you clear that up for us? To simplify, is the limit the high reached after leaving the FL, i.e. the high of the rally in the RBR? or is it the high reached before the FTB to the demand of the FL? I.E. not the s/r of the FL? I'll draw an example.

Hi all, I've been holding back from posting as i gather my thought's on the exact way I want to trade.

Something I have been having trouble with is clearing defining a trading plan. I'm very aware of my personality type and i need a plan to suit it or I will be doomed to fail. I have been trading a very small account to really pick up on my flaws. I've had mixed results, some very good trades, some trades where my SL has been too close, or another way of putting it is that I've been too greedy. I have jumped in the market when i shouldn't have and I've chased positions.

I've traded at my best when I've made a logical decision and set targets based upon where i think price will turn and not where i want price to go to meet a monetary goal.

My aim is consistency and this is now my main focus, ridding myself of anything that will make me inconsistent. Primarily, actions without reasons.

So far it is quite straight forward creating the plan, the hard part is WHAT I'm going to trade and defining the specific conditions I require. For me, I need this proven concept, something that i can rinse and repeat, day in, day out.

I'm finding it hard to define the concept that suits me, I like the idea of decisions being made rather than price just simply failing to return, the decision to engulf (which is made before an engulf) is logically more important than price failing to return after an engulf. I say this because the decision must be the origin of the imbalance therefore where the orders are, a failure to return is just a reaction, not a decision. When something is a decision and a failure to return that's a whole different thing and I would say is very important.

Where I was going wrong in my definition of FL's was not accepting we can made new FLs as we engulf each FL in a single move. I was placing more importance on the FL that made the most important decision. I now accept this and am happy to stick with it.

Something else that I have been working on is that everything moves in threes and that the institutions are lazy. the strength of their moves are repeated, over and over again and this creates symmetry. we can see this through making basic S/R lines.Id we look at the structure of RBR's and DBD's in every time frame we can see that the moves are measured, they don not look the same but from decision to decision the carry a very similar strength. This is going to require a bit more nailing down but you'll see how it ties in with s and d levels to the left, quite convenient.

That's my 2 cents for the day.

Good trading everyone.
