Guys you're over thinking it. I take lots of trades. I lose lots of trades. Yeah that's right, I lose and I love it, it frees my mind up to reanalyse and focus on new opportunities! I suffered a long time trying to be a perfectionist but ultimately you cannot be right 100% of the time so create your edge elsewhere! Something like 50-60% of the time I get stopped out for 5-15 pips. I share the ones that look pretty and I purposely leave my stop where it is (instead of moving it to BE out of FEAR) so you can see the ridiculous risk:reward I achieve. The edge is pretty much in everything else in your trading plan that isn't your entry.

Here take this for example. This is just having a bit of fun but look past that and see that I simply took retests at new demand with minor s/r as confluence in an uptrend. The ones that failed did not sit at the right spots and I was punished, but I was able to refocus on the task at hand as a positive outcome of failing.

Not every trade you take has to be some picture perfect S/R that you looked at in a text book. Immerse yourself in the market and follow what price is intending to do.

The aftermath

I know you didn't direct this at me, but I also monitor a large number of pairs - the way I manage it is as follows: - I always only ever have one chart at a time fullscreened - I condense my view (zoom out a lot) - you need to be able to see as much context as possible at all times, to get a feel for the big picture - widescreen monitors are not good for this, it squashes all the PA too much vertically.

Either use a monitor with a more square aspect ratio, or use the fixed chart scale option a lot to stretch things out vertically - the more vertically exaggerated the PA, the easier it is to read - I cycle through each chart first thing in the morning on M15/H1, and mark the nearest levels that I want to look for trades at above and below where price currently is - you MUST use alerts if you want to trade this many instruments. Many times, it's just a case of marking the best levels above/below price for each chart. setting alerts, and then just waiting for price to reach them. The main benefit to trading this many instruments is that you can trade only the more significant levels without too much waiting in between. Something usually hits something halfway significant every hour or two - I either play some computer game whilst I wait, or I just randomly click through each chart if I am bored, and cycle timeframes, to see if there are any scalps available that catch my eye

I am just no good with these hand drawn charts. I get that it helps some folk understand the basics of price action but ultimately they're all just made up and don't contain the necessary information for me to provide a qualified response, I never look at one chart and make a Go/No go decision. I like to drill down...and zoom out....flick between 2-4 time frames, look at correlations. I like to know what's happening in the bigger picture. Where is price coming from, where is it going to. What other levels are there that price has turned from. That's just the way I operate, so I cannot give you a definitive answer to your question nor will I attempt one.

Look at it this way, if you're confused with your current understanding of a concept, anything I or anyone tells you one way or the other will not give you the fool proof answer to apply to the same future scenarios for you to profit 100% of the time, so there's no point in me telling you what I would do....my recommendation comes in the way of these three choices: 1. Price has violated your original plan, you do nothing, you move on to your next opportunity. 2. Price has violated your original plan, but PA is providing an opportunity in your original desired direction, it fits within your risk profile, so you just take the trade and see what happens. That's what taking risks is about.

3. Price has violated your original plan, but PA is providing an opportunity opposite to your original desired direction, it fits within your risk profile, so you just take the trade and see what happens. That's what taking risks is about.

Over time you're going to gain a much better understanding through just giving trades a go and answering your own questions with empirical evidence from your own trading data.

Just to add my 2 cents (I hope you don't mind Shadow):

Origins and their engulfs are not a "rule". Really, there are no 100% rules in the market. There are just things which we can expect to happen more often than they do not when we put together all of the information at our disposal.

In actuality, MPL of an origin of a major swing or FTR just represents a good *area* to look for a trade. A lot of the time, the origin gets FO'd into the space between origin MPL and the swing/FTR MPL.

This is actually one of my favourite places to look for a trade - if the origin is in the form of a very prominent "hook", I will trade the very pip edge of it, expecting a FO into the space aforementioned. There is usually excellent RR available with low pip risk, if you fancy taking it.

Hello wom25,

Your screenshot suggests to me you're missing the key components required to know what you're looking for, but I will let you reconcile that for yourself after you read the following. You're close, but you need to be really specific about what each attribute means for you to exploit the inefficiency of the market you're in.

It's very important to dedicate the time to really absorb the teachings of the QM article and relevant examples in the Homework section and spend a lot of time concentrating and observing the key attributes that make up the pattern, once you sequentially identify each attribute, it is impossible to get it wrong. I guarantee you will get a firm grip of the form of the pattern if you can label the key attributes below, if you have to force the pattern or cross your eyes to see a QM setup to label the chart, you best move on to another chart or timeframe. Also whilst you're at it, in the process, don't forget to start asking questions why the pattern occurs, what is the psychological makeup that allows this trick to be performed time and time again? Who's buying and who's selling at each step of the process? You can then even start exploring why Diamonds begin to occur, how is that a HHH or LLL will occur, what are the factors that contribute to that extra push?

So what are the key attributes for a sell QM? 1. Left shoulder (a high) 2. New demand (low) 3. The head (higher-high) 4. An engulf of the new demand (lower-low) - for higher probability you want a good surge in price, a break with a bit of conviction! 5. A retracement of price to around the left shoulder or nice supply structure around the area (anticipating a lower-high)

Once you understand the key framework and can apply it to the chart you can begin to fine tune the trade by combining the zone with confluencing factors and other recognisable patterns on LTFs such as FLs or DBDs.

So in the best interest of actually getting a handle of this beautiful pattern and remaining in the present, please do the following for me (just for now): ignore the left of the chart, ignore the bigger picture and simply work to observe a decent quantity of them. At this stage of your learning. I recommend you forget about looking for them on the daily charts and get down on the M1/M5 charts and start mapping them out, they happen fast and they happen frequently (at least once or twice a session on each pair). Once you get the hang of retrospectively identifying them, demo trade the darn things real time! There is no substitute for first hand experience of anticipation. Don't spend too much time backtesting historical data. Forward test your ability to recognise the pattern in real time, you will only ever learn what to do through stepping yourself through the process over and over again. Wait for the left shoulder, wait for the higher high, wait for the engulf, place a limit order for the right shoulder, place your stop beyond the head, and target an obvious fresh zone. Forget about R:R at this stage. Trade management and fine tuning will come with time.

I discovered this site a little over a week ago, from the recommendation of a friend. I've been studying intently ever since, and believe I've got a pretty good grasp on the fundamental concepts. I quit out of work last December to try to learn to trade - I only wish I'd found this site back then!

I've made some great trades, that I've planned, and waited for patiently, and many more horrific trades. The first trade of the day seems to set the tone - if I get a winner, I'm happy to be patient for the next trade. If I lose, I want revenge. I should just step away from the computer at times like this.

Also I'd just like to express my gratitude to IF and the community at large for marking this such a great place to learn.

Cheers Simon

Ok, well typically, after a good day yesterday, I got massively overconfident. Such a problem for me - I stop doing the things which made me trade well the day before.

I tried to go long on EU, and the corresponding short on UCHF, failing to notice that both had turned at significant levels, and sellers were still in control on EU, buyers on UC.

Getting stopped out on both, but convinced I was still correct, but had just not spotted the FO level, I went in again - on both. And got stopped out again - on both. Good job I'm only on a demo account eh

My reasoning, H1 UCHF:

What I failed to spot:

So basically, the next important level below hadn't actually been engulfed, so sellers weren't still in control as I thought.

After 4 losing trades back to back, I'll make this a study day, to avoid making more emotional decisions, and probably more mistakes.

Key for me is being able to determine who is in control at any given time - buyers or sellers, then I know whether to look for entries long or short. If the last significant engulf was of a short level, then buyers are in control, and look for longs on RT. And vice versa. If we have just reacted to a strong level short however, with no engulf, then sellers in control until shown otherwise.

Obviously these levels exists on all TFs - buyers could be in control on M5, but overall sellers are in control in the H1/H4 picture.

Something for me to bear in mind.

posts.text:
One more thing - I need to get my analysis straight. I'm spending too much time stuck in H1/M30 etc, but still missing the big picture. Analysis needs to start from the top down - M1/W1/D1/H4/H1.

The trades on which I've been completely incorrect whether buyers or sellers are in control have been because I haven't actually looked at a daily chart, beyond a perfunctory glance. There may have been some engulf on H1 or H4 signifying a potential reversal, but nothing on the daily to indicate the same. Of course, an H1/H4 engulf can be significant, but only if you know you're coming off a daily or weekly FTR.

Take NU for instance. It can clearly be seen on the daily chart, that the last move down engulfed a very strong daily FTR in the other direction. Where was the source of that engulf? Somewhere inside the D1 FL shown in red.

Dropping TF to H1, the engulfed D1 FTR is poking in from the left, and we can narrow down the source of the engulf to the H1 supply area shown.

Dropping even further into M1 to pinpoint the source of the move, we can see there is a lovely cap on price, with a little hook into supply right at the top.

Fast forward to this week...

There would have been a beautiful limit available there, with a 70 pip stop (10 pips = 1 point for me, so I guess most people would call this a 7 pip stop). This trade would be up over 20R by now. There was also a very nice re-entry available on a RT, had I actually realised what the previous top had come off!

I can see exactly how some guys on here take trades like this, the problem is I only manage to see them in hindsight at present, hah.

Lesson learned. Get my bearings on W1/D1 first, and work down from there.

Ok, last entry this week. I've identified 2 methods that work for me, I just now need to stick to them. I find myself clicking aimlessly through the charts at times, before I realise I'm not paying attention. I've had the lurgy these past couple of days (hopefully not ebola - typing up my journal with my nose will be difficult if my arms get eaten by a virus), so I've not been concentrating very well.

It's a simple process, as outlined on my charts from yesterday.

Method 1: "Safe", very good RR

1. Identify HTF Suppy/Demand or SR Flip or FTR of Significance 2. Wait for price to hit the zone 3. Establish the limits of the significant flag that needs to be broken to indicate a reversal 4. Wait for break of FL (with additional engulfs preferentially) 5. Enter on RT to source of break of FL

Method 2: Riskier, but sometimes necessary because if price CPs into our zone, we're not going to have a clearly defined FL to trade the break of.

1. Identify HTF Suppy/Demand or SR Flip or FTR of Significance 2. Observe price CP'ing into zone 3. TT edge of zone

And here are a few examples from today, for my own benefit to cement this process in my mind, and to share with anyone else who might find this helpful. As my understanding is developing, I'm beginning to see that price reactions can usually be anticipated in advance equally as much by drawing zones from ignored FTRs that we've momo'd over, as opposed to precise SR flip locations.

Before, I was fixated on drawing very exact SR lines, and then trying to pinpoint the immediate supply or demand level to the left that caused the engulf, or was an FTR formed from the engulf.

My odds of spotting higher strength higher probability reversal zones have gone up greatly when I go up a couple of TFs, and draw in the actual supply or demand zone at the top/base of the ignored FTR, rather than just using a precise line.

If the D1/W1 trend is down, we've reacted short with an eng off the HTF zone, and then I can see a CP move back up to a good supply level - I'll take that all day long.

I trade off HTF zones in the sense that I wait for LTF reaction from them, and then use that as my directional bias to enter a trade in what is most likely to be the correct direction.

posts.author: smimon
posts.text:
I'll probably avoid going short on CJ and UJ at the same time again in future.

When trading any crosspair, it's important to consider whether it's moving in one direction solely because of the strength or weakness of only one of its constituents. ITs often like to play currencies as a whole to my knowledge, rather than focusing on individual pairs. The best trades come when one part is weak and the other part is strong, resulting in swift movements.

CJ and UJ obviously share JPY as a common component. Any strength in JPY will therefore push them lower. However, CAD and USD are almost opposing currencies -over 80% of the value of the trade-weighted CADX index comes from USDCAD. Therefore usually as USD moves up, CAD moves down, and vice versa.

For this reason, we can see that the only way CJ and UJ will both go down convincingly is in the event of significant JPY strength. If JPY remains neutral, then the sole driver of the pairs will be USD, meaning that if UJ starts going down in the face of JPY neutrality, then CJ will start going up.

Which is essentially what's happening to my 2 trades up the moment, see-sawing off each other. A strong kick from JPY will push them both down, but I've effectively bet 50% against myself.

A good way to look at things is in triplets of pairings. Let's say EURUSD is going down in HTF trend - we therefore know that USD is stronger than EUR. Let's also say however that GBPUSD is headed up in HTF trend. GBP is stronger than USD. Logic then dictates that the strongest moves should be coming short on EURGBP. USD is stronger than EUR, but GBP is stronger than USD, and so therefore far stronger than EUR.

This is of course all academic, and it's possible to trade the currency pairs perfectly well in isolation, but it's always worth bearing in mind so you not only don't bet against yourself, but also so that you can pick up on something that's really looking like it's going to run.

I wanted to add some ideas for consideration on this one. I can see two options that allows one to be conservative but help maximize returns.

1. Expect the FO zone on the other side of the supply/demand and only trade that. In other words, instead of picking the entry in the supply zone, pick the entry in the FO zone above the supply. You will missing some trades but you will have a smaller stop loss to deal with.

2. The other idea is a hybrid of your style and my #1. Trade a portion of your risk at the supply zone and another portion in the FO zone. I spent a lot of time reading the FO or Engulf thread in the Homework room and it dawned on me that often price will FO to the decision point on the other side of the most recent supply/demand zone. So, why not play 2 trades. One at the edge of the obvious zone (S or D) and another in the DP beyond the S/D zone. Essentially if you had $100 to risk per trade and you see a nice supply zone with a FO area above, well, you take a $50 position near the edge of the supply zone and another $50 near the DP of the FO zone. That way you get a chance for 2 tickets to the party.

Quick something I knocked up to monitor my average position when adding to a trade in progress, and show me where multiplying my total lots by a factor of x will put my average position. It moves up and down as the bid price moves up and down. The idea is that I wait for a sufficiently deep retrace that I can double my lots (or whatever) and keep my average position behind a "safe" extreme - typically a FTR, the engulfing of which would mean I would consider the trade dead in the water.

Once a trade is in progress and you double (or whatever) up, you essentially go double or quits. You're either out for a lot more at your target, or you lose the lot at B/E at your new average position level if price reaches it.

It's a concept called "Space management" I found on another forum some time ago. The idea isn't new of course. If you're feeling really bold, and your trade has run almost all the way to target, you can do something silly like x10 your lots for the final stretch, "compressing" your space. You can also remove lots to a trade in progress if it looks like it's getting into trouble, putting some in the bank, and moving your average position further out, "expanding" your space, and giving yourself more room to survive a deep RT. If the RT ends up continuing back in your original trade direction, you can "compress" the space back again.

It's more suited for swing or position type trades I think, running over many hours, days, or even weeks, but you can still use it on a LTF trade, as I am attempting to do here.

Something I hope to master, is if I get on something that goes on a good run over several hours, is to "compress" up my space upon every successful retest and hold of freshly created FLs after engulfs.

posts.text:
Ok, so here's something I'm currently pondering. Below is a condensed chart of UJ, M15, with some important levels marked.

Bear with me, as I go through what I'm thinking.

First of all, an observation - I've noticed that quite often, when you have a HTF FTR, or S/D extreme in general, price will react to the first lower TF FTR formed after the initial move away from the extrme. Not only react to it, but almost like clockwork, you get a tiny FO into the LTF level that the first FTR formed off, and away it goes.

UJ has currently come short off such a level - the hollow box at the top is the first lower TF FTR at the edge of a prominent D1 FTR.

Here's the daily chart, and why I think it is important:

And here's M15 of that area, showing the level we've recently had a short reaction to:

Now, like good traders, we don't just dive in immediately, but we wait for an engulf of a significant opposing FTR to give us some idea that the move has got legs, and then enter on a RT.

Referring back to the topmost chart, just below this level we're currently having a long reaction to, is a level I've marked W1S. It was a weekly supply extreme, which in fact formed from the daily FTR we've now had a move short off.

The initial move down from the top engulfed both the FTR from the upwards engulf of this W1S, and also the source of the move that engulfed the W1S. After travelling a little further down, we've had a strong retrace off the level that was the source of the engulf of the short level I've marked "1st FTR" - this was the 1st large FTR formed after the top of the W1S when we fell away from it way back in 2007.

Now, to my mind, the level we are currently coming long off is less "significant" in the scheme of things. The W1S was a weekly supply extreme, and so presumably required a good shove to push through. We then took out this "shove" level from the first drop.

What I'm thinking is that price is now likely to RT back to the first new FTR formed from the recent drop (marked on the chart, also a QM level), which should then open the way up for a drop down to at least the level I've marked "Eng src of next FTR" - it being, as the name suggests, the source of the move which pushed through the next FTR in line from the down move in 2007. However, time and again, I've seen these seemingly "innocuous" levels actually turn into massive trend continuations.

I'm wondering - is it just down to my currently flawed understanding of the market that I get things like this wrong? Or am I just being far too ambitious in even trying to predict what level we're going to fall down to, given that the current level we've reacted long from hasn't actually been engulfed yet? I presume the concepts of PAZ apply on weekly and daily charts, just the same as they do on H4, H1, M30 etc, it's just that it takes a lot longer to play out.

I'm sure it's possible to rate the relative importance of each FTR on the scheme of things - whether it was a daily/weekly level, where it formed, what the move from that level took out, and thereby derive an understanding of where we think price is likely to go. I'm just perhaps not very good at it yet, and require more chart time and seeing things play out in order to get better at the analysis.

One last quick observation - we've currently had a small short move off a FTR that formed at the same level as the last upwards FTR before the recent high extreme. I've noticed that quite often these are also significant levels - in the same way that the first FTR after a move from an extreme, so can be the level that the last FTR of the upward (or downward) move formed at, when we revisit the other side of it.

posts.author: smimon
posts.text:
And just one more last "last" observation

I'm getting so wrapped up I think currently in zooming my charts out, to micro-analyse where FTRs formed, and where FTRs were engulfed, that I'm forgetting to do basic HTF Supply/Demand zone analysis.

Where are we likely to RT to, if we've formed a nice short move off a HTF FTR? A fresh H4 supply level formed near the edge. I've seen a lot of the time, that if you draw a line from the body close of the candle prior to the momo candle (the two taken together defining the S/D zone), it gives you a good idea of where price might bounce from, allowing you to hone in on any important LTF levels around the vicinity.

Here is a chart showing some H4 supply zones that were created as UJ moved short from the top, with lines drawn from the body closes of the previous candles.

Here are the same lines, but shown on M15 - helpful to narrowing our levels down.

They also usually form nice SR lines we can watch for reactions to in the future.

You can also drop down through the timeframes, H1, M30 etc, and repeat the same technique to find the H1/whatever fresh supply zones "inside" the H4 supply zone, narrowing the range of nice RT levels even further.

Also, if the level has already had a wick through it, but hasn't been taken out, it can still be used as a point of reference in the future. Here's an example from GJ:

H1

LTF

I believe this works because really what you're seeing when you draw these body lines is minor SR flip zones, or in fact the other side of ignored LTF FTRs, that are subsequently momo'd over when price makes a big surge.

This doesn't always work of course - it depends entirely on whether the H4 (or whatever) S/D level is actually significant in the scheme of things, depending on what we're coming off on Daily, what we've engulfed etc.

Anyway, excuse my ramblings, I still sometimes feel like I'm failing to see the wood for the trees, but I know it'll all gel perfectly well given more chart time.

posts.text:
For me, there are only 2 things I need to take a trade: - a zone that could turn price, be it a FL, FTR, QM, whatever - a reason to enter the trade

Finding zones is what RTM is all about. The excellent analysis techniques provide us with the means to identify possible turning points ahead of time. We could just set POs, and trust that more will work than will not, which is no doubt a profitable way of trading provided you're getting at least 2 or 3R on your trades.

But if we really want to bump up our win %age, we need a good reason to enter the trade at the zone, merely apart from the fact that price has arrived there. What's a good reason? PA of course. We let the market tell us the intentions of the ITs.

What's a good type of PA to look out for? For me at least, it's the initial surge from a level that engs something significant, and then returns to source. That's where we enter.

I like to use D1/H4/H1 for my zones, and M15/M5 for my entry PA. Once you get used to spotting these types of trades, they're everywhere. Some may only make a small surge up to the next zone, some may keep going for much longer - that's when your HTF analysis comes into play.

To my mind though, I'm quite happy grabbing 3 or 4R off a good surge in 30 mins. If I want to hit the equivalent of 20R on a trade, I've got 2 options - leave it running for ages, and risk my HTF analysis being wrong, or if I'm confident in my win %age, rolling the profits of the first trade into a second. If I lose, then I'm just back to where I started for the day. If I win the second, that's getting on for some decent account gain, depending on your risk level.

I like to trade between 2 and 4% risk depending on how much I like the look of things. If I hit 3R off a 4% trade (12%), and then roll that into a second and do it again (12 x 3 = 36, plus the original 12 = 48%) then I've almost increased my account by 50% just off 2 single 3R trades, which can usually play out in an hour or less.

I've even written it down so I can see it in front of me - "3R, and then 3R, that's all you need".

Obviously you need to be quite consistent to get this to work well, which is why I use the two steps mentioned above. I'll just post a couple of quick examples so I can illustrate what I mean.

#1

#2

As always, this is nothing new. Many others have said this already, and better than I.

I seem to keep wanting to make trading more complicated than this, by micro-analysing things on M1, but in truth, it's really not necessary for simple, quick results. You can be in and out, with your 3/5/10/20/50% whatever, off a couple of trades in less than an hour, and then go and do something else with your day.

This method doesn't always work - sometimes you get V-shaped bottoms or tops, where price just runs away. C'est la vie, we don't need to be on every single move the market makes. I'd rather miss out on these, than risk getting 50% of them wrong by using "blind" POs at certain levels.

There are of course other tell-tale signs, such as CP into a level, etc. But for me at least, this is the most blindingly obvious PA to look out for.

Here's the candle body line concept in action again. I first learned of this idea a while back, when I was still in the wilderness before RTM, from a great trader on another forum, who called the concept a "zero line" (or "z line" for short), because it's quite frequently the point where breakout traders will have their trades zeroed out by a RT after they've moved their stops to B/E, before their stops are hit and add fuel to the fire, and the move continues on its way.

We can't just use them blindly, there has to exist a confluence of factors to strengthen the decision.

And of course, obviously, they do just represent a place within a supply or demand zone. But they represent a great place for us to start narrowing down our search for pinpoint trades. I've seen price bounce off them almost to the pip so many times over the time I've been trading, that it would be foolish of me not to include them in my toolkit.

Why do they work? Most of the time, if you draw them in and drop timeframe, you'll find that what has been marked is actually some local SR which held price up or down for a while before a surge, or also quite often the edge of the last LTF FTR which get's momo'd over by a surge, which then becomes an ignored SD level. Both of these things we know are usually good for a bounce.

Here's a daily chart of NU, where I've marked in some z lines and shown where price reacted to them. You can find them on any timeframe, but obviously the higher timeframe ones are more probable for big bounces.

Here's today's NU surge and drop on LTF.

When it comes down to it, it's all just boxes (FL/FTR SD zones) and lines (SR, z lines etc). Why anyone would waste time with squiqqly line indicators all over their chart is beyond me.

posts.text:
Sunday's always a good time to play around with some code. After falling afoul of losing sight of the big picture last week, I've been messing around with a good way to superimpose HTF S/D zones on top of each other, in a clear, easily visually identifiable manner. I was previously using outline boxes with borders of various thickness, but I quickly ended up with a confusing mess of lines on my chart.

As I'm sure anyone who has experimented with drawing rectangles on top of each other in MT4 knows, it's got an annoying habit of flipping colours of overlapping shapes, so that you end up with weird and wonderful shades, none of which was what you originally wanted. It's possible to apply a bitwise negation to a rectangle's colour before drawing it in order to counter this effect, but you still run into problems when one part of a rectangle overlaps another, and one part does not.

The only way I could reliably find to achieve the effect I was looking for was to convert the rectangle's price/time co-ordinates to x/y using the built in function, and then draw a rectangle label exactly on top of the original one. Rectangle labels do not suffer from the aforementioned colour flipping problem, but they are fixed in position - as you scroll the chart, they remain fixed in the same place. As such, you have to implement a timer function to redraw them every couple of hundred milliseconds in the correct position, which is a bit of a bodge (there is a lag effect as you scroll the chart quickly), but works. Also some other small caveats like making sure you sort your list of rectangles into descending order of timeframe (W1 then D1 then H4 etc) so that the correct drawing order is respected.

All a bit geeky, but I'm still a software developer at heart, and I always like trying to come up with creative solutions to work around the limitations of software. The end result is quite nice - here's a recent chart of GBPCHF, where we can see price hitting the nested H1/H4/D1/W1 supply zones, and falling off nicely.

Next up on the list is a way for me to quickly indicate which zones are engulf sources, and getting some good colours to indicate engulfed zones on various TFs. The more information I can assimilate from a single glance at a chart, the quicker I can make decisions about which direction to try and look for entries on LTF, and trade accordingly.

As an aside, this approach also lends itself quite nicely to a S/D radar, which will show me, once the zones are drawn, at a glance for all pairs I trade which ones are currently in tradeable zones.

Eng or FO?

Here's something which was puzzling me for a while, the number of times that a FL appears to have been engulfed, only for the move to continue in its original direction -seemingly a "failed engulf".

In terms of a bullish move, consider that many times a FL forms just after a FTR is momo'd over, or ignored. When price retraces later, and appears to have engulfed our FL, in actual fact what has happened is that it has dipped slightly lower to bounce off the ignored level that the FL formed above.

This will of course be clearer with an example. Here's a recent one on EU.

It may be the case that there's something on the tick chart in these occasions, but I don't have the data.

I'm not going to treat any eng of a few pixels as a real eng - there are too many reasons why it might be FO. When a genuine eng happens, it's usually by a lot more than a pip or two - and even if you miss a few valid ones, you'll keep yourself out of a lot of bad ones too.

Hey pal. They're both indicators I wrote, I strangely enough really enjoy coding for MQL, I've pretty much know it inside out after getting enraged at it for the last 10 months!

The marker one shows news events, past and present, that are applicable to the pairing you're looking at. I use a javascript bookmarklet to parse the calendar from FxStreet into a text file, and the indi reads it.. Different colours dependent on the expected volatility, future events shown with a dotted vline so I don't forget what's in store for the week, could also add alerts, although haven't done so yet.

First journal update of the new year, so I'll take the opportunity to wish you all a Happy New Year.

So my first 3 months with the RTM material were a real ray of light in the darkness of the "trading without a clue" wilderness that had come before. I'd gained the ability to make some great trades, but was still haemorrhaging losers all over the place. After once already revisiting all the material once from scratch, I decided to read through the RTM thread on Forex Factory to see if I could glean any further nuggests from it. It's a great read, I recommend it to anyone who hasn't seen it yet. The main thing I picked up was the importance of FLs above all else. So many times a seemingly strong FTR gets taken out, only for you to then realise we just went deeper into the FL that caused it. In particular, this sentence from IF about FOs struck home and made a lot of sense - "Say price is coming up to a supply. The only way we can be sure that supply will hold price down is if that supply has already visited the extreme set of orders in the flag limit to its left. If the supply fell short of that, we can anticipate a FO to those extreme orders." (the link to the thread is here by the way - www.forexfactory.com/showthread.php?t=420159 )

With this information in mind, and resolving that this year I will turn this trading style into a science, rather than an art, I'm trying to take fewer trades, and analyse the charts as thoroughly as possible to spot the important FLs, and engulfs thereof. I'm sure I'll still get some wrong, but I aim to get those down to the utter minimum. It really is possible not to take any full stop outs if you know what you're doing.

posts.text:
Hey pal, thanks for stopping by.

I simply wait for an engulf of an important FL (making sure we've checked on M1 if it's real, or a fakeout), and then assume price is going to reach the other side of the PAZ down (or up) to the next important FL on whatever TF we're on. It's then a case of waiting through the RT after the engulf until it gets to a likely level, and entering. Even better is when it reaches the last possible level that it can react to before it has to continue on its way. If you've read your engulfs correctly, those are almost a guaranteed trade, and the depth of the RT opens up a ton of space to trade into. 2 PAZs might only be 10 pips apart, but when you've had a 50 pip RT after an engulf, you've got a nice trade.

Longer term bias doesn't necessarily matter for a single trade - a valid setup is a valid setup after all - but if we're coming off a daily or weekly level, in line with the HTF trend, then I am more likely to hold on to a trade and let it run as far as possible. This is something I need to work on more really - my UJ trade went much further, but I'm still finding my feet, so when I've got good profit on the table, I tend to bag it quickly. The confidence for longer holds will come with time.

With counter trend trades, I will take everything at the first target, no exceptions, and then look to reverse if possible - the target for one trade is often a great place to enter an opposing one. With trades that go with the long term trend, then it's up to your discretion whether you want to keep hold of it in the hope it will blast through a few more levels - you can always monitor PA and get out when it looks like you've had an important FL eng go against you.

Bear in mind too that PAZs exist on W1, D1, H4 etc etc. Which PAZ we've engulfed into on which timeframe is a good way to give ourselves a directional compass for our longer term bias.

Hope that helps in some way.

Wow, place looks busy all of a sudden, guessing that's because the main site URL came back online.

Anyone struggling a bit with fitting everything together - I'd really urge you to go and read the RTM thread on Forex Factory. It's absolute gold. Since sitting down with it at the start of this week, my trading has suddenly shot to a new level, when I realised the importance of FLs at important levels.

Trading wise, little bit shabby today. I got into an EJ long after seeing an important engulf north last night, realised it wasn't going well, and thought to myself - "what's the lowest possible point it could RT to before the entire move is dead". I decided to move my stop out there, using some of the excess profit I'd built up during the week. Price went down to 1 pip above where my stop was, and then came all the way back up into profit. If I'd just set a PO at the edge level...

It made me realise something - it's always worth waiting for the deepest possible retrace after you see an engulf to set a PO. You can literally get in with a 1 pip stop on the edge of these zones if you've spotted them correctly. If price hasn't yet tested the extreme orders in a FL, then it will sooner or later. Whenever you see what you think is an FTR - draw a box around it. Now drag that box back in time until you find the FL it was formed from. That is the real level you want to trade, the "apparent" FTR itself is just ripe for a FO if it wasn't formed off the very edge of the flag.

Stopped myself out of a UJ long after FOMC last night, which would have made about 20R. Panicked, and didn't trust my entry. Took b/e 4 times on the gold up move today, after seeing the engulf south of the important FL. I had a PO on the deepest possible RT level, but by this point I was in PTSD mode. I got taken in by a pip, and then price flagged slowly down from the top. I went b/e again too soon - price dropped like a stone, missed about 15R on that one.

I've just sat and watched UCAD come off a level I was monitoring within 0.5 pip.

I'm certainly not there yet, but I'm starting to see some amazingly accurate trade levels, even if at the moment I seem to keep making a hash of getting on them. Trading is starting to seem more like a science to me now, as it should do, instead of a bit of a dark art.

posts.text:
Personally, I only draw the lowest or highest edges of a bullish or bearish flag respectively, rather than a box around the whole thing, since it seems to me that these are the important edges, but I'm sure there's a reason why most of the academy students draw the entire box. There are tons of examples in my journal.

This is an example of one of the charts I trade from. These levels have just accumulated over time, I occasionally have to spring clean my charts to clean them up. There are probably more levels on here than I need, but I'm still in the process of refining my identification of which levels matter most.

i.imgur.com/EFkP3XO.png

I try to find only the important engulfed flags/FTRs, and nothing else. I find them by looking left, and seeing what engulfed what. The HTF engulfed flags (shown in grey with a red or green "tab" at the end) are more important, the LTF engulfed flags (greyish dark green or red) act as guidelines to how we're going to get from FTR to FTR.

I will use HTF initially to find the more prominent FLs/FTRs - but as soon as I've marked it on H4/D1/W1 whatever, I drop on to M1/M5, and extend the zone to the left until I find the actual FL it formed off.

In this way, I know straight away which are the more important flags I should be looking at. I'll use PAZ formed by FTRs corresponding to H1/H4/D1 FL engulfs as a directional guideline, and the LTF FLs as a way of tracking how I'm going to get there, and which level we're likely to RT from.

Sorry if this is a bit confusing, but it's quite hard to summarise in a few paragraphs a process that it's taken me 3 months of staring at charts about 10 hours a day to figure at. It's really all about just starting with the basic building blocks, the engulf and the FTR, and then applying it over and over again in your chart history, until it's become second nature. I must have marked up a 1000 different places on various charts at one point or another. Sometimes if I'm bored, I just scroll back to 2009 or another random year, and start making on where I think the important levels are, and then scroll forward in time to see if I was right. Alternatively, just find somewhere a massive move originated from, draw a horizontal line from the top/bottom, and then scroll back until you find the place it started from, and see if you can figure out why.

What you tend to find with these sort of SR flips is that if you bring up the tick chart, there is almost always a tiny FTR exactly in line with the base of the pole. I was playing with the 3 tick chart on Dukascopy last night, and it's great for seeing "inside" a big M1 pole. It's a shame MT4 doesn't natively support tick charts, there are indis which will collect it for you, but they require MT4 to be running 24/7 to collect the data. zhao wrote: A question how you manage these two point in your trading: 1 the decision point that make the move to break the important FL/FTR, 2 the FL/FTR that formed after the break. When price RT, where you put your enter point? I read many charts, but still confusing. which point is more important? Price can stop at either of these points or even RT to the origin of the move. How you handle it in your trading?

The FTR is always the important level that we must consider the engulf of when defining a FTR PAZ to trade with. The DP to engulf is quite often an important level in its own right, and we can quite often see a big bounce from these levels, but it's the FTRs and the engulfs of the FTRs (not forgetting to include the FL that caused the FTR within our zone) that give us our heads up on how to trade. The only caveat to consider is if the DP to engulf is also an important FTR in its own right. I can show you a quick example from UJ from memory (excuse the small text, I had to resize chart, it should still be legible):

Further to this, I'd like to amend my initial comments.

The place where a strong decision was made to engulf an important FL can also be an important level in its own right, provided it's relatively close to the FTR (on the relevant timeframe). I've been working under the assumption, and indeed been told independently that only the FTR is the important level, but I've just seen too many times that a FTR gets taken out, only for the DP to cause a massive reaction, and reverse the whole move. The Dax seems to be especially bad for this.

It's not all bad news though - quite often, when we have a decision to engulf an important level followed by a RT and then FTR, the FTR sits almost on top of the original DP. In these cases, we can just treat both DP and FTR as a single zone - it gives us a FO area when looking for entries from a FTR.

When there is a big gap between DP and FTR, I don't expect the DP to be as important.

In my opinion, FTB to any level where there are large amount of untested orders is valid for a PO. Remember, all this FL/FTR analysis is merely an enhancement to basic Supply/Demand trading, and it's to help us locate the levels on the charts where the unfilled orders are. If we see an engulf in the favour of the trade first, then great - we've got a confirmed trade. However even if we don't see this, there are still many levels where we can be reasonably sure of a big bounce - certainly enough to get some profit out of, and then leave the rest to run to see what happens. These I believe are called SAS trades - "scalp and see". You'll probably never get 100% trade success with this method, but you can still take plenty of profit, and avoid taking any full stop out in most cases if you manage the trade properly.

We knew there were significant amounts of buy orders in that FL, because of how it formed - after the engulf of an important opposing level. We also could see there had been a large surge from the level. We could also see that the extreme edge of the FL had not yet been tested. All of these were good reasons to expect a reaction.

The best way to manage these types of trades for me currently is to enter the order in 2 parts. Take some profit where you see the first likely trouble area, and then hold the rest as long as PA supports it.

Seem to be at the stage now where I can pinpoint most of the minor intraday turns in the market within a few pips, by just applying a few simple rules. Many major ones too. Took a combined 40R off 2 gold shorts on Friday using the method.

- important FLs: start off on MN1, work down TFs, mark on any engulfed FTRs, or just engulfed large swings (although I don't consider the engulf of a LTF swing high/low important (unless it was a reaction to the extreme of an important FL), the return to a FTR from the engulf of a swing high/low which lasted days or weeks is going to definitely produce a tradeable reaction on LTF) - origins - SR flips from poles/last small FTR into the top/bottom

Confirmed entries are of course better using this method, but quite often you can get the first top/bottom to a few pips, and then take a second entry off what would have been your confirmed entry had you waited. This works for continuation moves also.

posts.author: smimon
posts.text:
Haha, no worries.

Go Tools --> Options and set the number of bars in history/chart to something 1,000,000 - the option isn't in the dropdown, but you can overtype it. You need to close and relaunch MT4 for this setting to get picked up correctly. i.imgur.com/c652DOJ.png

Next, press F2 to go to history centre, find the symbol you want on the left, and click download. This might take a while. Everything going well, all the history should then appear. However, the history handling in MT4 isn't the best. You might have to click download again, and get it to "recalculate all timeframes", or right click on the chart and hit "Refresh" if strange gaps appear in the data. Also a relaunch doesn't hurt. i.imgur.com/YZ8uvwe.png

Eventually, it settles down and should be ok.

A warning though - if you've got a number of charts open, having this many history bars can use a lot of memory, and MT4 can start bugging or crashing out. Gaps can randomly appear in the data, or it gets stuck on "Waiting for update" when you switch TF. A relaunch usually fixes this.

In the worst case, it will crash completely, with the "Metatrader has stopped working" windows dialog, Every time you relaunch, after 30 seconds it happens again. To clear this, you have to open, quickly close down all charts, close, relaunch with no charts open, and then it's fine.

1,000,000 seems to be about the sweet spot, I only get very occasional crashes with this. Any more, and it becomes almost unusable. I actually have a separate instance of MT4 with 5,000,000 bars so I can look back on M1 about a decade, which I just fire up when I need it, and then close down again.

Have fun;-)

I've seen the question "how do you know if a FL is important or not" a few times, so as best as I can explain it:

- it is important is there is a big surge from it - it is important if it holds price up/down several times - this is perhaps the key indicator - it is important if it is the last s urge into a top/bottom, that is a FTR from taking out an opposing important FL

When you bear these 3 things in mind, the level on Gold was important because:

In terms of "knowing" it will hold, you don't - at least I don't with that much confidence! However what I do know is we are guaranteed to get a decent bounce from it - there are simply too many orders in levels like that for it not to give a good bounce. It's a scalp-and-see PO really when you try and pick a top like that. If you've analysed the level correctly, it's a great potential runner. If you've analysed it wrong, you're usually stopped out in 10 seconds;-)

Analysis starts on MN1, and goes down through the TFs. Look for what MN/W1/D1/H4/H1 levels have been engulfed (in decreasing order of importance), and look for the FTRs formed by these.

Here's the area of W1 supply we reacted to, on D1. Important W1/D1 engulfed FLs marked, and the FTRs marked. Note that 2 of the lower D1 FTRs have been engulfed already.

Here's the same area, on H1. Note the sharp clean FTR after taking out the last D1 FL into the top.

M1 of our trade area - the initial drop from the edge of the H1 FTR identified earlier took out both of the FLs formed from the engulf of the daily levels. We bounced once from the shoulder of the pole base, and then again from deeper inside it. It's a fair bet there's not a lot of demand left in here now. Therefore, the retrace to origin is a valid place to expect a decent reaction. Take some profit quickly at the first opposing FL, and then you've got the confidence to let the rest run as far as PA shows you it's going to go.

posts.author: smimon
posts.text:
The most common mistake I see on here (not to try and sound all high and mighty - I make plenty of my own!) is people simply drawing a line from a swing high/low, and then treating it as engulf. We've got to consider that every FTR forms as a reaction to some FL. Whenever you see a swing high or low, mark it with a horizontal line, and look left, however far back in time you have to go back, until you find the FL that caused it on LTF. Draw a box around the whole FL, and if the FTR didn't reach the very edge of those orders in the FL, then a FO is always possible.

A couple of examples immediately springs to mind from recent PA on UJ. Here's H4:

Both these levels looked like they'd been engulfed. But both of them were FOs of the apparent obvious levels. How could we have known this? Simple, by dropping down to LTF, and extending our rectangles further back in time to find the FL that caused them.

Here's the top one M5:

Here's the bottom one M5:

Now let's look at that H4 chart again:

Both apparent FTRs were caused from reactions to a FL, but we hadn't reached the extreme set of orders (very edge of the FL) in either of them. We can't treat a FTR as engulfed until the FL that caused the FTR is also engulfed too.

Engulf DP's aren't the levels we should be looking for, it's FTRs. Remember price is fractal - we get larger swings, which are themselves comprised of smaller swings. The key is to keep looking for the first significant FTR of a up or down move, starting from higher TFs, and working down to M1. posts.author: smimon
posts.text:
By_Tor2114 wrote: I think the tricky part is knowing when a swing is a reaction to a flag limit, or when a swing actually is a flag limit.

You just need to look left (and possibly left again) and see if there is any obvious RBR or DBD that was formed after breaking a level, that price is reacting to. That is then the level that you look for the break of, not the swing itself. This way, you can avoid FOs, by being aware of where the actual edge of the important FL is. Sometimes you get a series of stacked FTRs all on top of a FL - this is then compression.

Sometimes the levels look insignificant, like the one on GU. But the market tells us it is important, because the last FTR into the top formed after bouncing from it. Therefore the break of this FL (also bearing in mind what we'd bounced from above) was significant.

Without the added information of bouncing from a HTF/big FTR/FL above, then it's harder to gauge the importance of a FL breaking. FL break without apparent reason for the break = no trade for me. I will only take the ones where I can clearly see a reason for the bounce and break.

Hope that helps.

posts.text:
My style of trading has changed somewhat over the last couple of weeks.

Back in the day, before RTM, I used to just try and trade pin bars for reversals. Obviously, without a deeper understanding of how to read price, this was hit and miss at best. Sometimes pins indicate rejection of price, sometimes they represent consumption of supply/demand before a move continues. Having the context in which to understand these is vital - and RTM gives us that context.

Now, I'm moving back towards PA-based trading, but combined with the experience gained by applying RTM techniques. The 2 main things I'm focusing on are surges in price, and signs of rejection on M1 after a engulf + RT - pins, inverted pins, signs of momentum fading.

PBs/IPBs immediately following a strong surge that breaks through a range are usually a great place to get a quick continuation. PBs/IPBs following an eng + RT are also a great place to take an entry, with a longer hold available. Just the pins by themselves aren't enough however - you need to have identified that the pins are occurring in a logical zone to turn price. Sometimes after an eng we get a shallow RT, sometimes a deep RT. PA gives me the clue as to whether we're going shallow or deep in these instances.

I like this style for 2 reasons - first, it's essentially confirmation trades only. No more guessing where price might turn, you simply wait for the market to tell you what's going on. Secondly, by sizing your position aggressively with a stop just above/below the pins (this results in a stop of 2 or 3 pips normally, I'll usually then remove the stop and manage the trade manually - it's possible to get stopped out by half a pip otherwise) you can hit 3 or 4R within the next 3 or 4 M1 bars, and if it really takes off, you can get 20R or more without too much trouble.

This style works best during the periods of highest volatility (0730 - 0930/1000 & 1330 -1630). The faster price moves around, the more exaggerated PA becomes, and the easier it is to read it. It's a highly aggressive style, definitely not suited for everyone, and you need to be able to tolerate high levels of risk and think quickly to pull it off.

I'm coding up a couple of alerting systems - one that goes off whenever a strong surge in price occurs which breaks through the range of at least 10 previous bars (arbitrary number, might adjust this), and one that goes off when we have a cluster of PBs/IPBs. They're not the kind of signals that you could feed into an EA - they're "look, something is potentially happening, open up the chart and analyse it, and see what's going on" signals. This means I can effectively monitor several charts without having to sit here staring at them. I can be playing a game, watching a movie, reading a book or whatever, and periodically something will bleep at me, and give me a heads up.

I'm entering the end of my learning phase now (at least, the learning phase required to go live - the learning never stops!), and I've realised it's quite possible to hit 10R daily off these sorts of setups if handled correctly, sometimes an awful lot more. There are probably about 10 or 20 tradeable setups across 6 charts every day. I'm back to 4% risk, and so I'll make it my aim to hit 40% daily for the next couple of weeks. If I can do that, I've truly convinced myself beyond a shadow of a doubt that I'm good enough to trade my real cash, and multiply it rapidly. 40% compounded twice is nearly 100%, so it'd be doubling an account every 2 days if I can pull it off. I'm sure that's not sustainable indefinitely - there simply aren't enough orders in the market beyond a point, but that's a nice problem to dream about having!

I'm almost never totally, hideously wrong with a decision any more, so I'm happy to trade without a stop using this method, jumping out at b/e on a RT if I've read price wrong and the trade goes against me. Worst case scenario - I take a big painful loss, but that's the risk you take with aggressive trading.

Sorry to waffle on, just airing my thoughts!

Here's a screenie of EU, showing the surge detection code currently in testing. It basically looks for a bullish/bearish run of bars that breaks the range of at least 10 bars. It needs a bit of tweaking, it's missing a few of them due to needing to make some adjustments to the algorithm to handle inside bars, it's quite simplistic at present.

Pins by themselves crop up all over the place, but pins in the correct zones in the context of preceding PA are a great way to take a tight entry. It's how I'm being able to generate 8R or more off 4 M1 bars in some instances with the morning's volatility.

In this case, the strong drop from the daily level and RT to this important FTR (remember the first FTR after eng into a CP PAZ is good for a FTB trade) would have been enough to make me take the pins, especially with the news lurking just ahead. Usually if you see something in a great place to turn price, in the context of HTF PA, just ahead of news, then you've got a good trade.

I will use a stop line just above the pins to size my trade with my calc tool, and then usually remove the stop and manage the trade manually - in case, as you say, price decides it wants to go a couple of pips above or below before moving the right way, which often happens. In this case, with the news coming, I'd have used a hard stop just above the whole FTR zone for safety, I won't ever go into news without a stop, just in case something horrendous happens.

Credit goes to Blackhawk for the suggestion to just get used to trading small lot sizes with no stop - it really forces you to analyse step-by-step what's going on with price movement, and bail on a trade if it looks like it's going against you. There is a tendency I find to ignore signs the trade is going wrong when you've placed a stop above what you believe to be a good zone - you sort of think "well, it looks bad, but I'm sure my stop will hold" - and then it doesn't!

Maybe I'm guilty of perfectionism - but the truth is, I've still got several months of time to play with before I get into dire financial straits, and I intend to use that time wisely to get as completely tuned in with the charts as I can before I put cash on the line. If the difference is - go live now, be conservative, add 10% daily, stress myself out because I'm not confident in my ability to read price movement properly - or wait another month or so, completely master what I'm doing, and be able to add 50-100% daily by compounding winnings - then I know what I prefer. I know now I'm merely a whisker away from where I want to be.

I'm still improving on a daily basis, I'm really trying now to hone my "feel" for price, that which can't really be quantified. The speed at which the candles are forming, how quickly they are rejecting from a level, momentum, where the last surge in price was, mentally combining M1 candles into M2/M3 PA etc - all of these things help us get a read on what's likely to come next. When you can get this skill down, there are suddenly 20 or more opportunities on M1 on every chart on every single day, instead of having to wait hours for a setup. The ability to read the market intention by analysing the movement of M1 PA becomes your "confirmation", in addition to all the excellent RTM techniques.

Hi smimon.

You will find that a real account is different from a demo for two main reasons: 1. It is real money and you need to deal with it. 2. Demo trading gives you perfect execution because it assumes inifnite liquidity. Real life trading has liquidity issues, and that leads to slippage and to trades setups that are not triggered.

I think you need to taste that, because it will affect the outcome of your current plans.

Also, I know it;s a personal choice, but I think that the stop loss gives you freedom. You won't need to spend an unknown amount of time managing a bad trade. Instead you can use that time scanning the market for the next setup without stress.

The more you know, the simpler it all seems to become...

Would it surprise you to know that everything you need to know about how to trade accurately, and with confirmation, is in a single post on the first page of the ForexFactory RTM thread? www.forexfactory.com/showthread.php? p=6585047#post6585047

Hi All,

I too have been following the topic of 'finding the origins' for a few weeks now. And like Smimon said, there is gold in the first page of the FF thread. I review those charts often to remind myself of how the IT's think and play tricks.

I wanted to add that there are 2 other gems in the 'origin' story right here under our noses.

Go to the videos link: www.readthemarket.com/index.php/education/education-videos and watch the videos named "What's an engulf" and "The FTR Trade" at least 3 times. Listen to every word. For me, the light-bulb lit up the last time I watched those 2 videos.

Next, get to work identifying origins on the charts. Watch what happens when price comes back. There are only 2 options, engulf or respect. When you get an engulf, what happens next? When the level is respected, what happens next? I find that the M30 or H1 chart is often low enough to see the ITs plans in advance.

@Kossack - you don't need tick data for identifying origins. Check what IF does in the FTR trade video - he starts with weekly and drops to daily. Tick data is nice to have if you plan on basing your trades on M1 charts. But even then, I think you can often pinpoint the same entries on M1 by seeing between the lines of the candles. It all really boils down to your trading style.

And the concept of fractals is interesting too. Watching origins on a M30 chart provides the same signals (engulf/respected levels) as an M1 chart. There are just way more of them in M1. At the same time, your targets in M1 are closer to the origins. So, use M30 and swing trade or M1 and scalp, it is all the same. Engulfs, FL and Origins work the same in any time frame. At least that is how I see it today.

GJ.

In other words, the potential for compounding is enormous when you can pick levels... even using higher time frame charts. I can also recommend, if you have not already, reading about 'SPACE' from Cap N Crunch. I do not like the method but I like the process. In a simple form, you start with your seed money and wait for price to come into an area of high probability. Then you enter using your seed money. If you are wrong... you start over. If you are right, you start the process of compounding... taking profits, entering again on retracements/FTRs all the while being more aggressive with house money. When you reach some pre-set goal, you liquidate and start the process over again.

I tend to get slaughtered on anything less than 30 mins, but using H1 and H4, the drive for liquidity is getting easier and easier to see and using compounding gives me flexibility to start with a wide range to enter the market (ie, small lot size, large stop loss). Once the market moves in my favor, I build and build and build my position.

I played around with trading futures (demo) this way and starting with $200 in seed risk capital, gains of $10,000 were doable in a week or less. My demo account expired so I went back to playing with IC Markets.. but futures trading is a logical next steps after being successful with a live account.

Time to vent some spleen.

Went live last week, and I'm having an utter nightmare. Everything I touch seems to turn to sh*t at the moment. I'm getting stopped out by 0.1 pip here, having a PO missed by 0.1 pip there, having price turn seemingly in thin air against me. I understand that this is all due to deficencies in my reading.

The psychology is difficult. When I win my first trade, I trade well. When I lose, for each successive trade my decision making just becomes worse and worse. The hardest part is patience - after I lose a trade, I just want to be straight back into the market again, which is obviously not a good idea.

I'm not sure what anyone else thinks about this, and it may just be my misconception since I'm not doing so well at present - but I swear price reading seems to be an order of magnitude more difficult than even 6 months ago. So many more FOs than I can remember, which really muddy the picture, because it's difficult to understand whether what you are seeing is a genuine engulf, or a FO.

The mechanical science of "this FL engulfed that important FL, which engulfed that important FL" just does not hold up as it should half the time. The important FL gets engulfed, just for price to turn off some seemingly random cluster in the middle of nowhere. Which if you look back far enough, you can always find some sort of swap or SR flip to explain - but if you drew all of these on your chart, all the time, you wouldn't be able to see the screen for the number of lines you'd have across it.

If indeed price reading is a science, then my textbook is missing half the pages, and I'm not sure where to find them right now.

I'll keep plugging away, my time on demo has convinced me that I can trade perfectly well, but the confidence is taking a battering right now. Conditions have been so slow these past few weeks as well, which makes things more difficult.

Anyway, that's enough complaining. Back to the grindstone. I will persevere eventually.

One of the most common mistakes I make, and have to work hard to eliminate, is to always try to fade a surge in price.

Most of the time, when a massive range expansion in price takes place like that, the market is telling you something - price wants to continue going up.

I want to help you and even though my price reading skills are lower than yours, there is something I think I can help with. The above post and a few before this have a somewhat negative tone. Each and every experience we have in life presents 2 possible outcomes. It can be either negative or positive. If you chose to interpret the results as negative, then you will have a negative experience. If you chose to interpret the results as positive, then you will have a positive experience.

It does not matter what happens to you, it is only your choice to interpret it either as positive or negative. So, you have an intention to read the market and I sense that you feel it is not working. This whole thing is like a hammer. If you use the wrong end of the hammer (you define your results as being negative) it will take a lot longer to drive the nail. If you define your results as positive, NO MATTER WHAT THEY ARE OR HOW CLOSELY THEY MATCH YOUR EXPECTATIONS, then you are using the hammer the proper way.

Everything we do in life is about abundance. You just happen to have an abundance of frustration at the moment. That is what I sense. Be grateful for your abundance. Embrace your abundance no matter what it is. The road from A to B often passes through C, D, E, F, G, H, I, J etc.

Where do you go from here? Ask the question. What do I want to do right now that gives me the most excitement that I am not doing at this moment?

The answer may have nothing to do with trading. No matter what the answer, practice acting on your excitement in every moment. Slowly you will train yourself to act when you need to do so and your circumstances will begin to change to match your desires and intentions.

I realize that on the surface this may appear to have nothing to do with trading and I encourage you to just try it out. Life is abundance. Enjoy your abundance, no matter what it is and eventually you will be given more and more of the things that are in alignment with your desires.

JC.

posts.text:
Well, at the risk of getting ahead of myself, I feel like I've finally turned the corner on live.

Going from demo to live was more of a massive leap than I thought it was going to be The intensity of the emotional battle can't be compared. But as a positive, the lessons you learn on live stick with you a lot more than anything on demo. Ultimately, demo doesn't matter, there are no real consequences to loss, other than damage to your ego. Worst comes to worst, you just press the "reset" button. There isn't that option on live, and you really have to start thinking a hell of a lot more about what you are doing.

The main thing I have learned really over the last few weeks - there are some areas on the chart, if you do your FTR analysis correctly, that it is basically impossible to lose from. Either price reacts to the zone as expected, and you profit, or price breaks the zone, but due to its importance and perhaps the number of stops outside the zone, a decent sized RT begins almost immediately, allowing you to average out of an initial bad entry. I have taken perhaps only one or two full losses in the last 2 weeks, and that was just from my own error in entering in a stupid place through impatience. Every other entry I've taken, I've been able to average out of it it went wrong - this means using no SL of course, but once you are confident that you're always going to get a chance to get out if the zone breaks (provided you always wait to enter at the most important levels), then it's not a problem.

Also - a zone is merely a place to look for important SR/flip lines which you can expect to turn price. A zone 30 pips wide - price cannot turn anywhere inside it, there are always 1 or 2 key SR/flip lines which are the places to look for reversal PA on M1. An important zone (FTR) is just a container for SR/flip lines, inside which you can expect them to have a much greater probability of bouncing price strongly.

Once you understand that price turns from within a few pips of a line inside a zone, and not just "somewhere" in the entire zone, you can then avoid even thinking about taking a trade until price reaches the line within the zone, and you see some M1 PA indicating that opposing orders are going in. In this way, all of the fake tops/bottoms the ITs create before price reaches the real turning point mean nothing to you, because you know price is not yet at the correct line, and you end up actually welcoming a huge LQ surge into your zone that stops dead at the line you have marked. When you see a huge momo candle stop dead on your important line in your important zone, and start to flicker a bit - you just know you can hit it. Even better if price makes an engulf before the LQ surge up to your line, since this is now almost certain to form a diamond.

There are 4 or 5 main "species" of these SR lines. In no particular order, they come from: - a QM from a previously important FL edge that was faked, before price continued (we call this a FOFLQM - a Faked-Out FL that provides a QM) - a standard QM - the flip from the last *important* small scale FL into the top/bottom before the reverse (even better if this came from a diamond reversal) - the top/bottom of a LQ push that broke an important level, and falls inside the resultant FTR (or even just outside for a FO) - support/resistance from a previously important high scale FL edge in history

Whenever you find an important FTR, there is always at least one of these types of SR line near the edge of it. Sometimes you even find multiple types lining up on the same spot, which is even better. Then all you need to do is watch the price approach, wait for price to hit the line, form some kind of rejection PA, and hit the thing. Even it it breaks, price is going to make a RT, so you just wait for the next M1 reversal PA to appear, and enter again, averaging out easily.

I've only got a micro account, because I'm broke and that's all I can afford at the moment! I initially deposited £100, lost it, then another £50, and dropped that down to £15. However that was when I started getting my act together, and since then I've quadrupled it in 2 weeks, and so now my next goal is to get all my original cash back.

I'm aiming for a daily profit target of 10-15%. This will double my account approximately weekly. It's not so hard to do, if you are confident on your entries, and prepared to use decent risk. Sooner or later, you've seen price reactions at levels so many times, you just know when one is going to appear.

The next thing I need to work on, is running my trades. I am shocking at it. I always exit my trades far too quickly, sometimes taking only 5% of the pips on offer. I've lost count of the number of times I've been in my trade with 1 pip of the edge of a 200 pip move, and I've taken only 10 pips from it. This is really the hardest thing for me at this stage, I just have nightmares about the open profit I've got all disappearing back to zero. I had such a bad start to live I've mentally conditioned myself to expect to lose. I understand this will take time to de-program out of my brain, but I am not worried, because I know if I keep doing the right things, and keep taking entries in the correct place, I will keep winning most of my trades, and my confidence will increase.

Excuse the long winded nature of this post, but I haven't chronicled my thoughts for a while. These are my stats for the last 2 weeks. I know I can actually improve on this - I had a run of 24 wins in a row in the middle of this period, I am seeing already how it is entirely possible to never lose a trade. That 7% DD figure was at 3% for most of this time, until I had a single moment of madness and entered 2 trades in stupid places one after the other. Once I've realised I've entered in a stupid place. and price has gone against me - I drop the thing instantly. Do not try to average out of an entry you've taken mid-PAZ, because awful things can happen.

Most importantly, I've now kept this run going for long enough, and seen price do the things I expect it to at the places I expect it to so many times, that I now have instilled belief that I am good at this, and I will continue to be good, and only improve from here. Once I've actually made some decent profit off this account, enough to live off, then I will be able to relax a bit, and perhaps even enjoy my trading instead of finding it stressful

Eventually, I will just end up taking fewer trades with larger risk, but I'm happy to be taking a lot of quick trades at the moment, since it's excellent practise for reading M1 rejection PA and honing my skills for getting in at the best price.

Whenever you find an important FTR, there is always at least one of these types of SR line near the edge of it. Sometimes you even find multiple types lining up on the same spot, which is even better. Then all you need to do is watch the price approach, wait for price to hit the line, form some kind of rejection PA, and hit the thing. Even it it breaks, price is going to make a RT, so you just wait for the next M1 reversal PA to appear, and enter again, averaging out easily.

I've only got a micro account, because I'm broke and that's all I can afford at the moment! I initially deposited £100, lost it, then another £50, and dropped that down to £15. However that was when I started getting my act together, and since then I've quadrupled it in 2 weeks, and so now my next goal is to get all my original cash back.

I'm aiming for a daily profit target of 10-15%. This will double my account approximately weekly. It's not so hard to do, if you are confident on your entries, and prepared to use decent risk. Sooner or later, you've seen price reactions at levels so many times, you just know when one is going to appear.

The next thing I need to work on, is running my trades. I am shocking at it. I always exit my trades far too quickly, sometimes taking only 5% of the pips on offer. I've lost count of the number of times I've been in my trade with 1 pip of the edge of a 200 pip move, and I've taken only 10 pips from it. This is really the hardest thing for me at this stage, I just have nightmares about the open profit I've got all disappearing back to zero. I had such a bad start to live I've mentally conditioned myself to expect to lose. I understand this will take time to de-program out of my brain, but I am not worried, because I know if I keep doing the right things, and keep taking entries in the correct place, I will keep winning most of my trades, and my confidence will increase.

Excuse the long winded nature of this post, but I haven't chronicled my thoughts for a while. These are my stats for the last 2 weeks. I know I can actually improve on this - I had a run of 24 wins in a row in the middle of this period, I am seeing already how it is entirely possible to never lose a trade. That 7% DD figure was at 3% for most of this time, until I had a single moment of madness and entered 2 trades in stupid places one after the other. Once I've realised I've entered in a stupid place. and price has gone against me - I drop the thing instantly. Do not try to average out of an entry you've taken mid-PAZ, because awful things can happen.

Most importantly, I've now kept this run going for long enough, and seen price do the things I expect it to at the places I expect it to so many times, that I now have instilled belief that I am good at this, and I will continue to be good, and only improve from here. Once I've actually made some decent profit off this account, enough to live off, then I will be able to relax a bit, and perhaps even enjoy my trading instead of finding it stressful

Eventually, I will just end up taking fewer trades with larger risk, but I'm happy to be taking a lot of quick trades at the moment, since it's excellent practise for reading M1 rejection PA and honing my skills for getting in at the best price.
