Also - a zone is merely a place to look for important SR/flip lines which you can expect to turn price. A zone 30 pips wide - price cannot turn anywhere inside it, there are always 1 or 2 key SR/flip lines which are the places to look for reversal PA on M1. An important zone (FTR) is just a container for SR/flip lines, inside which you can expect them to have a much greater probability of bouncing price strongly.

Once you understand that price turns from within a few pips of a line inside a zone, and not just "somewhere" in the entire zone, you can then avoid even thinking about taking a trade until price reaches the line within the zone, and you see some M1 PA indicating that opposing orders are going in. In this way, all of the fake tops/bottoms the ITs create before price reaches the real turning point mean nothing to you, because you know price is not yet at the correct line, and you end up actually welcoming a huge LQ surge into your zone that stops dead at the line you have marked. When you see a huge momo candle stop dead on your important line in your important zone, and start to flicker a bit - you just know you can hit it. You cannot ever hope to analyse a chart properly, and find important levels, if all you are ever looking at is just the PA that fits on the current screen.

Hi Smimon,

I am going to be a stickler here for a few of reasons as your overall lesson (An FTR lesson more or less) gives me mixed emotions(some of which you have already addressed in your markup, but I do want to highlight the nuance of it all): 1. Neutral narratives I am a big fan of neutral narratives when it comes to trading, to remain flexible and open to a dynamic and complex environment and it helps to minimize confirmation bias associated with words which can have negative connotations or reckless optimism i.e. labeling price points as 'important' vs 'not-important' or 'correct' vs 'incorrect'. (I am guilty of doing the opposite of what I am preaching here, that's what makes some of us good story tellers vs robots!) In fact, I would argue that all price points/swings/engulfs/levels/zones/horizontal lines can be made important in their own context (as you have so rightly highlighted). But yes I agree with you, in the context of FTR what you have described is correct.

2. What makes an FTR? Yes your lesson on FTR is logically sound. However, the only reason why an FTR becomes so in your illustration is because it goes on to engulf the RT you have labelled as 'not an important level'. But I can see the context you are trying to portray in your example, and the message rings true in a very simplistic academic way, which aligns quite well with the FTR article, so kudos for your take, it is refreshing.

3. Nuance Outside of the scope of your lesson, but an important point to raise; in my experience, these not-important levels you have identified, once engulfed, very often form immediate resistance (support), that cannot be portrayed accurately in paint diagrams. The structure is very nuanced because 1. each pair has its own personality, 2. what happens to the definition when one trader draws a zone using the wicks and the other only uses the bodies? and 3. it gets into the territory of what is an FTR vs a FL and how do we codify that? Have a look through my journal and you will see most of my 'best' trades are taken immediately after these price structures form. Somewhat important if you want to profit from it

I am just mindful as some beginners might take your labeling as 100% fact in all situations, true or false, and then discount that information in the future when it could actually assist their trading to acknowledge it, and use it as a secondary trading opportunity, and saving the forming of the FTR for another trade when price does come back... An FTR is very primitive on its own without the rest of the tools in our kit though (As you kindly pointed out:) How price left the level, how it arrived, where it came from, where its going to, on what time frames, at what time of the day, using what risk management, and experience in trade management *takes a deep breathe*)

I often have to remind myself that markets are very complex systems that cannot simply be coded to if/then statements to be 100% correct all of the time, in all past and future conditions.

posts.author: smimon
posts.text:
Thank you for the excellent comment, I agree completely.

It did occur to me as I posted the previous diagrams that this was a gross over-simplification of how the market actually works, and it was not my intent to state the above as an immutable law of the markets - but then, every lesson in the Markepedia is along the same lines.

The theory taught here on RTM is along the lines of "If the market was a perfect model, this is how it should behave". You then go on to realise there are layers and layers of subtlety and nuance on top of all the basic building blocks, the mastering of which is what takes 1000s of hours of chart time, and enables you to make the leap from "competent but inconsistent trader" into "consistent and highly profitable trader".

However, as over-simplifications go, I believe that my second diagram is a much more useful over-simplification than the first one, and if a beginner were to adhere religiously to one price model they would be better served by using this.

As you say, the market is an inherently complex entity. The only way we can begin to make sense of it is by having a set of rules which should hold true *most* of the time. We then have to learn under what conditions they might *not* hold true, by repeated application and study of when they failed, and trying to consider *why* they failed in terms of the behaviour of ITs creating liquidity to fill large positions.

Every scale has PAZ. We are either at the edges or in the middle of a PAZ on every single scale at any given time. We have a "where we are coming from" and "where we are probably headed to" in play on every scale at the same time. The smaller scale FTR and PAZ give us a "how we are going to get to the likely destination" in terms of our larger scale PAZ. Sometimes an engulf happens, which does not play out for days or weeks, until price has RT'd all the way back to the opposite side of the PAZ on the scale on which it formed. Sometimes price only makes a shallow RT. Sometimes you believe you've seen an engulf, but it turns out to be a FO only after a lot more price action has played out, and confirms it as such. Sometimes you have what appear to be opposing engulfs in play at the same time on the same scale. Sometimes new price action plays out which invalidates your previous assumption, and you must remain flexible enough to change your mind quickly - sticking to a flawed assumption in the face of conflicting evidence is a recipe for disaster.

Really, it can be an utter nightmare for a beginner to wrap their heads around as we know, which is why we must start from a simplified model, and extrapolate exceptions and nuances from that point.

As we know, the further you are from a PAZ edge on any given scale, the lower the probabilities that price is going to behave in a logically consistent manner. As you get closer and closer to the edges of a PAZ, and factor in how price approached, what engulfs are in play etc, then the probabilities of you being able to take a successful entry at a level increase greatly - the fuzziness begins to come more sharply into focus. The greater the scale of the PAZ edge, the sharper the focus and the higher the probability of a successful trade from the level.

Over time, one realises (or I did at least), that 99% of the time the best thing to do in the market is wait. Wait until price arrives at a level in the manner you expect, when as many pre-conditions of "is this trade likely to be successful" are met. Pre-conditions include, but not limited to: - is price moving away from a valid target? - is there a supporting engulf in play? - have we had a LTF engulf of FTA coming off a HTF level? - is this FTB to this level? - is this the deepest possible RT level on this scale? - can price FO this level, and if so, where can it FO to? - how did we approach the level? - what is the scale of this level? - is there any high volatility news approaching? - can I see any LTF rejection PA from this level to confirm opposing orders going in? - is there a confluence of important SR near MPL of this zone?

The list is large, and this list is probably not exhaustive, but only when all things are taken into account can you start hitting high win rates.

Anyway, I've rambled on a bit here Good to hear from you pal, please feel free to disagree/critique anything I've said here also, debate is how we learn and refine our ideas!

posts.author: smimon
posts.text:
I've been live for around 3 or 4 months now (can't remember the exact date). I'm pretty broke, so have only been able to fund a micro account. In that time, I have blown the account 3 times, and had to redeposit funds.

Am I losing 75% of my trades? Far from it. I win around 80%, some days I don't even take a loss, but then I get offside badly on a single trade sequence, refuse to admit I am wrong, and get margin called. I'm probably now on my 5th or 6th cycle of "double, treble or even quadruple my account in a 2-3 week period with a 80%+ win rate, and then hand it all back again with one stupid trade sequence".

Naturally, this has to stop. It's absurd to win 80% of your trades, and then blow your account.

One of the main reasons I've been able to keep the win rate so high, has been not using a SL. By only entering at important larger levels, and keeping the big picture in mind, it's been possible to average out of 95% of my bad entries - but then there's that 5% that break, and never come back... Sometimes, price is just on an uber trend, and will blow through levels you could have sworn should have given a decent reaction with no more than a 5 pip flicker.

I believe that with more experience, I'd probably be able to understand when price is in this sort of mood, and step aside. But it's only been just over a year since I found RTM, and although I am good at this point, I am not that good. And I've got bills to pay, soon.

One plus that has come out of not using a SL, it that is has really sharpened up my analysis skills - I only try and trade zones where there was another obvious cluster nearby that could bounce and let me out if things went wrong. In the process of trading like this, I learned that a lot of the most profitable trades come not from trading a level directly, but from trading the FO of the level. I've also become extremely tuned in to M1 PA, and can recognise a reversal forming usually before the candle is even finished.

Put it this way - how many times does price respect a valid level, as expected? And how many times does it either FO, or engulf it but immediately begin to RT afterwards? I'd say the latter scenario happens about 4 times more often. When you think about it in terms of ITs needing LQ for their positions, they aren't going to get much when price makes a valid bounce from a very obvious FTR. When price breaks above (or below) and comes off some random cluster instead though? They'll get tons. And with time and experience, you can spot these seemingly "unimportant" clusters well ahead of time, and be ready.

Now let me preface this next section with the following - this is not a whine, or a rant, and I am fully responsible for my own decisions I've made. I am also eternally thankful to this community for teaching me what I need to know to make money out of the markets.

With that out of the way, there is one small issue I'd like to highlight about RTM, and member's journals - almost no-one is honest about how many they lose or posts up their losing trades more than once in a blue moon. (this goes for me too of course)

I think the reason for this is obvious - we're putting ourselves on public display in a community of our peers, and our own egos coupled with a desire to earn the respect of said peers means we generally only post up our trades when we are winning. It's fine, and it's natural.

However - this creates a pretty toxic false impression that everyone else except you is winning all the time. This leads you into thoughts of "What am I doing wrong? Why do I lose so many? What do they know that I don't?"

In truth, I have probably been good enough to make a ton of cash from the markets for 6 months now. But I have become obsessed with never taking a loss. Things like when IF posts up a screenshot of someone with 125 wins in a row doesn't help someone like me - I am competitive and a perfectionist, and I firmly believe that anything anyone else can do, I can do if I put my mind to it.

All of these weeks and months of trading with no SL, all the time, have been as a direct result of me going on an ego trip needing to never be wrong, and under the impression that it is possible to win every single trade, and that there are a bunch of "high level" people on the forum doing it day in, day out.

Shadowpit yesterday had the candour to admit that he loses 50% of his trades, for small risk - but losses nonetheless. Which directly led to me sitting here thinking "What the hell am I doing wiping out my account every 3 weeks, when all I just need to do is take a win or take a loss, and move on?"

I don't want to blow my own trumpet, but I am really good now at finding price turning points that react within 1-2 pips. If I were to just take these levels with a tight SL on M1 -a lot of the time I could be making 20R+ several times over the course of the day. What then does it matter if I lose 5 trades?

So anyway this is just a cathartic tirade, but the upshot of it is from next week, I will go back to using a SL, and take my profits when I get them, and the losses too, in the full knowledge that I will end up massively up on average if I just stick to my guns. It's going to be a bit of a learning curve again - I need to learn how to stay calm, and not become emotional after losing a few trades in a row, which was traditionally a big problem for me.

Another benefit to trading a large number of instruments - correlations. Think CADJPY is about to go long? Quickly check UCAD - is it at a level it could go short from? Great, take the trade. Is it in the middle of a PAZ? Probably better wait.

As discussed previously, individual instruments do not exist in a vacuum. The Fx market is driven by money flowing from one set of currencies into others. It is no coincidence that when an entire currency is about to make a turn, it's major and minors are usually all at significant levels at the same time. In this way we can also usually get a good guess at which directions large news announcements are going to go - 5-10 mins out from GBP news for example, go check the big picture on all GBP crosses, see if they are sat at important levels, or have just turned from important levels 30 mins ago etc.

If you're looking at a setup on an individual minor crosspair, and none of the other crosses for this currency are reflecting the same PA or are at good levels, then you should probably wait.

I wrote this indi a little while back to help me out with this - it enables me to quickly look at all crosses for a given currency at once, without needing the chart open. It inverts those crosses that need inverting, so that they're all the correct way up with respect to the currency being viewed.

posts.author: jon

posts.author: smimon
posts.text:
Certainly, it's just a single piece of information out of many that must be taken into consideration. But the engulf is one of our main weapons of determining how far a move can potentially go.

The theory being that there are key price levels in the market, as defined by important FTRs (amongst other things), that contain many orders, which are defended. Once those orders are removed, price is therefore free to travel to the next important cluster, or the edge of the next PAZ.

The confusion comes when you realise there are many more types of level price can make a valid bounce from, not just FTRs. In this way, an important FTR can appear to be engulfed, but in fact price has made a valid turn from another type of level. The more that price FOs, the more confusing this picture becomes, and the harder it is to know exactly how far we can hold a trade.

Higher highs and lower lows are by themselves somewhat meaningless unless viewed in the context of FTRs/PAZ. A higher high that was rejected from MPL of an important bearish FTR is in fact a reversal signal, not a continuation signal for instance.

posts.author: smimon
posts.text: Ideally, when we enter a trade, we want to see price engulf the nearest important level in our favour. This is then our cue to try and hold the trade further. The harder it is to define a valid engulf however, the harder it is to have confidence to understand where price may be headed next.

posts.text:
Personally, all analysis begins from FTRs, from weekly downwards.

I then fit DPs on SR etc into the context of these FTRs. If the structure of the FTR appears to support it, I will attempt a trade from near MPL, otherwise I start looking for seemingly unimportant DPs on S/D levels that price can FO into or react from - but it's always in the context of important higher scale FTRs - these are our best roadmap of what price wants to do. We then fit the IT tricks in and around these.

posts.author: smimon
posts.text:
Example - GJ short I took today i.imgur.com/MyECRTi.png

After a while, it's just the same old tricks, over and over again. The key is to learn to recognise: - which levels are likely to get ignored/faked, and where they are going to fake into - which important FTRs are good to trade from the near the edge without them breaking

I prefer the first scenario personally, because then I am either trading a reversal from genuine FO, or I am trading the RT cycle after an eng of an important level which can be large sometimes. A valid reaction to a valid levels happens far less often than the combined amount of times a FO or eng + RT happens.

The second scenario is totally valid however, and works well a lot of the time. The key to recognising which FTR edges are more likely to work is to recognise the smaller scale structure near the edge, and where it is located in relation to the next significant orders. This comes largely from experience, but generally you want to see something on smaller scale that can be faked, and something for it to fake into. Remember the ITs can't generate much LQ from turning price at a massively obvious level - if you can see if that obviously, so can the rest of the world.

One of the biggest breakthroughs in my trading came recently when I started trying to "think like the ITs". When considering the trade of any level, I now first ask myself - how much LQ can the ITs generate at this level?

A lot of traders are a lot more S/D savvy than they used to be. A valid turn from an obvious valid level means the ITs aren't going to get too many of their orders filled for big positions.

Instead, when considering a level, it's always a good idea to look nearby, and see if there is a better level that price was turned just before, such as this example here in the PA that is developing from the move up on GN. No guarantees this will work here - but the presence of that swing low "hovering" above the QM gives a great low risk/high RR opportunity upon return.

Always be suspicious of the "too obvious" FTR floating just above a really nice DP on a QM or SR...

posts.text:
If any of you are anything like me, you probably have markup on your charts all the time, showing zones of interest, marking where engulfs occurred, etc. Indeed, I've even written a ton of indicators to help me out with this, including a FlagLimit indicator which allows FLs to be defined on multiple scales, finds if they have been engulfed or not, monitors them for price proximity/enter/engulf etc.

Since I like to adopt a currency based approach to my trading, I trade all USD and EUR crosses, in conjunction with 7 currency indexes (I don't trade CHF crosses just because the spread on most of them is terrible (apart from ECHF and UCHF) and because the index confluence doesn't work too well). This means I've got over 15 charts open across 2 instances of MT4, all with marked zones and alerts on them. At any given time, especially in times of high volatility in the markets, there are alerts going off every 2 minutes. You can have been waiting patiently for a setup, and watching price, and suddenly another 4 alerts go off, and your concentration is pulled all over the place. My head is a mess, my thinking is muddled.

I am also guilty of having a proximity alert to one of my zones go off, and then just thinking "I'll go stare at something else, and wait for the alert to go off that price has actually entered the zone before I decide whether to hit it or not". As a result, when price does enter the zone, I've not been paying attention, and I am out of tune with the approach, the speed of it, the way the candles are forming etc, and I tend to just make a rushed hasty decision to hit the level without a second thought. Sometimes it's fine if I've analysed the zone correctly, sometimes it goes instantly wrong as I've misjudged the strength of the move.

Also, whether you are aware of it or not, the second you place a single piece of markup on your charts, a single line, box, whatever - your thinking is influenced from that point forwards. Every time you look at that chart, you are starting with a single default assumption based on your markup, and everything subsequently is viewed through this lens. If your markup is valid and accurate - great; but if it's not, everything you try to trade from that point forwards will be biased towards being incorrect. Think - how many times have you drawn a zone, and then later in the day some more price action plays out, and you realised it was totally incorrect?

All of this is to say - less is more.

I've realised that the only thing holding me back from consistent success (my equity is up and down like a yo-yo at present) is my mental approach and organisation. I need a clear mind, need to be able to focus, need to be reading price clearly every time I sit down and not base my thinking on a load of assumptions I made 2 days ago.

To this end, I now only set alerts on my currency index charts (crosspairs don't usually make turns until the relevant currency index is at the correct level anyway), and at the start of every day, I wipe every single object off my charts. This cleaning of the charts has 2 benefits - it not only makes sure you are really reading what's going on with no previous assumptions, it also over time will dramatically improve your speed of analysis by eye, until you get to the point where you can just eyeball a chart and know pretty much what's going on in under 10 seconds, and where the next likely levels in play will be. I also now do not allow myself to use "zone entered" alerts - if I receive a proximity alert for a zone, i turn everything else off, and force myself to stare at that chart until the setup plays out.

You can glean a lot more information out of a naked chart than a chart with 43 boxes and lines all over it. Don't forget, the manner in which price is moving (surging, driving, compressing, flagging etc) is one of the biggest clues we have as to future intent, or whether what we think is an engulf is actually a FO. Yoy simple cannot see this piece of information clearly with clutter everywhere.

posts.text:
Well, a nice end to the week. I have been treading water on live for nearly 6 months now, in an endless cycle of boom and bust. Every bust is caused by me getting mad and doubling and trebling down on losing trades. But I'm seeing improvement in my mental approach. My chart skills are not the issue at this stage

EU faked some HTF lows off the news, and I saw the initial M1 candle get rejected all the way back up to the top, then closed down at the low as it was forming - this was a pretty good sign that a reversal was occurring. I waited for a clean engulfing surge, and then tried to gauge the depth of the retracement. One of my strongest skills is PA reading during times of high volatility, I just find it laughably easy because everything is so exaggerated.

In these cases, I look for what I've seen referred to as a "key reversal" bar (KR) in order to confirm that the current LTF swing is about to reverse. A KR bar (let's say a bullish one), has a low outside the current range, but closes right back up high into the range, with almost no top wick. As with all PA, it has to happen at a level which makes sense.

I waited for the KR bar, entered with SL just below it, and targeted the area of the origin of the last swing down on HTF, and walked away from the PC - because I know if I sit there and stare at it, I will meddle. End result was a nice 23R trade in a little over an hour.

EU M1

Here is a close up of the KR bar. In this case, I used the z-line of the cluster that formed after the news retracement as my "level to make the PA make sense".

Ah dudu, a typically constructive post delivered in your usual eloquent manner.

If anyone needs a translation I believe what dudu is trying to say is "I am surprised you are not having consistent returns. I tried RTM for a while, but could not find consistency with the method, so I returned to a simpler method of trading."

Well, it's a valid point. I've seen a lot of people come and go just over the last year on here, initially excited by the prospect of making 0 pip entries, and then leaving in frustration some time later, usually cursing IF. Let me say a few things in response.

First, the freely available material on RTM is NOT going to teach you how to make 0 pip entries. That would be madness to give away for nothing. What is does teach you are the concepts which you need to know, and apply over and over again, in order to develop your own understanding to the point where you can make 0 pip trades. Believe me, I've done it myself a large number of times by now. As IF has said, he has also given enough hints without spelling it out directly. I put together what he has said on here, and especially over at the FF thread, and figured out how he does it, and have been able to replicate it to a lesser extent. He's still much better at it than me though

Second, the reason I am not consistent has nothing to do with RTM, it's entirely my own fault. For me, trading is 25% skill, 75% mental control. I'm overconfident and impatient by nature and I hate to lose - I think it's not too hard to see why this is an awful combination for trading. Every time I sit down, I'm not only analysing charts, I'm also trying to fight my base personality. I hit far too many unconfirmed entries at dodgy levels, I boredom scalp, I use too much risk, I revenge trade.

But you see the difference between dudu and I, is that when I am failing to find consistency with a method that others are employing successfully, instead of cursing the system and the mentor who gave us the concepts. I assume ownership of my failure, and admit that the reason I'm not succeeding is due to my own failings. This is something we call intellectual honesty

Of course, the other option is to protect your ego, and tell yourself some pretty lie that the reason you didn't succeed with a proven method is not because you personally failed to apply it properly, but because the teacher is "BS".

Don't forget people - trading is HARD. There is pretty much zero chance you're going to pick this up and run with consistent profits in less than 12 months, at an absolute minimum. Sure, you can gain the analysis skills in much less time than that, but learning to control your own mental state and fight those elements of your brain that are constantly striving to sabotage you - well, that's the real battle, and that's what takes years of endless repetition. You also need this amount of time to really develop that "feel" for price, which cannot be quantified.

I've added 1000% to my account over a 12 day period. I've added 100% to my account even in a single day. But then I've gone on a madness revenge spiral and given it all back, or blown my account with a single stupid trade with no SL, which I kept adding to all the way.

As soon as I can stop self-sabotaging, my consistent returns and large sums of money are waiting for me. The only variable in the equation I still need to solve is me

posts.author: smimon
posts.text:
Yes, couldn't agree more.

Step 1 is to identify the repeating mental patterns which cause us to make bad decisions.

Step 2 is to then implement rules or working practices which give us a fighting chance of not making the same mistake again.

Step 3 is to not get mad at yourself if you fail, simply to calmly realise your mistake, and reset to try again.

A "favourite" of mine - I am bored waiting for price to reach a level I want to trade, so I start scalping silly midrange PA on M1 in times of low volatility (M1 PA is much tougher to read when the market is slow). I then lose 0.5%. Annoyed, I try to make it back quickly. I lose another 1%. Then I get more annoyed, and double down on my next scalp. Then I lose 4%. Before I know it, I'm 15% in the red, and trebling my lot size on stupid scalps trying to just "win it all back in one go". All started from one silly boredom scalp.

When we stare at charts for many hours, it is easy to zone out. These are the times of real danger, because your conscious mind is not fully focused on what you are doing, and you can quite easily end up doing strange things that you wouldn't normally have dreamed of doing. I'm learning to spot when my mind has started drifting, and this is my cue to take a break and refocus.

Also, if you have entered a trade based on a setup, and find yourself wanting to close it long before it gets to the target, there are 2 options - write down on a piece of paper the reasons why you entered and why you think you should hold it to TG, and every time you find yourself wanting to exit too soon, just read what you've written. The second option, and the one I prefer, is to take partial profit, and just walk away from the desk and come back hours later. Many of my best trades are overnight POs which have had 8 hours to move in my favour without me messing with them

geejay wrote: I realize that this seems like a 'crutch' but it is my coping mechanism at the moment and it gives me peace to know that while I may not be fully mature at reading price, I can still make trades and learn successful money management skills at the same time.

Not in the slightest, there's no point in ever allowing a trade that was in decent profit turn into an overall loss.

We can't possible ever *know* what the markets are going to do next, just be able to make a highly informed guess with good probability of success. We may think the planets have lined up in our favour, only to realise we've been mislead by a FO, or that what we thought was an engulf was a flip from some ignored level or SR etc.

It's just good sense to take some profit when it's on the table - whether that's in the form of taking most of the trade off at FTA or doing what you prefer and taking only enough profit to cover the SL, setting yourself up for a big payday if the setup works out.

And for sure, it's never a bad idea to leave your SL where you originally placed it, since price can so easily return to our entry levels hours or even days after we initially entered (in the case of higher scale setups), only to then later make it to our target.

posts.author: smimon
posts.text:
The "solution", to call it such, would be to understand the move in terms of the higher scales, and also to study the move away from the FO level.

Let's say we are coming north strongly out of a W1 FTR, showing a engulf north on the D1 chart, price then "engulfs" south but shoots away from the zone like a rocket - then by combining all pieces of information available to us, we can be pretty certain that it was a FO, not an engulf.

Conversely, if there was a W1 eng south in play, price had RT'd up to some D1 bearish FTR, not broken it, and had then come down and "engulfed" the level - then we can be more certain in this case that it was an engulf, and not a FO.

Each piece of information the market gives us must be understood in context of the larger scale moves that are going on, and also considering how price approaches the level, and how it moves away.

posts.author: smimon
posts.text:
Well, it's there on the chart really.

A bearish FTR has to engulf a bullish level south, make a RT north, and then *make lower lows*.

If price comes up north, RTs south, but then *does not make lower lows* and then goes on to *make higher highs*, then it cannot be a bearish FTR by definition. The swing high point is therefore *a place where a RT south started*, as opposed to *the edge of a bearish FTR*.

As discussed previously, individual instruments do not exist in a vacuum. The Fx market is driven by money flowing from one set of currencies into others. I've developed a style which is working well for me - I wait until highest probability levels only, based on higher timeframes and bigger picture analysis, then hit the market with very high risk (10-15%) sized over M10 ATR. This gives me the wiggle room to still get out of the trade with a profit even if my entry level breaks - provided I've waited until MPL to enter. I usually just run the trade to LTF FTA, looking for 1R, or whatever I can get. I have a daily profit TG of 15%, and I can usually hit it in 1 or 2 trades.

This is a deliberate strategy however - 15% daily for 66 days compounds £100 into £1,000,000. MPL = max pain limit. It basically means the very last possible place price can turn from at the edge of a FTR, the last set of orders.

What you'll note is that very often, when an important level is broken, price makes an immediate quick RT back inside. Therefore if you wait only til MPL to enter, with a wider stop, you have every chance to escape what would been a loss with a profit instead.

My trading method is focused on the highest probability events only.

A price reaction from just inside MPL of an important FTR, or an engulf of MPL and then quick RT, are very high probability events. It allows me to profit 90% of the time. If price turns some distance away from MPL (although there is usually a good LTF reason for it to do so), then I just let it go without me. No problem, it won't be long to wait for the next chance.

If you were to look for shorts immediately when a level breaks like this, then you are essentially breakout trading, which is a high risk approach. Quite often price can make a deep RT after the engulf of a significant level. Safest is to wait for deepest possible RT level, and then enter short.

That was just some random PA from UJ M5 months ago. You can find examples of this phenomenon everywhere on any instrument. Just look for how price behaves when it reaches important levels - see how many times you get a valid reaction from FTB, and how many times it engulfs and then starts a RT.

Price can also smash straight through the level and not come back, but this generally means you read the HTF picture totally wrong, or were trying to enter from a non-important level.

posts.author: smimon
posts.text:
I've had to steadily develop a range of mental hacks to keep me from doing stupid stuff as I've gone along.

As I've discussed, I devised a trading style whereby I would always enter with a SL based on an ATR multiple to give me wiggle room, and size my risk over this distance. The entry was always to be taken using a button on my LotCalc EA, which would calculate the position size automatically, and place the SL for me.

The stop was not supposed to be moved, the position was not supposed to be added to, I was to have a daily loss limit, and I even coded rules into my EA to this effect... but I moved my stops, and had an awful habit of popping open the Alt + T quick trade dialog and taking multiple "revenge" positions to try and average out of a bad entry, circumventing all the rules I'd coded. Unhelpfully, this averaging usually worked... but on the odd times I was 100% wrong on the big picture read, price would rip against me, and I would get margin called, wiping out most of the account. I lost count of the number of times this happened. Admittedly, a large part of this was inexperience in trying to enter from levels I'd misanalysed, but there's no point in wiping yourself out just because you're still not the finished article.

I did some research online, and find a way to code a C# app which intercepts the Alt + T keypress at a system level, and blocks it. No more quick trade panel. This method of circumventing my rules now being disabled, my EA is able to enforce the "no more than 1 entry", and daily loss limit rules I coded in. I also made my EA log the initial SL position when a trade is taken, and automatically detect when I've moved it, and put it right back again. This now forces me to wait until the best possible place to enter, when I can get my ATR stop behind the next level which can bounce, should the one I am entering from break.

I was also having some issues with the steadily increasing balance of my account causing me to become anxious, and affecting my decision making. So to counter this, I now never open the terminal window, so I have nothing more than a rough idea what is in my account and how much £ I have in open P/L, and have configured my EA to show me nothing except %age figures. % up/down on the day, % up/down current position, all open positions etc.

This way, every single trade is executed (as best as I can fool myself) the same regardless of whether I've got £100 or £100,000 in my account (I wish;-) )

Anecdotally - I lift weights at the gym a lot. I realised that after you've learned the correct training methods, getting an impressive physique is really 25% time in the gym, and 75% diet.

Trading follows a similar ratio for me. Once you've learned how to read a chart, it's 25% analysis skills, 75% learning to control yourself and not self-sabotage. Getting good at that 75% takes a lot of experience, and even some little hacks and tricks such as I just described.

Also key is to realise when you have enough analysis skills to spot the potential for good trades, but it's just your execution that is causing you to fail. At this stage, you are better served by settling on a style you prefer to take your entries and run your trades, and then just repeating it mindlessly for month after month. Only in this way will you start to see consistent improvement.

Constantly chopping and changing your approach, or always thinking you "just need to know a bit more information" and scanning the journals of 10 expert level traders (all of whom have years more experience than you) - will in the long run just hold you back from progressing as quickly as you might if you just pick a style and stick with it. Just realise when you are "good enough", and will be better served by more practise, rather than more reading.

Hey, thought I'd check in and journal where I'm currently at, in the interests of keeping myself honest.

Well, I'm still not a millionaire.

As mentioned previously, my natural temperament is really not suited for trading -overconfident, impulsive, impatient. So as such, curbing this is taking a very long time, one painful iterative step after another.

The good news - progress is being made. Every time I make a cock up, I learn a bit more about what I'm good at, and what doesn't suit my personality, and I am able to make steps to adjust and hopefully correct the problem.

I am currently, and have been for some time, extremely good at spotting high probability reaction levels in the market. This is without doubt my strongest area. It's the rest of the skillset around this that has been letting me down.

I've been "ego trading" for some time now. What's the ultimate goal of trading? Is it to have a high win rate, and stroke your ego? Or is to make money as quickly as possible, regardless of the method provided that it is effective?

By ego trading to avoid loss, instead of trading to win, I have been cutting winners short, and really making life hard for myself in terms of having to sustain a high win rate. And in fairness, I can usually hold up a 90% or greater win rate. But when you're only snatching 0.5R off most of these, you feel compelled to up your risk to compensate. Risk 10%, to make 5%, and hope you can keep winning 80-90%.

When it works, it's fine. When you start losing a few, it's very tough to handle. I usually go for 2 weeks without significant loss, and then have a bad day which knocks the wheels off everything.

So... first thing is I have to learn to accept loss. And I have to reduce my risk, and aim for at least 2R off every trade. Remember, you only to need to win 33% at 2R to break even, it's not a lot.

Second - I simply cannot be trusted to TT. You know how the banks' algos are designed to surge price around in such a manner as to stir up maximal emotion and excitement in the market participants, causing them to act impulsively and without due thought and planning? Well, they certainly work on me. Of course, knowing that more often than not price is just surging into a reversal makes it worse in many ways - as soon as I see a huge surge, all thought goes out the window, and I start looking to fade the thing. Often it works, but when it does not, instant pain. Unplanned trades caused by excitement, impatience.

To this end, my EA now only allows POs. I am to maximise profit from my skill in finding very high probability reaction levels, and in this way I will only be taking planned trades. I never have the patience to wait for PA anyway, so at least this way I am ensuring I get best price.

At this stage, it's tweaks, not a total overhaul. My live account is not large, but doubling it weekly has become commonplace. In the past, I would unfortunately hand it all back every so often in a disastrous day. Now, I have a daily loss limit in place which I can't break, but I've still had 3 losing days back to back this week, which hasn't happened for a very long time. First day wasn't too bad, second I wiped out within 30 minutes of sitting down trying to fade a surge, and by the third I'd gone to bits chasing stupid PA at stupid levels, taking ridiculous TTs just trying to win it back. We all know how that ends.

So I'm upbeat anyway, confident I will sort this out and find the constant account growth consistency which has been eluding me thus far.

In other news, I'm working on a really cool piece of software which finds very tightly correlated baskets of crosspairs, and allows you to generate synthetic instruments to use for confluence. It's not uncommon at present for me to be looking for 10-way confluence on a trade decision.

The market in general is in a very highly correlated state at present, owing to the large financial flows going on between oil, stock indexes, and a large number of currencies.

Here's a screenshot of the work in progress.

i.imgur.com/1rL64DI.png

Basically, by following the chains of positive and negative correlations, and using a bit of deductive logic, it's possible to separate linked correlations into two separate "flows" which do not conflict with one another, and from that provide the ability to generate custom synthetic instruments, one for each currency involved in the basket, and one overall synthetic representing the whole basket.

Look at that one at the bottom right, Flow1 - it's a synthetic made up of the average of 15 crosspairs, and it works. When that index turns, so do all of the 15 pairs it is related to at the same time (more or less). These correlations are basically the footprint of pro money in the markets. If you can read a normal chart, you can read the synthetic - it works exactly the same.

I'm also currently working on a system to enable me to take basket trades against these synthetics - set an order on the synthetic chart, and when price reaches it, it will automatically take a position long or short on all of the components at the same time.

A couple of weeks ago, I predicted the daily move of about 12 crosspairs at the same time, and my friend traded it and every single one was correct - but it was only on demo

I've been "ego trading" for some time now. What's the ultimate goal of trading? Is it to have a high win rate, and stroke your ego? Or is to make money as quickly as possible, regardless of the method provided that it is effective?

By ego trading to avoid loss, instead of trading to win, I have been cutting winners short, and really making life hard for myself in terms of having to sustain a high win rate. And in fairness, I can usually hold up a 90% or greater win rate. But when you're only snatching 0.5R off most of these, you feel compelled to up your risk to compensate. Risk 10%, to make 5%, and hope you can keep winning 80-90%.

When it works, it's fine. When you start losing a few, it's very tough to handle. I usually go for 2 weeks without significant loss, and then have a bad day which knocks the wheels off everything.

So... first thing is I have to learn to accept loss. And I have to reduce my risk, and aim for at least 2R off every trade. Remember, you only to need to win 33% at 2R to break even, it's not a lot.

Second - I simply cannot be trusted to TT. You know how the banks' algos are designed to surge price around in such a manner as to stir up maximal emotion and excitement in the market participants, causing them to act impulsively and without due thought and planning? Well, they certainly work on me. Of course, knowing that more often than not price is just surging into a reversal makes it worse in many ways - as soon as I see a huge surge, all thought goes out the window, and I start looking to fade the thing. Often it works, but when it does not, instant pain. Unplanned trades caused by excitement, impatience.

To this end, my EA now only allows POs. I am to maximise profit from my skill in finding very high probability reaction levels, and in this way I will only be taking planned trades. I never have the patience to wait for PA anyway, so at least this way I am ensuring I get best price.

At this stage, it's tweaks, not a total overhaul. My live account is not large, but doubling it weekly has become commonplace. In the past, I would unfortunately hand it all back every so often in a disastrous day. Now, I have a daily loss limit in place which I can't break, but I've still had 3 losing days back to back this week, which hasn't happened for a very long time. First day wasn't too bad, second I wiped out within 30 minutes of sitting down trying to fade a surge, and by the third I'd gone to bits chasing stupid PA at stupid levels, taking ridiculous TTs just trying to win it back. We all know how that ends.

So I'm upbeat anyway, confident I will sort this out and find the constant account growth consistency which has been eluding me thus far.

In other news, I'm working on a really cool piece of software which finds very tightly correlated baskets of crosspairs, and allows you to generate synthetic instruments to use for confluence. It's not uncommon at present for me to be looking for 10-way confluence on a trade decision.

The market in general is in a very highly correlated state at present, owing to the large financial flows going on between oil, stock indexes, and a large number of currencies.

Here's a screenshot of the work in progress.

i.imgur.com/1rL64DI.png

Basically, by following the chains of positive and negative correlations, and using a bit of deductive logic, it's possible to separate linked correlations into two separate "flows" which do not conflict with one another, and from that provide the ability to generate custom synthetic instruments, one for each currency involved in the basket, and one overall synthetic representing the whole basket.

Look at that one at the bottom right, Flow1 - it's a synthetic made up of the average of 15 crosspairs, and it works. When that index turns, so do all of the 15 pairs it is related to at the same time (more or less). These correlations are basically the footprint of pro money in the markets. If you can read a normal chart, you can read the synthetic - it works exactly the same.

I'm also currently working on a system to enable me to take basket trades against these synthetics - set an order on the synthetic chart, and when price reaches it, it will automatically take a position long or short on all of the components at the same time.

A couple of weeks ago, I predicted the daily move of about 12 crosspairs at the same time, and my friend traded it and every single one was correct - but it was only on demo

posts.author: smimon
posts.text:
Thought I'd wait for the "spirited" debate to die down before commenting.

Dudu is no fan of RTM, that much is clear at this stage, but I wish him well with his preferred analysis style, if it's making him good, consistent money. That's all we're in this game for at the end of the day.

Personally, I love RTM-style analysis. Is it perfect? Is it a panacea? No, not at all. Especially since the markets seems to be getting harder and harder to read recently (or maybe that's just me). It does however remain a sound and effective model to form a basis for looking for levels.

When I want to take an entry, I want to do so from a level that has "orders" (I'm not sure this can be thought of in the literal sense, but it's a good analogy for referring to important buying/selling levels on the chart). A FL/FTR that was formed after taking out a key opposing level - well, it's just a very good place to look for orders. Of course FLs/FTRs themselves don't "move the market" - the only thing that moves the market is people actually hitting the market with active buying and selling.

I've been using this approach for over a year now, and know that it forms the nucleus of a very successful, accurate method of trading. There are of course many exceptions and nuances, which take a long time to learn, and even when you "know it all", you still face the even larger battle of controlling yourself and your emotions - a battle which I am still nowhere near winning.

When I fuck up, I know it's my own fault, and no-one else's. Sometimes I make a total misread, but most of the time I'm just self-sabotaging. There's nothing wrong with the RTM style, provided you realise it's not a set of literal rules which MUST BE OBEYED AT ALL TIMES. Nothing works like that in trading.

The reality is, you have to take some of this, some of that, put the pieces together. Which HTF levels are in play, the trend, style of movement, PA, FLs/FTRs, engulfs, key SR (PAZ boundary, QM etc), even a bit of volume profiling, and a huge amount of experience.

There are many ways to skin a cat. I like this method because it gives me precision to anticipate massive price turns within a few pips, if I do my homework correctly. I'm interested in RR, and % on the account. Number of pips gained, number of trades won etc are useless metrics. All that matters is the money going on your account, and the quicker the better

The end result is to get rich. However you get there is largely irrelevant. We're all going to have our preferred styles, and be extremely defensive about them, that's just human nature.

posts.author: smimon
posts.text:
Buying/selling symmetry levels are just clear places on the chart where you can see heavy buying/selling took place in the past. Very often, price will make a reaction upon returning to them.

If you want to sell for instance, it makes sense to look for levels on the chart where you can see evidence of strong selling in the past.

A QM, if you think about it, is just buying/selling symmetry followed by a FO. The "real" orders go in, price then FOs to stop out those with early entries and get some more people going the wrong way, it reverses and an engulf occurs, and then price returns to the "real" level where the first orders went in.

As it happens, that level on CJ gave only a very small reaction, which was to be expected really given the strength of the up move.

You can't just blindly fade and take FTB to every old FL on every lower timeframe. You have to put everything together in terms of the bigger picture, and learn when it's best to step aside instead of trying to fade, or indeed look for the quick continuation instead.

posts.text:
Volume profiling is another tool I've started to make more use of recently. If I can see large amounts of activity at a particular price level, inside an important FL, that lines up with some important SR, it's almost a certainty price will react there.

Take this level for example (AUDNZD H1, but could be anything):

Initially, looks hard to spot a level

We draw a custom volume profile around the top part, and immediately a high volume node (HVN) is quite clear. Out of all the accumulation that occurred within this choppy region, these were the price levels which showed the most activity. I believe this is a result of the way the banks' algorithms work - they perhaps instruct them to fill a big order at a certain price, and as price chops around it, it keeps taking small bites until their position is filled. Normally, we wouldn't be able to see this by eye, but the presence of the HVN gives it away.

Now also if we look, there is a clear FL that was faked out, before the move continued. What appears to have happened here - a bull FL was engulfed, and a new bear FL was created, the top edge of this being the key price level. ITs then wanted to load up on positions for a bigger move south, and so price chopped around the area, faking the FL north, for some time, until their positions were filled and price dropped off strongly. The presence of the HVN on the same level as the FOFL (faked-out flag limit) gives us an A+ very accurate price reaction level.

Ok, here's how to do it.

If you don't have a TradingView subscription, you will only be able to view D1 and above. If yo it's pretty cheap for a year), you can view lower timeframes as well.

One thing to note - this calculation isn't perfect. When calculating a composite index for let's s component is raised to the power of a certain weighting. When the base currency of the cross currency (for AUD, this would be a cross like EURAUD), the weighting requires inverting (or u same effect). In addition, the cross candle's high/low values must be flipped. TradingView is n this, the end result being that the candles on lower timeframes get a "hairy" look about them, higher timeframes, this is not as noticeable. The open/close values of the candles are correct

The basic approach: - raise each cross component to the power of 1/7 (approx. 0.143) (the sum of all the weights n there are 7 crosses for each currency) - for those crosses where the base currency is the "wrong way around", we take 1/(cross^1/7 - sum all components together

Example for AUDX: AUDCAD^0.143+AUDCHF^0.143+1/EURAUD^0.143+1/GBPAUD^0.143+AUDJPY^0.143+AU

If you paste that into the symbol bar in TradingView, you end up with a chart which looks like

The AUDX produced by my indicator in MT4 looks like this:

So as you can see, pretty similar.

This should be enough info for you to recreate the other average indexes.

I'm always playing with various new tools I've coded up to help me make better decisions on which crosspairs to hit. When you trade using 8 average currency indexes as your basis, you are essentially trading all 28 crosses in the market.

A big part of trading successfully intraday is the ability to be familiar with your chosen instruments, to hold the story of how the various higher timeframes are fitting together into a coherent map in your mind. The brain is only of limited capacity however, and whilst you might be able to do this for 4-8 instruments, you'd have to be an Einstein level genius to manage it for 28.

To confuse things further, moves of differing sizes are always happening simultaneously on different scales. GBPUSD might be the strongest pair in the market for the week, but chopping on the day, and actually the weakest over the last 2 hours. Again if you only trade a small number of instruments, this is easier to keep track of in your mental map, but when you trade the same small set of instruments every day you run the risk of just staring at hours of chop some days when all the big moves are elsewhere in the market.

I came close to a grand unified theory of tracking currency correlations a while back, which enabled me to trade baskets of 10 or more crosspairs from a single synthetic instrument, but ultimately had to abandon it, despite several times successfully predicting the daily move of 2/3 of the market. I was basically trading a brand new set of instruments and synthetic charts every single day, and just couldn't keep up with the ever changing nature of it.

So as it is, I have settled on using the 8 average currency indexes as my basis for all entries. I can just about manage to keep up with everything this way. My basic strategy is to fade nice approaches to key FTB levels, ideally as HTF trend continuations, but even against trend will yield some few pips 90% of the time or more.

Even this has its complications however. Let's say GBPX is surging long towards a level you want to fade - which crosses to hit? You have a choice of 7.

If you pick only one, you risk selecting the worst one of the bunch which goes nowhere, due to the other currency component not showing any strength against GBP in that moment, even as all the other crosses move as expected. It's actually amazing how often this seems to happen, sod's law I guess.

The safest idea is to hedge your bets across 2-3 crosses which are showing the most strength/weakness against GBP at that moment in time, since logically, these should be the ones which reflect the bounce in the most promising fashion.

To that end, I knocked up a simple tool yesterday which allows me to draw a box around an area of price on my currency index, and see currency & cross performance graphs for that section of time. As always, pictures are worth a thousand words, so I'll show a quick example.

This was GBPX M5 as we were coming up to London open on Friday morning. Price was moving strongly towards a key HTF FL, FTB. This is always especially nice to see 5-10 minutes out from 0800, since very often the volatility from London open gives you a nice move.

Which crosses to fade it against though? You can always do a visual inspection of the other 7 currency charts, but this is quite a lot to manage in the heat of the moment. So, using the new tool, I would have seen this:

This is a performance graph of the period of time encompassing the 6 or so M5 bars which comprised the surge into the level on GBPX. Using this, I now can very quickly see that USD, CHF and EUR were the 3 strongest currencies in the market during this time, and so the 3 trades to take would have been: short GU, short GCHF, long EG. I'd of course have wanted to make sure that these 3 were at some sort of semi-logical place for a price bounce to happen.

There is one drawback to this method however - sometimes when an entire currency makes a HTF turn, the money flows out of it into a different currency which right up until the turn was the weakest currency in the market. But you can't predict this reliably (or I've not figured out how to yet, I suspect you could use short-term correlations for a clue), and it's adding extra complication to the method. Often if you've zoned out during the day and an alert that you'd set earlier goes off, you only have 5 minutes to make a snap decision, so you want the process to be as simple as possible.

Excuse my rant the other day, frustrations just got on top of me.

There's really no need to be able to read every single move on every chart, just that we can spot and profit from the most obvious setups. I've put a string of large profit days together since then, all is well.

I've been thinking about a way to reduce the risk of my preferred "unconfirmed FTB to key MPL" strategy. 70-80% of the time, it works, you get a nice clean bounce, and an easy ride to at least LTF FTA.

Sometimes however, when the trend is really against you, price will bounce only a very small distance, won't even reach LTF FTA, and then continue brutally the way it was going, leaving you badly offside (I don't really use a SL apart from to size my initial entry, I prefer to always try to manage an average position back onside).

You can minimise the risk of this happening by making sure that: a) you are not trying to fade one of the strongest intraday trends in the whole market (strongest vs weakest currencies) b) you analyse the chart properly to make sure that if the level you are attempting to enter from breaks, there is somewhere nearby of some importance which has a very good chance to bounce price

However, accidents do happen.

From experience of doing this for a long time now, there are few scenarios which can play out when price surges into a fresh important FL: a) v-shaped clean bounce straight to FTA (does not happen often) b) initial clean bounce which stops some distance short of FTA. Price then comes back to re-test the initial entry level, or forms a LTF QM, stopping out those who entered early, before then going on to make it all the way to FTA, and often beyond c) initial bounce which stops short of FTA, turns around and keeps going

I'm in the business of trying to "never lose" an overall trade sequence, whilst trying not to cheat myself out of profit by being too cautious.

Obviously, we don't want to go b/e on our initial entry unless we've managed to get in with 0-1 pip accuracy on a massive M1 rejection candle. Similarly, I don't want to set a SL outside the zone, get an initial bounce, and then have price just keep going and stop me out. I'm also not a huge fan of taking out enough of the position to cover the SL at the first chance, because it really gimps profit if the trade turns into a big runner. Running full position as far as possible is key.

What I aim to do from next week is: 1) hit the initial surge into MPL, as close to MPL as possible, with decent size 2) at the very first indication that the initial bounce is faltering, drop the whole thing 3) this is now "the market's money", which I can use as "armour" if you like to protect my next entry 4) I then wait for price to come back and make a double top/bottom, or a LTF QM, and I throw all the money I just banked at the trade, using a fixed, tight SL 5) Now I've got the best of both worlds. A no-risk trade, with much bigger lot than I originally was willing to risk. I also now have the chance to just walk away and let the thing run, if it is showing good signs it wants to

This is quite a bit to think about in the moment, so I'll code something into my EA to help out with it.

The downside is that I will potentially cut myself out of any v-shape reversals without properly running it, but this doesn't happen that often, and I'm primarily interested in reducing the riskiness of my approach.

posts.text:
Anticipating a news setup using currency index confluence:

It's a safe bet to assume most economic announcements are always leaked. This usually presents us with good opportunities to predict the direction the news will go, since we understand the tricks the ITs like to play in order to get people offside.

Every week or two, GBP has 3 days in the week where medium importance economic announcements come out at 0930 GMT. Whilst these rarely produce huge moves, they always increase GBP volatility for 30-60 mins afterwards, and present nice opportunities for quick profit.

The general approach is: - check the currency index for the relevant currency. See where it is. Has it engulfed a level 30 mins earlier, and is making a RT? Is it sat at a strong level showing rejection PA 10-15 mins ahead? Is it making a straight line move into a key level? Is it mid-paz, but moving strongly already in direction of HTF trend? - check the other currency indexes to find the best opposing currency to hit it against. This can be either one which is itself at a key level and can bounce, or one that is already moving strongly in the correct direction as compared to the direction we want to trade GBP, with room to run - from the 2-3 crosspairs you have perhaps filtered down to, perform the same checks as on the indexes. Levels, PA etc - wait until 5-10 mins before the news to enter. Most of the time you can enter 10 seconds before the news hits. Ideally, you want to see a LTF surge going *against* the direction you think the news will go, right up until it hits. This is usually a trick to make people think the news is going to go the other way. Another type of very nice setup we can see, is price making an uninterrupted surge for 30 minutes right into the news, into a key level.

So, for today's 0930 GBP news, we start with GBPX M15

As we can see here, GBPX is currently in a range, held by 2 FLs above and below. The HTF trend is down, so it is more likely the lower one will break. However, with 15 mins to go before the news, GBPX was sat right at the bottom of the range, and had not broken it. In my experience, it is extremely unusual for price to be sat at a valid level, and for a news surge to suddenly break it *and keep going*. Much more likely, is that an engulf has already happened in the lead up to the news, and then the news continues the move; or the initial news stab breaks the level, but then price RTs sharply the other way, to complete the move at a later date. This chart favoured GBP going long. (remember, we're not necessarily looking for a huge move, just to ride the volatility for 5-10 mins after the news hits. We can use our understanding of the bigger picture to inform a decision as to whether it's worth trying for a longer hold or not)

I won't post all the other currency indexes, but the one that caught my eye at this time was USDX:

USD had what appeared to be a short term trend reversal day yesterday, unrelenting buying pressure. However, we had reacted to a key FL overnight, hit support, and then made a clean push deeper into it. Whilst you couldn't bet on this reversing the move short, it was an important level, and the 2TB offered the chance of secondary, smaller bounce. This chart supported USD selling off for a short period of time.

Combining the 2, we deduce that GU is a good pair to try and go long on for the news. So the next step is to look at the chart of GU itself.

This a section of an GU H1 chart.

What catches the eye is a decent DP, which was spiked through very quickly, circled (I believe this was FOMC last week that did this). There is a decent chance that orders were not filled at this level, so we can realistically expect some sort of bounce upon return. The slightly higher line is key SR from a PAZ boundary. Price was sat just above the lower line 10-15 mins out from the news.

So we now have 2 currency indexes and the cross itself supporting the possibility of a short-term long move from the news. We would not really expect a large move, because the HTF pictures on GBPX and USDX do not support it at this time. The final step is to examine M5/M15 PA for the candles leading up to 0930. Here is GU M5:

Circled, we can see price has surged down strongly (herd is now selling) and is showing nice M5 rejection PA from a place we anticipated in the period 0915-0925. Seeing this, I entered 10 minutes out from the news, keeping an eye on proceedings. Had price started to shoot up with just a few minutes to go, I most likely would have exited, since as mentioned this is usually a contrarian indicator. However, as it was, the 0925 candle, the last one before the news, closed bearish, which was enough confidence for me to hold into the release.

Finally M1 of how the trade played out:

On this timeframe, we can actually see a small FL just below the very obvious SR line. This made for a good initial target (and indeed, final target in this case), since most of the herd will be expecting price to reach this SR line, and turning price before it gets there represents a good opportunity for the ITs to confuse. The news itself gapped open slightly lower, before recovering strongly, and coming through for a nice quick 25 pips in 10 minutes.

Seems like a lot of work for 25 pips? Perhaps, but when you consider a) with enough time and experience, this entire mental process can be performed in under 60 seconds b) putting all of the factors together, we end up with a probability of being correct most likely in excess of 90%

then I believe it's worth it.

Although today, this move was small and against the larger picture, it was still extremely predictable, and using the method outlined above, on many other days with other news setups, there will be a lot more on the table.

Starting with previous posts, showing the complete trades from opening to close in addition to overview analysis.

My main trading time frames are H4 & H1. I might use the minimum
indicators for confluence sake, such as Trend Lines, Channels and
sometimes Oscillators for divergence signals.

The core of my trading technique is tracing the order flow and trading Price Action at decision areas.

Based on this equation Volatility = High Volume + Low Liquidity, I will be using some terms that might have the same meaning as follows:

Base = Cluster = Equilibrium = Indecision = Balance = Stable = Normal = Efficient = Range = Consolidation = Flag

Decision = Imbalance = Unstable = Abnormal = Inefficient = Momentum = Impulse = Liquidity Gap/Spike = Engulf = Pole

Corrective Moves = Rebalancing

Level = Zone = Area

Decision Point = Supply / Demand

Pivot Zone = S/R Flip/Swap = Key Level

Broken = Ignored

False Breakout = Fakeout = Stop Run = Stop Hunt = Trap

Positioning / Accumulation = Liquidation / Distribution

You can find my following articles in the
	Markepedia
, and I recommend reading all of the other great articles in there:

1).
	Order Flow

2).
	Trend Direction / Highs & Lows

3).
	Key Levels and Price Action There

4).
	Stacked Orders/Zones

All comments and critics are most welcomed.

posts.author: FX.Sniffer
posts.text:
I've posted this in another topic and thought its time to bring it here.

Supply and Demand zones presents a stack of unfilled orders either offers or bids.

Stacked zones presents stacked groups of unfilled orders (limit orders), in every zone there are unfilled stacked orders on top of each other.

As Sam Seiden explained in a webinar - Unfilled orders moves market prices, the chart line/candles/bars represent filled/executed orders and the white space around it represent the unfilled orders (limit orders) thus we need to focus on the big unfilled orders (limit orders).

What I'll explain here based on my understanding of the market, so is the attached chart. The following example applies to the stacked zones as well as to stacked orders inside a zone.

In case of a supply zone scenario, offers shall be stacked above each other (the wider the zone the more orders at different prices) logically the majority would sell high and this is why unfilled orders would increase higher into the zone, and with every return of price to the zone the sell orders are decrease/consumed.....now this doesn't mean the smart or big money would be sitting at the highest prices....nope not necessarily....they are the smart money and they know where to set and distribute their offers...well, it could be among the highest offers and "for example" this is where a compression ends, or it might be among the lowest offers and this is when we see a spike or a quick touch of the zone's lower edge then price bounce and drops for a long distant before returning back and starts pressuring or forming ascending triangle to consumes the entire zone.

Of course the strength of buyers and sellers plays a big role in this process every time it happens, thus comes the importance of how did the price leave the zone, and how is price returning to the zone.

I hope I made it simple and clear.

P.S. The attached chart present Buy/Sell limit orders.
