What did Pyrrho teach? That the greatest aim of life is Eudemonia. This is a Greek term that means happiness or living the good life - careful, don’t confuse it with pleasure or success – for them is living a contemplative life and embodying the truth and living from Good.

Philosophy is about what is true. Pyrrhonism says that nothing can be known for certain because you have two ways of accessing reality. The first one is the senses and the other one is reasoning. The problem is that they are not reliable and can trick us very easily. Therefore, we have to be honest and admit that we cannot know reality for sure. Neither perceptions nor reasoning tell us the ultimate truth. Moreover, he taught us that reasoning or proof is either, circular, or involves an infinite regress that is ultimately groundless.

How do we usually know what is true? We claim something and then back it up with justifications and proofs and evidence, but if we really think about it this is groundless because for any evidence you provide, you will need more evidence to prove itself and so on. You cannot basically ground anything because you don’t any grounding proof. You cannot say something is true because with each statement, its contradiction may be advanced with equal justification. THEREFORE, PYRRHONISTS REFUSE TO TAKE ANY POSITIONS BECAUSE WE DON’T HAVE GROUNDS FOR TAKING IT. THEY REFUSE TO TAKE SIDES. They will doubt anything beyond appearances because they cannot be ultimately proven. They also oppose that nothing can be known. The problem with the modern skeptic is that they doubt their own skepticism. You cannot know if nothing can be known. To make that sort of claim would be dogmatic.

“Skepticism is an ability or mental attitude with opposes judgement in any way whatsoever, with the results that, we are brought to a state of mental suspense, and then to a state of quietude. Suspense is a state of mental rest in which we don’t deny or affirm anything. Quietude is a tranquil condition of the soul. The main basic principle of the skeptic system is that of opposing to every proposition, an opposite proposition for we believe that as a consequence o this, we end to seizing to dogmatize.”

“The strength of man’s position in the world depends on his degree of adequacy of his perception of the world and reality. The less adequate, the more insecure he is and, hence, he is in need of idols to lean on and find security. The more adequate it is, the more he can stand on his own feet and has his center within himself.”

I'm learning about: Deficiency Cognition/Perception vs Being Cognition/Perception

Maslow’s Definition for B-Cognition: "A self-actualizing person is more able to perceive the world as if it were independent, not only of him, but also of human beings in general. Therefore, he can look upon nature as if it were there in itself and for itself and not as a human playground put there for human purposes. He can more easily refrain from projecting human purposes onto it and in a word, he can see it is there in its own being rather than a something to be used or something to be afraid of or something to be reacted to in some other human way. A section of cancer seen through a microscope, if only we can forget it is a cancer, can be seen as a beautiful and inspiring organization. A mosquito is a wonderful object if seen as an end by itself.”

- the ability to look at things holistically, as they actually are in a very attentive way, without judging or classifying these things. - no ego, no self-agenda perception; it is unmotivated, impersonal, desireless, unselfish, not needing and detached.

It is the ability to perceive an object for itself, not the way it is for us. Our desires and fears and emotions don’t get reflected into the object (physical, living object, institutions, etc.). How we perceive an object is very important since it dictates how we will react to it. If we perceive an object for itself (i.e. for the benefit and for the longlasting survival of itself) we get the most accurate representation of it. If we perceive an object as it is for us (for our benefit and for our own survival needs), we get a distorted view of it. We don’t project ourself and our desires into the things we are perceiving.

“Self-actualizing people take a non-valuing, non-judging, not-condemning attitude towards others. A desireless-ness and a choiceless awareness; this understanding permits a more clear and insightful perception about what is actually there.”

“Concrete perceiving of the whole of the object implies also that it is seen with care; the care that a mother would give to his infant, or the lover at his beloved. This will surely produce a more complete perception than the usual and casual one.”

It is the difference between looking at something and seeing it as it is vs what we normally call perception.

D-Cognition: Ordinary perception; partial and incomplete form of experience. It is a deficient and anxiety based way of perceiving the world. It is driven by the ego and our self-agenda. The degree in which we have deficiencies and need safety (money, girls, etc), that is the degree to which we are gonna evaluate the things we look at to see if they can give us something that we need. Our mind is very brilliant to filter what is relevant and what is not relevant. We perceive things in regard of what we need and want, not what it is in reality. We are constantly judging reality! The D-Perception is anthropocentric, it is the way humans look at the world; It is rigidly rational and abstract (we create our personal model of reality to fit into our self-agenda and ego). We confuse abstractions with perception itself.

People cannot stand paradox in d-cognition. It also is ideological and pragmatic.

“In ordinary cognition, the object is it is seen not so much per say, but as a member of a class, as an instance of a larger category. This kind of perception is described as classifying and, again, what you need to realize is that this is not a full perception of the object as it is a kind of classifying and labeling. It implies comparing and contrasting.”

“Abstractions, to the extent that they are useful, are also false. In a word, to perceive an object abstractly means not to perceive some aspects of it; it clearly implies selection of some attributes, discarding some others and creation and distortion of some others.”

“In order to perceive reality fully you need to suspend judgments and classifying, to need and to use. The moment we classify reality we cut the possibility to see it as a beautiful thing.”

“Fully disinterested and holistic perception of another human being becomes possible when nothing is needed from him.”

“Self-actualizing people can abstract without giving up concreteness and vice versa.”

Our own egoic deficiencies distorts reality. The very interaction of us and reality is compromised by our lack of mental health and the accuracy of our perceptions depends on our emotional and mental maturity (the distortion is huge, even though we don’t realize it) and many of the issues we have in our life are created by this distortions. THE PROBLEMS THAT WE HAVE ARE CREATED BY OUR PERCEPTIONS.

We need to start to notice how our mind distorts and judge reality. Our mind creates model of reality and then tries to fit actual reality in it rather than seeing it as it really is. (curve-fitting)

We are living in an augmented reality. We are the only organism that live in an augmented reality distorted by our concepts, fantasies and ideas (we don’t realize of this augmentation). The ego creates a kind of smog that doesn’t let us see reality as it is.

“Thoughts is always doing a great deal, but it tends to say that it hasn’t done anything, that it is telling you the way things really are but it distorts everything. What thoughts takes to be perception it’s actually highly affected by it. Thought can produce experiences without us being aware that they were produces by thoughts. It is this deceptive feature of thought that we have to look for. You need to see that thought is actually participating in perception.”

We all MUST realize that this is a systemic problem and the mind is biased by itself.

What can we do? Create awareness around this topic and realize that we perceive life from our own deficiencies. WE NEED TO REALIZE HOW WE REFLECT Y\OUR OWN AGENDA INTO REALITY, PEOPLE AND SITUATIONS. We need to start looking at objects and people for themselves as they actually are (existing for and only for themselves), not how they are for us.

Projections of our mind that are not features of reality itself:

- Labels and names that we give to objects

- Categories and hierarchies

- Meanings, judgements, values, usefulness and purpose

- Emotional Triggers (every time we get emotionally triggered by situations, are also creations of our mind)

- Relationships between objects: In reality, everything in the universe is extremely related to everything else in the universe; relationships are infinite. Everything is more complex than we can imagine.

- Separations and boundaries: Objects themselves are creations of our mind. If we look upon reality with complete lucidity we will see that there is no single object and boundary in it.

- Problems: Problems are creations of the mind, reality has no problems.

How to change our perception? It requires practice (10,000 hours). Select an object or person that we either hate or love and then see it for (and only for) itself as it actually is. See it independent of our and its values. Look at the object as God (and/or the multi-universe) was looking at it. Look at it not even as an object (since it is just an abstraction of our mind).

Enlightenment is the dissolution of the ego smog; same thing for meditation and mindfulness.

We may self-actualize after we improve our cognition. We cannot self-actualize if we maintain our ego (enlightenment). We can improve our life without enlightenment but we will not get to that part of life that it is really juicy and satisfying. We need to make the following choice:

- Are we gonna stay faithful to our self-agenda or to reality?

Self-agenda is the distortion of reality. - ever heard of the story “The monster and the little boy metaphor”?

If we are wise enough to see the greater good, we will create an extraordinary life!

Note: If you read this, you may be wondering whether or not I'm going crazy sharing something that has nothing to do with trading method, let alone RTM method. If you are, then I'm just guessing you are still close-minded and still very ego centric (i.e. always thinking "what's in it for me anyway"). Only through a paradigm change, I can start to look at things from many different perspectives and grow a little better. It is not easy, indeed, but simply live-able. Hopefully, those who read this can help him/herself change his/her perspective about seeing RTM and also many other facets of life. posts.author: staurum
posts.text:
Understand the context::

We do NOT really care about the facts, if we are really honest. We only care about making sense of things. We care about understanding. When it comes to making sense or understanding something, that very much hinges upon getting the *right* context.

Such that: even if we get the right content but the wrong context, we WILL still be wrong. And vice versa, if we get the right context, but we screw up the content a little bit (we get our facts wrong a little bit), we are still going to be right (in the big picture). ---> the reasons on why mind fucks happen.

GBPUSD trade setup:

Monthly on GBPUSD for me the bias is up, clearly pointing to the supply far up in the heavens.

DAILY: On the daily chart, price has been in an uptrend since July 2012, currently standing at a place from where it was rejected twice earlier, April 2012 and September 2012, Currently also, price is starting to project weakness, having been rejected for the third time in December.

Image 1: Daily linegraph for trendline and S/R flip. Black thick line is the S/R flip.

Image 2: Daily chart showing rejections of the price from the supply zone. The supply zone marked in green happens to be the Weekly and Daily supply zone.

Image 3: H4 chart. The take home message for me from this chart is break of the uptrend by the engulf of the source of the final upmove shown in light blue rectangle.

The white areas in the green zone are the untouched decisions made by the price to move lower.

Image4: M30 chart shows the decision made by the price to break the S/R line. Decision is marked in Golden color. The price is now compressing into the decision.

Image5: M5 chart helps us to zoom into the area where it was decided price is too expensive to go above the S/R flip and price moved further down.

Image 6: Target for the trade

In the event of the failure of the trade setup, the next setup would be to trade the untouched decision points shown on the H4 chart.

Advice and comments welcome!

Here is an AUDUSD long which I took: There is a very important lesson learnt in this trade.

Scenario: I took this trade, both in demo as well as in my live account. With a well sought and thought out analysis, chose my targets and stoploss. When I got into the trade I knew I was going to take it to the take profit, no shortcuts but I also knew there was 'DBD supply sitting right in between at 76, which can stop my trade. So, the greed took the best of me and I closed my trade, for a decent 50 pips, but the point of story is "I sold my trade cheaply to the bastards"

Here is something we all must understand, when we are planning our trades, we must know where our stop losses should be and where our most logical take profits should be. There must be a reason for every why and why not, if you dont have a reason, there should be no trade.

I really believe here at RTM, we have the education good enuf for all of us to be able to trade profitably with people like IF, Doctor and many others around on this website, who are more than willing to help us become good at it but at the end of the day, what we need is, to believe in ourselves. If we cannot believe in our own analysis, however much these guys help us out, we wont be able to improve.

Hi Hoto,

There is no single rule to find where you want to trade. We trade supply and demand, lot of people trade ranges, support and resistance, trend line, Fibonaccis and what not. All these places are good enough to see price action. A DBD or a RBD, they both are a good places to look for PA, and if PA is happening at any place where it makes sense to happen, our duty is to take that trade.

We dont need to make a million analysis before taking every trade....keep your Reward:Risk high enough, trade with some kind of logical setup which gives you winning trades, and you are on your way.

Settle down on a setup which you like to trade, observe it like hell, in every time frame, every situation, every place it forms, trade it and see when it works, when it does not work. Think why it worked and why it did not work. You can ask 1000 questions, no body here at RTM will mind, we all are here to help each other, that is the motive or RTM, but in the end, it will come down to you and your trading style. Understand your trading style like the back of your hand and you will be all good. You dont need a 100 ways to trade, find 1 that suits your style.

Feel free to ask as many questions as you want, I will try my best to answer them. If I can not, I am sure somebody else will definitely.

Good luck man.

Ans. I dont pay attention to single candle engulfings but I pay more attention to swing engulfings. If you understand the reason why I enter the trade then use it in reverse, and you will have my reason for exiting a trade.

When the price approaches to a significant demand or supply level belonging to higher time frames, I follow the price on m30, and when the last swing high/low gets engulfed, I exit. This is my way of trailing.

Now you can figure out why I did not close the trade on first of my charts.

On the gold trade, when price makes engulf of a level, it is more often than not going to the next level above or below, so I knew what I was targeting before I opened the trade. About price coming back in, it doesnt scare me because when I look up, it made a new engulfing, which clearly said to me, we are going up, if you want you can add another position at the point when price came down again

Hope this helps.

Hi Rex,

Thanks for asking the question.

Here is the answer: If you see just below my entry, there is a blue rectangle, only partially visible. It says H1 FTR. The chart which you are looking at is an M5. You have a valid reasoning for going short on m5 when price comes back after making the engulf, but the problem is there is no HTF supply above it to support the engulf on the short side.

HTF tells you where the price is standing currently with respect to big players and LTF gives you entries. Try not to fixate on LTFs only coz you want to take more trades. Instead, go out to H4, daily, weekly, monthly and mark out each and every demand and supply which is created. wait for the price to come back to these zones and then watch the PA on LTFs. Then when you have the signal, trade it. By LTFs I dont mean M1,M5 but atleast H1 to get engulf, then pin point your entries on M5, M1 to enter the trade.

In short: "demand/supply H4 or higher, watch PA on return to these zones on M30/H1, got engulf, pin point your entries on M1/5/15. SL above the zone. Target, oppostite zone on the time frame on which you are taking the trade"

Good luck and keep the questions coming.

Hi Chanya,

Sunny doesn't enter a trade as soon as there is an engulf, engulfs happen all the time, in both directions. We need to identify which engulfs are most significant and trade from them.

In that chart most likely on the HTF there was a supply area above the high, price did not want to go any higher and engulfed the last significant demand which lead to a push up to the supply, this shows buyers are no longer in control and we should be looking to short which will be from the origin of the engulfing of the demand.

For price to return to the origin it needs to go higher and so will be engulfing on the move up, we know these won’t be significant as all price is trying to do is each the origin to get in more sellers and push price down.

That’s how I view it anyway but I would like to see Sunny’s response as well.

posts.text:
sunnytrader1984 wrote:

romant wrote: Nice trade! btw, Sunny. There's a post on the previous page with my question. Could you answer please?

Hi Romant,

If you want me to tell you in one line why I took all those trades, the answer would be: The only common thing in all my trades is ENGULFING. Now, you have to understand the engulfing, looks good, looks weak etc, Where it forms, ofcourse if you see it is forming in HTF Demand and Supply zones, it is good. If not then what, can be ftr, can support/resistance, can be Moving averages. If it is happening, there must be a reason, and the reason is, big money is interested in pushing the price in the direction of engulf. That is all the confirmation I need.

When you see any of my charts, they are most likely marked with my reason to enter a trade. I really try to make my charts look as simple as possible they can be, coz I myself dont understand as much as some of these other guys do. I try to keep it simple so that it can make some sense in my stupid head. If you think, I dont get loosers, I do, but they are small. Sometimes I am saved from falling into the trap of a bad trade because there is no engulf.

If I was to give you one thing that can help you become successful, I would give you ENGULFING. Take it, use it, understand it, why it works, why it did not work. Take trades based on engulfing.....they will start coming together.

I hope my rant makes some kind of sense. Keep posting your charts, setups and you will get comments on them, if not from me, then somebody else on this community.

Have a nice day.

Excellent sir!. Simplicity at its best

posts.author: Ifmyante
posts.text:
Supply and Demand, Support and Resistance, and Price Action are the very basis of everything we do in trading. So, which came first, S/D or PA? Or of course, S/R To me, there's no difference between them. Both are simply decisions made on the value of an asset and what happens to price when it returns to these decision points. Price simply bounces from decision point to decision point. Take a look at this video to see what I mean

I truly hope this video has shown you how unbelievably simple it is to grasp price dynamics. And the great thing is, it works (more often than not) in every timeframe, on every pair!

Thx guys.. nice analysis..

One question i was looking somebody to ask positions size. After all I took a bit of adventures trade on with the first entry as there was no PA config at the entry point..

When I take on this kind of trades i start with small position. in this case first entry was 0.5 second std 1 lot and third one was 2 lots. However, stops for the second and the third entry were just above the previous peak while for the first entry it was just above the h4 supply.

My trading mainly based on spotting where noticeable buyers and sellers are.. all other tech stuff comes after.

Keep in mind position sizing must be relevant to your account size. My view is that if you open a micro account it should be at least $5.000, for trading mini lots it shouldn't be less than $20.000 and for standard lots $100k + if you want want to survive and possibly get somewhere in markets.

Whiteout, there are times I risk up-to 5% but I try to keep it around 2% for any one of my accounts.

Sometimes, I have 10 or 15 open trades running with any one account. Then some may ask how the heck I can keep it within 2-5% account risk ratio. No, I don't have zillion $ accounts. Once any one of my trades locked, means at least stop moved to be +spread then that trade is no longer included in my risk pool.

One day I'll try to put together an article about "Risk Management" if and when I get around to do it. Risk management is THE Holly Grail of trading.

Tyoon wrote:

Its only a BEflag if you see it as a BEflag. Try and see what else it could be beyond face-value.

These 'patterns' happen at times. Here is one on GU also.

You've highlighted the typical dangers of patterns - traders tend to see patterns too frequently and see what they want to see rather than what is actually there.

This is one of the reasons understanding what is actually happening in patterns like flags in terms of the price action helps to assess the 'quality' of the pattern and the likelihood of it working out.

The most common mistake I see people make (not on here - just generally) is with regards H&S patterns, people see them in all shapes and sizes without regard of the location relative to other TF's and to the market generally - let alone an understanding on what is actually occurring in an H&S pattern from a true price action perspective.

You've also highlighted the nuances off going from a relatively quiet session (Asia) to Frankfurt / London open - it's easy to see Asian low liquidity and thus tight consolidation as a flag or other pattern, taking care when you are approaching such a big jump in volume is always prudent IMO.

With regards flags specifically, another thing I would generally comment on is to remember what a flag is:

1. It's a continuation of a strong momentum move - it's a brief pause while price clears demand (for a short setup) and then moves on it's way. Thus it is logical that if the pole forms say over 2 hours and then price consolidates in the flag for 12 hours then the 'chances' of the flag working have somewhat decreased - because you're looking for that same momentum (which is a strong supply / demand imbalance) being present and price moving in the same vein it did when forming the pole.

2. The chances of a flag also working out if it retraces the whole pole distance are also decreased, why, because as a I said above a flag is a momentum continuation move so if price is retracing the whole move what does that tell us about the strength of the move that caused the pole - that supply / demand imbalance has been completely retraced.

Of course that latter could turn out to be compression back into the source of the pole for example, but then that's something different and not a flag.

I find when first understanding patterns if people (a) remember to think about what the pattern represents should be happening (b) understand the price action occurring within the pattern (c) remember to check the location and surrounding TF's and (d) check the market generally it helps to keep them out of trouble and focussing on identifying the more straight forward and obvious setups which helps to build confidence before moving onto more advanced concepts.

Quickly scanned the charts to find two examples of more obvious straightforward flags. Notice how price moved after it forms the flag lows/highs i.e. hits supply for the short and demand for the long (you should always be able to identify a clear supply / demand zone where price will start to move with high momentum and breakout of the flag).

The advantage of having the above knowledge is you know how price should move and where it should move from and thus can get into a trade at the biggest discount and easily cut the trade when price isn't doing what it should. Catching moves like this when you're in at the source of the flag provide some very big risk/reward opportunities.

posts.author: Tyoon
posts.text:
Josh wrote: let alone an understanding on what is actually occurring in an H&S pattern from a true price action perspective.

That goes for any pattern. They are face-value bi-products or results of order flow. There is logic to every pattern and to why it plays out the way it does.

Josh wrote: You've also highlighted the nuances off going from a relatively quiet session (Asia) to Frankfurt / London open - it's easy to see Asian low liquidity and thus tight consolidation as a flag or other pattern, taking care when you are approaching such a big jump in volume is always prudent IMO.

Asian session are not typically low in liquidity. They only seem like that because they usually run their circular trade phase to build positions for the European opens. When the rolls are switched the Asians can make very large moves just like you would see in typical NY and London sessions. If Asians do stick to a tight range the key is to watch how the range widens during Franky and London open.

Josh wrote: With regards flags specifically, another thing I would generally comment on is to remember what a flag is

A flag is either one of two things; profit taking or consumption. Why do you see constantly flags at key levels before they break? At key levels there are a crap load of orders sitting there (lovely liquidity) in which the market makers take advantage of to re-accumulate. If they were net long for example and price gets to a level of sell orders, they use it as an opportunity to add to their positions - consuming them. When they get to their level of taking profits they will release their longs as sales into the market which creates a beflag pattern. It consolidates but does not drop too much because they release them slowly to keep it within a price range to maintain profit.

posts.author: MitchWorse
posts.text:
<nerdmode> supply && demand == market

The name of this topic describes the understanding of price in its purest form.

When 2 people want to buy 1 available object, the object will go to the highest bid. Demand > Supply, price goes up.

When 2 people want to sell an identical object and there is 1 buyer who needs 1 object, the buyer will go for the lowest ask. Supply > Demand, price goes down.

When there is no supply or demand, there is no price.

When you look at a chart with price history(from any object), you will spot recent levels at which price reacted; A base/range where buyers and sellers agreed on price followed by an impulse. That impulse was triggered by a decision that caused supply and demand to go out of balance.

The level where this decision was made should be marked on your chart. There will be supply or demand left at that zone.

When buyers and sellers disagree on price, price will move to a previous level of agreement.

How price moves between levels is called Price Action(PA).

Since price is based on the opinions from buyers and sellers and not solely on facts, trading can't be science, therefor it must be an art. </nerdmode>

posts.author: Simon
posts.text:
I feel like there are many trading opportunities that I am missing, particularly the intraday ones.

I've noticed that there seems to be quite a lot of emphasis on S/R "flip zones", and traders advocating touch-trades at the first test.

One thing that I have found confusing with this is that in order to establish a horizontal line at the flip-zone one will need to cut through candles.

Sam Seiden, who I would consider my trading mentor has offered many examples of the areas that he considers supply or demand. And crucially, one will often hear Sam say that in order to mark out the level, "We NEVER cut through candles".

The one person who made total sense to me from day one of my trading journey is Sam Seiden. There are also a number of guys on here who seem to have taken supply/demand trading to the next level (pun-intended):)

I'd be grateful if anyone can help me disambiguate the cutting through candles process into one that also fits

into Sam's type of supply/demand trading method.

posts.author: Ifmyante
posts.text:
Hi Simon.

Just so I can be sure we're gonna talk about the same thing, would you mind showing me a chart example of "cutting through candles"?

posts.author: Simon
posts.text:
Hi If,

Thanks for the quick reply.

I've attached a current chart of USDCHF which was a long trade that I recently took. It's in the D1 timeframe but I believe that the same principles should still apply across the other timeframes.

1. Demand level

2. All bear candles into the level and then buy.

3. Sam Seiden would often talk about the "path of least resistance" to the nearest opposing level. On that basis the opportunity here looked really good.

4. SR flip zone established. In order to consider the SR flip zone once I had bought

at the original demand level, horizontal line would need to "cut through" the red candles.

If I had considered the SR flip when taking the trade then I could have considered taking profits at the white circle, which also forms a confluence with a 76.4 fib retrace.

In the event I did makes pips but do feel that with a little more craft it would have been possible to take a lot more of what the market was offering.

Hope this makes sense!

posts.author: C-12
posts.text:
I've watched a few XLT videos where the instructors talk about "What was once demand then becomes supply".

The reason given was that that once a demand zone has been weakened and then removed it can leave unfilled orders sell orders behind. It makes sense really if a large entity places a large sell order that not all their orders will be filled.

Just from observation there seams to be lot of competition for fills at these flip levels and price can often reverse a few pips before the level.

posts.author: Ifmyante
posts.text:
Simon wrote: One thing that I have found confusing with this is that in order to establish a horizontal line at the flip-zone one will need to cut through candles.

Sam Seiden, who I would consider my trading mentor has offered many examples of the areas that he considers supply or demand. And crucially, one will often hear Sam say that in order to mark out the level, "We NEVER cut through candles".

Now I think I get what you mean, thanks for explaining.

We look for decisions on value, and decision points both respected and broken.

If a demand gets broken, and price shoots down from it, we look for the point where the decision was made to break it. Ideally we look for a break, and then a rally back into it which fails miserably. This "Epic Fail" point is the decision that price has broken the level and the level is staying broken. We can't just expect price to break this DP easily, as lots of sell orders await price's return there.

That's why price will often need to bounce from S/R flips back to the last DP before advancing.

In the case of your chart, the Deman you have shown is a reaction to something on the left - the decision to break a beautiful Supply. See what happened lately when price came back up from your buy line and hit that old supply?

posts.text:
Hello,

If price form a flag before reaching S or D area, what does it mean and how to deal with it? I am sorry if I am in the wrong thread to ask.

posts.author: Tyoon
posts.text:
rokuhaato wrote: If price form a flag before reaching S or D area, what does it mean and how to deal with it?

I am sorry if I am in the wrong thread to ask.

When you see something that looks like a flag before a level, it is most likely consumption of that level. So if you see a buflag at supply it could be that the buyers are consuming the supply orders to break through.

If you think of a level of supply and a level of demand (or support and resistance), price either consumes one level and rejects off of the other. So price can be consuming supply then rejecting off of demand. So, the way to deal with it is to find your levels and watch the PA interaction between them within the flag keeping the bigger picture in mind.

posts.author: Emene
posts.text:
WRB: Wide Range Bodies = BIG CANDLES, lots of orders, heavy money making the price move fast and wild.

Hidden gaps: there is no space between the candles, so it is not a true gap. HOWEVER, a WRB candle is called a hidden gap because this very candle must be filled, some people are trapped at the other end of it because it moved too fast. I personnally call them price inconsistencies. The price action is not clean, price has not been retest.

In the way we teach here, hidden gaps are the sources of the poles (you know, poles, flag?). A flag fills the pole and comes back to source. Then the hiddne gap is closed and price can resume in the same direction.

satman wrote: Hello everyone.

Along with Acegazette i have also been watching some of Sam Seiden"s video's from (site not mentioned) about supply and demand. Sam doesn't consider the swing high's & lows as demand & support levels, he always seem to reference supply/demand levels as a brief pause just after a swing high or low, i'd naturally think that the swing high and low would be the proper supply and demand levels (confused)

For example with a strong move he say's that there are stacks of unfilled buy orders remaining and if strong decline stacks of unfilled sell orders, is the reason for the unfilled orders due to the move being so quick? and what is the significance of that, can we expect another move in the opposite direction to the move to eat up all the left over orders?

Just trying to get my head around it all.

Regards Marc

Hi Marc, What you are asking is really about the basics of supply and demand trading and it's important that you understand it. I wrote an article about Basic Supply & Demand some time ago, you can find it here: www.acegazette.com/en/trading-articles/s...s-levels-by-mel.html

This is important to know that price moves from Supply to Demand and from Demand to Supply. Why does price move from Demand to Supply? Simply because Buyers were in control at this particular point. Why does price move from Supply to Demand? Simply because Sellers were in control at this particular point.

Why is it that price can break Supply and become Demand? Simply because Buyers were in control at this particular point. Why is it that price can break Demand and become Supply? Simply because Sellers were in control at thos particular point.

Our edge is based on this simple facts. When price re-visit a Fresh Demand, we look to buy because there is a good chance that Big Money will have orders placed there and vice versa for a re-vist of a Fresh Supply.

I suspect that the "brief pause" you are reffering to is what we call a Base. You can find more info about it by clicking on the link to the article.

Now about the Swing high and low, imo, those are mostly just retests of a previous Supply & Demand areas...

I have marked a chfjpy chart for you with some thoughts on it, Hopefully it helps. Best, Mel

EDIT: Nr 5 has to be " Imediate test of Supply" and not Demand

You are definitely looking at important areas for your entry and tg levels!

Upon first glance at your money management (mm) your trade is a little better than 1:1 which by many standards is too low. If you popped into the smaller timeframes I am sure you could fine tune the decision points and describe the price action around the area.

I say this because Just looking at the 4 hr could hold you back on understanding the value decisions going on in the lower timeframes. You may not have the time to be around the charts perusing ltf all day but you could tighten up your stops or look for trades in between. Where you have your stop loss set could be a tg for a short trade should your entry level break and price action gives you a sign with an rbd after break kind of thing.

Also your tg could be a good aread to reverse your trade should it go in your favor given a good aproach.

So viewing from a multi timeframe perspective can increase your reward but also open other trade opportunities.

Given most of us are relatively new at this, which I do not know your experience, 1:1 risk reward trading can lead to alot of head banging at break even and taking trades at less desirable levels, even though your areas are good.

Thats my 2 cents for the day

You are definitely looking at important areas for your entry and tg levels!

Upon first glance at your money management (mm) your trade is a little better than 1:1 which by many standards is too low. If you popped into the smaller timeframes I am sure you could fine tune the decision points and describe the price action around the area.

I say this because Just looking at the 4 hr could hold you back on understanding the value decisions going on in the lower timeframes. You may not have the time to be around the charts perusing ltf all day but you could tighten up your stops or look for trades in between. Where you have your stop loss set could be a tg for a short trade should your entry level break and price action gives you a sign with an rbd after break kind of thing.

Also your tg could be a good aread to reverse your trade should it go in your favor given a good aproach.

So viewing from a multi timeframe perspective can increase your reward but also open other trade opportunities.

Given most of us are relatively new at this, which I do not know your experience, 1:1 risk reward trading can lead to alot of head banging at break even and taking trades at less desirable levels, even though your areas are good.

Thats my 2 cents for the day

posts.author: Warren
posts.text:
Alientrader,

Thank you for your question.

I have limited time and there is no set time slot when i can say, ok, this week i can spend the same 3 hours at my screen every day. And to be really honest i dont want to sit at my screen for hours.

My trading style works round my lifestyle, not the other way round. You see i have traded full time, but i found it boring and i felt i needed to be in the market all the time to make money. These days i dont chase price around, i let the market come to me!

So considering that i can not always be there to pull the trigger or even watch the approach. I set buy / sell limit orders on really good zones that are fresh, with a view on HTF. This affords me time and you generally get good momentum away from the zone, i can then switch to trade management mode.

I set zones on my laptop or desktop, and have alarms by my entries, these alarms send an email and text to my mobile phone.I have an app for my platform on my phone. So, if i am busy at least i know a trade has been triggered.

When i get an hour or so to watch, i scan through pairs, suss the general trend and sometimes i get in on a uptrending market on a pull back to demand. Like catching a move part way through, as im sure you know, price can give us multiple opportunities to get into a move.

The 2 charts above, are both good zones. But, one thing i am looking at more is, where is price going to turn and how can i see that before hand. Most of the time i know that price will react to a zone, but how can i be accurate with my limit orders.

1 thing that frustrates me is when entering a zone, does price react on the spikes or bodies of candles. To me they both seem to happen. So here is my latest logic.

Lets say my account is £10,000

My total risk on any one trade is 1%, that = £100, for me to risk in a zone

so in a marked box zone of 50 pips top to bottom

This allows me a lot size of £2 per pip. So if my trade fails i have only lost £100 or 1% of my account.

Now, if i have 1 limit order with the above equation, it allows me one chance to enter the market.

But if i break the lot size down to 0.50p per pip, i can have 4 limit orders at various areas in the zone. And still only risk 1%!

So when price enters my zone it could pick up some or all orders.

This allows me with metatrader to also take part profits on 1 or 2 of those micro orders, as price hits mid targets. If i have one order on IBFX, i can not part close 1 large order.

Sorry the explanation was long winded,hopefully you can see my full reasoning behind a method that suits my trading and my lifestyle.

Regards

posts.author: Pedini
posts.text:
Hey guys, if I may,

When I first started looking into Supply and Demand I found Sam S work and used to think "shit, how does he do it?!" I never used to miss his webinars (even if they ran at 2am my time) and used to mark all his zones on my charts. I had a basic understanding on how it worked, but that was as far as it went, the very basics of supply and demand, and nothing of PA.

After IF brought us his online material, and after I started to learn it. I found myself less and less compelled to watch Sams webinars. Not because I didn't think they were good, but because I already knew what to look for, and WHY.

I think I have come a long way since I first found SD trading, and I don't even watch Sams webinars anymore as I can find all the important zones on the charts myself. Not only that but I understand the PA too! which we know is most of the story.

Again, Sams works are really cool to understand the basics, but the team here at RTM have really taken it to the next level.

Hey Dappa,

i have defined the base with black square (or box). To my understanding - price gets "trapped" between two important prices. (The high of the box and the low of the box.) The price has been given a limited range where it can move. (To understand why it limits the price - you should check engulfing, order-flow and flag limit articles.) Price needs a push from bigger money to break (engulf) the high or the low of the box (HTF can help you getting an idea in which way it will break.) Its indeed almost an equalibrium of price - from where a decision will be needed inin order to break bulish or bearish.

Ofcourse you have 100 pip and 5 pip ranges (bases) . In my case: It wasnt clear to me, and didnt wanna risk it - so i just closed the position.

Hi Heath,

That's a good question, you have here. When I first started to look at Supply and Demand, I did so many "researches" on my charts in order to locate some "bases" /S/D. Then, I remember hearing Sam S. talking about Fresh zones in his video and this is when the "troubles" started for me.

I looked at the zones I had marked on my charts and they all seemed to be not fresh....! I can tell you, I was scratching my head because I wanted to know why all the bases were already tested lol

After looking and searching, I realized that there was something very intresting and powerfull that happened all the time on the charts. A supply took place, was tested once, retested twice (sometimes more) and bammmme the magic happened...... This Supply BECAME Demand! (and vice versa for Demand becoming Supply)

You see, for something to be called Fresh, it has to be New, untouched and how in the world is this going to happen? Well I concluded that a Fresh zone can only exists when there is a swap in decision.

IF did a video about Decision Point, it helped me understand it even more. When a new decision is made, you'll see a Decision point/ base forming and this is when a Fresh Supply/Demand exists.

Hope this helps, Mel

So this whole game is really looking at:

Past price action: This is where we mark of past supply/Demand and key levels.

Approach: This is where we look at price action to come back to these levels from the past. We look for CP, 3 drive, momentum, or stacked zones.

Reaction: Based how it returns we look for price action to offer us entries. This could be in the form of Engulf,QM,diamond, fake outs, or the cancan.

The issue I am having is how does the return of price and the reaction relate? In other words if price rockets back into an old supply level, you would not take that short. If price rockets back and then engulfs/caps, then you short the return to that engulf/cap. Right?

So what if price CP's back to the old supply level? Since all the demand has already been removed why would you wait for a reaction? Price should hit that supply and turn almost immediately. Right?

because if the rise after the FL is consumed, does not go high enough, it often falls back to test the last swing low, in that case it reacted there but went even lower later. this is less probable trade of course but is one of the plays in the flag. this whole scenario of FL engulfed and price dropping is a trap and happens way too often if you look for it. why? because it catches whoever bought at the place you wanted to buy.

posts.author: floating brick

Hi Heath,

In answer to your question: how do you determine say in a section that all demand has beed cleared so the only way is down... or viceversa)

I feel the answer is the PA has the answer, in a strong move up or down, all the buyers or sellers have had their demand satisfied, when a reversal occurs short the buyers have all filled their orders until the price falls to a level where there are buyers, where the market perceives the price is to cheap, and it all starts over again, buyers, sellers, to cheep indecision, market movement....

I hope this helps, what has helped me are Iffys video tutorials on this site and Sam Sneddon videos on the FX street site.

posts.author: rcmacf
posts.text:
I'll have a go.

To be a true FTR of the S/R line you have marked, it should not manage to get back above the that same S/R line. However, as the decision to break and go low is an engulf, you should always be aware that it can retrace up to the supply which created the engulf - the "source".

When price moves away from this area for some time, and then returns, the FTR below the S/R line is a preferable touch trade, as if the FTR is created higher (red) then you have to then consider that price is moving up to stacked zones, so you need to watch PA more carefully.

Also, if you use the red FTR as your entry point on the FTB then you shall also need to consider that you have broken the S/R line to the upside, and so that line has now become a demand zone, which reduces your R:R for your first TG.

Maybe this makes it clearer:

a'lot of people ask questions on this site, and no one really gives straight out answers, so i will try and clarify my insight and knowledge that i gained from a great trader and friend and all praise goes out to him (redsword)

what iv'e learnt and seen for my self, are that markets are very simple by nature. so don't try and complicate things which i tend to sometimes do. in general, price move's from source to source, that is, Supply & Demand. ASK YOUR SELF, what is supply and what does price do at supply. ask your self the same thing at Demand.

chart im showing below is silver 4h bare chart, no lines no markings, nothing. before continuing check out the chart, and try and spot the "Demand (first source) & Supply (second source)"

(silver 4H) chartupload.com/images/19502173077647496207.png

after looking at it, have you spotted the supply & demand?

now continuing from above, price moves from source to source. what i mean by that is price will want to move back to the source. the source is where trades are made, placed, entered, what ever you want to call it. that is where you look at to enter/renter the market.

chart below are the supply & demand marked out.

chartupload.com/images/31578998783755156644.png

looking at the source and the candles them self's, we need to find buyers and sellers. as the famous saying goes, "price does not move with out "engulfing". do u see at the source, engulfing candles marked out in red and blue? do u see how price moves away hard from there in White marked out? now this is the first part, spotting credible and reliable levels.

the second part is going down a TF or a few TF, and looking at the micro structure of PA with in the marked out levels. this is the tricky part thou since levels (or source) can be at higher or lower levels that u marked out. so u need to spend time at the charts reading, reading and more reading, the charts that is and its structure.

it u look closely at the zoomed in chart, u will see "flips" at the Demand and supply. what i mean by flips, is at the demand u will get an r/s flip (resistance turned support) and at supply u will get a s/r flip (support turned resistance). that is the source. that is where you look to enter the trade.

chartupload.com/images/47457093265920484275.png

this is the simple nature and most common form of PA that moves from "source to source" understand what i talk about and see it for your self and you are well on your way to being a successful trader

chartupload.com/images/94126533463886997901.png

I know that price is typically guided by Flag Limits (FL) and it’s the break of the FL that's important as it allows prices to move into a new zone; and the FL defines the edge of the zone. As such I am starting to see FL as my guiding compass, telling me where price wants to go. If done properly, from my limited studies, you can look at the FL in each time frame to keep in the right side of the market at all times to ensure you are trading in the right direction and from the edge of the zone.

At present, the Time Frame (TF) that makes sense to me is the H4. I can see how the FL marked is containing price. When a FL breaks, price will often flag and the FL defines the edge of the flag. I want to see price as flags and poles as that is how IF sees price and I want to see price the same way IF does.

posts.author: polymorph
posts.text:
The middle section of the Supply/Demand article describes DBR/RBD/DBD/RBR's. On your charts start by focusing on the B's (the bases) in those formations and extend them out as far as they seem to matter. Regarding your yellow circles, why did you draw them there? Don't tell us, show us by using boxes on your own chart and extending them to the right to see what happens. Don't be afraid to drop to lower time frames (LTF) and refine your areas of supply and demand.

As for how wide to draw them, stop and think about what is really happening as you're doing this homework - real buying and selling is creating the picture on the chart. So in the pic I uploaded, the blue supply box is drawn around the area where buying and selling was fairly equal right before a clear decision by the market to take price lower. That's essentially what a base is: balance in price before clear imbalance, in this case price moved sideways and then selling far exceeded buying, which always means that price must fall. It also might help to think of it as decisions (If has a wholevideo on it that is phenomenal!) - where did the market make clear decisions on price? That's a base and for this homework it's what you want to mark.

posts.author: Jurij
posts.text:
OK now I understand what you mean.

An MPL is inside an FTR/FL, it is the extreme set of unfilled orders. An FTR is made (and confirmed) once a new high (HH) or low (LL) is made after a break of some barrier (SR etc...). So without HH in case of the above chart there is no FTR and thus no MPL.

Also this, not all QMs are MPLs but an MPL (inside an FTR/FL) can be a QM.

As staurum said, this is really explained everywhere on this site and especially in the videos/webinars.

(specially recently omidfxt and salivan), one should not use HTF FL/FTR

zone where you want to trade, then you can go to LTF and finetune the
entry for max R:R.

Found them while reading IF's journal..

Ifmyante wrote: I've just been
reading Deenius' journal, where I found the answers to pretty much every
 question I could ever be asked, so I'm stealing his fine work and
putting it here

deenius wrote: Ok, I would like to restart my journal with my favorite Ifmyante quotes. I think, it is really important stuff.

Ifmyante quotes

If the signal is given by the market mover (an engulf into a new
 zone), then price is very unlikely to break the extreme of the zone it
just came from. So, if you have the patience to wait at the last
remaining set of unfilled orders in the origin, you can be almost
certain that that price will be respected.

There is absolute order in the market. Nothing at all there happens
by chance. That's why it's so easy to read what's going to happen next.
There are rules which are strictly followed; so much so you'd imagine
it's all run by algorithms, up to the moment when the signal is decided
upon, and straight away thereafter. There is zero chaos in the market.
It's elegantly designed; a beauty to behold.

Fakeouts are extremely easy to predict. Most SD traders still look
directly left, which is the big shortcoming of Supply/Demand trading.
It's further left again we should be looking.

Say price is coming up to a supply. The only way we can be sure that
 supply will hold price down is if that supply has already visited the
extreme set of orders in the flag limit to its left. If the supply fell
short of that, we can anticipate a FO to those extreme orders. Extremely
 simple stuff.

We always look to what S or D are reactions to, rather than just S or D themselves.

Look for tricks being played on approach to a place where a trick was played, and you'll find where price will turn.

If you can look beyond S/D, you'll see that the Flag Limit is the only true place to look for PA for a trade. Trade these levels and you're taking gambling out of your method.

All we can ever hope for is a bounce at these levels, unless we are
certain that this level is the deepest possible point of retrace after a
 previous engulf. Without that, we must watch PA as it develops, both
before and during the trade. Set and Forget trades can only be taken
once the signal is given and the target is clear.

Being patient is absolutely vital for making giant trades. We must
wait for the very best possible places before we enter; the places where
 you'd expect great PA to react.

If you're around to watch the PA unfold, it's rare your stop should
get hit. Price will so very often retrace enough for you to get out
without a loss. That's why I wait for the very best price to TT - it
tends to keep me in the black.

I'm not even a part time trader now, so I miss nearly every piece of
 action there is. If I ever open the charts and see a trade opp right in
 front of me, I take it. However, I usually get between 10R and 25R per
trade. If I lose, it's usually no more than the spread and commission.
There are between 5 and 20 such confirmed trades available every day.

First of all, we need to understand that time has no place in any
read of the market. The only way to be completely sure of where a FL is,
 is to be there when the break occurs, and mark the highs and lows as
they occur. Within a minute they can be obscured by a candle, but we'll
know exactly where they are. If we're not there to watch and mark, we
must use the full candle as a FL.

If we've had an engulf and are getting in on a RT, we must always be
 ready for a diamond to occur, especially if price hasn't yet hit MPL of
 the zone the original bounce was a reaction to. So, if we're not going
to be around to watch PA, our stop must be beyond the original FL.

Funny you should say that, as I teach to always and only trade
within a flag. Sometimes the flag will already have developed, and
sometimes the flag is to be made while you're in the trade. Either way, always trade within a flag.

Attune yourself to what the buggers are doing, and don't let them
fool you. Just know they've got orders to fill at a level, watch them
fill some on approach (CP), see the momentum, and watch them come back
to fill more orders 'til they've had their fill.

This perhaps should be the first thing that anybody ever reads regarding trading: We're
 always looking for signs of what the big guys are doing at significant
areas, and if we don't see what they're doing, there's no trade. So,
 on approach, if we see the big guys trying to hide their orders in the
market, we see compression, and can feel pretty sure of their intentions
 - to get in as many orders as they can before the turn If we don't see
this, we can be pretty sure that it won't just turn immediately, as
there usually won't be enough orders against them to fill all the orders
 they must fill. This is why we wait for an engulf. This shows their intention to reverse price. Then we watch them trying to hide their orders in the market on a retrace, ready to take price to the origin of the move.

When we see decent CP coming into the base of a pole, we are very
often safe to touch trade the base. The safest thing to do however is to
 await the first engulf into the cp zone as confirmation.

Very often a zone will break strongly and price will retrace but
fail to retouch it. This is still the FTR - the confirmation of a new
trend (do a study of how price reacts and how far it goes after hitting
this spot). So an FTR can be first time back, but doesn't need to be.

During holidays, volume in the market is often greatly diminished.
This would lead some to imagine that price hardly moves. But. Say
someone decided to put a truckload of orders into the market. If there's
 nobody else in the market to oppose these orders, price can do nothing
but shoot away. So remember. Low Volume can = High Volatility.

Until now I have been so unfocused on the charts that my exits have
been very sloppy. My trade plan now has a couple of variables, but
essentially I'll let price travel back to the other edge of the last PAZ
 in the TF I'm trading. If it engulfs, I'll exit on a RT or a break of
the next LTF FL. If it rejects, I'll let the trade run and await exit
PA.

It's all about getting into the mind of the market makers and trading as they do. Nothing special.

Most of my analysis comes in after the trade is entered. Before
taking the trade, I do as you said - simple - it's really easy to find
pockets of orders which will bounce price, and if they happen to be at
great htf levels, even better - there's the highest chance of them
giving maximum pips. What I do certainly looks like touch trading -
picking tops and bottoms, but what you said belies that. These are not
tops and bottoms, but retraces to the best price to re enter. Once I'm
in though, I'm never guaranteed massive returns - sure price will bounce
 where I enter, but I'm never complacent until I've seen the engulf. In
fact, I'm never really complacent at all. If PA tells me to get out, I
must get out!

Many might misconstrue us as pattern recognition traders - we're
not. Certainly while learning we look for recurring patterns in the
market. But once we understand them, what becomes most important is WHY
the ITs made them. It's paramount to understand that it's not enough for
 the ITs to simply move price. They must also get massive amounts of
orders filled in order to make maximum gains. They must also refrain
from giving other ITs false signals, which could ultimately cause chaos
for everybody. Think of these things as you study, and you'll be able to
 get into the mind of the market mover.

Here are just a few targets for price, and the QM level is a big
one. Certainly we need to get PA for entry before or once it's hit.

If it breaks, then the same level can have the opposite effect on return.

Once price engulfs a level, all that's important is how far it
retraces before hitting its target. While the pockets of orders remain
in this RT, it remains strong. If price totally compresses (picking up
all orders) forward from the tip of the RT, then we will look primarily
for the orders at the entrance to said CP.

To the ITs, candle closes don't mean a damned thing, so please don't use them in your own analysis.

A line is not the answer. Certainly, you may draw a line, but you
must then go into the LTF to find a DBR/RBD on the right side of the
LL/HH swing which covers that line. That RBD/DBR will be your box. You
can scalp from each of these, knowing that it may only be a scalp. If
you're simply setting a PO, then you must set your stop beyond the FL
the HH/LL is a reaction to.

The usable engulf is the one which hasn't hit its target. Every engulf has a very specific target.

Apply that statement to your charts and eventually you'll see what I mean.

Being only a sporadic trader (I really couldn't sit and watch the
charts all day anymore!), I tend to open the charts from time to time
and ask myself what's coming up in the next few minutes for me to take.
If I'm lucky, I'll open the charts when we're at an HTF level. If not,
I'll gladly take whatever high R M1 or whatever is there for the
picking. 30 pips with a 3 pip stop is exactly the same as 150 pips with a
 15. If there's nothing decent to take, I shut the charts.

If I were asked where to trade, in one word, I'd say: Stops

I'm way too disorganised to use limit orders! I just open the charts
 from time to time, and if I see the ITs scaring the retailers into
closing good trades at a good level, I enter. I'll take off some of the
position at the first target, so if my stop gets taken I can profit
overall, then watch PA level by level. If price doesn't get into a big
zone quickly, I'll usually get bored and go flat, having made enough to
cover my next week's expenses. If I were truly meticulous, I'd treat my
exits the same as my entries, and trade up and down all day, but trading
 is usually way down on my to-do list.

Certainly there's an awful lot to learn here. But if I were to
summarise what I think is most important, I'd say look to an engulf into
 free space that hasn't yet hit the origin (tg). Very often it will
retrace deeply before advancing to the origin. Learn to spot these, and
you'll be better equipped than most other traders out there.

Price moves from PAZ to PAZ. The clear target for any trade after an
 engulf is the other end of the PAZ in that TF. If you zoom out to HTFs,
 you may find the TG is even further, but if not, stick to the TF you're
 in.

I just want to warn you though that watching candles is an absolute
waste of time. It distracts you from reading the story of price. The
chart is a page, and a candle is a word. A word in itself has little
meaning; it can be taken out of context. Sure, a sentence can be very
powerful, as can a group of candles. But to get a real sense of the
story, we need to view it all as a whole - be aware of how this
paragraph relates to one many chapters back, and get a sense of where
the story will lead in the future.

In essence, we know that if price engulfs South, it wants to move down to the last engulf North.

We want to read the story of price, and believe me, price has a
story! You'll need to go further left to get your analysis right. Yes,
you've marked levels well, but what are those levels a reaction to?
Without knowing this, you're just gambling. So, look left, read the
story, and be better equipped to predict what'll come next.

Ask yourself "Why did price shoot up from there?" You'll answer
"Because someone wanted to buy a lorryload, but there was nobody willing
 to sell at that price, so price shot up to find sellers." The next
question you'll ask yourself is "Will he have left orders to buy again
at that price?" The answer is usually "yes". Next question is "will
price reverse from there?" The answer is, "Well, it may well bounce form
 there, but we won't know if it'll reverse until an engulf tells us it's
 reversed"

Of course, the extremes in one TF can be midrange in another TF,
which is why it's vital to manage your adds in the lower TF until they
break into HTF trades.

Okay! One giant clue: If something which should have been important got ignored, then it will be given great import on return.

Personally, I love to dissect the HTF zone, in LTF, and look for a
DBR or RBD within it, where price had broken out of a box and failed to
get back in.

Whipsaw engulfing - a fakeout followed by a quick return breaking the last zone. It's great PA.

An excellent Supply or Demand zone is one where the future has
already been written. Having done some study of the markets, we know
that once we have an engulf of a zone, price will want to go to the
origin. So we look to where the trend change was confirmed - FTR.

You must study the zone which is being reacted to just as much as the reaction itself.

Just consider the manipulation of hope and fear at turning points, and you'll have a very valuable eureka moment.

When you begin to see the symmetry in the market, you're making one of the final steps in reading and predicting it.

High R is High R, and these trades happen with great frequency. I
applaud this easy way of making good money. If you're at the MPL of an
HTF level, however, think about taking enough at LTF tg1 to cover the
HTF stop, and letting the trade run.

A bit of simple advice, to avoid overtrading and impulse trading:
Draw up the most important looking zones, and look for trades only
there.

We absolutely must have an hard stop, always. But if we don't
 have an engulf before entry, we don't put it directly above the high or
 below the low, where all the retail stops lie. Instead, we find a
lovely LTF RBD/DBR just beyond, and put it on the other side of that, so
 that we have the best chance to get out at BE or in big profit from the
 usual RT.

There's no indication that a demand has been respected until the source above has been engulfed.

Ifmyante wrote: First, we must dissect the kink, and mark all the clean orders in it.

Then we watch the approach for distinct stop hunts into these levels.

We can trade each and any of them, taking profits to cover trips to the next sets of clean orders.

Say our first minor set of clean orders breaks. Price will, sooner or
later get to the next one. It could first retrace for ten pips, or ten
thousand. But it will get there. So, essentially, our minor level hasn't
 turned price.

Can you think of a way to manage a trade taken at a kink which broke,
allowing for no loss and the possibility of a giant retrace?

This Journal is the record of my thought process regarding analysis, approach, execution and management of trades. Successful and failed trades will be logged here for historic purposes and further analysis. Comments are more than welcome. Like with all projects there has to be a purpose and a plan. The purpose is what drives me and the plan is how i intend to get there

The purpose

From a young age i wanted to be free and have freedom of choice, a tall order of understanding for someone of 16yrs old. You learn as you get older as dreams come and go, that they were more of a whim/wish than anything else..........but the fire is still in the belly. Maturity changes things and you can look at things how they are. I do believe there is a place for us all. But i must get to know myself first, by discovering what my purpose is. Trading knowledge is a tool that i will continue to acquire that i can hone my skills to be a more comfortable trader, this will allow me to;

To create more time freedom

To create more choice

To help others and see them grow

To protect what i have

To treat others as i want to be treated

To be fit in mind, body and soul.

Notice i have not spoken about money yet. That’s because for me it is only a tool. It will come and it does already but it is not the primary. It’s just numbers! Targets, well, i will take what the market is prepared to give. I cannot name a % per month or £ per day. Let’s see that the account grows and i can move through the ranks and learn along the way.

The plan

Broker: IBFX

Amount: £5000

Leverage:400-1

Risk: 2% maximum of total account, could include more than one trade, or trades with locked in profit.

Timeframe: w,d,h4,h1. I believe as a trader i need to be flexible and to work across multiple timeframes, it’s a skill that i must master. The clues are hidden in the candles.

RR 2:1 minimum

Stop loss: subjective to timeframe, but must be in line with 2% risk and lot size

Method: mark and review every Sunday supply and demand zones, set alarms. Use boxes drawn to set stop loss and targets. Entry, to use different methods touch, touch..engulf...retest. quasi. Compression.Trendline confluence.

I will share and discuss not only my trading charts and experiences, but others as well and understand we are all working toward a common goal. I will encourage, question and listen. I wish to grow, but be a part of other growth as well.

posts.author: Warren
posts.text:
Do not ever tell me pending trades do not yield pips on daily supply and demand.

Many of us work and do not have the time to monitor possible trades, but do not fool yourself into thinking others that can spend all day by their pc will make this work and because you are part time, it is like an uphill struggle.

Listen and listen good, the more time i spend away from the screen the better, i personally didnt learn trading so i could stare at the screen for hours and hours. I wanted to be free and earn some nice money doing it.

Most of my trades are triggered by pending orders, so i am not even there when my good decision pays off and my trade is triggered. When that trade is triggered its not just the entry that is set. The whole trade is, my stop, my take profit/s. Very mechanical!

All i do is highlight once an evening possible zones, and if they are good i set a pending on it. It triggers or it doesn't. it stops me out or it doesn't, i dont really care!

Why do i not care...........................because the math works!

I do not think for one minute that me staring at the screen and using the power of my mind it will make the market go my way! Is that what you do?

I just walk away and let it play out.

Infest,

I do Daily charts because, the turning points or zones are stronger and quite often you get a reaction even if it ends up countertrend.

Daily charts afford me time, if a trade triggers, i also have set an alarm that texts my phone, so i know "ok, thats another trade i am in" I do not know what time you have and how easy it is for you to monitor your trade once triggered. Targets could take days or weeks to hit. I would say that if you plotted pending trades on 1hr zone, look for tp on 1hr also.

Rules i set pendings by.

They must be REALLY good zones

Consider the trend

Consider the approach

What shape is pair in fundimentally.

I look once in evening and once in morning.takes me about 15 minutes each time. I may need to update zones, set pendings or mark charts with any additional notes. Now, i have had people say "do you have to wait days or weeks for a trade" Well not with 40 pairs. Here is the biggy!

If a trade doesnt trigger for a number of days, there are always exsisting trades to manage. So you could have 4 or 5 nice trades on the go at once.

Find what works for you, stick to it, master it.

posts.author: Warren
posts.text:
Harry,

You and IF are right, it doesnt take many pips to really take the pressure off and be comfortable. I know it sounds great to "smash the markets" up as some people say. Some days i do have time and scalp a little, thats why i like trading, i decide what, when and how much.

I do not think any job on earth is this flexible.

Compound interest is the key, it helped me build a very small live account into quite a substanital amount of money in 4 years. That sounds like a long time.

When i started my live account i was trading 0.05p per pip or 500 units which ever way you want to call it.

I remember thinking "It is going to take me years before my account will grow enough so it can make a difference to my lifestyle. At first it grew so slow, real slow, coupled with the fact that i was still learning.

But as the years pass, things get more interesting. Your larger account means that you can use bigger lot size, the two grow your account at an ever increasing rate.

The Snowball Effect

I do not think it really hit home until i was able to comfortably place trades at 1 standard lot. Thats the point when all the hardwork is worth it.

All the TV i missed, the facebook updates and all the silly games, the midweek drowning sorrows at the bar. Was it worth missing this for a few years?

Do not put off the things you should do now, because life will pass you by.

Hi Warren, some great thoughts have been expressed here. Keep it up.

I trade in a similar fashion in terms of using limit orders. I used to watch charts looking for small pips before I found SD and understood it. Watching didn't help then and I don't need to know.

I do most of my analysis in the evenings too. I write up my plan for each trade with Entry, SL and Targets and actions to be taken at each target level if necessary. This has helped a lot as I know what to expect in a trade ahead of time and I have a plan for how I will react. When I started out, I never really understood how important this was which let to frustration over closing too early or moving stops out of fear etc. Now I just set the orders in the market and set alerts on my iPhone for when price hits my levels so I know when I am in or out of a trade. If I need to take action I know when and where as it's written in my plan for each trade. I save this in the cloud so I can access it at any time should I need to.

A mechanical approach has served me well and seems to work for you too. My 1st 2:1 + trades were when I started trading SD and my best ones where when I was no where near my PC. I noticed that if I watched too much I might interfere. If I don't watch, the trades just do their thing and I am right or wrong.

I also check for trades in the morning and do the same thing setting limts etc.

Obviously if market conditions change I may modify the trade but ideal with that if and when it happens.

I mainly trade from 30m to H4 from Daily/Weekly zones but I've recently been looking more at doing ltf entries from those higher charts for when I'm around to catch them.

Thanks

Before beginning my studies with S/D I would often see (the next day) the Frankie or London spikes that often occur and say: "Well, there is no way I could use a pending to trade that. Thanks Alientrader,

Here is a story that i was told years back and it made me think, what is important?

Makes you question how many pips is enough, i asked myself and the answer was pretty similar to the fisherman in the story below.

No amount of pips can buy me, Health, Family, Friends and Love.

There was once a businessman who was sitting by the beach in a small Brazilian village. As he sat, he saw a Brazilian fisherman rowing a small boat towards the shore having caught quite a few big fish. The businessman was impressed and asked the fisherman, “How long does it take you to catch so many fish?” The fisherman replied, “Oh, just a short while.”

“Then why don’t you stay longer at sea and catch even more?” The businessman was astonished.

“This is enough to feed my whole family,” the fisherman said.

The businessman then asked, “So, what do you do for the rest of the day?” The fisherman replied, “Well, I usually wake up early in the morning, go out to sea and catch a few fish, then go back and play with my kids. In the afternoon, I take a nap with my wife, and evening comes, I join my buddies in the village for a drink — we play guitar, sing and dance throughout the night.”

The businessman offered a suggestion to the fisherman. “I am a PhD in business management. I could help you to become a more successful person. From now on, you should spend more time at sea and try to catch as many fish as possible. When you have saved enough money, you could buy a bigger boat and catch even more fish. Soon you will be able to afford to buy more boats, set up your own company, your own production plant for canned food and distribution network. By then, you will have moved out of this village and to Sao Paulo, where you can set up HQ to manage your other branches.”

The fisherman continues, “And after that?”

The businessman laughs heartily, “After that, you can live like a king in your own house, and when the time is right, you can go public and float your shares in the Stock Exchange, and you will be rich.”

The fisherman asks, “And after that?”
